title: Ergonomics

sections.title: Unit Overview
sections.html:
Unit Overview

Welcome to Unit A1.1: Ergonomics! In this unit, we will explore how ergonomic considerations profoundly influence product design. You'll learn about designing things to fit people, rather than forcing people to adapt to ill-fitting designs. This is crucial for creating products that are not just functional, but also comfortable, safe, and efficient.

We'll dive into various aspects of human interaction with products, systems, and environments, making the design process truly human-centered. Let's get started! 💡

Recommended Time Allocation: 10 hours (SL and HL)

sections.title: 1.1.1 Ergonomics Defined
sections.html:
1.1.1 Ergonomics Defined

Core Understanding: Ergonomics is the study of the relationship and interaction between people (considering aspects of the human body) and the products, systems, and environments they use. It's about designing things to fit people, not forcing people to adapt to ill-fitting designs.

Knowledge Requirement: You must be able to describe how ergonomics is used to improve a product's design. The focus is on making the design:

  • More efficient: Reduces wasted effort and energy, allows tasks to be completed faster.
  • Usable: Intuitive and easy to learn, reducing frustration for the user.
  • Functional: Effective in meeting its intended purpose; fulfills its primary task well.
  • Effective: Achieves the intended results with minimal error or difficulty.
  • Safe: Minimizes the risk of injury, strain, or other health problems for the user.

Case Study: OXO Good Grips

Let's examine the OXO Good Grips line of kitchen utensils. These products were developed with ergonomics at their core. Consider how their soft, non-slip handles are designed to be comfortable and easy to grip, even for users with arthritis or limited hand strength.

Think about how this design improves the efficiency, usability, and safety of simple kitchen tasks.

Case Study: Clear RX Prescription Bottles

The Clear RX bottles focused heavily on usability. Traditional prescription bottles often had small labels, confusing instructions, and a generic appearance. Clear RX redesigned these bottles to be more intuitive, with larger fonts, clear labeling for common uses and cautions, and a distinct shape to help differentiate medications.

How do these design changes improve the overall usability and safety for patients, especially those who might be elderly or have visual impairments?

sections.title: 1.1.2 Anthropometrics
sections.html:
1.1.2 Anthropometrics

Core Understanding: Anthropometrics involves measuring human physical dimensions and expressing them in the percentile range. This is often shown using static data and dynamic data.

Knowledge Requirement: You must be able to discuss how age, gender, ethnicity, and disability affect the anthropometric data.

  • Static Anthropometric Data: These are measurements taken while the body is in a fixed position (e.g., standing height, arm length, hip width). Think about measuring someone standing still.
  • Dynamic Anthropometric Data: These are measurements taken while the body is in motion (e.g., reach distance, range of motion, grip strength). Think about how far you can comfortably reach when sitting.

Activity: "Measure Up!"

Let's take some static and dynamic anthropometric data ourselves! In pairs, you will measure each other's standing height, sitting eye level, and forward reach distance (while seated without leaning forward). We will also try to estimate our comfortable grip strength for a common object like a water bottle.

Discussion: Do you notice variations in measurements within the class? How might age, gender, ethnicity, and disability lead to even greater differences in anthropometric data across a larger population?

sections.title: 1.1.3 Percentiles
sections.html:
1.1.3 Percentiles

Core Understanding: Percentiles aid in the selection of appropriate anthropometric data to satisfy a user population.

Knowledge Requirement: You must be able to identify where 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles are appropriate for a given design scenario.

A percentile describes how a data point compares to all data in that set, divided into 100 equal parts. For a given demographic (gender, race, age), the 50th percentile is the median. The 5th and 95th percentiles represent the lower and upper limits of most of the population. Designers use these to ensure products accommodate a wide range of users.

  • 5th Percentile: Represents the smallest 5% of the population for a given measurement. If you design for this, it means 95% of people will be larger than this measurement.
  • 50th Percentile: Represents the average measurement. Designing only for this might exclude a large portion of the population.
  • 95th Percentile: Represents the largest 5% of the population for a given measurement. If you design for this, it means 95% of people will be smaller than this measurement.

Activity: "Percentile Power!"

Let's consider a practical design challenge. Imagine you are designing the height of a public bus grab handle.

Task: Discuss in groups:

  • Would you design this for the 5th, 50th, or 95th percentile for standing height? Why?
  • What would be the consequences of designing it only for the 95th percentile? Or only for the 5th percentile?

Discussion: We'll share our reasoning and see how designing for different percentiles impacts user access and comfort. This is crucial for inclusive design!

sections.title: 1.1.4 Adjustability and Range of Sizes
sections.html:
1.1.4 Adjustability and Range of Sizes

Core Understanding: To ensure products are appropriate for a range of percentiles, designers design products to be adjustable and/or produced in a range of sizes.

Knowledge Requirement: You must be able to explain the reasons why designers chose adjustability and/or range of sizes for the design, and identify products that use one or both strategies.

  • Adjustability: The ability of a product to be changed in size, configuration, or function to better suit the individual user. It commonly increases the range of percentiles catered to by a single product design. (e.g., office chairs, car seats).
  • Range of Sizes: A selection of specific sizes that a product is manufactured in to cater to the needs of a majority of a target market (e.g., clothing sizes, shoe sizes).

Activity: "Adjust or Size?"

Think about different products around you or that you use regularly.

Task: In groups, identify products that utilize:

  • Only adjustability (e.g., a bicycle helmet). Explain why this is the best approach.
  • Only a range of sizes (e.g., a pair of gloves). Explain why this is the best approach.
  • A combination of both (e.g., a backpack with adjustable straps and different sizes). Explain why both are needed.

Discussion: We will compare our examples and discuss the trade-offs (cost, complexity, effectiveness) designers consider when choosing between these strategies.

sections.title: 1.1.5 Workspace Envelopes, Reach, Clearance, Adjustability, and Range of Sizes
sections.html:
1.1.5 Workspace Envelopes, Reach, Clearance, Adjustability, and Range of Sizes

Core Understanding: In design, consideration must be given to work envelopes, reach, clearance, adjustability, and range of sizes.

Knowledge Requirement: You must be able to explain the importance of workspace envelopes, adjustability, reach, and range of sizes clearance in relation to percentiles and how they are used when designing products.

  • Workspace Envelope: A 3D space (physical and/or virtual) with defined permissible boundaries of movement and operation. It defines the optimal arrangement of elements within a workspace to maximize efficiency and safety.
  • Reach: The range a person can stretch to touch or grasp an object from a specified position, considering physical limitations. Crucial for placing controls and objects within easy access.
  • Clearance: The physical space required between two objects or between a user and an object. Important to avoid collisions, ensure ease of access, and prevent discomfort (e.g., wheelchair-accessible doorways).

Activity: "Desk Detective"

Let's apply these concepts to your own desk or workstation.

Task: Individually, observe your own workspace:

  • Are frequently used items within your primary reach zone (your workspace envelope)?
  • Do you have enough clearance to move comfortably?
  • Are your chair and screen adjustable to fit your individual dimensions (considering percentiles)?
  • If this desk was fixed, for which percentile do you think it would be most comfortable?

Discussion: Share your observations. How could your personal workspace be improved using these ergonomic principles? Consider the standing desk example from your handout.

sections.title: 1.1.6 Physiology
sections.html:
1.1.6 Physiology

Core Understanding: Physiology is the study of systems and biomechanics within the human body, their responses, limitations and capabilities.

Knowledge Requirement: You must be able to explain limiting aspects of user capabilities, including users' visual accuracy, color perception, strengths, fatigue, muscle control and hearing thresholds.

Physiological factors are human factor data related to physical characteristics used to optimize the user's safety, health, comfort, and performance. This includes understanding the biomechanics of the human body.

  • Visual Accuracy: How well we can see details. Design implications: font size, icon clarity.
  • Color Perception: How we interpret colors (important for indicators, warnings). Design implications: avoiding red/green for warnings due to color blindness.
  • Strengths: The force a person can exert. Design implications: ease of opening packaging, button resistance.
  • Fatigue: How quickly a person tires. Design implications: weight of tools, repetitive tasks, need for breaks.
  • Muscle Control: Precision and coordination. Design implications: small buttons vs. large buttons, fine motor tasks.
  • Hearing Thresholds: The range of sounds a person can hear. Design implications: alarm volumes, notification sounds.

Activity: "Designer's Challenge: Physiological Limits"

Let's consider how physiological limitations impact design.

Task: In small groups, choose one of the following products and discuss how physiological limitations would influence its design:

  • A child's toy
  • A smartphone app for the elderly
  • A power tool for construction workers
For your chosen product, identify at least three physiological factors (e.g., grip strength, visual accuracy, fatigue) and explain how the design would need to accommodate these limits.

Discussion: Share your group's ideas and insights into how thoughtful design can overcome physiological challenges.

sections.title: 1.1.7 Psychology
sections.html:
1.1.7 Psychology

Core Understanding: Psychology is concerned with the study of the human mind and involves the study of all human senses involved in sending information to the brain.

Knowledge Requirement: You must be able to discuss how human senses (smell, sound, touch, taste, and vision) are used to influence the design and development of products.

Psychological factors are human factor data related to psychological interpretations caused by light, smell, sound, taste, temperature, and texture. Understanding these factors is crucial for creating emotionally resonant and intuitive designs.

  • Vision: How we perceive visuals (colors, shapes, patterns). Influences branding, interface design, safety signs.
  • Sound: How we interpret auditory cues (alerts, feedback, ambient noise). Influences alarm design, product sounds (e.g., a satisfying click of a button).
  • Touch (Haptics/Tactile): How we experience physical interaction (texture, temperature, vibration). Influences material choices, button feel, phone vibrations.
  • Smell: How odors affect perception and memory. Influences product materials, car interiors, cleaning products.
  • Taste: While less common in DT, relevant for products that interact with food or drink. Influences material safety, purity.

Activity: "Sensory Design Challenge"

Let's explore how our senses influence product experience beyond just sight.

Task: Choose one everyday product. Brainstorm in your groups:

  • How does each of the five senses (vision, sound, touch, smell, taste) interact with this product?
  • How have designers intentionally (or unintentionally) used these senses to influence your perception or experience of the product?
  • How could you enhance the product experience by focusing on a less obvious sense (e.g., sound for a door handle, texture for a pen)?

Discussion: Share your findings and discuss how integrating multi-sensory design can lead to richer, more memorable user experiences.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.html:
Key Takeaways

Here are the essential concepts to remember from our Ergonomics unit:

Human-Centered Approach:

Emphasizes the importance of designing with a deep understanding of human physical and cognitive capabilities.

Data-Driven Design:

Underlines the need to use measurable data (anthropometric data, physiological data, and sensory data) to inform design decisions.

Adaptability:

Highlights the importance of designing for a range of users, rather than a "one size fits all" approach, using adjustability and range of sizes.

Safety and Usability:

Stresses the need to prioritize safety and ease of use in all design decisions.

Thinking about ALL People:

Highlights that factors such as age, gender, ethnicity and disability affect the anthropometric data.

How this knowledge translates to practical design skills:

  • You will be able to conduct user research to gather relevant data on the target demographic.
  • You will understand how to apply that data to create safer, more efficient, and more comfortable products.
  • You will be able to evaluate existing products from an ergonomic perspective, identifying both strengths and areas for improvement.

sections.title: Extended Exam Practice
sections.html:
Extended Exam Practice

Let's test your understanding with some practice questions across different formats. Remember to use specific examples and terminology from the unit in your answers.

Multiple Choice Questions

1. When designing a hiking jacket suitable for an adult, what anthropometric data is most crucial to support the development of a comfortable and functional fit for a wide range of users?

  • A. Adult torso data for 5th percentile
  • B. Adult waist data for 95th percentile
  • C. Adult shoulder range 95th percentile
  • D. Adult torso data for 50th percentile

2. What type of anthropometric data would be most relevant when designing a new, interactive children's play structure that requires climbing and reaching activities?

  • A. Static data, such as standing height.
  • B. Dynamic data, such as reach envelopes.
  • C. Historical anthropometric data from adults.
  • D. Psychological data on color preference.

3. A designer is creating a new kitchen tool. They choose to make the handle with a soft, non-slip texture to improve grip and reduce hand strain. Which ergonomic factor is primarily being addressed?

  • A. Visual accuracy
  • B. Hearing threshold
  • C. Tactile (touch) perception
  • D. Color perception

Short Answer Questions

1. Define Ergonomics and provide one specific example of how it improves a product's usability.

2. Explain the difference between static and dynamic anthropometric data, providing an example for each in the context of designing a bicycle.

sections.title: Glossary of Key Terms for A1.1
sections.html:
Glossary of Key Terms for A1.1

Here are the key terms from our unit to help you remember important concepts:

Adjustability

The ability of a product to be changed in size, configuration, or function to better suit the individual user. It commonly increases the range of percentiles catered to by a single product design.

Context: Ergonomics often seeks to accommodate a diverse range of users. Example: Adjustable office chairs (seat height, backrest angle, armrest height) allow multiple users to find comfortable and supportive postures.

Anthropometrics

The aspect of ergonomics that deals with body measurements and proportions. This includes static and dynamic human characteristics.

Context: Crucial for designing products that physically interact with the human body. Example: Determining the appropriate size and shape of handles for tools (gardening tools, kitchen utensils) requires anthropometric data on hand size and grip strength.

Biomechanics

Research and analysis of the mechanics of the human body (e.g., operation of muscles, joints, tendons, etc.).

Context: Provides insights into how the body moves and exerts force, helping designers prevent strain and injury. Example: Analyzing the biomechanics of lifting heavy objects informs the design of ergonomic handles and lifting aids.

Clearance

The physical space required between two objects or between a user and an object.

Context: Important to avoid collisions, ensure ease of access, and prevent discomfort. Example: Designing wheelchair-accessible doorways and hallways requires ensuring adequate clearance for the wheelchair and the person using it to move freely.

Dynamic Data

Human body measurements taken while the subject is in motion. Measurements show a range in their motion and interactions.

Context: This will often have a variety of ranges that one will find appropriate for different purposes, and will assist designers in understanding motion and activity. Example: Range of reach or joint rotation.

Efficiency (Ergonomics)

Ergonomic designs aim to minimize physical and mental effort required to complete tasks. This can lead to increased productivity and reduced fatigue.

Context: A core goal of ergonomics. Example: A well-designed tool that requires less force to operate, reducing user fatigue over long periods.

Ergonomics

The application of scientific information concerning the relationship between human beings and the design of products, systems, and environments. It's about optimizing human well-being and overall system performance.

Context: The overarching principle guiding good design in this area. Example: Designing a car dashboard so that all controls are easily reachable and visible by the driver without causing distraction or requiring unnatural movements.

Functionality (Ergonomics)

Ergonomic designs focus on creating products that effectively fulfill their intended purpose. This involves considering factors such as comfort, stability, and durability.

Context: Ensures a product performs its core job well while being comfortable to use. Example: A backpack with well-padded, adjustable straps and balanced weight distribution serves its primary function of carrying items while maximizing user comfort.

Human-Centered Approach

Emphasizes the importance of designing with a deep understanding of human physical and cognitive capabilities.

Context: The core philosophy behind ergonomics and UCD. Example: Before designing a new medical instrument, observing surgeons to understand their movements, stress points, and cognitive load during operations.

Percentile

A term that describes how a data point compares to all data in that set, divided into 100 equal parts.

Context: Used to understand the distribution of human measurements and design for the "average" user or a wider range. Example: The 50th percentile represents the median, while the 5th and 95th represent the lower and upper limits of most of the population.

Percentile Range (Upper/Lower Limits)

The proportion of a population with a dimension at or less than a given value. For a given demographic (gender, race, age), the 50th percentile is the median.

Context: This is a key consideration for product usability. Example: Designing a door handle for a certain user group to meet their comfort levels across the 5th to 95th percentile.

Physiology Factors

Human factor data related to physical characteristics used to optimize the user's safety, health, comfort, and performance.

Context: These are data used to support and test designs for the design's usability. Example: Designing a workstation for extended use to ensure health for a wide demographic, considering factors like visual accuracy, strength, and fatigue.

Psychology Factors

Human factor data related to psychological interpretations caused by light, smell, sound, taste, temperature, and texture.

Context: Crucial for understanding how sensory input influences user experience and perception. Example: The use of calming colors and soft lighting in a hospital room to reduce patient anxiety, or the satisfying "click" of a well-designed button.

Range of Sizes

A selection of specific sizes that a product is manufactured in to cater to the needs of a majority of a target market.

Context: An alternative or supplement to adjustability; useful when adjustability is impractical or undesirable. Example: Clothing sizes (small, medium, large, etc.) cater to a range of body shapes.

Reach

The range a person can stretch to touch or grasp an object from a specified position, considering physical limitations.

Context: Important for placing controls and objects within easy access. Example: Positioning the controls on a microwave within a comfortable reach for someone using a wheelchair.

Safety (Ergonomics)

Ergonomics helps prevent injuries and accidents by designing products that reduce the risk of hazards. This includes factors like proper posture, strain prevention, and hazard mitigation.

Context: A paramount concern in ergonomic design. Example: Designing tools with anti-vibration handles to prevent hand-arm vibration syndrome, or furniture that supports proper posture to avoid back pain.

Static Data

Human body measurements when the subject is still (refers to measurements taken while the subject is in a fixed or standard position, e.g., arm length and overhead reach).

Context: Important for situations when one has to hold still for the best ergonomics, rather than move one's body into an uncomfortable angle. Example: Measurement of hand or arm circumference for glove sizing.

Usability (Ergonomics)

A product is considered usable if it can be easily understood and operated by its intended users. Ergonomics ensures that controls are intuitive, information is clear, and layouts are logical.

Context: A core ergonomic goal. Example: A coffee machine with clearly labeled buttons and a straightforward brewing process is highly usable.

Workspace Envelope

A 3D space (physical and/or virtual) with defined permissible boundaries of movement and operation.

Context: Used to define the optimal arrangement of elements within a workspace to maximize efficiency and safety. Example: A cockpit layout where all essential controls are within easy reach and view of the pilot.

syllabus.title: Ergonomics
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How do ergonomic considerations influence the design of a product?

statements.text: Ergonomics is the relationship and interaction between people (aspects of the human body) and the products, systems and environments they use.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe how ergonomics is used to improve the design of a product by making a design more efficient, usable, functional, effective and safe.

statements.text: Anthropometrics involves the measurement of human physical dimensions expressed in the percentile range. This method specifically focuses on determining and presenting the range of individuals’ physical characteristics.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain and use static and dynamic anthropometric data to design for different people and be able to discuss how factors such as age, gender, ethnicity and disability affect the anthropometric data.

statements.text: Percentiles aid in the selection of appropriate anthropometric data to satisfy the majority of a user population.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify where the 5th, 50th and 5th–95th percentiles are appropriate for a design scenario.

statements.text: To ensure products are appropriate to a range of percentiles, designers can choose to design products to be adjustable and/or to be produced in a range of sizes.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the reasons why designers choose adjustability and/or range of sizes for a product, and identify products that use one or both strategies.

statements.text: In design, consideration must be given to work envelopes, reach, clearance, adjustability and range of sizes.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the importance of workspace envelopes, adjustability, reach and range of sizes clearance in relation to percentiles and how they are used when designing products.

statements.text: Physiology is the study of systems and biomechanics within the human body, their responses, limitations and capabilities.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain limiting aspects of user capabilities, including users’ visual accuracy, colour perception, strengths, fatigue, muscle control and hearing thresholds.

statements.text: Psychology is concerned with the study of the human mind and involves the study of all the human senses that may be involved in sending information to the brain.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss how human senses (smell, sound, touch, taste and vision) are used to influence the design and development of products.

activity.title: Reach versus clearance
steps: In pairs, measure comfortable seated forward reach and seated hip breadth three times; record units.
Pool anonymous measurements. Identify sample limitations before selecting any percentile.
Mark a control panel and a seat width using contrasting small-user reach and large-user clearance decisions.
Test both layouts with three classmates; record failures and propose adjustability.
activity.debrief: Why does one percentile not suit every dimension?

exam.question: Explain why a control should be positioned using small-user reach data. [2]
exam.answer: A person with shorter reach must still be able to operate the control; placing it within their reach also usually accommodates people with greater reach. Distinguish reach from clearance.
exam.label: Additional teacher-authored exam-style practice; indicative answer

activities.title: Activity: "Measure Up!"
activities.text: Activity: "Measure Up!" Let's take some static and dynamic anthropometric data ourselves! In pairs, you will measure each other's standing height, sitting eye level, and forward reach distance (while seated without leaning forward). We will also try to estimate our comfortable grip strength for a common object like a water bottle. Discussion: Do you notice variations in measurements within the class? How might age, gender, ethnicity, and disability lead to even greater differences in anthropometric data across a larger population?
activities.html:
Let's take some static and dynamic anthropometric data ourselves! In pairs, you will measure each other's standing height, sitting eye level, and forward reach distance (while seated without leaning forward). We will also try to estimate our comfortable grip strength for a common object like a water bottle.

Discussion: Do you notice variations in measurements within the class? How might age, gender, ethnicity, and disability lead to even greater differences in anthropometric data across a larger population?

activities.title: Activity: "Percentile Power!"
activities.text: Activity: "Percentile Power!" Let's consider a practical design challenge. Imagine you are designing the height of a public bus grab handle. Task: Discuss in groups: Would you design this for the 5th, 50th, or 95th percentile for standing height? Why? What would be the consequences of designing it only for the 95th percentile? Or only for the 5th percentile? Discussion: We'll share our reasoning and see how designing for different percentiles impacts user access and comfort. This is crucial for inclusive design !
activities.html:
Let's consider a practical design challenge. Imagine you are designing the height of a public bus grab handle.

Task: Discuss in groups:

  • Would you design this for the 5th, 50th, or 95th percentile for standing height? Why?
  • What would be the consequences of designing it only for the 95th percentile? Or only for the 5th percentile?

Discussion: We'll share our reasoning and see how designing for different percentiles impacts user access and comfort. This is crucial for inclusive design!

activities.title: Activity: "Adjust or Size?"
activities.text: Activity: "Adjust or Size?" Think about different products around you or that you use regularly. Task: In groups, identify products that utilize: Only adjustability (e.g., a bicycle helmet). Explain why this is the best approach. Only a range of sizes (e.g., a pair of gloves). Explain why this is the best approach. A combination of both (e.g., a backpack with adjustable straps and different sizes). Explain why both are needed. Discussion: We will compare our examples and discuss the trade-offs (cost, complexity, effectiveness) designers consider when choosing between these strategies.
activities.html:
Think about different products around you or that you use regularly.

Task: In groups, identify products that utilize:

  • Only adjustability (e.g., a bicycle helmet). Explain why this is the best approach.
  • Only a range of sizes (e.g., a pair of gloves). Explain why this is the best approach.
  • A combination of both (e.g., a backpack with adjustable straps and different sizes). Explain why both are needed.

Discussion: We will compare our examples and discuss the trade-offs (cost, complexity, effectiveness) designers consider when choosing between these strategies.

activities.title: Activity: "Desk Detective"
activities.text: Activity: "Desk Detective" Let's apply these concepts to your own desk or workstation. Task: Individually, observe your own workspace: Are frequently used items within your primary reach zone (your workspace envelope )? Do you have enough clearance to move comfortably? Are your chair and screen adjustable to fit your individual dimensions (considering percentiles)? If this desk was fixed, for which percentile do you think it would be most comfortable? Discussion: Share your observations. How could your personal workspace be improved using these ergonomic principles? Consider the standing desk example from your handout.

activities.title: Activity: "Designer's Challenge: Physiological Limits"
activities.text: Activity: "Designer's Challenge: Physiological Limits" Let's consider how physiological limitations impact design. Task: In small groups, choose one of the following products and discuss how physiological limitations would influence its design: A child's toy A smartphone app for the elderly A power tool for construction workers For your chosen product, identify at least three physiological factors (e.g., grip strength, visual accuracy, fatigue) and explain how the design would need to accommodate these limits. Discussion: Share your group's ideas and insights into how thoughtful design can overcome physiological challenges.

  • A child's toy
  • A smartphone app for the elderly
  • A power tool for construction workers
For your chosen product, identify at least three physiological factors (e.g., grip strength, visual accuracy, fatigue) and explain how the design would need to accommodate these limits.

Discussion: Share your group's ideas and insights into how thoughtful design can overcome physiological challenges.

activities.title: Activity: "Sensory Design Challenge"
activities.text: Activity: "Sensory Design Challenge" Let's explore how our senses influence product experience beyond just sight. Task: Choose one everyday product. Brainstorm in your groups: How does each of the five senses (vision, sound, touch, smell, taste) interact with this product? How have designers intentionally (or unintentionally) used these senses to influence your perception or experience of the product? How could you enhance the product experience by focusing on a less obvious sense (e.g., sound for a door handle, texture for a pen)? Discussion: Share your findings and discuss how integrating multi-sensory design can lead to richer, more memorable user experiences.

(e.g., office chairs, car seats). range of sizes: a selection of specific sizes that a product is manufactured in to cater to the needs of a majority of a target market (e.g., clothing sizes, shoe sizes). activity: "adjust or size?" think about different products around you or that you use regularly. task: in groups, identify products that utilize: only adjustability (e.g., a bicycle helmet). explain why this is the best approach. only a range of sizes (e.g., a pair of gloves). explain why this is the best approach. a combination of both (e.g., a backpack with adjustable straps and different sizes). explain why both are needed. discussion: we will compare our examples and discuss the trade-offs (cost, complexity, effectiveness) designers consider when choosing between these strategies. 1.1.5 workspace envelopes, reach, clearance, adjustability, and range of sizes core understanding: in design, consideration must be given to work envelopes , reach , clearance , adjustability , and range of sizes . knowledge requirement: you must be able to explain the importance of workspace envelopes , adjustability , reach , and range of sizes clearance in relation to percentiles and how they are used when designing products. workspace envelope: a 3d space (physical and/or virtual) with defined permissible boundaries of movement and operation. it defines the optimal arrangement of elements within a workspace to maximize efficiency and safety . reach: the range a person can stretch to touch or grasp an object from a specified position, considering physical limitations. crucial for placing controls and objects within easy access. clearance: the physical space required between two objects or between a user and an object. important to avoid collisions, ensure ease of access, and prevent discomfort (e.g., wheelchair-accessible doorways). activity: "desk detective" let's apply these concepts to your own desk or workstation. task: individually, observe your own workspace: are frequently used items within your primary reach zone (your workspace envelope )? do you have enough clearance to move comfortably? are your chair and screen adjustable to fit your individual dimensions (considering percentiles)? if this desk was fixed, for which percentile do you think it would be most comfortable? discussion: share your observations. how could your personal workspace be improved using these ergonomic principles? consider the standing desk example from your handout. 1.1.6 physiology core understanding: physiology is the study of systems and biomechanics within the human body, their responses, limitations and capabilities. knowledge requirement: you must be able to explain limiting aspects of user capabilities, including users' visual accuracy, color perception, strengths, fatigue, muscle control and hearing thresholds. physiological factors are human factor data related to physical characteristics used to optimize the user's safety , health, comfort, and performance. this includes understanding the biomechanics of the human body. visual accuracy: how well we can see details. design implications: font size, icon clarity. color perception: how we interpret colors (important for indicators, warnings). design implications: avoiding red/green for warnings due to color blindness. strengths: the force a person can exert. design implications: ease of opening packaging, button resistance. fatigue: how quickly a person tires. design implications: weight of tools, repetitive tasks, need for breaks. muscle control: precision and coordination. design implications: small buttons vs. large buttons, fine motor tasks. hearing thresholds: the range of sounds a person can hear. design implications: alarm volumes, notification sounds. activity: "designer's challenge: physiological limits" let's consider how physiological limitations impact design. task: in small groups, choose one of the following products and discuss how physiological limitations would influence its design: a child's toy a smartphone app for the elderly a power tool for construction workers for your chosen product, identify at least three physiological factors (e.g., grip strength, visual accuracy, fatigue) and explain how the design would need to accommodate these limits. discussion: share your group's ideas and insights into how thoughtful design can overcome physiological challenges. 1.1.7 psychology core understanding: psychology is concerned with the study of the human mind and involves the study of all human senses involved in sending information to the brain. knowledge requirement: you must be able to discuss how human senses (smell, sound, touch, taste, and vision) are used to influence the design and development of products. psychological factors are human factor data related to psychological interpretations caused by light, smell, sound, taste, temperature, and texture. understanding these factors is crucial for creating emotionally resonant and intuitive designs. vision: how we perceive visuals (colors, shapes, patterns). influences branding, interface design, safety signs. sound: how we interpret auditory cues (alerts, feedback, ambient noise). influences alarm design, product sounds (e.g., a satisfying click of a button). touch (haptics/tactile): how we experience physical interaction (texture, temperature, vibration). influences material choices, button feel, phone vibrations. smell: how odors affect perception and memory. influences product materials, car interiors, cleaning products. taste: while less common in dt, relevant for products that interact with food or drink. influences material safety, purity. activity: "sensory design challenge" let's explore how our senses influence product experience beyond just sight. task: choose one everyday product. brainstorm in your groups: how does each of the five senses (vision, sound, touch, smell, taste) interact with this product? how have designers intentionally (or unintentionally) used these senses to influence your perception or experience of the product? how could you enhance the product experience by focusing on a less obvious sense (e.g., sound for a door handle, texture for a pen)? discussion: share your findings and discuss how integrating multi-sensory design can lead to richer, more memorable user experiences. key takeaways here are the essential concepts to remember from our ergonomics unit: human-centered approach: emphasizes the importance of designing with a deep understanding of human physical and cognitive capabilities. data-driven design: underlines the need to use measurable data ( anthropometric data , physiological data , and sensory data) to inform design decisions. adaptability: highlights the importance of designing for a range of users, rather than a "one size fits all" approach, using adjustability and range of sizes . safety and usability: stresses the need to prioritize safety and ease of use in all design decisions. thinking about all people: highlights that factors such as age, gender, ethnicity and disability affect the anthropometric data. how this knowledge translates to practical design skills: you will be able to conduct user research to gather relevant data on the target demographic. you will understand how to apply that data to create safer, more efficient, and more comfortable products. you will be able to evaluate existing products from an ergonomic perspective, identifying both strengths and areas for improvement. extended exam practice let's test your understanding with some practice questions across different formats. remember to use specific examples and terminology from the unit in your answers. multiple choice questions 1. when designing a hiking jacket suitable for an adult, what anthropometric data is most crucial to support the development of a comfortable and functional fit for a wide range of users? a. adult torso data for 5th percentile b. adult waist data for 95th percentile c. adult shoulder range 95th percentile d. adult torso data for 50th percentile 2. what type of anthropometric data would be most relevant when designing a new, interactive children's play structure that requires climbing and reaching activities? a. static data, such as standing height. b. dynamic data, such as reach envelopes. c. historical anthropometric data from adults. d. psychological data on color preference. 3. a designer is creating a new kitchen tool. they choose to make the handle with a soft, non-slip texture to improve grip and reduce hand strain. which ergonomic factor is primarily being addressed? a. visual accuracy b. hearing threshold c. tactile (touch) perception d. color perception short answer questions 1. define ergonomics and provide one specific example of how it improves a product's usability . 2. explain the difference between static and dynamic anthropometric data , providing an example for each in the context of designing a bicycle. 3. outline how inclusive design principles can improve a standard water bottle for users with limited dexterity or grip strength. longer answer questions 1. a designer is developing a new office chair. discuss how the use of percentiles , adjustability , and workspace envelopes are crucial in creating an ergonomically sound product that caters to a diverse user population. 2. evaluate the statement: "focusing solely on the 50th percentile in design is the most efficient way to create products for the majority of users." refer to concepts from anthropometrics , physiological factors , and adjustability in your answer, providing relevant examples. 3. explain how a primary persona was used to develop the design of a yoga equipment organizer, referencing how anthropometrics , physiological , and psychological factors informed the design decisions. we will discuss strategies for answering these questions effectively, focusing on structure, use of terminology, and illustrative examples. glossary of key terms for a1.1 here are the key terms from our unit to help you remember important concepts: adjustability the ability of a product to be changed in size, configuration, or function to better suit the individual user. it commonly increases the range of percentiles catered to by a single product design. context: ergonomics often seeks to accommodate a diverse range of users. example: adjustable office chairs (seat height, backrest angle, armrest height) allow multiple users to find comfortable and supportive postures. anthropometrics the aspect of ergonomics that deals with body measurements and proportions. this includes static and dynamic human characteristics. context: crucial for designing products that physically interact with the human body. example: determining the appropriate size and shape of handles for tools (gardening tools, kitchen utensils) requires anthropometric data on hand size and grip strength. biomechanics research and analysis of the mechanics of the human body (e.g., operation of muscles, joints, tendons, etc.). context: provides insights into how the body moves and exerts force, helping designers prevent strain and injury. example: analyzing the biomechanics of lifting heavy objects informs the design of ergonomic handles and lifting aids. clearance the physical space required between two objects or between a user and an object. context: important to avoid collisions, ensure ease of access, and prevent discomfort. example: designing wheelchair-accessible doorways and hallways requires ensuring adequate clearance for the wheelchair and the person using it to move freely. dynamic data human body measurements taken while the subject is in motion. measurements show a range in their motion and interactions. context: this will often have a variety of ranges that one will find appropriate for different purposes, and will assist designers in understanding motion and activity. example: range of reach or joint rotation. efficiency (ergonomics) ergonomic designs aim to minimize physical and mental effort required to complete tasks. this can lead to increased productivity and reduced fatigue. context: a core goal of ergonomics. example: a well-designed tool that requires less force to operate, reducing user fatigue over long periods. ergonomics the application of scientific information concerning the relationship between human beings and the design of products, systems, and environments. it's about optimizing human well-being and overall system performance. context: the overarching principle guiding good design in this area. example: designing a car dashboard so that all controls are easily reachable and visible by the driver without causing distraction or requiring unnatural movements. functionality (ergonomics) ergonomic designs focus on creating products that effectively fulfill their intended purpose. this involves considering factors such as comfort, stability, and durability. context: ensures a product performs its core job well while being comfortable to use. example: a backpack with well-padded, adjustable straps and balanced weight distribution serves its primary function of carrying items while maximizing user comfort. human-centered approach emphasizes the importance of designing with a deep understanding of human physical and cognitive capabilities. context: the core philosophy behind ergonomics and ucd. example: before designing a new medical instrument, observing surgeons to understand their movements, stress points, and cognitive load during operations. percentile a term that describes how a data point compares to all data in that set, divided into 100 equal parts. context: used to understand the distribution of human measurements and design for the "average" user or a wider range. example: the 50th percentile represents the median, while the 5th and 95th represent the lower and upper limits of most of the population. percentile range (upper/lower limits) the proportion of a population with a dimension at or less than a given value. for a given demographic (gender, race, age), the 50th percentile is the median. context: this is a key consideration for product usability. example: designing a door handle for a certain user group to meet their comfort levels across the 5th to 95th percentile. physiology factors human factor data related to physical characteristics used to optimize the user's safety, health, comfort, and performance. context: these are data used to support and test designs for the design's usability. example: designing a workstation for extended use to ensure health for a wide demographic, considering factors like visual accuracy, strength, and fatigue. psychology factors human factor data related to psychological interpretations caused by light, smell, sound, taste, temperature, and texture. context: crucial for understanding how sensory input influences user experience and perception. example: the use of calming colors and soft lighting in a hospital room to reduce patient anxiety, or the satisfying "click" of a well-designed button. range of sizes a selection of specific sizes that a product is manufactured in to cater to the needs of a majority of a target market. context: an alternative or supplement to adjustability; useful when adjustability is impractical or undesirable. example: clothing sizes (small, medium, large, etc.) cater to a range of body shapes. reach the range a person can stretch to touch or grasp an object from a specified position, considering physical limitations. context: important for placing controls and objects within easy access. example: positioning the controls on a microwave within a comfortable reach for someone using a wheelchair. safety (ergonomics) ergonomics helps prevent injuries and accidents by designing products that reduce the risk of hazards. this includes factors like proper posture, strain prevention, and hazard mitigation. context: a paramount concern in ergonomic design. example: designing tools with anti-vibration handles to prevent hand-arm vibration syndrome, or furniture that supports proper posture to avoid back pain. static data human body measurements when the subject is still (refers to measurements taken while the subject is in a fixed or standard position, e.g., arm length and overhead reach). context: important for situations when one has to hold still for the best ergonomics, rather than move one's body into an uncomfortable angle. example: measurement of hand or arm circumference for glove sizing. usability (ergonomics) a product is considered usable if it can be easily understood and operated by its intended users. ergonomics ensures that controls are intuitive, information is clear, and layouts are logical. context: a core ergonomic goal. example: a coffee machine with clearly labeled buttons and a straightforward brewing process is highly usable. workspace envelope a 3d space (physical and/or virtual) with defined permissible boundaries of movement and operation. context: used to define the optimal arrangement of elements within a workspace to maximize efficiency and safety. example: a cockpit layout where all essential controls are within easy reach and view of the pilot. adjustability anthropometrics clearance ergonomics percentile range (upper and lower limits) psychology factors physiology factors percentile range of sizes static data dynamic data reach biomechanics workspace envelope efficiency (ergonomics) functionality (ergonomics) human-centered approach percentile range (upper/lower limits) safety (ergonomics) usability (ergonomics) ergonomics is the relationship and interaction between people (aspects of the human body) and the products, systems and environments they use. anthropometrics involves the measurement of human physical dimensions expressed in the percentile range. this method specifically focuses on determining and presenting the range of individuals’ physical characteristics. percentiles aid in the selection of appropriate anthropometric data to satisfy the majority of a user population. to ensure products are appropriate to a range of percentiles, designers can choose to design products to be adjustable and/or to be produced in a range of sizes. in design, consideration must be given to work envelopes, reach, clearance, adjustability and range of sizes. physiology is the study of systems and biomechanics within the human body, their responses, limitations and capabilities. psychology is concerned with the study of the human mind and involves the study of all the human senses that may be involved in sending information to the brain.

title: User-centred research methods

sections.title: Lesson 1: Core Principles of User-Centred Design
sections.html:
A2.1.1 Core Principles of UCD ~45 min

Lesson 1: Core Principles of User-Centred Design

User-centred design begins with a simple but demanding idea: designers must set aside their own assumptions and immerse themselves in a user's lived experience. This lesson introduces the vocabulary and mental model — empathy, pain points, and the User Experience Trinity — that underpins every research method and case study in this unit.

Hook: The MRI Scanner Nobody Wanted to Use

Watch engineer Doug Dietz describe the moment he realised his award-winning MRI scanner was terrifying young patients. As you watch, note: was the actual problem the machine's technology, or something else entirely?

Watch: Doug Dietz — Transforming Healthcare for Children and Their Families (TEDxSanJoseCA).

1. Empathy & Pain Points

Definition: Designers set aside their own assumptions and immerse themselves in a user's lived experience to uncover pain points — points of friction or frustration a user may struggle to describe themselves.

Context: Doug Dietz discovered that around 80% of paediatric MRI patients needed sedation — not because of the technology itself, but because of the cold, clanking, unfamiliar tunnel, a pain point families struggled to put into words.

Materials/Examples: Empathy interviews, contextual inquiry, immersion/shadowing sessions.

Application: Used at the very start of the design cycle, and revisited whenever later testing reveals a gap in understanding.

2. The User Experience (UX) Trinity

Definition: Every interaction sits at the intersection of the User (abilities, age, prior experience), the Task (the action and its steps), and the Environment (the physical, social or technological context of use). Change one, and the other two must be reconsidered.

Context: An MRI scan is the same Task, but is experienced completely differently by a frightened child (User) inside a clinical scan room (Environment) than by a calm adult patient.

Materials/Examples: UX Trinity diagrams, context-of-use mapping.

Application: Used to diagnose exactly which factor — User, Task or Environment — is the true source of a pain point, rather than assuming the product itself is at fault.

3. Iterative Design & Outcomes

Definition: UCD loops — insights from testing feed back into research and concept work, refining the team's understanding of the user across repeated cycles rather than a single pass. The outcome is intuitive, accessible, efficient products that reduce user frustration and increase satisfaction.

Context: Dietz's team didn't redesign the MRI hardware once — they repainted scanners, trained staff, and refined the "pirate-ship adventure" framing repeatedly. Sedation rates fell from roughly 80% to under 10%, and patient satisfaction scores rose by 90%, using the same underlying machine.

Materials/Examples: Repeated test-and-refine cycles, staff training updates, low-cost interventions (paint, scripts) rather than hardware redesign.

Application: Reminds teams that UCD does not end at launch — insight keeps looping back into research and concept work.

Practical Engagement: "Pain-Point Safari"

In pairs: Student A wears thick gloves or tapes two fingers together to simulate reduced dexterity, then attempts three everyday tasks while Student B silently observes and times them — opening a snack packet, sending a text message, and cutting along a line with scissors. Student B logs each hesitation or workaround under three columns: Task / Observed Pain Point / Possible Design Response.

Swap roles, then debrief as a class: was each pain point rooted in the User, the Task, or the Environment? Discuss why direct observation revealed more than simply asking "what's hard about this?" would have.

ConceptDefinitionWhy It Matters
EmpathySetting aside assumptions to understand a user's lived experience and uncover pain points.Surfaces frustrations a user may not be able to describe themselves.
UX TrinityThe interacting User, Task and Environment behind every interaction.Diagnoses which factor is really causing a problem.
Iterative DesignInsights from testing loop back into research and concept work.Refines understanding across repeated cycles, not a single pass.

sections.title: Lesson 2: UCD Definition and Stages
sections.html:
A2.1.2 UCD Definition and Stages ~60 min

Lesson 2: UCD Definition and Stages

UCD is a process that involves users at all stages of the design cycle, not just at final testing. The Five Stages of UCD move from Research (understand user and context) → Concept (broad ideas informed by that research) → Design (refine into a detailed, testable solution) → Implementation (engineer for manufacture) → Launch (release to market, sometimes in stages). The OXO Good Grips story — one of the most cited case studies in design — traces a single product through every stage.

1. Research

Definition: The first stage of UCD — gathering data on user needs, behaviours and context before any concepts are proposed.

Context: In the late 1980s, Sam Farber watched his wife Betsey, who had mild arthritis, struggle to grip a standard thin metal vegetable peeler.

Materials/Examples: Observation, interviews, contextual inquiry into daily frustrations.

Application: Anchors every later stage in evidence rather than assumption.

2. Concept

Definition: The stage where broad ideas are generated in direct response to research findings.

Context: Farber partnered with the New York firm Smart Design, which produced dozens of foam and rubber handle sketches.

Materials/Examples: Sketch storms, foam/rubber material sampling, rapid low-fidelity mock-ups.

Application: Converts a research insight (e.g. "gripping is painful") into a wide range of possible solutions before narrowing down.

3. Design

Definition: The stage where a concept is refined into a detailed, testable solution.

Context: The team tested prototypes with people who had arthritis alongside able-bodied users of all ages, refining a soft, wide, ridged handle.

Materials/Examples: Iterative prototype testing, ridge-pattern and diameter refinement, mixed-ability user trials.

Application: Confirms the concept actually works for the full range of intended users, not just the most extreme case.

4. Implementation

Definition: The stage where a finalised design is engineered for manufacture, including tooling and production processes.

Context: New tooling and a supply chain for moulding rubber over plastic had to be developed from scratch, since nothing like it existed for kitchenware.

Materials/Examples: Production tooling, moulding processes, supply-chain development.

Application: Turns a validated prototype into something that can actually be manufactured at scale.

5. Launch

Definition: The stage where a product is released to the market, sometimes in a staged or trial form.

Context: OXO launched the Good Grips line in 1990 at a premium price. It became one of the best-selling kitchen tool ranges in US history — a foundational case of inclusive design, where designing for an "extreme" user produced a better product for almost everyone (sometimes called the curb-cut effect).

Materials/Examples: Market release planning, pricing strategy, staged or trial rollouts.

Application: Closes one iteration of the UCD cycle — though feedback after launch often restarts it.

Advantages of UCDDisadvantages of UCD
  • Enhanced satisfaction — products feel intuitive and enjoyable to the intended user
  • Increased usability — interfaces and controls are easier to navigate
  • Reduced costs — usability issues caught early avoid expensive late-stage changes
  • Inclusive design — considering diverse needs widens a product's real market, as with OXO Good Grips
  • Time-consuming — extensive research and iteration slows development
  • High initial costs — user research and prototyping (and new tooling, as at OXO) are expensive
  • Complexity — balancing conflicting user needs against technical feasibility is difficult
  • Scope creep — constant feedback can trigger frequent changes that delay launch

Practical Engagement: "Sequence the Stages" Card Sort

Provide small groups with six shuffled cards describing moments from the OXO Good Grips story above, plus one distractor card (e.g. "the packaging is redesigned five years later using recycled cardboard" — a post-launch iteration, not one of the five original stages).

Groups sequence the five genuine cards into Research → Concept → Design → Implementation → Launch, explain their reasoning, and identify why the distractor doesn't belong. Discuss: if OXO had skipped straight from Research to Implementation, which disadvantage from the table above would apply?

Groups sequence the five genuine cards into Research → Concept → Design → Implementation → Launch, explain their reasoning, and identify why the distractor doesn't belong. Discuss: if OXO had skipped straight from Research to Implementation, which disadvantage from the table above would apply?

sections.title: Lesson 3: Multidisciplinary UCD Teams
sections.html:
A2.1.3 Multidisciplinary UCD Teams ~45 min

Lesson 3: Multidisciplinary UCD Teams

Successful UCD often requires a multidisciplinary team, since no single designer can hold the full picture of psychology, ergonomics, engineering and social context that governs how varied users behave. Collaborative disciplines may include designers, engineers, software programmers, psychologists and sociologists.

1. Why UCD Needs a Multidisciplinary Team

Definition: No single designer can hold the full 360-degree picture of psychology, ergonomics, engineering and social context that governs how varied users behave — successful UCD relies on specialists from different fields collaborating.

Context: A team designing a child-friendly asthma inhaler needs more than a product designer alone — an ergonomic specialist to size the trigger for small hands, a psychologist to understand a frightened 6-year-old's behaviour, and a nurse to check real-world hygiene and handling.

Materials/Examples: Cross-disciplinary design reviews, joint field visits, shared research repositories.

Application: Ensures a 360-degree understanding that no single specialist could reach alone.

2. Specialist Contributions

Definition: Psychologists explain mental processes like perception and reasoning; ergonomic specialists guide the physical sizing of controls for specific users (e.g. arthritic hands); nurses or other secondary personas identify practical difficulties in handling or hygiene.

Context: An ergonomic specialist recommending the trigger-grip diameter for a child-friendly asthma inhaler works alongside a psychologist advising on how a frightened child behaves under stress, and a nurse (a secondary persona) confirming the device can be cleaned and checked by a caregiver.

Materials/Examples: Ergonomic sizing charts, secondary-persona interviews (e.g. nurses, caregivers), psychology-informed interface reviews.

Application: Each specialist's contribution targets a different potential failure point — physical, cognitive, practical or social.

Case Study: The NeoNurture Infant Incubator

Standard donated incubators shipped to rural hospitals in Nepal often failed within months, because trained biomedical technicians and replacement parts were not available locally and power was unreliable. A multidisciplinary team of biomedical engineers, industrial designers, and local Nepali doctors and technicians — who understood which parts actually stayed maintained in that context — co-designed the NeoNurture infant incubator almost entirely from car parts: sealed-beam headlights for radiant heat, a dashboard fan for air circulation, a motorcycle battery for backup power. Because every village mechanic already knew how to repair those specific components, the incubators stayed functional for years after conventional Western-designed alternatives had been abandoned. Neither engineers alone, nor medical staff alone, could have reached this solution.

Practical Engagement: "Design the Team" Role Debate

Brief: Design a child-friendly asthma inhaler that a 6-year-old can operate correctly, unaided, during an attack.

Distribute role cards — Ergonomic specialist, Psychologist, Nurse (secondary persona for the caregiver), Software programmer (companion reminder app), Sociologist — each listing that specialist's core concern. In groups of five, one student per role argues for their concern being prioritised; the group must then agree a final combined requirement list containing at least one contribution from every discipline, modelling how real UCD teams negotiate trade-offs.

sections.title: Lesson 4: User-Centred Research Methods
sections.html:
A2.1.4 User-Centred Research Methods ~60 min

Lesson 4: User-Centred Research Methods

Designers draw on a toolkit of research methods, each suited to a different kind of question — some reveal authentic, unspoken behaviour; others collect opinions at scale. Choosing the right method (or combination of methods) is itself a design decision.

Hook: Which Method Finds What?

Watch the clip below, then predict: which research method would have been most likely to reveal a problem the researchers didn't already know to ask about?

Watch: Usability, User Testing & Task Analysis (explainer).

1. Field Research

Definition: First-hand observation of users in their natural environment, to see how they interact with products authentically.

Context: In 2009, with almost no growth, Airbnb's founders flew from San Francisco to New York and went door to door, staying with hosts and photographing listings themselves.

Materials/Examples: On-site observation, contextual visits, photo/video documentation of real use.

Application: Reveals authentic behaviour that users may not think to mention when simply asked.

2. Task Analysis

Definition: A complex process broken down into sequential steps to identify bottlenecks, inefficiencies, or points of user error.

Context: Sequencing every step of "packing your bag after class" to circle the single step most likely to cause an item to be forgotten.

Materials/Examples: Step-by-step observation sheets, numbered task lists.

Application: Targets the exact failing step for redesign, rather than the whole product or process.

3. User Observation

Definition: Watching users interact with a product to identify unspoken behaviours, workarounds, or difficulties.

Context: Silently watching a partner attempt an everyday task — such as opening a snack packet with reduced dexterity — reveals hesitations and workarounds a user might never mention in an interview.

Materials/Examples: Silent observation logs, video recordings, hesitation/workaround tallies.

Application: Surfaces problems the user themselves may not be able to put into words.

4. Interviews

Definition: Direct, qualitative conversations to uncover user frustrations, motivations and expectations.

Context: Asking an elderly participant open questions about their daily medication routine can surface motivations a tick-box survey never would.

Materials/Examples: Open-question scripts, one-to-one conversations, follow-up probing questions.

Application: Best for depth and "why" — understanding motivations behind a behaviour, not just counting it.

5. Surveys and Questionnaires

Definition: Structured methods for collecting quantitative data on user demographics and preferences from a larger audience.

Context: A 3-question tick-box survey handed to classmates about their bag-packing habits collects comparable, gradable data quickly — but can only answer questions the researcher already thought to ask.

Materials/Examples: Tick-box questionnaires, rating scales, closed-question forms.

Application: Best for scale — reaching a large sample fast — but weaker than field research or interviews at surfacing unexpected insights.

6. Focus Groups

Definition: Group discussions used to reveal a range of user perceptions and attitudes toward a design concept.

Context: A panel of elderly residents discussing their reactions to an early medication-organiser prototype together can build on and challenge each other's opinions in a way a one-to-one interview cannot replicate.

Materials/Examples: Moderated group discussion, concept boards, reaction/rating exercises.

Application: Useful for testing reactions to a specific concept once early research has already narrowed the options.

Case Study: Airbnb's Photography Pivot

Rather than run more surveys, Airbnb's founders discovered — through direct field research and user observation — that listings were failing largely because host-taken photos were low quality, a pain point no survey had surfaced, since a survey can only answer questions researchers already think to ask. Within weeks of the founders manually replacing amateur photos with professional ones for New York listings, revenue in that city doubled — a finding that later became Airbnb's professional photography programme.

Practical Engagement: "Method Match" Stations

Three 6-minute rotations, all studying the same everyday task — how classmates pack their bag after class:

  • Station 1 (Field research / observation): silently watch and note behaviour for 4 minutes, asking no questions.
  • Station 2 (Interview): ask a partner four pre-written open questions about frustrations with their bag.
  • Station 3 (Survey): hand three classmates a 3-question tick-box survey on packing habits.

Regroup and compare: what did observation reveal that the interview didn't, and vice versa? Which method produced quantitative data suitable for graphing, and which produced richer but harder-to-compare qualitative detail? Extend into task analysis by having students individually sequence the steps of "packing your bag after class" and circle the step most likely to cause an item to be forgotten.

MethodData TypeBest For
Field ResearchQualitativeAuthentic behaviour in a real environment.
Task AnalysisQualitative / process dataPinpointing the exact step that causes error or delay.
User ObservationQualitativeUnspoken behaviours and workarounds.
InterviewsQualitativeMotivations, frustrations, the "why" behind behaviour.
Surveys/QuestionnairesQuantitativeComparable data from a large sample, quickly.
Focus GroupsQualitativeRange of reactions and attitudes to a specific concept.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Personas, Scenarios, and Population Stereotypes
sections.html:
A2.1.5 Personas, Scenarios & Population Stereotypes ~45 min

Lesson 5: Personas, Scenarios, and Population Stereotypes

Research data on its own is hard to design against. Personas and scenarios translate raw findings into specific, human tools a whole team can design around — while a sharp eye for population stereotypes keeps those tools honest.

1. Primary Persona

Definition: A profile of a fictional character representing a major user group, based on real, behaviour-based research. Personas save time by focusing development on real cases rather than unlikely edges.

Context: EasiDose's "Grace, 78" persona represents common patterns of mild memory lapses and finger stiffness among the medication organiser's target users.

Materials/Examples: Persona templates (name, age, goals, frustrations, quote, key habits).

Application: Gives the whole team a consistent, evidence-based reference point for design decisions, instead of designing around rare or extreme scenarios.

2. Secondary Persona

Definition: A profile representing a secondary user group whose needs also influence the design, though they are not the main user.

Context: A nurse or family caregiver who also needs to check that a patient has taken their EasiDose correctly is a secondary persona alongside the primary user, Grace.

Materials/Examples: Secondary-user interviews, caregiver-focused checklists.

Application: Ensures a design doesn't unintentionally fail the people who support or maintain the primary user's experience.

3. Scenario

Definition: An imagined sequence of events in the daily life of a persona, used to simulate how they might interact with a product in a specific context.

Context: A short scenario describing Grace opening her EasiDose organiser at breakfast after a poor night's sleep tests whether the design still works under realistic, imperfect conditions — not just an ideal use case.

Materials/Examples: 4–6 sentence written scenarios, storyboard panels.

Application: Pressure-tests a persona's needs against a specific, believable situation rather than an abstract profile.

4. Population Stereotypes

Definition: Assumptions widespread across a demographic (e.g. assuming elderly users cannot use technology), which are often factually incorrect.

Context: The EasiDose team initially assumed elderly users would reject digital reminder features — but field research found many participants already used smartphones daily for video calls with grandchildren, directly disproving the stereotype.

Materials/Examples: Stereotype-checking exercises, evidence logs that confirm or challenge an assumption.

Application: Every assumption about a user group should be tested against real research before it shapes a design decision.

Case Study: Microsoft's Persona Spectrum

Microsoft's Inclusive Design team plots disability across three states for the same limitation: Permanent (a person with one arm), Temporary (a person with an arm in a cast), and Situational (a new parent holding a baby in one arm). All three need the same one-handed solution — for example, packaging or a games controller that can be opened or operated with one hand. Designing only for the "permanent" case, or assuming (a population stereotype) that only permanently disabled users need such features, badly under-serves real demand, since a large proportion of any population is temporarily or situationally in that state at any given time.

Practical Engagement: "Build-a-Persona" for Our School Context

Brief: Design a reusable water bottle for use around school.

In pairs, students complete a one-page Primary Persona template (name, age, goals, frustrations, a representative quote, key habits) after a 2-minute mini-interview with a nearby classmate about their current bottle habits. They then write a 4–6 sentence Scenario describing a specific school-day moment where this persona uses the redesigned bottle.

Finally, each pair is handed one Population Stereotype card (e.g. "teenagers don't care about sustainability") and must state, with a reason drawn from their own research, whether their persona supports or challenges it.

Linking Questions

Use these to bridge A2.1 to other parts of the syllabus and to build the kind of cross-topic thinking Paper 2 extended-response questions reward.

A1.1 Ergonomics: How are user-centred research methods used to collect human factor data?
B1.1 UCD: How important is a good understanding of research methods to ensure effective UCD?
B2.2 Prototyping: To what extent are these strategies useful for gathering feedback on models?
C1.2 Inclusive Design: To what extent can designers remove personal bias when using research methods?
C3.1 Product Analysis: Which methods can impact the effectiveness of product evaluation?
