sections.title: Exam Practice: Topic A2.1
sections.html:
A2.1 Exam Practice AO1 / AO2 / AO3

Exam Practice: Topic A2.1

The following questions are written in the style of IB DP Design Technology Paper 1 and Paper 2. A stimulus is provided below; use it to anchor every question, as the real IB papers do.

Stimulus

EasiDose is a weekly medication organiser developed by a multidisciplinary design team for elderly users living independently. During Research, the team spent two weeks conducting field research in participants' own homes, observing (without suggesting solutions) how residents currently managed their medication. They found many participants already used smartphones daily for video calls with grandchildren — challenging the team's initial assumption that this user group would reject any digital reminder features. The team then built a Primary Persona, "Grace, 78", representing common patterns of mild memory lapses and finger stiffness, to guide Concept and Design work. Production tooling for the organiser's ridged, easy-grip lid was finalised during Implementation, ahead of a staged Launch trialling EasiDose in three local pharmacies before nationwide release.

Section A: Multiple Choice (AO1)

Question 1 [1 mark]

Which UCD research method did the design team use during their two weeks in participants' homes?

  • Focus group
  • Field research
  • Survey
  • Task analysis

Examiner Insight: This is a direct AO1 recall/identify question. The stimulus explicitly describes first-hand observation of users in their own environment — the definition of one specific term.

Reveal Answer
B. Field research. [1]

Question 2 [1 mark]

The team's initial belief that elderly users would reject digital reminder features is an example of a:

  • Primary persona
  • Scenario
  • Population stereotype
  • Secondary persona

Examiner Insight: Tests whether students can distinguish a population stereotype (an assumption about a demographic, shown here to be inaccurate) from the other UCD tools listed as distractors.

Reveal Answer
C. Population stereotype. [1]

Question 3 [1 mark]

Finalising the production tooling for the organiser's lid took place during which stage of the UCD process?

  • Concept
  • Design
  • Implementation
  • Launch

Examiner Insight: AO1 identify question requiring precise placement of an activity within the five-stage UCD model — tooling and manufacture belong to Implementation, not Design or Launch.

Reveal Answer
C. Implementation. [1]

Section B: Short Answer (AO1 / AO2)

Question 4 [2 marks]

State two components of the User Experience Trinity relevant to Grace's use of EasiDose.

Examiner Insight: "State" requires technical terms only — no explanation. Examiners generally mark on the first two points given; write single terms, not sentences.

Reveal Answer

1. User (Grace, and her memory/finger stiffness); 2. Task (taking the correct pill on the correct day). Environment also accepted as a second or third point. [2]

Question 5 [3 marks]

Explain how using a primary persona, "Grace, 78", helped the EasiDose team avoid designing for unlikely edge cases.

Examiner Insight: "Explain" requires a logical chain: Point → Mechanism → Consequence, using connectives like "because" or "therefore".

Reveal Answer

The team created a fictional but research-based profile representing a major, realistic user group (Point). This gave the whole team a consistent shared reference point for decisions about grip, text size and reminder frequency, rather than designing around rare or extreme scenarios (Mechanism). As a result, the Concept and Design stages stayed focused on the needs of the largest proportion of real users, saving development time (Consequence). [3]

Section C: Long Answer (AO2 / AO3)

Question 6 [6 marks]

Justify the design team's decision to use field research rather than a survey to understand how elderly users currently manage their medication.

Examiner Insight: "Justify" requires valid evidence supporting a conclusion. At 6 marks, build a fuller case: a strength of field research, a limitation, a comparison with the alternative (survey), and a concluding judgement.

Reveal Answer

Field research allowed the team to observe unspoken behaviours first-hand, which is how they discovered that many participants already used smartphones daily — a finding a scripted survey would likely have missed, since a survey can only answer questions the researchers already thought to ask. However, field research is time-consuming and costly, and the two-week sample was small. A survey would have reached a larger, more quantifiable sample faster, but at the cost of this depth of insight. For a small, high-stakes user group like this, where an incorrect stereotype could have led to a poorly received product, the deeper accuracy of field research justifies its higher cost — though a follow-up survey could later confirm the finding at scale. [6]

Question 7 [8 marks]

Evaluate the effectiveness of the user-centred design research methods used to develop EasiDose, and design one modification to the "Grace, 78" persona that would make it more inclusive of visually impaired users.

Examiner Insight: A two-part question combining "Evaluate" (weigh strengths and limitations to a balanced conclusion) with "Design" (identify a weakness and propose a specific, justified change). Award roughly half the marks to each command term.

Reveal Answer

Evaluate: The team's field research grounded the design in real user behaviour and corrected a costly, incorrect population stereotype about elderly users and technology, reducing the risk of an unwelcome late-stage redesign. However, the two-week home-visit sample was small and may not represent the full diversity of the elderly population, particularly users with different mobility or vision levels; this depth of research is also expensive and slow to repeat. On balance, the methods were effective for the specific problem investigated (memory and grip), but their narrow scope limits how confidently the findings generalise to other needs within the same user group. Design: The current persona documents memory lapses and finger stiffness but no visual data. A modification would be to add a stated visual acuity/contrast-sensitivity level to Grace's profile (e.g. reduced ability to distinguish low-contrast text), and require any packaging text or day labels to be tested against that data. This broadens the design's usability beyond hand dexterity alone, reflecting the same 360-degree, multidisciplinary understanding that underpins effective UCD. [8]
sections.text: A2.1 Exam Practice AO1 / AO2 / AO3 Exam Practice: Topic A2.1 The following questions are written in the style of IB DP Design Technology Paper 1 and Paper 2. A stimulus is provided below; use it to anchor every question, as the real IB papers do. Stimulus EasiDose is a weekly medication organiser developed by a multidisciplinary design team for elderly users living independently. Production tooling for the organiser's ridged, easy-grip lid was finalised during Implementation, ahead of a staged Launch trialling EasiDose in three local pharmacies before nationwide release. [1] Question 2 [1 mark] The team's initial belief that elderly users would reject digital reminder features is an example of a: Primary persona Scenario Population stereotype Secondary persona Examiner Insight: Tests whether students can distinguish a population stereotype (an assumption about a demographic, shown here to be inaccurate) from the other UCD tools listed as distractors. sections.html:
A2.1 Glossary

Glossary: Topic A2.1 — User-Centred Research Methods

Every key term from this unit, its IB-style definition, and a real-world example that shows the term in use. Click on a term to reveal its definition.

User-Centred Design (UCD)
IB Definition: A design process that involves real users at every stage of the design cycle, from research through to launch.
Real-World Context: OXO Good Grips kitchenware, developed around the needs of an arthritic user, Betsey Farber.
Empathy
IB Definition: The ability of a designer to understand and share the feelings and experiences of a user, in order to uncover real-world pain points.
Real-World Context: Doug Dietz embedding himself in a children's hospital to understand why young patients feared MRI scans.
Pain Point
IB Definition: A specific point of friction, frustration or failure that a user experiences, which they may not be able to articulate themselves.
Real-World Context: A weak, thin peeler handle causing hand pain for a user with arthritis.
User Experience (UX) Trinity
IB Definition: The three interacting factors a designer must understand for any interaction: the User, the Task, and the Environment.
Real-World Context: An MRI scan (Task) experienced very differently by a frightened child (User) inside a clinical scan room (Environment).
Iterative Design
IB Definition: A cyclical process of prototyping, testing and refining a solution based on repeated rounds of user feedback.
Real-World Context: EasiDose trialled in three pharmacies before being refined and released nationwide.
Research (UCD stage)
IB Definition: The first stage of UCD: gathering data on user needs, behaviours and context before any concepts are proposed.
Real-World Context: Two weeks of home visits to elderly users before any EasiDose concept was sketched.
Concept (UCD stage)
IB Definition: The stage where broad ideas are generated in direct response to research findings.
Real-World Context: Smart Design's early foam and rubber handle sketches for OXO Good Grips.
Design (UCD stage)
IB Definition: The stage where a concept is refined into a detailed, testable solution.
Real-World Context: Refining the Santoprene rubber grip diameter and ridge pattern through repeated user testing.
Implementation (UCD stage)
IB Definition: The stage where a finalised design is engineered for manufacture, including tooling and production processes.
Real-World Context: Developing new rubber-over-plastic moulding tooling that did not previously exist for kitchenware.
Launch (UCD stage)
IB Definition: The stage where a product is released to the market, sometimes in a staged or trial form.
Real-World Context: EasiDose's staged release in three local pharmacies ahead of nationwide sale.
Inclusive Design
IB Definition: A design approach that considers the full diversity of user needs, often widening a product's appeal beyond its original target user.
Real-World Context: OXO Good Grips, designed for an arthritic user, became a bestseller with able-bodied users of all ages (the "curb-cut effect").
Scope Creep
IB Definition: The tendency for a project's requirements to keep expanding as ongoing user feedback generates new demands, delaying launch.
Real-World Context: A design team repeatedly redesigning a feature after every new round of focus-group feedback.
Multidisciplinary Team
IB Definition: A team of specialists from different fields collaborating to gain a full, 360-degree understanding of a design problem.
Real-World Context: Engineers, doctors and local technicians co-designing the NeoNurture infant incubator from car parts for rural Nepal.
Ergonomic Specialist
IB Definition: A specialist who advises on the physical sizing and shape of controls or products to suit a specific user group.
Real-World Context: An ergonomist recommending grip diameter for an asthma inhaler designed for a 6-year-old's hand.
Field Research
IB Definition: First-hand observation of users in their own, natural environment.
Real-World Context: Airbnb's founders visiting and photographing host apartments in New York in person in 2009.
Task Analysis
IB Definition: Breaking a complex process down into sequential steps to identify bottlenecks, inefficiencies or points of user error.
Real-World Context: Mapping every step of packing a school bag to find the step most likely to cause a forgotten item.
User Observation
IB Definition: Watching users interact with a product to identify unspoken behaviours, workarounds, or difficulties.
Real-World Context: Silently observing how residents currently opened medication bottles before EasiDose was designed.
Interviews
IB Definition: Direct, qualitative conversations used to uncover a user's frustrations, motivations and expectations.
Real-World Context: Asking an elderly participant open questions about their daily medication routine.
Surveys and Questionnaires
IB Definition: Structured methods for collecting quantitative data on user demographics and preferences from a larger audience.
Real-World Context: A 3-question tick-box survey on classmates' backpack-packing habits.
Focus Groups
IB Definition: Group discussions used to reveal a range of user perceptions and attitudes toward a design concept.
Real-World Context: A panel of elderly residents discussing their reactions to an early EasiDose prototype together.
Primary Persona
IB Definition: A profile of a fictional character representing a major user group, built from real, behaviour-based research.
Real-World Context: "Grace, 78" — representing common patterns of memory lapses and finger stiffness among EasiDose's target users.
Secondary Persona
IB Definition: A profile representing a secondary user group whose needs also influence the design, though they are not the main user.
Real-World Context: A nurse or family caregiver who also needs to check that a patient has taken their EasiDose correctly.
Scenario
IB Definition: An imagined sequence of events in a persona's daily life, used to simulate how they might interact with a product in context.
Real-World Context: A short story describing Grace opening her EasiDose organiser at breakfast after a poor night's sleep.
Population Stereotype
IB Definition: A response or assumption that is widespread across a specific demographic, which may be factually incorrect.
Real-World Context: Microsoft's "Persona Spectrum" showing that assuming only permanently disabled users need one-handed products is inaccurate.
Secondary Research
IB Definition: Research undertaken by someone other than the original researcher, used to provide background information.
Real-World Context: Reading a published market report on elderly medication non-adherence before starting original field research.
Research Question
IB Definition: A focused question that directs research toward the specific answers a design team requires.
Real-World Context: "What causes elderly users to forget a scheduled dose?" guiding the EasiDose team's field research.

A particular group of customers or potential customers for whom a product, system or environment is designed.

A research activity where the user is observed interacting with a product or completing a task to find pain points in the process or interaction.
The range of users for a particular product or system.

syllabus.title: User-centred research methods
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How do designers understand the relationship between users, the product and the environment?

statements.text: Understanding the needs, wants and limitations of end-users is the key to user-centred design (UCD).
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how developing empathy with users through an understanding of their needs and carrying out (behaviours) tasks in a specified environment leads to better design.

statements.text: UCD is a design process that pays particular attention to the needs of potential users of a product through involvement of users at all stages of the design process.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the five stages of UCD and the advantages and disadvantages of UCD when designing products that meet the requirements of a diverse range of user needs and capabilities.

statements.text: UCD teams are multidisciplinary and develop a deep understanding of the user, task and the environment.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how different disciplines contribute to a better understanding of target user, task and environment when designing to meet the needs of specific target users.

statements.text: User-centred research methods can be used to understand a user population(s).
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how user-centred research methods (field research, task analysis, user observation, interviews, surveys and focus groups) can be used to discover the true nature of a user population.

statements.text: Design development uses persona, scenarios and population stereotypes early in the design process.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss how a primary persona, scenarios, population stereotypes and demographics can be used to guide design development, and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using them when engaging with UCD.

activity.title: Research detectives
steps: Choose a classroom object that causes difficulty. Write a neutral research question.
Observe a partner completing a normal task without coaching. Separate observations from interpretations.
Ask two non-leading interview questions; compare their answers with observed behaviour.
Select a further research method and explain what new evidence it could contribute.
activity.debrief: When might reported preferences conflict with observed behaviour?

exam.question: Explain one advantage and one limitation of observing users in context. [4]
exam.answer: Natural settings reveal real task demands and workarounds, improving the relevance of requirements. Observation can alter behaviour and may not explain motivations; combine it with interviews.
exam.label: Additional teacher-authored exam-style practice; indicative answer

activities.title: Practical Engagement: "Pain-Point Safari"
activities.text: Practical Engagement: "Pain-Point Safari" In pairs: Student A wears thick gloves or tapes two fingers together to simulate reduced dexterity, then attempts three everyday tasks while Student B silently observes and times them — opening a snack packet, sending a text message, and cutting along a line with scissors. Student B logs each hesitation or workaround under three columns: Task / Observed Pain Point / Possible Design Response. Swap roles, then debrief as a class: was each pain point rooted in the User, the Task, or the Environment? Discuss why direct observation revealed more than simply asking "what's hard about this?" would have.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: "Sequence the Stages" Card Sort
activities.text: Practical Engagement: "Sequence the Stages" Card Sort Provide small groups with six shuffled cards describing moments from the OXO Good Grips story above, plus one distractor card (e.g. "the packaging is redesigned five years later using recycled cardboard" — a post-launch iteration, not one of the five original stages). Groups sequence the five genuine cards into Research → Concept → Design → Implementation → Launch, explain their reasoning, and identify why the distractor doesn't belong. Discuss: if OXO had skipped straight from Research to Implementation, which disadvantage from the table above would apply?

activities.title: Practical Engagement: "Design the Team" Role Debate
activities.text: Practical Engagement: "Design the Team" Role Debate Brief: Design a child-friendly asthma inhaler that a 6-year-old can operate correctly, unaided, during an attack. Distribute role cards — Ergonomic specialist, Psychologist, Nurse (secondary persona for the caregiver), Software programmer (companion reminder app), Sociologist — each listing that specialist's core concern. In groups of five, one student per role argues for their concern being prioritised; the group must then agree a final combined requirement list containing at least one contribution from every discipline, modelling how real UCD teams negotiate trade-offs.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: "Method Match" Stations
activities.text: Practical Engagement: "Method Match" Stations Three 6-minute rotations, all studying the same everyday task — how classmates pack their bag after class: Station 1 (Field research / observation): silently watch and note behaviour for 4 minutes, asking no questions. Station 2 (Interview): ask a partner four pre-written open questions about frustrations with their bag. Station 3 (Survey): hand three classmates a 3-question tick-box survey on packing habits. Regroup and compare: what did observation reveal that the interview didn't, and vice versa? Which method produced quantitative data suitable for graphing, and which produced richer but harder-to-compare qualitative detail? Extend into task analysis by having students individually sequence the steps of "packing your bag after class" and circle the step most likely to cause an item to be forgotten.
activities.html:
Three 6-minute rotations, all studying the same everyday task — how classmates pack their bag after class:

  • Station 1 (Field research / observation): silently watch and note behaviour for 4 minutes, asking no questions.
  • Station 2 (Interview): ask a partner four pre-written open questions about frustrations with their bag.
  • Station 3 (Survey): hand three classmates a 3-question tick-box survey on packing habits.

Regroup and compare: what did observation reveal that the interview didn't, and vice versa? Which method produced quantitative data suitable for graphing, and which produced richer but harder-to-compare qualitative detail? Extend into task analysis by having students individually sequence the steps of "packing your bag after class" and circle the step most likely to cause an item to be forgotten.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: "Build-a-Persona" for Our School Context
activities.text: Practical Engagement: "Build-a-Persona" for Our School Context Brief: Design a reusable water bottle for use around school. In pairs, students complete a one-page Primary Persona template (name, age, goals, frustrations, a representative quote, key habits) after a 2-minute mini-interview with a nearby classmate about their current bottle habits. They then write a 4–6 sentence Scenario describing a specific school-day moment where this persona uses the redesigned bottle. Finally, each pair is handed one Population Stereotype card (e.g. "teenagers don't care about sustainability") and must state, with a reason drawn from their own research, whether their persona supports or challenges it.

searchText: user-centred research methods a2.1.1 core principles of ucd ~45 min lesson 1: core principles of user-centred design user-centred design begins with a simple but demanding idea: designers must set aside their own assumptions and immerse themselves in a user's lived experience. this lesson introduces the vocabulary and mental model — empathy, pain points, and the user experience trinity — that underpins every research method and case study in this unit. hook: the mri scanner nobody wanted to use watch engineer doug dietz describe the moment he realised his award-winning mri scanner was terrifying young patients. as you watch, note: was the actual problem the machine's technology, or something else entirely? watch: doug dietz — transforming healthcare for children and their families (tedxsanjoseca). 1. empathy & pain points definition: designers set aside their own assumptions and immerse themselves in a user's lived experience to uncover pain points — points of friction or frustration a user may struggle to describe themselves. context: doug dietz discovered that around 80% of paediatric mri patients needed sedation — not because of the technology itself, but because of the cold, clanking, unfamiliar tunnel, a pain point families struggled to put into words. materials/examples: empathy interviews, contextual inquiry, immersion/shadowing sessions. application: used at the very start of the design cycle, and revisited whenever later testing reveals a gap in understanding. 2. the user experience (ux) trinity definition: every interaction sits at the intersection of the user (abilities, age, prior experience), the task (the action and its steps), and the environment (the physical, social or technological context of use). change one, and the other two must be reconsidered. context: an mri scan is the same task, but is experienced completely differently by a frightened child (user) inside a clinical scan room (environment) than by a calm adult patient. materials/examples: ux trinity diagrams, context-of-use mapping. application: used to diagnose exactly which factor — user, task or environment — is the true source of a pain point, rather than assuming the product itself is at fault. 3. iterative design & outcomes definition: ucd loops — insights from testing feed back into research and concept work, refining the team's understanding of the user across repeated cycles rather than a single pass. the outcome is intuitive, accessible, efficient products that reduce user frustration and increase satisfaction. context: dietz's team didn't redesign the mri hardware once — they repainted scanners, trained staff, and refined the "pirate-ship adventure" framing repeatedly. sedation rates fell from roughly 80% to under 10%, and patient satisfaction scores rose by 90%, using the same underlying machine. materials/examples: repeated test-and-refine cycles, staff training updates, low-cost interventions (paint, scripts) rather than hardware redesign. application: reminds teams that ucd does not end at launch — insight keeps looping back into research and concept work. practical engagement: "pain-point safari" in pairs: student a wears thick gloves or tapes two fingers together to simulate reduced dexterity, then attempts three everyday tasks while student b silently observes and times them — opening a snack packet, sending a text message, and cutting along a line with scissors. student b logs each hesitation or workaround under three columns: task / observed pain point / possible design response. swap roles, then debrief as a class: was each pain point rooted in the user, the task, or the environment? discuss why direct observation revealed more than simply asking "what's hard about this?" would have. concept definition why it matters empathy setting aside assumptions to understand a user's lived experience and uncover pain points. surfaces frustrations a user may not be able to describe themselves. ux trinity the interacting user, task and environment behind every interaction. diagnoses which factor is really causing a problem. iterative design insights from testing loop back into research and concept work. refines understanding across repeated cycles, not a single pass. a2.1.2 ucd definition and stages ~60 min lesson 2: ucd definition and stages ucd is a process that involves users at all stages of the design cycle, not just at final testing. the five stages of ucd move from research (understand user and context) → concept (broad ideas informed by that research) → design (refine into a detailed, testable solution) → implementation (engineer for manufacture) → launch (release to market, sometimes in stages). the oxo good grips story — one of the most cited case studies in design — traces a single product through every stage. 1. research definition: the first stage of ucd — gathering data on user needs, behaviours and context before any concepts are proposed. context: in the late 1980s, sam farber watched his wife betsey, who had mild arthritis, struggle to grip a standard thin metal vegetable peeler. materials/examples: observation, interviews, contextual inquiry into daily frustrations. application: anchors every later stage in evidence rather than assumption. 2. concept definition: the stage where broad ideas are generated in direct response to research findings. context: farber partnered with the new york firm smart design, which produced dozens of foam and rubber handle sketches. materials/examples: sketch storms, foam/rubber material sampling, rapid low-fidelity mock-ups. application: converts a research insight (e.g. "gripping is painful") into a wide range of possible solutions before narrowing down. 3. design definition: the stage where a concept is refined into a detailed, testable solution. context: the team tested prototypes with people who had arthritis alongside able-bodied users of all ages, refining a soft, wide, ridged handle. materials/examples: iterative prototype testing, ridge-pattern and diameter refinement, mixed-ability user trials. application: confirms the concept actually works for the full range of intended users, not just the most extreme case. 4. implementation definition: the stage where a finalised design is engineered for manufacture, including tooling and production processes. context: new tooling and a supply chain for moulding rubber over plastic had to be developed from scratch, since nothing like it existed for kitchenware. materials/examples: production tooling, moulding processes, supply-chain development. application: turns a validated prototype into something that can actually be manufactured at scale. 5. launch definition: the stage where a product is released to the market, sometimes in a staged or trial form. context: oxo launched the good grips line in 1990 at a premium price. it became one of the best-selling kitchen tool ranges in us history — a foundational case of inclusive design, where designing for an "extreme" user produced a better product for almost everyone (sometimes called the curb-cut effect). materials/examples: market release planning, pricing strategy, staged or trial rollouts. application: closes one iteration of the ucd cycle — though feedback after launch often restarts it. advantages of ucd disadvantages of ucd enhanced satisfaction — products feel intuitive and enjoyable to the intended user increased usability — interfaces and controls are easier to navigate reduced costs — usability issues caught early avoid expensive late-stage changes inclusive design — considering diverse needs widens a product's real market, as with oxo good grips time-consuming — extensive research and iteration slows development high initial costs — user research and prototyping (and new tooling, as at oxo) are expensive complexity — balancing conflicting user needs against technical feasibility is difficult scope creep — constant feedback can trigger frequent changes that delay launch practical engagement: "sequence the stages" card sort provide small groups with six shuffled cards describing moments from the oxo good grips story above, plus one distractor card (e.g. "the packaging is redesigned five years later using recycled cardboard" — a post-launch iteration, not one of the five original stages). groups sequence the five genuine cards into research → concept → design → implementation → launch, explain their reasoning, and identify why the distractor doesn't belong. discuss: if oxo had skipped straight from research to implementation, which disadvantage from the table above would apply? a2.1.3 multidisciplinary ucd teams ~45 min lesson 3: multidisciplinary ucd teams successful ucd often requires a multidisciplinary team, since no single designer can hold the full picture of psychology, ergonomics, engineering and social context that governs how varied users behave. collaborative disciplines may include designers, engineers, software programmers, psychologists and sociologists. 1. why ucd needs a multidisciplinary team definition: no single designer can hold the full 360-degree picture of psychology, ergonomics, engineering and social context that governs how varied users behave — successful ucd relies on specialists from different fields collaborating. context: a team designing a child-friendly asthma inhaler needs more than a product designer alone — an ergonomic specialist to size the trigger for small hands, a psychologist to understand a frightened 6-year-old's behaviour, and a nurse to check real-world hygiene and handling. materials/examples: cross-disciplinary design reviews, joint field visits, shared research repositories. application: ensures a 360-degree understanding that no single specialist could reach alone. 2. specialist contributions definition: psychologists explain mental processes like perception and reasoning; ergonomic specialists guide the physical sizing of controls for specific users (e.g. arthritic hands); nurses or other secondary personas identify practical difficulties in handling or hygiene. context: an ergonomic specialist recommending the trigger-grip diameter for a child-friendly asthma inhaler works alongside a psychologist advising on how a frightened child behaves under stress, and a nurse (a secondary persona) confirming the device can be cleaned and checked by a caregiver. materials/examples: ergonomic sizing charts, secondary-persona interviews (e.g. nurses, caregivers), psychology-informed interface reviews. application: each specialist's contribution targets a different potential failure point — physical, cognitive, practical or social. case study: the neonurture infant incubator standard donated incubators shipped to rural hospitals in nepal often failed within months, because trained biomedical technicians and replacement parts were not available locally and power was unreliable. a multidisciplinary team of biomedical engineers, industrial designers, and local nepali doctors and technicians — who understood which parts actually stayed maintained in that context — co-designed the neonurture infant incubator almost entirely from car parts: sealed-beam headlights for radiant heat, a dashboard fan for air circulation, a motorcycle battery for backup power. because every village mechanic already knew how to repair those specific components, the incubators stayed functional for years after conventional western-designed alternatives had been abandoned. neither engineers alone, nor medical staff alone, could have reached this solution. practical engagement: "design the team" role debate brief: design a child-friendly asthma inhaler that a 6-year-old can operate correctly, unaided, during an attack. distribute role cards — ergonomic specialist, psychologist, nurse (secondary persona for the caregiver), software programmer (companion reminder app), sociologist — each listing that specialist's core concern. in groups of five, one student per role argues for their concern being prioritised; the group must then agree a final combined requirement list containing at least one contribution from every discipline, modelling how real ucd teams negotiate trade-offs. a2.1.4 user-centred research methods ~60 min lesson 4: user-centred research methods designers draw on a toolkit of research methods, each suited to a different kind of question — some reveal authentic, unspoken behaviour; others collect opinions at scale. choosing the right method (or combination of methods) is itself a design decision. hook: which method finds what? watch the clip below, then predict: which research method would have been most likely to reveal a problem the researchers didn't already know to ask about? watch: usability, user testing & task analysis (explainer). 1. field research definition: first-hand observation of users in their natural environment, to see how they interact with products authentically. context: in 2009, with almost no growth, airbnb's founders flew from san francisco to new york and went door to door, staying with hosts and photographing listings themselves. materials/examples: on-site observation, contextual visits, photo/video documentation of real use. application: reveals authentic behaviour that users may not think to mention when simply asked. 2. task analysis definition: a complex process broken down into sequential steps to identify bottlenecks, inefficiencies, or points of user error. context: sequencing every step of "packing your bag after class" to circle the single step most likely to cause an item to be forgotten. materials/examples: step-by-step observation sheets, numbered task lists. application: targets the exact failing step for redesign, rather than the whole product or process. 3. user observation definition: watching users interact with a product to identify unspoken behaviours, workarounds, or difficulties. context: silently watching a partner attempt an everyday task — such as opening a snack packet with reduced dexterity — reveals hesitations and workarounds a user might never mention in an interview. materials/examples: silent observation logs, video recordings, hesitation/workaround tallies. application: surfaces problems the user themselves may not be able to put into words. 4. interviews definition: direct, qualitative conversations to uncover user frustrations, motivations and expectations. context: asking an elderly participant open questions about their daily medication routine can surface motivations a tick-box survey never would. materials/examples: open-question scripts, one-to-one conversations, follow-up probing questions. application: best for depth and "why" — understanding motivations behind a behaviour, not just counting it. 5. surveys and questionnaires definition: structured methods for collecting quantitative data on user demographics and preferences from a larger audience. context: a 3-question tick-box survey handed to classmates about their bag-packing habits collects comparable, gradable data quickly — but can only answer questions the researcher already thought to ask. materials/examples: tick-box questionnaires, rating scales, closed-question forms. application: best for scale — reaching a large sample fast — but weaker than field research or interviews at surfacing unexpected insights. 6. focus groups definition: group discussions used to reveal a range of user perceptions and attitudes toward a design concept. context: a panel of elderly residents discussing their reactions to an early medication-organiser prototype together can build on and challenge each other's opinions in a way a one-to-one interview cannot replicate. materials/examples: moderated group discussion, concept boards, reaction/rating exercises. application: useful for testing reactions to a specific concept once early research has already narrowed the options. case study: airbnb's photography pivot rather than run more surveys, airbnb's founders discovered — through direct field research and user observation — that listings were failing largely because host-taken photos were low quality, a pain point no survey had surfaced, since a survey can only answer questions researchers already think to ask. within weeks of the founders manually replacing amateur photos with professional ones for new york listings, revenue in that city doubled — a finding that later became airbnb's professional photography programme. practical engagement: "method match" stations three 6-minute rotations, all studying the same everyday task — how classmates pack their bag after class: station 1 (field research / observation): silently watch and note behaviour for 4 minutes, asking no questions. station 2 (interview): ask a partner four pre-written open questions about frustrations with their bag. station 3 (survey): hand three classmates a 3-question tick-box survey on packing habits. regroup and compare: what did observation reveal that the interview didn't, and vice versa? which method produced quantitative data suitable for graphing, and which produced richer but harder-to-compare qualitative detail? extend into task analysis by having students individually sequence the steps of "packing your bag after class" and circle the step most likely to cause an item to be forgotten. method data type best for field research qualitative authentic behaviour in a real environment. task analysis qualitative / process data pinpointing the exact step that causes error or delay. user observation qualitative unspoken behaviours and workarounds. interviews qualitative motivations, frustrations, the "why" behind behaviour. surveys/questionnaires quantitative comparable data from a large sample, quickly. focus groups qualitative range of reactions and attitudes to a specific concept. a2.1.5 personas, scenarios & population stereotypes ~45 min lesson 5: personas, scenarios, and population stereotypes research data on its own is hard to design against. personas and scenarios translate raw findings into specific, human tools a whole team can design around — while a sharp eye for population stereotypes keeps those tools honest. 1. primary persona definition: a profile of a fictional character representing a major user group, based on real, behaviour-based research. personas save time by focusing development on real cases rather than unlikely edges. context: easidose's "grace, 78" persona represents common patterns of mild memory lapses and finger stiffness among the medication organiser's target users. materials/examples: persona templates (name, age, goals, frustrations, quote, key habits). application: gives the whole team a consistent, evidence-based reference point for design decisions, instead of designing around rare or extreme scenarios. 2. secondary persona definition: a profile representing a secondary user group whose needs also influence the design, though they are not the main user. context: a nurse or family caregiver who also needs to check that a patient has taken their easidose correctly is a secondary persona alongside the primary user, grace. materials/examples: secondary-user interviews, caregiver-focused checklists. application: ensures a design doesn't unintentionally fail the people who support or maintain the primary user's experience. 3. scenario definition: an imagined sequence of events in the daily life of a persona, used to simulate how they might interact with a product in a specific context. context: a short scenario describing grace opening her easidose organiser at breakfast after a poor night's sleep tests whether the design still works under realistic, imperfect conditions — not just an ideal use case. materials/examples: 4–6 sentence written scenarios, storyboard panels. application: pressure-tests a persona's needs against a specific, believable situation rather than an abstract profile. 4. population stereotypes definition: assumptions widespread across a demographic (e.g. assuming elderly users cannot use technology), which are often factually incorrect. context: the easidose team initially assumed elderly users would reject digital reminder features — but field research found many participants already used smartphones daily for video calls with grandchildren, directly disproving the stereotype. materials/examples: stereotype-checking exercises, evidence logs that confirm or challenge an assumption. application: every assumption about a user group should be tested against real research before it shapes a design decision. case study: microsoft's persona spectrum microsoft's inclusive design team plots disability across three states for the same limitation: permanent (a person with one arm), temporary (a person with an arm in a cast), and situational (a new parent holding a baby in one arm). all three need the same one-handed solution — for example, packaging or a games controller that can be opened or operated with one hand. designing only for the "permanent" case, or assuming (a population stereotype) that only permanently disabled users need such features, badly under-serves real demand, since a large proportion of any population is temporarily or situationally in that state at any given time. practical engagement: "build-a-persona" for our school context brief: design a reusable water bottle for use around school. in pairs, students complete a one-page primary persona template (name, age, goals, frustrations, a representative quote, key habits) after a 2-minute mini-interview with a nearby classmate about their current bottle habits. they then write a 4–6 sentence scenario describing a specific school-day moment where this persona uses the redesigned bottle. finally, each pair is handed one population stereotype card (e.g. "teenagers don't care about sustainability") and must state, with a reason drawn from their own research, whether their persona supports or challenges it. linking questions use these to bridge a2.1 to other parts of the syllabus and to build the kind of cross-topic thinking paper 2 extended-response questions reward. a1.1 ergonomics: how are user-centred research methods used to collect human factor data? b1.1 ucd: how important is a good understanding of research methods to ensure effective ucd? b2.2 prototyping: to what extent are these strategies useful for gathering feedback on models? c1.2 inclusive design: to what extent can designers remove personal bias when using research methods? c3.1 product analysis: which methods can impact the effectiveness of product evaluation? a2.1 exam practice ao1 / ao2 / ao3 exam practice: topic a2.1 the following questions are written in the style of ib dp design technology paper 1 and paper 2. a stimulus is provided below; use it to anchor every question, as the real ib papers do. stimulus easidose is a weekly medication organiser developed by a multidisciplinary design team for elderly users living independently. during research, the team spent two weeks conducting field research in participants' own homes, observing (without suggesting solutions) how residents currently managed their medication. they found many participants already used smartphones daily for video calls with grandchildren — challenging the team's initial assumption that this user group would reject any digital reminder features. the team then built a primary persona, "grace, 78", representing common patterns of mild memory lapses and finger stiffness, to guide concept and design work. production tooling for the organiser's ridged, easy-grip lid was finalised during implementation, ahead of a staged launch trialling easidose in three local pharmacies before nationwide release. section a: multiple choice (ao1) question 1 [1 mark] which ucd research method did the design team use during their two weeks in participants' homes? focus group field research survey task analysis examiner insight: this is a direct ao1 recall/identify question. the stimulus explicitly describes first-hand observation of users in their own environment — the definition of one specific term. reveal answer b. field research. [1] question 2 [1 mark] the team's initial belief that elderly users would reject digital reminder features is an example of a: primary persona scenario population stereotype secondary persona examiner insight: tests whether students can distinguish a population stereotype (an assumption about a demographic, shown here to be inaccurate) from the other ucd tools listed as distractors. reveal answer c. population stereotype. [1] question 3 [1 mark] finalising the production tooling for the organiser's lid took place during which stage of the ucd process? concept design implementation launch examiner insight: ao1 identify question requiring precise placement of an activity within the five-stage ucd model — tooling and manufacture belong to implementation, not design or launch. reveal answer c. implementation. [1] section b: short answer (ao1 / ao2) question 4 [2 marks] state two components of the user experience trinity relevant to grace's use of easidose. examiner insight: "state" requires technical terms only — no explanation. examiners generally mark on the first two points given; write single terms, not sentences. reveal answer 1. user (grace, and her memory/finger stiffness); 2. task (taking the correct pill on the correct day). environment also accepted as a second or third point. [2] question 5 [3 marks] explain how using a primary persona, "grace, 78", helped the easidose team avoid designing for unlikely edge cases. examiner insight: "explain" requires a logical chain: point → mechanism → consequence, using connectives like "because" or "therefore". reveal answer the team created a fictional but research-based profile representing a major, realistic user group (point) . this gave the whole team a consistent shared reference point for decisions about grip, text size and reminder frequency, rather than designing around rare or extreme scenarios (mechanism) . as a result, the concept and design stages stayed focused on the needs of the largest proportion of real users, saving development time (consequence) . [3] section c: long answer (ao2 / ao3) question 6 [6 marks] justify the design team's decision to use field research rather than a survey to understand how elderly users currently manage their medication. examiner insight: "justify" requires valid evidence supporting a conclusion. at 6 marks, build a fuller case: a strength of field research, a limitation, a comparison with the alternative (survey), and a concluding judgement. reveal answer field research allowed the team to observe unspoken behaviours first-hand, which is how they discovered that many participants already used smartphones daily — a finding a scripted survey would likely have missed, since a survey can only answer questions the researchers already thought to ask. however, field research is time-consuming and costly, and the two-week sample was small. a survey would have reached a larger, more quantifiable sample faster, but at the cost of this depth of insight. for a small, high-stakes user group like this, where an incorrect stereotype could have led to a poorly received product, the deeper accuracy of field research justifies its higher cost — though a follow-up survey could later confirm the finding at scale. [6] question 7 [8 marks] evaluate the effectiveness of the user-centred design research methods used to develop easidose, and design one modification to the "grace, 78" persona that would make it more inclusive of visually impaired users. examiner insight: a two-part question combining "evaluate" (weigh strengths and limitations to a balanced conclusion) with "design" (identify a weakness and propose a specific, justified change). award roughly half the marks to each command term. reveal answer evaluate: the team's field research grounded the design in real user behaviour and corrected a costly, incorrect population stereotype about elderly users and technology, reducing the risk of an unwelcome late-stage redesign. however, the two-week home-visit sample was small and may not represent the full diversity of the elderly population, particularly users with different mobility or vision levels; this depth of research is also expensive and slow to repeat. on balance, the methods were effective for the specific problem investigated (memory and grip), but their narrow scope limits how confidently the findings generalise to other needs within the same user group. design: the current persona documents memory lapses and finger stiffness but no visual data. a modification would be to add a stated visual acuity/contrast-sensitivity level to grace's profile (e.g. reduced ability to distinguish low-contrast text), and require any packaging text or day labels to be tested against that data. this broadens the design's usability beyond hand dexterity alone, reflecting the same 360-degree, multidisciplinary understanding that underpins effective ucd. [8] a2.1 glossary glossary: topic a2.1 — user-centred research methods every key term from this unit, its ib-style definition, and a real-world example that shows the term in use. click on a term to context: an mri scan (task) experienced very differently by a frightened child (user) inside a clinical scan room (environment). iterative design ib definition: a cyclical process of prototyping, testing and refining a solution based on repeated rounds of user feedback. real-world context: easidose trialled in three pharmacies before being refined and released nationwide. research (ucd stage) ib definition: the first stage of ucd: gathering data on user needs, behaviours and context before any concepts are proposed. real-world context: two weeks of home visits to elderly users before any easidose concept was sketched. concept (ucd stage) ib definition: the stage where broad ideas are generated in direct response to research findings. real-world context: smart design's early foam and rubber handle sketches for oxo good grips. design (ucd stage) ib definition: the stage where a concept is refined into a detailed, testable solution. real-world context: refining the santoprene rubber grip diameter and ridge pattern through repeated user testing. implementation (ucd stage) ib definition: the stage where a finalised design is engineered for manufacture, including tooling and production processes. real-world context: developing new rubber-over-plastic moulding tooling that did not previously exist for kitchenware. launch (ucd stage) ib definition: the stage where a product is released to the market, sometimes in a staged or trial form. real-world context: easidose's staged release in three local pharmacies ahead of nationwide sale. inclusive design ib definition: a became a bestseller with able-bodied users of all ages (the "curb-cut effect"). scope creep ib definition: the tendency for a project's requirements to keep expanding as ongoing user feedback user-centred design (ucd). ucd is a design process that pays particular attention to the needs of potential users of a product through involvement of users at all stages of the design process. ucd teams are multidisciplinary and develop a deep understanding of the user, task and the environment. user-centred research methods can be used to understand a user population(s). design development uses persona, scenarios and population stereotypes early in the design process.

title: Prototyping techniques

sections.title: Unit Overview
sections.html:
Unit Overview

Welcome to Unit A2.2: Prototyping Techniques! This unit is designed to be an interactive and comprehensive exploration into the crucial role of prototyping in design. We will investigate why prototyping is essential for learning, communication, and risk reduction, and you'll develop both theoretical knowledge and practical skills.

Across four parts, you will compare different prototyping fidelities, analyze drawing techniques, explore the worlds of physical and virtual models, and evaluate cutting-edge rapid prototyping technologies.

Lesson Objectives:

  • Explain the purpose and value of prototyping at different stages of the design process.
  • Compare and contrast low-fidelity and high-fidelity prototyping techniques.
  • Analyze the advantages and disadvantages of manual vs. CAD drawing techniques.
  • Discuss the purpose and application of physical and virtual prototypes.
  • Evaluate the use of emerging rapid prototyping technologies.
  • Apply your knowledge to select the most appropriate prototyping technique for a given design challenge.

sections.title: Part 1: The Why & The Chess Piece Challenge
sections.html:
Part 1: The Why & The Chess Piece Challenge

The Big Picture: A Dress Rehearsal for Design

Prototyping is not just about building a final product; it’s about learning, communicating ideas, and reducing risk before committing significant resources. Think of it as a "dress rehearsal" for a play—it’s the chance to find out what works and what doesn't before the main performance.

Low-Fidelity Prototyping

Low-fidelity prototypes are quick, cheap, and simple to create, often using materials like paper or cardboard. Their main purpose is to test core concepts and user flow in the early stages of design.

High-Fidelity Prototyping

In contrast, high-fidelity prototypes are much more realistic and closer to the final product. They are often digital, interactive, and are used to test detailed interactions and the aesthetic qualities of a design.

Activity: The 'Pawn to King: From Foam to 3D Print' Challenge ♟️

This challenge tasks you with designing a unique chess piece, taking it from a simple low-fidelity foam model to a detailed high-fidelity 3D print. The goal is to experience firsthand how different prototyping methods serve different purposes at different stages.

The Task: Design and create a single, unique chess piece.

Constraints: The piece must have a stable, circular base and have a height that is proportional to a standard chess piece.

Step 1: Ideation and Lo-Fi Foam Prototyping ✍️➡️✂️

First, sketch 2-3 ideas for your chosen piece on paper, based on a class theme (e.g., sci-fi, mythology). Then, select your best idea and carve a lo-fi prototype from a foam block. Focus on speed and the overall form, silhouette, and proportions—this is your chance to see if the design works in 3D.

Step 2: Digital Conversion & Hi-Fi Modeling 💻

Using your foam model as a physical guide, build your chess piece in a 3D modeling software like Tinkercad. In this high-fidelity stage, you can add details impossible to carve in foam, such as smooth curves, engraved patterns, and perfectly precise geometry.

Step 3: 3D Printing and Review 🖨️

Once the digital models are complete, they can be 3D printed. Finally, present your lo-fi foam model next to your hi-fi 3D print and discuss how the simple prototype informed the detailed final version.

sections.title: Part 2: The Art of Drawing
sections.html:
Part 2: The Art of Drawing

The Purpose of Design Drawing

Designers use drawings for three core reasons: to explore initial ideas, to refine concepts with more detail, and to communicate those ideas clearly to others, such as clients or manufacturers.

Free-Hand Sketching

Free-hand sketching is the fastest and most fluid way for designers to explore a wide range of initial concepts without the constraints of tools or software.

Formal Drawing Techniques

Formal drawings provide the accuracy and detail needed for manufacturing. Key types include:

  • Orthographic Projection: A 2D representation of a 3D object, showing separate top, front, and side views.
  • Isometric Drawing: A 3D representation of an object on a 2D surface.
  • Exploded Drawing: Shows a product's components separated but in the correct relative position for assembly.

Manual vs. CAD

While manual drawings are quick and accessible for early ideation, Computer-Aided Design (CAD) is essential for creating precise, complex virtual prototypes and generating the final documentation needed for modern manufacturing.

Watch these videos to see how sketching and CAD are used in professional car design.

sections.title: Part 3: Virtual and Physical Worlds
sections.html:
Part 3: Virtual and Physical Worlds

Prototypes come in two main forms: physical and virtual. Both are used to explore ideas, gather feedback, and refine a product before it goes into final production.

Physical Prototypes

These are tangible models that can be physically interacted with. Common types include:

  • Scale Models: Used for products that are too large or small to test at their final size.
  • Aesthetic Models: Focus on the look and feel of a product but are not functional.
  • Functional Prototypes: Working models that simulate the final product's real-world use.

Virtual Prototypes and Advanced Techniques

CAD software is used to create powerful virtual models. These can be simple **surface models** (showing only the outer appearance) or complete **solid models** (containing a full dataset for manufacturing). Modern technology has introduced several advanced virtual prototyping techniques:

Generative Design

This is an AI-driven process where software generates a range of optimal design solutions based on a set of constraints (like weight, material, and cost) provided by the designer. This often results in complex, organic-looking parts that are incredibly strong yet lightweight.

Finite Element Analysis (FEA)

FEA is a powerful simulation tool used to test how a design will perform under stress, heat, or vibration. For instance, car companies use FEA to digitally simulate crash tests, saving the time and expense of building numerous physical prototypes.

Digital Humans & Motion Capture

These tools are used to test a product's ergonomics and biomechanics. A designer can use a digital human model to see how a person interacts with a product, like testing the comfort of a car's interior or the effectiveness of a running shoe.

Augmented Reality (AR) & Virtual Reality (VR)

AR and VR allow designers and clients to experience a prototype in a simulated or mixed-reality environment. For example, an architect can use an AR app on a tablet to overlay a 3D model of a new building onto the actual construction site to see how it fits in the real world.

sections.title: Part 4: The Speed of Rapid Prototyping
sections.html:
Part 4: The Speed of Rapid Prototyping

Rapid prototyping refers to a group of techniques used to quickly fabricate a physical part or model from a 3D CAD model. This process is transformative because it allows designers to get physical feedback on their designs quickly, helping to refine the product and significantly reduce development time.

Emerging Technologies

Some of the most common rapid prototyping technologies include:

  • Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM): This is the most common and accessible type of 3D printing. It works by depositing layers of melted material (like plastic) to build up a model. It's excellent for creating durable, functional prototypes.
  • Stereolithography (SLA): This technique uses an ultraviolet laser to harden a liquid photosensitive polymer, layer by layer. SLA is known for producing models with very high detail and a smooth surface finish.
  • Selective Laser Sintering (SLS): A professional-grade technique that uses a high-powered laser to fuse powdered materials, such as plastic or metal, into a solid object. SLS produces strong, functional parts and does not require support structures, allowing for complex geometries.

Advantages and Disadvantages

The key advantages of rapid prototyping are speed, the ability to create complex geometries that are difficult to machine, and the ease of customization. However, disadvantages can include the high cost of some machines and materials, limitations on material selection, and the need for post-processing to finish the part.

Case Study: Rapid Prototyping in Medicine

Rapid prototyping has revolutionized medicine. Surgeons can 3D print patient-specific anatomical models from CT scans to practice complex operations. Similarly, companies use techniques like SLA to create highly detailed, customized prototypes for medical implants before manufacturing the final device.

sections.title: Extended Exam Practice
sections.html:
Extended Exam Practice

Test your understanding with these practice questions, structured like those you'll find on your IB exams.

Multiple Choice Questions (Paper 1 Style)

1. A designer creates a cardboard model of a new packaging box for user testing. This type of prototype is best described as:

A. An aesthetic prototype.
B. A high-fidelity prototype.
C. A low-fidelity prototype.
D. A functional prototype.

2. Which virtual prototyping tool is best for analyzing stress on a bridge design to find weak points before construction?

A. Generative design
B. Motion capture
C. Haptic technology
D. Finite Element Analysis (FEA)

Short Answer Questions (Paper 2 Style)

(a) State one advantage of using a free-hand sketch over a CAD model in the early stages of a design process.

Reveal Answer

One advantage is speed and fluidity. Free-hand sketching allows for rapid exploration of many different ideas without the technical constraints of software, making it ideal for initial brainstorming.

(b) Explain one reason why a formal drawing technique, such as an exploded drawing, is necessary for communicating a design to a manufacturer.

Reveal Answer

An exploded drawing is necessary because it clearly shows how different components of a product fit together. It provides an unambiguous, visual guide for the assembly process, reducing the chance of errors during manufacturing and ensuring all parts are correctly placed.

Long Answer Question (Paper 2 Style)

Discuss the extent to which rapid prototyping technologies have influenced the design process for products requiring a high degree of customization, such as prosthetics or customized athletic footwear. Your answer should refer to at least two specific rapid prototyping techniques.

Reveal Answer

Rapid prototyping technologies have had a profound influence on the design of customized products by dramatically shortening the development cycle and enabling patient- or user-specific solutions that were previously impractical.

One key technique is Selective Laser Sintering (SLS). For a product like a prosthetic limb, SLS can be used to create strong, durable, and lightweight final parts directly from a 3D scan of a patient's residual limb. This allows for a perfect, custom fit that improves comfort and functionality. The influence is that it merges the prototype and final product stages, allowing for the rapid creation of a highly personalized, functional item.

Another technique is Stereolithography (SLA). In the development of customized athletic footwear, a designer could use SLA to produce highly detailed, aesthetically finished prototypes of a custom shoe sole. This allows the athlete to see and feel the design before final production. The influence here is the ability to get fast, high-quality physical feedback on a unique design, enabling quick iterations to optimize performance and fit.

In both cases, these technologies move the design process away from mass production toward mass customization, fundamentally changing how personalized products are developed.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
Glossary

Aesthetic Prototype: A physical model developed to look and feel like the final product, but that does not function.

Augmented Reality (AR): A technology that superimposes a computer-generated image onto a user's view of the real world.

Computer-Aided Design (CAD): The use of computer software to aid the design process.

Digital Human: A digital simulation of various mechanical and biological aspects of the human body.

Exploded Drawing: A formal drawing that shows components of a product apart but in a relative position to show how they assemble.

Finite Element Analysis (FEA): A digital simulation used to calculate and visualize unknown factors like stress in a product using a CAD model.

Functional Prototype: A working model that functions in the same way as the final product to simulate real-world use.

Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM): A 3D printing method that deposits melted layers of material to build a model.

Generative Design: An AI-driven software that generates a range of design solutions based on constraints provided by the designer.

High-Fidelity Prototype: A model that is as functionally and aesthetically similar to the final product as possible.

Low-Fidelity Prototype: A simplified model created in the early stages to test a few aspects of a design idea.

Motion Capture: The process of recording human or animal movement for digital use.

Orthographic Projection: A formal 2D drawing technique used to depict the top, side, and front views of a 3D object.

Prototype: A physical or virtual model built to test a concept or process.

Rapid Prototyping: Manufacturing techniques used to quickly create a physical object from a CAD model for testing.

Selective Laser Sintering (SLS): An additive manufacturing technique that uses a laser to fuse small particles of material into a mass that has a desired 3D rapid prototyping shape.

Solid Model: A virtual (digital) model that provides a complete set of data for the product, including its interior.

Stereolithography (SLA): An additive manufacturing technique that creates 3D physical prototypes layer by layer by hardening molecules of a photosensitive liquid polymer using a laser beam.

Surface Model: A virtual (digital) model presenting the outer appearance and form, offering some machining data. Surface digital models contain no data about the interior of the part.

Virtual Prototype: Photorealistic digital computer-aided design (CAD) based interactive models that use surface and solid modelling.

Virtual Reality (VR): The ability to simulate a real situation on the screen and interact with it in a near-natural way.

A 3D printing method that deposits melted layers of material to build a model.
An AI-driven software that generates a range of design solutions based on constraints provided by the designer.
A model that is as functionally and aesthetically similar to the final product as possible.
A simplified model created in the early stages to test a few aspects of a design idea.
The process of recording human or animal movement for digital use.
A formal 2D drawing technique used to depict the top, side, and front views of a 3D object.
A physical or virtual model built to test a concept or process.
Manufacturing techniques used to quickly create a physical object from a CAD model for testing.
An additive manufacturing technique that uses a laser to fuse small particles of material into a mass that has a desired 3D rapid prototyping shape.
A virtual (digital) model that provides a complete set of data for the product, including its interior.
An additive manufacturing technique that creates 3D physical prototypes layer by layer by hardening molecules of a photosensitive liquid polymer using a laser beam.

syllabus.title: Prototyping techniques
syllabus.guidingQuestion: Why is it necessary for designers to prototype ideas as part of a design process?

statements.text: There are two techniques used in iterative design and development: low fidelity and high fidelity.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the advantages and disadvantages of using low- and high-fidelity prototyping within a design process.

statements.text: Drawings, either manual or prepared using computer-aided design (CAD) software, are used to explore, refine and communicate ideas.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline why designers use drawings to explore, refine and communicate ideas (including informal drawing techniques such as free-hand sketching and formal drawing techniques such as assembled drawing (isometric), orthographic projection and exploded drawings), the advantages and disadvantages of using informal and formal drawing processes, and understand how these techniques are used at different stages of design development.

statements.text: Prototypes can be developed in both physical and virtual (digital) form.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss the purpose of prototyping and how it is used in design and product development.

statements.text: Physical prototypes are used to test ideas and gather insights that inform the development of a product.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how and why designers use physical prototypes (including scale, aesthetics, materials, function and performance) to enhance the development towards a final product.

statements.text: CAD is used to create virtual prototypes to test ideas and gather insights that inform the development of a product.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how and why designers use virtual prototypes, including the use of surface and solid models, generative design, digital humans, motion capture, haptic technology, virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR), and finite element analysis (FEA).

statements.text: Rapid prototyping is used to create physical prototypes quickly for potential users and design teams to interact with them and provide feedback to drive design development forward.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to respond to emerging technologies and describe the advantages and disadvantages of why designers use rapid prototyping techniques, such as: stereolithography (SLA), fused deposition modelling (FDM) and selective laser sintering (SLS).

activity.title: One idea, three fidelities
steps: Choose a handheld classroom product and define a test question about grip, appearance or function.
Create a paper sketch, card mock-up and a labelled proposal for a functional prototype.
Exchange prototypes and gather one useful finding from each representation.
Rank the methods for the test question, time and resources; justify the next prototype.
activity.debrief: When does higher fidelity create false confidence?

exam.question: Explain why a low-fidelity prototype may be appropriate early in development. [2]
exam.answer: It is quick and inexpensive to modify, enabling alternatives to be tested before committing substantial resources.

activities.title: Activity: The 'Pawn to King: From Foam to 3D Print' Challenge ♟️
activities.text: Activity: The 'Pawn to King: From Foam to 3D Print' Challenge ♟️ This challenge tasks you with designing a unique chess piece, taking it from a simple low-fidelity foam model to a detailed high-fidelity 3D print. The goal is to experience firsthand how different prototyping methods serve different purposes at different stages. The Task: Design and create a single, unique chess piece. Constraints: The piece must have a stable, circular base and have a height that is proportional to a standard chess piece. Step 1: Ideation and Lo-Fi Foam Prototyping ✍️➡️✂️ First, sketch 2-3 ideas for your chosen piece on paper, based on a class theme (e.g., sci-fi, mythology). Then, select your best idea and carve a lo-fi prototype from a foam block. Focus on speed and the overall form, silhouette, and proportions—this is your chance to see if the design works in 3D. Step 2: Digital Conversion & Hi-Fi Modeling 💻 Using your foam model as a physical guide, build your chess piece in a 3D modeling software like Tinkercad. In this high-fidelity stage, you can add details impossible to carve in foam, such as smooth curves, engraved patterns, and perfectly precise geometry. Step 3: 3D Printing and Review 🖨️ Once the digital models are complete, they can be 3D printed. Finally, present your lo-fi foam model next to your hi-fi 3D print and discuss how the simple prototype informed the detailed final version.

Step 2: Digital Conversion & Hi-Fi Modeling 💻

Using your foam model as a physical guide, build your chess piece in a 3D modeling software like Tinkercad. In this high-fidelity stage, you can add details impossible to carve in foam, such as smooth curves, engraved patterns, and perfectly precise geometry.
