searchText: prototyping techniques unit overview welcome to unit a2.2: prototyping techniques ! this unit is designed to be an interactive and comprehensive exploration into the crucial role of prototyping in design. we will investigate why prototyping is essential for learning, communication, and risk reduction, and you'll develop both theoretical knowledge and practical skills. across four parts, you will compare different prototyping fidelities, analyze drawing techniques, explore the worlds of physical and virtual models, and evaluate cutting-edge rapid prototyping technologies. lesson objectives: explain the purpose and value of prototyping at different stages of the design process. compare and contrast low-fidelity and high-fidelity prototyping techniques. analyze the advantages and disadvantages of manual vs. cad drawing techniques. discuss the purpose and application of physical and virtual prototypes. evaluate the use of emerging rapid prototyping technologies. apply your knowledge to select the most appropriate prototyping technique for a given design challenge. part 1: the why & the chess piece challenge the big picture: a dress rehearsal for design prototyping is not just about building a final product; it’s about learning, communicating ideas, and reducing risk before committing significant resources. think of it as a "dress rehearsal" for a play —it’s the chance to find out what works and what doesn't before the main performance. low-fidelity prototyping low-fidelity prototypes are quick, cheap, and simple to create, often using materials like paper or cardboard. their main purpose is to test core concepts and user flow in the early stages of design. high-fidelity prototyping in contrast, high-fidelity prototypes are much more realistic and closer to the final product. they are often digital, interactive, and are used to test detailed interactions and the aesthetic qualities of a design. activity: the 'pawn to king: from foam to 3d print' challenge ♟️ this challenge tasks you with designing a unique chess piece, taking it from a simple low-fidelity foam model to a detailed high-fidelity 3d print. the goal is to experience firsthand how different prototyping methods serve different purposes at different stages. the task: design and create a single, unique chess piece. constraints: the piece must have a stable, circular base and have a height that is proportional to a standard chess piece. step 1: ideation and lo-fi foam prototyping ✍️➡️✂️ first, sketch 2-3 ideas for your chosen piece on paper, based on a class theme (e.g., sci-fi, mythology). then, select your best idea and carve a lo-fi prototype from a foam block. focus on speed and the overall form, silhouette, and proportions—this is your chance to see if the design works in 3d. step 2: digital conversion & hi-fi modeling 💻 using your foam model as a physical guide, build your chess piece in a 3d modeling software like tinkercad. in this high-fidelity stage, you can add details impossible to carve in foam, such as smooth curves, engraved patterns, and perfectly precise geometry. step 3: 3d printing and review 🖨️ once the digital models are complete, they can be 3d printed. finally, present your lo-fi foam model next to your hi-fi 3d print and discuss how the simple prototype informed the detailed final version. part 2: the art of drawing the purpose of design drawing designers use drawings for three core reasons: to explore initial ideas, to refine concepts with more detail, and to communicate those ideas clearly to others, such as clients or manufacturers. free-hand sketching free-hand sketching is the fastest and most fluid way for designers to explore a wide range of initial concepts without the constraints of tools or software. formal drawing techniques formal drawings provide the accuracy and detail needed for manufacturing. key types include: orthographic projection: a 2d representation of a 3d object, showing separate top, front, and side views. isometric drawing: a 3d representation of an object on a 2d surface. exploded drawing: shows a product's components separated but in the correct relative position for assembly. manual vs. cad while manual drawings are quick and accessible for early ideation, computer-aided design (cad) is essential for creating precise, complex virtual prototypes and generating the final documentation needed for modern manufacturing. watch these videos to see how sketching and cad are used in professional car design. part 3: virtual and physical worlds prototypes come in two main forms: physical and virtual. both are used to explore ideas, gather feedback, and refine a product before it goes into final production. physical prototypes these are tangible models that can be physically interacted with. common types include: scale models: used for products that are too large or small to test at their final size. aesthetic models: focus on the look and feel of a product but are not functional. functional prototypes: working models that simulate the final product's real-world use. virtual prototypes and advanced techniques cad software is used to create powerful virtual models. these can be simple **surface models** (showing only the outer appearance) or complete **solid models** (containing a full dataset for manufacturing). modern technology has introduced several advanced virtual prototyping techniques: generative design this is an ai-driven process where software generates a range of optimal design solutions based on a set of constraints (like weight, material, and cost) provided by the designer. this often results in complex, organic-looking parts that are incredibly strong yet lightweight. finite element analysis (fea) fea is a powerful simulation tool used to test how a design will perform under stress, heat, or vibration. for instance, car companies use fea to digitally simulate crash tests, saving the time and expense of building numerous physical prototypes. digital humans & motion capture these tools are used to test a product's ergonomics and biomechanics. a designer can use a digital human model to see how a person interacts with a product, like testing the comfort of a car's interior or the effectiveness of a running shoe. augmented reality (ar) & virtual reality (vr) ar and vr allow designers and clients to experience a prototype in a simulated or mixed-reality environment. for example, an architect can use an ar app on a tablet to overlay a 3d model of a new building onto the actual construction site to see how it fits in the real world. part 4: the speed of rapid prototyping rapid prototyping refers to a group of techniques used to quickly fabricate a physical part or model from a 3d cad model. this process is transformative because it allows designers to get physical feedback on their designs quickly, helping to refine the product and significantly reduce development time. emerging technologies some of the most common rapid prototyping technologies include: fused deposition modeling (fdm): this is the most common and accessible type of 3d printing. it works by depositing layers of melted material (like plastic) to build up a model. it's excellent for creating durable, functional prototypes. stereolithography (sla): this technique uses an ultraviolet laser to harden a liquid photosensitive polymer, layer by layer. sla is known for producing models with very high detail and a smooth surface finish. selective laser sintering (sls): a professional-grade technique that uses a high-powered laser to fuse powdered materials, such as plastic or metal, into a solid object. sls produces strong, functional parts and does not require support structures, allowing for complex geometries. advantages and disadvantages the key advantages of rapid prototyping are speed, the ability to create complex geometries that are difficult to machine, and the ease of customization. however, disadvantages can include the high cost of some machines and materials, limitations on material selection, and the need for post-processing to finish the part. case study: rapid prototyping in medicine rapid prototyping has revolutionized medicine. surgeons can 3d print patient-specific anatomical models from ct scans to practice complex operations. similarly, companies use techniques like sla to create highly detailed, customized prototypes for medical implants before manufacturing the final device. extended exam practice test your understanding with these practice questions, structured like those you'll find on your ib exams. multiple choice questions (paper 1 style) 1. a designer creates a cardboard model of a new packaging box for user testing. this type of prototype is best described as: a. an aesthetic prototype. b. a high-fidelity prototype. c. a low-fidelity prototype. d. a functional prototype. 2. which virtual prototyping tool is best for analyzing (a) state one advantage of using a free-hand sketch over a cad model in the early stages of a design process. reveal answer one advantage is speed and fluidity . free-hand sketching allows for rapid exploration of many different ideas without the technical constraints of software, making it ideal for initial brainstorming. (b) explain one reason why a formal drawing technique, such as an exploded drawing, is necessary for communicating a design to a manufacturer. reveal answer an exploded drawing is necessary because it clearly shows how different components of a product fit together . it provides an unambiguous, visual guide for the assembly process, reducing the chance of errors during manufacturing and ensuring all parts are correctly placed. long answer question (paper 2 style) discuss the extent to which rapid prototyping technologies have influenced the design process for products requiring a high degree of customization, such as prosthetics or customized athletic footwear. your answer should refer to at least two specific rapid prototyping techniques. reveal answer rapid prototyping technologies have key technique is selective laser sintering (sls) . for a product like a prosthetic limb, sls can be used to create strong, durable, and lightweight final parts directly from a 3d scan of a patient's residual limb. this allows for a perfect, custom fit that improves comfort and functionality. the influence is that it merges the prototype and final product stages, allowing for the rapid creation of title: Material classification and properties

sections.title: Lesson 1: Physical Properties
sections.html:
3.1.1 Classification 3.1.4 Physical Properties 1 Hour

Lesson 1: Physical Properties

Since you need to cover all of these for your Design Technology course, it helps to view them as "Trade-offs." In design, you rarely get a material that is perfect in every category—you choose the one that fits the specific environment of your product.

1. Density (ρ)

Definition: The mass of a material per unit volume (ρ = m/V).

Context: Primary factor in "Specific Strength" (strength-to-weight ratio). In transport design, lower density equals better fuel efficiency.

Materials: Low: Polypropylene, Balsa Wood, Aluminum (2,700 kg/m3). High: Steel (7,850 kg/m3), Lead, Gold.

Application: A drone frame needs low density (Carbon Fiber) to stay airborne, while a ship's keel needs high density (Lead) for stability.

2. Thermal Expansion

Definition: The degree to which a material expands or contracts when subjected to temperature changes.

Context: Measured by the Coefficient of Thermal Expansion. If a product uses two different materials (like a metal engine part inside a plastic housing), they must have compatible expansion rates or the product will crack.

Materials: High: Most Thermoplastics, Aluminum. Low: Tungsten, Glass-ceramics.

Application: Dental fillings must have the same thermal expansion as tooth enamel, or drinking hot coffee would cause the filling to pop out or crack the tooth.

3. Thermal Conductivity

Definition: The rate at which heat passes through a material.

Context: Materials with high conductivity are "Heat Sinks"; those with low conductivity are "Insulators."

Materials: Conductors: Copper, Silver, Graphite. Insulators: Polystyrene (Styrofoam), Wood, Ceramic.

Application: Space Shuttle tiles are made of high-tech ceramics with incredibly low thermal conductivity to protect the ship from the heat of re-entry.

4. Electrical Resistivity vs. Conductivity

These are two sides of the same coin.

Electrical Resistivity (ρe)

Definition: How strongly a material opposes the flow of electric current.

Context: High resistivity is essential for safety and preventing "leakage" of electricity.

Application: Protective gloves for electricians are made of high-resistivity rubber.

Electrical Conductivity (σ)

Definition: How easily a material allows electrons to flow through it. It is the mathematical reciprocal of resistivity (σ = 1/ρe).

Context: Vital for power distribution and signal processing.

Application: Gold is often used on high-end headphone jacks—not just because it conducts well, but because it doesn't corrode (maintainng a clean connection).

5. Melting Point

Definition: The temperature at which a material changes from a solid to a liquid state.

Context: Determines "Service Temperature" (max temp before losing structural integrity). Metals with high melting points are harder/more expensive to cast.

Materials: High: Tungsten (3,422°C), Tantalum. Low: Solder (183°C), Lead, Tin.

Application: Jet engine turbine blades are made of "Superalloys" because they must remain solid and strong at temperatures very close to their melting point.

Quick Comparison Table for your Notes

Property High Value Example Low Value Example DT Design Focus
Density Steel (Heavy) Aluminum (Light) Portability & Buoyancy
Thermal Expansion Plastic (High) Invar (Low) Dimensional Stability
Thermal Conductivity Copper Glass Fiber Heat Dissipation/Insulation
Elec. Resistivity Rubber Silver Safety & Insulation
Melting Point Ceramics Solder Manufacturing & Safety

sections.title: Lesson 2: The Stress Test (Mechanical Properties I)
sections.html:
3.1.1 Mechanical Intro 3.1.6 Strength/Stiffness/Hardness 1 Hour

Lesson 2: The Stress Test (Mechanical Properties I)

In mechanical engineering, the way a material responds to physical force determines its "personality." A material can be incredibly strong but useless if it is too flexible, or it can be extremely hard but shatter the moment it's dropped. Here is a deeper breakdown of the four fundamental mechanical properties.

1. Tensile Strength (Pulling Force)

The maximum stress a material can withstand while being stretched or pulled before necking or breaking.

The Mechanics: Pulling atoms away from each other. In metals, atomic planes slide; in polymers, chains uncoil. Designers usually look at Yield Strength (permanent deformation point).
  • Steel Cables: Used in suspension bridges; high tensile "ductility" gives warning before snapping.
  • Spider Silk: Nature's wonder; pound-for-pound stronger than many steel alloys.
  • Carbon Fiber: Exceptional strength but brittle—fails suddenly without stretching.

2. Compressive Strength (Squeezing Force)

The capacity to withstand loads that tend to reduce size. The polar opposite of tensile strength.

The Mechanics: Pushing atoms together. Failure happens via buckling (bending sideways) or crushing. Some materials (Stone/Concrete) are "anisotropic"—great at compression, terrible at tension.
  • Concrete Pillars: Designed to hold up massive highway overpasses.
  • Cast Iron: Absorbs vibration and resists crushing; used for heavy engine bases.
  • Shoe Soles (EVA): "Compression set resistance"—foam springs back after crushing.

3. Stiffness (Young's Modulus)

Strength is "when will it break?"; Stiffness is "how much does it bend before it breaks?"

The Mechanics: Measured by Young's Modulus (E). High E = Rigid (Diamond); Low E = Flexible (Rubber). In aerospace, stiffness is critical for control.
  • Bicycle Frames: Aluminum is stiffer than Steel, providing a "snappy" but harsh ride.
  • Glass: Extremely stiff (High E) but zero ductility—shatters without bending.

4. Hardness (Surface Resistance)

Resistance to localized plastic deformation (scratching, abrasion, indentation). A surface property.

The Mechanics: Tight atomic bonding. Measured by Mohs, Rockwell, or Brinell scales. Trade-off: Harder materials often become more brittle.
  • Tungsten Carbide: Drill bits/saw teeth; stays hard even when red-hot.
  • Sapphire Glass: Watch faces; scratch-proof except against diamond.
  • Case-Hardened Steel: Hard outside for wear resistance, soft inside for toughness.

Mechanical Property Summary Chart

Property High Performance Low Performance Failure Mode
Tensile Kevlar / Carbon Fiber Concrete / Glass Snapping / Tearing
Compressive Granite / Cast Iron Rubber / Wood (across grain) Crushing / Buckling
Stiffness Ceramics / Steel Lead / Nylon Sagging / Warping
Hardness Diamond / Tool Steel Gold / Plastic Scratching / Gouging

Activity: Mohs Scale Testing

Your Task: Use the provided scratch test kit (fingernail, penny, glass slide, steel file). Rank the sample materials from softest to hardest based on which material can scratch the other.

Glass: Extremely stiff (High E ) but zero ductility—shatters without bending. 4. Hardness (Surface Resistance) Resistance to localized plastic deformation (scratching, abrasion, indentation). A surface property. The Mechanics: Tight atomic bonding. Measured by Mohs, Rockwell, or Brinell scales. Trade-off: Harder materials often become more brittle. Tungsten Carbide: Drill bits/saw teeth; stays hard even when red-hot. Sapphire Glass: Watch faces; scratch-proof except against diamond. Case-Hardened Steel: Hard outside for wear resistance, soft inside for toughness. Rank the sample materials from softest to hardest based on which material can scratch the other.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Bending Without Breaking (Mechanical Properties II)
sections.html:
3.1.6 Ductility/Malleability/Toughness 1 Hour

Lesson 3: Bending Without Breaking (Mechanical Properties II)

While Strength and Stiffness tell us how much a material can carry, these five properties—Plasticity, Elasticity, Ductility, Malleability, and Toughness—tell us how a material behaves when it is pushed beyond its limits. In engineering, these are often called "deformation characteristics."

1. Elasticity (The "Spring" Factor)

The ability of a material to deform under stress and return to its original dimensions once that stress is removed.

The Mechanics: Atomic bonds stretch but don't break (atomic-scale bungee cord). The limit is the Elastic Limit.

Engineering Context: Metals have an elastic range. Bridges sink and spring back; if not, they fail.

Example: A silicone gasket or a slingshot.

2. Plasticity (The Permanent Change)

The opposite of elasticity. The ability to undergo permanent deformation without localized failure (cracking).

The Mechanics: Stress is high enough that atomic planes slide and "lock" into new positions.

Engineering Context: Vital for manufacturing (stamping car doors, bending paperclips).

Example: Wet clay or lead.

3. Ductility (Stretchability)

A specific type of plasticity referring to the ability to be stretched or "drawn" out into a thin wire without snapping.

The Mechanics: Materials "neck" down before breaking. Provides a visual safety warning.

Engineering Context: Copper is king. Pulled through dies to create wiring.

Example: Low-carbon steel and Gold.

4. Malleability (Flattenability)

The ability to be compressed, hammered, or rolled into thin sheets without cracking. (Squeezing vs Pulling).

The Mechanics: Atoms spread laterally under pressure.

Industrial Design Context: Aluminum is highly malleable (foil measured in microns).

Example: Aluminum foil, Gold leaf, heated wrought iron.

5. Toughness (Impact Energy Absorption)

The ability to absorb energy and deform plastically before fracturing. Combination of Strength + Ductility.

The Mechanics: Fights the crack. Uses impact energy to move atoms (plasticity) rather than cracking.

The Paradox: Diamond = Strong but Low Toughness (shatters). Rubber = High Toughness but Low Strength.

Example: Polycarbonate (bulletproof glass), Car Bumpers.

Summary of Deformation Properties

Property Primary Action Real-World Application Why Designers Care
Elasticity Recover Springs, Seals, Foundations Predicts if a part will "sag" permanently.
Plasticity Form Die-stamping, Forging Essential for making complex metal shapes.
Ductility Pull Wiring, Cables Provides a "safety warning" before breaking.
Malleability Squeeze Foil, Beverage Cans Allows for thin-walled, lightweight containers.
Toughness Absorb Helmets, Bumpers, Tools Prevents "catastrophic failure" during impact.

The "Grand Finale" Comparison

To see how these all interact, imagine a Glass Marble vs. a Copper Ball:

  • Both are Hard (resist scratching).
  • The glass is Stiff (won't bend), but the copper is Ductile (will stretch).
  • If you hit them with a hammer, the glass shatters (Brittle failure) because it lacks Toughness. The copper flattens (Malleable deformation) because it has high Plasticity.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Chemical Properties & Material Selection
sections.html:
3.1.3 Identifying Materials 3.1.5 Chemical Properties 1 Hour

Lesson 4: Chemical Properties & Material Selection

When selecting materials for industrial design or engineering, chemical properties are often more critical than mechanical ones. A part that is strong enough but dissolves in rain or leaches toxins into food is a failure. Here is an expanded look at the four key chemical properties.

1. Corrosion & Oxidation Resistance

This is a material's ability to resist deterioration caused by chemical reactions with its environment (usually oxygen or moisture).

The Mechanics: Many metals form an "oxide layer." For Steel, this layer (rust) is porous and flakes off. For Aluminum or Titanium, it is "passivating"—creating a microscopic, airtight seal.

Engineering Context: In Reinforced Concrete, "concrete cancer" occurs when internal steel rebar corrodes, expands, and cracks the concrete.

  • Stainless Steel (316 Grade): Contains Molybdenum to resist salt-water corrosion.
  • Gold: The ultimate non-reactive metal; used for high-end electrical connectors.
  • Fiberglass: Used for underground chemical storage tanks because it never "rusts."

2. Reactivity & Chemical Compatibility

Reactivity determines how a material behaves when it touches acids, bases, or solvents. Primary concern for Food Safety and Medical Devices.

The Mechanics: High reactivity leads to "leaching." Inert materials (Glass, Teflon) are used for zero interaction.

Critical Context: BPA in plastics is a reactivity concern; it can mimic hormones if leaches into food.

  • HDPE (Plastic #2): Highly non-reactive; used for milk jugs and bleach containers.
  • Copper: Reactive with acids. Cooking tomato sauce in unlined copper dissolves copper into food.
  • Titanium: Biocompatible (zero reactivity with human tissue), standard for bone implants.

3. Hygroscopy (Moisture Sensitivity)

The tendency of a material to absorb water molecules from the surrounding atmosphere.

The Mechanics: Absorption causes Dimensional Instability (swelling), loss of insulation, or "hydrolysis" (bond breaking).

The "Hidden" Problem: In 3D printing, "wet" plastic turns to steam during processing, creating bubbles/weak spots.

  • Nylon (PA): Can absorb up to 10% weight in water, swelling and becoming flexible.
  • Wood: Classic hygroscopic material. Plywood uses cross-lamination to fight warping.
  • Silica Gel: Engineered specifically for high hygroscopy to protect electronics.

4. Flammability & Thermal Decomposition

Measures how easily a material ignites (Flash Point) and whether it supports combustion or self-extinguishes.

The Mechanics: Polymers often burn easily. Flame Retardants (like Bromine) interfere with the reaction.

The Danger of Off-gassing: PVC releases deadly Hydrogen Cyanide gas when it burns.

  • Nomex: Inherently flame-resistant aramid; used for racing suits/firefighter gear.
  • Polycarbonate: Often "Self-Extinguishing" (UL94 V-0 rating).
  • Magnesium: Highly flammable in thin sheets/powder form (machining risk).

Chemical Properties Summary Chart

Property High Performance Low Performance Key Design Question
Corrosion Titanium / Ceramic Carbon Steel Will this be used outdoors or near salt?
Reactivity Glass / PTFE (Teflon) Untreated Aluminum Is it touching food or human skin?
Hygroscopy Acrylic (PMMA) Nylon / Wood Will the part size change if it gets humid?
Flammability Silicone / Nomex Polyethylene / Polystyrene Does it need to pass building fire codes?

Synthesis Activity: "The Acid Tank"

Design Challenge: You need to select a material to store a corrosive industrial acid.

  • Why might you reject Steel? (Corrosion risk)
  • Why might you reject Glass? (Brittle/Mechanical failure risk)
  • Solution? Specific polymers like HDPE (High-Density Polyethylene) offer chemical resistance and toughness.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Origins & Structural Design
sections.html:
3.1.2 Classification (Origin) 1 Hour

Lesson 5: Origins & Structural Design

Classification by Origin

Natural Materials: Sourced from nature. Examples: Timber, cotton, wool, leather.
Synthetic Materials: Man-made. Examples: Polymers, alloys, glass.

Deep Dive: Structural Mechanics

In engineering and industrial design, the magic happens in how structures manage internal stresses (tension, compression, and torsion) and how they fail. Here is a deeper look into the four categories.

1. Frame Structures (Skeleton-like)

A network of thin components (members) that support the load. Strength lies in geometry, not mass.

The Mechanics: Deals primarily with bending and buckling. Triangles (trusses) are used for inherent rigidity.

Engineering Context: Loads redistribute if a member fails. (e.g., A crane doesn't collapse if one brace bends).

  • Industrial: Steel skyscrapers (curtain wall is skin, not support).
  • Nature: Spiderwebs (tension-only frame).
  • Product Design: Laptop internal magnesium chassis.

2. Shell Structures (Thin-Skinned)

Thin, often curved outer layers distribute loads across the entire surface. Acts as both "skin" and "support."

The Mechanics: Membrane stress. Loads on curves convert to compressive forces traveling to the base.

The Weakness: Stiff but brittle. Cracks/dents significantly reduce load capacity.

  • Industrial: Pressure vessels, airplane fuselages (Monocoque).
  • Nature: Tortoise shell, coconut.
  • Product Design: Plastic milk jug (liquid inside prevents buckling).

3. Solid Structures (Mass-Based)

Rely on sheer weight and volume to resist forces. Usually held together by gravity.

The Mechanics: Designed for compression. Poor at handling tension.

Design Intent: "Set and forget" durability or when material is cheap.

  • Industrial: Great Pyramids, dams, heavy machine tool bases.
  • Nature: Mountains, thick tree trunks.
  • Product Design: Cast-iron skillet, marble countertop.

4. Combination Structures

"Form follows function." Different parts have different mechanical needs.

The Mechanics: Integrated Design. Frame for heavy lifting, shell for ergonomics/protection.

Deep Context: Modern cars use a Unibody (pillars = frame, floorpan = shell).

  • House: Wooden frame + Drywall shell + Concrete solid foundation.
  • Umbrella: Foldable frame (ribs) + Fabric shell (canopy).
  • Bridge: Solid towers + Steel truss frame + Cable tension system.

Quick Comparison Reference

Structure Type Main Strength Main Weakness Design Goal
Frame Lightweight / Modular Complex Joints Efficiency
Shell High Surface Area Protection Buckling/Denting Weight Reduction
Solid Extreme Durability Massive Material Use Stability
Combination Versatility High Manufacturing Cost Performance

Design Challenge (10 mins)

Task: Sketch a chair design using ONLY a Frame structure. Then, sketch a second chair using ONLY a Shell structure.

sections.title: Lesson 6: Strength in Numbers (Composites)
sections.html:
3.1.7 Composites 1 Hour

Lesson 6: Strength in Numbers (Composites)

What is a Composite?

Definition: A Matrix (glue/binder) + A Reinforcement (fiber/particle).

Common examples: Reinforced Concrete (Steel + Concrete), Carbon Fiber (Epoxy + Carbon strands), GRP (Glass Reinforced Plastic).

Why use them? We combine materials to get the "best of both worlds."
  • Concrete is good in compression, but bad in tension.
  • Steel is good in tension.
  • Reinforced Concrete handles both forces well.

Case Study: The Boeing 787 Dreamliner

This was the first major airliner to use 50% composite materials.

  • Benefits: Lighter (fuel efficiency), no corrosion (unlike aluminum), allows for higher cabin pressure (better passenger comfort).
  • Drawbacks: Difficult to repair; lightning strike management requires extra engineering (copper mesh).

Activity: "Composite Analysis"

Task: Examine a skateboard deck or a snowboard. Why do they layer wood with fiberglass? What property does each layer provide?

Composite Materials Reference Data

Composite Material Young's Modulus (E) Tensile Strength (σ) Context Common Applications
1. Reinforced Concrete 25−35 GPa 2−5 MPa* By far the most widely used man-made composite on Earth. Cement matrix + aggregate (sand/gravel). Reinforced with steel rebar for tensile loads. Foundations, bridges, skyscrapers, dams.
2. Fiberglass (GFRP) 20−45 GPa 200−600 MPa Glass Fiber Reinforced Polymer. Fine glass fibers embedded in plastic resin (polyester/epoxy). Lightweight, corrosion-resistant, cheap. Boat hulls, wind turbine blades, storage tanks.
3. Carbon Fiber (CFRP) 50−150 GPa 600−1,500 MPa The "gold standard". Carbon fibers for extreme rigidity and tensile strength. Lighter than aluminum, stronger than steel. Aerospace structures, F1 cars, high-end sports gear.
4. Plywood 8−12 GPa 30−60 MPa Classic "engineered wood". Thin veneer layers glued with grain perpendicular to the next. "Cross-graining" prevents splitting/warping. Formwork, furniture, cabinetry, structural flooring.
5. Kevlar (Aramid) 30−80 GPa 400−1,400 MPa Aramid fibers known for heat resistance and energy absorption. Woven into sheets with resins. virtually puncture-proof. Body armor, radial tires, mooring lines.
6. Metal Matrix (MMC) 90−120 GPa 400−600 MPa Metal matrix (Aluminum/Magnesium) reinforced with ceramic/carbon fibers. Higher stiffness, better extreme temp performance. Jet engine parts, automotive pistons, tank armor.
7. Ceramic Matrix (CMC) 200−300 GPa 200−400 MPa Ceramic fibers in ceramic matrix. Resists "crack propagation" unlike brittle standard ceramics. Tough against thermal shock. Space shuttle tiles, gas turbines, brake discs.
8. Wood-Plastic (WPC) 3−6 GPa 15−35 MPa Mix of wood flour/fiber and thermoplastics (PE/PVC). Aesthetic of wood, durability of plastic. Outdoor decking, railings, landscaping timber.
9. Engineered Bamboo 15−20 GPa 120−160 MPa Sustainable. Bamboo fibers/strands bonded with resins. Outperforms traditional hardwoods in hardness/stability. Sustainable architecture, flooring, furniture.
10. Honeycomb Panel 70 GPa* 200−300 MPa* Structural composite. Honeycomb core (aluminum/Nomex) sandwiched between two skins. Highest stiffness-to-weight ratio. Aircraft bulkheads, satellites, transit interiors.

* Note: Values are approximate and depend heavily on the specific grade and manufacturing process.

sections.title: Lesson 7: The Future (Smart Materials)
sections.html:
3.1.8 Smart Materials 1 Hour

Lesson 7: The Future (Smart Materials)

Smart materials are often called "responsive materials." Unlike traditional materials that are static, these have properties that can be significantly changed in a controlled fashion by external stimuli (like stress, temperature, or light).

1. Piezoelectricity

The Stimulus: Mechanical stress (pressure) or Electrical voltage.
How it works: When you deform a piezoelectric crystal (squeeze it), it generates an electric charge. Conversely, if you apply electricity to it, the material changes shape (vibrates).

Context: Used for sensing and ultra-precise movement.

  • Sensors: Airbag sensors in cars (detecting the impact force).
  • Actuators: High-end speakers and inkjet printer heads that need to move tiny amounts.
  • Energy Harvesting: Floor tiles in busy train stations that generate electricity from footsteps.

2. Shape Memory Alloys (SMA)

The Stimulus: Heat (Temperature change).
How it works: These materials (usually Nitinol—a Nickel-Titanium alloy) can be "programmed" to remember a specific shape. If you bend them out of shape while cold, they will instantly return to their original "remembered" shape when heated.

Context: Eliminates the need for bulky mechanical motors or levers.

  • Medical: Stents for clogged arteries (expand to shape at body temp).
  • Aerospace: Flaps on wings that move without heavy hydraulic systems.
  • Frames: "Unbreakable" glasses frames that pop back into shape.

3. Photochromicity

The Stimulus: Light (specifically UV radiation).
How it works: A material changes its optical properties (transparency or color) when exposed to light. When the light source is removed, the material returns to its original state.

Context: Used for light management and UV protection.

  • Transition Lenses: Glasses that turn into sunglasses when you step outside.
  • Smart Windows: Buildings that darken their glass automatically in bright sunlight to reduce cooling costs.

4. Magneto-rheostatic (MR) & Electro-rheostatic (ER)

The Stimulus: Magnetic fields (MR) or Electric fields (ER).
How it works: Typically fluids containing tiny particles. When a field is applied, particles align instantly, changing the fluid into a near-solid or very thick "grease."

Context: Used for instant, "real-time" damping and shock absorption.

  • MR Fluids: High-end car suspension (Audi/Ferrari). Adjusts from "soft" to "sport" in milliseconds.
  • ER Fluids: Industrial valves or clutches that engage/disengage instantly without mechanical wear.

5. Thermoelectricity

The Stimulus: Temperature Difference (ΔT).
How it works: (Seebeck Effect) A temperature difference between two conductors creates voltage. (Peltier Effect) Apply electricity, and one side gets hot while the other gets cold.

Context: Converting "waste heat" into useful energy or cooling without moving parts.

  • Thermoelectric Generators (TEGs): Powering remote sensors using heat from a pipe or engine.
  • Solid-state Cooling: Portable 12V camping fridges (no compressor/coolant gas).

Summary Checklist for Selection

Smart Material Stimulus Reaction Key DT Benefit
Piezoelectric Pressure Electricity Sensing & precision
SMA (Nitinol) Heat Shape Change No motors needed
Photochromic UV Light Color Change Light/Heat control
MR / ER Fluids Mag/Elec Field Viscosity Change Instant dampening
Thermoelectric Temp Gradient Electricity Waste heat recovery

Unlike traditional materials that are static, these have properties that can be significantly changed in a controlled fashion by external stimuli (like stress, temperature, or light). 1. Piezoelectricity The Stimulus: Mechanical stress (pressure) or Electrical voltage. How it works: When you deform a piezoelectric crystal (squeeze it), it generates an electric charge. Conversely, if you apply electricity to it, the material changes shape (vibrates). Context: Used for sensing and ultra-precise movement. Sensors: Airbag sensors in cars (detecting the impact force). Actuators: High-end speakers and inkjet printer heads that need to move tiny amounts. Energy Harvesting: Floor tiles in busy train stations that generate electricity from footsteps. 2. If you bend them out of shape while cold, they will instantly return to their original "remembered" shape when heated. Context: Eliminates the need for bulky mechanical motors or levers. Medical: Stents for clogged arteries (expand to shape at body temp). Aerospace: Flaps on wings that move without heavy hydraulic systems. Frames: "Unbreakable" glasses frames that pop back into shape. 3. Photochromicity The Stimulus: Light (specifically UV radiation). sections.title: Lesson 8: Biomaterials & The Circular Economy
sections.html:
3.1.9 Biodegradable Materials Unit Review 1 Hour

Lesson 8: Biomaterials & The Circular Economy

1. Defining Biodegradability

Definition: A material's ability to be broken down by microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, or algae) into natural substances like water, CO2, and biomass, without leaving toxic residue.
  • The Stimulus: Moisture, heat, and oxygen.
  • The Timeline: To be truly "biodegradable" in a design context, it should break down within a reasonable timeframe (months to years), rather than centuries.

2. Biomaterials in the Circular Economy

A. Designing Out Waste

Traditional designers used a "Linear Economy" (Take → Make → Dispose). Modern DT designers use biomaterials to ensure that the "Dispose" phase actually feeds the next "Make" phase.

Case Study: Instead of using expanded polystyrene (EPS) for packaging—which lasts 500 years—designers use Mycelium (mushroom roots). Once the customer receives their package, they can break the Mycelium down and put it in their garden as fertilizer.

B. Renewable Feedstocks

Biomaterials are often Bio-based, meaning they are made from renewable resources like corn starch, sugarcane, or cellulose. This reduces the reliance on finite resources like crude oil.

3. Key Biodegradable Materials for DT

1. PLA (Polylactic Acid)

Source: Fermented plant starch (corn, sugarcane).

Circular Benefit: Can be melted and reshaped (recycling) or industrially composted.

App: 3D printing filaments, food containers.

2. Mycelium (Mushroom Roots)

Source: Fungi roots grown on agricultural waste.

Circular Benefit: "Grows" into shape with low energy. 100% home-compostable replacement for Styrofoam.

App: Protective packaging (Dell/IKEA), fashion leather.

3. PHA (Polyhydroxyalkanoate)

Source: Bacterial fermentation of sugar/lipids.

Circular Benefit: Marine-biodegradable. Breaks down in ocean water (unlike PLA).

App: Agricultural mulch films, medical staples.

4. Algae-based Bioplastics

Source: Seaweed and algae.

Circular Benefit: Carbon-negative (absorbs CO2). Grows fast without land/freshwater.

App: Edible water sachets (Ooho), dissolvable pods.

5. Chitosan (Chitin)

Source: Shells of crustaceans (shrimp, crabs).

Circular Benefit: Turns waste into high-value material. Natural antimicrobial properties.

App: Biodegradable cling film, wound dressings.

6. Bacterial Cellulose

Source: Bacteria grown in tea/sugar mixture.

Circular Benefit: Grown to exact pattern shape (zero-waste manufacturing).

App: Sustainable "vegan leather" jackets/shoes.

7. Hempcrete

Source: Hemp inner hurd mixed with lime.

Circular Benefit: Carbon-sequestering. Can be crushed into soil conditioner at end-of-life.

App: Non-load-bearing insulation walls.

8. Bagasse (Sugarcane Fiber)

Source: Fibrous residue from crushed sugarcane.

Circular Benefit: Uses waste residue. Highly compostable, low energy processing.

App: Takeaway containers, heat-resistant plates.

sections.title: Exam Preparation & Practice
sections.html:
Exam Practice Time: 25 Mins 15 Marks Total

Exam Preparation & Practice

Test your knowledge with these IB-style questions. Attempt the question first, then reveal the markscheme to check your understanding.

Section A: Multiple Choice (3 Marks)

1. Which mechanical property describes a material's ability to undergo permanent deformation without fracturing?

  • Elasticity
  • Plasticity
  • Stiffness
  • Density
Reveal Answer
Correct Answer: B (Plasticity)

2. A designer is selecting a material for a kitchen spatula. Which combination of properties is most critical?

  • High thermal conductivity and high plasticity.
  • High electrical conductivity and high toughness.
  • Low thermal conductivity and high non-reactivity (food safety).
  • Low density and high magnetism.
Reveal Answer
Correct Answer: C
(Low thermal conductivity prevents burns; high non-reactivity ensures food safety).

3. Which of the following best describes a "Smart Material"?

  • A material that is composed of two or more distinct substances.
  • A material that breaks down naturally in the environment.
  • A material derived strictly from natural sources.
  • A material with properties that change significantly in response to external stimuli.
Reveal Answer
Correct Answer: D
(Properties change in response to stimuli like heat, light, or electricity).

Section B: Short Answer (4 Marks)

4. Distinguish between 'ductility' and 'malleability'. (2 marks)

Reveal Markscheme
  • Award [1] for defining ductility as the ability of a material to be drawn into a wire (under tension).
  • Award [1] for defining malleability as the ability of a material to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets (under compression).

5. Define the term 'composite material' and state one advantage of using a composite over a pure metal in the aerospace industry. (2 marks)

Reveal Markscheme
  • Award [1] for defining a composite as a material made from two or more constituent materials with significantly different physical/chemical properties that remain separate within the finished structure.
  • Award [1] for one valid advantage, such as:
    • Higher strength-to-weight ratio.
    • Increased corrosion resistance.
    • Ability to tailor properties (anisotropy) to direction of load.

sections.title: Glossary of Terms
sections.html:
Quick Reference Definitions

Glossary of Terms

Click on a term to reveal its definition.

Density

The mass per unit volume of a material. Important for portability and weight constraints (e.g. Aerospace).

Stiffness (Young's Modulus)

The resistance of an elastic body to deformation by an applied force. A stiff material resists bending.

Toughness

The ability of a material to absorb energy and plastically deform without fracturing. (Area under the stress-strain curve).

Composite

A material made from two or more constituent materials with significantly different physical or chemical properties that, when combined, produce a material with characteristics different from the individual components.

Smart Material

Materials that have one or more properties that can be significantly changed in a controlled fashion by external stimuli, such as stress, temperature, moisture, pH, electric or magnetic fields.

Toughness The ability of a material to absorb energy and plastically deform without fracturing. (Area under the stress-strain curve). Composite A material made from two or more constituent materials with significantly different physical or chemical properties that, when combined, produce a material with characteristics different from the individual components. Smart Material Materials that have one or more properties that can be significantly changed in a controlled fashion by external stimuli, such as stress, temperature, moisture, pH, electric or magnetic fields.

glossary.definition: Any material created by, or derived from, biological organisms, including plants, animals, bacteria and fungi.
A property of a material that only becomes evident during or after a chemical reaction.

An economic model in which resources remain in use for as long as possible, from which maximum value is extracted while in use, and the products and materials are recovered and regenerated at the end of the product life cycle.
A material comprised of two or more materials to improve their physical, mechanical and chemical properties and/or aesthetics characteristics.
The ability of a material to withstand being pushed or squashed.
The ability of a material to withstand damage caused by oxidization or other chemical reactions.

The mass per unit of volume of a material. Its importance is in portability of a product’s weight and size. Design contexts include food packaging, because pre-packaged food is sold by weight and volume, and packing foams.
The ability of a material to be drawn or extruded into an extended shape such as a wire.
The extent to which a material will return to its original shape after being deformed, once the force causing the deformation is removed.
The measure of a material’s ability to conduct electricity. A material with low resistivity will conduct electricity well.
This smart property relates to a fluid that can undergo a dramatic change in its viscosity when exposed to an electric field. This effect is reversed when the electric field is removed.
A measure of how quickly a material can be ignited and how quickly it burns.
A chemical property of a material that has the ability to absorb moisture from the surrounding environment.
A hard, brittle and typically transparent amorphous solid made by rapidly cooling a fusion of sand, soda and lime.
The resistance a material offers to penetration or scratching.
This smart property relates to a fluid that can undergo a dramatic change in its viscosity when exposed to a magnetic field. This effect is reversed when the magnetic field is removed.
A material’s ability to be plastically deformed under compressive forces.
A material that does not occur naturally in the world. It is synthetic or artificial.
Properties of a material that involve the relationship between stress and strain or a reaction to an applied force.
The temperature a material transforms from a solid into a liquid.
Materials that occur in the natural world.
A property of a smart material. A photochromic material changes colour in response to an increase in light. When the light source is removed, it returns to its original colour.

Any property that is measurable and that describes a state of materials, including density, thermal expansion, thermal conductivity, melting point, electrical resistivity and electrical conductivity. These properties tend to be the characteristics of materials that can be identified through non-destructive testing.
A property of a smart material. A piezoelectric material gives off a small electrical discharge when deformed and experiences an increase in its volume when an electrical current passes through it.
The ability of a material to be changed in shape permanently.
Synthetic materials made from chemical compounds commonly referred to as “plastics”.
A chemical property of a material that represents the extent to which a material will react with another (including air) to become unsafe for use to come in contact with food.
A material that “remembers” and returns to a predefined shape after being deformed. This is achieved in response to changes in temperature or stress.

Materials that have been designed to have one or more properties that can be modified when subject to an external stimulus in a way that the output can be controlled. This modification (change) is reversible and can be repeated.
A material’s ability to resist deflection (bending deformation) and maintain its shape.
The ability of a material to withstand pulling forces.
A cloth or woven fabric material.
The measure of how fast heat is conducted through a slab of material with a given temperature difference across the slab.
A measure of the degree of increase in dimensions (length, area or volume) when an object is heated.
This refers to a smart material comprised of two dissimilar conductors that produce an electric current when heated.
Wood harvested from trees prepared for use in manufacturing, construction and carpentry. Categorized as softwoods and hardwoods depending on the type of tree it is sourced from.
The ability of a material to resist the propagation of cracks.
The resistance of an elastic body to deformation by an applied force. A stiff material resists bending.

A material made from two or more constituent materials with significantly different physical or chemical properties that, when combined, produce a material with characteristics different from the individual components.
Materials that have one or more properties that can be significantly changed in a controlled fashion by external stimuli, such as stress, temperature, moisture, pH, electric or magnetic fields.

syllabus.title: Material classification and properties
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How do material properties and classifications aid material selection for a specified manufacturing process or product?

statements.text: Materials are classified based on their physical, chemical and mechanical properties.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how and why materials are classified and discuss the advantages of classifying materials in terms of physical, chemical and mechanical properties.

statements.text: Materials are classified according to their source or origin.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss frame, shell, solid and combination (for example, frame and shell) structures, and how they are used in the design of products. They need to understand that materials are classified into natural and human-made, including for example timbers, polymers, metals, glass, textiles, composites, smart materials and biomaterials.

statements.text: Identifying the most suitable material for a product is a complex and challenging task, involving the consideration of physical, chemical and mechanical properties and aesthetic characteristics.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to evaluate the physical, chemical and mechanical properties to ensure the selection of the most appropriate material for a specific purpose.

statements.text: Physical properties include aspects of a material that can be measured and observed without it changing in any way.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain density, thermal expansion, thermal conductivity, melting point, electrical resistivity and electrical conductivity.

statements.text: Chemical properties include aspects of a material that lead to it chemically reacting with another.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain corrosion resistance, reactivity (food safe), hygroscopy and flammability.

statements.text: Mechanical properties include aspects of a material affected by the application of a force.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain tensile and compressive strength, stiffness, toughness, hardness, malleability, elasticity, plasticity and ductility.

statements.text: Composites consist of two or more materials combined to enhance their properties.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain why combining materials can create composite materials more suitable for a specific purpose or context using an example.

statements.text: Smart materials are materials that have one or more properties that can be significantly changed in response to changes in their environment.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how materials can be selected to react to external stimuli, including piezoelectricity, shape memory, photochromicity, magneto-rheostatic, electro-rheostatic and thermoelectricity.

statements.text: Biodegradable materials break down in the environment after disposal or at the end of their useful life.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how biomaterials are a key part of a circular economy and can be used by designers to design out waste.
