searchText: material classification and properties 3.1.1 classification 3.1.4 physical properties 1 hour lesson 1: physical properties since you need to cover all of these for your design technology course, it helps to view them as "trade-offs." in design, you rarely get a material that is perfect in every category—you choose the one that fits the specific environment of your product. 1. density ( ρ ) definition: the mass of a material per unit volume ( ρ = m/v ). context: primary factor in "specific strength" (strength-to-weight ratio). in transport design, lower density equals better fuel efficiency. materials: low: polypropylene, balsa wood, aluminum (2,700 kg/m 3 ). high: steel (7,850 kg/m 3 ), lead, gold. application: a drone frame needs low density (carbon fiber) to stay airborne, while a ship's keel needs high density (lead) for stability. 2. thermal expansion definition: the degree to which a material expands or contracts when subjected to temperature changes. context: measured by the coefficient of thermal expansion. if a product uses two different materials (like a metal engine part inside a plastic housing), they must have compatible expansion rates or the product will crack. materials: high: most thermoplastics, aluminum. low: tungsten, glass-ceramics. application: dental fillings must have the same thermal expansion as tooth enamel, or drinking hot coffee would cause the filling to pop out or crack the tooth. 3. thermal conductivity definition: the rate at which heat passes through a material. context: materials with high conductivity are "heat sinks"; those with low conductivity are "insulators." materials: conductors: copper, silver, graphite. insulators: polystyrene (styrofoam), wood, ceramic. application: space shuttle tiles are made of high-tech ceramics with incredibly low thermal conductivity to protect the ship from the heat of re-entry. 4. electrical resistivity vs. conductivity these are two sides of the same coin. electrical resistivity ( ρ e ) definition: how strongly a material opposes the flow of electric current. context: high resistivity is essential for safety and preventing "leakage" of electricity. application: protective gloves for electricians are made of high-resistivity rubber. electrical conductivity ( σ ) definition: how easily a material allows electrons to flow through it. it is the mathematical reciprocal of resistivity ( σ = 1/ρ e ). context: vital for power distribution and signal processing. application: gold is often used on high-end headphone jacks—not just because it conducts well, but because it doesn't corrode (maintainng a clean connection). 5. melting point definition: the temperature at which a material changes from a solid to a liquid state. context: determines "service temperature" (max temp before losing structural integrity). metals with high melting points are harder/more expensive to cast. materials: high: tungsten (3,422°c), tantalum. low: solder (183°c), lead, tin. application: jet engine turbine blades are made of "superalloys" because they must remain solid and strong at temperatures very close to their melting point. quick comparison table for your notes property high value example low value example dt design focus density steel (heavy) aluminum (light) portability & buoyancy thermal expansion plastic (high) invar (low) dimensional stability thermal conductivity copper glass fiber heat dissipation/insulation elec. resistivity rubber silver safety & insulation melting point ceramics solder manufacturing & safety 3.1.1 mechanical intro 3.1.6 strength/stiffness/hardness 1 hour lesson 2: the stress test (mechanical properties i) in mechanical engineering, the way a material responds to physical force determines its "personality." a material can be incredibly strong but useless if it is too flexible, or it can be extremely hard but shatter the moment it's dropped. here is a deeper breakdown of the four fundamental mechanical properties. 1. tensile strength (pulling force) the maximum stress a material can withstand while being stretched or pulled before necking or breaking. the mechanics: pulling atoms away from each other. in metals, atomic planes slide; in polymers, chains uncoil. designers usually look at yield strength (permanent deformation point). steel cables: used in suspension bridges; high tensile "ductility" gives warning before snapping. spider silk: nature's wonder; pound-for-pound stronger than many steel alloys. carbon fiber: exceptional strength but brittle—fails suddenly without stretching. 2. compressive strength (squeezing force) the capacity to withstand loads that tend to reduce size. the polar opposite of tensile strength. the mechanics: pushing atoms together. failure happens via buckling (bending sideways) or crushing. some materials (stone/concrete) are "anisotropic"—great at compression, terrible at tension. concrete pillars: designed to hold up massive highway overpasses. cast iron: absorbs vibration and resists crushing; used for heavy engine bases. shoe soles (eva): "compression set resistance"—foam springs back after crushing. 3. stiffness (young's modulus) strength is "when will it break?"; stiffness is "how much does it bend before it breaks?" the mechanics: measured by young's modulus ( e ). high e = rigid (diamond); low e = flexible (rubber). in aerospace, stiffness is critical for control. bicycle frames: aluminum is stiffer than steel, providing a "snappy" but harsh ride. glass: extremely stiff (high e ) but zero ductility—shatters without bending. 4. hardness (surface resistance) resistance to localized plastic deformation (scratching, abrasion, indentation). a surface property. the mechanics: tight atomic bonding. measured by mohs, rockwell, or brinell scales. trade-off: harder materials often become more brittle. tungsten carbide: drill bits/saw teeth; stays hard even when red-hot. sapphire glass: watch faces; scratch-proof except against diamond. case-hardened steel: hard outside for wear resistance, soft inside for toughness. mechanical property summary chart property high performance low performance failure mode tensile kevlar / carbon fiber concrete / glass snapping / tearing compressive granite / cast iron rubber / wood (across grain) crushing / buckling stiffness ceramics / steel lead / nylon sagging / warping hardness diamond / tool steel gold / plastic scratching / gouging activity: mohs scale testing your task: use the provided scratch test kit (fingernail, penny, glass slide, steel file). rank the sample materials from softest to hardest based on which material can scratch the other. 3.1.6 ductility/malleability/toughness 1 hour lesson 3: bending without breaking (mechanical properties ii) while strength and stiffness tell us how much a material can carry, these five properties—plasticity, elasticity, ductility, malleability, and toughness—tell us how a material behaves when it is pushed beyond its limits. in engineering, these are often called "deformation characteristics." 1. elasticity (the "spring" factor) the ability of a material to deform under stress and return to its original dimensions once that stress is removed. the mechanics: atomic bonds stretch but don't break (atomic-scale bungee cord). the limit is the elastic limit . engineering context: metals have an elastic range. bridges sink and spring back; if not, they fail. example: a silicone gasket or a slingshot. 2. plasticity (the permanent change) the opposite of elasticity. the ability to undergo permanent deformation without localized failure (cracking). the mechanics: stress is high enough that atomic planes slide and "lock" into new positions. engineering context: vital for manufacturing (stamping car doors, bending paperclips). example: wet clay or lead. 3. ductility (stretchability) a specific type of plasticity referring to the ability to be stretched or "drawn" out into a thin wire without snapping. the mechanics: materials "neck" down before breaking. provides a visual safety warning. engineering context: copper is king. pulled through dies to create wiring. example: low-carbon steel and gold. 4. malleability (flattenability) the ability to be compressed, hammered, or rolled into thin sheets without cracking. (squeezing vs pulling). the mechanics: atoms spread laterally under pressure. industrial design context: aluminum is highly malleable (foil measured in microns). example: aluminum foil, gold leaf, heated wrought iron. 5. toughness (impact energy absorption) the ability to absorb energy and deform plastically before fracturing. combination of strength + ductility. the mechanics: fights the crack. uses impact energy to move atoms (plasticity) rather than cracking. the paradox: diamond = strong but low toughness (shatters). rubber = high toughness but low strength. example: polycarbonate (bulletproof glass), car bumpers. summary of deformation properties property primary action real-world application why designers care elasticity recover springs, seals, foundations predicts if a part will "sag" permanently. plasticity form die-stamping, forging essential for making complex metal shapes. ductility pull wiring, cables provides a "safety warning" before breaking. malleability squeeze foil, beverage cans allows for thin-walled, lightweight containers. toughness absorb helmets, bumpers, tools prevents "catastrophic failure" during impact. the "grand finale" comparison to see how these all interact, imagine a glass marble vs. a copper ball : both are hard (resist scratching). the glass is stiff (won't bend), but the copper is ductile (will stretch). if you hit them with a hammer, the glass shatters ( brittle failure) because it lacks toughness . the copper flattens ( malleable deformation) because it has high plasticity . 3.1.3 identifying materials 3.1.5 chemical properties 1 hour lesson 4: chemical properties & material selection when selecting materials for industrial design or engineering, chemical properties are often more critical than mechanical ones. a part that is strong enough but dissolves in rain or leaches toxins into food is a failure. here is an expanded look at the four key chemical properties. 1. corrosion & oxidation resistance this is a material's ability to resist deterioration caused by chemical reactions with its environment (usually oxygen or moisture). the mechanics: many metals form an "oxide layer." for steel, this layer (rust) is porous and flakes off. for aluminum or titanium, it is "passivating"—creating a microscopic, airtight seal. engineering context: in reinforced concrete, "concrete cancer" occurs when internal steel rebar corrodes, expands, and cracks the concrete. stainless steel (316 grade): contains molybdenum to resist salt-water corrosion. gold: the ultimate non-reactive metal; used for high-end electrical connectors. fiberglass: used for underground chemical storage tanks because it never "rusts." 2. reactivity & chemical compatibility reactivity determines how a material behaves when it touches acids, bases, or solvents. primary concern for food safety and medical devices. the mechanics: high reactivity leads to "leaching." inert materials (glass, teflon) are used for zero interaction. critical context: bpa in plastics is a reactivity concern; it can mimic hormones if leaches into food. hdpe (plastic #2): highly non-reactive; used for milk jugs and bleach containers. copper: reactive with acids. cooking tomato sauce in unlined copper dissolves copper into food. titanium: biocompatible (zero reactivity with human tissue), standard for bone implants. 3. hygroscopy (moisture sensitivity) the tendency of a material to absorb water molecules from the surrounding atmosphere. the mechanics: absorption causes dimensional instability (swelling), loss of insulation, or "hydrolysis" (bond breaking). the "hidden" problem: in 3d printing, "wet" plastic turns to steam during processing, creating bubbles/weak spots. nylon (pa): can absorb up to 10% weight in water, swelling and becoming flexible. wood: classic hygroscopic material. plywood uses cross-lamination to fight warping. silica gel: engineered specifically for high hygroscopy to protect electronics. 4. flammability & thermal decomposition measures how easily a material ignites (flash point) and whether it supports combustion or self-extinguishes. the mechanics: polymers often burn easily. flame retardants (like bromine) interfere with the reaction. the danger of off-gassing: pvc releases deadly hydrogen cyanide gas when it burns. nomex: inherently flame-resistant aramid; used for racing suits/firefighter gear. polycarbonate: often "self-extinguishing" (ul94 v-0 rating). magnesium: highly flammable in thin sheets/powder form (machining risk). chemical properties summary chart property high performance low performance key design question corrosion titanium / ceramic carbon steel will this be used outdoors or near salt? reactivity glass / ptfe (teflon) untreated aluminum is it touching food or human skin? hygroscopy acrylic (pmma) nylon / wood will the part size change if it gets humid? flammability silicone / nomex polyethylene / polystyrene does it need to pass building fire codes? synthesis activity: "the acid tank" design challenge: you need to select a material to store a corrosive industrial acid. why might you reject steel? (corrosion risk) why might you reject glass? (brittle/mechanical failure risk) solution? specific polymers like hdpe (high-density polyethylene) offer chemical resistance and toughness. 3.1.2 classification (origin) 1 hour lesson 5: origins & structural design classification by origin natural materials: sourced from nature. examples: timber, cotton, wool, leather. synthetic materials: man-made. examples: polymers, alloys, glass. deep dive: structural mechanics in engineering and industrial design, the magic happens in how structures manage internal stresses (tension, compression, and torsion) and how they fail. here is a deeper look into the four categories. 1. frame structures (skeleton-like) a network of thin components (members) that support the load. strength lies in geometry, not mass. the mechanics: deals primarily with bending and buckling. triangles (trusses) are used for inherent rigidity. engineering context: loads redistribute if a member fails. (e.g., a crane doesn't collapse if one brace bends). industrial: steel skyscrapers (curtain wall is skin, not support). nature: spiderwebs (tension-only frame). product design: laptop internal magnesium chassis. 2. shell structures (thin-skinned) thin, often curved outer layers distribute loads across the entire surface. acts as both "skin" and "support." the mechanics: membrane stress. loads on curves convert to compressive forces traveling to the base. the weakness: stiff but brittle. cracks/dents significantly reduce load capacity. industrial: pressure vessels, airplane fuselages (monocoque). nature: tortoise shell, coconut. product design: plastic milk jug (liquid inside prevents buckling). 3. solid structures (mass-based) rely on sheer weight and volume to resist forces. usually held together by gravity. the mechanics: designed for compression. poor at handling tension. design intent: "set and forget" durability or when material is cheap. industrial: great pyramids, dams, heavy machine tool bases. nature: mountains, thick tree trunks. product design: cast-iron skillet, marble countertop. 4. combination structures "form follows function." different parts have different mechanical needs. the mechanics: integrated design. frame for heavy lifting, shell for ergonomics/protection. deep context: modern cars use a unibody (pillars = frame, floorpan = shell). house: wooden frame + drywall shell + concrete solid foundation. umbrella: foldable frame (ribs) + fabric shell (canopy). bridge: solid towers + steel truss frame + cable tension system. quick comparison reference structure type main strength main weakness design goal frame lightweight / modular complex joints efficiency shell high surface area protection buckling/denting weight reduction solid extreme durability massive material use stability combination versatility high manufacturing cost performance design challenge (10 mins) task: sketch a chair design using only a frame structure. then, sketch a second chair using only a shell structure. 3.1.7 composites 1 hour lesson 6: strength in numbers (composites) what is a composite? definition: a matrix (glue/binder) + a reinforcement (fiber/particle). common examples: reinforced concrete (steel + concrete), carbon fiber (epoxy + carbon strands), grp (glass reinforced plastic). why use them? we combine materials to get the "best of both worlds." concrete is good in compression, but bad in tension. steel is good in tension. reinforced concrete handles both forces well. case study: the boeing 787 dreamliner this was the first major airliner to use 50% composite materials. benefits: lighter (fuel efficiency), no corrosion (unlike aluminum), allows for higher cabin pressure (better passenger comfort). drawbacks: difficult to repair; lightning strike management requires extra engineering (copper mesh). activity: "composite analysis" task: examine a skateboard deck or a snowboard. why do they layer wood with fiberglass? what property does each layer provide? composite materials reference data composite material young's modulus (e) tensile strength (σ) context common applications 1. reinforced concrete 25−35 gpa 2−5 mpa* by far the most widely used man-made composite on earth. cement matrix + aggregate (sand/gravel). reinforced with steel rebar for tensile loads. foundations, bridges, skyscrapers, dams. 2. fiberglass (gfrp) 20−45 gpa 200−600 mpa glass fiber reinforced polymer. fine glass fibers embedded in plastic resin (polyester/epoxy). lightweight, corrosion-resistant, cheap. boat hulls, wind turbine blades, storage tanks. 3. carbon fiber (cfrp) 50−150 gpa 600−1,500 mpa the "gold standard". carbon fibers for extreme rigidity and tensile strength. lighter than aluminum, stronger than steel. aerospace structures, f1 cars, high-end sports gear. 4. plywood 8−12 gpa 30−60 mpa classic "engineered wood". thin veneer layers glued with grain perpendicular to the next. "cross-graining" prevents splitting/warping. formwork, furniture, cabinetry, structural flooring. 5. kevlar (aramid) 30−80 gpa 400−1,400 mpa aramid fibers known for heat resistance and energy absorption. woven into sheets with resins. virtually puncture-proof. body armor, radial tires, mooring lines. 6. metal matrix (mmc) 90−120 gpa 400−600 mpa metal matrix (aluminum/magnesium) reinforced with ceramic/carbon fibers. higher stiffness, better extreme temp performance. jet engine parts, automotive pistons, tank armor. 7. ceramic matrix (cmc) 200−300 gpa 200−400 mpa ceramic fibers in ceramic matrix. resists "crack propagation" unlike brittle standard ceramics. tough against thermal shock. space shuttle tiles, gas turbines, brake discs. 8. wood-plastic (wpc) 3−6 gpa 15−35 mpa mix of wood flour/fiber and thermoplastics (pe/pvc). aesthetic of wood, durability of plastic. outdoor decking, railings, landscaping timber. 9. engineered bamboo 15−20 gpa 120−160 mpa sustainable. bamboo fibers/strands bonded with resins. outperforms traditional hardwoods in hardness/stability. sustainable architecture, flooring, furniture. 10. honeycomb panel 70 gpa* 200−300 mpa* structural composite. honeycomb core (aluminum/nomex) sandwiched between two skins. highest stiffness-to-weight ratio. aircraft bulkheads, satellites, transit interiors. * note: values are approximate and depend heavily on the specific grade and manufacturing process. 3.1.8 smart materials 1 hour lesson 7: the future (smart materials) smart materials are often called "responsive materials." unlike traditional materials that are static, these have properties that can be significantly changed in a controlled fashion by external stimuli (like stress, temperature, or light). 1. piezoelectricity the stimulus: mechanical stress (pressure) or electrical voltage. how it works: when you deform a piezoelectric crystal (squeeze it), it generates an electric charge. conversely, if you apply electricity to it, the material changes shape (vibrates). context: used for sensing and ultra-precise movement. sensors: airbag sensors in cars (detecting the impact force). actuators: high-end speakers and inkjet printer heads that need to move tiny amounts. energy harvesting: floor tiles in busy train stations that generate electricity from footsteps. 2. shape memory alloys (sma) the stimulus: heat (temperature change). how it works: these materials (usually nitinol—a nickel-titanium alloy) can be "programmed" to remember a specific shape. if you bend them out of shape while cold, they will instantly return to their original "remembered" shape when heated. context: eliminates the need for bulky mechanical motors or levers. medical: stents for clogged arteries (expand to shape at body temp). aerospace: flaps on wings that move without heavy hydraulic systems. frames: "unbreakable" glasses frames that pop back into shape. 3. photochromicity the stimulus: light (specifically uv radiation). how it works: a material changes its optical properties (transparency or color) when exposed to light. when the light source is removed, the material returns to its original state. context: used for light management and uv protection. transition lenses: glasses that turn into sunglasses when you step outside. smart windows: buildings that darken their glass automatically in bright sunlight to reduce cooling costs. 4. magneto-rheostatic (mr) & electro-rheostatic (er) the stimulus: magnetic fields (mr) or electric fields (er). how it works: typically fluids containing tiny particles. when a field is applied, particles align instantly, changing the fluid into a near-solid or very thick "grease." context: used for instant, "real-time" damping and shock absorption. mr fluids: high-end car suspension (audi/ferrari). adjusts from "soft" to "sport" in milliseconds. er fluids: industrial valves or clutches that engage/disengage instantly without mechanical wear. 5. thermoelectricity the stimulus: temperature difference (δt). how it works: (seebeck effect) a temperature difference between two conductors creates voltage. (peltier effect) apply electricity, and one side gets hot while the other gets cold. context: converting "waste heat" into useful energy or cooling without moving parts. thermoelectric generators (tegs): powering remote sensors using heat from a pipe or engine. solid-state cooling: portable 12v camping fridges (no compressor/coolant gas). summary checklist for selection smart material stimulus reaction key dt benefit piezoelectric pressure electricity sensing & precision sma (nitinol) heat shape change no motors needed photochromic uv light color change light/heat control mr / er fluids mag/elec field viscosity change instant dampening thermoelectric temp gradient electricity waste heat recovery 3.1.9 biodegradable materials unit review 1 hour lesson 8: biomaterials & the circular economy 1. defining biodegradability definition: a material's ability to be broken down by microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, or algae) into natural substances like water, co 2 , and biomass, without leaving toxic residue. the stimulus: moisture, heat, and oxygen. the timeline: to be truly "biodegradable" in a design context, it should break down within a reasonable timeframe (months to years), rather than centuries. 2. biomaterials in the circular economy a. designing out waste traditional designers used a "linear economy" (take → make → dispose). modern dt designers use biomaterials to ensure that the "dispose" phase actually feeds the next "make" phase. case study: instead of using expanded polystyrene (eps) for packaging—which lasts 500 years—designers use mycelium (mushroom roots). once the customer receives their package, they can break the mycelium down and put it in their garden as fertilizer. b. renewable feedstocks biomaterials are often bio-based, meaning they are made from renewable resources like corn starch, sugarcane, or cellulose. this reduces the reliance on finite resources like crude oil. 3. key biodegradable materials for dt 1. pla (polylactic acid) source: fermented plant starch (corn, sugarcane). circular benefit: can be melted and reshaped (recycling) or industrially composted. app: 3d printing filaments, food containers. 2. mycelium (mushroom roots) source: fungi roots grown on agricultural waste. circular benefit: "grows" into shape with low energy. 100% home-compostable replacement for styrofoam. app: protective packaging (dell/ikea), fashion leather. 3. pha (polyhydroxyalkanoate) source: bacterial fermentation of sugar/lipids. circular benefit: marine-biodegradable. breaks down in ocean water (unlike pla). app: agricultural mulch films, medical staples. 4. algae-based bioplastics source: seaweed and algae. circular benefit: carbon-negative (absorbs co 2 ). grows fast without land/freshwater. app: edible water sachets (ooho), dissolvable pods. 5. chitosan (chitin) source: shells of crustaceans (shrimp, crabs). circular benefit: turns waste into high-value material. natural antimicrobial properties. app: biodegradable cling film, wound dressings. 6. bacterial cellulose source: bacteria grown in tea/sugar mixture. circular benefit: grown to exact pattern shape (zero-waste manufacturing). app: sustainable "vegan leather" jackets/shoes. 7. hempcrete source: hemp inner hurd mixed with lime. circular benefit: carbon-sequestering. can be crushed into soil conditioner at end-of-life. app: non-load-bearing insulation walls. 8. bagasse (sugarcane fiber) source: fibrous residue from crushed sugarcane. circular benefit: uses waste residue. highly compostable, low energy processing. app: takeaway containers, heat-resistant plates. exam practice time: 25 mins 15 marks total exam preparation & practice test your knowledge with these ib-style questions. attempt the question first, then reveal the markscheme to check your understanding. section a: multiple choice (3 marks) 1. which mechanical property describes a material's ability to undergo permanent deformation without fracturing? elasticity plasticity stiffness density reveal answer correct answer: b (plasticity) 2. a designer is selecting a material for a kitchen spatula. which combination of properties is most critical? high thermal conductivity and high plasticity. high electrical conductivity and high toughness. low thermal conductivity and high non-reactivity (food safety). low density and high magnetism. reveal answer correct answer: c (low thermal conductivity prevents burns; high non-reactivity ensures food safety). 3. which of the following best describes a "smart material"? a material that is composed of two or more distinct substances. a material that breaks down naturally in the environment. a material derived strictly from natural sources. a material with properties that change significantly in response to external stimuli. reveal answer correct answer: d (properties change in response to stimuli like heat, light, or electricity). section b: short answer (4 marks) 4. distinguish between 'ductility' and 'malleability'. (2 marks) reveal markscheme award [1] for defining ductility as the ability of a material to be drawn into a wire (under tension). award [1] for defining malleability as the ability of a material to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets (under compression). 5. define the term 'composite material' and state one advantage of using a composite over a pure metal in the aerospace industry. (2 marks) reveal markscheme award [1] for defining a composite as a material made from two or more constituent materials with significantly different physical/chemical properties that remain separate within the finished structure. award [1] for one valid advantage, such as: higher strength-to-weight ratio. increased corrosion resistance. ability to tailor properties (anisotropy) to direction of load. quick reference definitions glossary of terms click on a term to reveal its definition. density the mass per unit volume of a material. important for portability and weight constraints (e.g. aerospace). stiffness (young's modulus) the resistance of an elastic body to deformation by an applied force. a stiff material resists bending. toughness the ability of a material to absorb energy and plastically deform without fracturing. (area under the stress-strain curve). composite a material made from two or more constituent materials with significantly different physical or chemical properties that, when combined, produce a material with characteristics different from the individual components. smart material materials that have one or more properties that can be significantly changed in a controlled fashion by external stimuli, such as stress, temperature, moisture, ph, electric or magnetic fields. bio-materials chemical properties circular economy composite material compressive strength corrosion resistance density ductility elasticity electrical resistivity (electrical conductivity) electro-rheostatic flammability hygroscopy glass hardness magneto-rheostatic malleability manufactured material mechanical properties melting point natural materials photochromicity physical properties piezoelectricity plasticity polymer reactivity (food safe) shape memory material smart materials stiffness tensile strength textiles thermal conductivity thermal expansion thermoelectricity timber (lumber) toughness stiffness (young's modulus) composite smart material materials are classified based on their physical, chemical and mechanical properties. materials are classified according to their source or origin. identifying the most suitable material for a product is a complex and challenging task, involving the consideration of physical, chemical and mechanical properties and aesthetic characteristics. physical properties include aspects of a material that can be measured and observed without it changing in any way. chemical properties include aspects of a material that lead to it chemically reacting with another. mechanical properties include aspects of a material affected by the application of a force. composites consist of two or more materials combined to enhance their properties. smart materials are materials that have one or more properties that can be significantly changed in response to changes in their environment. biodegradable materials break down in the environment after disposal or at the end of their useful life.

title: Introduction to structural systems

sections.title: Lesson Overview
sections.html:
Lesson Overview

Overview of Objectives

By the end of this unit, you will be able to recognize structural components, analyze forces, evaluate equilibrium, and apply structural principles to your own product designs.

You will be able to:

  • Recognize that structures are ubiquitous in both natural and human-made environments.
  • Classify structures into frame, shell, solid, and combinations.
  • Identify structural components (various beams and columns) and how they distribute loads.
  • Analyze how static and dynamic forces (compression, tension, torsion, bending, shear) act on structures.
  • Interpret stress-strain graphs and understand the application of materials with different Young's Moduli.
  • Evaluate structural equilibrium, identify weak points (like joints), and apply strengthening techniques (struts, shapes, lamination).
  • Calculate and justify the use of a Safety Factor (SF) in product design.
  • Connect structural principles to Syllabus topics (Ergonomics, Material Selection) and your Internal Assessment (Criterion C).

sections.title: Part 1: The Ubiquity and Classification of Structures
sections.html:
Part 1: The Ubiquity and Classification of Structures

Context & Explanation:

Structures are everywhere. Whether they are natural (like honeycomb cells, spider webs, or the hollow strength of bones) or human-made (like bridges, towers, and furniture), they are designed to support loads, maintain stability, and resist forces.

Classification of Structures

Designers classify structures into three main types:

1. Frame Structures

Made from a network of connected parts (like beams or tubes). They are lightweight but strong in multiple directions (e.g., scaffolding, bicycle frames).

2. Shell Structures

Rely on a thin outer surface to support loads and hold shape. They enclose space efficiently without an internal frame (e.g., eggshells, crash helmets, car bodies).

3. Solid Structures

Made from a solid mass, relying on bulk and weight for strength (e.g., bricks, statues).

Combinations

Most modern products use a combination. A car uses a metal frame, a shell for body panels, and solid tires.

Multimedia Resources

Biomimicry: How Designers Are Learning from Nature (Vox)

National Geographic: How do you cool a building without air conditioning?

Practical Engagement: The "Structure Scavenger Hunt"

Take a 15-minute walk around your school campus or neighborhood. Photograph and classify at least one frame, shell, solid, and combination structure, noting what loads you believe the structure is holding.

sections.title: Part 2: Forces, Loads, and Components
sections.html:
Part 2: Forces, Loads, and Components

Context & Explanation:

Structures fail or succeed based on how they handle loads. Designers must calculate these to prevent collapse.

Loads and Forces

  • Loads: Dead Loads are the permanent weight of the structure itself, while Live Loads are variable weights (people, furniture). Environmental loads include wind and earthquakes.
  • Forces: Static forces are constant and unchanging, whereas Dynamic forces change over time.

Specific Forces Acting on Materials

Force Type Action
CompressionSquashing or shortening.
TensionPulling or stretching.
TorsionTwisting around an axis.
BendingA mix of compression on top and tension on the bottom.
ShearParts sliding past each other in opposite directions.

Structural Components

Columns

Upright pillars designed to carry compressive, vertical loads.

Beams

Horizontal members to handle forces. Types include Simply Supported Beams (resting on two ends), Fixed Beams (rigid at both ends), Cantilevers (supported at one end only, like a diving board), and Continuously Supported Beams.

Multimedia Resource

Understanding Shear Force and Bending Moment Diagrams

Practical Engagement: The Cantilever Challenge

Gather some raw spaghetti and marshmallows (or similar building materials). Challenge yourself to build the longest cantilever beam that extends off the edge of your desk and can hold the weight of a single tea bag. Consider where the tension and compression forces are concentrated in your design.

sections.title: Part 3: Material Behavior & Young’s Modulus
sections.html:
Part 3: Material Behavior & Young’s Modulus

Context & Explanation:

How do we know when a material will stretch, bend, or break? We use a Stress-Strain Graph.

Interpreting the Graph

Young’s Modulus (Elastic Region)

The initial straight slope indicating stiffness. Steeper slope = stiffer material. High Young's Modulus materials (like steel or carbon fiber) are used for rigid support, while low Young's Modulus materials (like rubber or silicone) are used for flexibility and shock absorption.

Yield Strength

The elastic limit. Past this point, the material permanently deforms (plastic deformation).

Ultimate Strength

The maximum stress before weakening or "necking".

Fracture Point

Where the material finally snaps or breaks.

Practical Engagement: The Bend Test

Find three 30cm rulers (or similar flat items) made of different materials like wood, steel, and flexible plastic. Gently apply a bending force to each and rank the materials based on their perceived Young's Modulus (their stiffness).

sections.title: Part 4: Equilibrium, Weak Points, and Strengthening
sections.html:
Part 4: Equilibrium, Weak Points, and Strengthening

Context & Explanation:

A structure is stable when in equilibrium — meaning all vertical forces, horizontal forces, and turning moments equal zero.

Why Do Structures Fail at Joints?

Often, a structure won't fail in the middle of a beam, but at its joints and corners due to:

  • Stress Concentration: Forces gather at sharp corners.
  • Material Discontinuity: Imperfections where two pieces join, like a weld.

Strengthening Techniques

To counteract this, designers use various techniques:

Struts

Members that resist compression and transfer loads.

Shape

Using triangles (trusses) or arches to distribute loads effectively.

Lamination

Bonding multiple layers (like plywood) to reduce weak points.

Composite Materials

Combining materials (like carbon fiber) to maximize strength-to-weight ratios.

Practical Engagement: Triangles vs. Squares

Using craft sticks and split pins (or strips of cardboard and pushpins), build a square frame and push on the corner to see how it collapses (shears). Next, add a single diagonal strut to create two triangles within your frame. Push again to observe how the geometry dramatically improves stability.

sections.title: Part 5: Factor of Safety (SF)
sections.html:
Part 5: Factor of Safety (SF)

Context & Explanation:

Humans will always push the limits of a product! Therefore, designers must include a Factor of Safety (SF).

Formula

Safety Factor = Maximum Load ÷ Working Load

If a beam must hold 2,500 N but is designed to withstand 10,000 N, its SF is 4.

Why use an SF?

Unpredictable loads, material variability (defects), wear/aging, and user misuse. An SF of 1.5 to 2.0 is common for non-critical applications, but essential safety components (like elevators) require 2.5 to 4.0+.

Multimedia Resource: Case Study

Research the "Hyatt Regency walkway collapse" to explore what happens when structural equilibrium and safety factors are miscalculated.

Practical Engagement: Elevator Pitch

Calculate the required maximum load for a new school elevator that is intended to hold 10 people (Working Load = ~750kg). Apply a Safety Factor of 4 and specify the ultimate load capacity the structural cables must be able to withstand.

sections.title: Part 6: The Bigger Picture (Syllabus Links & IA Application)
sections.html:
Part 6: The Bigger Picture (Syllabus Links & IA Application)

Context & Explanation:

Understanding structures isn't just about passing a test; it is fundamentally tied to your personal design projects.

Syllabus Connections

Columns vs. Beams

Remember that while beams handle horizontal loads (bending/shear), columns are upright pillars specifically designed to carry compressive, vertical loads.

Internal Assessment (IA) Alignment

When you reach Criterion C (Ideation and Modelling) of your IA, you must evaluate the feasibility of your redesigns. If you design a chair, can the legs (columns) handle the compressive load? Will the seat (beam) bend under a dynamic force?

Ergonomics (A1.1)

How does the structural rigidity or flexibility of a product affect user comfort?

Material Selection (B3.1)

How does a material's Young's Modulus dictate its structural application?

Life-Cycle Analysis (C3.2)

Applying a massive Safety Factor might make a product safer, but it also means using more raw materials. How does over-engineering impact a product's environmental footprint?

Practical Engagement: The IA Structural Audit

Take out a sketch or prototype from one of your past or current design projects. Annotate it using the vocabulary from this unit: identify the structural type (frame, shell, solid), locate areas of high tension or compression, and estimate where the structure might fail (fracture point) without proper strengthening techniques.

sections.title: Exam Practice Session
sections.html:
Exam Practice Session

Test your knowledge with these typical exam questions for Topic A 3.2.

Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ)

1. Which of the following best describes a shell structure?

A) A structure made from a network of connected beams and rods.
B) A structure made from a solid mass of material relying on weight for strength.
C) A 3D hollow structure with a relatively small wall thickness compared to its overall size.
D) A beam resting on more than two supports along its length.

2. On a stress-strain graph, what does the yield strength represent?

A) The maximum stress a material can withstand before breaking.
B) The exact point where the material breaks into two pieces.
C) The initial slope indicating the stiffness of the material.
D) The maximum amount of stress a material can withstand before undergoing permanent plastic deformation.

Short Answer Questions (SAQ)

1. Differentiate between static forces and dynamic forces acting on a structure. (2 marks)

Reveal Answer

Static forces are constant and unchanging over time, such as the dead weight of a building's roof.

Dynamic forces are changing or moving forces that vary in size or direction, such as wind pushing against a skyscraper or moving vehicles on a bridge.

2. Outline why joints and corners are often the weakest points in a structure. (2 marks)

Reveal Answer

Joints and corners suffer from stress concentration, where forces like tension and compression gather at sharp corners.

They also suffer from material discontinuity, as slight imperfections or differing material alignments at a weld or connection can weaken the overall strength.

Long Answer Questions (LAQ)

1. Explain, using an example, how a designer might use a combination of frame, shell, and solid structures to optimize a product. (4 marks)

Reveal Mark Scheme
  • Identify that combinations are used to achieve specific goals like strength, weight reduction, and functionality. Provide an example, such as a modern car.
  • Explain the frame aspect: The car utilizes a metal frame (chassis) which provides lightweight, multi-directional structural integrity to support the engine and passengers.
  • Explain the shell aspect: It uses curved outer body panels (shell structure) to distribute aerodynamic forces evenly without needing heavy internal frames.
  • Explain the solid aspect: Solid structures (rubber tires) rely on bulk material to bear the compressive load of the car against the road.

2. Discuss the importance of incorporating a Safety Factor (SF) in structural design, providing the formula and two specific reasons why it is necessary. (6 marks)

Reveal Mark Scheme
  • Formula: Safety Factor = Maximum Load / Working Load.
  • Basic Premise: An SF ensures the structure is significantly stronger than the required functional load, protecting users from harm.
  • Reason 1 (Unpredictable Loads/Misuse): Humans often overload products or use them in unintended ways. An SF protects against this dynamic variable.
  • Reason 2 (Material Degradation/Variability): Materials can weaken over time due to wear, fatigue, or corrosion, and manufacturing processes can have defects, meaning a material's true strength might be slightly lower than its theoretical strength.

sections.title: Topic A 3.2 Glossary
sections.html:
Topic A 3.2 Glossary

Click on any term to reveal its IB Design Technology definition.

Bending force / moment

A load applied to a material a certain distance from one of its fixed positions that causes it to bend. Bending Moment (M) = Force (F) × Distance (d).

Built environment

The collective name for constructed structures, features and facilities where people live and work.

Cantilever beam

A rigid structure that is fixed on one end and extends horizontally without support on the other.

Column

An upright pillar typically used to support beams in structures.

Composite material

A material comprised of two or more materials to improve their physical, mechanical and chemical properties and/or aesthetics characteristics.

Compression (force)

A force that squeezes or causes a material to shorten.

Continuously supported beam

A beam that is supported at more than two points along its length.

Dynamic force

Moving forces exerted on structures. Such forces may be produced by the wind, vehicles, etc.

Equilibrium (force)

A state of balance. When a system is subject to equal but opposite forces.

Fixed beam

A member in a structure that is fixed on both ends to supports.

Fracture point

The point at which a material breaks due to stress, permanently deforming.

Frame structure

Any structure comprised of beams and columns that can support its own weight without an outer shell.

Lamination

Covering the surface of a material with a thin sheet of another material using adhesion for protection, preservation, durability, rigidity and stiffness or aesthetic reasons.

Safety factor (SF)

The ratio of how much load a structure can bear compared to its normal expected load.

Shear force

Two opposite and equal forces that act on an object but are not aligned. A cutting force.

Shell structure

A 3D hollow structure with a relatively small wall thickness compared to its overall size.

Simply supported beams

A beam that is supported at either end.

Solid structure

A structure with few, or no, open spaces inside it. Solid structures resist a change in shape when subjected to a load.

Static force

Stationary forces acting on a structure. Such forces include a structure’s own weight, the load it carries.

Strain

The response of a material due to stress, defined as the change in length divided by the original length.

Stress

A force on a material divided by the cross-sectional area of that material.

Strut

A beam forming part of a framework designed to resist compression and support other beams.

Tension (force)

A pulling or stretching force.

Torsion (force)

A twisting force.

Ultimate strength

The maximum stress a material can withstand before breaking.

Yield strength

The maximum amount of stress a material can withstand before undergoing plastic deformation.

Young’s Modulus

A measure of the stiffness of an elastic material, defined by stress or strain.

syllabus.title: Introduction to structural systems
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How are structures present in everyday products?

statements.text: Structures are ubiquitous in nature and the built environment.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to analyse and interpret a variety of human-made and natural structures.

statements.text: Structures can be classified in different ways.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss frame, shell and solid structures, and how they are used in the design of products.

statements.text: Structures are often comprised of multiple parts.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify simply supported beams, fixed beams, cantilever beams, continuously supported beams, and columns, and explain their function.

statements.text: Static and dynamic forces can be identified according to how they act on a structure.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how compression, tension, torsion, bending and shear forces act within a structure, and differentiate between static and dynamic forces.

statements.text: In structures, it is important to know how and when an object or material will stretch, bend or break.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe the relationship between stress and strain on a material under stress, and be able to outline Young’s Modulus, yield strength, ultimate strength and fracture in the context of a stress-strain graph.

statements.text: Materials with differing Young’s Modulus are chosen for specific applications.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to compare materials with a high Young’s Modulus and those with a low Young’s Modulus in terms of how they react when placed under stress, and explain why this is important when designing structures.

statements.text: When forces on a structure are in equilibrium, the structure is stable.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe when a structure is in equilibrium and identify the conditions where a structure will fail (not in equilibrium).

statements.text: The overall design of a structure can be improved by applying strengthening techniques.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how structures can be strengthened by using struts, shape, lamination and composite materials.

statements.text: Structures are typically designed with a safety factor (SF) in case of overloading.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to define an SF as a ratio of a structure’s absolute strength to the allowable load, and explain why structures are designed to include an SF.

statements.text: Structures are typically designed to withstand higher loads than required.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline what an SF of 1 means for a structure, and explain why most structures have an SF above 1.

activity.title: The paper beam laboratory
activity.materials: Paper strips, books, small masses, ruler
steps: Bridge a fixed gap with a flat paper strip. Add small equal loads and measure deflection.
Fold a second strip into a channel using the same material quantity and repeat.
Draw load and reaction arrows; identify likely tension, compression and bending regions.
Compare results and control span, loading position and material quantity.
activity.debrief: Why can a change in section improve performance without changing material?

exam.question: Explain how increasing a beam’s depth can reduce deflection. [2]
exam.answer: More material is distributed farther from the neutral axis, increasing the second moment of area and resistance to bending for the same material and span.

loads are variable weights (people, furniture). environmental loads include wind and earthquakes. forces: static forces are constant and unchanging, whereas dynamic forces change over time. specific forces acting on materials force type action compression squashing or shortening. tension pulling or stretching. torsion twisting around an axis. bending a mix of compression on top and tension on the bottom. shear parts sliding past each other in opposite directions. structural components columns upright pillars designed to carry compressive, vertical loads. beams horizontal members to handle forces. types include simply supported beams (resting on two ends), fixed beams (rigid at both ends), cantilevers (supported at one end only, like a diving board), and continuously supported beams . multimedia resource understanding shear force and bending moment diagrams practical engagement: the cantilever challenge gather some raw spaghetti and marshmallows (or similar building materials). challenge yourself to build the longest cantilever beam that extends off the edge of your desk and can hold the weight of a single tea bag. consider where the tension and compression forces are concentrated in your design. part 3: material behavior & young’s modulus context & explanation: how do we know when a material will stretch, bend, or break? we use a stress-strain graph . interpreting the graph young’s modulus (elastic region) the initial straight slope indicating stiffness. steeper slope = stiffer material. high young's modulus materials (like steel or carbon fiber) are used for rigid support, while low young's modulus materials (like rubber or silicone) are used for flexibility and shock absorption. yield strength the elastic limit. past this point, the material permanently deforms (plastic deformation). ultimate strength the maximum stress before weakening or "necking". fracture point where the material finally snaps or breaks. practical engagement: the bend test find three 30cm rulers (or similar flat items) made of different materials like wood, steel, and flexible plastic. gently apply a bending force to each and rank the materials based on their perceived young's modulus (their stiffness). part 4: equilibrium, weak points, and strengthening context & explanation: a structure is stable when in equilibrium — meaning all vertical forces, horizontal forces, and turning moments equal zero. why do structures fail at joints? often, a structure won't fail in the middle of a beam, but at its joints and corners due to: stress concentration: forces gather at sharp corners. material discontinuity: imperfections where two pieces join, like a weld. strengthening techniques to counteract this, designers use various techniques: struts members that resist compression and transfer loads. shape using triangles (trusses) or arches to distribute loads effectively. lamination bonding multiple layers (like plywood) to reduce weak points. composite materials combining materials (like carbon fiber) to maximize strength-to-weight ratios. practical engagement: triangles vs. squares using craft sticks and split pins (or strips of cardboard and pushpins), build a square frame and push on the corner to see how it collapses (shears). next, add a single diagonal strut to create two triangles within your frame. push again to observe how the geometry dramatically improves stability. part 5: factor of safety (sf) context & explanation: humans will always push the limits of a product! therefore, designers must include a factor of safety (sf) . formula safety factor = maximum load ÷ working load if a beam must hold 2,500 n but is designed to withstand 10,000 n, its sf is 4. why use an sf? unpredictable loads, material variability (defects), wear/aging, and user misuse. an sf of 1.5 to 2.0 is common for non-critical applications, but essential safety components (like elevators) require 2.5 to 4.0+. multimedia resource: case study research the "hyatt regency walkway collapse" to explore what happens when structural equilibrium and safety factors are miscalculated. practical engagement: elevator pitch calculate the required maximum load for a new school elevator that is intended to hold 10 people (working load = ~750kg). apply a safety factor of 4 and specify the ultimate load capacity the structural cables must be able to withstand. part 6: the bigger picture (syllabus links & ia application) context & explanation: understanding structures isn't just about passing a test; it is fundamentally tied to your personal design projects. syllabus connections columns vs. beams remember that while beams handle horizontal loads (bending/shear), columns are upright pillars specifically designed to carry compressive, vertical loads. internal assessment (ia) alignment when you reach criterion c (ideation and modelling) of your ia, you must evaluate the feasibility of your redesigns. if you design a chair, can the legs (columns) handle the compressive load? will the seat (beam) bend under a dynamic force? ergonomics (a1.1) how does the structural rigidity or flexibility of a product affect user comfort? material selection (b3.1) how does a material's young's modulus dictate its structural application? life-cycle analysis (c3.2) applying a massive safety factor might make a product safer, but it also means using more raw materials. how does over-engineering impact a product's environmental footprint? practical engagement: the ia structural audit take out a sketch or prototype from one of your past or current design projects. annotate it using the vocabulary from this unit: identify the structural type (frame, shell, solid), locate areas of high tension or compression, and estimate where the structure might fail (fracture point) without proper strengthening techniques. exam practice session test your knowledge with these typical exam questions for topic a 3.2. multiple choice questions (mcq) 1. which of the following best describes a shell structure? a) a structure made from a network of connected beams and rods. b) a structure made from a solid mass of material relying on weight for strength. c) a 3d hollow structure with a relatively small wall thickness compared to its overall size. d) a beam resting on more than two supports along its length. 2. on a stress-strain graph, what does the yield strength represent? a) the maximum stress a material can withstand before breaking. b) the exact point where the material breaks into two pieces. c) the initial slope indicating the stiffness of the material. d) the maximum amount of stress a material can withstand before undergoing permanent plastic deformation. short answer questions (saq) 1. differentiate between static forces and dynamic forces acting on a structure. (2 marks) reveal answer static forces are constant and unchanging over time, such as the dead weight of a building's roof. dynamic forces are changing or moving forces that vary in size or direction, such as wind pushing against a skyscraper or moving vehicles on a bridge. 2. outline why joints and corners are often the weakest points in a structure. (2 marks) reveal answer joints and corners suffer from stress concentration , where forces like tension and compression gather at sharp corners. they also suffer from material discontinuity , as slight imperfections or differing material alignments at a weld or connection can weaken the overall strength. long answer questions (laq) 1. explain, using an example, how a designer might use a combination of frame, shell, and solid structures to optimize a product. (4 marks) reveal mark scheme identify that combinations are used to achieve specific goals like strength, weight reduction, and functionality. provide an example, such as a modern car. explain the frame aspect: the car utilizes a metal frame (chassis) which provides lightweight, multi-directional structural integrity to support the engine and passengers. explain the shell aspect: it uses curved outer body panels (shell structure) to distribute aerodynamic forces evenly without needing heavy internal frames. explain the solid aspect: solid structures (rubber tires) rely on bulk material to bear the compressive load of the car against the road. 2. discuss the importance of incorporating a safety factor (sf) in structural design, providing the formula and two specific reasons why it is necessary. (6 marks) reveal mark scheme formula: safety factor = maximum load / working load. basic premise: an sf ensures the structure is significantly stronger than the required functional load, protecting users from harm. reason 1 (unpredictable loads/misuse): humans often overload products or use them in unintended ways. an sf protects against this dynamic variable. reason 2 (material degradation/variability): materials can weaken over time due to wear, fatigue, or corrosion, and manufacturing processes can have defects, meaning a material's true strength might be slightly lower than its theoretical strength. topic a 3.2 glossary click on any term to reveal its ib design technology definition. bending force / moment a load applied to a material a certain distance from one of its fixed positions that causes it to bend. bending moment (m) = force (f) × distance (d). built environment the collective name for constructed structures, features and facilities where people live and work. cantilever beam a rigid structure that is fixed on one end and extends horizontally without support on the other. column an upright pillar typically used to support beams in structures. composite material a material comprised of two or more materials to improve their physical, mechanical and chemical properties and/or aesthetics characteristics. compression (force) a force that squeezes or causes a material to shorten. continuously supported beam a beam that is supported at more than two points along its length. dynamic force moving forces exerted on structures. such forces may be produced by the wind, vehicles, etc. equilibrium (force) a state of balance. when a system is subject to equal but opposite forces. fixed beam a member in a structure that is fixed on both ends to supports. fracture point the point at which a material breaks due to stress, permanently deforming. frame structure any structure comprised of beams and columns that can support its own weight without an outer shell. lamination covering the surface of a material with a thin sheet of another material using adhesion for protection, preservation, durability, rigidity and stiffness or aesthetic reasons. safety factor (sf) the ratio of how much load a structure can bear compared to its normal expected load. shear force two opposite and equal forces that act on an object but are not aligned. a cutting force. shell structure a 3d hollow structure with a relatively small wall thickness compared to its overall size. simply supported beams a beam that is supported at either end. solid structure a structure with few, or no, open spaces inside it. solid structures resist a change in shape when subjected to a load. static force stationary forces acting on a structure. such forces include a structure’s own weight, the load it carries. strain the response of a material due to stress, defined as the change in length divided by the original length. stress a force on a material divided by the cross-sectional area of that material. strut a beam forming part of a framework designed to resist compression and support other beams. tension (force) a pulling or stretching force. torsion (force) a twisting force. ultimate strength the maximum stress a material can withstand before breaking. yield strength the maximum amount of stress a material can withstand before undergoing plastic deformation. young’s modulus a measure of the stiffness of an elastic material, defined by stress or strain. bending force built environment cantilever beam compression (force) column composite material continuously supported beam dynamic force equilibrium (force) fixed beam forces fracture point frame structure lamination safety factor (sf) shear force shell structure simply supported beams solid structure static force strain strut stress stress-strain graph tension (force) torsion (force) ubiquitous ultimate strength yield strength young’s modulus bending force / moment structures are ubiquitous in nature and the built environment. structures can be classified in different ways. structures are often comprised of multiple parts. static and dynamic forces can be identified according to how they act on a structure. in structures, it is important to know how and when an object or material will stretch, bend or break. materials with differing young’s modulus are chosen for specific applications. when forces on a structure are in equilibrium, the structure is stable. the overall design of a structure can be improved by applying strengthening techniques. structures are typically designed with a safety factor (sf) in case of overloading. structures are typically designed to withstand higher loads than required.

A3.3.1 Types of Motion A3.3.2 Input–Process–Output A3.3.3 Mechanical Advantage ~120 min

Lesson 1: Motion, Input–Process–Output & Mechanical Advantage

Every mechanical system, however complex, is built from the same underlying ideas: a type of motion, a chain of input–process–output, and a trade-off between the force a user applies and the force a system delivers. This lesson establishes that shared vocabulary so it can be applied to every mechanism studied for the rest of the unit.

Hook: Mechanisms Hiding in Plain Sight

Look around the room right now. A door hinge, a stapler, a pair of scissors, a window blind, a swivel chair — every one of them relies on a mechanism most people never consciously notice. Before any theory is introduced, list five mechanical products within arm's reach and, for each, guess what type of motion goes in and what type comes out. Keep your list — you will revisit it at the end of this lesson.

1. Types of Motion

Designers must identify four basic types of mechanical motion in order to design efficient systems.

1. Linear Motion

Definition: Movement of an object in a straight line, with every point on the object travelling the same distance in the same direction.

Context: A train moving along a straight section of track — the whole carriage travels the same distance in the same direction at once.

Materials/Examples: Conveyor belts, elevator cars, drawer slides, sliding doors.

Application: Used wherever a product must move an object or user directly from one point to another without changing direction.

2. Rotary Motion

Definition: Circular motion of an object around a fixed central point or axis.

Context: A spinning wheel turns continuously around its axle, with every point on the rim tracing a full circle.

Materials/Examples: Motor shafts, wheels, gears, drill bits.

Application: The most common output of motors and engines, and the starting point for most gear, belt and cam systems.

3. Oscillating Motion

Definition: Back-and-forth movement in an arc about a central point.

Context: A swinging pendulum, or a child's playground swing, sweeps repeatedly through the same arc.

Materials/Examples: Metronomes, windscreen wipers, wrecking balls.

Application: Chosen when a product needs to repeatedly sweep across an area, such as clearing a windscreen.

4. Reciprocating Motion

Definition: Linear, repetitive back-and-forth motion.

Context: A piston inside an engine, or the needle of a sewing machine, repeatedly moves up and down (or in and out) along the same straight line.

Materials/Examples: Engine pistons, jigsaw blades, hand saws.

Application: Chosen whenever a system needs to repeatedly cut, punch, or drive something along a fixed line.

Activity: Mechanical Motion Matching Challenge

Identify the primary type of motion (Linear, Rotary, Oscillating, or Reciprocating) for each real-world object below.

  1. Windshield wiper sweeping across a car's glass
  2. Elevator car travelling from floor 1 to floor 10
  3. Hand saw cutting back and forth through timber
  4. Ferris wheel turning at a carnival
  5. Pneumatic jackhammer chisel breaking up concrete
  6. Wrecking ball swinging into a wall
  7. Conveyor belt moving boxes straight down an assembly line
  8. Ceiling fan blades spinning on high speed
Reveal Answers
  1. Oscillating — the wiper sweeps back and forth through the same arc.
  2. Linear — the car travels a straight vertical path.
  3. Reciprocating — the blade repeats a straight back-and-forth cutting stroke.
  4. Rotary — the wheel turns fully around its central axle.
  5. Reciprocating — the chisel repeatedly strikes along a straight line.
  6. Oscillating — the ball swings through an arc about its suspension point.
  7. Linear — boxes move in a single straight direction.
  8. Rotary — the blades spin around a central axis.

2. Input–Process–Output Model

Mechanical systems are designed to convert an initial input into a desired output through a specific process.

1. Input

Definition: The initial energy or force applied to a system.

Context: Turning a handle or pressing a pedal supplies the energy that the rest of the system will act upon.

Materials/Examples: A rider's push on a pedal, a hand-crank, a motor shaft.

Application: Always the starting point of the chain — every mechanism needs an initial force or motion to work with.

2. Process

Definition: The mechanism of components (gears, cams, levers) that manipulate the input energy.

Context: A bicycle's chain transmits motion from the pedals to the rear sprocket, changing speed and torque along the way.

Materials/Examples: Chains, gear trains, cams, levers, linkages.

Application: This is where a designer's choice of mechanism determines how the input is transformed — changing its speed, direction, or force.

3. Output

Definition: The resulting action the system is designed to produce.

Context: Rotating a wheel, lifting a load, or the rear wheel of a bicycle rotating to move it forward.

Materials/Examples: A rotating wheel, a lifted load, a cut piece of material.

Application: The output is judged against the product's specification — if it fails to deliver the intended action, the process stage must be redesigned.

Activity: Input–Process–Output Breakdown Challenge

Deconstruct each of the four everyday mechanical systems below into its Input, Process, and Output.

  1. Manual Hand-Crank Pencil Sharpener
  2. Bicycle Cable Brakes
  3. Hand-Operated Water Well Pump
  4. Winged Corkscrew (Lever Corkscrew)
Reveal Answer Key

1. Manual Hand-Crank Pencil Sharpener
Input: Rotational force applied by turning the hand crank.
Process: Internal gears turn cylindrical cutting blades around the pencil tip.
Output: Wood and graphite shaved away to create a sharp point.

2. Bicycle Cable Brakes
Input: Squeezing force applied by the rider's hand on the brake lever.
Process: Cable tension pulls two caliper arms inward against a spring.
Output: Friction rubber pads press against the wheel rim, slowing or stopping the bike.

3. Hand-Operated Water Well Pump
Input: Downward force applied by pushing down on the pump handle lever.
Process: The lever lifts a piston rod within a cylinder, opening and closing internal valves to create suction.
Output: Water drawn up from below ground and discharged through the spout.

4. Winged Corkscrew
Input: Downward force applied by pushing down the two raised side levers.
Process: Interlocking gear teeth (rack and pinion) on the levers pull the central shaft straight up.
Output: The cork extracted vertically out of the bottle neck.

3. Mechanical Advantage (MA)

Mechanical Advantage

Definition: The ratio of output force (load) to input force (effort), allowing a user to apply less force to move a load.

Context: Manual winches use a ratchet and pawl to allow motion in only one direction, providing a high MA to lift heavy boat loads with minimal user effort.

Materials/Examples: Levers, pulleys, gear trains, winches.

Application: Simple systems multiply force or change its direction to make tasks easier and more efficient for the user.

Formula: Mechanical Advantage (MA) = Load ÷ Effort

Activity: Mechanical Advantage Calculation & Application Challenge

Apply the formula MA = Load ÷ Effort and your understanding of mechanical systems to solve these four scenarios.

  1. Calculating MA: A mechanic uses a lever to lift an engine out of a car frame. The engine exerts a load force of 800 N, and the mechanic applies an effort force of 160 N. What is the mechanical advantage of the lever?
  2. Finding Required Effort: A compound pulley system on a crane provides a mechanical advantage of 5. How much effort force must the winch motor exert to lift a 2,500 N steel beam?
  3. Determining Maximum Load: A boat winch has a mechanical advantage of 8. If a person can exert 200 N of effort force on the hand crank, what is the maximum load force the winch can move?
  4. Identifying Components: When using a nutcracker to crack a walnut, identify what acts as the Load and what acts as the Effort.
Reveal Answer Key

1. MA = 5. MA = Load ÷ Effort = 800 N ÷ 160 N = 5.

2. Effort = 500 N. Effort = Load ÷ MA = 2,500 N ÷ 5 = 500 N.

3. Load = 1,600 N. Load = MA × Effort = 8 × 200 N = 1,600 N.

4. Load: the structural resistance of the walnut shell resisting being crushed. Effort: the squeezing force applied by the user's hand on the long handles.

Linear MotionMovement in a straight lineA train on a track
Rotary MotionCircular motion about an axisA spinning wheel
Oscillating MotionBack-and-forth arc about a pointA swinging pendulum
Reciprocating MotionLinear, repetitive back-and-forth motionAn engine piston
Input–Process–OutputA system converts an input into a desired output via a processPedalling (input) → chain (process) → rear wheel turning (output)
Mechanical AdvantageMA = Load ÷ EffortA ratchet winch lifting a boat with minimal effort

Process: Cable tension pulls two caliper arms inward against a spring.
Output: Friction rubber pads press against the wheel rim, slowing or stopping the bike.

3. Hand-Operated Water Well Pump
Input: Downward force applied by pushing down on the pump handle lever.
Process: The lever lifts a piston rod within a cylinder, opening and closing internal valves to create suction.
Output: Water drawn up from below ground and discharged through the spout.

4. Winged Corkscrew
Input: Downward force applied by pushing down the two raised side levers.
Process: Interlocking gear teeth (rack and pinion) on the levers pull the central shaft straight up.
Output: The cork extracted vertically out of the bottle neck.

activities.text: Activity: Mechanical Advantage Calculation & Application Challenge Apply the formula MA = Load ÷ Effort and your understanding of mechanical systems to solve these four scenarios. Calculating MA: A mechanic uses a lever to lift an engine out of a car frame. The engine exerts a load force of 800 N, and the mechanic applies an effort force of 160 N. What is the mechanical advantage of the lever? Finding Required Effort: A compound pulley system on a crane provides a mechanical advantage of 5. How much effort force must the winch motor exert to lift a 2,500 N steel beam? Determining Maximum Load: A boat winch has a mechanical advantage of 8. If a person can exert 200 N of effort force on the hand crank, what is the maximum load force the winch can move? Identifying Components: When using a nutcracker to crack a walnut, identify what acts as the Load and what acts as the Effort. Reveal Answer Key 1. MA = 5. MA = Load ÷ Effort = 800 N ÷ 160 N = 5. 2. Effort = 500 N. Effort = Load ÷ MA = 2,500 N ÷ 5 = 500 N. 3. Load = 1,600 N. Load = MA × Effort = 8 × 200 N = 1,600 N. 4. Load: the structural resistance of the walnut shell resisting being crushed.
