sections.title: Lesson 2: Gear-Driven Systems, Ratios, Torque & Efficiency
sections.html:
A3.3.4 Gear-Driven Systems A3.3.5 Gear Ratios & Torque A3.3.6 Efficiency of Gear Systems ~150 min

Lesson 2: Gear-Driven Systems, Ratios, Torque & Efficiency

Gears consist of rotating toothed wheels that mesh to transmit rotary motion and power between shafts. In any pair of meshing gears, the gear connected to the power source (e.g. a motor, an engine, or a hand crank) is the driver gear, and the gear it turns is the driven gear. This lesson covers the main gear types, then how their size and arrangement can be used to deliberately trade speed for torque — and what that trade costs in efficiency.

1. Types of Gear Systems

1. Spur Gears

Definition: Gears used for parallel shafts, with teeth that project parallel to the gear's axis.

Context: Simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth mesh side-by-side on parallel shafts to transfer motion in a basic gearbox.

Materials/Examples: Basic gearboxes, clocks, hand-cranked machinery.

Application: The simplest and most efficient gear type; the baseline against which other gear types are compared.

2. Bevel Gears

Definition: Gears used for intersecting shafts, typically at a 90° angle.

Context: Hand drills employ bevel gears to transmit power between the intersecting horizontal handle shaft and vertical drill bit shaft.

Materials/Examples: Hand drills, eggbeaters, car differentials.

Application: Chosen whenever power must change direction between shafts that meet at an angle rather than running parallel.

3. Rack and Pinion

Definition: A mechanism that converts rotary motion into linear motion, using a fixed toothed bar (the rack) engaged with a smaller toothed wheel (the pinion).

Context: Car steering systems use a pinion gear on the steering column to drive the rack, converting the driver's rotary input into the linear motion that turns the wheels.

Materials/Examples: Car steering, sliding security gates, some 3D printers.

Application: Used whenever rotary input must be converted directly into a straight-line output.

4. Worm Gear

Definition: A screw-shaped gear providing high torque and low speed; non-reversible (self-locking).

Context: Guitar tuning pegs utilise worm gears to ensure the strings remain under tension without slipping backward.

Materials/Examples: Guitar tuning pegs, boat winches, electric wheelchair tilt mechanisms.

Application: Chosen specifically for its self-locking property, which lets a lifted or tensioned load hold safely in place without a separate brake.

5. Ratchet and Pawl

Definition: A mechanical device that allows motion in one direction only; a spring-loaded pawl fits into the teeth of a toothed ratchet wheel, preventing it from rotating backward while still allowing it to rotate forward.

Context: Manual winches use a ratchet and pawl to allow motion in only one direction, providing a high mechanical advantage to lift heavy boat loads with minimal user effort.

Materials/Examples: Socket wrenches, boat winches, seatbelt retractors.

Application: Chosen whenever a mechanism must build up motion in repeated small strokes without slipping backward between strokes.

6. Idler Gear

Definition: A gear placed between the driving and driven gears to change the rotational direction of the driven gear, or to fill a gap between them, without affecting the overall gear ratio.

Context: On a conveyor line, a driving gear needs to turn a driven gear on a parallel shaft in the same direction, so a middle idler gear is added between them to correct the direction.

Materials/Examples: Timing gear trains, multi-gear drivetrains, bicycle derailleurs.

Application: Used whenever the output direction needs correcting, or extra centre distance needs bridging, without changing the speed or torque relationship between the driver and driven gears.

7. Compound Gear

Definition: Two or more gears fixed to the same shaft, so the output of one gear becomes the input for the next gear in the system, enabling complex speed/torque relationships in a compact space.

Context: The internal mechanism of a mechanical wristwatch uses several compound gear stages to convert the fast rotation of the mainspring into the very slow rotation of the second, minute, and hour hands.

Materials/Examples: Wristwatches, gearboxes, cordless drill gear trains.

Application: Chosen when a single gear pair cannot achieve the needed speed or torque change within the available space, so several smaller ratio changes are stacked in series.

8. Planetary (Epicyclic) Gear

Definition: A compact gear system in which small "planet" gears rotate around a central "sun" gear while both are enclosed within an outer "ring" gear, allowing several teeth to share the load at once.

Context: An automatic car gearbox uses planetary gear sets to shift smoothly between multiple gear ratios without ever disengaging the gears, by locking or releasing different parts of the assembly.

Materials/Examples: Automatic transmissions, bicycle hub gears, cordless drill gearboxes, wind turbine gearboxes.

Application: Chosen when a very high gear ratio or torque multiplication is needed within a small, compact housing, since load is shared across multiple planet gears rather than a single tooth pair.

Activity: Gear-Driven Systems Identification Challenge

Match each scenario below with the correct gear mechanism (Spur Gears, Bevel Gears, Rack and Pinion, Worm Gear, Ratchet and Pawl, Idler Gear, Compound Gear, or Planetary Gear).

  1. Eggbeater Mixer: Turning a handle on a horizontal axle spins beaters mounted on vertical axles at a 90° angle.
  2. Automated Sliding Gate: A motor turns a small circular gear that drives a long, straight toothed bar to slide the gate open.
  3. Heavy Equipment Hoist: A motor turns a threaded screw shaft that drives a gear wheel to lift heavy loads, locking the load safely if power is lost.
  4. Drive Belt Conveyor Line: A driving gear needs to turn a driven gear on a parallel shaft in the same direction, so a middle gear is added between them.
  5. Socket Wrench: A spring-loaded catch engages angled teeth, clicking freely in one direction while applying force in the other.
  6. Multi-Stage Clockwork Mechanism: A watchmaker mounts two gears of different sizes onto the same central axle for a high reduction ratio in a compact case.
  7. Basic Parallel Gearbox: Simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth mesh side-by-side on parallel shafts.
  8. Automatic Car Transmission: A central sun gear, three surrounding planet gears on a rotating carrier, and an outer ring gear work together in a compact housing to provide multiple gear ratios without ever disengaging the gears.
Reveal Answers
  1. Bevel Gears — transmits motion between intersecting shafts, usually at 90°.
  2. Rack and Pinion — converts the rotary motion of the gear into linear motion of the gate.
  3. Worm Gear — provides high torque/speed reduction and is non-reversible to prevent slipping.
  4. Idler Gear — changes output direction back to the original input direction without altering the overall gear ratio.
  5. Ratchet and Pawl — restricts motion to a single direction while allowing slipping in reverse.
  6. Compound Gear — two gears fixed to the same shaft for compact, multi-stage speed/torque adjustments.
  7. Spur Gears — simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth meshing on parallel shafts.
  8. Planetary Gear — a sun, planet, and ring gear share the load between them to provide multiple ratios within a compact space.

2. Gear Size, Ratios and Torque

Module (tooth size): m = Pitch Diameter ÷ Number of Teeth. Because meshing gears share the same module, a gear's diameter is directly proportional to its number of teeth — a large-diameter gear always carries more teeth than a small-diameter gear from the same gear train.

Small Gear (fewer teeth)

Definition: Completes one full rotation faster than a meshing large gear — associated with higher speed.

Context: On a bicycle, the small chainring at the pedals spins the chain quickly for each pedal stroke.

Materials/Examples: Small front chainrings, drill's highest speed setting.

Application: Selected as the driver gear when high output speed is the design priority.

Large Gear (more teeth)

Definition: Completes one full rotation more slowly than a meshing small gear — associated with higher torque.

Context: A bicycle's larger rear sprocket, used in a low ("climbing") gear, turns more slowly but with greater turning force per pedal stroke.

Materials/Examples: Large rear sprockets, a drill's low-speed/high-torque setting.

Application: Selected as the driven gear when high output torque is needed, e.g. climbing a hill or lifting a heavy load.

Gear Ratio (GR): GR = Number of Teeth on Driven Gear ÷ Number of Teeth on Driver Gear  (equivalently, GR = Diameter of Driven Gear ÷ Diameter of Driver Gear, since tooth count is proportional to diameter)
  • A gear ratio greater than 1 (e.g. 4:1) means a small driver gear turns a large driven gear: output speed decreases and output torque increases — useful for climbing hills or lifting heavy loads.
  • A gear ratio less than 1 (e.g. 1:4, sometimes called an "overdrive") means a large driver gear turns a small driven gear: output speed increases and output torque decreases — useful for high-speed travel, such as a bicycle's top gear on a flat road or a drill's highest speed setting.

Watch: an explanation of how gear ratios trade speed for torque, e.g. in a car gearbox — high torque in 1st gear to accelerate from a standstill, and a low-torque/high-speed ratio in top gear for efficient highway cruising.

Torque

Definition: The rotational (turning) equivalent of force — how much a force twists an object around a pivot or shaft. Torque = Force × Perpendicular Distance from the Pivot, measured in newton-metres (Nm).

Context: An electric screwdriver uses a compound gear train to convert the motor's naturally fast, low-torque rotation into the slow, high-torque rotation needed to drive a screw into wood without stalling.

Materials/Examples: Screwdrivers, car gearboxes, bicycle gear systems.

Application: Ignoring friction losses, Input Torque × Input Speed ≈ Output Torque × Output Speed — a gear train cannot create extra power, it can only trade speed for torque, or torque for speed, just as a lever trades effort distance for load force.

Activity: Gear Ratio, Torque and Speed Calculation Challenge

Apply GR = Teeth on Driven Gear ÷ Teeth on Driver Gear to solve these scenarios.

  1. Calculating Gear Ratio: A driver gear has 12 teeth and meshes with a driven gear that has 60 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and will the output speed be faster or slower than the input speed?
  2. Finding Output Speed: A driver gear with 15 teeth rotates at 300 rpm and meshes with a driven gear that has 45 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and what is the resulting output speed of the driven gear?
  3. Selecting a Gear Ratio for Torque: A cordless drill needs to multiply the motor's torque to drive large screws without stalling. Should the designer choose a gear ratio greater than 1 or less than 1? Justify your answer.
  4. Explaining a Trade-off: Using the concept of torque and speed, explain why a bicycle rider shifts to a gear ratio greater than 1 (a "low gear") when climbing a steep hill.
Reveal Answer Key

1. GR = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 (a ratio of 5:1). Because GR > 1, the output speed will be slower than the input speed, and output torque will be higher.

2. GR = 45 ÷ 15 = 3 (a ratio of 3:1). Output speed = 300 rpm ÷ 3 = 100 rpm.

3. Greater than 1. A gear ratio above 1 (small driver turning a large driven gear) reduces output speed while increasing output torque, giving the drill enough turning force to drive the screw without stalling.

4. Shifting to a gear ratio greater than 1 trades speed for torque: the rear wheel turns more slowly for each pedal rotation, but the torque delivered to the wheel increases, giving the rider enough turning force to overcome the extra resistance of the incline with less effort per pedal stroke.

Practical Engagement: The "Gear Ratio Race"

Task: Using sets of spur gears, build a system that either maximises output speed (small gear driving large) or maximises power/torque (large gear driving small).

Outcome: Count the teeth on each gear used and calculate the actual gear ratio achieved. Compare it against the measured change in speed and torque, and explain how altering the gear ratio changed your system's performance and efficiency.

3. Efficiency of Gear Systems

Formula: Efficiency = (Output Energy ÷ Input Energy) × 100%

In gear systems, efficiency is reduced mainly by friction between meshing teeth, heat generated in the lubricant, and losses in the supporting bearings. Gears that roll against each other with minimal sliding (spur, helical, and bevel gears) are highly efficient, typically 96–99% per gear mesh. Worm gears rely on a sliding, screw-like contact rather than rolling contact, so they lose far more energy to friction — efficiencies can range from roughly 20% to 90% depending on the design, even though worm gears are prized for their high torque and self-locking (non-reversible) properties. Efficiency losses also compound in a gear train: if a system uses two gear meshes that are each 90% efficient, the overall efficiency of the train is only 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, or 81% — a key reason designers try to minimise the number of gear meshes in a drivetrain.

Case Study: Efficiency Trade-offs in Practice

Electric vehicles typically use a single-speed helical gear reduction (rather than a multi-speed gearbox) partly because it keeps the drivetrain simple and highly efficient, maximising the vehicle's range from the battery. In contrast, guitar tuning pegs and boat winches deliberately use lower-efficiency worm gears, because the trade-off — the mechanism locking in place and not slipping backward under load — is more valuable than raw efficiency.

Activity: Gear Efficiency Challenge

  1. Calculating Efficiency: An electric screwdriver's motor supplies 12 J of input energy to its gear train. Only 10.2 J is delivered as useful output energy at the screw tip. What is the efficiency of the gear train?
  2. Comparing Gear Types: A designer is choosing between a helical gear set (98% efficient) and a worm gear set (55% efficient) to drive a conveyor belt that runs continuously for 10 hours a day. Which would you recommend, and why?
  3. Justifying a Trade-off: Despite being less efficient than spur or helical gears, worm gears are still commonly chosen for winches and lifting hoists. Explain why.
Reveal Answer Key

1. Efficiency = (10.2 ÷ 12) × 100% = 85%.

2. The helical gear set, because its higher efficiency (98% vs 55%) wastes far less energy as heat over a continuously running system, reducing electricity costs and the risk of the mechanism overheating during long operating hours.

3. Worm gears are non-reversible (self-locking): once the motor stops turning, the driven gear cannot turn the worm shaft backward. This means a winch or hoist holds a lifted load safely in place without needing a separate brake, which is a critical safety benefit that outweighs the lower energy efficiency.

Automated Sliding Gate: A motor turns a small circular gear that drives a long, straight toothed bar to slide the gate open. Heavy Equipment Hoist: A motor turns a threaded screw shaft that drives a gear wheel to lift heavy loads, locking the load safely if power is lost. Drive Belt Conveyor Line: A driving gear needs to turn a driven gear on a parallel shaft in the same direction, so a middle gear is added between them. Socket Wrench: A spring-loaded catch engages angled teeth, clicking freely in one direction while applying force in the other. Multi-Stage Clockwork Mechanism: A watchmaker mounts two gears of different sizes onto the same central axle for a high reduction ratio in a compact case. Basic Parallel Gearbox: Simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth mesh side-by-side on parallel shafts. Automatic Car Transmission: A central sun gear, three surrounding planet gears on a rotating carrier, and an outer ring gear work together in a compact housing to provide multiple gear ratios without ever disengaging the gears. Worm Gear — provides high torque/speed reduction and is non-reversible to prevent slipping. Idler Gear — changes output direction back to the original input direction without altering the overall gear ratio. Ratchet and Pawl — restricts motion to a single direction while allowing slipping in reverse. Compound Gear — two gears fixed to the same shaft for compact, multi-stage speed/torque adjustments. Spur Gears — simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth meshing on parallel shafts. Planetary Gear — a sun, planet, and ring gear share the load between them to provide multiple ratios within a compact space.

activities.title: Activity: Gear Ratio, Torque and Speed Calculation Challenge
activities.text: Activity: Gear Ratio, Torque and Speed Calculation Challenge Apply GR = Teeth on Driven Gear ÷ Teeth on Driver Gear to solve these scenarios. Calculating Gear Ratio: A driver gear has 12 teeth and meshes with a driven gear that has 60 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and will the output speed be faster or slower than the input speed? Finding Output Speed: A driver gear with 15 teeth rotates at 300 rpm and meshes with a driven gear that has 45 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and what is the resulting output speed of the driven gear? Selecting a Gear Ratio for Torque: A cordless drill needs to multiply the motor's torque to drive large screws without stalling. Should the designer choose a gear ratio greater than 1 or less than 1? Justify your answer. Explaining a Trade-off: Using the concept of torque and speed, explain why a bicycle rider shifts to a gear ratio greater than 1 (a "low gear") when climbing a steep hill. Reveal Answer Key 1. GR = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 (a ratio of 5:1). Because GR > 1, the output speed will be slower than the input speed, and output torque will be higher. 2. GR = 45 ÷ 15 = 3 (a ratio of 3:1). Output speed = 300 rpm ÷ 3 = 100 rpm. 3. Greater than 1. A gear ratio above 1 (small driver turning a large driven gear) reduces output speed while increasing output torque, giving the drill enough turning force to drive the screw without stalling. 4. Shifting to a gear ratio greater than 1 trades speed for torque: the rear wheel turns more slowly for each pedal rotation, but the torque delivered to the wheel increases, giving the rider enough turning force to overcome the extra resistance of the incline with less effort per pedal stroke.

Activity: Gear Ratio, Torque and Speed Calculation Challenge

Apply GR = Teeth on Driven Gear ÷ Teeth on Driver Gear to solve these scenarios.

  1. Calculating Gear Ratio: A driver gear has 12 teeth and meshes with a driven gear that has 60 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and will the output speed be faster or slower than the input speed?
  2. Finding Output Speed: A driver gear with 15 teeth rotates at 300 rpm and meshes with a driven gear that has 45 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and what is the resulting output speed of the driven gear?
  3. Selecting a Gear Ratio for Torque: A cordless drill needs to multiply the motor's torque to drive large screws without stalling. Should the designer choose a gear ratio greater than 1 or less than 1? Justify your answer.
  4. Explaining a Trade-off: Using the concept of torque and speed, explain why a bicycle rider shifts to a gear ratio greater than 1 (a "low gear") when climbing a steep hill.
Reveal Answer Key

1. GR = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 (a ratio of 5:1). Because GR > 1, the output speed will be slower than the input speed, and output torque will be higher.

2. GR = 45 ÷ 15 = 3 (a ratio of 3:1). Output speed = 300 rpm ÷ 3 = 100 rpm.

3. Greater than 1. A gear ratio above 1 (small driver turning a large driven gear) reduces output speed while increasing output torque, giving the drill enough turning force to drive the screw without stalling.

4. Shifting to a gear ratio greater than 1 trades speed for torque: the rear wheel turns more slowly for each pedal rotation, but the torque delivered to the wheel increases, giving the rider enough turning force to overcome the extra resistance of the incline with less effort per pedal stroke.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: The "Gear Ratio Race"
activities.text: Practical Engagement: The "Gear Ratio Race" Task: Using sets of spur gears, build a system that either maximises output speed (small gear driving large) or maximises power/torque (large gear driving small). Outcome: Count the teeth on each gear used and calculate the actual gear ratio achieved. Compare it against the measured change in speed and torque, and explain how altering the gear ratio changed your system's performance and efficiency.

activities.title: Activity: Gear Efficiency Challenge
activities.text: Activity: Gear Efficiency Challenge Calculating Efficiency: An electric screwdriver's motor supplies 12 J of input energy to its gear train. Only 10.2 J is delivered as useful output energy at the screw tip. What is the efficiency of the gear train? Comparing Gear Types: A designer is choosing between a helical gear set (98% efficient) and a worm gear set (55% efficient) to drive a conveyor belt that runs continuously for 10 hours a day. Which would you recommend, and why? Justifying a Trade-off: Despite being less efficient than spur or helical gears, worm gears are still commonly chosen for winches and lifting hoists. Explain why. Reveal Answer Key 1. Efficiency = (10.2 ÷ 12) × 100% = 85%. 2. The helical gear set, because its higher efficiency (98% vs 55%) wastes far less energy as heat over a continuously running system, reducing electricity costs and the risk of the mechanism overheating during long operating hours. 3. Worm gears are non-reversible (self-locking): once the motor stops turning, the driven gear cannot turn the worm shaft backward. This means a winch or hoist holds a lifted load safely in place without needing a separate brake, which is a critical safety benefit that outweighs the lower energy efficiency.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Belts, Cams, Levers and Linkages
sections.html:
A3.3.7 Belt-Driven Systems A3.3.8 Cam and Follower Systems A3.3.9 Lever Systems A3.3.10 Linkage Systems ~90 min

Lesson 3: Belts, Cams, Levers and Linkages

Not every mechanical system relies on toothed gears. This lesson covers four further families of mechanism — belts, cams, levers and linkages — each suited to a different job: transferring motion over distance, converting rotary motion into precise reciprocating movement, multiplying force around a pivot, or redirecting motion through an assembly of rigid links.

1. Belt-Driven and Pulley Systems

Belt-Driven Systems

Definition: A drive system that uses pulleys (grooved wheels) connected by flexible belt loops to transfer rotary motion over longer distances.

Context: Washing machines use belt-driven systems and pulleys to rotate the drum quietly while absorbing shock during heavy, unbalanced loads.

Materials/Examples: Pulleys, flat belts, V-belts, timing belts, tensioners.

Application: Quieter than gears and absorbs shock well, but may slip under very heavy loads — a useful overload-protection feature as well as a limitation.

Activity: Belt-Driven and Pulley Systems Challenge

  1. Distance Transfer: Why would a system designer prefer a belt-driven pulley system over a series of spur gears to transmit rotary motion between two shafts spaced 2 metres apart?
  2. System Protection: How does the tendency of standard belts to "slip under very heavy loads" act as an unintentional safety benefit for a motor compared to rigid gear teeth?
  3. Component Function: What specific component is added to a belt-driven system to maintain proper belt tightness and prevent slippage as the belt wears or stretches over time?
  4. Belt Matching: Match each belt type (Flat belt, V-belt, or Timing belt) to its application: (A) high-torque transmission using a wedge shape in grooved pulleys; (B) precise, non-slip synchronisation with teeth engaging pulley grooves (e.g. 3D printers, engine timing); (C) simple, high-speed power transfer across flat cylindrical pulleys over longer distances.
  5. Shock Absorption: Why are washing machines designed with belt systems rather than direct gear trains to rotate the washing drum during unbalanced spin cycles?
Reveal Answer Key

1. Belts efficiently span long distances using flexible loops, whereas gears would require a heavy, complex, and costly train of intermediate idler gears to bridge the same gap.

2. Slippage allows the belt to spin freely if the output jams, protecting the motor from burning out and preventing structural damage to other components.

3. A tensioner — it applies constant force to the belt to maintain proper tension and eliminate slack.

4. A: V-belt. B: Timing belt. C: Flat belt.

5. Belts absorb mechanical shocks and vibrations caused by sloshing water and heavy, shifting clothes, keeping the appliance quiet and preventing mechanical fatigue.

2. Cam and Follower Systems

Cam and Follower

Definition: A cam is a specially shaped rotating disc that pushes a follower to convert rotary motion into reciprocating or oscillating motion.

Context: Automobile engines use cams to convert rotary motion into the reciprocating motion required to open and close valves at precise intervals.

Materials/Examples: Pear, circular (eccentric), triangular, oval, and snail cam profiles dictate the timing and movement of the follower.

Application: Chosen whenever a repeating, precisely-timed reciprocating or oscillating movement must be driven from a continuously rotating shaft.

Discussion

Watch the cam animation above. As the disc rotates at a constant speed, does the follower always move at a constant speed? Why might a designer deliberately choose an irregular cam profile (like a snail or pear shape) rather than a simple circular one?

3. Lever Systems

A lever is a rigid bar pivoting on a fulcrum, with effort applied to move a load. The order of the fulcrum, effort and load determines the class of lever, and Mechanical Advantage can also be expressed as MA = Length of Effort Arm ÷ Length of Resistance Arm.

1st Class Lever

Definition: The fulcrum is located between the effort and the load.

Context: Scissors and a seesaw both pivot on a central point between the effort applied by the user and the load being cut or lifted.

Materials/Examples: Scissors, seesaws, pliers, crowbars.

Application: Can be used to multiply force, multiply distance/speed, or simply change direction, depending on where the fulcrum sits relative to the load and effort.

2nd Class Lever

Definition: The load is located between the effort and the fulcrum.

Context: Wheelbarrows use second-class levers to allow users to move heavy construction materials with reduced effort.

Materials/Examples: Wheelbarrows, bottle openers, nutcrackers.

Application: Always produces a mechanical advantage greater than 1, making it well suited to lifting heavy loads.

3rd Class Lever

Definition: The effort is located between the fulcrum and the load.

Context: Tweezers, and the human forearm, apply effort between the pivot and the object being held.

Materials/Examples: Tweezers, fishing rods, the human forearm.

Application: Trades force for speed and range of movement — useful for precise or fast movements rather than heavy lifting.

4. Linkage Systems

Linkages are assemblies of rigid links (bars) connected by pivots, used to change the direction or magnitude of a force or motion.

Parallel Linkage

Definition: Keeps input and output motion in the same direction.

Context: Car suspensions use parallel linkages so the wheel can move up and down while staying aligned with the car body.

Materials/Examples: Car suspension arms, some desk lamp arms.

Application: Used when output motion must mirror input motion without changing its direction.

Reverse Linkage

Definition: Moves the output in the opposite direction to the input.

Context: Windshield wipers use reverse linkages so that as one arm sweeps one way, a connected arm sweeps the opposite way.

Materials/Examples: Windscreen wiper linkages, some scissor mechanisms.

Application: Used whenever a mechanism needs an output that mirrors the input in the opposite direction.

Bell Crank

Definition: Transfers motion around corners, usually through a 90° angle.

Context: Bicycle brake systems use a bell crank where the cable pull must change direction to reach the calipers; bicycle steering also uses this principle to ensure handlebar input results in the desired steering direction.

Materials/Examples: Bicycle brake and steering linkages, aircraft control surfaces.

Application: Used whenever a force or motion must be redirected around a corner rather than transmitted in a straight line.

Practical Engagement: Mechanical Disassembly Audit

Task: Take apart a manual product (e.g. a hand drill, wind-up toy, or can opener). Before disassembly, predict the mechanism's function to test your observation skills.

Outcome: Identify each component (gears, cams, levers, linkages) and map the full Input–Process–Output chain for the product, noting the class of any levers and the type of any gears you find.

SystemFunctionReal-World Example
Belt-Driven SystemTransfers rotary motion over distance; quiet and shock-absorbingWashing machine drum
Cam and FollowerConverts rotary motion into precisely-timed reciprocating/oscillating motionEngine valve timing
1st Class LeverFulcrum between effort and loadScissors
2nd Class LeverLoad between effort and fulcrumWheelbarrow
3rd Class LeverEffort between fulcrum and loadTweezers
Parallel LinkageOutput moves in the same direction as inputCar suspension
Reverse LinkageOutput moves opposite to inputWindscreen wipers
Bell CrankRedirects motion, usually through 90°Bicycle brake cable routing

Linking Questions

Use these to connect Topic A3.3 to other areas of the syllabus and to stimulate class discussion or extended-response practice.

C1.2 Inclusive Design: How can mechanical advantage (levers and gear ratios) be used to enable inclusive design for users with reduced strength?
B1.1 User-Centred Design: How might a task analysis of a product reveal that a mechanical system, rather than the product's overall form, is the true source of a usability pain point?
C4.1 Design for Manufacture: Why might a designer choose a less efficient mechanism (e.g. a worm gear) if it reduces the number of components needed elsewhere in the product?

sections.title: Exam Practice: Topic A3.3
sections.html:
A3.3 Exam Practice AO1 / AO2 / AO3

Exam Practice: Topic A3.3

Questions below follow the command-term expectations and mark-allocation logic used in Paper 1 and Paper 2. Sample/indicative answers for teacher use follow each question.

Section A: Multiple Choice (2 questions, 1 mark each)

1. Which type of motion is best described as a repetitive back-and-forth movement in a straight line?

  • Rotary
  • Oscillating
  • Reciprocating
  • Linear
Reveal Answer
C. Reciprocating. [1]

2. A driver gear with 10 teeth meshes with a driven gear with 40 teeth. Which statement correctly describes the output of the driven gear compared to the input of the driver gear?

  • Higher speed, lower torque
  • Lower speed, higher torque
  • Same speed, same torque
  • Higher speed, higher torque
Reveal Answer
B. Lower speed, higher torque. [1]

Section B: Short Answer (2 questions)

Question 3 [3 marks]

Describe the input, process, and output of a bicycle's chain and sprocket system.

Reveal Answer

[3] Award for Input (the user applies force/rotary motion to the pedals); for Process (the chain transmits motion to the rear sprocket); and for Output (the rear wheel rotates to move the bicycle forward).

Question 4 [3 marks]

A gear train used in a cordless drill has an overall efficiency of 80%. If the motor supplies 15 J of input energy, calculate the useful output energy delivered to the drill bit, and state one reason why the gear train is not 100% efficient.

Reveal Answer

[3] Award for correct substitution into the efficiency formula; award for the correct answer (Output = 0.80 × 15 J = 12 J); award for a valid reason (e.g. friction between meshing teeth, heat loss, or bearing/lubrication losses).

Section C: Extended Response (2 questions)

Question 5 [4 marks]

Explain how a multidisciplinary design team might use mechanical systems to enable inclusive design for elderly users.

Reveal Answer

[4] Identify that mechanical advantage is the key factor. Explain how engineers (multidisciplinary team) might use levers or gear ratios to reduce the physical effort needed for a task (e.g. a jar opener or stair lift), thereby making the product usable for those with reduced muscle strength or arthritis.

Question 6 [4 marks]

Discuss why a designer might choose a worm gear system over a spur gear system for an electric wheelchair's tilt mechanism, despite the worm gear being less energy efficient.

Reveal Answer

[4] Award for identifying that worm gears are non-reversible/self-locking, meaning the tilt mechanism cannot slip backward under the user's weight if power is lost, which is a critical safety requirement. Award for acknowledging the trade-off that worm gears have lower efficiency (more energy/heat lost to friction from sliding contact) than spur gears. Award for a balanced conclusion that safety and reliability outweigh the efficiency cost in this safety-critical application.

sections.html:
A3.3 Glossary

Glossary: Topic A3.3 — Mechanical Systems (HL)

Click on a term to reveal its definition.

1st-class lever
A lever where the fulcrum is located between the effort force and the load (resistance force). For example, a seesaw or a pair of scissors.
2nd-class lever
A lever where the load (resistance force) is located between the effort force and the fulcrum. For example, a wheelbarrow.
3rd-class lever
A lever where the effort force is located between the fulcrum and the load (resistance force). For example, tweezers and most human limbs are 3rd-class levers.
Belt-driven system
A drive system where a belt transfers power between at least two pulleys. One pulley drives the belt (driver pulley) and the other is driven by the belt (driven pulley).
Bell crank linkage
A linkage that allows vertical movement to be converted into horizontal movement. It also works the opposite way around.
Bevel gear
A pair of toothed rotating gears used to transfer power between two gear shafts at an angle, usually 90°, to the original.
Cam
A mechanical component used to transform rotational motion into linear motion.
Compound gear
Comprises two or more gears forming a connected system. The output of one gear is used as the input for another gear in the same system.
Driver/driven gear
The driver gear is directly connected to the power source and initiates motion; the driven gear is turned by the driver (directly or through intermediate gears). For example, in a car steering system, the pinion gear on the steering column is the driver, and the rack it moves along is the driven component.
Efficiency (mechanical)
The ratio of useful output energy (or power) to input energy (or power) in a system, expressed as a percentage; real systems are always below 100% due to losses such as friction and heat. For example, a helical gear reduction in an electric car drivetrain is around 97–98% efficient, helping maximise the vehicle's driving range.
Fulcrum (lever)
The fixed point around which the lever rotates, also known as a "pivot".
Gears
A toothed wheel that interlocks with another to transmit motion or change the speed and/or direction of motion.
Gear ratio
The ratio of the number of teeth on the driven gear to the number of teeth on the driver gear, used to predict how a gear system changes output speed and torque. For example, a bicycle in a 5:1 low gear turns the pedals five times to rotate the rear wheel once, trading speed for the extra torque needed to climb a hill.
Idler gear
A gear in a gear train that is used between the driving and driven gears. It is used to change the rotational direction of the driven gear or to fill a gap between the gears without affecting the speed ratio.
Lever
A beam resting on a fulcrum that has effort applied to it to move a load. The order of the fulcrum, effort and load determines the class of lever.
Levers (Mechanical Advantage)
Mechanical Advantage (MA) = Length of Effort Arm (EA) ÷ Length of Resistance Arm (RA).
Load
An amount of force applied to a surface or body.
Linear motion
Movement in a straight line.
Linkage
A mechanical device comprised of components that are joined together in a defined sequence in order to change the direction or magnitude of a force.
Mechanical advantage
The ratio of output force compared to input force in a mechanical system.
Mechanical system
A set of physical components that convert an input force and motion into a desired output force and motion.
Module (gear)
A measure of tooth size, calculated as pitch diameter divided by the number of teeth; gears must share the same module to mesh correctly. For example, replacement gears in a repaired machine must be manufactured to the same module as the originals or they will not mesh with the surrounding gears.
Oscillating motion
The motion of an object that repeatedly moves over a point.
Parallel linkage
A central moving point of the linkage that is constrained to travel on a nearly straight line.
Pulley
A grooved wheel that uses a rope, cord, chain or cable to transmit energy and motion.
Rack and pinion
A mechanical device using a fixed bar that engages with a smaller toothed wheel that converts rotary to linear motion.
Ratchet and pawl
A mechanical device that allows motion in one direction only. The pawl fits into the teeth of the toothed ratchet and prevents it from rotating backwards, while allowing it to rotate forwards.
Reciprocating motion
A repetitive motion in a straight line.
Reverse linkage
A linkage that is used to move the force in the opposite direction.
Rotary motion
The motion of an object that spins on its own axis.
Spur gear
A toothed gear where the teeth project parallel to the gear's axis.
Torque
The rotational (turning) equivalent of force, calculated as force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot, measured in newton-metres (Nm). For example, an electric screwdriver uses a gear train to convert its motor's fast, low-torque rotation into the slow, high-torque rotation needed to drive a screw without stalling.
Worm gear
A mechanical component typically formed as a threaded shaft that interlocks with a toothed gear or worm wheel.

syllabus.title: Introduction to mechanical systems
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How are mechanisms present in everyday products?

statements.text: There are four types of motion involved in mechanical systems.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify the four basic types of mechanical motion: linear; rotary; oscillating; and reciprocating.

statements.text: Mechanical systems convert an input into an output.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe inputs, processes and outputs in the context of mechanical systems.

statements.text: Mechanical systems can provide a mechanical advantage to the user.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline a mechanical advantage and suggest how simple mechanical systems may improve performance in terms of function and efficiency.

statements.text: Mechanical systems are used to increase or decrease the speed, direction or power of a motion.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify gear-driven, belt-driven, cam, lever and linkage systems.

statements.text: The four types of motion can be combined to create simple or complex mechanical systems.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the basic principles of mechanical motion and discuss how gears, pulleys, cams, levers and linkages can be combined to create complex mechanical systems.

statements.text: Gears transmit rotary motion from one gear shaft to another, and have a number of teeth.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify the different types of gear systems (spur, bevel, rack and pinion, worm, ratchet and pawl, idler and compound) and their components, and outline how they are used providing examples.

statements.text: Belt-driven systems are driven by pulleys.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify components of pulley systems, and outline how they are used providing examples.

statements.text: The shape of a cam dictates the type of motion.
statements.guidance: Students must be able identify different shaped cams (pear, circular, triangular, eccentric, oval and snail) and outline how they are used providing examples.

statements.text: Levers comprise a beam acting on a fulcrum (pivot) and are classed based on the relative position of the fulcrum to an applied load and effort.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify the three types of levers (1st class, 2nd class and 3rd class) and the position of the Load (L), Effort (E) and the Fulcrum, and outline how they are used providing examples.

statements.text: Linkages are used to change the direction of a movement, alter the magnitude of a force or make parts of a system move in a particular way.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify parallel, reverse and bell crank linkages, and outline how they are used providing examples.

exam.question: A 12-tooth driver turns a 36-tooth driven gear. Calculate the output speed for a 90 rpm input. [2]
exam.answer: Output speed = input speed × driver teeth / driven teeth = 90 × 12 / 36 = 30 rpm. External gears rotate in opposite directions.

activities.title: Activity: Mechanical Motion Matching Challenge
activities.text: Activity: Mechanical Motion Matching Challenge Identify the primary type of motion (Linear, Rotary, Oscillating, or Reciprocating) for each real-world object below. Windshield wiper sweeping across a car's glass Elevator car travelling from floor 1 to floor 10 Hand saw cutting back and forth through timber Ferris wheel turning at a carnival Pneumatic jackhammer chisel breaking up concrete Wrecking ball swinging into a wall Conveyor belt moving boxes straight down an assembly line Ceiling fan blades spinning on high speed Reveal Answers Oscillating — the wiper sweeps back and forth through the same arc. Linear — the car travels a straight vertical path. Reciprocating — the blade repeats a straight back-and-forth cutting stroke. Rotary — the wheel turns fully around its central axle. Reciprocating — the chisel repeatedly strikes along a straight line. Oscillating — the ball swings through an arc about its suspension point. Linear — boxes move in a single straight direction. Rotary — the blades spin around a central axis.
activities.html:
Identify the primary type of motion (Linear, Rotary, Oscillating, or Reciprocating) for each real-world object below.

  1. Windshield wiper sweeping across a car's glass
  2. Elevator car travelling from floor 1 to floor 10
  3. Hand saw cutting back and forth through timber
  4. Ferris wheel turning at a carnival
  5. Pneumatic jackhammer chisel breaking up concrete
  6. Wrecking ball swinging into a wall
  7. Conveyor belt moving boxes straight down an assembly line
  8. Ceiling fan blades spinning on high speed
Reveal Answers
  1. Oscillating — the wiper sweeps back and forth through the same arc.
  2. Linear — the car travels a straight vertical path.
  3. Reciprocating — the blade repeats a straight back-and-forth cutting stroke.
  4. Rotary — the wheel turns fully around its central axle.
  5. Reciprocating — the chisel repeatedly strikes along a straight line.
  6. Oscillating — the ball swings through an arc about its suspension point.
  7. Linear — boxes move in a single straight direction.
  8. Rotary — the blades spin around a central axis.

activities.title: Activity: Input–Process–Output Breakdown Challenge
activities.text: Activity: Input–Process–Output Breakdown Challenge Deconstruct each of the four everyday mechanical systems below into its Input, Process, and Output. Manual Hand-Crank Pencil Sharpener Bicycle Cable Brakes Hand-Operated Water Well Pump Winged Corkscrew (Lever Corkscrew) Reveal Answer Key 1. Manual Hand-Crank Pencil Sharpener Input: Rotational force applied by turning the hand crank. Process: Internal gears turn cylindrical cutting blades around the pencil tip. Output: Wood and graphite shaved away to create a sharp point. 2. Bicycle Cable Brakes Input: Squeezing force applied by the rider's hand on the brake lever. Process: Cable tension pulls two caliper arms inward against a spring. Output: Friction rubber pads press against the wheel rim, slowing or stopping the bike. 3. Hand-Operated Water Well Pump Input: Downward force applied by pushing down on the pump handle lever. Process: The lever lifts a piston rod within a cylinder, opening and closing internal valves to create suction. Output: Water drawn up from below ground and discharged through the spout. 4. Winged Corkscrew Input: Downward force applied by pushing down the two raised side levers. Process: Interlocking gear teeth (rack and pinion) on the levers pull the central shaft straight up. Output: The cork extracted vertically out of the bottle neck.

  1. Manual Hand-Crank Pencil Sharpener
  2. Bicycle Cable Brakes
  3. Hand-Operated Water Well Pump
  4. Winged Corkscrew (Lever Corkscrew)
Reveal Answer Key

1. Manual Hand-Crank Pencil Sharpener
Input: Rotational force applied by turning the hand crank.

Output: Wood and graphite shaved away to create a sharp point.

2. Bicycle Cable Brakes

3. Hand-Operated Water Well Pump

4. Winged Corkscrew

activities.title: Activity: Mechanical Advantage Calculation & Application Challenge
activities.text: Activity: Mechanical Advantage Calculation & Application Challenge Apply the formula MA = Load ÷ Effort and your understanding of mechanical systems to solve these four scenarios. Calculating MA: A mechanic uses a lever to lift an engine out of a car frame. The engine exerts a load force of 800 N, and the mechanic applies an effort force of 160 N. What is the mechanical advantage of the lever? Finding Required Effort: A compound pulley system on a crane provides a mechanical advantage of 5. How much effort force must the winch motor exert to lift a 2,500 N steel beam? Determining Maximum Load: A boat winch has a mechanical advantage of 8. If a person can exert 200 N of effort force on the hand crank, what is the maximum load force the winch can move? Identifying Components: When using a nutcracker to crack a walnut, identify what acts as the Load and what acts as the Effort. Reveal Answer Key 1. MA = 5. MA = Load ÷ Effort = 800 N ÷ 160 N = 5. 2. Effort = 500 N. Effort = Load ÷ MA = 2,500 N ÷ 5 = 500 N. 3. Load = 1,600 N. Load = MA × Effort = 8 × 200 N = 1,600 N. 4. Load: the structural resistance of the walnut shell resisting being crushed. Effort: the squeezing force applied by the user's hand on the long handles.
activities.html:
Apply the formula MA = Load ÷ Effort and your understanding of mechanical systems to solve these four scenarios.

  1. Calculating MA: A mechanic uses a lever to lift an engine out of a car frame. The engine exerts a load force of 800 N, and the mechanic applies an effort force of 160 N. What is the mechanical advantage of the lever?
  2. Finding Required Effort: A compound pulley system on a crane provides a mechanical advantage of 5. How much effort force must the winch motor exert to lift a 2,500 N steel beam?
  3. Determining Maximum Load: A boat winch has a mechanical advantage of 8. If a person can exert 200 N of effort force on the hand crank, what is the maximum load force the winch can move?
  4. Identifying Components: When using a nutcracker to crack a walnut, identify what acts as the Load and what acts as the Effort.
Reveal Answer Key

1. MA = 5. MA = Load ÷ Effort = 800 N ÷ 160 N = 5.

2. Effort = 500 N. Effort = Load ÷ MA = 2,500 N ÷ 5 = 500 N.

3. Load = 1,600 N. Load = MA × Effort = 8 × 200 N = 1,600 N.

4. Load: the structural resistance of the walnut shell resisting being crushed. Effort: the squeezing force applied by the user's hand on the long handles.

activities.title: Activity: Gear-Driven Systems Identification Challenge
activities.text: Activity: Gear-Driven Systems Identification Challenge Match each scenario below with the correct gear mechanism (Spur Gears, Bevel Gears, Rack and Pinion, Worm Gear, Ratchet and Pawl, Idler Gear, Compound Gear, or Planetary Gear). Eggbeater Mixer: Turning a handle on a horizontal axle spins beaters mounted on vertical axles at a 90° angle. Automated Sliding Gate: A motor turns a small circular gear that drives a long, straight toothed bar to slide the gate open. Heavy Equipment Hoist: A motor turns a threaded screw shaft that drives a gear wheel to lift heavy loads, locking the load safely if power is lost. Drive Belt Conveyor Line: A driving gear needs to turn a driven gear on a parallel shaft in the same direction, so a middle gear is added between them. Socket Wrench: A spring-loaded catch engages angled teeth, clicking freely in one direction while applying force in the other. Multi-Stage Clockwork Mechanism: A watchmaker mounts two gears of different sizes onto the same central axle for a high reduction ratio in a compact case. Basic Parallel Gearbox: Simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth mesh side-by-side on parallel shafts. Automatic Car Transmission: A central sun gear, three surrounding planet gears on a rotating carrier, and an outer ring gear work together in a compact housing to provide multiple gear ratios without ever disengaging the gears. Reveal Answers Bevel Gears — transmits motion between intersecting shafts, usually at 90°. Rack and Pinion — converts the rotary motion of the gear into linear motion of the gate. Worm Gear — provides high torque/speed reduction and is non-reversible to prevent slipping. Idler Gear — changes output direction back to the original input direction without altering the overall gear ratio. Ratchet and Pawl — restricts motion to a single direction while allowing slipping in reverse. Compound Gear — two gears fixed to the same shaft for compact, multi-stage speed/torque adjustments. Spur Gears — simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth meshing on parallel shafts. Planetary Gear — a sun, planet, and ring gear share the load between them to provide multiple ratios within a compact space.
activities.html:
Match each scenario below with the correct gear mechanism (Spur Gears, Bevel Gears, Rack and Pinion, Worm Gear, Ratchet and Pawl, Idler Gear, Compound Gear, or Planetary Gear).

  1. Eggbeater Mixer: Turning a handle on a horizontal axle spins beaters mounted on vertical axles at a 90° angle.
  2. Automated Sliding Gate: A motor turns a small circular gear that drives a long, straight toothed bar to slide the gate open.
  3. Heavy Equipment Hoist: A motor turns a threaded screw shaft that drives a gear wheel to lift heavy loads, locking the load safely if power is lost.
  4. Drive Belt Conveyor Line: A driving gear needs to turn a driven gear on a parallel shaft in the same direction, so a middle gear is added between them.
  5. Socket Wrench: A spring-loaded catch engages angled teeth, clicking freely in one direction while applying force in the other.
  6. Multi-Stage Clockwork Mechanism: A watchmaker mounts two gears of different sizes onto the same central axle for a high reduction ratio in a compact case.
  7. Basic Parallel Gearbox: Simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth mesh side-by-side on parallel shafts.
  8. Automatic Car Transmission: A central sun gear, three surrounding planet gears on a rotating carrier, and an outer ring gear work together in a compact housing to provide multiple gear ratios without ever disengaging the gears.
Reveal Answers
  1. Bevel Gears — transmits motion between intersecting shafts, usually at 90°.
  2. Rack and Pinion — converts the rotary motion of the gear into linear motion of the gate.
  3. Worm Gear — provides high torque/speed reduction and is non-reversible to prevent slipping.
  4. Idler Gear — changes output direction back to the original input direction without altering the overall gear ratio.
  5. Ratchet and Pawl — restricts motion to a single direction while allowing slipping in reverse.
  6. Compound Gear — two gears fixed to the same shaft for compact, multi-stage speed/torque adjustments.
  7. Spur Gears — simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth meshing on parallel shafts.
  8. Planetary Gear — a sun, planet, and ring gear share the load between them to provide multiple ratios within a compact space.

activities.title: Activity: Gear Ratio, Torque and Speed Calculation Challenge
activities.text: Activity: Gear Ratio, Torque and Speed Calculation Challenge Apply GR = Teeth on Driven Gear ÷ Teeth on Driver Gear to solve these scenarios. Calculating Gear Ratio: A driver gear has 12 teeth and meshes with a driven gear that has 60 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and will the output speed be faster or slower than the input speed? Finding Output Speed: A driver gear with 15 teeth rotates at 300 rpm and meshes with a driven gear that has 45 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and what is the resulting output speed of the driven gear? Selecting a Gear Ratio for Torque: A cordless drill needs to multiply the motor's torque to drive large screws without stalling. Should the designer choose a gear ratio greater than 1 or less than 1? Justify your answer. Explaining a Trade-off: Using the concept of torque and speed, explain why a bicycle rider shifts to a gear ratio greater than 1 (a "low gear") when climbing a steep hill. Reveal Answer Key 1. GR = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 (a ratio of 5:1). Because GR > 1, the output speed will be slower than the input speed, and output torque will be higher. 2. GR = 45 ÷ 15 = 3 (a ratio of 3:1). Output speed = 300 rpm ÷ 3 = 100 rpm. 3. Greater than 1. A gear ratio above 1 (small driver turning a large driven gear) reduces output speed while increasing output torque, giving the drill enough turning force to drive the screw without stalling. 4. Shifting to a gear ratio greater than 1 trades speed for torque: the rear wheel turns more slowly for each pedal rotation, but the torque delivered to the wheel increases, giving the rider enough turning force to overcome the extra resistance of the incline with less effort per pedal stroke.

Apply GR = Teeth on Driven Gear ÷ Teeth on Driver Gear to solve these scenarios.

  1. Calculating Gear Ratio: A driver gear has 12 teeth and meshes with a driven gear that has 60 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and will the output speed be faster or slower than the input speed?
  2. Finding Output Speed: A driver gear with 15 teeth rotates at 300 rpm and meshes with a driven gear that has 45 teeth. What is the gear ratio, and what is the resulting output speed of the driven gear?
  3. Selecting a Gear Ratio for Torque: A cordless drill needs to multiply the motor's torque to drive large screws without stalling. Should the designer choose a gear ratio greater than 1 or less than 1? Justify your answer.
  4. Explaining a Trade-off: Using the concept of torque and speed, explain why a bicycle rider shifts to a gear ratio greater than 1 (a "low gear") when climbing a steep hill.
Reveal Answer Key

1. GR = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 (a ratio of 5:1). Because GR > 1, the output speed will be slower than the input speed, and output torque will be higher.

2. GR = 45 ÷ 15 = 3 (a ratio of 3:1). Output speed = 300 rpm ÷ 3 = 100 rpm.

3. Greater than 1. A gear ratio above 1 (small driver turning a large driven gear) reduces output speed while increasing output torque, giving the drill enough turning force to drive the screw without stalling.

4. Shifting to a gear ratio greater than 1 trades speed for torque: the rear wheel turns more slowly for each pedal rotation, but the torque delivered to the wheel increases, giving the rider enough turning force to overcome the extra resistance of the incline with less effort per pedal stroke.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: The "Gear Ratio Race"
activities.text: Practical Engagement: The "Gear Ratio Race" Task: Using sets of spur gears, build a system that either maximises output speed (small gear driving large) or maximises power/torque (large gear driving small). Outcome: Count the teeth on each gear used and calculate the actual gear ratio achieved. Compare it against the measured change in speed and torque, and explain how altering the gear ratio changed your system's performance and efficiency.

activities.title: Activity: Gear Efficiency Challenge
activities.text: Activity: Gear Efficiency Challenge Calculating Efficiency: An electric screwdriver's motor supplies 12 J of input energy to its gear train. Only 10.2 J is delivered as useful output energy at the screw tip. What is the efficiency of the gear train? Comparing Gear Types: A designer is choosing between a helical gear set (98% efficient) and a worm gear set (55% efficient) to drive a conveyor belt that runs continuously for 10 hours a day. Which would you recommend, and why? Justifying a Trade-off: Despite being less efficient than spur or helical gears, worm gears are still commonly chosen for winches and lifting hoists. Explain why. Reveal Answer Key 1. Efficiency = (10.2 ÷ 12) × 100% = 85%. 2. The helical gear set, because its higher efficiency (98% vs 55%) wastes far less energy as heat over a continuously running system, reducing electricity costs and the risk of the mechanism overheating during long operating hours. 3. Worm gears are non-reversible (self-locking): once the motor stops turning, the driven gear cannot turn the worm shaft backward. This means a winch or hoist holds a lifted load safely in place without needing a separate brake, which is a critical safety benefit that outweighs the lower energy efficiency.

activities.title: Activity: Belt-Driven and Pulley Systems Challenge
activities.text: Activity: Belt-Driven and Pulley Systems Challenge Distance Transfer: Why would a system designer prefer a belt-driven pulley system over a series of spur gears to transmit rotary motion between two shafts spaced 2 metres apart? System Protection: How does the tendency of standard belts to "slip under very heavy loads" act as an unintentional safety benefit for a motor compared to rigid gear teeth? Component Function: What specific component is added to a belt-driven system to maintain proper belt tightness and prevent slippage as the belt wears or stretches over time? Belt Matching: Match each belt type (Flat belt, V-belt, or Timing belt) to its application: (A) high-torque transmission using a wedge shape in grooved pulleys; (B) precise, non-slip synchronisation with teeth engaging pulley grooves (e.g. 3D printers, engine timing); (C) simple, high-speed power transfer across flat cylindrical pulleys over longer distances. Shock Absorption: Why are washing machines designed with belt systems rather than direct gear trains to rotate the washing drum during unbalanced spin cycles? Reveal Answer Key 1. Belts efficiently span long distances using flexible loops, whereas gears would require a heavy, complex, and costly train of intermediate idler gears to bridge the same gap. 2. Slippage allows the belt to spin freely if the output jams, protecting the motor from burning out and preventing structural damage to other components. 3. A tensioner — it applies constant force to the belt to maintain proper tension and eliminate slack. 4. A: V-belt. B: Timing belt. C: Flat belt. 5. Belts absorb mechanical shocks and vibrations caused by sloshing water and heavy, shifting clothes, keeping the appliance quiet and preventing mechanical fatigue.

1. Distance Transfer: Why would a system designer prefer a belt-driven pulley system over a series of spur gears to transmit rotary motion between two shafts spaced 2 metres apart?
  2. System Protection: How does the tendency of standard belts to "slip under very heavy loads" act as an unintentional safety benefit for a motor compared to rigid gear teeth?
  3. Component Function: What specific component is added to a belt-driven system to maintain proper belt tightness and prevent slippage as the belt wears or stretches over time?
  4. Belt Matching: Match each belt type (Flat belt, V-belt, or Timing belt) to its application: (A) high-torque transmission using a wedge shape in grooved pulleys; (B) precise, non-slip synchronisation with teeth engaging pulley grooves (e.g. 3D printers, engine timing); (C) simple, high-speed power transfer across flat cylindrical pulleys over longer distances.
  5. Shock Absorption: Why are washing machines designed with belt systems rather than direct gear trains to rotate the washing drum during unbalanced spin cycles?
Reveal Answer Key

1. Belts efficiently span long distances using flexible loops, whereas gears would require a heavy, complex, and costly train of intermediate idler gears to bridge the same gap.

2. Slippage allows the belt to spin freely if the output jams, protecting the motor from burning out and preventing structural damage to other components.

3. A tensioner — it applies constant force to the belt to maintain proper tension and eliminate slack.

4. A: V-belt. B: Timing belt. C: Flat belt.

5. Belts absorb mechanical shocks and vibrations caused by sloshing water and heavy, shifting clothes, keeping the appliance quiet and preventing mechanical fatigue.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Mechanical Disassembly Audit
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Mechanical Disassembly Audit Task: Take apart a manual product (e.g. a hand drill, wind-up toy, or can opener). Outcome: Identify each component (gears, cams, levers, linkages) and map the full Input–Process–Output chain for the product, noting the class of any levers and the type of any gears you find.

searchText: introduction to mechanical systems a3.3.1 types of motion a3.3.2 input–process–output a3.3.3 mechanical advantage ~120 min lesson 1: motion, input–process–output & mechanical advantage every mechanical system, however complex, is built from the same underlying ideas: a type of motion, a chain of input–process–output, and a trade-off between the force a user applies and the force a system delivers. this lesson establishes that shared vocabulary so it can be applied to every mechanism studied for the rest of the unit. hook: mechanisms hiding in plain sight look around the room right now. a door hinge, a stapler, a pair of scissors, a window blind, a swivel chair — every one of them relies on a mechanism most people never consciously notice. before any theory is introduced, list five mechanical products within arm's reach and, for each, guess what type of motion goes in and what type comes out. keep your list — you will revisit it at the end of this lesson. 1. types of motion designers must identify four basic types of mechanical motion in order to design efficient systems. 1. linear motion definition: movement of an object in a straight line, with every point on the object travelling the same distance in the same direction. context: a train moving along a straight section of track — the whole carriage travels the same distance in the same direction at once. materials/examples: conveyor belts, elevator cars, drawer slides, sliding doors. application: used wherever a product must move an object or user directly from one point to another without changing direction. 2. rotary motion definition: circular motion of an object around a fixed central point or axis. context: a spinning wheel turns continuously around its axle, with every point on the rim tracing a full circle. materials/examples: motor shafts, wheels, gears, drill bits. application: the most common output of motors and engines, and the starting point for most gear, belt and cam systems. 3. oscillating motion definition: back-and-forth movement in an arc about a central point. context: a swinging pendulum, or a child's playground swing, sweeps repeatedly through the same arc. materials/examples: metronomes, windscreen wipers, wrecking balls. application: chosen when a product needs to repeatedly sweep across an area, such as clearing a windscreen. 4. reciprocating motion definition: linear, repetitive back-and-forth motion. context: a piston inside an engine, or the needle of a sewing machine, repeatedly moves up and down (or in and out) along the same straight line. materials/examples: engine pistons, jigsaw blades, hand saws. application: chosen whenever a system needs to repeatedly cut, punch, or drive something along a fixed line. activity: mechanical motion matching challenge identify the primary type of motion (linear, rotary, oscillating, or reciprocating) for each real-world object below. windshield wiper sweeping across a car's glass elevator car travelling from floor 1 to floor 10 hand saw cutting back and forth through timber ferris wheel turning at a carnival pneumatic jackhammer chisel breaking up concrete wrecking ball swinging into a wall conveyor belt moving boxes straight down an assembly line ceiling fan blades spinning on high speed reveal answers oscillating — the wiper sweeps back and forth through the same arc. linear — the car travels a straight vertical path. reciprocating — the blade repeats a straight back-and-forth cutting stroke. rotary — the wheel turns fully around its central axle. reciprocating — the chisel repeatedly strikes along a straight line. oscillating — the ball swings through an arc about its suspension point. linear — boxes move in a single straight direction. rotary — the blades spin around a central axis. 2. input–process–output model mechanical systems are designed to convert an initial input into a desired output through a specific process. 1. input definition: the initial energy or force applied to a system. context: turning a handle or pressing a pedal supplies the energy that the rest of the system will act upon. materials/examples: a rider's push on a pedal, a hand-crank, a motor shaft. application: always the starting point of the chain — every mechanism needs an initial force or motion to work with. 2. process definition: the mechanism of components (gears, cams, levers) that manipulate the input energy. context: a bicycle's chain transmits motion from the pedals to the rear sprocket, changing speed and torque along the way. materials/examples: chains, gear trains, cams, levers, linkages. application: this is where a designer's choice of mechanism determines how the input is transformed — changing its speed, direction, or force. 3. output definition: the resulting action the system is designed to produce. context: rotating a wheel, lifting a load, or the rear wheel of a bicycle rotating to move it forward. materials/examples: a rotating wheel, a lifted load, a cut piece of material. application: the output is judged against the product's specification — if it fails to deliver the intended action, the process stage must be redesigned. activity: input–process–output breakdown challenge deconstruct each of the four everyday mechanical systems below into its input, process, and output. manual hand-crank pencil sharpener bicycle cable brakes hand-operated water well pump winged corkscrew (lever corkscrew) reveal answer key 1. manual hand-crank pencil sharpener input: rotational force applied by turning the hand crank. process: internal gears turn cylindrical cutting blades around the pencil tip. output: wood and graphite shaved away to create a sharp point. 2. bicycle cable brakes input: squeezing force applied by the rider's hand on the brake lever. process: cable tension pulls two caliper arms inward against a spring. output: friction rubber pads press against the wheel rim, slowing or stopping the bike. 3. hand-operated water well pump input: downward force applied by pushing down on the pump handle lever. process: the lever lifts a piston rod within a cylinder, opening and closing internal valves to create suction. output: water drawn up from below ground and discharged through the spout. 4. winged corkscrew input: downward force applied by pushing down the two raised side levers. process: interlocking gear teeth (rack and pinion) on the levers pull the central shaft straight up. output: the cork extracted vertically out of the bottle neck. 3. mechanical advantage (ma) mechanical advantage definition: the ratio of output force (load) to input force (effort), allowing a user to apply less force to move a load. context: manual winches use a ratchet and pawl to allow motion in only one direction, providing a high ma to lift heavy boat loads with minimal user effort. materials/examples: levers, pulleys, gear trains, winches. application: simple systems multiply force or change its direction to make tasks easier and more efficient for the user. formula: mechanical advantage (ma) = load ÷ effort activity: mechanical advantage calculation & application challenge apply the formula ma = load ÷ effort and your understanding of mechanical systems to solve these four scenarios. calculating ma: a mechanic uses a lever to lift an engine out of a car frame. the engine exerts a load force of 800 n, and the mechanic applies an effort force of 160 n. what is the mechanical advantage of the lever? finding required effort: a compound pulley system on a crane provides a mechanical advantage of 5. how much effort force must the winch motor exert to lift a 2,500 n steel beam? determining maximum load: a boat winch has a mechanical advantage of 8. if a person can exert 200 n of effort force on the hand crank, what is the maximum load force the winch can move? identifying components: when using a nutcracker to crack a walnut, identify what acts as the load and what acts as the effort. reveal answer key 1. ma = 5. ma = load ÷ effort = 800 n ÷ 160 n = 5. 2. effort = 500 n. effort = load ÷ ma = 2,500 n ÷ 5 = 500 n. 3. load = 1,600 n. load = ma × effort = 8 × 200 n = 1,600 n. 4. load: the structural resistance of the walnut shell resisting being crushed. effort: the squeezing force applied by the user's hand on the long handles. concept key idea real-world efficiency of gear systems ~150 min lesson 2: gear-driven systems, ratios, torque & efficiency gears consist of rotating toothed wheels that mesh to transmit rotary motion and power between shafts. in any pair of meshing gears, the gear connected to the power source (e.g. a motor, an engine, or a hand crank) is the driver gear , and the gear it turns is the driven gear . this lesson covers the main gear types, then how their size and arrangement can be used to deliberately trade speed for torque — and what that trade costs in efficiency. 1. types of gear systems 1. spur gears definition: gears used for parallel shafts, with teeth that project parallel to the gear's axis. context: simple cylindrical gears with straight teeth mesh side-by-side on parallel shafts to transfer motion in a basic gearbox. materials/examples: basic gearboxes, clocks, hand-cranked machinery. application: the simplest and most efficient gear type; the baseline against which other gear types are compared. 2. bevel gears definition: gears used for intersecting shafts, typically at a 90° angle. context: hand drills employ bevel gears to transmit power between the intersecting horizontal handle shaft and vertical drill bit shaft. materials/examples: hand drills, eggbeaters, car differentials. application: chosen whenever power must change direction between shafts that meet at an angle rather than running parallel. 3. rack and pinion definition: a mechanism that converts rotary motion into linear motion, using a fixed toothed bar (the rack) engaged with a smaller toothed wheel (the pinion). context: car steering systems use a pinion gear on the steering column to drive the rack, converting the driver's rotary input into the linear motion that turns the wheels. materials/examples: car steering, sliding security gates, some 3d printers. application: used whenever rotary input must be converted directly into a straight-line output. 4. worm gear definition: a screw-shaped gear providing high torque and low speed; non-reversible (self-locking). context: guitar tuning pegs utilise worm gears to ensure the strings remain under tension without slipping backward. materials/examples: guitar tuning pegs, boat winches, electric wheelchair tilt mechanisms. application: chosen specifically for its self-locking property, which lets a lifted or tensioned load hold safely in place without a separate brake. 5. ratchet and pawl definition: a mechanical device that allows motion in one direction only; a spring-loaded pawl fits into the teeth of a toothed ratchet wheel, preventing it from rotating backward while still allowing it to rotate forward. context: manual winches use a ratchet and pawl to allow motion in only one direction, providing a high mechanical advantage to lift heavy boat loads with minimal user effort. materials/examples: socket wrenches, boat winches, seatbelt retractors. application: chosen whenever a mechanism must build up motion in repeated small strokes without slipping backward between strokes. 6. idler gear definition: a gear placed between the driving and driven gears to change the rotational direction of the driven gear, or to fill a gap between them, without affecting the overall gear ratio. context: on a conveyor line, a driving gear needs to turn a driven gear on a parallel shaft in the same direction, so a middle idler gear is added between them to correct the direction. materials/examples: timing gear trains, multi-gear drivetrains, bicycle derailleurs. application: used whenever the output direction needs correcting, or extra centre distance needs bridging, without changing the speed or torque relationship between the driver and driven gears. 7. compound gear definition: two or more gears fixed to the same shaft, so the output of one gear becomes the input for the next gear in the system, enabling complex speed/torque relationships in a compact space. context: the internal mechanism of a mechanical wristwatch uses several compound gear stages to convert the fast rotation of the mainspring into the very slow rotation of the second, minute, and hour hands. materials/examples: wristwatches, gearboxes, cordless drill gear trains. application: chosen when a single gear pair cannot achieve the needed speed or torque change within the available space, so several smaller ratio changes are stacked in series. 8. planetary (epicyclic) gear definition: a compact gear system in which small "planet" gears rotate around a central "sun" gear while both are enclosed within an outer "ring" gear, allowing several different parts of the assembly. materials/examples: automatic transmissions, bicycle hub gears, cordless drill gearboxes, wind turbine gearboxes. application: chosen when a very high gear ratio or
