efficiency = (output energy ÷ input energy) × 100% in gear systems, efficiency is reduced mainly by friction between meshing teeth, heat generated in the lubricant, and losses in the supporting bearings. gears that roll against each other with minimal sliding (spur, helical, and bevel gears) are highly efficient, typically 96–99% per gear mesh. worm gears rely on a sliding, screw-like contact rather than rolling contact, so they lose far more energy to friction — efficiencies can range from roughly 20% to 90% depending on the design, even though worm gears are prized for their high torque and self-locking (non-reversible) properties. efficiency losses also compound in a gear train: if a system uses two gear meshes that are each 90% efficient, the overall efficiency of the train is only 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, or 81% — a key reason designers try to minimise the number of gear meshes in a drivetrain. case study: efficiency trade-offs in practice electric vehicles typically use a single-speed helical gear reduction (rather than a multi-speed gearbox) partly because it keeps the drivetrain simple and highly efficient, maximising the vehicle's range from the battery. in contrast, guitar tuning pegs and boat winches deliberately use lower-efficiency worm gears, because the trade-off — the mechanism locking in place and not slipping backward under load — is more valuable than raw efficiency. activity: gear efficiency challenge calculating efficiency: an electric screwdriver's motor supplies 12 j of input energy to its gear train. only 10.2 j is delivered as useful output energy at the screw tip. what is the efficiency of the gear train? comparing gear types: a designer is choosing between a helical gear set (98% efficient) and a worm gear set (55% efficient) to drive a conveyor belt that runs continuously for 10 hours a day. which would you recommend, and why? justifying a trade-off: despite being less efficient than spur or helical gears, worm gears are still commonly chosen for winches and lifting hoists. explain why. reveal answer key 1. efficiency = (10.2 ÷ 12) × 100% = 85%. 2. the helical gear set, because its higher efficiency (98% vs 55%) wastes far less energy as heat over a continuously running system, reducing electricity costs and the risk of the mechanism overheating during long operating hours. 3. worm gears are non-reversible (self-locking): once the motor stops turning, the driven gear cannot turn the worm shaft backward. this means a winch or hoist holds a lifted load safely in place without needing a separate brake, which is a critical safety benefit that outweighs the lower energy efficiency. a3.3.7 belt-driven systems a3.3.8 cam and follower systems a3.3.9 lever systems a3.3.10 linkage systems ~90 min lesson 3: belts, cams, levers and linkages not every mechanical system relies on toothed gears. this lesson covers four further families of mechanism — belts, cams, levers and linkages — each suited to a different job: transferring motion over distance, converting rotary motion into precise reciprocating movement, multiplying force around a pivot, or redirecting motion through an assembly of rigid links. 1. belt-driven and pulley systems belt-driven systems definition: a drive system that uses pulleys (grooved wheels) connected by flexible belt loops to transfer rotary motion over longer distances. context: washing machines use belt-driven systems and pulleys to rotate the drum quietly while absorbing shock during heavy, unbalanced loads. materials/examples: pulleys, flat belts, v-belts, timing belts, tensioners. application: quieter than gears and absorbs shock well, but may slip under very heavy loads — a useful overload-protection feature as well as a limitation. activity: belt-driven and pulley systems challenge distance transfer: why would a system designer prefer a belt-driven pulley system over a series of spur gears to transmit rotary motion between two shafts spaced 2 metres apart? system protection: how does the tendency of standard belts to "slip under very heavy loads" act as an unintentional safety benefit for a motor compared to rigid gear teeth? component function: what specific component is added to a belt-driven system to maintain proper belt tightness and prevent slippage as the belt wears or stretches over time? belt matching: match each belt type (flat belt, v-belt, or timing belt) to its application: (a) high-torque transmission using a wedge shape in grooved pulleys; (b) precise, non-slip synchronisation with teeth engaging pulley grooves (e.g. 3d printers, engine timing); (c) simple, high-speed power transfer across flat cylindrical pulleys over longer distances. shock absorption: why are washing machines designed with belt systems rather than direct gear trains to rotate the washing drum during unbalanced spin cycles? reveal answer key 1. belts efficiently span long distances using flexible loops, whereas gears would require a heavy, complex, and costly train of intermediate idler gears to bridge the same gap. 2. slippage allows the belt to spin freely if the output jams, protecting the motor from burning out and preventing structural damage to other components. 3. a tensioner — it applies constant force to the belt to maintain proper tension and eliminate slack. 4. a: v-belt. b: timing belt. c: flat belt. 5. belts absorb mechanical shocks and vibrations caused by sloshing water and heavy, shifting clothes, keeping the appliance quiet and preventing mechanical fatigue. 2. cam and follower systems cam and follower definition: a cam is a specially shaped rotating disc that pushes a follower to convert rotary motion into reciprocating or oscillating motion. context: automobile engines use cams to convert rotary motion into the reciprocating motion required to open and close valves at precise intervals. materials/examples: pear, circular (eccentric), triangular, oval, and snail cam profiles dictate the timing and movement of the follower. application: chosen whenever a repeating, precisely-timed reciprocating or oscillating movement must be driven from a continuously rotating shaft. discussion watch the cam animation above. as the disc rotates at a constant speed, does the follower always move at a constant speed? why might a designer deliberately choose an irregular cam profile (like a snail or pear shape) rather than a simple circular one? 3. lever systems a lever is a rigid bar pivoting on a fulcrum, with effort applied to move a load. the order of the fulcrum, effort and load determines the class of lever, and mechanical advantage can also be expressed as ma = length of effort arm ÷ length of resistance arm. 1st class lever definition: the fulcrum is located between the effort and the load. context: scissors and a seesaw both pivot on a central point between the effort applied by the user and the load being cut or lifted. materials/examples: scissors, seesaws, pliers, crowbars. application: can be used to multiply force, multiply distance/speed, or simply change direction, depending on where the fulcrum sits relative to the load and effort. 2nd class lever definition: the load is located between the effort and the fulcrum. context: wheelbarrows use second-class levers to allow users to move heavy construction materials with reduced effort. materials/examples: wheelbarrows, bottle openers, nutcrackers. application: always produces a mechanical advantage greater than 1, making it well suited to lifting heavy loads. 3rd class lever definition: the effort is located between the fulcrum and the load. context: tweezers, and the human forearm, apply effort between the pivot and the object being held. materials/examples: tweezers, fishing rods, the human forearm. application: trades force for speed and range of movement — useful for precise or fast movements rather than heavy lifting. 4. linkage systems linkages are assemblies of rigid links (bars) connected by pivots, used to change the direction or magnitude of a force or motion. parallel linkage definition: keeps input and output motion in the same direction. context: car suspensions use parallel linkages so the wheel can move up and down while staying aligned with the car body. materials/examples: car suspension arms, some desk lamp arms. application: used when output motion must mirror input motion without changing its direction. reverse linkage definition: moves the output in the opposite direction to the input. context: windshield wipers use reverse linkages so that as one arm sweeps one way, a connected arm sweeps the opposite way. materials/examples: windscreen wiper linkages, some scissor mechanisms. application: used whenever a mechanism needs an output that mirrors the input in the opposite direction. bell crank definition: transfers motion around corners, usually through a 90° angle. context: bicycle brake systems use a bell crank where the cable pull must change direction to reach the calipers; bicycle steering also uses this principle to ensure handlebar input results in the desired steering direction. materials/examples: bicycle brake and steering linkages, aircraft control surfaces. application: used whenever a force or motion must be redirected around a corner rather than transmitted in a straight line. practical engagement: mechanical disassembly audit task: take apart a manual product (e.g. a hand drill, wind-up toy, or can opener). before disassembly, predict the mechanism's function to test your observation skills. outcome: identify each component (gears, cams, levers, linkages) and map the full input–process–output chain for the product, noting the class of any levers and the type of any gears you find. system function real-world example belt-driven system transfers rotary motion over distance; quiet and shock-absorbing washing machine drum cam and follower converts rotary motion into precisely-timed reciprocating/oscillating motion engine valve timing 1st class lever fulcrum between effort and load scissors 2nd class lever load between effort and fulcrum wheelbarrow 3rd class lever effort between fulcrum and load tweezers parallel linkage output moves in the same direction as input car suspension reverse linkage output moves opposite to input windscreen wipers bell crank redirects motion, usually through 90° bicycle brake cable routing linking questions use these to connect topic a3.3 to other areas of the syllabus and to stimulate class discussion or extended-response practice. c1.2 inclusive design: how can mechanical advantage (levers and gear ratios) be used to enable inclusive design for users with reduced strength? b1.1 user-centred design: how might a task analysis of a product reveal that a mechanical system, rather than the product's overall form, is the true source of a usability pain point? c4.1 design for manufacture: why might a designer choose a less efficient mechanism (e.g. a worm gear) if it reduces the number of components needed elsewhere in the product? a3.3 exam practice ao1 / ao2 / ao3 exam practice: topic a3.3 questions below follow the command-term expectations and mark-allocation logic used in paper 1 and paper 2. sample/indicative answers for teacher use follow each question. section a: multiple choice (2 questions, 1 mark each) 1. which type of motion is best described as a repetitive back-and-forth movement in a straight line? rotary oscillating reciprocating linear reveal answer c. reciprocating. [1] 2. a driver gear with 10 teeth meshes with a driven gear with 40 teeth. which statement correctly describes the output of the driven gear compared to the input of the driver gear? higher speed, lower torque lower speed, higher torque same speed, same torque higher speed, higher torque reveal answer b. lower speed, higher torque. [1] section b: short answer (2 questions) question 3 [3 marks] describe the input, process, and output of a bicycle's chain and sprocket system. reveal answer [3] award for input (the user applies force/rotary motion to the pedals); for process (the chain transmits motion to the rear sprocket); and for output (the rear wheel rotates to move the bicycle forward). question 4 [3 marks] a gear train used in a cordless drill has an overall efficiency of 80%. if the motor supplies 15 j of input energy, calculate the useful output energy delivered to the drill bit, and state one reason why the gear train is not 100% efficient. reveal answer [3] award for correct substitution into the efficiency formula; award for the correct answer (output = 0.80 × 15 j = 12 j); award for a valid reason (e.g. friction between meshing teeth, heat loss, or bearing/lubrication losses). section c: extended response (2 questions) question 5 [4 marks] explain how a multidisciplinary design team might use mechanical systems to enable inclusive design for elderly users. reveal answer [4] identify that mechanical advantage is the key factor. explain how engineers (multidisciplinary team) might use levers or gear ratios to reduce the physical effort needed for a task (e.g. a jar opener or stair lift), thereby making the product usable for those with reduced muscle strength or arthritis. question 6 [4 marks] discuss why a designer might choose a worm gear system over a spur gear system for an electric wheelchair's tilt mechanism, despite the worm gear being less energy efficient. reveal answer [4] award for identifying that worm gears are non-reversible/self-locking, meaning the tilt mechanism cannot slip backward under the user's weight if power is lost, which is a critical safety requirement. award for acknowledging the trade-off that worm gears have lower efficiency (more energy/heat lost to friction from sliding contact) than spur gears. award for a balanced conclusion that safety and reliability outweigh the efficiency cost in this safety-critical application. a3.3 glossary glossary: topic a3.3 — mechanical systems (hl) click on a term to reveal its definition. 1st-class lever a lever where the fulcrum is located between the effort force and the load (resistance force). for example, a seesaw or a pair of scissors. 2nd-class lever a lever where the load (resistance force) is located between the effort force and the fulcrum. for example, a wheelbarrow. 3rd-class lever a lever where the effort force is located between the fulcrum and the load (resistance force). for example, tweezers and most human limbs are 3rd-class levers. belt-driven system a drive system where a belt transfers power between at least two pulleys. one pulley drives the belt (driver pulley) and the other is driven by the belt (driven pulley). bell crank linkage a linkage that allows vertical movement to be converted into horizontal movement. it also works the opposite way around. bevel gear a pair of toothed rotating gears used to transfer power between two gear shafts at an angle, usually 90°, to the original. cam a mechanical component used to transform rotational motion into linear motion. compound gear comprises two or more gears forming a connected system. the output of one gear is used as the input for another gear in the same system. driver/driven gear the driver gear is directly connected to the power source and initiates motion; the driven gear is turned by the driver (directly or through intermediate gears). for example, in a car steering system, the pinion gear on the steering column is the driver, and the rack it moves along is the driven component. efficiency (mechanical) the ratio of useful output energy (or power) to input energy (or power) in a system, expressed as a percentage; real systems are always below 100% due to losses such as friction and heat. for example, a helical gear reduction in an electric car drivetrain is around 97–98% efficient, helping maximise the vehicle's driving range. fulcrum (lever) the fixed point around which the lever rotates, also known as a "pivot". gears a toothed wheel that interlocks with another to transmit motion or change the speed and/or direction of motion. gear ratio the ratio of the number of teeth on the driven gear to the number of teeth on the driver gear, used to predict how a gear system changes output speed and torque. for example, a bicycle in a 5:1 low gear turns the pedals five times to rotate the rear wheel once, trading speed for the extra torque needed to climb a hill. idler gear a gear in a gear train that is used between the driving and driven gears. it is used to change the rotational direction of the driven gear or to fill a gap between the gears without affecting the speed ratio. lever a beam resting on a fulcrum that has effort applied to it to move a load. the order of the fulcrum, effort and load determines the class of lever. levers (mechanical advantage) mechanical advantage (ma) = length of effort arm (ea) ÷ length of resistance arm (ra). load an amount of force applied to a surface or body. linear motion movement in a straight line. linkage a mechanical device comprised of components that are joined together in a defined sequence in order to change the direction or magnitude of a force. mechanical advantage the ratio of output force compared to input force in a mechanical system. mechanical system a set of physical components that convert an input force and motion into a desired output force and motion. module (gear) a measure of tooth size, calculated as pitch diameter divided by the number of teeth; gears must share the same module to mesh correctly. for example, replacement gears in a repaired machine must be manufactured to the same module as the originals or they will not mesh with the surrounding gears. oscillating motion the motion of an object that repeatedly moves over a point. parallel linkage a central moving point of the linkage that is constrained to travel on a nearly straight line. pulley a grooved wheel that uses a rope, cord, chain or cable to transmit energy and motion. rack and pinion a mechanical device using a fixed bar that engages with a smaller toothed wheel that converts rotary to linear motion. ratchet and pawl a mechanical device that allows motion in one direction only. the pawl fits into the teeth of the toothed ratchet and prevents it from rotating backwards, while allowing it to rotate forwards. reciprocating motion a repetitive motion in a straight line. reverse linkage a linkage that is used to move the force in the opposite direction. rotary motion the motion of an object that spins on its own axis. spur gear a toothed gear where the teeth project parallel to the gear's axis. torque the rotational (turning) equivalent of force, calculated as force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot, measured in newton-metres (nm). for example, an electric screwdriver uses a gear train to convert its motor's fast, low-torque rotation into the slow, high-torque rotation needed to drive a screw without stalling. worm gear a mechanical component typically formed as a threaded shaft that interlocks with a toothed gear or worm wheel. 1st-class lever 2nd-class lever 3rd-class lever belt-driven system bell crank linkage bevel gear cam compound gear fulcrum (lever) gears idler gear lever levers (effort) levers (load) levers (mechanical advantage) load linear motion linkage mechanical advantage mechanical system oscillating motion parallel linkage pulley rack and pinion ratchet and pawl reciprocating motion reverse linkage rotary motion spur gear worm gear driver/driven gear efficiency (mechanical) gear ratio module (gear) torque there are four types of motion involved in mechanical systems. mechanical systems convert an input into an output. mechanical systems can provide a mechanical advantage to the user. mechanical systems are used to increase or decrease the speed, direction or power of a motion. the four types of motion can be combined to create simple or complex mechanical systems. gears transmit rotary motion from one gear shaft to another, and have a number of teeth. belt-driven systems are driven by pulleys. the shape of a cam dictates the type of motion. levers comprise a beam acting on a fulcrum (pivot) and are classed based on the relative position of the fulcrum to an applied load and effort. linkages are used to change the direction of a movement, alter the magnitude of a force or make parts of a system move in a particular way.

title: Introduction to electronic systems

sections.title: Lesson 1: The System Model & Designer Responsibility
sections.html:
3.4.1 System Model 3.4.2 Ubiquity & Responsibility ~50 min

Lesson 1: The System Model & Designer Responsibility

Electronic systems can be analysed as input, process and output. Some systems also use feedback from a measured output to control their behaviour. A thermostat measures achieved temperature; a simple presence sensor is an input, not necessarily output feedback.

Hook: Cruise Control

Closed-loop example: a thermostat senses actual room temperature, compares it with a set point and switches the heater. The resulting temperature is measured again. A hand-presence sensor simply supplies an input unless a controlled output is measured.

1. The System Model: Input, Process, Output, Feedback

Definition: Input is a signal or data — from a sensor or switch — that initiates the process. Process is the circuitry or component (e.g. a microcontroller) that transforms the input signal. Output is the final result, action or display the system produces. Feedback is information about the output returned to the system to adjust the process and maintain stability.

Closed-loop example: a thermostat senses actual room temperature, compares it with a set point and switches the heater. The resulting temperature is measured again. A hand-presence sensor simply supplies an input unless a controlled output is measured.

Materials/Examples: Torch, motion-sensor light, musical greeting card, cruise control.

Application: Try this — take any unfamiliar product and label its four stages without opening the casing.

Practical Activity: The Black Box Challenge

Choose a safe, low-voltage everyday electronic product without opening it. From observation, sketch input → process → output. Identify whether a controlled output is actually measured; include feedback only where you can justify it. Swap diagrams and challenge one assumption.

2. Ubiquity and Responsibility

Definition: Electronics are embedded in nearly every modern product. Designers must identify products that are safe for the user, and must prioritise energy efficiency and minimal energy use.

Context: A phone charger left plugged in still draws a small "phantom load" 24/7; a poorly insulated smart-home hub can overheat. Designers are responsible for choices most users never see — from standby power draw to the plastic casing that stops a child touching a live wire.

Materials/Examples: Phone chargers, smart-home hubs, plastic casings, child-safety design.

Application: Next time you look at an everyday device, weigh up its safety and energy-efficiency trade-offs, not just what it does.

Practical Activity: 60-Second Electronics Audit

Scan the room (or recall your journey to school) and list as many electronic products as you can in 60 seconds. In pairs, pick your top 3 and rate each 1–5 for safety design and 1–5 for energy efficiency, then be ready to justify your harshest score to the class in one sentence.

StageRoleThermostat example
InputMeasured signal and user settingRoom temperature and selected set point
ProcessCompare input with targetController decides whether heating is required
OutputActuator changes the systemHeater supplies thermal energy
FeedbackMeasure the controlled resultSensor measures achieved room temperature again

sections.title: Lesson 2: Analogue vs. Digital Systems
sections.html:
3.4.3–3.4.5 Analogue vs Digital ~50 min

Lesson 2: Analogue vs. Digital Systems

Now that you can see a system's stages, this lesson asks what kind of signal is actually moving through them. The analogue/digital distinction sounds abstract until you tie it to something you touch every day: a dimmer switch versus a light switch, or a vinyl record versus a streamed song.

Hook: Dimmer or Switch?

Picture a dimmer switch next to a standard light switch. Which one gives you infinite control, and which one only gives you two states? That's the whole lesson in one comparison.

1. Analogue Systems

Definition: Analogue systems use continually changing signals, often shown as sine waves, and are described by voltage, current and frequency.

Context: A dimmer switch allows infinite brightness levels — a continuously variable signal, not a set of steps.

Materials/Examples: Dimmer switches, vinyl records, thermometers with a needle dial.

Application: Look for continuous, smooth change rather than discrete steps — that's your clue it's analogue.

2. Digital Systems

Definition: Digital systems store and process information as discrete values — binary digits (0/1) or on/off signals — and rely on logic gates to control signal flow.

Context: A standard light switch controlling an LED driver is digital — fully on or fully off — even though the light itself looks smooth to the eye.

Materials/Examples: Streaming audio, smartphones, digital thermostats.

Application: Don't assume "looks smooth" means analogue — digital systems can simulate continuity through very fine steps.

Case Study: Vinyl vs Streaming

Vinyl records are analogue sound waves cut physically into a groove. Streaming audio carries the same sound broken into millions of binary snapshots. Both can sound identical to your ear — the difference is entirely in how the signal is stored and processed.

Practical Activity: Dimmer vs. Switch, Live

Using a real (or simulated) dimmer switch and a toggle switch on identical bulbs, sketch the signal each produces over time — a smooth wave for the dimmer, a stepped on/off line for the switch — and label which is analogue and which is digital, with one reason each.

PropertyAnalogueDigital
Signal typeContinuously variableDiscrete values (0/1, on/off)
Described byVoltage, current, frequencyBinary digits, logic states
Control elementDirect physical variationLogic gates
ExampleDimmer switch, vinyl recordLED on/off, streamed audio

sections.title: Lesson 3: Electronic Components — Passive vs. Active
sections.html:
3.4.6 Electronic Components ~50 min

Lesson 3: Electronic Components — Passive vs. Active

Every circuit is built from components that either just sit there shaping the flow of electricity, or actively make decisions about it. Once you can sort components into passive and active, you've got the vocabulary to describe what's actually happening inside the "process" stage of any system.

Hook: Inside a Torch

Inside a torch, the resistor protecting the LED is passive — it just limits current. So what's the difference between a component that limits something and one that switches something on and off in response to a signal?

1. Passive Components

Definition: Passive components do not control the flow of electricity — this group includes fixed and variable resistors, capacitors, switches and relays.

Context: A fixed resistor in a torch limits current so the LED doesn't burn out — it shapes the flow but never makes a decision about it.

Materials/Examples: Resistors, capacitors, switches, relays.

Application: Look for components that limit, store or route current without amplifying or switching it based on a signal — those are your passives.

2. Active Components

Definition: Active components control or amplify the flow of electricity — this group includes diodes and transistors.

Context: The transistor switching a motor on and off in response to a signal is active — it's making a decision about current flow, not just limiting it.

Materials/Examples: Diodes, transistors, integrated circuits.

Application: Look for components that respond to or amplify a signal, effectively "deciding" what happens next in the circuit — those are your actives.

Practical Activity: Component Sort-Off

In small groups, you'll get a mixed bag (or image set) of components: resistor, capacitor, switch, relay, diode, transistor. In 3 minutes, sort them into two piles — Passive and Active — and be ready to defend one tricky choice (relay or switch) when asked.

ComponentTypeRole in a Circuit
Fixed / variable resistorPassiveLimits current flow
CapacitorPassiveStores an electric charge; smooths fluctuations
SwitchPassivePhysically opens/closes a circuit
RelayPassive (borderline — discuss)Uses an electromagnet to switch a separate circuit
DiodeActiveAllows current flow in one direction only

sections.text: 3.4.6 Electronic Components ~50 min Lesson 3: Electronic Components — Passive vs. Active Every circuit is built from components that either just sit there shaping the flow of electricity, or actively make decisions about it. Once you can sort components into passive and active, you've got the vocabulary to describe what's actually happening inside the "process" stage of any system. Hook: Inside a Torch Inside a torch, the resistor protecting the LED is passive — it just limits current. So what's the difference between a component that limits something and one that switches something on and off in response to a signal? 1. Passive Components Definition: Passive components do not control the flow of electricity — this group includes fixed and variable resistors, capacitors, switches and relays. Context: A fixed resistor in a torch limits current so the LED doesn't burn out — it shapes the flow but never makes a decision about it. Materials/Examples: Resistors, capacitors, switches, relays. Application: Look for components that limit, store or route current without amplifying or switching it based on a signal — those are your passives. 2. Active Components Definition: Active components control or amplify the flow of electricity — this group includes diodes and transistors. Context: The transistor switching a motor on and off in response to a signal is active — it's making a decision about current flow, not just limiting it. Materials/Examples: Diodes, transistors, integrated circuits. Application: Look for components that respond to or amplify a signal, effectively "deciding" what happens next in the circuit — those are your actives. Practical Activity: Component Sort-Off In small groups, you'll get a mixed bag (or image set) of components: resistor, capacitor, switch, relay, diode, transistor. In 3 minutes, sort them into two piles — Passive and Active — and be ready to defend one tricky choice (relay or switch) when asked. sections.title: Lesson 4: System Stages in Detail — Input, Processing & Output Devices
sections.html:
3.4.7–3.4.10 Input, Processing & Output Devices ~50–60 min

Lesson 4: System Stages in Detail — Input, Processing & Output Devices

This lesson zooms back out to the full system loop from Lesson 1, but now fills each stage with real hardware. You'll move from naming "input, process, output" in the abstract to naming the actual sensor, microcontroller and output device a real product would use.

Hook: The Hand Dryer, Revisited

An automatic hand dryer: an infrared sensor (input) detects hands, a microcontroller (process) checks the signal against a threshold, and a motor and heater (outputs) activate. Swap the sensor for a sound sensor and the same processing logic could trigger a completely different product.

1. Input Devices

Definition: Input devices detect environmental stimuli — switches and sensors for light, temperature, humidity and sound.

Context: An LDR (Light Dependent Resistor) detects when it gets dark to trigger a street light — the sensor is the system's connection to the physical world.

Materials/Examples: Light sensors, temperature sensors, humidity sensors, sound sensors, switches.

Application: Given a design scenario, practise matching the stimulus (light, heat, sound) to the correct sensor type.

2. Processing Devices

Definition: Processing devices translate input into output — signal conditioning for analogue data, program control for digital data. A microcontroller (PIC) acts as the programmable "brain" carrying out processing tasks.

Context: An Arduino board's microcontroller is the same kind of "brain" used by students to build functional prototypes in the design lab.

Materials/Examples: Microcontrollers (PIC, Arduino), signal-conditioning circuits.

Application: Be ready to explain what "processing" actually does to a signal — it's not just a black box, it's a decision-making or conditioning step.

3. Output Devices

Definition: Output devices perform a function in response to a stimulus — motors, haptics, buzzers, speakers, headphones, printers, lights, plotters, relays, braille displays, LEDs and LCDs.

Context: A buzzer provides an audible alert in a microwave when the timer reaches zero — a simple, single-purpose output.

Materials/Examples: Motors, buzzers, LEDs, LCDs, speakers, braille displays.

Application: When choosing an output device for a design scenario, think about the user first (e.g. braille displays for accessibility).

Practical Activity: Design-a-Response Sprint

Working alone, choose one everyday product (automatic tap, streetlight, fire alarm, vending machine) and complete a 4-box diagram naming a specific real input device, processing device, and output device for it. If you finish first with a correct diagram, you'll read it aloud for the class to guess the product.

ProductInput DeviceProcessing DeviceOutput Device
Automatic hand dryerInfrared sensorMicrocontroller (threshold check)Motor + heater
Street lightLDR (light sensor)MicrocontrollerLED lamp
Microwave timerTimer / keypad switchMicrocontroller (countdown logic)Buzzer

sections.title: Lesson 5: Advanced Control & Representation
sections.html:
3.4.11–3.4.14 Advanced Control & Representation ~50–60 min

Lesson 5: Advanced Control & Representation

This final lesson raises the sophistication of the system model: does the system correct itself, or just run blind on a timer? You'll also meet the amplifiers and embedded computers that make modern feedback possible, and the standard symbols used to document it all — the shared language that leads directly into B3.4.

Hook: Toaster vs. Thermostat

A toaster on a timer is open-loop — it stops when the clock runs out, whether the toast is burnt or not. A thermostat is closed-loop — it keeps checking the room temperature against a target and adjusts continuously. Which would you trust to cook an egg perfectly?

1. Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Systems

Definition: Open-loop systems have no feedback; closed-loop systems are self-regulating via feedback.

Context: A toaster on a timer (open-loop) vs. a thermostat (closed-loop) — both are common household devices, but only one corrects itself.

Materials/Examples: Toaster, thermostat, oven timer, cruise control, kettle, automatic blinds.

Application: To classify a product as open- or closed-loop, ask yourself: does it check its own output?

2. Operational Amplifiers (Op-Amps)

Definition: Operational amplifiers are high-gain voltage amplifiers used to amplify weak sensor signals in analogue circuits.

Context: An op-amp can amplify the tiny electrical signal from a heart rate monitor so it can be displayed on a screen.

Materials/Examples: Heart rate monitors, weak analogue sensor circuits.

Application: Be ready to explain why a weak sensor signal often needs amplifying before a processing device can use it.

3. Embedded Systems

Definition: Embedded systems are computerised systems built into everyday products to increase automation and efficiency.

Context: The dedicated computer system inside an Anti-lock Braking System (ABS) in a car is an embedded system — purpose-built for one job.

Materials/Examples: ABS in cars, smart appliances, IoT devices.

Application: Remember: embedded systems are computers dedicated to a single product function, not general-purpose computers.

4. Circuit Diagrams & Standard Symbols

Definition: Circuit diagrams represent electronic functions using standardised symbols for all components covered in this unit.

Context: Both a toaster and a thermostat would be documented using the same standard circuit symbols, regardless of whether they're open- or closed-loop.

Materials/Examples: Resistor, capacitor, diode, transistor and switch symbols.

Application: Practise drawing and recognising standard symbols so you can read circuit diagrams consistently across any product.

Case Study: Cruise Control as Closed-Loop

Cruise control continuously checks vehicle speed against the target speed and adjusts the throttle — a textbook closed-loop system, and a natural bridge back to the feedback stage you met in Lesson 1.

Practical Activity: Open Loop, Closed Loop, Go!

Your teacher will call out household products (toaster, thermostat, oven timer, cruise control, kettle, automatic blinds). Move to one side of the room for "open-loop" and the other for "closed-loop" within 5 seconds — no discussion. After debriefing any disagreements as a class, sketch the standard circuit symbol for two components of your choice.

sections.title: Exam Prep: A3.4 Introduction to Electronic Systems
sections.html:
A3.4 Exam Prep

Exam Prep: A3.4 Introduction to Electronic Systems

Test yourself on this unit. Work through the multiple choice questions first, then try the short answers before revealing the markscheme — you'll learn more from attempting an answer than from reading one.

Section A: Multiple Choice

1. In the input–process–output–feedback model, which stage is responsible for adjusting the process to maintain stability?

  • Input
  • Process
  • Output
  • Feedback
Reveal Answer
D — Feedback. [1] Feedback returns information about the output to the system so the process can be adjusted.

2. Which of the following is an active component?

  • Fixed resistor
  • Capacitor
  • Transistor
  • Switch
Reveal Answer
C — Transistor. [1] Transistors control or amplify the flow of electricity; the other options are passive.

3. A thermostat that continuously checks room temperature and adjusts the heater is an example of:

  • An open-loop system
  • A closed-loop system
  • An analogue-only system
  • A passive system
Reveal Answer
B — Closed-loop system. [1] The output (room temperature) is fed back in as an input, making the system self-regulating.

Section B: Short Answer

4. Distinguish between analogue and digital systems, using an example of each. [4 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Analogue systems use a continually/permanently variable signal, described by voltage, current and frequency.

[1] Example: a dimmer switch, which allows a continuous range of brightness.

[1] Digital systems store/process information as discrete values — binary digits (0/1) or on/off signals.

[1] Example: a streamed audio file, which represents sound as binary snapshots.

5. Explain, with reference to a named product, the role of an input device, a processing device, and an output device in an electronic system. [6 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Named product identified, e.g. automatic hand dryer.

[2] Input device named and explained, e.g. an infrared sensor detects the presence of hands beneath the nozzle.

[2] Processing device named and explained, e.g. a microcontroller checks the sensor signal against a threshold to decide whether to activate.

[1] Output device named, e.g. a motor and heater activate to dry the hands.

6. Discuss the responsibility of a designer when incorporating electronic systems into a product, referring to safety and energy efficiency. [4 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Designers must ensure products are safe for the user, e.g. casing that prevents contact with live components.

[1] Example given, e.g. a child unable to touch a live wire due to protective casing.

[1] Designers must prioritise energy efficiency / minimal energy use, e.g. reducing standby "phantom load".

[1] Example given, e.g. a phone charger drawing power even when not charging a device.

sections.title: Glossary of Key Terms
sections.html:
A3.4 Glossary

Glossary of Key Terms

Click on a term to reveal its definition.

Active Components
IB Definition: Electronic components that control the flow of electricity.
Real-World Example: Transistors used to amplify weak signals or act as switches in computers.
Ampere
IB Definition: An electrical current.
Real-World Example: Measuring the current draw of a motor to ensure a battery won't drain too quickly.
Analogue System
IB Definition: An electronic system that has a permanently variable signal.
Real-World Example: A dimmer switch that allows for a continuous range of light brightness.
Binary Digit
IB Definition: A digit that has either a value of 0 or 1.
Real-World Example: The fundamental language used by a microcontroller to process data.
Buzzer
IB Definition: An electronic device that emits a buzzing noise when activated.
Real-World Example: Providing an audible alert in a microwave when the timer reaches zero.
Capacitor
IB Definition: An electronic component used to store an electric charge.
Real-World Example: Used in power supplies to smooth out voltage fluctuations and prevent flickering.
Closed-Loop System
IB Definition: A self-regulating, automated system where the output is considered feedback and acts as an input back into the system.
Real-World Example: A thermostat that monitors room temperature and adjusts the heater to maintain a set point.
Current
IB Definition: The flow of electricity in a circuit resulting from the movement of charged particles.
Real-World Example: Like the amount of water flowing through a hose; limited by resistance.
Control Circuit
IB Definition: A circuit that carries signals that direct the performance of a controller.
Real-World Example: The internal logic of a washing machine that dictates when the drum should spin or drain.
Digital System
IB Definition: An electronic system that uses binary signals (0 or 1, on or off).
Real-World Example: Modern computers and smartphones that process data as discrete packets of information.
Diode
IB Definition: An electronic device that allows the flow of current in one direction only.
Real-World Example: Acts as a one-way valve to protect sensitive circuits from incorrect battery insertion.
Embedded System
IB Definition: A computerized system designed to perform a specific set of real-world functions.
Real-World Example: The dedicated computer system inside an Anti-lock Braking System (ABS) in a car.
Feedback Loop
IB Definition: A process in which an output is "fed back" to the system as an input.
Real-World Example: Adjusting the speed of a drone's motors based on wind resistance detected by sensors.
Hertz (Hz)
IB Definition: The standard unit of frequency; equal to one cycle per second.
Real-World Example: The refresh rate of a computer monitor or the frequency of a radio signal.
Integrated Circuit
IB Definition: A small component comprised of a self-contained circuit that performs the same function as a larger circuit.
Real-World Example: A microchip in a calculator that contains thousands of individual components in one package.
Internet of Things (IoT)
IB Definition: Everyday objects interconnected through the internet, enabling them to send and receive data.
Real-World Example: A smart refrigerator that notifies your phone when you are low on milk.
Logic Gate
IB Definition: A device performing a Boolean function that controls whether a signal can pass to the output.
Real-World Example: A security alarm that only sounds if (Sensor A AND Sensor B) are both triggered.
Microcontroller
IB Definition: An electronic device used to control specific operations in an embedded system; a compact integrated circuit.
Real-World Example: The "brain" of an Arduino board used by students to build functional prototypes.
Operational Amplifier
IB Definition: A high-gain voltage amplifier that amplifies weak signals.
Real-World Example: Amplifying the tiny electrical signal from a heart rate monitor so it can be displayed on a screen.
Passive Components
IB Definition: Electronic components that do not have any control over the flow of electricity.
Real-World Example: Fixed resistors used to limit current so an LED doesn't burn out.
Power
IB Definition: The rate at which electrical energy is transferred by an electric circuit (measured in Watts).
Real-World Example: Calculating how much energy a power tool uses to ensure the circuit breaker won't trip.
Resistance
IB Definition: The opposition to the flow of electrons in an electrical circuit.
Real-World Example: Like sand in a water hose that slows down the flow; measured in Ohms (Ω).
Sensor
IB Definition: An electronic input device that detects or measures an input from the physical environment.
Real-World Example: An LDR (Light Dependent Resistor) that detects when it gets dark to turn on a street light.
Voltage
IB Definition: An electromotive force that pushes electrons through a circuit; also considered electric pressure.
Real-World Example: Like the water pressure in a hose that determines how much "push" the electricity has.

Voltage V is measured in volts (V), current I in amperes (A), resistance R in ohms (Ω), power P in watts (W), time t in seconds (s), and frequency f in hertz (Hz). The quantity symbol and unit symbol are different roles: write I = 0.020 A.

Case matters: 1 mΩ = 0.001 Ω while 1 MΩ = 1,000,000 Ω. Convert prefixes before substituting into equations. For a 2.2 kΩ resistor with 3 mA: V = IR = 0.003 × 2200 = 6.6 V.

Four-minute prefix relay

sections.title: Feedback measures the controlled result · A3.4.11
sections.html:
A closed-loop system compares a measured output with a target and adjusts its action. A thermostat measures achieved room temperature and switches heating to reduce the difference from the set point. An open-loop timer runs a heater for a fixed duration without measuring achieved temperature.

Detecting hands is an input to a hand dryer. Rechecking whether hands remain does not by itself prove that the dryer measures its controlled output. Always name the controlled quantity and the sensor that measures it before identifying output feedback.

Feedback detective · 5 minutes

Sketch two irrigation systems: one waters for ten minutes on a timer; the other measures soil moisture and stops at a target. Label input, process, output and feedback where present. Predict what each does after heavy rain.

sections.title: Circuit symbols: read, draw and trace
sections.html:
Read the circuit before building it

Common component symbols communicate electrical connections rather than physical layout. The LED arrows point outwards; the LDR arrows point towards the light-sensitive resistor. A cell uses unequal parallel lines. A battery is represented by multiple cell pairs.

Draw, trace, explain · 8 minutes

  1. Sketch a cell, switch, resistor and LED in one series loop. Mark the LED orientation and the positive terminal.
  2. Trace conventional current around the closed circuit. Explain why opening the switch interrupts the current.
  3. Calculate a suitable resistor in the Light it responsibly virtual lab before a teacher-supervised low-voltage build.
  4. Swap drawings. Identify one error in connectivity rather than changing the physical placement.

These are simplified educational symbols. Use the symbol convention specified by your teacher and the component datasheet.

glossary.definition: Electronic components that control the flow of electricity.
An electrical current.
An electronic system that has a permanently variable signal.
A binary digit has either a value of 0 or 1.
An electronic device that emits a buzzing noise when activated.
An electronic component used to store an electric charge.
A self-regulating, automated system where the output is considered feedback and acts as an input back into the system.
The flow of electricity in a circuit that results from the movement of electrically charged particles.
A circuit that carries signals that direct the performance of a controller.
An electronic system that uses binary signals, i.e. 0 or 1, on or off.
An electronic device that allows the flow of current in one direction only.
A selection of electronic components joined together via a conducting material in a system that performs a function.
A system powered by electricity that receives an input as information, processes that information and produces a desired output.
A computerized system designed to perform a specific set of real-world functions.
An essential element to create a closed system, a feedback loop is a process in which an output is “fed back” to the system as an input.
The standard unit of frequency in an electrical system. One hertz is equal to one cycle per second.
A resistor that has a defined value of electrical resistance that is not adjustable.
The rate at which current changes from positive to negative per second in a signal measure in hertz (Hz).
What is put into a system.
A component of a system used to put information into that system. For example, a switch or a sensor.
A small component comprised of a self-contained electrical circuit that performs the same function as a larger circuit made from individual components.
Everyday objects and devices that contain computing devices that are interconnected through the internet, enabling them to send and receive data.
An electronic device that allows the flow of current in one direction only, and glows when current runs through it.
An electronic device that consists of a flat panel display that uses liquid crystal molecules controlled by an electric field.
A device that performs a Boolean function in a digital system that controls whether an input signal can pass through to the output.
An electronic device used to control specific operations in an embedded system. It is a compact integrated circuit.
An electronic device that converts electrical energy into a rotary motion.
A unit of electrical resistance.
A control system that does not have any feedback.
An electronic device that amplifies weak signals.
What comes out of a system.
Electronic components that do not have any control over the flow of electricity.
The rate at which electrical energy is transferred by an electric circuit. See resistance.
Components that are responsible for interpreting, manipulating and storing data in an electronic system.

A small component comprised of a self-contained electrical circuit that performs the same function as a larger circuit made from individual components and that can be programmed to respond in a certain way.
An electronic device that is activated by current or a signal to open or close another circuit.

The opposition to the flow of electrons in an electrical circuit. The relationship between voltage (V), current (I) and resistance (R) is known as Ohm’s law: V = I × R. I is measured in amperes (A), R in ohms (Ω).
An electronic input device that detects or measures an input from the physical environment.
The processing of an analogue signal that prepares it for the next stage of processing.
An electrical component used to connect or disconnect the conducting path in an electrical circuit.
An electrical component that is a semiconductor and has three connections capable of regulating current or voltage flow and amplification.
A resistor that has an adjustable value of electrical resistance.
An electromotive force from a power source that pushes electrons through a circuit, also considered as electric pressure.
A unit of power equivalent to one joule per second.
IB Definition: Electronic components that control the flow of electricity. Real-World Example: Transistors used to amplify weak signals or act as switches in computers.
IB Definition: An electronic system that has a permanently variable signal. Real-World Example: A dimmer switch that allows for a continuous range of light brightness.
IB Definition: An electronic system that uses binary signals (0 or 1, on or off). Real-World Example: Modern computers and smartphones that process data as discrete packets of information.
IB Definition: A high-gain voltage amplifier that amplifies weak signals. Real-World Example: Amplifying the tiny electrical signal from a heart rate monitor so it can be displayed on a screen.
IB Definition: Electronic components that do not have any control over the flow of electricity. Real-World Example: Fixed resistors used to limit current so an LED doesn't burn out.

syllabus.title: Introduction to electronic systems
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How are electronics present in everyday products?

statements.text: Electronic systems comprise of an input, process, output and feedback loop.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe an electronic system in terms of input, process, output and feedback.

statements.text: Electronics are ubiquitous and designers need to consider how they can be created so that they may be used responsibly in homes, industry and society as well as improving aspects of modern-day life.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify electronic products that are safe, energy-efficient and utilize minimal energy.

statements.text: Electronic systems can be either analogue or digital.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to distinguish between analogue and digital systems.

statements.text: An analogue system uses continually changing signals such as sine waves.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe analogue systems in terms of voltage, current, resistance, frequency and power using the International System of Units (SI): ampere (A), second (s), hertz (Hz), watt (W), volt (V), ohm (Ω). Students must be able to use the following SI multipliers: p, n, μ, m, k, M, G, T.

statements.text: A digital system is designed to store, process and communicate information in digital form.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe digital systems in terms of using discrete values such as binary digits and on and off signals. Students must be able to define logic gates.

statements.text: Electronic systems are composed of electronic components that have a specific purpose.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the purpose of passive electronic components, including fixed and variable resistors, capacitors, switches, relays and active components such as diodes and transistors.

statements.text: Electronic systems utilize input devices to identify a change in an environment that requires a response.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the purpose of basic analogue and digital input electronic components, including switches and sensors (including light, temperature, humidity and sound).

statements.text: Processing devices translate an input into an output.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to compare and differentiate basic analogue and digital electronic process components, including signal conditioning (analogue) and program control (digital).

statements.text: Many everyday electronic devices contain control circuits to monitor and control.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe the use of a microcontroller as a programmable integrated circuit (PIC) into which software can be loaded to carry out a range of processing tasks.

statements.text: Electronic systems utilize output devices to perform a function in response to an initial stimulus.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline basic analogue and digital electronic output components. Electronic output components are restricted to motors, haptic devices, buzzers, speakers, headphones, printers, lights, plotters, relays, braille display, light-emitting diode (LED) and liquid crystal display (LCD).

statements.text: Electronic systems utilize feedback to monitor an environment and respond to a stimulus if required.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to compare open- and closed-loop electronic systems, identify where open- and closed-loop systems are used, and explain the purpose of feedback in a closed-loop system.

statements.text: An operational amplifier (op-amp) is a high-gain voltage amplifier with differential inputs and a single output. It is one of the basic building blocks of analogue circuits.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe the common applications of op-amps, such as analogue or digital signal amplifiers used to amplify signals from sensors in internet of things (IoT) home appliances.

statements.text: Digital systems communicate with each other through the use of embedded systems to perform a specific task.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to define an embedded system, encompassing its role in augmenting everyday products’ functionality, efficiency and automation.

statements.text: Electronic components are combined to perform a function in an electronic circuit, which is represented in a circuit diagram.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify the symbols used in a circuit diagram for fixed and variable resistors, capacitors, switches, relays, diodes, transistors, operational amplifiers and input and output devices.

activity.title: Human logic circuit
activity.materials: Input cards marked 0 and 1, gate cards
steps: Assign two students as inputs, one as an AND gate and one as the output indicator.
Test every input combination and record the truth table.
Repeat with OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR; predict before revealing.
Combine two gates to model a practical condition and explain the output.
activity.debrief: How would a sensor signal become a binary input?

exam.question: State the output of an XOR gate when both inputs are 1 and explain your answer. [2]
exam.answer: The output is 0. XOR gives 1 only when its two inputs differ.

activities.title: Practical Activity: The Black Box Challenge
activities.text: Practical Activity: The Black Box Challenge In pairs, you'll receive a simple electronic product (a torch, a musical greeting card, a motion-sensor light) that you're not allowed to open. Working from observation and testing only, sketch an input → process → output → feedback diagram for it in 6 minutes, then swap diagrams with another pair to spot what you missed.
activities.html: Choose a safe, low-voltage electronic product without opening it. Sketch its input, process and output. Include feedback only if a controlled output quantity is measured; explain your evidence. Compare diagrams with another pair.

title: Manufacturing techniques

sections.title: Overview: Why Manufacturing Technique Selection Matters
sections.html:
Theme A — Materials HL only 20 hours Sub-topics 4.1.1–4.1.11

Overview: Why Manufacturing Technique Selection Matters

No single manufacturing process can economically produce every product. A method that is ideal for a one-off prototype (such as FDM 3D printing) is rarely suitable for a production run of 500,000 units (which favours injection moulding), and a process that produces a beautifully smooth surface finish (SLA) may be far slower and more expensive than one that does not (FDM).

Designers therefore select — and combine — manufacturing techniques based on the material being processed, the required production volume, the geometric complexity of the part, the tolerances and finish required, cost and lead time, and the environmental impact of the process across the product's life cycle. This topic organises the huge range of available techniques into five categories so that this decision-making process becomes systematic rather than a matter of memorising isolated facts about individual machines.

Guiding question

Why are different manufacturing techniques used for producing different products? Keep this question in mind across every sub-topic — each technique below is a response to a specific combination of material, volume, geometry, tolerance, cost and environmental impact.

sections.title: Lesson 1: The Five Categories of Manufacturing
sections.html:
4.1.1 Five Categories of Manufacturing Links: C3.1

Lesson 1: The Five Categories of Manufacturing

Every manufactured product is the result of one or more categories of process applied to a material. Recognising these categories allows a designer to think critically about how a component's geometry, tolerances and surface qualities were achieved, and to judge whether an alternative technique might produce a lighter, cheaper or more sustainable outcome.

1. Additive

Definition: Builds an object layer by layer, adding only the material that is needed.

Context: Typically generates comparatively little waste compared with other categories.

2. Subtractive (wasting)

Definition: Starts with a larger block, sheet or bar of material and cuts, mills or turns material away until the desired form remains.

Context: Waste material (swarf) is an inherent feature of the process.

3. Forming

Definition: Reshapes a fixed mass of material — using heat, pressure or a mould — without adding or removing material.

Context: The material's volume is conserved throughout the process.

4. Joining

Definition: Brings two or more components together to create an assembly from separate parts.

Context: May be permanent (e.g. welding) or temporary (e.g. a bolted joint).

5. Finishing

Definition: Applied last, to protect a component from corrosion, wear or UV degradation, and/or to enhance its aesthetic appeal.

Context: In practice, almost no product is made using only one category — most combine several.

A confident understanding of A4.1 depends on being able to identify which category — or combination of categories — was used to produce each component of a familiar object, and to justify why.

Key terms: Additive · Subtractive (wasting) · Forming · Joining · Finishing

Classroom engagement — Reverse-engineering a bicycle

In small groups, students examine a bicycle (or a high-resolution exploded diagram if a real one is unavailable) and classify the manufacturing category used to create each component: the welded aluminium frame (joining, following a forming/extrusion process for the tubing), the injection-moulded plastic pedals (forming), the CNC-machined chainring (subtractive), the chrome-plated handlebar stem (finishing), and the woven brake-cable outer sheath (joining). Each group must justify its classification with reference to the material used and the tolerance, strength or surface finish required. This activity directly rehearses the skill needed for linking question C3.1 — using product analysis to identify manufacturing techniques — and can be repeated later in the topic with a more complex product once all five categories have been taught in full.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Additive Techniques (3D Printing)
sections.html:
4.1.2 Additive Techniques (3D Printing)

Lesson 2: Additive Techniques (3D Printing)

Additive manufacturing — commonly known as 3D printing — constructs a three-dimensional object from a digital CAD file by depositing or fusing material in successive thin layers (typically 0.05–0.3 mm) until the object is complete. Because material is only placed where it is structurally needed, additive processes can achieve complex internal geometries (such as lattices or channels) that would be impossible, or prohibitively expensive, to produce by subtractive machining.

1. Laminated Object Manufacture (LOM)

Definition: Builds an object by bonding successive layers of sheet material (often paper, plastic or metal foil) together, using a laser or blade to cut the outline of each layer before the next sheet is applied; unused material is then peeled away.

2. Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM)

Definition: The most widely used and most affordable additive technique. Feeds a thermoplastic filament (commonly PLA or ABS) through a heated nozzle, which melts it and extrudes it along a pre-programmed path onto a build plate, where it cools and fuses to the layer below.

3. Stereolithography (SLA)

Definition: Uses an ultraviolet laser to selectively cure a liquid photopolymer resin in a vat, solidifying it one thin cross-section at a time.

Context: Produces a notably smoother surface finish and finer detail than FDM, at greater cost.

Key terms: Additive manufacturing · LOM · FDM · SLA · Photopolymer resin

Classroom engagement — Same design, three processes

If the school has access to an FDM printer (e.g. a desktop Creality or Prusa machine) and can source SLA-printed samples (many resin-printer owners, dental labs, or jewellers can supply an offcut), students compare an identical small design produced by both processes: layer lines, surface smoothness, print time and cost. Where hardware is unavailable, students instead analyse a real product made using SLA at industrial scale — Invisalign clear dental aligners, which are digitally 3D-modelled from a scan of the patient's teeth and mass-customised using resin-based additive printing — and evaluate why SLA (rather than FDM) is appropriate for a product requiring biocompatibility, high dimensional accuracy and a smooth, comfortable surface against skin.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Rapid Prototyping vs. Production
sections.html:
4.1.3 Rapid Prototyping vs. Production

Lesson 3: Rapid Prototyping vs. Production

Students must be able to distinguish between manufacturing techniques used to create initial base models for testing and validation, and those used for the production of refined, final products.

1. Rapid Prototyping

Definition: Most commonly desktop FDM or SLA 3D printing. Prioritises speed, low cost per unit, and ease of design iteration over surface finish, material properties or unit economics at scale.

Context: A single prototype can be redesigned in CAD and reprinted within hours, allowing a design team to test form, fit and basic function before committing to expensive production tooling.

2. Production Manufacturing

Definition: Techniques such as injection moulding, die casting or industrial additive processes, which require significant upfront investment — most notably in tooling, such as a steel injection mould, which can cost tens of thousands of dollars and take weeks to manufacture.

Context: This investment only becomes economical at high volumes, where the tooling cost is amortised across many thousands of identical, high-quality units produced at a low marginal cost per part. Choosing the wrong technique for the intended volume — for example, attempting to injection-mould ten units, or FDM-printing fifty thousand — is a common and costly design error.

Key terms: Rapid prototyping · Production manufacturing · Tooling · Unit cost · Design iteration

Classroom engagement — The Dyson iteration case study

Students research James Dyson's well-documented development of the cyclone vacuum cleaner, which went through 5,127 prototypes before reaching a production-ready design. Using this case, students map which stages of development would realistically have used rapid, low-cost modelling (early cyclone geometry testing) versus which stages required production-representative tooling to validate (final injection-moulded housing, motor housing tolerances). Students then produce a simple cost-versus-volume sketch graph showing why the break-even point between prototyping and mass-production tooling shifts depending on order quantity — reinforcing the economic reasoning, not just the technical description, behind technique selection.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Industrial Additive Manufacturing
sections.html:
4.1.4 Industrial Additive Manufacturing

Lesson 4: Industrial Additive Manufacturing

Beyond desktop prototyping, industrial additive manufacturing is increasingly used for genuine low-volume production runs across aerospace, medical, automotive and consumer-goods industries — particularly where a part's complexity or customisation would make subtractive or forming methods impractical.

1. Powder Bed Fusion (PBF)

Definition: Spreads a thin layer of powdered material (commonly a metal alloy or nylon) across a build platform, then uses a laser or electron beam to selectively fuse the powder particles together according to the cross-section of that layer; the platform lowers, a new layer of powder is spread, and the process repeats, with unfused powder providing support for overhangs.

2. Material Extrusion

Definition: Dispenses material — typically a thermoplastic, though industrial systems can also extrude fibre-reinforced composites or even concrete — through a heated nozzle in a continuous bead, building the part layer by layer.

Context: Industrial-scale FDM is a form of material extrusion.

3. Selective Laser Sintering (SLS)

Definition: A specific powder bed fusion process that uses a high-powered laser as the energy source to sinter (fuse without fully melting) powdered polymer or metal.

Context: Produces strong, functional parts that require no support structures, because surrounding unsintered powder supports the geometry during the build.

Key terms: Powder Bed Fusion (PBF) · Material Extrusion · Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) · Sintering · Support structures

Watch / Read

GE Aviation: 100,000th 3D-printed fuel nozzle (3DPrint.com)

Classroom engagement — Redesigning the fuel nozzle

GE Aviation redesigned the fuel nozzle for its LEAP jet engine using metal powder bed fusion, consolidating a component that previously required 20 separately machined and welded parts into a single printed part that is around 25% lighter and up to five times more durable. Students examine before/after diagrams of the nozzle and are asked to justify, in writing, why PBF was selected over conventional subtractive machining and welding for this specific component — considering internal cooling channels, weight-critical aerospace requirements, and the relatively low production volume (thousands, not millions, of units per year) that makes the high per-part cost of metal PBF economically viable.

Students examine before/after diagrams of the nozzle and are asked to justify, in writing, why PBF was selected over conventional subtractive machining and welding for this specific component — considering internal cooling channels, weight-critical aerospace requirements, and the relatively low production volume (thousands, not millions, of units per year) that makes the high per-part cost of metal PBF economically viable.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Emerging Additive Technologies — 4D Printing
sections.html:
4.1.5 Emerging Additive Tech — 4D Printing

Lesson 5: Emerging Additive Technologies — 4D Printing

4D printing extends 3D printing by adding a fourth dimension: time. A 4D-printed object is manufactured using standard additive processes, but is built from a smart material — most commonly a shape memory polymer — that is programmed, during printing, to change its physical or chemical state in response to an external stimulus after manufacture, such as changes in pH, temperature, exposure to water, or light. The object therefore continues to 'develop' after it leaves the printer, transforming from its printed shape into a second, pre-programmed shape without any additional human intervention, electronics or motors.

1. Origins

Definition: The concept was first popularised by Skylar Tibbits of the MIT Self-Assembly Lab.

Context: Early demonstrations included a printed strand that folded itself into the letters 'MIT' when submerged in water.

2. Applications

Materials/Examples: Medical stents that are printed in a compact form for minimally invasive insertion and then expand to their functional shape once they reach body temperature, and self-tightening or self-adjusting consumer products.

Key terms: 4D printing · Shape memory polymer · External stimulus · Self-assembly

Classroom engagement — Design a stimulus-responsive product

After watching Skylar Tibbits' TED talk introducing 4D printing, students work in pairs to sketch a concept product that would benefit from a shape-change stimulus — for example, a flat-packed shelving bracket that assembles itself when heated with a hairdryer, or an irrigation valve that opens automatically as soil moisture (and therefore humidity) rises. For each concept, students must specify the intended stimulus (heat, water, pH, light), explain in their own words how a shape memory polymer achieves the transformation, and evaluate one practical limitation of 4D printing at the current stage of the technology (for example, the limited range of materials that reliably exhibit shape memory behaviour, and the difficulty of achieving precise, repeatable transformations at production scale).

sections.title: Lesson 6: Emerging Additive Technologies — 5D Printing
sections.html:
4.1.6 Emerging Additive Tech — 5D Printing Links: A3.1

Lesson 6: Emerging Additive Technologies — 5D Printing

5D printing extends additive manufacturing further by adding rotational movement to the build process itself. In standard 3D printing, the print head moves only in the X, Y and Z axes while the object is built as a stack of flat, horizontal layers. In 5D printing, both the extruder head and the print bed can rotate, adding two further axes of motion, so that layers can be deposited at an angle and follow the curved contours of the part being produced, rather than being restricted to flat horizontal planes.

1. Why it's stronger

Definition: Because the printed layers align with the direction of mechanical stress the finished part will experience in use, 5D-printed components are significantly stronger than an equivalent 3D-printed part for a given amount of material.

Context: Current research suggests strength improvements in the order of several times that of conventionally layered prints.

2. Applications

Application: Particularly suited to complex, long-lasting, load-bearing components in biomedical (custom joint implants that must withstand curved loading), automotive, and aerospace applications, where component failure carries a high safety and financial cost.

Key terms: 5D printing · Multi-axis printing · Layer orientation · Load-bearing strength

Classroom engagement — Layer lines and load paths

Using a simple 3D-printed test piece (or a diagram if a printer is unavailable), students identify the visible layer lines and predict, then physically test where possible, where the piece is weakest — typically along the layer boundary, where inter-layer adhesion is lower than the strength of the filament itself. Students then sketch how a 5D-printed equivalent of a curved bracket or hip-implant stem could orient its layers to follow the load path instead of stacking flat, and explain — referencing linking question A3.1 — how this changes the relationship between the printing process and the mechanical properties of the finished component.

sections.title: Lesson 7: Subtractive (Wasting) Techniques
sections.html:
4.1.7 Subtractive (Wasting) Techniques

Lesson 7: Subtractive (Wasting) Techniques

Subtractive — or wasting — techniques remove material from an initial three-dimensional mass or flat sheet of material until the desired form remains. Because material is removed rather than added, subtractive processes generate waste (swarf, chips or dust) and are generally most efficient when working with a low-complexity outer geometry cut from a strong, homogeneous material such as metal or hardwood.

1. Cutting

Definition: Using a saw or laser to separate material along a line.

2. Milling

Definition: A rotating multi-point cutting tool removes material from a workpiece held in a fixed position, used to produce flat faces, slots and pockets.

3. Turning

Definition: The workpiece itself rotates on a lathe while a single-point cutting tool removes material, producing cylindrical or conical forms such as shafts and bolts.

4. Abrading

Definition: Uses friction — via sandpaper, a grinding wheel, or an abrasive belt — to gradually wear away a material's surface.

Context: Typically used to refine a shape, remove tool marks, or prepare a surface for a subsequent finishing process.

Key terms: Machining · Milling · Turning · Abrading · Swarf

Classroom engagement — CNC milling case study

Students examine the unibody aluminium chassis of a modern laptop (e.g. a MacBook), which is CNC-milled from a single solid block of aluminium rather than assembled from pressed sheet-metal panels. Using photographs or a physical device, students identify visible evidence of the subtractive process (internal pockets, fillet radii left by the rotating cutter, consistent wall thickness) and are asked to explain why a manufacturer would choose a slower, more wasteful subtractive process over faster forming techniques for this specific product — considering rigidity, precision, and the premium aesthetic and structural qualities that milling from solid metal can deliver, in trade-off against the significant material waste generated.

sections.title: Lesson 8: Forming Techniques
sections.html:
4.1.8 Forming Techniques

Lesson 8: Forming Techniques

Forming techniques modify the shape of a material — usually using heat, pressure, or both — without adding or removing material, so the material's volume and mass remain constant.

1. Bending / Press-forming

Definition: Uses a punch and die to permanently deform sheet metal into a new shape.

Context: For example, pressing flat steel blanks into a curved car body panel.

2. Casting

Definition: Pouring a liquid material (commonly molten metal) into a mould cavity, where it solidifies into the shape of the mould before being removed.

3. Injection moulding

Definition: Forces molten plastic under high pressure into a precision steel mould cavity, producing highly accurate, repeatable parts at high volume.

Materials/Examples: LEGO bricks, manufactured to tolerances of around ±0.002 mm.

4. Extrusion moulding

Definition: Continuously forces heated plastic through a shaped die to create long, constant-cross-section profiles.

Materials/Examples: Drinking straws, pipes, or window frames.

5. Rotational moulding

Definition: Rotates a heated hollow mould on two axes so that powdered plastic evenly coats and fuses to the internal mould surface, producing seamless hollow parts.

Materials/Examples: Kayaks and traffic cones.

6. Blow moulding

Definition: Inflates a heated tube of plastic (a parison) inside a mould using compressed air, forming thin-walled hollow containers.

Materials/Examples: PET drinks bottles.

7. Vacuum moulding

Definition: Heats a plastic sheet until pliable, then uses a vacuum to draw it tightly over a mould, producing shallow, detailed forms.

Materials/Examples: Blister packaging or chocolate-box trays.
ProcessMechanismTypical Product
Injection mouldingMolten plastic forced into a steel mould cavityLEGO bricks
Extrusion mouldingHeated plastic forced through a shaped dieDrinking straws, pipes
Rotational mouldingPowdered plastic rotated inside a heated mouldKayaks, traffic cones
Blow mouldingHeated parison inflated inside a mouldPET drinks bottles
Vacuum mouldingHeated sheet drawn over a mould by vacuumBlister packaging

Key terms: Press-forming · Casting · Injection moulding · Extrusion moulding · Rotational moulding · Blow moulding · Vacuum moulding

Classroom engagement — One material, five moulding processes

Students bring in (or are shown images of) five everyday plastic objects, each made using a different moulding process: a LEGO brick (injection moulding), a length of plastic guttering or a drinking straw (extrusion moulding), a traffic cone or kayak (rotational moulding), a PET water bottle (blow moulding), and a blister pack or chocolate box tray (vacuum moulding). In groups, students must correctly match each object to its process, identify one visible clue that supports their answer (a sprue/gate mark, a consistent cross-section, a seam line, a pinch-off point, or a thin uniform wall thickness), and justify why that specific process suits the object's required wall thickness, hollowness, or production volume.
