sections.title: Lesson 9: Joining Techniques
sections.html:
4.1.9 Joining Techniques

Lesson 9: Joining Techniques

Joining techniques combine two or more components — of similar or dissimilar materials — into a single product or assembly, and may be designed to be permanent or temporary/demountable.

1. Adhering

Definition: Uses glues or bonding agents to chemically bond surfaces together.

Context: Modern structural and waterproof adhesives are increasingly used in place of mechanical fasteners in products such as smartphones, where an adhesive seal also improves water resistance.

2. Mechanical joining

Definition: Uses fastening (screws, bolts, rivets, snap-fits) to hold components together, often allowing disassembly for repair or recycling; also includes stitching (thread passed through layers of a flexible material) and weaving (interlacing individual threads or filaments into a single structure).

3. Fusion joining (Welding)

Definition: Permanently joins parts, typically metal, by heating the joint area to melting point so that the materials fuse together and solidify as one continuous piece on cooling.

Materials/Examples: Common welding processes include arc welding and spot welding.

Key terms: Adhering · Mechanical fastening · Stitching · Weaving · Welding (fusion)

Classroom engagement — Flat-pack vs. welded vs. woven

Students compare three products that each rely on a different joining strategy for a clear functional reason: flat-pack furniture (such as an IKEA bookcase), which uses demountable mechanical fasteners — cam locks and dowels — specifically so the product can be transported flat and assembled by the customer; a steel bicycle frame, which uses fusion welding to create a permanent, rigid structural joint capable of withstanding repeated dynamic loads; and a knitted trainer upper (such as Nike Flyknit or adidas Primeknit), which uses weaving to create a single, largely seamless textile structure that reduces material waste and stitched seams compared to a traditional cut-and-sew upper. Students explain, for each case, why the alternative joining methods would be inappropriate.

sections.title: Lesson 10: Finishing Techniques
sections.html:
4.1.10 Finishing Techniques

Lesson 10: Finishing Techniques

Finishing techniques are applied to a component's surface, after forming or joining, to protect it and/or improve its appearance and longevity. Several finishing processes work by depositing or growing a protective layer on the base material.

1. Anodizing

Definition: An electrochemical process, most commonly applied to aluminium, that thickens and hardens the material's naturally occurring oxide layer, improving corrosion and wear resistance and allowing the surface to be dyed a durable colour.

Materials/Examples: Used extensively on aluminium consumer electronics and cookware.

2. Electro-plating

Definition: Uses an electric current to deposit a thin layer of one metal (commonly chromium, nickel, gold or zinc) onto the surface of another, improving corrosion resistance, wear resistance or appearance.

Materials/Examples: Chrome-plated taps and vehicle trim.

3. Galvanizing

Definition: Coats iron or steel with a protective layer of zinc, most often by hot-dip immersion, to prevent rust.

Materials/Examples: Widely used for structural steel, crash barriers and roofing.

4. Powder coating

Definition: Applies a dry, electrostatically charged powder to a (usually metal) surface, which is then cured under heat to form a tough, even, decorative layer.

Materials/Examples: Commonly used on outdoor furniture, bicycle frames and domestic appliances.

5. Polishing / sealants

Definition: Uses mechanical abrasion (polishing, buffing) or an applied layer such as oil, wax or silicone to reduce surface friction, enhance appearance, and protect materials such as wood, stone or leather from moisture and wear.

Key terms: Anodizing · Electro-plating · Galvanizing · Powder coating · Polishing/sealants

Classroom engagement — Why does this surface look/feel like this?

Students are given (or shown close-up images of) four finished surfaces: an anodized, brightly coloured aluminium water bottle; a chrome-plated bathroom tap; a galvanized steel crash barrier or roofing sheet; and a powder-coated steel garden chair. For each, students identify the finishing process, describe one functional benefit (corrosion resistance, wear resistance, colour durability) and one aesthetic benefit, and are challenged to explain why the manufacturer selected that specific finishing process rather than one of the others — for example, why galvanizing (a thicker, less decorative zinc coating) is preferred over anodizing for an outdoor steel barrier exposed to weather and impact, whereas anodizing (a thinner, colourable oxide layer) is preferred for a consumer product where appearance matters more than impact resistance.

sections.title: Lesson 11: Combining Techniques
sections.html:
4.1.11 Combining Techniques Links: A3.1 · C3.1

Lesson 11: Combining Techniques

Most real products cannot be produced using a single manufacturing category in isolation. Instead, designers combine additive, subtractive, forming, joining and finishing techniques — selecting each one to suit the specific material, function, tolerance and finish required by an individual component, before those components are brought together into a finished assembly. A confident A4.1 candidate can look at an everyday product, break it down into its constituent parts, and justify why each part was manufactured the way it was — this is the culminating skill of the whole topic, and is also the skill directly assessed by linking question C3.1.

Key terms: Combining techniques · Assembly · Design justification

Classroom engagement — Full product breakdown: the office chair

As a capstone task, students carry out a full manufacturing breakdown of an office chair (or an equally multi-component product, such as a power drill or a kettle). For each component, students state the category, name the specific technique, and justify the choice using at least one material property (linking question A3.1) and one production-volume or cost consideration (4.1.3).

sections.text: 4.1.11 Combining Techniques Links: A3.1 · C3.1 Lesson 11: Combining Techniques Most real products cannot be produced using a single manufacturing category in isolation. Instead, designers combine additive, subtractive, forming, joining and finishing techniques — selecting each one to suit the specific material, function, tolerance and finish required by an individual component, before those components are brought together into a finished assembly. A confident A4.1 candidate can look at an everyday product, break it down into its constituent parts, and justify why each part was manufactured the way it was — this is the culminating skill of the whole topic, and is also the skill directly assessed by linking question C3.1. sections.title: Exam Prep: Topic A4.1
sections.html:
Exam Prep: Topic A4.1

The following questions are written in the style of IB Design Technology Paper 1 and Paper 2, and use official IB command terms.

Command termWhat it requires
DefineGive the precise meaning of a word, phrase or physical quantity.
Identify / OutlineGive a brief account or summary; state the main point(s) with little or no supporting detail.
DistinguishMake clear the differences between two or more concepts or items.
DescribeGive a detailed account, including all relevant characteristics, events or processes.
ExplainGive a detailed account including reasons or causes — the 'how' and 'why', not just the 'what'.
DiscussOffer a considered and balanced review of a topic, including a range of arguments, factors or hypotheses; opinions/conclusions should be presented clearly and supported by evidence.
Evaluate / To what extentMake an appraisal by weighing up strengths and limitations, arriving at a balanced, evidence-based judgement.

Section A — Multiple Choice (3 questions, 1 mark each)

1. Which manufacturing technique is best classified as forming?

  • A. CNC milling
  • B. Injection moulding
  • C. Selective laser sintering
  • D. Anodizing
Reveal Answer
[1] B — Injection moulding.

2. Which additive manufacturing technique uses a laser to selectively cure a liquid photopolymer resin?

  • A. Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM)
  • B. Laminated Object Manufacture (LOM)
  • C. Stereolithography (SLA)
  • D. Selective Laser Sintering (SLS)
Reveal Answer
[1] C — Stereolithography (SLA).

3. A component made from a shape memory polymer that changes form only after exposure to heat is best described as an example of:

  • A. 3D printing
  • B. 4D printing
  • C. 5D printing
  • D. Subtractive manufacturing
Reveal Answer
[1] B — 4D printing.

Section B — Short Answer

4. Distinguish between additive and subtractive manufacturing, using one named example of each. [4 marks]

Reveal Answer

Indicative content: Award marks for: a clear statement that additive manufacturing builds an object by adding material layer by layer while subtractive manufacturing removes material from a larger mass [1]; a valid named additive example, e.g. FDM, SLA, SLS [1]; a valid named subtractive example, e.g. CNC milling, turning [1]; credit for noting the waste-material implication of each — additive generates little waste, subtractive generates swarf [1].

5. Outline two differences between rapid prototyping and production manufacturing techniques. [4 marks]

Reveal Answer

Indicative content: Award one mark per valid difference outlined, to a maximum of two differences (two marks each if elaborated): tooling cost — prototyping requires little/no tooling; production requires significant up-front tooling investment, e.g. an injection mould; unit cost at volume — prototyping has a high cost per unit at scale, production has a low marginal cost per unit once tooling is amortised; speed of design iteration — prototyping allows fast redesign, production tooling is slow and costly to modify; typical processes cited, e.g. desktop FDM vs. injection moulding.

Section C — Long Answer

6. Explain, using an example, why 5D printing might be selected over standard 3D printing for a component used in the aerospace industry. [6 marks]

Reveal Answer

Mark scheme guidance

Level 1 (1–2 marks): Basic description of 5D printing (rotating extruder/bed, prints on five axes) with little or no reference to aerospace application.

Level 2 (3–4 marks): Explains that 5D printing allows layers to follow the curved contours/load path of a part, and links this to increased strength compared with flat-layered 3D printing.

Level 3 (5–6 marks): Fully explains the causal link between layer orientation and mechanical strength (referencing material properties, A3.1), and applies this convincingly to a plausible or named aerospace component (e.g. a curved structural bracket) where weight-critical strength and safety justify the additional process complexity and cost of 5D printing over conventional 3D printing.

7. A company is designing a reusable plastic water bottle intended to fit within a circular economy. The bottle body is produced by blow moulding, the cap by injection moulding, and a metal carry-clip is joined to the body. Discuss the extent to which these manufacturing choices support circular economy principles. [8 marks]

Reveal Answer

Mark scheme guidance: Award marks for a balanced discussion that considers both supporting and limiting factors.

Supporting: blow moulding and injection moulding both produce durable, reusable components suited to a long product life; both processes are well suited to using recycled polymer feedstock; separable joining (rather than adhesive or fusion joining) of the clip could support end-of-life disassembly and material recovery.

Limiting: if the cap, body and clip use dissimilar materials that are permanently joined, this can hinder recycling/disassembly; moulding processes require energy-intensive tooling and processing; single-polymer design and mechanical (demountable) joining would better support circularity than permanent joining of mixed materials.

Top-level responses reach a clear, justified conclusion on the overall extent to which the technique choices support circularity, referencing linking question C2.2.

sections.title: Glossary of Key Terms — Topic A4.1
sections.html:
Glossary of Key Terms — Topic A4.1

Click on a term to reveal its definition.

3D Printing
Definition: The process of creating physical objects from a 3D digital model by building up material layer by layer.
Example: Rapid functional prototypes and custom medical implants.
Additive Manufacturing
Definition: A process of making a three-dimensional solid object from a digital file by adding material layer by layer.
Example: Industrial SLS printing used to manufacture lightweight aerospace engine parts.
Laminated Object Manufacture (LOM)
Definition: An additive process that builds an object by bonding and cutting successive layers of sheet material.
Example: Early full-colour architectural scale models built from bonded paper sheets.
Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM)
Definition: An additive process that melts and extrudes a thermoplastic filament through a heated nozzle, layer by layer.
Example: Desktop 3D printers used to prototype phone cases and enclosures.
Stereolithography (SLA)
Definition: An additive process that uses a laser to selectively cure liquid photopolymer resin into solid layers.
Example: Invisalign-style clear dental aligners custom-printed from a tooth scan.
Rapid Prototyping
Definition: The fast production of a scale model or working model using additive or other quick-turnaround processes, to test and validate a design before committing to production tooling.
Example: An FDM-printed housing used to test the fit of internal electronics before injection-mould tooling is ordered.
Powder Bed Fusion (PBF)
Definition: An industrial additive process in which thermal energy (laser or electron beam) selectively fuses regions of a bed of powdered material.
Example: GE Aviation's metal-printed LEAP engine fuel nozzle.
Material Extrusion
Definition: An additive process that dispenses material through a nozzle in a continuous bead to build an object layer by layer.
Example: Industrial-scale FDM printing of functional end-use parts and jigs.
Selective Laser Sintering (SLS)
Definition: An additive process that uses a laser as a power source to sinter (fuse) powdered material, typically without support structures.
Example: Lightweight, complex nylon brackets used in low-volume automotive and aerospace parts.
4D Printing
Definition: Using 3D printing to create a physical object that can change its shape or properties when exposed to a stimulus such as water, heat, light or an electric current.
Example: A medical stent that expands to its functional shape once it reaches body temperature.
5D Printing
Definition: An additive process similar to 3D printing, but with a rotating extruder head and print bed that allow printing on five axes.
Example: Curved aerospace or biomedical components whose printed layers follow the part's load path for extra strength.
Shape Memory Polymer
Definition: A smart material that can be deformed and then returns to a pre-programmed shape when triggered by an external stimulus.
Example: Self-tightening product fastenings and self-folding packaging.
Subtractive Manufacturing
Definition: Any manufacturing process in which a 3D object is created by removing material from a solid block.
Example: CNC milling a laptop's unibody aluminium chassis from a solid block.
Machining
Definition: A family of subtractive processes, including cutting, milling and turning, that remove material using a cutting tool.
Example: Turning a steel bolt shaft on a lathe.
Abrading
Definition: A subtractive process that uses friction to gradually wear away a material's surface.
Example: Sanding a wooden skateboard deck before applying a finish.
Forming
Definition: A manufacturing process that changes the shape of a material — usually with heat and/or pressure — without adding or removing material.
Example: Press-forming a flat steel blank into a curved car door panel.
Casting
Definition: A forming process in which a liquid material is poured into a mould cavity and solidifies into the mould's shape.
Example: Casting a cast-iron frying pan from molten iron.
Injection Moulding
Definition: A forming process that injects molten plastic under pressure into a precision mould cavity to produce highly accurate, repeatable parts.
Example: Mass-produced LEGO bricks, moulded to tolerances of around ±0.002 mm.
Extrusion Moulding
Definition: A forming process that continuously forces heated material through a shaped die to create a constant cross-section profile.
Example: Plastic guttering, pipes and drinking straws.
Rotational Moulding
Definition: A forming process in which powdered plastic is rotated on two axes inside a heated mould to evenly coat the internal surface, producing a seamless hollow part.
Example: Traffic cones and kayaks.
Blow Moulding
Definition: A forming process in which a heated tube of plastic is inflated with compressed air inside a mould to create a thin-walled hollow container.
Example: PET plastic drinks bottles.
Vacuum Moulding
Definition: A forming process in which a heated plastic sheet is drawn tightly over a mould using a vacuum, producing shallow, detailed forms.
Example: Blister packaging and chocolate-box trays.
Joining
Definition: Combining two or more components, of similar or dissimilar materials, to form a single product or assembly.
Example: Welding the tubular frame of a bicycle together.
Adhering
Definition: A joining process that uses glues or bonding agents to chemically bond surfaces together.
Example: Adhesive-sealed waterproof joints in a smartphone casing.
Mechanical Fastening
Definition: A joining process that uses fasteners such as screws, bolts or snap-fits, often allowing later disassembly.
Example: Cam-lock and dowel fixings in flat-pack furniture.
Weaving
Definition: A joining process that interlaces individual threads or filaments into a single structural textile.
Example: A knitted trainer upper, such as Nike Flyknit.
Welding
Definition: A fusion joining process used to permanently join parts, typically metal, by heating them to melting point and allowing them to solidify together.
Example: Arc welding used in the construction of steel bridge structures.
Finishing
Definition: A final process applied to the surface of a product to improve appearance and/or performance and protect it from degradation.
Example: Anodizing an aluminium smartphone case to give it a durable, coloured finish.
Anodizing
Definition: An electrochemical finishing process, usually applied to aluminium, that thickens the natural oxide layer to improve corrosion resistance and allow colouring.
Example: Brightly coloured anodized aluminium water bottles and cookware.
Electro-plating
Definition: A finishing process that uses an electric current to deposit a thin layer of metal onto the surface of another material.
Example: Chrome-plated bathroom taps and vehicle trim.
Galvanizing
Definition: A finishing process that coats iron or steel with a protective layer of zinc, typically by hot-dip immersion, to prevent rust.
Example: Galvanized steel crash barriers and roofing sheets.
Powder Coating
Definition: A finishing process in which dry, electrostatically charged powder is applied to a surface and cured under heat to form a tough, even coating.
Example: Powder-coated steel garden furniture and bicycle frames.

A 3D rapid prototyping printing methodology that deposits melted layers of material on a bed to build up a 3D model.

A system that virtually slices a 3D computer-aided design (CAD) model into thin layers, then cuts out each layer from a roll of material using a laser or plotter cutter. The layers can then be glued in the correct order to create a 3D model.

A suite of manufacturing techniques that uses a mould to shape material into a desired form.

A group of manufacturing techniques used to manufacture a physical object quickly for testing aspects of a product. Typically, 3D computer-aided design (CAD) models are used.

Definition: A finishing process that uses an electric current to deposit a thin layer of metal onto the surface of another material. Example: Chrome-plated bathroom taps and vehicle trim.

Definition: A finishing process in which dry, electrostatically charged powder is applied to a surface and cured under heat to form a tough, even coating. Example: Powder-coated steel garden furniture and bicycle frames.

syllabus.title: Manufacturing techniques
syllabus.guidingQuestion: Why are different manufacturing techniques used for producing different products?

statements.text: Manufacturing techniques can be organized into five categories.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline additive, subtractive (wasting), forming, joining and finishing techniques, relevant to the properties of the selected material(s).

statements.text: An additive technique is the process of creating an object by constructing it one layer at a time and typically refers to 3D printing.
statements.guidance: Students must be aware of current and emerging 3D printing techniques to explain how components are produced using additive manufacturing techniques, including laminated object manufacture (LOM), fused deposition modelling (FDM) and stereolithography (SLA).

statements.text: Rapid prototyping is the creation of an object based on a computer model developed in a 3D modelling (CAD) program.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to distinguish between rapid prototyping techniques used for creating initial base models, which serve as a foundation for testing and validation, as opposed to techniques used in the production of the refined products.

statements.text: Additive manufacturing is used in various industries for low-volume production runs.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe additive manufacturing techniques used in manufacturing, including powder bed fusion (PBF), material extrusion, and selective laser sintering (SLS).

statements.text: 4D printing is an extension of 3D printing, where the physical and chemical state of a 3D printed object changes over time due to external stimuli such as pH, temperature, water and light.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how the use of shape memory polymers can be deployed for printing 4D objects and provide examples of their potential use.

statements.text: 5D dimensional additive manufacturing involves the rotation of the extruder head and the print bed in order to print in five different axes.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how 5D technology can be used to produce long-lasting and complex components in biomedical, automobile and aerospace applications.

statements.text: Subtractive techniques involve removing material from an initial 3D mass to achieve a desired shape and can also be applied to 2D or flat materials to modify or change the shape.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how components are produced using wasting manufacturing techniques, including machining (cutting, milling, turning) and abrading processes, which are applied to both 3D and 2D materials.

statements.text: Forming techniques modify the shape of a material without adding or removing any materials.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how components are produced using forming techniques, including bending, press-forming, casting, moulding (injection, extrusion, rotational, blow, vacuum) processes.

statements.text: Joining techniques can temporarily or permanently join two or more similar or dissimilar materials together.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how components are assembled using joining techniques, including adhering, fastening, stitching, weaving and welding processes.

statements.text: Finishing techniques are used to protect and enhance the surface of a component, contributing to its longevity and an overall increase in product life.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to suggest how natural and human-made finishing techniques (such as anodizing, electro-plating, galvanizing), coatings (such as powder-coating), polishing, sealants (such as oils, wax, silicone) enhance a product’s aesthetics, level of protection, durability, longevity and the ease of maintenance of natural and human-made materials.

statements.text: A combination of additive, subtractive, forming, joining and finishing techniques are needed to create components and products.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to suggest why specific manufacturing techniques have been used to create a given component.

activity.title: Manufacturing route cards
activity.materials: Sample products or images, process cards
steps: Compare a hollow plastic bottle, sheet-metal bracket and timber chair component.
Identify form, material and production-volume constraints for each.
Select suitable shaping, joining and finishing processes and place them in order.
Swap routes with another team and challenge one process choice using the product requirements.
activity.debrief: When would a technically possible process be an unsuitable choice?

exam.question: Explain why injection moulding is suitable for high-volume manufacture of identical polymer casings. [2]
exam.answer: High tooling cost is spread across many parts, while short repeatable cycles produce consistent complex shapes with a low unit cost at sufficient volume.

activities.title: Classroom engagement — Reverse-engineering a bicycle
activities.text: Classroom engagement — Reverse-engineering a bicycle In small groups, students examine a bicycle (or a high-resolution exploded diagram if a real one is unavailable) and classify the manufacturing category used to create each component: the welded aluminium frame (joining, following a forming/extrusion process for the tubing), the injection-moulded plastic pedals (forming), the CNC-machined chainring (subtractive), the chrome-plated handlebar stem (finishing), and the woven brake-cable outer sheath (joining). Each group must justify its classification with reference to the material used and the tolerance, strength or surface finish required. This activity directly rehearses the skill needed for linking question C3.1 — using product analysis to identify manufacturing techniques — and can be repeated later in the topic with a more complex product once all five categories have been taught in full.

activities.title: Classroom engagement — Same design, three processes
activities.text: Classroom engagement — Same design, three processes If the school has access to an FDM printer (e.g. a desktop Creality or Prusa machine) and can source SLA-printed samples (many resin-printer owners, dental labs, or jewellers can supply an offcut), students compare an identical small design produced by both processes: layer lines, surface smoothness, print time and cost. Where hardware is unavailable, students instead analyse a real product made using SLA at industrial scale — Invisalign clear dental aligners, which are digitally 3D-modelled from a scan of the patient's teeth and mass-customised using resin-based additive printing — and evaluate why SLA (rather than FDM) is appropriate for a product requiring biocompatibility, high dimensional accuracy and a smooth, comfortable surface against skin.

activities.title: Classroom engagement — Redesigning the fuel nozzle
activities.text: Classroom engagement — Redesigning the fuel nozzle GE Aviation redesigned the fuel nozzle for its LEAP jet engine using metal powder bed fusion, consolidating a component that previously required 20 separately machined and welded parts into a single printed part that is around 25% lighter and up to five times more durable. Students examine before/after diagrams of the nozzle and are asked to justify, in writing, why PBF was selected over conventional subtractive machining and welding for this specific component — considering internal cooling channels, weight-critical aerospace requirements, and the relatively low production volume (thousands, not millions, of units per year) that makes the high per-part cost of metal PBF economically viable.

activities.title: Classroom engagement — Design a stimulus-responsive product
activities.text: Classroom engagement — Design a stimulus-responsive product After watching Skylar Tibbits' TED talk introducing 4D printing, students work in pairs to sketch a concept product that would benefit from a shape-change stimulus — for example, a flat-packed shelving bracket that assembles itself when heated with a hairdryer, or an irrigation valve that opens automatically as soil moisture (and therefore humidity) rises. For each concept, students must specify the intended stimulus (heat, water, pH, light), explain in their own words how a shape memory polymer achieves the transformation, and evaluate one practical limitation of 4D printing at the current stage of the technology (for example, the limited range of materials that reliably exhibit shape memory behaviour, and the difficulty of achieving precise, repeatable transformations at production scale).

activities.title: Classroom engagement — Layer lines and load paths
activities.text: Classroom engagement — Layer lines and load paths Using a simple 3D-printed test piece (or a diagram if a printer is unavailable), students identify the visible layer lines and predict, then physically test where possible, where the piece is weakest — typically along the layer boundary, where inter-layer adhesion is lower than the strength of the filament itself. Students then sketch how a 5D-printed equivalent of a curved bracket or hip-implant stem could orient its layers to follow the load path instead of stacking flat, and explain — referencing linking question A3.1 — how this changes the relationship between the printing process and the mechanical properties of the finished component.

activities.title: Classroom engagement — One material, five moulding processes
activities.text: Classroom engagement — One material, five moulding processes Students bring in (or are shown images of) five everyday plastic objects, each made using a different moulding process: a LEGO brick (injection moulding), a length of plastic guttering or a drinking straw (extrusion moulding), a traffic cone or kayak (rotational moulding), a PET water bottle (blow moulding), and a blister pack or chocolate box tray (vacuum moulding). In groups, students must correctly match each object to its process, identify one visible clue that supports their answer (a sprue/gate mark, a consistent cross-section, a seam line, a pinch-off point, or a thin uniform wall thickness), and justify why that specific process suits the object's required wall thickness, hollowness, or production volume.

activities.title: Classroom engagement — Why does this surface look/feel like this?
activities.text: Classroom engagement — Why does this surface look/feel like this? Students are given (or shown close-up images of) four finished surfaces: an anodized, brightly coloured aluminium water bottle; a chrome-plated bathroom tap; a galvanized steel crash barrier or roofing sheet; and a powder-coated steel garden chair. For each, students identify the finishing process, describe one functional benefit (corrosion resistance, wear resistance, colour durability) and one aesthetic benefit, and are challenged to explain why the manufacturer selected that specific finishing process rather than one of the others — for example, why galvanizing (a thicker, less decorative zinc coating) is preferred over anodizing for an outdoor steel barrier exposed to weather and impact, whereas anodizing (a thinner, colourable oxide layer) is preferred for a consumer product where appearance matters more than impact resistance.

activities.title: Classroom engagement — Full product breakdown: the office chair
activities.text: Classroom engagement — Full product breakdown: the office chair As a capstone task, students carry out a full manufacturing breakdown of an office chair (or an equally multi-component product, such as a power drill or a kettle). For each component, students state the category, name the specific technique, and justify the choice using at least one material property (linking question A3.1) and one production-volume or cost consideration (4.1.3).

moulding), and a process that produces a beautifully smooth surface finish (sla) may be far slower and more expensive than one that does not (fdm). designers therefore select — and combine — manufacturing techniques based on the material being processed, the required production volume, the geometric complexity of the part, the tolerances and finish required, cost and lead time, and the environmental impact of the process across the product's life cycle. this topic organises the huge range of available techniques into five categories so that this decision-making process becomes inherent feature of the process. 3. forming definition: reshapes a fixed mass of material — using heat, pressure or a mould — without adding or removing material. context: the material's volume is conserved throughout the process. 4. joining definition: brings two or more components together to create an assembly from separate parts. context: may be permanent (e.g. welding) or temporary (e.g. a bolted joint). 5. finishing definition: applied last, to protect a component from corrosion, wear or uv degradation, and/or to enhance its aesthetic appeal. context: in practice, almost no product is made using only one category — most combine several. a confident understanding of a4.1 depends on being able to identify which category — or combination of categories — was used to produce each (or are shown images of) five everyday plastic objects, each made using a different moulding process: a lego brick (injection moulding), a length of plastic guttering or a drinking straw (extrusion moulding), a traffic cone or kayak (rotational moulding), a pet water bottle (blow moulding), and a blister pack or chocolate box tray (vacuum moulding). in groups, students must correctly match each object to its process, identify one visible clue that supports their answer (a sprue/gate mark, a consistent cross-section, a seam line, a pinch-off point, or a thin uniform wall thickness), and justify why that specific process suits the object's required wall thickness, hollowness, or production volume. 4.1.9 joining techniques lesson 9: joining techniques joining techniques combine two or more components — of similar or dissimilar materials — into a single product or assembly, and may be designed to be permanent or temporary/demountable. 1. adhering definition: uses glues or bonding agents to chemically bond surfaces together. context: modern structural and waterproof adhesives are increasingly used in place of mechanical fasteners in products such as smartphones, where an adhesive seal also improves water resistance. 2. mechanical joining definition: uses fastening (screws, bolts, rivets, snap-fits) to hold components together, often allowing disassembly for repair or recycling; also includes stitching (thread passed through layers of a flexible material) and weaving (interlacing individual threads or filaments into a single structure). 3. fusion joining (welding) definition: permanently joins parts, typically metal, by heating the joint area to melting point so that the materials fuse together and solidify as one continuous piece on cooling. materials/examples: common welding processes include arc welding and spot welding. key terms: adhering · mechanical fastening · stitching · weaving · welding (fusion) classroom engagement — flat-pack vs. welded vs. woven students compare three products that each rely on a different joining strategy for a clear functional reason: flat-pack furniture (such as an ikea bookcase), which uses demountable mechanical fasteners — cam locks and dowels — specifically so the product can be transported flat and assembled by the customer; a steel bicycle frame, which uses fusion welding to create a permanent, rigid structural joint capable of withstanding repeated dynamic loads; and a knitted trainer upper (such as nike flyknit or adidas primeknit), which uses weaving to create a single, largely seamless textile structure that reduces material waste and stitched seams compared to a traditional cut-and-sew upper. students explain, for each case, why the alternative joining methods would be inappropriate. 4.1.10 finishing techniques lesson 10: finishing techniques finishing techniques are applied to a component's surface, after forming or joining, to protect it and/or improve its appearance and longevity. several finishing processes work by depositing or growing a protective layer on the base material. 1. anodizing definition: an electrochemical process, most commonly applied to aluminium, that thickens and hardens the material's naturally occurring oxide layer, improving corrosion and wear resistance and allowing the surface to be dyed a durable colour. materials/examples: used extensively on aluminium consumer electronics and cookware. 2. electro-plating definition: uses an electric current to deposit a thin layer of one metal (commonly chromium, nickel, gold or zinc) onto the surface of another, improving corrosion resistance, wear resistance or appearance. materials/examples: chrome-plated taps and vehicle trim. 3. galvanizing definition: coats iron or steel with a protective layer of zinc, most often by hot-dip immersion, to prevent rust. materials/examples: widely used for structural steel, crash barriers and roofing. 4. powder coating definition: applies a dry, electrostatically charged powder to a (usually metal) surface, which is then cured under heat to form a tough, even, decorative layer. materials/examples: commonly used on outdoor furniture, bicycle frames and domestic appliances. 5. polishing / sealants definition: uses mechanical abrasion (polishing, buffing) or an applied layer such as oil, wax or silicone to reduce surface friction, enhance appearance, and protect materials such as wood, stone or leather from moisture and wear. key terms: anodizing · electro-plating · galvanizing · powder coating · polishing/sealants classroom engagement — why does this surface look/feel like this? students are given (or shown close-up images of) four finished surfaces: an anodized, brightly coloured aluminium water bottle; a chrome-plated bathroom tap; a galvanized steel crash barrier or roofing sheet; and a powder-coated steel garden chair. for each, students identify the finishing process, describe one functional benefit (corrosion resistance, wear resistance, colour durability) and one aesthetic benefit, and are challenged to explain why the manufacturer selected that specific finishing process rather than one of the others — for example, why galvanizing (a thicker, less decorative zinc coating) is preferred over anodizing for an outdoor steel barrier exposed to weather and impact, whereas anodizing (a thinner, colourable oxide layer) is preferred for a consumer product where appearance matters more than impact resistance. 4.1.11 combining techniques links: a3.1 · c3.1 lesson 11: combining techniques most real products cannot be produced using a single manufacturing category in isolation. instead, designers combine additive, subtractive, forming, joining and finishing techniques — selecting each one to suit the specific material, function, tolerance and finish required by an individual component, before those components are brought together into a finished assembly. a confident a4.1 candidate can look at an everyday product, break it down into its constituent parts, and justify why each part was manufactured the way it was — this is the culminating skill of the whole topic, and is also the skill directly assessed by linking question c3.1. key terms: combining techniques · assembly · design justification classroom engagement — full product breakdown: the office chair as a capstone task, students carry out a full manufacturing breakdown of an office chair (or an equally multi-component product, such as a power drill or a kettle). for each component, students state the category, name the specific technique, and justify the choice using at least one material property (linking question a3.1) and one production-volume or cost consideration (4.1.3). component category technique plastic seat shell forming injection moulding five-star base forming die casting (aluminium) gas-lift cylinder housing subtractive / forming cnc machining or extrusion steel frame beneath upholstery joining welding metal components (visible) finishing powder coating fabric upholstery joining stitching / stapling ergonomics test model additive rapid prototyping (fdm/sla) linking questions use these questions to connect a4.1 to other parts of the design technology course. they are well suited to plenary discussion, homework extension, or as scaffolding for the internal assessment and extended essay. code linking question a3.1 how might material properties influence the selection of manufacturing techniques? b2.2 to what extent are manufacturing techniques for commercial products used for modelling and prototyping potential design solutions? c2.2 which manufacturing techniques should be avoided when designing products for a circular economy? c3.1 how can product analysis be used to identify the manufacturing techniques used to create a product? c3.2 how can the selection of a manufacturing technique affect the outcome of a life-cycle analysis (lca) on a product? exam prep: topic a4.1 the following questions are written in the style of ib design technology paper 1 and paper 2, and use official ib command terms. command term what it requires define give the precise meaning of a word, phrase or physical quantity. identify / outline give a brief account or summary; state the main point(s) with little or no supporting detail. distinguish make clear the differences between two or more concepts or items. describe give a detailed account, including all relevant characteristics, events or processes. explain give a detailed account including reasons or causes — the 'how' and 'why', not just the 'what'. discuss offer a considered and balanced review of a topic, including a range of arguments, factors or hypotheses; opinions/conclusions should be presented clearly and supported by evidence. evaluate / to what extent make an appraisal by weighing up strengths and limitations, arriving at a balanced, evidence-based judgement. section a — multiple choice (3 questions, 1 mark each) 1. which manufacturing technique is best classified as forming? a. cnc milling b. injection moulding c. selective laser sintering d. anodizing reveal answer [1] b — injection moulding. 2. which additive manufacturing technique uses a laser to selectively cure a liquid photopolymer resin? a. fused deposition modelling (fdm) b. laminated object manufacture (lom) c. stereolithography (sla) d. selective laser sintering (sls) reveal answer [1] c — stereolithography (sla). 3. a component made from a shape memory polymer that changes form only after exposure to heat is best described as an example of: a. 3d printing b. 4d printing c. 5d printing d. subtractive manufacturing reveal answer [1] b — 4d printing. section b — short answer 4. distinguish between additive and subtractive manufacturing, using one named example of each. [4 marks] reveal answer indicative content: award marks for: a clear statement that additive manufacturing builds an object by adding material layer by layer while subtractive manufacturing removes material from a larger mass [1] ; a valid named additive example, e.g. fdm, sla, sls [1] ; a valid named subtractive example, e.g. cnc milling, turning [1] ; credit for noting the waste-material implication of each — additive generates little waste, subtractive generates swarf [1] . 5. outline two differences between rapid prototyping and production manufacturing techniques. [4 marks] reveal answer indicative content: award one mark per valid difference outlined, to a maximum of two differences (two marks each if elaborated): tooling cost — prototyping requires little/no tooling; production requires significant up-front tooling investment, e.g. an injection mould; unit cost at volume — prototyping has a high cost per unit at scale, production has a low marginal cost per unit once tooling is amortised; speed of design iteration — prototyping allows fast redesign, production tooling is slow and costly to modify; typical processes cited, e.g. desktop fdm vs. injection moulding. section c — long answer 6. explain, using an example, why 5d printing might be selected over standard 3d printing for a component used in the aerospace industry. [6 marks] reveal answer mark scheme guidance level 1 (1–2 marks): basic description of 5d printing (rotating extruder/bed, prints on five axes) with little or no reference to aerospace application. level 2 (3–4 marks): explains that 5d printing allows layers to follow the curved contours/load path of a part, and links this to increased strength compared with flat-layered 3d printing. level 3 (5–6 marks): fully explains the causal link between layer orientation and mechanical strength (referencing material properties, a3.1), and applies this convincingly to a plausible or named aerospace component (e.g. a curved structural bracket) where weight-critical strength and safety justify the additional process complexity and cost of 5d printing over conventional 3d printing. 7. a company is designing a reusable plastic water bottle intended to fit within a circular economy. the bottle body is produced by blow moulding, the cap by injection moulding, and a metal carry-clip is joined to the body. discuss the extent to which these manufacturing choices support circular economy principles. [8 marks] reveal answer mark scheme guidance: award marks for a balanced discussion that considers both supporting and limiting factors. supporting: blow moulding and injection moulding both produce durable, reusable components suited to a long product life; both processes are well suited to using recycled polymer feedstock; separable joining (rather than adhesive or fusion joining) of the clip could support end-of-life disassembly and material recovery. limiting: if the cap, body and clip use dissimilar materials that are permanently joined, this can hinder recycling/disassembly; moulding processes require energy-intensive tooling and processing; single-polymer design and mechanical (demountable) joining would better support circularity than permanent joining of mixed materials. top-level responses reach a clear, justified conclusion on the overall extent to which the technique choices support circularity, referencing linking question c2.2. glossary of key terms — topic a4.1 click on a term to reveal its definition. 3d printing definition: the process of creating physical objects from a 3d digital model by building up material layer by layer. example: rapid functional prototypes and custom medical implants. additive manufacturing definition: a process of making a three-dimensional solid object from a digital file by adding material layer by layer. example: industrial sls printing used to manufacture lightweight aerospace engine parts. laminated object manufacture (lom) definition: an additive process that builds an object by bonding and cutting successive layers of sheet material. example: early full-colour architectural scale models built from bonded paper sheets. fused deposition modelling (fdm) definition: an additive process that melts and extrudes a thermoplastic filament through a heated nozzle, layer by layer. example: desktop 3d printers used to prototype phone cases and enclosures. stereolithography (sla) definition: an additive process that uses a laser to selectively cure liquid photopolymer resin into solid layers. example: invisalign-style clear dental aligners custom-printed from a tooth scan. rapid prototyping definition: the fast production of a scale model or working model using additive or other quick-turnaround processes, to test and validate a design before committing to production tooling. example: an fdm-printed housing used to test the fit of internal electronics before injection-mould tooling is ordered. powder bed fusion (pbf) definition: an industrial additive process in which thermal energy (laser or electron beam) selectively fuses regions of a bed of powdered material. example: ge aviation's metal-printed leap engine fuel nozzle. material extrusion definition: an additive process that dispenses material through a nozzle in a continuous bead to build an object layer by layer. example: industrial-scale fdm printing of functional end-use parts and jigs. selective laser sintering (sls) definition: an additive process that uses a laser as a power source to sinter (fuse) powdered material, typically without support structures. example: lightweight, complex nylon brackets used in low-volume automotive and aerospace parts. 4d printing definition: using 3d printing to create a physical object that can change its shape or properties when exposed to a stimulus such as water, heat, light or an electric current. example: a medical stent that expands to its functional shape once it reaches body temperature. 5d printing definition: an additive process similar to 3d printing, but with a rotating extruder head and print bed that allow printing on five axes. example: curved aerospace or biomedical components whose printed layers follow the part's load path for extra strength. shape memory polymer definition: a smart material that can be deformed and then returns to a pre-programmed shape when triggered by an external stimulus. example: self-tightening product fastenings and self-folding packaging. subtractive manufacturing definition: any manufacturing process in which a 3d object is created by removing material from a solid block. example: cnc milling a laptop's unibody aluminium chassis from a solid block. machining definition: a family of subtractive processes, including cutting, milling and turning, that remove material using a cutting tool. example: turning a steel bolt shaft on a lathe. abrading definition: a subtractive process that uses friction to gradually wear away a material's surface. example: sanding a wooden skateboard deck before applying a finish. forming definition: a manufacturing process that changes the shape of a material — usually with heat and/or pressure — without adding or removing material. example: press-forming a flat steel blank into a curved car door panel. casting definition: a forming process in which a liquid material is poured into a mould cavity and solidifies into the mould's shape. example: casting a cast-iron frying pan from molten iron. injection moulding definition: a forming process that injects molten plastic under pressure into a precision mould cavity to produce highly accurate, repeatable parts. example: mass-produced lego bricks, moulded to tolerances of around ±0.002 mm. extrusion moulding definition: a forming process that continuously forces heated material through a shaped die to create a constant cross-section profile. example: plastic guttering, pipes and drinking straws. rotational moulding definition: a forming process in which powdered plastic is rotated on two axes inside a heated mould to evenly coat the internal surface, producing a seamless hollow part. example: traffic cones and kayaks. blow moulding definition: a forming process in which a heated tube of plastic is inflated with compressed air inside a mould to create a thin-walled hollow container. example: pet plastic drinks bottles. vacuum moulding definition: a forming process in which a heated plastic sheet is drawn tightly over a mould using a vacuum, producing shallow, detailed forms. example: blister packaging and chocolate-box trays. joining definition: combining two or more components, of similar or dissimilar materials, to form a single product or assembly. example: welding the tubular frame of a bicycle together. adhering definition: a joining process that uses glues or bonding agents to chemically bond surfaces together. example: adhesive-sealed waterproof joints in a smartphone casing. mechanical fastening definition: a joining process that uses fasteners such as screws, bolts or snap-fits, often allowing later disassembly. example: cam-lock and dowel fixings in flat-pack furniture. weaving definition: a joining process that interlaces individual threads or filaments into a single structural textile. example: a knitted trainer upper, such as nike flyknit. welding definition: a fusion joining process used to permanently join parts, typically metal, by heating them to melting point and allowing them to solidify together. example: arc welding used in the construction of steel bridge structures. finishing definition: a final process applied to the surface of a product to improve appearance and/or performance and protect it from degradation. example: anodizing an aluminium smartphone case to give it a durable, coloured finish. anodizing definition: an electrochemical finishing process, usually applied to aluminium, that thickens the natural oxide layer to improve corrosion resistance and allow colouring. example: brightly coloured anodized aluminium water bottles and cookware. electro-plating definition: a finishing process that uses an electric current to deposit a thin layer of metal onto the surface of another material. example: chrome-plated bathroom taps and vehicle trim. galvanizing definition: a finishing process that coats iron or steel with a protective layer of zinc, typically by hot-dip immersion, to prevent rust. example: galvanized steel crash barriers and roofing sheets. powder coating definition: a finishing process in which dry, electrostatically charged powder is applied to a surface and cured under heat to form a tough, even coating. example: powder-coated steel garden furniture and bicycle frames. 3d printing 4d printing 5d printing abrading additive manufacturing adhering anodizing casting computer-aided design (cad) die-casting electroplating fastening finishing techniques form forming techniques fused deposition modelling (fdm) galvanizing injection moulding joining techniques laminated object manufacture (lom) machining (manufacturing) manufacturing techniques mass customization material extrusion moulding polishing powder bed fusion (pbf) press-forming rapid prototyping scale of production selective laser sintering (sls) stereolithography (sla) stitching subtractive manufacturing weaving welding shape memory polymer machining forming extrusion moulding rotational moulding blow moulding vacuum moulding joining mechanical fastening finishing electro-plating powder coating manufacturing techniques can be organized into five categories. an additive technique is the process of creating an object by constructing it one layer at a time and typically refers to 3d printing. rapid prototyping is the creation of an object based on a computer model developed in a 3d modelling (cad) program. additive manufacturing is used in various industries for low-volume production runs. 4d printing is an extension of 3d printing, where the physical and chemical state of a 3d printed object changes over time due to external stimuli such as ph, temperature, water and light. 5d dimensional additive manufacturing involves the rotation of the extruder head and the print bed in order to print in five different axes. subtractive techniques involve removing material from an initial 3d mass to achieve a desired shape and can also be applied to 2d or flat materials to modify or change the shape. forming techniques modify the shape of a material without adding or removing any materials. joining techniques can temporarily or permanently join two or more similar or dissimilar materials together. finishing techniques are used to protect and enhance the surface of a component, contributing to its longevity and an overall increase in product life. a combination of additive, subtractive, forming, joining and finishing techniques are needed to create components and products.

title: User-centred design

sections.title: Lesson 1: UCD Planning
sections.html:
B1.1.1 UCD Planning ~45 min

Lesson 1: UCD Planning

A successful UCD process begins with a structured plan to research user needs and engage potential end-users throughout the design cycle. Designers must define research questions, identify potential end-users, and schedule the entire cycle from initial research through to manufacturing. A well-structured plan ensures that the resulting design insights are relevant and that research is conducted efficiently — without it, teams risk designing for assumptions rather than evidence.

Think about it

Imagine you had to design a product for someone whose daily routine, physical abilities, and frustrations are completely different from your own. Where would you even start? UCD planning is the answer: a structured way of finding out before you start sketching.

1. Defining Research Questions

Definition: Focused questions that a design team must answer through user research before any solution is sketched — they turn a vague brief into a targeted investigation.

Context: Rather than assuming "students want a faster kiosk," a well-planned research question asks "at what time of day do queues form, and why?" — a question that can actually be tested.

Materials/Examples: Interview scripts, survey question banks, observation checklists.

Application: Used at the very start of the design cycle to steer every subsequent research method.

2. Identifying End-Users

Definition: The process of recognising that a product may serve several distinct groups of people, each with different needs, abilities, and contexts of use.

Context: A school water-refill station is used very differently by a Year 7 student between classes and a PE teacher carrying several bottles at once — a single "average user" assumption would miss both.

Materials/Examples: Stakeholder maps, demographic breakdowns, user-group lists.

Application: Ensures research and later personas represent the real range of people who will use the product.

3. Scheduling the UCD Cycle

Definition: Mapping out realistic time-frames for every stage of the design process, from initial research through to manufacture, so that user engagement happens continuously rather than only at the start.

Context: A schedule might allocate two weeks for research, one week for persona-building, three weeks of iterative prototyping with user feedback, and a final manufacturing window — with users consulted at each checkpoint.

Materials/Examples: Gantt charts, timelines, project-planning software.

Application: Prevents user research from being treated as a one-off box to tick, keeping the "user" central throughout.

Further viewing: Explain UX with User-Centered Design (NN/Group) — a concise explanation of why planning around real users, not assumptions, drives the whole UCD cycle.

Practical Engagement: Plan a Real Research Sprint (20 min)

Scenario: the school wants to redesign its water-refill station because students complain it is slow and hard to use between classes.

  • In pairs, write 3 focused research questions the design team should answer before sketching any solution (e.g. "What time of day causes the longest queues?").
  • Identify 2 distinct end-user groups (e.g. Year 7 students vs. PE staff carrying multiple bottles) whose needs might differ.
  • Sketch a one-line timeline from research → persona-building → prototyping → manufacture, with a rough date for each stage.
Planning StagePurposeExample Output
Research QuestionsTurn assumptions into testable investigations"When do queues peak at the refill station?"
End-User IdentificationEnsure no user group is designed outYear 7 students; PE staff; students with limited mobility
Cycle SchedulingKeep users involved from research to manufactureResearch → personas → prototyping → manufacture timeline

sections.title: Lesson 2: Targeting Populations and Personas
sections.html:
B1.1.2 Targeting Populations B1.1.3 Personas & Journey Maps ~60 min

Lesson 2: Targeting Populations and Personas

Designers use specific research methods — interviews, surveys, observations — to target demographics and develop a deep understanding of their intended users. This data is used to create primary personas: fictional representations that reflect the attributes, goals, and motivations of a user population. Research data is also translated into user journey maps (often storyboards), which visually plot a user's experience over time to highlight "pain points" — moments of friction that become concrete design opportunities.

1. Research Methods for Targeting Populations

Definition: Structured techniques — interviews, surveys, and direct observation — used to gather first-hand data about a target demographic's needs, goals, and behaviours.

Context: A short intercept survey at a library self-checkout can reveal exactly which step causes first-time visitors to hesitate, in a way that assumptions never could.

Materials/Examples: Structured interview scripts, online survey tools, observation logs.

Application: Provides the raw evidence base that personas and journey maps are built from.

2. Primary Personas

Definition: Fictional representations, built from real research data, that reflect the attributes, goals, and motivations of a target user population.

Context: "Kofi, a first-time visitor unfamiliar with self-service technology" gives a design team a specific, memorable person to design for — sharper than a vague target market description.

Materials/Examples: Persona templates (name, goals, frustrations, quote), research synthesis boards.

Application: Keeps every later design decision anchored to a specific, evidence-based user rather than the design team's own assumptions.

3. User Journey Maps & Pain Points

Definition: A visual plot (often a storyboard) of a persona's experience over time, used to highlight "pain points" — moments of friction that become concrete design opportunities.

Context: Mapping a hospital patient's journey from admission to discharge can reveal the exact moment a patient struggles to locate the call button while in pain — an invisible frustration turned into a targetable opportunity.

Materials/Examples: Six-panel storyboards, journey-map templates, sticky-note timelines.

Application: Converts a persona's lived experience into specific, actionable design briefs.

Case Study: "Divya"

A university library research team creates the persona "Divya," a focused student who needs a quiet study space between lectures. Every subsequent decision — seating layout, noise policy, signage — is tested against whether it would genuinely help Divya, keeping the whole redesign anchored to real user research rather than guesswork.

Practical Engagement A: The Gift-Giving Challenge (15 min)

  • Empathize: in pairs, interview your partner about their morning routine.
  • Define: identify one specific frustration they experience.
  • Ideate: sketch a "gift" product that solves that one frustration, and name the persona it is designed for.

Practical Engagement B: User Journey Storyboarding

Using the persona created above (or the water-refill station scenario), draw a 6-panel storyboard tracking that persona's experience from start to finish. Circle the single panel that represents the biggest "pain point," and annotate it with one design intervention that could remove it.

Further viewing/reading: How to Create & Use Personas in UX (Sarah Doody) and Storyboards Help Visualize UX Ideas (NN/Group).

sections.title: Lesson 3: Usability Objectives
sections.html:
B1.1.4 Usability Objectives ~50 min

Lesson 3: Usability Objectives

Products are analysed against five key usability objectives to identify specific areas for improvement.

1. Learnability

Definition: How easy is it for users to accomplish basic tasks the first time they use the product?

Context: Google Search is highly learnable because it uses a simple, intuitive interface that requires no training.

Materials/Examples: First-use walkthroughs, onboarding tooltips, icon clarity testing.

Application: Tested by observing brand-new users attempting a task with no instruction.

2. Efficiency

Definition: How quickly and accurately can users perform tasks once they are familiar with the system?

Context: Amazon's "One-Click" checkout speeds up the purchasing process for returning customers.

Materials/Examples: Task-timing studies, click-count analysis, shortcut design.

Application: Measured by timing an experienced user completing a familiar task.

3. Memorability

Definition: How well can a user remember how to operate the product after a period of non-use?

Context: A returning smart-thermostat user who has not opened the app in three months forgets how the schedule icons work, even though a first-time user found them easy to learn.

Materials/Examples: Return-visit usability tests, consistent icon systems.

Application: Tested by bringing back a user after a gap of weeks or months.

4. Errors

Definition: What is the frequency and severity of mistakes made by the user, and how does the system help them recover?

Context: An ATM that requires a confirmation step before dispensing cash reduces the severity of a mis-entered amount, and clearly explains how to correct it.

Materials/Examples: Error logs, confirmation dialogues, undo functions.

Application: Assessed by counting mistakes and recovery time during task testing.

5. Satisfaction

Definition: How pleasant and rewarding is the overall experience of using the product?

Context: An Apple iPhone's smooth animations and intuitive interface create a satisfying user experience beyond pure task completion.

Materials/Examples: Post-use surveys, satisfaction ratings, qualitative feedback interviews.

Application: Gathered through user feedback after a task has been completed successfully.

ObjectiveGuiding QuestionExample
LearnabilityCan a first-time user complete a basic task?Google Search's intuitive interface
EfficiencyHow fast/accurate is a familiar user?Amazon "One-Click" checkout
MemorabilityCan a returning user recall how it works?Smart-thermostat schedule icons
ErrorsHow often/severely do users make mistakes?ATM confirmation step before cash is dispensed
SatisfactionHow pleasant is the overall experience?iPhone's smooth, intuitive animations

Practical Engagement: Usability Audit

In groups, choose a school service you use regularly — e.g. the lunch ordering system, the timetable app, or the library self-checkout — and evaluate it against all five usability objectives. For each objective, propose one specific, actionable improvement (not just "make it better").

Further reading: Usability 101: Introduction to Usability (NN/Group) — the original framework these five objectives are drawn from.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Task Analysis
sections.html:
B1.1.5 Task Analysis ~45 min

Lesson 4: Task Analysis

Task analysis is a strategy used to deconstruct a complex process into individual steps. By observing a user performing a specific task — e.g. brushing teeth or riding a bike — designers can identify critical points of failure, delay, or frustration. These identified points are targeted for design enhancements to streamline the process and reduce user error.

1. Deconstructing Complex Processes

Definition: Breaking a task down into its individual, observable steps so that every part of the interaction can be examined on its own.

Context: Analysing the steps of using a manual can opener — reaching for it, aligning the blade, gripping and turning — makes it possible to find exactly where users with arthritis struggle most.

Materials/Examples: Step-by-step observation sheets, numbered task lists, video recordings of use.

Application: Used before redesigning any product where the interaction sequence itself may be the problem.

2. Identifying Points of Failure

Definition: Pinpointing the exact step in a deconstructed task where a user hesitates, makes an error, or gives up — the moment task analysis is designed to reveal.

Context: An elderly user struggling at the exact moment they must align a plug with a wall socket hidden behind furniture is a pain point identified through task analysis, not a general usability rating.

Materials/Examples: Annotated step lists, hesitation/error markers, timing data per step.

Application: Directly targeted for design enhancement — the single failing step, not the whole product, is redesigned.

Case Study: Redesigning a Kettle Handle

A design team studying users with arthritis conducts a task analysis of pouring an electric kettle. It reveals two pain points: difficulty gripping the handle when the kettle is full and heavy, and difficulty triggering the lid-release catch with reduced finger strength. These findings directly justify prioritising Errors (reducing spills/scalds) and Satisfaction (a handle that feels comfortable and safe) in the redesign.

Practical Engagement: Step-by-Step Observation

Watch a partner use the school vending machine, a locker, or a public water fountain. Write down every single step as a numbered list (aim for 8–12 steps — be exhaustive). Circle the step where hesitation, confusion, or error occurred, and propose one design change that would remove it.

Further reading: How to Improve Your UX Designs with Task Analysis (Interaction Design Foundation).

Linking Questions

Use these to connect Topic B1.1 to other areas of the syllabus and to stimulate class discussion or extended-response practice.

A1.1 Ergonomics: To what extent does UCD rely on a strong foundation of ergonomics to ensure user satisfaction and safety?
A2.1 Research: How important is a deep understanding of user-centred research methods to ensure an effective UCD strategy?
B2.2 Prototyping: How can modelling and prototyping be used to gather the feedback necessary to iterate a UCD solution?
C1.2 Inclusive Design: To what extent should a UCD process prioritize "designing for extremes" to ensure universal accessibility?
C3.1 Product Analysis: What influence does product analysis have on identifying usability opportunities within UCD?

sections.title: Exam Practice: Topic B1.1
sections.html:
B1.1 Exam Practice AO1 / AO2 / AO3

Exam Practice: Topic B1.1

Command terms and mark-allocation logic follow the IB Design Technology assessment objectives (AO1 Knowledge, AO2 Application, AO3 Synthesis). Sample/indicative answers for teacher use follow each question.

Section A: Multiple Choice (3 questions, 1 mark each)

1. Which of the following best defines a "primary persona" in the UCD process?

  • A record of every possible user of a product
  • A fictional character representing the attributes, goals, and motivations of a target user group
  • A technical specification document used for manufacturing
  • A survey completed by the design team
Reveal Answer
B. A fictional character representing the attributes, goals, and motivations of a target user group. [1]

2. A first-time user of a smart thermostat app can complete the "set schedule" task easily without instructions, but a returning user who has not opened the app in three months forgets how the icons work. Which pair of usability objectives does this scenario contrast?

  • Efficiency and Satisfaction
  • Learnability and Memorability
  • Errors and Efficiency
  • Satisfaction and Errors
Reveal Answer
B. Learnability and Memorability. [1]

3. A designer observes an elderly user struggling at the exact moment they must align a plug with a wall socket hidden behind furniture. In UCD, this observed moment of difficulty is best described as a:

  • Usability objective
  • Primary persona
  • Pain point identified through task analysis
  • Design specification
Reveal Answer
C. Pain point identified through task analysis. [1]

Section B: Short Answer (2 questions)

Question 4 [1 + 3 = 4 marks]

A public library wants to redesign its self-checkout kiosk after noticing many first-time visitors struggle to locate the "scan" button.

(a) Identify one user-centred design research method the library could use to understand visitor needs. [1]

(b) Describe how creating a primary persona of a "first-time visitor" could help the design team improve the kiosk's usability. [3]

Reveal Answer

(a) [1] Award for a valid method named precisely, e.g. observation of visitors at the current kiosk; a short intercept survey; a structured interview with library staff. Technical term only — no explanation required.

(b) [3] Award up to 3 using Point → Evidence → Effect: the persona (e.g. "Kofi, a first-time visitor unfamiliar with self-service technology") (1) focuses the team on his specific confusion — not locating the scan button (1) — which justifies enlarging/relabelling the scan icon and adding on-screen prompts so first-time use matches expert use (1).

Question 5 [2 + 2 = 4 marks]

A design team is developing a new electric kettle for users with arthritis, following task analysis observations of users attempting to lift and pour a full kettle.

(a) Outline two "pain points" a task analysis of kettle use might reveal for a user with limited grip strength. [2]

(b) State two usability objectives the design team should prioritize when redesigning the kettle handle. [2]

Reveal Answer

(a) [2] Award 1 each for two distinct, plausible pain points, e.g. difficulty gripping the handle when the kettle is full and heavy; difficulty triggering the lid-release catch with reduced finger strength.

(b) [2] Award 1 each for two named objectives with a one-phrase justification, e.g. Errors — to reduce spills/scalds; Satisfaction — so the product feels comfortable and safe to use daily.

Section C: Long Answer (2 questions)

Question 6 [4 marks]

Explain how user journey mapping (storyboarding) can be used by a design team to identify design opportunities when developing a new product for hospital patients.

Reveal Answer

[4] Award marks for a logical chain (Point → Mechanism → Consequence). E.g. A design team maps a hospital patient's journey from admission to discharge (Point); this visualises each touchpoint — such as the confusing moment a patient must locate the call button while in pain or under medication (Mechanism); therefore the storyboard converts an invisible frustration into a concrete, targetable design opportunity, such as relocating or redesigning the call button (Consequence). Full marks require at least one named pain point and one resulting design opportunity.

Question 7 [6 marks]

Evaluate the effectiveness of conducting a usability audit against all five usability objectives (learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, satisfaction) as a strategy for improving an existing product, such as a school's online lunch-ordering system.

Reveal Answer

[6] Use the Strength/Opportunity — Limitation/Threat — Comparison — Synthesis structure. Strength: auditing against all five objectives surfaces problems a single-lens review would miss (e.g. a system can be efficient for regular users yet fail Learnability for new Year 7 students). Limitation: audits are time-consuming and subjective without real user testing data, and improving one objective (e.g. Efficiency, via fewer clicks) can conflict with another (e.g. Errors, if steps are skipped). Comparison: contrast with simply collecting complaints, which is reactive and unstructured. Conclusion: on balance, a five-objective audit is most effective when paired with direct observation of real users, since it converts vague dissatisfaction into specific, actionable design requirements for each objective.

sections.title: Glossary: Topic B1.1
sections.html:
B1.1 Glossary

Glossary: Topic B1.1

Key terms, IB definitions, and real-world contextual examples for User-Centred Design. Click on a term to reveal its definition.

User-Centred Design (UCD)
IB Definition: A design philosophy and process that pays particular attention to user needs at all stages.
Real-World Context: The guiding approach for the IA project, focusing on redesigning products for a specific user.
Primary Persona
IB Definition: A representative fictional character created based on user research.
Real-World Context: Creating "Divya," a focused student who needs a quiet study space, to guide the design of a library product.
Usability
IB Definition: How effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily a user can interact with a product.
Real-World Context: Evaluating an ATM interface to ensure it is simple enough for first-time users (Learnability).
Efficiency
IB Definition: A usability objective concerning the speed and accuracy of task performance.
Real-World Context: Amazon's "One-Click" checkout speeds up the purchasing process for returning customers.
Learnability
IB Definition: The extent to which a user can operate a product at a defined level of competence after initial use.
Real-World Context: Google Search is highly learnable because it uses a simple, intuitive interface that requires no training.
Satisfaction
IB Definition: How pleasant a product is to use; the degree to which needs and preferences are met.
Real-World Context: An Apple iPhone's smooth animations and intuitive interface create a satisfying user experience.
Task Analysis
IB Definition: A strategy used to break down a process into steps to identify critical points for improvement.
Real-World Context: Analysing the steps of using a manual can opener to find where users with arthritis struggle most.
