syllabus.title: User-centred design
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How does understanding user needs directly impact the design of products and services?

statements.text: User-centred design (UCD) requires a plan to structure an inquiry using user-centred research methods.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to construct a plan for a UCD process based on research questions that engage with user-centred research methods.

statements.text: UCD uses specific research methods to target persona populations and it develops empathy and understanding of users’ demographics.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to apply a variety of user-centred research methods (field research, user observation, interviews, questionnaires and focus groups) and analyse data to establish users’ characteristics, behaviours, and the wants and needs of the target population defined by their demographics.

statements.text: Data collected from user-centred research is used to determine personae that represent attributes of user populations.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to create a primary persona or personae based on user-centred research to aid design development.

statements.text: Products can be analysed by using usability objectives to identify opportunities for improvement.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain and apply five usability objectives (learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors and satisfaction) in order to evaluate a product.

statements.text: A task analysis is a strategy used to develop empathy and gain understanding of how users perform a task to achieve their intended goal.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to apply task analysis techniques to break down a process into steps and identify the critical points for design improvement.

activity.title: Usability test swap
steps: Set a measurable task such as finding a feature or adjusting a product.
Test two designs with consenting classmates using the same instructions and conditions.
Record completion time, errors and a short satisfaction rating.
Use evidence to propose one revision; distinguish usability findings from personal preference.
activity.debrief: Can a product be usable but fail to meet a real need?

exam.question: Explain how involving users during development can improve usability. [2]
exam.answer: Testing reveals specific difficulties with learning or operating a product. Designers can revise features in response and retest whether errors or effort decrease.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Plan a Real Research Sprint (20 min)
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Plan a Real Research Sprint (20 min) Scenario: the school wants to redesign its water-refill station because students complain it is slow and hard to use between classes. In pairs, write 3 focused research questions the design team should answer before sketching any solution (e.g. "What time of day causes the longest queues?"). Identify 2 distinct end-user groups (e.g. Year 7 students vs. PE staff carrying multiple bottles) whose needs might differ. Sketch a one-line timeline from research → persona-building → prototyping → manufacture, with a rough date for each stage.

searchText: user-centred design b1.1.1 ucd planning ~45 min lesson 1: ucd planning a successful ucd process begins with a structured plan to research user needs and engage potential end-users throughout the design cycle. designers must define research questions, identify potential end-users, and schedule the entire cycle from initial research through to manufacturing. a well-structured plan ensures that the resulting design insights are relevant and that research is conducted efficiently — without it, teams risk designing for assumptions rather than evidence. think about it imagine you had to design a product for someone whose daily routine, physical abilities, and frustrations are completely different from your own. where would you even start? ucd planning is the answer: a structured way of finding out before you start sketching. 1. defining research questions definition: focused questions that a design team must answer through user research before any solution is sketched — they turn a vague brief into a targeted investigation. context: rather than assuming "students want a faster kiosk," a well-planned research question asks "at what time of day do queues form, and why?" — a question that can actually be tested. materials/examples: interview scripts, survey question banks, observation checklists. application: used at the very start of the design cycle to steer every subsequent research method. 2. identifying end-users definition: the process of recognising that a product may serve several distinct groups of people, each with different needs, abilities, and contexts of use. context: a school water-refill station is used very differently by a year 7 student between classes and a pe teacher carrying several bottles at once — a single "average user" assumption would miss both. materials/examples: stakeholder maps, demographic breakdowns, user-group lists. application: ensures research and later personas represent the real range of people who will use the product. 3. scheduling the ucd cycle definition: mapping out realistic time-frames for every stage of the design process, from initial research through to manufacture, so that user engagement happens continuously rather than only at the start. context: a schedule might allocate two weeks for research, one week for persona-building, three weeks of iterative prototyping with user feedback, and a final manufacturing window — with users consulted at each checkpoint. materials/examples: gantt charts, timelines, project-planning software. application: prevents user research from being treated as a one-off box to tick, keeping the "user" central throughout. further viewing: explain ux with user-centered design (nn/group) — a concise explanation of why planning around real users, not assumptions, drives the whole ucd cycle. practical engagement: plan a real research sprint (20 min) scenario: the school wants to redesign its water-refill station because students complain it is slow and hard to use between classes. in pairs, write 3 focused research questions the design team should answer before sketching any solution (e.g. "what time of day causes the longest queues?"). identify 2 distinct end-user groups (e.g. year 7 students vs. pe staff carrying multiple bottles) whose needs might differ. sketch a one-line timeline from research → persona-building → prototyping → manufacture, with a rough date for each stage. planning stage purpose example output research questions turn assumptions into testable investigations "when do queues peak at the refill station?" end-user identification ensure no user group is designed out year 7 students; pe staff; students with limited mobility cycle scheduling keep users involved from research to manufacture research → personas → prototyping → manufacture timeline b1.1.2 targeting populations b1.1.3 personas & journey maps ~60 min lesson 2: targeting populations and personas designers use specific research methods — interviews, surveys, observations — to target demographics and develop a deep understanding of their intended users. this data is used to create primary personas: fictional representations that reflect the attributes, goals, and motivations of a user population. research data is also translated into user journey maps (often storyboards), which visually plot a user's experience over time to highlight "pain points" — moments of friction that become concrete design opportunities. 1. research methods for targeting populations definition: structured techniques — interviews, surveys, and direct observation — used to gather first-hand data about a target demographic's needs, goals, and behaviours. context: a short intercept survey at a library self-checkout can reveal exactly which step causes first-time visitors to hesitate, in a way that assumptions never could. materials/examples: structured interview scripts, online survey tools, observation logs. application: provides the raw evidence base that personas and journey maps are built from. 2. primary personas definition: fictional representations, built from real research data, that reflect the attributes, goals, and motivations of a target user population. context: "kofi, a first-time visitor unfamiliar with self-service technology" gives a design team a specific, memorable person to design for — sharper than a vague target market description. materials/examples: persona templates (name, goals, frustrations, quote), research synthesis boards. application: keeps every later design decision anchored to a specific, evidence-based user rather than the design team's own assumptions. 3. user journey maps & pain points definition: a visual plot (often a storyboard) of a persona's experience over time, used to highlight "pain points" — moments of friction that become concrete design opportunities. context: mapping a hospital patient's journey from admission to discharge can reveal the exact moment a patient struggles to locate the call button while in pain — an invisible frustration turned into a targetable opportunity. materials/examples: six-panel storyboards, journey-map templates, sticky-note timelines. application: converts a persona's lived experience into specific, actionable design briefs. case study: "divya" a university library research team creates the persona "divya," a focused student who needs a quiet study space between lectures. every subsequent decision — seating layout, noise policy, signage — is tested against whether it would genuinely help divya, keeping the whole redesign anchored to real user research rather than guesswork. practical engagement a: the gift-giving challenge (15 min) empathize: in pairs, interview your partner about their morning routine. define: identify one specific frustration they experience. ideate: sketch a "gift" product that solves that one frustration, and name the persona it is designed for. practical engagement b: user journey storyboarding using the persona created above (or the water-refill station scenario), draw a 6-panel storyboard tracking that persona's experience from start to finish. circle the single panel that represents the biggest "pain point," and annotate it with one design intervention that could remove it. further viewing/reading: how to create & use personas in ux (sarah doody) and storyboards help visualize ux ideas (nn/group). b1.1.4 usability objectives ~50 min lesson 3: usability objectives products are analysed against five key usability objectives to identify specific areas for improvement. 1. learnability definition: how easy is it for users to accomplish basic tasks the first time they use the product? context: google search is highly learnable because it uses a simple, intuitive interface that requires no training. materials/examples: first-use walkthroughs, onboarding tooltips, icon clarity testing. application: tested by observing brand-new users attempting a task with no instruction. 2. efficiency definition: how quickly and accurately can users perform tasks once they are familiar with the system? context: amazon's "one-click" checkout speeds up the purchasing process for returning customers. materials/examples: task-timing studies, click-count analysis, shortcut design. application: measured by timing an experienced user completing a familiar task. 3. memorability definition: how well can a user remember how to operate the product after a period of non-use? context: a returning smart-thermostat user who has not opened the app in three months forgets how the schedule icons work, even though a first-time user found them easy to learn. materials/examples: return-visit usability tests, consistent icon systems. application: tested by bringing back a user after a gap of weeks or months. 4. errors definition: what is the frequency and severity of mistakes made by the user, and how does the system help them recover? context: an atm that requires a confirmation step before dispensing cash reduces the severity of a mis-entered amount, and clearly explains how to correct it. materials/examples: error logs, confirmation dialogues, undo functions. application: assessed by counting mistakes and recovery time during task testing. 5. satisfaction definition: how pleasant and rewarding is the overall experience of using the product? context: an apple iphone's smooth animations and intuitive interface create a satisfying user experience beyond pure task completion. materials/examples: post-use surveys, satisfaction ratings, qualitative feedback interviews. application: gathered through user feedback after a task has been completed successfully. objective guiding question example learnability can a first-time user complete a basic task? google search's intuitive interface efficiency how fast/accurate is a familiar user? amazon "one-click" checkout memorability can a returning user recall how it works? smart-thermostat schedule icons errors how often/severely do users make mistakes? atm confirmation step before cash is dispensed satisfaction how pleasant is the overall experience? iphone's smooth, intuitive animations practical engagement: usability audit in groups, choose a school service you use regularly — e.g. the lunch ordering system, the timetable app, or the library self-checkout — and evaluate it against all five usability objectives . for each objective, propose one specific, actionable improvement (not just "make it better"). further reading: usability 101: introduction to usability (nn/group) — the original framework these five objectives are drawn from. b1.1.5 task analysis ~45 min lesson 4: task analysis task analysis is a strategy used to deconstruct a complex process into individual steps. by observing a user performing a specific task — e.g. brushing teeth or riding a bike — designers can identify critical points of failure, delay, or frustration. these identified points are targeted for design enhancements to streamline the process and reduce user error. 1. deconstructing complex processes definition: breaking a task down into its individual, observable steps so that every part of the interaction can be examined on its own. context: analysing the steps of using a manual can opener — reaching for it, aligning the blade, gripping and turning — makes it possible to find exactly where users with arthritis struggle most. materials/examples: step-by-step observation sheets, numbered task lists, video recordings of use. application: used before redesigning any product where the interaction sequence itself may be the problem. 2. identifying points of failure definition: pinpointing the exact step in a deconstructed task where a user hesitates, makes an error, or gives up — the moment task analysis is designed to reveal. context: an elderly user struggling at the exact moment they must align a plug with a wall socket hidden behind furniture is a pain point identified through task analysis, not a general usability rating. materials/examples: annotated step lists, hesitation/error markers, timing data per step. application: directly targeted for design enhancement — the single failing step, not the whole product, is redesigned. case study: redesigning a kettle handle a design team studying users with arthritis conducts a task analysis of pouring an electric kettle. it reveals two pain points: difficulty gripping the handle when the kettle is full and heavy, and difficulty triggering the lid-release catch with reduced finger strength. these findings directly justify prioritising errors (reducing spills/scalds) and satisfaction (a handle that feels comfortable and safe) in the redesign. practical engagement: step-by-step observation watch a partner use the school vending machine, a locker, or a public water fountain. write down every single step as a numbered list (aim for extent should a ucd process prioritize "designing for extremes" to ensure universal accessibility? c3.1 product analysis: what influence does product analysis have on identifying usability opportunities within ucd? b1.1 exam practice ao1 / ao2 / ao3 exam practice: topic b1.1 command terms and mark-allocation logic follow the ib design technology assessment objectives (ao1 knowledge, ao2 application, ao3 synthesis). sample/indicative answers for teacher use follow each question. section a: multiple choice (3 questions, 1 mark each) 1. which of the following best defines a "primary persona" in the ucd process? a record of every possible user of a product a fictional character representing the attributes, goals, and motivations of a target user group a technical specification document used for manufacturing a survey completed by the design team reveal answer b. a fictional character representing the attributes, goals, and motivations of a target user group. [1] 3. a designer observes an elderly user struggling at the exact moment they must align a plug with a wall socket hidden behind furniture. in ucd, this observed moment of difficulty is best described as a: usability objective primary persona pain point identified through task analysis design specification reveal answer c. pain point identified through task analysis. (a) identify one user-centred design research method the library could use to understand visitor needs. [1] (b) describe how creating a primary persona of a "first-time visitor" could help the design team improve the kiosk's usability. [3] reveal answer (a) [1] award for a valid method named precisely, e.g. observation of visitors at the current kiosk; a short intercept survey; a structured interview with library staff. technical term only — no explanation required. (b) [3] award up to 3 using point → evidence → effect: the persona (e.g. "kofi, a first-time visitor unfamiliar with self-service technology") (1) focuses the team on his specific confusion — not locating the scan button (1) — which justifies enlarging/relabelling the scan icon and adding on-screen prompts so first-time use matches expert use (1) . question 5 [2 + 2 = 4 marks] a design team is developing a new electric kettle for users with arthritis, following task analysis observations of users attempting to lift and pour a full kettle. (a) outline two "pain points" a task analysis of kettle use might reveal for a user with limited grip strength. [2] (b) state two usability objectives the design team should prioritize when redesigning the kettle handle. [2] reveal answer (a) [2] award 1 each for two distinct, plausible pain points, e.g. difficulty gripping the handle when the kettle is full and heavy; difficulty triggering the lid-release catch with reduced finger strength. (b) [2] award 1 each for two named objectives with a one-phrase justification, e.g. errors — to reduce spills/scalds; satisfaction — so the product feels comfortable and safe to use daily. section c: long answer (2 questions) question 6 [4 marks] explain how user journey mapping (storyboarding) can be used by a design team to identify design opportunities when developing a new product for hospital patients. reveal answer [4] award marks for a logical chain (point → mechanism → consequence). e.g. a design team maps a hospital patient's journey from admission to discharge (point) ; this visualises each touchpoint — such as the confusing moment a patient must locate the call button while in pain or under medication (mechanism) ; therefore the storyboard converts an invisible frustration into a concrete, targetable design opportunity, such as relocating or redesigning the call button (consequence) . full marks require at least one named pain point and one resulting design title: The design process

sections.title: Lesson 1: The Five Stages of the Design Process
sections.html:
B2.1.1 The Design Process ~60 min

Lesson 1: The Five Stages of the Design Process

Design Thinking is a non-linear, iterative process for tackling complex, ill-defined problems. Rather than treating its five stages as a checklist to complete in order, designers move fluidly between them, returning to earlier stages as new information emerges. This lesson — and the running case study it introduces — anchors every later lesson in the unit.

Hook: The Shopping Cart Challenge (10 min)

Before naming any stages, consider the classic case study of a design consultancy given five days to reinvent an everyday object nobody thinks twice about: the supermarket shopping cart. Individually, jot down what you think is wrong with a normal shopping cart — then reveal how a professional design team approached the same question.

As you watch the clip below, log every moment the team is: (a) talking to real shoppers, (b) sketching or arguing about ideas, and (c) building something with their hands. This primes you to notice Empathize, Ideate and Prototype in action before the vocabulary is introduced.

Watch (5 min excerpt): ABC Nightline — IDEO Shopping Cart Redesign.

The Five Stages

1. Empathize

Definition: Research to gain a deep understanding of user needs, motivations and challenges.

Context: The IDEO team watched real shoppers, store staff and even a child struggle with existing carts in the supermarket aisle.

Materials/Examples: Observation, interviews, contextual inquiry, video logging.

Application: Always the starting point of a design cycle — and revisited whenever a later stage reveals a gap in understanding.

2. Define

Definition: Synthesise research to clearly articulate the problem being solved — framing the design challenge.

Context: Problems clustered around theft, child safety, checkout speed and manoeuvrability — not just "the cart is old."

Materials/Examples: Affinity diagrams, problem statements, insight clustering.

Application: Turns scattered observations into a single, actionable brief the team can ideate against.

3. Ideate

Definition: Generate a wide range of potential solutions using divergent thinking.

Context: Rapid, no-judgement brainstorming produced dozens of concepts, from modular baskets to entirely new wheel systems.

Materials/Examples: Sticky-note brainstorms, sketch storms, "how might we" prompts.

Application: Quantity over quality at this stage — evaluation and narrowing happen later.

4. Prototype / Model

Definition: Create tangible low-to-high fidelity versions of ideas to test assumptions.

Context: A working cardboard-and-metal prototype was built from scratch within the five-day sprint.

Materials/Examples: Cardboard, paper, foam, 3D-printed or CAD models.

Application: Makes an idea testable — and often sends the team back to Ideate or even Empathize.

5. Present

Definition: Communicate the best tested solution, meeting design specifications and intentions.

Context: The team pitched the redesigned cart back to the client, justifying each feature against user needs.

Materials/Examples: Pitch decks, technical drawings, working models.

Application: Closes one iteration of the cycle — but rarely the last, as feedback often restarts it.

Practical Engagement: 45-Minute Mini Design Sprint

Brief: "Redesign the school bag/backpack experience for a Year 9 student who changes classrooms eight times a day."

  • Empathize (8 min) — In pairs, interview a classmate about their real backpack frustrations (weight, access, spilled contents, back pain). Record 3 direct quotes.
  • Define (5 min) — Write one problem statement per pair using the frame: "[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight]."
  • Ideate (10 min) — Sticky-note brainstorm: quantity over quality, no criticism allowed, build on others' ideas. Aim for 15+ ideas per pair.
  • Prototype (15 min) — Build a rapid low-fidelity model from paper, tape and recycled materials.
  • Present (7 min) — 30-second pitch to another pair: what problem it solves and for whom.

Debrief question: "Which stage did your pair want to skip, and what happened when you couldn't skip it?" — this surfaces the non-linear, iterative nature of the model (e.g. testing sends teams back to Ideate).

sections.title: Lesson 2: Research Methodologies
sections.html:
B2.1.2 Research in the Design Process ~60 min

Lesson 2: Research Methodologies

Research is not a single step at the start of the process — it is an ongoing activity used throughout to identify opportunities, validate assumptions, and generate feasible solutions.

1. Primary vs. Secondary Research

Definition: Primary research is first-hand data collected directly by the design team. Secondary research is data provided by a third party, used to support or validate primary findings.

Context: IDEO designers standing in supermarket aisles filming real shoppers wrestling with carts is primary research; a designer citing national obesity or road-safety statistics to justify a brief is secondary research.

Materials/Examples: Primary — observations, interviews, surveys, focus groups, material testing, product analysis. Secondary — internet research, government statistics, university research, literature searches.

Application: Strong specifications are usually built from both types working together, not one alone.

2. Qualitative vs. Quantitative Data

Definition: Qualitative data is descriptive — feelings, perceptions, and the why. Quantitative data is numerical and measurable — the what.

Context: "Users said the handle felt awkward and embarrassing to use in public" (qualitative) versus "68% of surveyed users could not open the jar within 15 seconds" (quantitative).

Materials/Examples: Interview transcripts and open survey responses (qualitative); timed task data and closed survey results (quantitative).

Application: Quantitative data shows scale; qualitative data explains cause — both are usually needed to justify a design decision.

Practical Engagement: Build a Research Plan

Brief: A company wants to design a reusable smart water bottle for secondary school students in a hot, humid climate (e.g. Hong Kong).

  • In groups of 3, design one primary research method (e.g. a 5-question survey, or a 3-question interview script) to uncover student hydration habits and frustrations.
  • List two secondary sources you would search for supporting statistics (e.g. WHO hydration guidelines, school health survey data).
  • Card sort: the teacher distributes 10 data "evidence cards" (e.g. "73% of students refill bottles less than twice a day" / "students say sports bottles feel childish"). Groups sort each card into Qualitative or Quantitative, then again into Primary or Secondary, justifying any card that could belong in more than one place.

Stretch Discussion

Why might a design team deliberately seek out contradictory data — primary evidence that seems to disagree with a secondary statistic? (Leads toward triangulation and the idea that quantitative data shows scale, while qualitative data explains cause.)

sections.title: Lesson 3: User-Centred Tools
sections.html:
B2.1.3 User Journey & Storyboarding C3.1 Product Analysis ~60 min

Lesson 3: User-Centred Tools

To keep the process genuinely human-centred, designers avoid designing for an imagined "everyone." Instead they use specific tools to keep a real, evidenced user at the centre of every decision.

Case Study: OXO Good Grips

A widely-cited example of user-centred design: OXO's founder noticed his wife, who had mild arthritis, struggling to grip a standard vegetable peeler. Rather than designing only for arthritic users, the company designed for the "extremes" — a soft, large, non-slip handle — which turned out to be more comfortable for every user, not just the target persona.

Three Tools

1. Primary Persona

Definition: A profile of a fictional character representing a key user group, built from real research data.

Context: OXO designing around a persona with reduced hand strength rather than "everyone" is what led to the Good Grips handle.

Materials/Examples: Persona cards (name, age, photo/sketch, goals, frustrations, quote).

Application: Humanises data and stops the team from vaguely designing for "everyone."

2. User Journey Mapping

Definition: A visual plot (often a storyboard) of a user's experience over time.

Context: Storyboarding a student's water bottle use from home to the final lesson of the day reveals exactly when and why it becomes a hassle to carry.

Materials/Examples: 6–8 frame storyboards, journey-map templates.

Application: Surfaces pain points — moments of frustration — which become concrete design opportunities.

3. Product Analysis

Definition: Systematic examination of existing products.

Context: Comparing two competitor water bottles for insulation performance and lid design reveals gaps a new design can exploit.

Materials/Examples: Strength/weakness tables, teardown photos, comparative testing.

Application: Identifies strengths, weaknesses and gaps that a new design can exploit.

Practical Engagement: Persona + Journey Map

  • Using the research generated in Lesson 2 (the smart water bottle brief), build a primary persona card: name, age, a photo/sketch, 3 goals, 3 frustrations, one direct quote.
  • Storyboard (6–8 frames) that persona's journey through a school day with their current water bottle — from filling it at home to the last lesson of the day.
  • Circle every frame that shows a pain point. For each one, write a one-line design opportunity, e.g. "Bottle sweats and soaks the bag → opportunity for an insulated, non-condensing exterior."
  • Swap storyboards with another group and run a rapid product analysis of one existing water bottle (theirs, or a photo provided) — list 2 strengths and 2 weaknesses against the persona's needs.

User Journey MappingA visual plot (often a storyboard) of a user's experience over time.Surfaces pain points — moments of frustration — which become concrete design opportunities.
Product AnalysisSystematic examination of existing products.Identifies strengths, weaknesses and gaps that a new design can exploit.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Defining the Problem and Success
sections.html:
B2.1.4 Problem Definition B2.1.5 Design Specification ~60 min

Lesson 4: Defining the Problem and Success

Once research has been gathered, it must be turned into a sharp problem statement and a clear set of success criteria — the design specification — against which every later prototype will be judged.

1. The Problem Statement

Definition: A concise, clear description of the specific challenge being addressed. It should be specific enough to guide ideation but not so specific that it presumes a solution.

Context: Weak: "We need a better water bottle." Strong: "Students need a way to keep water cold through a full school day without the bottle sweating onto shared bag contents."

Materials/Examples: The frame "[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight]."

Application: Bridges the Define stage of Design Thinking to the specifications that follow.

2. Essential Specifications

Definition: Non-negotiable requirements derived directly from research — if missing, the design has failed.

Context: "The jar opener must accommodate jar diameters from 50–90 mm (essential) so that it functions across the most common household jar sizes sold in the target market."

Materials/Examples: Requirement + Metric/Detail + Justification statements.

Application: Used to reject any prototype that fails to meet the minimum bar, regardless of other merits.

3. Desirable Specifications

Definition: Nice-to-have features that improve the design but whose absence would not make it unfit for purpose.

Context: A backpack being offered in a choice of five colours improves appeal but is not required for the backpack to function.

Materials/Examples: Wishlist features, aesthetic preferences, optional add-ons.

Application: Used to differentiate between competing designs that all meet the essential bar.

Practical Engagement: Specification Writing from Real IB Stimuli

Working from IB specimen assessment materials, practise turning stimulus information into formal specifications — exactly as examiners expect (Requirement + Metric/Detail + Justification).

  • Stimulus A — the yoga mat organiser designed around a primary persona and CAD-based testing/refinement.
  • Stimulus B — the geared jar opener, designed via the full design thinking cycle (Empathize → Define → Ideate → Model → Present) to optimise user satisfaction and efficiency.
  • Stimulus C — the Trekdesign hiking jacket, developed through user-centred design and anthropometric (5th–95th percentile) data.

In pairs, choose one stimulus and construct two design specifications (one essential, one desirable), each written as Requirement + Metric + Justification.

Check for understanding: Cold-call pairs to justify why their chosen requirement is essential rather than desirable — push them to defend the boundary, since this distinction is a common source of lost marks in Paper 2 extended-response questions.

sections.title: Lesson 5: The Model, Test, Refine Cycle
sections.html:
B2.1.8 Iterative Modelling, Testing & Refinement B2.1.9 Prototyping & User Testing ~60 min

Lesson 5: The Model, Test, Refine Cycle

Prototyping is not a single event but a repeating loop: build something, learn from it, and improve it. The cycle continues until the design specifications are met.

1. Model

Definition: Create an initial concept — a sketch, a digital model, or a physical prototype.

Context: A rough paper-and-tape mock-up of a redesigned backpack pocket layout, built in minutes rather than days.

Materials/Examples: Paper, card, CAD sketches, foam block models.

Application: Gives the team something concrete to react to, rather than debating ideas in the abstract.

2. Test

Definition: Evaluate the model through user testing or simulation to identify strengths and weaknesses.

Context: A "tester" role-plays the persona and attempts set tasks while thinking aloud, while the "designer" records feedback silently.

Materials/Examples: Think-aloud protocols, timed task lists, observation notes.

Application: Converts assumptions about a design into observed evidence.

3. Refine

Definition: Make improvements based on feedback, then repeat the cycle until specifications are met.

Context: Annotating a prototype directly with tester feedback, then sketching a refined version that labels exactly which specification each change addresses.

Materials/Examples: Annotated prototypes, revision sketches, specification checklists.

Application: Closes the loop — and often reveals that another Model/Test pass is still needed.

Levels of Fidelity

Designers deliberately choose how much time and finish to invest at each pass. Low-fidelity prototypes (e.g. cardboard, paper, foam mock-ups) are cheap and fast — ideal for testing early concepts and layout before committing resources. High-fidelity prototypes (e.g. a fully working, near-final model) are expensive and slow to build, but necessary to validate final performance, ergonomics and manufacturing feasibility.

Practical Engagement: Build → Test → Refine (in one lesson)

  • Model (15 min) — Using the persona and specifications from Lessons 3–4, build a low-fidelity paper/card prototype of the water bottle redesign (or the object chosen in Lesson 4). No electronics, no glue guns — the point is speed.
  • Test (12 min) — Swap prototypes with another group. The "tester" role-plays the persona and attempts 3 set tasks (e.g. "fill it one-handed," "check how much it sweats," "carry it in a bag for one minute") while thinking aloud. The "designer" records feedback silently — no defending the design.
  • Refine (10 min) — Annotate the prototype directly with feedback and sketch one refined version, labelling exactly which specification each change addresses.
  • Justify fidelity (5 min) — As a class, discuss: "What would we need to change about this test if we had built a high-fidelity prototype instead? What would we gain, and what would we risk by prototyping at high fidelity this early?"
StepWhat Happens
1. ModelCreate an initial concept — a sketch, a digital model, or a physical prototype.
2. TestEvaluate the model through user testing or simulation to identify strengths and weaknesses.
3. RefineMake improvements based on feedback, then repeat the cycle until specifications are met.

sections.title: Lesson 6: Communication, Presentation & Exam Practice
sections.html:
B2.1.10 Communicating Technical Details B2.1.11 Presenting the Final Solution ~60 min

Lesson 6: Communication, Presentation & Exam Practice

A design is only as good as a manufacturer's or client's ability to understand it. This lesson covers the standardised technical drawings designers use to communicate dimensions, scale and assembly, and how to pitch a finished, tested design.

1. Technical Drawings

Definition: A family of standardised drawings used to communicate a design's dimensions, scale and assembly to a manufacturer or client.

Context: Front and side orthographic views used to dimension a component for CNC machining, alongside an isometric sketch for a design portfolio.

Materials/Examples: CAD software, technical pens, scale rulers, set squares.

Application: The right drawing type is chosen for the audience — manufacture vs. client presentation.

Drawing TypeDescription
Component DrawingA single part, fully dimensioned.
Assembly DrawingHow multiple components fit together.
Orthographic ProjectionMultiple 2D views (front, side, plan) at true scale for manufacture.
Isometric DrawingA 3D view drawn on 120° axes, useful for showing form without perspective distortion.

2. Final Presentation

Definition: Communicating a finished design, highlighting key features and justifying improvements over existing products.

Context: A 90-second "Dragon's Den"-style pitch justifying a redesigned prototype to a panel.

Materials/Examples: Pitch scripts, rendered models, comparison boards.

Application: Closes the design cycle by proving the solution meets its specifications with evidence, not just claims.

Practical Engagement: Sketch → Pitch

  • Produce one rough orthographic sketch (front + side view, roughly to scale) and one isometric or perspective sketch of your refined prototype from Lesson 5.
  • Prepare a 90-second "Dragon's Den"-style pitch that: (a) states the problem statement, (b) shows the persona and one pain point it solves, (c) explains how the design meets at least one essential specification, and (d) justifies one improvement made during refinement.
  • Pitch to a small panel of classmates, who score the pitch against a simple 3-point rubric: Clarity of problem – Evidence of user-centred thinking – Justification of the final design.

C3.1 Product Analysis: Why is product analysis a fundamental aspect of the design process?
C4.1 Design for Manufacture: How does the process require the exploration of Design for Manufacture (DfM) strategies?

sections.html:
B2.1 Exam Practice AO1 / AO2 / AO3

Exam Practice: Topic B2.1

Questions below are modelled on the command-term expectations and mark-allocation logic used in Paper 1 and Paper 2, using original but exam-style contexts. Sample/indicative answers for teacher use follow each question.

Section A: Multiple Choice (3 questions, 1 mark each)

1. Which stage of the design thinking process primarily involves synthesising research to clearly articulate the problem being solved?

  • Empathize
  • Define
  • Ideate
  • Present
Reveal Answer
B. Define. [1]

2. A design team spends two days standing in train stations, filming and interviewing commuters as they struggle to use a ticket machine. This is best classified as:

  • Secondary, quantitative research
  • Primary, qualitative research
  • Secondary, qualitative research
  • A design specification
Reveal Answer
B. Primary, qualitative research. [1]

3. A design team is developing a new school backpack. Which of the following is a desirable (rather than essential) specification?

  • Must fit A4-sized folders without bending them
  • Should be available in a choice of five colours
  • Must weigh less than 800 g when empty
  • Must include a padded, ventilated back panel
Reveal Answer
B. Should be available in a choice of five colours. [1]

Section B: Short Answer (2 questions)

Question 4 [2 marks]

Outline one advantage of using a low-fidelity prototype during the early stages of testing a new product. [2]

Reveal Answer

[2] Award 1 mark for identifying a feature of low-fidelity prototyping (e.g. cheap materials, fast build time) + 1 mark for linking it to a specific benefit (e.g. allows many concepts to be tested before committing resources to one design).

Question 5 [3 marks]

Describe how a design team could use a user journey map to identify a pain point in the experience of a wheelchair user boarding a public bus. [3]

Reveal Answer

[3] Award marks using Action → Mechanism → Result: the team maps each stage of the boarding process (1) → observes/records where the wheelchair user is delayed or excluded, e.g. a gap between platform and bus door (1) → this pain point becomes a concrete design opportunity, e.g. a fold-out ramp specification (1).

Section C: Long Answer (2 questions)

Question 6 [4 marks]

Explain how primary and secondary research can be combined to inform the design specifications for a reusable smart water bottle aimed at secondary school students. [4]

Reveal Answer

[4] Award marks for a logical chain (Point → Mechanism → Consequence). E.g. Primary research (e.g. surveys/interviews with students) reveals specific user frustrations (Point); secondary research (e.g. published hydration or climate statistics) validates that the problem exists at scale and adds quantifiable targets (Mechanism); therefore combining both allows the team to write specifications that are both evidenced (secondary) and genuinely user-relevant (primary), e.g. "must keep contents below 15°C for 6 hours," informed by both surveyed preference and published thermal-comfort data (Consequence).

Question 7 [6 marks]

Evaluate the use of high-fidelity prototyping compared to low-fidelity prototyping when testing a new adjustable, ergonomic desk for a school computer lab. [6]

Reveal Answer

[6] Use the Strength/Limitation/Comparison/Conclusion structure. Strength of high-fidelity: validates real ergonomic performance (adjustment mechanism, stability under load) that a paper model cannot test. Limitation of high-fidelity: costly and slow to iterate, risking sunk-cost commitment to a flawed early concept. Strength of low-fidelity: fast, cheap, encourages honest early feedback and multiple concept variants. Limitation of low-fidelity: cannot validate mechanical/ergonomic performance claims. Conclusion: a justified recommendation that low-fidelity should dominate early concept testing, with a single high-fidelity prototype reserved for final validation once specifications have converged.

sections.title: Glossary: Topic B2.1 — The Design Process
sections.html:
B2.1 Glossary

Glossary: Topic B2.1 — The Design Process

Every key term from this unit, with a working definition and a real-world example drawn from the case studies used across the six lessons. Click on a term to reveal its definition.

Design Thinking
IB Definition: A non-linear, iterative, human-centred process for solving complex, ill-defined problems.
Real-World Context: IDEO's five-day sprint to redesign the supermarket shopping cart, moving fluidly between research, ideas and prototypes.
Empathize
IB Definition: Researching to gain a deep understanding of user needs, motivations and challenges.
Real-World Context: OXO's founder observing his wife's difficulty gripping a standard vegetable peeler.
Define
IB Definition: Synthesising research to clearly articulate the problem being solved.
Real-World Context: Turning scattered shopper complaints into the problem statement: "carts are unsafe for children and easily stolen."
Ideate
IB Definition: Generating a wide range of potential solutions using divergent thinking techniques.
Real-World Context: A sticky-note brainstorm producing 40+ shopping cart concepts before any are evaluated.
Prototype / Model
IB Definition: Creating tangible low-to-high fidelity versions of ideas to test assumptions.
Real-World Context: A cardboard-and-metal working shopping cart built within a five-day design sprint.
Present
IB Definition: Communicating the best tested solution, meeting design specifications and intentions.
Real-World Context: A design team pitching their final cart redesign back to the supermarket client.
Primary Research
IB Definition: First-hand data collected directly by the design team.
Real-World Context: Interviewing students about backpack frustrations in the school corridor.
Secondary Research
IB Definition: Data provided by a third party, used to support or validate primary findings.
Real-World Context: Citing WHO hydration guidelines to support a water bottle brief.
Qualitative Data
IB Definition: Descriptive data about feelings, perceptions and "the why."
Real-World Context: "Users said the bottle felt childish to carry in public."
Quantitative Data
IB Definition: Numerical data that can be measured; "the what."
Real-World Context: "68% of users could not open the jar within 15 seconds."
Primary Persona
IB Definition: A profile of a fictional character representing a key user group, built from research.
Real-World Context: OXO designing around a persona with reduced hand strength rather than "everyone."
User Journey Mapping
IB Definition: A visual plot (often a storyboard) of a user's experience over time, used to find pain points.
Real-World Context: Storyboarding a student's water bottle use from home to the final lesson of the day.
Pain Point
IB Definition: A moment of frustration in a user's journey that presents a design opportunity.
Real-World Context: A bottle "sweating" and soaking bag contents during a hot commute.
Product Analysis
IB Definition: Systematic examination of existing products to find strengths, weaknesses and opportunities.
Real-World Context: Comparing two competitor water bottles for insulation performance and lid design.
Problem Statement
IB Definition: A concise, clear description of the specific challenge being addressed.
Real-World Context: "Students need a way to keep water cold all day without it sweating onto bag contents."
Design Specification
IB Definition: A list of requirements and constraints derived from research, acting as success criteria.
Real-World Context: "Must keep contents below 15°C for 6 hours" for a water bottle.
Essential Specification
IB Definition: A must-have requirement; the design fails without it.
Real-World Context: A jar opener must accommodate the most common jar diameters sold in the target market.
Desirable Specification
IB Definition: A nice-to-have feature that improves but is not required for the design to succeed.
Real-World Context: A backpack being offered in a choice of five colours.
Model – Test – Refine Cycle
IB Definition: An iterative loop of building, evaluating and improving a design until specifications are met.
Real-World Context: Paper-prototyping a desk, user-testing it, then sketching a refined version based on feedback.
Low-Fidelity Prototype
IB Definition: A cheap, fast, rough mock-up (e.g. cardboard, paper) used for early concept testing.
Real-World Context: A taped-paper mock-up of a redesigned backpack pocket layout.
High-Fidelity Prototype
IB Definition: A near-final, fully working model used to validate final performance.
Real-World Context: A functioning, manufactured sample of an adjustable ergonomic desk.
Technical Drawing
IB Definition: Detailed, standardised drawings (component, assembly, orthographic, isometric, perspective) that communicate dimensions and assembly for manufacturing.
Real-World Context: Orthographic front/side views of a jar opener submitted to a manufacturer.
Orthographic Projection
IB Definition: Multiple 2D views (front, side, plan) drawn to true scale.
Real-World Context: Front and side views used to dimension a component for CNC machining.
Isometric Drawing
IB Definition: A 3D view drawn on 120° axes without perspective distortion.
Real-World Context: A 3D sketch of a prototype casing showing its true proportions for a design portfolio.
Final Presentation
IB Definition: Communicating a finished design, highlighting key features and justifying improvements over existing products.
Real-World Context: A 90-second "Dragon's Den"-style pitch justifying a redesigned prototype to a panel.

glossary.definition: The fourth stage in the DP design process, where the intended solution is developed through iterative model—test—refine cycles.
A list of requirements, constraints and considerations that a yet to be designed product must fulfil.
A non-linear, iterative process used to solve problems.
The first stage of the DP design process that prompts the user to discover the needs, motivations, behaviours and experiences of the intended user.
A group of people representing the target market or different personae assembled to discuss a product and provide feedback for the purpose of product development.
A series of tasks used to generate ideas for solutions to a problem, which can include brainstorming, mind mapping, sketching and SCAMPER.
A face-to-face consultation, typically with one person.
The use of consumer reports, newspapers, magazines, encyclopaedias, manufacturers' information, etc. To conduct research.

A cyclic development tool used in design to develop products swiftly, requiring designers to create models of their products, test them with users, and use the feedback to refine their design. The designer repeats the cycle until they have resolved all user requirements related to the product.
A digital scale or full-size representation of a product is used to test the mechanics and gain feedback from users.
See A2.1 User-centred research methods.
The examination of a product to determine its features, strengths and weaknesses and to identify opportunities for improvement.
The essential capabilities a product must have to be successful.
A concise and clear description of a problem in a few sentences that states what is to be addressed.
Typically, descriptive data is used to find out in depth the way people think or feel—their perception. Useful for research at the individual or small (focus) group level.
Data that can be measured and recorded using numbers. Examples include height, shoe size and the depth of a kitchen counter and the weight of a laptop.

A person’s perceptions and responses that result from the use, or anticipated use, of a product, system or service. A user’s journey shows empathy and is communicated through a storyboard.
A research activity where the user is observed interacting with a product or completing a task used to find pain points in the process or interaction.

syllabus.title: The design process
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How do designers approach problem-solving?

statements.text: The design process represents a design thinking model and is comprised of five sections.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline each stage of the design process (empathize; defining the project; ideation and modelling; designing a solution; presenting a solution).

statements.text: Research is an ongoing activity throughout the design process, critical to identifying design opportunities, understanding user needs and generating feasible real-world solutions to problems.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to distinguish between primary and secondary sources, qualitative and quantitative data and how they are used to identify design opportunities, develop an understanding of users and generate ideas for solutions to problems.

statements.text: Primary research involves the collection of first-hand data relevant to the design context.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to apply primary research methods to gather first-hand data (user observations, interviews, surveys, questionnaires, focus groups, material testing and product analysis) and analyse the data to establish user requirements and design specifications, develop a persona and suggest further developments of a solution.

statements.text: Secondary research involves the collection of data provided by a third party and is used to support or validate primary research.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to analyse secondary data sources (internet-based research, government data and statistics research, university research and literature search) to establish user requirements and design specifications, develop a persona and suggest further developments for a solution.

statements.text: When empathizing with the user, designers develop a persona used to represent a group of end-users they are solving a problem for.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify issues, problems and challenges using user-centred research methods and techniques, and to identify user needs for specific user groups to understand their experience, motivations and interactions with products and environments.

statements.text: Designers engage in user observation, mapping the user’s journey as they carry out a task. They use a storyboard to identify the steps in the design process and design opportunities.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to map a user’s journey using a storyboard and identify pain points within that journey that provide design opportunities.

statements.text: Product analysis is a tool used by designers to gain insight into the function, performance and features of an existing product.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to analyse a range of products that either provides a solution to a problem or can inspire a solution to a problem.

statements.text: The first step in solving a problem is to define it.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the nature of a problem by writing a problem statement that clearly defines their design intentions.

statements.text: Defining clear design specifications leads to clear parameters for the development of a solution.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to construct design specifications based on primary and secondary research that communicate the essential and desirable success criteria of the redesigned product.

statements.text: The ideation and modelling stage involves developing distinct ways to solve a particular problem that demonstrate different approaches to develop a solution.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to apply ideation techniques to develop a range of diverse and appropriate ideas that address a problem statement and respond to design specifications.

statements.text: Iterative analyses and evaluation of design ideas lead to improved design ideas.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to compare their ideas with the design specifications and user needs as they refine their solutions.

statements.text: When developing a solution, designers use an iterative model, test, refine cycle until all major design specifications and user requirements are satisfied.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to demonstrate iterative development of a design using the model, test, refine cycle.

statements.text: Models, prototypes and mock-ups of solutions are created to test their effectiveness and to gather feedback for further refinement and development.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to create feasible models of an intended solution at appropriate levels of fidelity that generate performance data when tested with end-users.

statements.text: The physical details of a new product need to be communicated for it to be manufactured.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to create detailed drawings of components and assembled products that communicate dimensions, scale and assembly details.

statements.text: When presenting a solution, it is important to communicate clearly the need for the solution, and the key features that demonstrate how it solves a given problem.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to create virtual representations of a solution, highlighting key usability features, and explain how it meets the design specifications and achieves the design intentions as a proposed solution or as an improvement to an existing product.

activity.title: Design process remix
steps: Arrange research, specification, ideation, modelling, testing and evaluation into a plausible process.
Reveal a failed prototype test and draw feedback arrows to earlier stages.
Write one measurable specification with its research evidence.
Explain where divergent and convergent thinking occur in your sequence.
activity.debrief: Why is a design process iterative rather than a fixed checklist?

exam.question: Explain how a measurable specification supports evaluation. [2]
exam.answer: It sets an explicit success threshold, allowing relevant test data to be compared against a criterion rather than relying on opinion.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: 45-Minute Mini Design Sprint
activities.text: Practical Engagement: 45-Minute Mini Design Sprint Brief: "Redesign the school bag/backpack experience for a Year 9 student who changes classrooms eight times a day." Empathize (8 min) — In pairs, interview a classmate about their real backpack frustrations (weight, access, spilled contents, back pain). Record 3 direct quotes. Define (5 min) — Write one problem statement per pair using the frame: "[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight]." Ideate (10 min) — Sticky-note brainstorm: quantity over quality, no criticism allowed, build on others' ideas. Aim for 15+ ideas per pair. Prototype (15 min) — Build a rapid low-fidelity model from paper, tape and recycled materials. Present (7 min) — 30-second pitch to another pair: what problem it solves and for whom. Debrief question: "Which stage did your pair want to skip, and what happened when you couldn't skip it?" — this surfaces the non-linear, iterative nature of the model (e.g. testing sends teams back to Ideate).

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Build a Research Plan
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Build a Research Plan Brief: A company wants to design a reusable smart water bottle for secondary school students in a hot, humid climate (e.g. Hong Kong). In groups of 3, design one primary research method (e.g. a 5-question survey, or a 3-question interview script) to uncover student hydration habits and frustrations. List two secondary sources you would search for supporting statistics (e.g. WHO hydration guidelines, school health survey data). Card sort: the teacher distributes 10 data "evidence cards" (e.g. "73% of students refill bottles less than twice a day" / "students say sports bottles feel childish"). Groups sort each card into Qualitative or Quantitative, then again into Primary or Secondary, justifying any card that could belong in more than one place.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Persona + Journey Map
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Persona + Journey Map Using the research generated in Lesson 2 (the smart water bottle brief), build a primary persona card: name, age, a photo/sketch, 3 goals, 3 frustrations, one direct quote. Storyboard (6–8 frames) that persona's journey through a school day with their current water bottle — from filling it at home to the last lesson of the day. Circle every frame that shows a pain point. For each one, write a one-line design opportunity, e.g. "Bottle sweats and soaks the bag → opportunity for an insulated, non-condensing exterior." Swap storyboards with another group and run a rapid product analysis of one existing water bottle (theirs, or a photo provided) — list 2 strengths and 2 weaknesses against the persona's needs.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Specification Writing from Real IB Stimuli
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Specification Writing from Real IB Stimuli Working from IB specimen assessment materials, practise turning stimulus information into formal specifications — exactly as examiners expect (Requirement + Metric/Detail + Justification). Stimulus A — the yoga mat organiser designed around a primary persona and CAD-based testing/refinement. Stimulus B — the geared jar opener, designed via the full design thinking cycle (Empathize → Define → Ideate → Model → Present) to optimise user satisfaction and efficiency. Stimulus C — the Trekdesign hiking jacket, developed through user-centred design and anthropometric (5th–95th percentile) data. In pairs, choose one stimulus and construct two design specifications (one essential, one desirable), each written as Requirement + Metric + Justification.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Build → Test → Refine (in one lesson)
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Build → Test → Refine (in one lesson) Model (15 min) — Using the persona and specifications from Lessons 3–4, build a low-fidelity paper/card prototype of the water bottle redesign (or the object chosen in Lesson 4). No electronics, no glue guns — the point is speed. Test (12 min) — Swap prototypes with another group. The "tester" role-plays the persona and attempts 3 set tasks (e.g. "fill it one-handed," "check how much it sweats," "carry it in a bag for one minute") while thinking aloud. The "designer" records feedback silently — no defending the design. Refine (10 min) — Annotate the prototype directly with feedback and sketch one refined version, labelling exactly which specification each change addresses. Justify fidelity (5 min) — As a class, discuss: "What would we need to change about this test if we had built a high-fidelity prototype instead? What would we gain, and what would we risk by prototyping at high fidelity this early?"

searchText: the design process b2.1.1 the design process ~60 min lesson 1: the five stages of the design process design thinking is a non-linear, iterative process for tackling complex, ill-defined problems. rather than treating its five stages as a checklist to complete in order, designers move fluidly between them, returning to earlier stages as new information emerges. this lesson — and the running case study it introduces — anchors every later lesson in the unit. hook: the shopping cart challenge (10 min) before naming any stages, consider the classic case study of a design consultancy given five days to reinvent an everyday object nobody thinks twice about: the supermarket shopping cart. individually, jot down what you think is wrong with a normal shopping cart — then reveal how a professional design team approached the same question. as you watch the clip below, log every moment the team is: (a) talking to real shoppers, (b) sketching or arguing about ideas, and (c) building something with their hands. this primes you to notice empathize, ideate and prototype in action before the vocabulary is introduced. watch (5 min excerpt): abc nightline — ideo shopping cart redesign . the five stages 1. empathize definition: research to gain a deep understanding of user needs, motivations and challenges. context: the ideo team watched real shoppers, store staff and even a child struggle with existing carts in the supermarket aisle. materials/examples: observation, interviews, contextual inquiry, video logging. application: always the starting point of a design cycle — and revisited whenever a later stage reveals a gap in understanding. 2. define definition: synthesise research to clearly articulate the problem being solved — framing the design challenge. context: problems clustered around theft, child safety, checkout speed and manoeuvrability — not just "the cart is old." materials/examples: affinity diagrams, problem statements, insight clustering. application: turns scattered observations into a single, actionable brief the team can ideate against. 3. ideate definition: generate a wide range of potential solutions using divergent thinking. context: rapid, no-judgement brainstorming produced dozens of concepts, from modular baskets to entirely new wheel systems. materials/examples: sticky-note brainstorms, sketch storms, "how might we" prompts. application: quantity over quality at this stage — evaluation and narrowing happen later. 4. prototype / model definition: create tangible low-to-high fidelity versions of ideas to test assumptions. context: a working cardboard-and-metal prototype was built from scratch within the five-day sprint. materials/examples: cardboard, paper, foam, 3d-printed or cad models. application: makes an idea testable — and often sends the team back to ideate or even empathize. 5. present definition: communicate the best tested solution, meeting design specifications and intentions. context: the team pitched the redesigned cart back to the client, justifying each feature against user needs. materials/examples: pitch decks, technical drawings, working models. application: closes one iteration of the cycle — but rarely the last, as feedback often restarts it. practical engagement: 45-minute mini design sprint brief: "redesign the school bag/backpack experience for a year 9 student who changes classrooms eight times a day." empathize (8 min) — in pairs, interview a classmate about their real backpack frustrations (weight, access, spilled contents, back pain). record 3 direct quotes. define (5 min) — write one problem statement per pair using the frame: "[user] needs a way to [need] because [insight]." ideate (10 min) — sticky-note brainstorm: quantity over quality, no criticism allowed, build on others' ideas. aim for 15+ ideas per pair. prototype (15 min) — build a rapid low-fidelity model from paper, tape and recycled materials. present (7 min) — 30-second pitch to another pair: what problem it solves and for whom. debrief question: "which stage did your pair want to skip, and what happened when you couldn't skip it?" — this surfaces the non-linear, iterative nature of the model (e.g. testing sends teams back to ideate). stage purpose in the shopping cart case study empathize research to gain a deep understanding of user needs, motivations and challenges. the team watched real shoppers, store staff and even a child struggle with existing carts. define synthesise research to clearly articulate the problem being solved. problems clustered around theft, / model create tangible low-to-high fidelity versions of ideas to test assumptions. a working cardboard-and-metal prototype was built within the five-day sprint. present communicate the best tested solution, meeting design specifications and intentions. the team pitched the redesigned cart back to the client. b2.1.2 research in the design process ~60 min lesson 2: research methodologies research is not a single step at the start of the process — it is an ongoing activity used throughout to identify opportunities, validate assumptions, and generate feasible solutions. 1. primary vs. secondary research definition: primary research is first-hand data collected directly by the design team. secondary research is data provided by a third party, used to support or validate primary findings. context: ideo designers standing in supermarket aisles filming real shoppers wrestling with carts is primary research; a designer citing national obesity or road-safety statistics to justify a brief is secondary research. materials/examples: primary — observations, interviews, surveys, focus groups, material testing, product analysis. secondary — internet research, government statistics, university research, literature searches. application: strong specifications are usually built from both types working together, not one alone. 2. qualitative vs. quantitative data definition: qualitative data is descriptive — feelings, perceptions, and the why . quantitative data is numerical and measurable — the what . context: "users said the handle felt awkward and embarrassing to use in public" (qualitative) versus "68% of surveyed users could not open the jar within 15 seconds" (quantitative). materials/examples: interview transcripts and open survey responses (qualitative); timed task data and closed survey results (quantitative). application: quantitative data shows scale; qualitative data explains cause — both are usually needed to justify a design decision. practical place. stretch discussion why might a design team deliberately seek out contradictory data — primary evidence that seems to disagree with a secondary statistic? (leads toward triangulation and the idea that quantitative data shows scale, while qualitative data explains cause.) type definition examples real-world instance primary research first-hand data collected directly by the design team. observations, interviews, surveys, focus groups, material testing, product analysis ideo designers standing in supermarket aisles filming real shoppers wrestling with carts. secondary research data provided by a third party, used to support or validate primary findings. internet research, government statistics, university research, literature searches a designer citing national obesity or road-safety statistics to justify a product brief. b2.1.3 user journey & storyboarding c3.1 product analysis ~60 min lesson 3: user-centred tools to keep the process genuinely human-centred, designers avoid designing for an imagined "everyone." instead they use specific tools to keep a real, evidenced user at the centre of every decision. case study: oxo good grips a widely-cited example of user-centred design: oxo's founder noticed his wife, who had mild arthritis, struggling to grip a standard vegetable peeler. rather than designing only for arthritic users, the company designed for the "extremes" — a soft, large, non-slip handle — which turned out to be more comfortable for every user, not just the target persona. three tools 1. primary persona definition: a profile of a fictional character representing a key user group, built from real research data. context: oxo designing around a persona with reduced hand strength rather than "everyone" is what led to the good grips handle. materials/examples: persona cards (name, age, photo/sketch, goals, frustrations, quote). application: humanises data and stops the team from vaguely designing for "everyone." 2. user journey mapping definition: a visual plot (often a storyboard) of a user's experience over time. context: storyboarding a student's water bottle use from home to the final lesson of the day reveals exactly when and why it becomes a hassle to carry. materials/examples: 6–8 frame storyboards, journey-map templates. application: surfaces pain points — moments of frustration — which become concrete design opportunities. 3. product analysis definition: systematic examination of existing products. context: comparing two competitor water bottles for insulation performance and lid design reveals gaps a new design can exploit. materials/examples: strength/weakness tables, teardown photos, comparative testing. application: identifies strengths, weaknesses and gaps that a new design can exploit. practical engagement: persona + journey map using the research generated in lesson 2 (the smart water bottle brief), build a primary persona card: name, age, a photo/sketch, 3 goals, 3 frustrations, one direct quote. storyboard (6–8 frames) that persona's journey through a school day with their current water bottle — from filling it at home to the last lesson of the day. circle every frame that shows a pain point. for each one, write a one-line design opportunity, e.g. "bottle sweats and soaks the bag → opportunity for an insulated, non-condensing exterior." swap storyboards with another group and run a rapid product analysis of one existing water bottle (theirs, or a photo provided) — list 2 strengths and 2 weaknesses against the persona's needs. tool what it is why it matters primary persona a profile of a fictional character representing a key user group, built from real research data. humanises data and stops the team from vaguely designing for "everyone." user journey mapping a visual plot (often a storyboard) of a user's experience over time. surfaces pain points — moments of frustration — which become concrete design opportunities. product analysis systematic examination of existing products. identifies strengths, weaknesses and gaps that a new design can exploit. b2.1.4 problem definition b2.1.5 design specification ~60 min lesson 4: defining the problem and success once research has been gathered, it must be turned into a sharp problem statement and a clear set of success criteria — the design specification — against which every later prototype will be judged. 1. the problem statement definition: a concise, clear description of the specific challenge being addressed. it should be specific enough to guide ideation but not so specific that it presumes a solution. context: weak: "we need a better water bottle." strong: "students need a way to keep water cold through a full school day without the bottle sweating onto shared bag contents." materials/examples: the frame "[user] needs a way to [need] because [insight]." application: bridges the define stage of design thinking to the specifications that follow. 2. essential specifications definition: non-negotiable requirements derived directly from research — if missing, the design has failed. context: "the jar opener must accommodate jar diameters from 50–90 mm (essential) so that it functions across the most common household jar sizes sold in the target market." materials/examples: requirement + metric/detail + justification statements. application: used to reject any prototype that fails to meet the minimum bar, regardless of other merits. 3. desirable specifications definition: nice-to-have features that improve the design but whose absence would not make it unfit for purpose. context: a backpack being offered in a choice of five colours improves appeal but is not required for the backpack to function. materials/examples: wishlist features, aesthetic preferences, optional add-ons. application: used to differentiate between competing designs that all meet the essential bar. practical engagement: specification writing from real ib stimuli working from ib specimen assessment materials, practise turning stimulus information into formal specifications — exactly as examiners expect (requirement + metric/detail + justification). stimulus a — the yoga mat organiser designed around a primary persona and cad-based testing/refinement. stimulus b — the geared jar opener, designed via the full design thinking cycle (empathize → define → ideate → model → present) to optimise user satisfaction and efficiency. stimulus c — the trekdesign hiking jacket, developed through user-centred design and anthropometric (5th–95th percentile) data. in pairs, choose one stimulus and construct two design specifications (one essential, one desirable), each written as requirement + metric + justification. check for understanding: cold-call pairs to justify why their chosen requirement is essential rather than desirable — push them to defend the boundary, since this distinction is a common source of lost marks in paper 2 extended-response questions. b2.1.8 iterative modelling, testing & refinement b2.1.9 prototyping & user testing ~60 min lesson 5: the model, test, refine cycle prototyping is not a single event but a repeating loop: build something, learn from it, and improve it. the cycle continues until the design specifications are met. 1. model definition: create an initial concept — a sketch, a digital model, or a physical prototype. context: a rough paper-and-tape mock-up of a redesigned backpack pocket layout, built in minutes rather than days. materials/examples: paper, card, cad sketches, foam block models. application: gives the team something concrete to react to, rather than debating ideas in the abstract. 2. test definition: evaluate the model through user testing or simulation to identify strengths and weaknesses. context: a "tester" role-plays the persona and attempts set tasks while thinking aloud, while the "designer" records feedback silently. materials/examples: think-aloud protocols, timed task lists, observation notes. application: converts assumptions about a design into observed evidence. 3. refine definition: make improvements based on feedback, then repeat the cycle until specifications are met. context: annotating a prototype directly with tester feedback, then sketching a refined version that labels exactly which specification each change addresses. materials/examples: annotated prototypes, revision sketches, specification checklists. application: closes the loop — and often reveals that another model/test pass is still needed. levels of fidelity designers deliberately choose how much time and finish to invest at each pass. low-fidelity prototypes (e.g. cardboard, paper, foam mock-ups) are cheap and fast — ideal for testing early concepts and layout before committing resources. high-fidelity prototypes (e.g. a fully working, near-final model) are expensive and slow to build, but necessary to validate final performance, ergonomics and manufacturing feasibility. practical engagement: build → test → refine (in one lesson) model (15 min) — using the persona and specifications
