gain, and what would we risk by prototyping at high fidelity this early?" step what happens 1. model create an initial concept — a sketch, a digital model, or a physical prototype. 2. test evaluate the model through user testing or simulation to identify strengths and weaknesses. 3. refine make improvements based on feedback, then repeat the cycle until specifications are met. b2.1.10 communicating technical details b2.1.11 presenting the final solution ~60 min lesson 6: communication, presentation & exam practice a design is only as good as a manufacturer's or client's ability to understand it. this lesson covers the standardised technical drawings designers use to communicate dimensions, scale and assembly, and how to pitch a finished, tested design. 1. technical drawings definition: a family of standardised drawings used to communicate a design's dimensions, scale and assembly to a manufacturer or client. context: front and side orthographic views used to dimension a component for cnc machining, alongside an isometric sketch for a design portfolio. materials/examples: cad software, technical pens, scale rulers, set squares. application: the right drawing type is chosen for the audience — manufacture vs. client presentation. drawing type description component drawing a single part, fully dimensioned. assembly drawing how multiple components fit together. orthographic projection multiple 2d views (front, side, plan) at true scale for manufacture. isometric drawing a 3d view drawn on 120° axes, useful for showing form without perspective distortion. perspective drawing a 3d view with vanishing points, closest to how the human eye actually sees an object — best for client-facing presentation. 2. final presentation definition: communicating a finished design, highlighting key features and justifying improvements over existing products. context: a 90-second "dragon's den"-style pitch justifying a redesigned prototype to a panel. materials/examples: pitch scripts, rendered models, comparison boards. application: closes the design cycle by proving the solution meets its specifications with evidence, not just claims. practical engagement: sketch → pitch produce one rough orthographic sketch (front + side view, roughly to scale) and one isometric or perspective sketch of your refined prototype from lesson 5. prepare a 90-second "dragon's den"-style pitch that: (a) states the problem statement, (b) shows the persona and one pain point it solves, (c) explains how the design meets at least one essential specification, and (d) justifies one improvement made during refinement. pitch to a small panel of classmates, who score the pitch against a simple 3-point rubric: clarity of problem – evidence of user-centred thinking – justification of the final design. linking questions use these to bridge b2.1 to other parts of the syllabus and to build the kind of cross-topic thinking paper 2 extended-response questions reward. c1.1 responsibility of the designer: how do requirements ensure students address the responsibility of the designer? b1.1 user-centred design: to what extent are the goals of the design process aligned with user-centred design (ucd)? c3.1 product analysis: why is product analysis a fundamental aspect of the design process? c4.1 design for manufacture: how does the process require the exploration of design for manufacture (dfm) strategies? b2.1 exam practice ao1 / ao2 / ao3 exam practice: topic b2.1 questions below are modelled on the command-term expectations and mark-allocation logic used in paper 1 and paper 2, using original but exam-style contexts. sample/indicative answers for teacher use follow each question. section a: multiple choice (3 questions, 1 mark each) 1. which stage of the design thinking process primarily involves synthesising research to clearly articulate the problem being solved? empathize define ideate present reveal answer b. define. [1] 2. a design team spends two days standing in train stations, filming and interviewing commuters as they struggle to use a ticket machine. this is best classified as: secondary, quantitative research primary, qualitative research secondary, qualitative research a design specification reveal answer b. primary, qualitative research. [1] 3. a design team is developing a new school backpack. which of the following is a desirable (rather than essential) specification? must fit a4-sized folders without bending them should be available in a choice of five colours must weigh less than 800 g when empty must include a padded, ventilated back panel reveal answer b. should be available in a choice of five colours. [1] section b: short answer (2 questions) question 4 [2 marks] outline one advantage of using a low-fidelity prototype during the early stages of testing a new product. [2] reveal answer [2] award 1 mark for identifying a feature of low-fidelity prototyping (e.g. cheap materials, fast build time) + 1 mark for linking it to a specific benefit (e.g. allows many concepts to be tested before committing resources to one design). question 5 [3 marks] describe how a design team could use a user journey map to identify a pain point in the experience of a wheelchair user boarding a public bus. [3] reveal answer [3] award marks using action → mechanism → result: the team maps each stage of the boarding process (1) → observes/records where the wheelchair user is delayed or excluded, e.g. a gap between platform and bus door (1) → this pain point becomes a concrete design opportunity, e.g. a fold-out ramp specification (1) . section c: long answer (2 questions) question 6 [4 marks] explain how primary and secondary research can be combined to inform the design specifications for a reusable smart water bottle aimed at secondary school students. [4] reveal answer [4] award marks for a logical chain (point → mechanism → consequence). e.g. primary research (e.g. surveys/interviews with students) reveals specific user frustrations (point) ; secondary research (e.g. published hydration or climate statistics) validates that the problem exists at scale and adds quantifiable targets (mechanism) ; therefore combining both allows the team to write specifications that are both evidenced (secondary) and genuinely user-relevant (primary), e.g. "must keep contents below 15°c for 6 hours," informed by both surveyed preference and published thermal-comfort data (consequence) . question 7 [6 marks] evaluate the use of high-fidelity prototyping compared to low-fidelity prototyping when testing a new adjustable, ergonomic desk for a school computer lab. [6] reveal answer [6] use the strength/limitation/comparison/conclusion structure. strength of high-fidelity: validates real ergonomic performance (adjustment mechanism, stability under load) that a paper model cannot test. limitation of high-fidelity: costly and slow to iterate, risking sunk-cost commitment to a flawed early concept. strength of low-fidelity: fast, cheap, encourages honest early feedback and multiple concept variants. limitation of low-fidelity: cannot validate mechanical/ergonomic performance claims. conclusion: a justified recommendation that low-fidelity should dominate title: Modelling and prototyping

sections.title: Lesson 1: Drawings for Communication
sections.html:
B2.2.1 Drawings for Communication ~90 min

Lesson 1: Drawings for Communication

Every product you own began as an idea inside someone's head. Between that idea and the object in your hand sits a chain of drawings, models, digital files and prototypes — each one a translation of the design into a form that a particular audience can understand, test or approve. A structural engineer cannot approve a design from a mood-board render; a customer on Kickstarter will not back a product from an orthographic drawing with tolerance callouts. Across this whole topic, keep coming back to one idea: every modelling and prototyping method exists to answer a specific question, for a specific audience, at a specific stage of the design cycle. Your exam answers should always say who the model is for and what question it answers — that is exactly what separates a Level 5–6 evaluate/justify answer from a Level 1–2 description.

Hook: Isometric vs. Orthographic (8 min)

Drawings are the oldest and still the fastest way to share a design idea — quick and cheap to produce and revise, so they are used constantly and iteratively throughout the design cycle, from a five-second concept sketch to a fully toleranced manufacturing drawing. Before naming any drawing types, watch the clip below and try to predict: which drawing style could a machinist actually measure directly off, and which one is closer to how the human eye sees the object?

Watch: Isometric Projection vs. Orthographic Projection Explained.

2D vs. 3D Representations

1. 2D Drawings

Definition: A representation of an object on a single flat plane, valued for clarity, simplicity and standardization — because they follow agreed conventions (line types, symbols, dimensioning rules such as ISO 128 or BS 8888), a technical drawing produced in Hong Kong can be read accurately by a manufacturer in Shenzhen or Germany without translation.

Context: An electrician wiring a building never sees the finished 3D space when they read the schematic — they read a standardized 2D symbol diagram that strips away everything except the information they need.

Materials/Examples: Electrical schematic diagrams, architectural floor plans, technical engineering drawings used on a factory floor.

Application: Good choice when precise dimensions, tolerances or standardized symbols must be communicated to a technically trained audience quickly and cheaply, and spatial/aesthetic appearance is not the priority.

2. 3D Models and Drawings

Definition: A representation that creates the illusion of depth and volume on a flat page or screen, so a viewer can understand how a form occupies space without needing to mentally reconstruct it from several 2D views.

Context: A photorealistic render shown to a client before an architectural project is built lets a non-technical audience judge form and proportion instantly.

Materials/Examples: Concept renders, client-facing pictorial visuals, marketing images.

Application: Good choice when the audience is non-technical, or when overall form, proportion and spatial relationship matter more than exact manufacturing dimensions — e.g. a concept render shown to a client for the first time.

3. Isometric Drawing

Definition: A 3D pictorial representation in which all three axes are equally foreshortened and set 120° apart. Because the foreshortening is equal on every axis, dimensions along each axis remain to scale — you can measure directly off an isometric drawing, unlike a perspective drawing where lines converge toward a vanishing point and distort scale.

Context: IKEA relies on isometric-style pictorial views inside its instruction booklets precisely because dimensions stay proportionally accurate — a customer can recognise which pre-drilled hole lines up with which dowel.

Materials/Examples: Isometric dot/grid paper, patent illustrations, self-assembly instructions.

Application: Good choice when you need a 3D pictorial view that can still be measured or scaled accurately — ideal for technical/engineering drawings, patent illustrations and self-assembly instructions.

4. Orthographic Projection

Definition: A set of separate, related 2D views — typically front, plan (top) and side elevation — each looking straight along one axis with no perspective distortion. Combined with dimension lines, hidden-detail lines and a title block, it communicates precise dimensions a single pictorial view cannot show.

Context: Before a building can be submitted for planning permission, an architect must supply a full orthographic set — plan, elevations and sections — because a single 3D render cannot specify wall thicknesses or window positions with the precision a contractor requires.

Materials/Examples: Dimension lines, hidden-detail lines, title blocks, scale rulers, CAD drawing sheets.

Application: Good choice when a part or building must be manufactured or constructed to an exact dimension or tolerance — the industry-standard language between designer and manufacturer.

5. Assembly Drawings

Definition: A drawing showing how the individual components of a product fit together in their final, joined position, usually alongside a numbered parts list (bill of materials) that references each component.

Context: Aircraft maintenance technicians work from assembly drawings to confirm that a replacement part has been correctly fitted and orientated before an aircraft is certified airworthy again.

Materials/Examples: Numbered bill of materials (BOM), joined-position CAD views.

Application: Good choice when a technician needs to check that parts are correctly located, orientated and fastened relative to each other in the finished product.

6. Exploded Drawings

Definition: A drawing that separates the components of a product along an axis while keeping them in their correct relative position and order, usually with numbered call-outs and dashed lines showing the direction of assembly.

Context: LEGO and IKEA instructions are almost entirely exploded drawings, and repair sites such as iFixit use them in teardown guides so a customer can order the exact numbered spare part they need.

Materials/Examples: Numbered call-outs, dashed assembly-direction lines.

Application: Good choice when a non-expert needs to assemble, disassemble or identify spare parts for a product without formal drawing-reading training.

Practical Engagement: Phone Stand Drawing Set

Using isometric dot paper and a simple object (e.g. a phone stand made of 3 parts):

  • Sketch it in isometric.
  • Produce a 2-view orthographic (front + side) of the same object, with dimensions.
  • Draw an exploded view with a numbered parts list.

Debrief: Which drawing would you send to a CNC machinist? Which to a customer? Why? This directly rehearses the "good choice when..." exam skill.

Drawing TypeWhat It ShowsBest Audience / Use
2D DrawingA single flat plane, using standardized symbols and conventions.Technically trained audiences needing precise dimensions or symbols (electricians, machinists).
3D Model / DrawingDepth and volume on a flat page or screen.Non-technical stakeholders judging overall form and proportion.
Isometric Drawing3D pictorial view on three 120° axes, true to scale.Technical/patent illustrations and self-assembly instructions that must still be measurable.
Orthographic ProjectionRelated front/plan/side 2D views with no perspective distortion.Manufacture or construction to an exact dimension or tolerance.
Assembly DrawingComponents shown in their final, joined position with a parts list.Checking parts are correctly located and fastened in the finished product.
Exploded DrawingComponents separated along an axis but kept in correct relative order.Non-experts assembling, disassembling or ordering spare parts.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Physical Prototypes
sections.html:
B2.2.2 Physical Prototypes ~60 min

Lesson 2: Physical Prototypes

A physical prototype is a tangible, three-dimensional object built to test an idea — and unlike a drawing or digital model, it can be picked up, operated, worn or dropped. That physicality lets designers and users evaluate things a drawing never can: ergonomics, weight, texture, assembly, real mechanical performance. Physical prototypes are built at different levels of fidelity (how closely they resemble the finished product) depending on what question they are trying to answer.

Hook: Five Days to Redesign a Shopping Cart

Watch the clip below. Note the exact moment the IDEO team stops talking about ideas and starts building something rough with their hands — that moment is the whole point of low-fidelity prototyping.

Watch: ABC Nightline — IDEO Shopping Cart.

Levels of Fidelity

1. Low-Fidelity Prototypes

Definition: Quick, cheap and simple models — often made from paper, card, foam board or tape — used early in the design process to test a basic concept or a user's first interaction with an idea, before any time is invested in materials, finish or mechanism.

Context: In their famous 1999 project for ABC Nightline, IDEO redesigned the supermarket shopping cart in five days. On day one, engineers built a rough cardboard, foam and wire mock-up purely to test whether a basket-swap concept even worked — long before anyone worried about colour, material or manufacturing.

Materials/Examples: Paper, card, foam board, tape.

Application: Use early, when speed and low cost matter more than realism, to test whether a concept works at all.

2. High-Fidelity Prototypes

Definition: Detailed versions that closely resemble the final product in look, feel and functionality. Because they are expensive and time-consuming to build, they are used later — for advanced user testing, investor pitches, or final stakeholder sign-off before committing to mass-production tooling.

Context: Smartphone manufacturers CNC-machine aluminium "unibody" prototypes that are visually and dimensionally identical to the production model, so designers can test in-hand feel, button travel and weight distribution before committing to expensive injection-mould tooling.

Materials/Examples: CNC-machined final-grade materials, working electronics, near-final finishes.

Application: Use later, when you need to test performance, finish or gain formal approval from a stakeholder who needs to see (almost) the real thing.

Types of Physical Models

3. Aesthetic Prototypes

Definition: Models that focus only on visual appearance — form, proportion, colour and surface finish — without functioning like the final product internally.

Context: Automotive studios (Ford, BMW, Tesla) still hand-sculpt full-size clay "aesthetic" models of new car bodies, because designers can judge how light reflects across a curved surface far more accurately on a physical clay form than on a screen render.

Materials/Examples: Clay, foam, paint, surface-finish samples.

Application: Choose to test look, branding or marketing reaction.

4. Functional Prototypes

Definition: Working models built to test mechanics, interactions and performance, even if they don't look anything like the finished product.

Context: A company developing a robotic prosthetic hand will 3D print an ugly, exposed functional prototype of just the gripping mechanism to test grip strength and object recognition, long before any cosmetic skin covering is designed.

Materials/Examples: 3D-printed mechanisms, breadboard electronics, exposed working parts.

Application: Choose to test engineering performance.

5. Scale Models

Definition: Models built larger or smaller than the real object to visualise spatial relationships for products that are too large or too small to prototype at final size.

Context: A 1:100 scale architectural model lets a planning committee understand a building's relationship to its street before a single brick is laid, while automotive engineers test 25% scale car models in a wind tunnel because a full-size rolling-road test is vastly more expensive.

Materials/Examples: Architectural scale models, wind-tunnel test models.

Application: Choose when the true size of the product makes full-size testing impractical or too costly.

Practical Engagement: The Coffee Cup Carrier Challenge

In teams, use identical basic materials (card, tape, foam, string) and 15 minutes to build a low-fidelity prototype of a device to carry three coffee cups one-handed. Test each prototype live, then discuss as a class: what did this rough model let us learn cheaply that we could never have learned from a drawing alone?

Follow with the IDEO shopping-cart video above as a professional case study of the same principle.

Model TypeFocusGood Choice When...
Low-FidelitySpeed and low cost over realism.Testing whether a basic concept works at all, early in the process.
High-FidelityRealism in look, feel and function.Advanced user testing, investor pitches or final sign-off.
AestheticVisual appearance only.Testing look, branding and marketing reaction.
FunctionalMechanics, interaction and performance.Testing engineering performance.
Scale ModelSpatial relationships at a different size.Product is too large or small to test at final size.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Computer-Aided Design (CAD)
sections.html:
B2.2.3 Computer-Aided Design (CAD) ~60 min

Lesson 3: Computer-Aided Design (CAD)

CAD is the use of computer software (e.g. SolidWorks, Fusion 360, Rhino, SketchUp) to visualise, modify and analyse a design before committing to physical production. Unlike a physical prototype, a CAD file can be changed in seconds, shared instantly across the world, measured with perfect precision, and fed directly into manufacturing (CAM) or simulation (FEA) software. CAD models exist at different levels of geometric detail, and choosing the right one depends on what you need the model to do.

1. Wireframe Models

Definition: The least detailed CAD models, representing an object using only lines and curves along its edges — essentially a see-through "skeleton" with no surfaces or volume.

Context: A designer sketching the very first digital concept of a new car's silhouette will often start with wireframe curves to check overall proportion and stance before any surface is applied — the file is tiny and every curve can be reshaped instantly.

Materials/Examples: Edge curves only, no surfaces — the lightest possible CAD file.

Application: Good for the earliest concept stage and checking basic proportion — but a wireframe cannot be 3D printed, rendered realistically, or used to calculate volume or mass.

2. Surface Models

Definition: Models that define only the outer "skin" or contours of an object, creating photorealistic images with no data about internal mass or structure — like a hollow shell with zero wall thickness.

Context: Car stylists use high-end surface modelling ("Class-A surfacing") to perfect the exact curvature of exterior body panels for a photorealistic marketing render — long before the engineering team has finalised the load-bearing structure hidden underneath.

Materials/Examples: NURBS surfaces, Class-A surfacing software.

Application: Good when visual appearance or a marketing/Kickstarter image matters more than manufacturability at that stage — but with no defined volume, a surface model cannot be used for FEA, mass/cost calculation, or most CNC/3D-printing workflows.

3. Solid Models

Definition: Complete 3D representations that define both the outer and inner surfaces (the full volume) of an object, so software can calculate mass, volume, centre of gravity and material cost. Most professional engineering CAD (feature-based, parametric modelling — extrude, revolve, fillet) works this way, and the solid model is normally the "master" file for detailed engineering, FEA and manufacturing.

Context: An engineer designing an injection-moulded plastic enclosure builds it as a solid model so the software can instantly report wall thickness, material volume and cost — and the exact same file exports straight into an FEA stress simulation and into the CNC toolpath software that cuts the mould.

Materials/Examples: Feature-based parametric operations — extrude, revolve, fillet.

Application: Essential whenever a design will be manufactured, simulated (FEA) or costed by material volume.

Practical Engagement: Wireframe → Surface → Solid

Using free CAD software (e.g. Tinkercad or Fusion 360), build the same simple bracket first as basic sketch geometry (wireframe-like), then loft/extrude it into a solid. Try to get a mass/volume readout at each stage and note when it becomes possible — this makes the wireframe → surface → solid progression concrete rather than abstract.

CAD ModelDetail LevelCan It Calculate Mass/Volume?Typical Use
WireframeEdges (lines/curves) only.NoEarliest concept stage, checking proportion.
SurfaceOuter "skin," zero wall thickness.NoPhotorealistic renders, marketing, Class-A surfacing.
SolidFull internal + external volume.YesEngineering, FEA, CNC/3D-printing, costing.
sections.text: B2.2.3 Computer-Aided Design (CAD) ~60 min Lesson 3: Computer-Aided Design (CAD) CAD is the use of computer software (e.g. SolidWorks, Fusion 360, Rhino, SketchUp) to visualise, modify and analyse a design before committing to physical production. Unlike a physical prototype, a CAD file can be changed in seconds, shared instantly across the world, measured with perfect precision, and fed directly into manufacturing (CAM) or simulation (FEA) software. CAD models exist at different levels of geometric detail, and choosing the right one depends on what you need the model to do. 1. Wireframe Models Definition: The least detailed CAD models, representing an object using only lines and curves along its edges — essentially a see-through "skeleton" with no surfaces or volume. Context: A designer sketching the very first digital concept of a new car's silhouette will often start with wireframe curves to check overall proportion and stance before any surface is applied — the file is tiny and every curve can be reshaped instantly. Materials/Examples: Edge curves only, no surfaces — the lightest possible CAD file. Application: Good for the earliest concept stage and checking basic proportion — but a wireframe cannot be 3D printed, rendered realistically, or used to calculate volume or mass. 2. Surface Models Definition: Models that define only the outer "skin" or contours of an object, creating photorealistic images with no data about internal mass or structure — like a hollow shell with zero wall thickness. Context: Car stylists use high-end surface modelling ("Class-A surfacing") to perfect the exact curvature of exterior body panels for a photorealistic marketing render — long before the engineering team has finalised the load-bearing structure hidden underneath. Materials/Examples: NURBS surfaces, Class-A surfacing software. Application: Good when visual appearance or a marketing/Kickstarter image matters more than manufacturability at that stage — but with no defined volume, a surface model cannot be used for FEA, mass/cost calculation, or most CNC/3D-printing workflows. 3. Solid Models Definition: Complete 3D representations that define both the outer and inner surfaces (the full volume) of an object, so software can calculate mass, volume, centre of gravity and material cost. Most professional engineering CAD (feature-based, parametric modelling — extrude, revolve, fillet) works this way, and the solid model is normally the "master" file for detailed engineering, FEA and manufacturing. Context: An engineer designing an injection-moulded plastic enclosure builds it as a solid model so the software can instantly report wall thickness, material volume and cost — and the exact same file exports straight into an FEA stress simulation and into the CNC toolpath software that cuts the mould. Materials/Examples: Feature-based parametric operations — extrude, revolve, fillet. Application: Essential whenever a design will be manufactured, simulated (FEA) or costed by material volume. Practical Engagement: Wireframe → Surface → Solid Using free CAD software (e.g. Tinkercad or Fusion 360), build the same simple bracket first as basic sketch geometry (wireframe-like), then loft/extrude it into a solid. Try to get a mass/volume readout at each stage and note when it becomes possible — this makes the wireframe → surface → solid progression concrete rather than abstract. sections.title: Lesson 4: Finite Element Analysis (FEA)
sections.html:
B2.2.4 Finite Element Analysis (FEA) ~60 min

Lesson 4: Finite Element Analysis (FEA)

FEA is a digital simulation tool that predicts how a part or assembly will perform under real-world physical conditions — stress, heat, vibration, airflow — without building it. The software divides ("discretizes") a solid CAD model into thousands of small connected elements (a mesh), applies the loads and constraints a designer specifies, and calculates the resulting stress, strain and deformation across every element.

Hook: Simulating Before You Build

Watch the clip below, then answer: what does FEA let an engineer find out about a part before a single physical prototype has been built?

Watch: What is Finite Element Analysis (FEA)? Explained Simply.

1. Benefits of FEA

Definition: FEA reduces the need for expensive, time-consuming physical prototypes and destructive testing, identifies failure points early — while changes are still cheap — and supports sustainable design by revealing exactly where material can be safely removed without compromising strength (lightweighting).

Context: Formula 1 teams run FEA on every carbon-fibre wishbone and chassis component before it is ever machined, because physically building and crash-testing a real part is vastly more expensive than simulating it first.

Materials/Examples: Mesh density settings, applied loads and constraints, material property data.

Application: Use when a part's structural or thermal performance needs to be predicted and optimised before committing to expensive tooling or materials.

2. Interpreting the Results

Definition: FEA results are usually displayed as a colour-coded stress map. As a general convention, red indicates areas of high stress and greatest risk of failure (often at corners, holes or sudden changes in cross-section), while blue indicates low stress, meaning that area is "over-engineered" and a candidate for material reduction.

Context: It is essential to read the map against its numerical scale bar rather than judging colour alone, and to remember that FEA is only as accurate as its mesh density, material data and assumed loads — real designers still validate FEA predictions with a small number of physical prototype tests rather than trusting simulation blindly.

Materials/Examples: Colour-coded stress maps, numerical scale bars.

Application: Use when a design needs to be made lighter or more sustainable without an expensive trial-and-error cycle of physical prototypes.

Case Study: GE Aviation's 80% Lighter Bracket

GE Aviation used FEA-guided topology optimization to redesign a jet engine bracket, removing material from every low-stress ("blue") region the simulation identified while keeping the high-stress ("red") load paths intact — the result was roughly 80% lighter than the original while meeting the same strength requirements, directly cutting fuel burn and material use.

Practical Engagement: Read the Stress Map

Look at a simple cantilever bracket stress-map image (search "FEA stress map bracket" or use a free Fusion 360 simulation study). Identify the red zones, the blue zones, and propose one specific change to the geometry that would reduce weight while keeping the red zones intact — connect this explicitly to sustainability and material efficiency.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Rapid Prototyping Effectiveness
sections.html:
B2.2.5 Rapid Prototyping Effectiveness ~90 min

Lesson 5: Rapid Prototyping Effectiveness

Rapid prototyping (RP) covers manufacturing techniques that build a physical object quickly and directly from a digital CAD file, layer by layer, without the moulds, jigs or tooling that traditional manufacturing requires. This is why RP is so effective at low volumes: it allows highly complex geometries impossible to machine (such as internal lattices) and lets designers iterate a physical model overnight instead of waiting weeks for tooling.

1. Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM)

Definition: Works by melting a thermoplastic filament (commonly PLA, ABS or PETG) and extruding it through a heated nozzle, building the object layer by layer.

Context: Desktop FDM printers are the workhorse of school workshops and product design studios worldwide because they are cheap to run — NASA has even sent an FDM printer to the International Space Station so astronauts can print replacement tools on demand instead of waiting months for a resupply launch.

Materials/Examples: PLA, ABS, PETG thermoplastic filament.

Application: Good choice when you need a cheap, fast, reasonably strong functional prototype and can accept visible layer lines and lower dimensional accuracy.

2. Stereolithography (SLA)

Definition: Uses a UV laser to selectively cure liquid photopolymer resin in a vat into a solid object, layer by layer, producing very high detail and a smooth surface finish.

Context: Jewellery designers 3D-print a wax-like castable resin "former" using SLA, then use the traditional lost-wax casting process to cast the exact same intricate form in silver or gold. Dental labs use the same resin-printing principle to produce precise models for clear aligners such as Invisalign.

Materials/Examples: Liquid photopolymer resin, UV laser.

Application: Good choice when fine surface detail and a smooth finish are critical — jewellery, dental models, miniatures — and the part does not need high mechanical strength.

3. Selective Laser Sintering (SLS)

Definition: Uses a high-power laser to fuse small particles of powder (typically nylon plastic, or metal powder in the related DMLS process) into a solid 3D object. Because the surrounding unfused powder itself supports the part during printing, no support structures are needed, allowing complex internal geometry and lattices that other processes cannot produce.

Context: SpaceX and Relativity Space 3D-print entire rocket engines from metal powder using laser-sintering processes, embedding internal cooling channels that would be impossible to machine conventionally, while functional nylon SLS parts are widely used for custom prosthetic sockets and drone components.

Materials/Examples: Nylon powder, metal powder (DMLS).

Application: Good choice when a strong, functional, end-use part with complex internal geometry is needed and support-free printing is an advantage — at a higher equipment cost than FDM or SLA.

FDMSLASLS
ProcessMelted filament extruded layer by layerUV laser cures liquid resin in a vatLaser fuses powdered material (plastic or metal)
Typical useCheap functional prototypes, jigs, classroom useHigh-detail aesthetic/dental/jewellery patternsStrong end-use functional parts, complex geometry
Surface finishVisible layer linesSmooth, highly detailedSlightly grainy/porous
Relative costLowMediumHigh
Support needed?Yes, for overhangsYes, for overhangsNo — powder bed self-supports

Read: FDM vs. SLA vs. SLS: 3D Printing Technology Comparison (Formlabs).

Practical Engagement: Card-Sort — Match the Process

Given six short product briefs (e.g. "a smooth wax pattern for a gold ring," "a cheap prototype bracket for a school project," "a strong drone arm with an internal lattice to save weight"), match each to FDM, SLA or SLS, justifying your choice using the comparison table above. This rehearses exactly the "apply the rule to a specific context" AO2 skill used in IB exam questions.

sections.title: Lesson 6: Data, Feedback and Stakeholder Communication
sections.html:
B2.2.6 Data and Feedback ~60 min

Lesson 6: Data, Feedback and Stakeholder Communication

A prototype is only useful if it generates data that improves the next version. Designers rely on a continuous model → test → refine cycle: build a version, test it against real users or real physical conditions, collect data (both quantitative, such as load-test results or task-completion times, and qualitative, such as user comfort or aesthetic preference), and use that evidence to refine the design before the next iteration. This cycle is what the syllabus term iterative design describes, and it repeats — sometimes hundreds of times — until the final product meets the design specification.

1. The Model → Test → Refine Cycle

Definition: An iterative loop in which designers build a version, test it against real users or physical conditions, collect quantitative and qualitative data, and use that evidence to refine the design before the next iteration.

Context: Sir James Dyson built and tested 5,127 prototypes of his cyclone vacuum cleaner separator over five years, measuring dust-separation performance at every stage and refining the geometry based on that data until it out-performed every bagged vacuum on the market.

Materials/Examples: Load-test results, task-completion times (quantitative); user comfort or aesthetic preference (qualitative).

Application: Repeats until the final product meets the design specification — this cycle is the syllabus term iterative design.

2. Stakeholder Communication

Definition: Non-technical stakeholders — clients, investors, everyday users — usually cannot read an orthographic drawing or interpret an FEA stress map. Presenting a physical or high-quality visual model instead lets these audiences understand shape, proportion, colour and use almost instantly, which is essential for gathering honest, useful feedback and for winning approval or investment.

Context: Crowdfunding campaigns on Kickstarter succeed or fail largely on rendered CAD images and short functional-prototype demo videos, not technical drawings, because backers are consumers, not engineers — while an architect presenting to a client will often bring a physical scale model into the room alongside renders, because clients read spatial relationships far more easily in a model they can walk around than in a stack of construction drawings.

Materials/Examples: Rendered CAD images, demo videos, physical scale models.

Application: Choose the model or drawing type to match the audience — technical language and orthographic drawings for engineers, physical models and everyday language for customers.

Practical Engagement: Explain It Twice

Role-play in pairs: one student is the "designer" and must explain the same design change twice — once to a "manufacturing engineer" partner (using technical/orthographic language) and once to a "customer" partner (using a physical model or render and everyday language). Debrief on how and why the communication method changed for each stakeholder.

Linking Questions

Use these to bridge B2.2 to other parts of the syllabus and to build the kind of cross-topic thinking Paper 2 extended-response questions reward.

B2.1 The Design Process: How does the model–test–refine cycle in B2.2 relate to the Prototype and Present stages of the design process?
B1.1 User-Centred Design: Why must the choice of model or prototype type be driven by the needs of the user or stakeholder being tested?
B3.3 Mechanical Systems — Application and Selection: How can FEA and functional prototyping be used to validate the performance of a mechanical system before manufacture?
C4.1 Design for Manufacture: How does the choice between rapid prototyping methods (FDM, SLA, SLS) anticipate the demands of full-scale manufacture?

sections.title: Exam Practice: Topic B2.2
sections.html:
B2.2 Exam Practice AO1 / AO2 / AO3

Exam Practice: Topic B2.2

The following questions are written in the style of IB DP Design Technology Paper 1 and Paper 2, following the command-term logic in Cracking the Command Terms (AO1 knowledge, AO2 application, AO3 synthesis). A short stimulus is provided below; use it to anchor the short-answer and long-answer questions, as the real IB papers do.

Stimulus

TrailLight is a small design company developing a collapsible, solar-powered camping lantern for backpackers. Early in development the team built a rough card-and-tape mock-up of the folding mechanism. Mid-way through development, the folding hinge bracket was modelled as a CAD solid model and FEA tested; the stress map showed a red (high-stress) zone at the hinge pin hole and a large blue (low-stress) zone across the flat base plate. For the final investor pitch, the team produced a high-fidelity, fully working prototype and a set of orthographic manufacturing drawings for their factory in China.

Section A: Multiple Choice (AO1)

Question 1 [1 mark]

What is the correct rapid prototyping technique for creating a smooth, castable wax-style pattern for jewellery?

  • Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM)
  • Stereolithography (SLA)
  • Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) of metal powder
  • Computer numerical control (CNC) milling

Command term focus: IDENTIFY — a simple, direct selection task with no reasoning required.

Reveal Answer
B. Stereolithography (SLA), chosen for its smooth, highly detailed surface finish suited to fine jewellery patterns. [1]

Question 2 [1 mark]

On the FEA stress map of TrailLight's hinge bracket, the red zone at the hinge pin hole indicates:

  • An area of low stress and excess material
  • An area of high stress and risk of failure
  • The exact location the part will be 3D printed
  • An area with no load applied

Command term focus: IDENTIFY — recognising a standard convention from the description given.

Reveal Answer
B. Red conventionally indicates high stress concentration and greatest risk of failure. [1]

Question 3 [1 mark]

Which CAD model type contains no data about a part's internal mass or volume, and therefore cannot be used to calculate weight or run an FEA simulation?

  • Wireframe model
  • Surface model
  • Solid model
  • Assembly model

Command term focus: IDENTIFY — matching a CAD model type to its defining property.

Reveal Answer
B. A surface model defines only the outer "skin" of the object, with zero internal volume data. [1]

Section B: Short Answer (AO1 / AO2)

Question 4 [2 marks]

Outline one reason why TrailLight's design team built a low-fidelity card-and-tape mock-up before developing the CAD solid model of the folding mechanism.

Command term focus: OUTLINE — a brief account combining a feature with its benefit.

Reveal Answer

A low-fidelity mock-up is quick and cheap to build (1), which lets the team test whether the basic folding concept and user interaction works before investing time and money in a detailed, accurate CAD model (1).

Question 5 [3 marks]

Explain how the FEA results described in the stimulus could support more sustainable design of the hinge bracket.

Command term focus: EXPLAIN — a three-step logic chain (A → B → C).

Reveal Answer

The FEA stress map shows a large blue, low-stress zone across the base plate (A) (1); because this material is barely loaded, the designer can remove or thin material from that region without weakening the part (B) (1); this reduces the mass of plastic or metal used per lantern, lowering material cost and the product's overall environmental footprint (C) (1).

Section C: Long Answer (AO2 / AO3)

Question 6 [6 marks]

Justify TrailLight's decision to produce a high-fidelity prototype and a set of orthographic manufacturing drawings for the investor pitch and factory handover, rather than relying on the early low-fidelity mock-up.

Command term focus: JUSTIFY — give valid evidence linking a physical feature to a higher-order goal (e.g. cost, sustainability, stakeholder need).

Reveal Answer

Structure: For each audience — identify the stakeholder + identify what they need to see/do + explain why the earlier model type could not meet that need + connective linking to outcome. Investors need to judge whether the finished product will look, feel and function like a market-ready item before committing funding (1); the low-fidelity card mock-up could never demonstrate real material finish, working electronics or genuine user experience, so only a high-fidelity prototype can convincingly secure investment (1–2). Separately, the factory in China needs exact, toleranced dimensions to manufacture interchangeable parts at scale (1); orthographic drawings — unlike a pictorial mock-up — communicate precise, measurable dimensions and hidden detail using an internationally standardised convention that the factory's machinists and quality-control staff can read without ambiguity (1–2), reducing costly manufacturing errors (1).

Question 7 [8 marks]

Evaluate TrailLight's use of Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) instead of Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) if they decide to 3D-print the final hinge bracket in low-volume production, and design one improvement to their prototyping process for the next product iteration.

Command term focus: EVALUATE — weigh advantages against disadvantages and reach a justified conclusion; may extend to DESIGN (identify a weakness and propose an innovation).

Reveal Answer

Structure: Advantage(s) of SLS + disadvantage(s)/trade-off + comparison to FDM + justified conclusion, then one specific, innovative process improvement. SLS produces stronger, functional end-use parts with no need for support structures, allowing the complex internal geometry an optimised hinge bracket might need after FEA-guided lightweighting (advantage); however, SLS equipment and material costs are significantly higher than FDM, and the slightly grainier surface finish may need secondary finishing for a consumer product (disadvantage). Because the hinge bracket is a structurally critical part rather than a purely cosmetic one, the extra cost of SLS is justified by its superior mechanical performance for this specific component, whereas FDM remains the better (cheaper, faster) choice for early concept iterations (justified conclusion). Improvement: TrailLight could introduce an intermediate FEA-validated functional prototype stage — printing the optimised geometry in cheap FDM first purely to physically validate the FEA prediction before committing to a costlier SLS production run, catching any simulation-to-reality gap earlier and more cheaply.
sections.text: B2.2 Exam Practice AO1 / AO2 / AO3 Exam Practice: Topic B2.2 The following questions are written in the style of IB DP Design Technology Paper 1 and Paper 2, following the command-term logic in Cracking the Command Terms (AO1 knowledge, AO2 application, AO3 synthesis). A short stimulus is provided below; use it to anchor the short-answer and long-answer questions, as the real IB papers do. Stimulus TrailLight is a small design company developing a collapsible, solar-powered camping lantern for backpackers. Early in development the team built a rough card-and-tape mock-up of the folding mechanism. Mid-way through development, the folding hinge bracket was modelled as a CAD solid model and FEA tested; the stress map showed a red (high-stress) zone at the hinge pin hole and a large blue (low-stress) zone across the flat base plate. For the final investor pitch, the team produced a high-fidelity, fully working prototype and a set of orthographic manufacturing drawings for their factory in China. Section A: Multiple Choice (AO1) Question 1 [1 mark] What is the correct rapid prototyping technique for creating a smooth, castable wax-style pattern for jewellery? Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) Stereolithography (SLA) Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) of metal powder Computer numerical control (CNC) milling Command term focus: IDENTIFY — a simple, direct selection task with no reasoning required. Reveal Answer B. Stereolithography (SLA), chosen for its smooth, highly detailed surface finish suited to fine jewellery patterns. [1] Question 2 [1 mark] On the FEA stress map of TrailLight's hinge bracket, the red zone at the hinge pin hole indicates: An area of low stress and excess material An area of high stress and risk of failure The exact location the part will be 3D printed An area with no load applied Command term focus: IDENTIFY — recognising a standard convention from the description given. Reveal Answer B. Red conventionally indicates high stress concentration and greatest risk of failure. [1] Question 3 [1 mark] Which CAD model type contains no data about a part's internal mass or volume, and therefore cannot be used to calculate weight or run an FEA simulation? Wireframe model Surface model Solid model Assembly model Command term focus: IDENTIFY — matching a CAD model type to its defining property. Reveal Answer B. A surface model defines only the outer "skin" of the object, with zero internal volume data. [1] Section B: Short Answer (AO1 / AO2) Question 4 [2 marks] Outline one reason why TrailLight's design team built a low-fidelity card-and-tape mock-up before developing the CAD solid model of the folding mechanism. Command term focus: OUTLINE — a brief account combining a feature with its benefit. Reveal Answer A low-fidelity mock-up is quick and cheap to build (1) , which lets the team test whether the basic folding concept and user interaction works before investing time and money in a detailed, accurate CAD model (1) . Question 5 [3 marks] Explain how the FEA results described in the stimulus could support more sustainable design of the hinge bracket. Command term focus: EXPLAIN — a three-step logic chain (A → B → C). Reveal Answer The FEA stress map shows a large blue, low-stress zone across the base plate (A) (1) ; because this material is barely loaded, the designer can remove or thin material from that region without weakening the part (B) (1) ; this reduces the mass of plastic or metal used per lantern, lowering material cost and the product's overall environmental footprint (C) (1) . Section C: Long Answer (AO2 / AO3) Question 6 [6 marks] Justify TrailLight's decision to produce a high-fidelity prototype and a set of orthographic manufacturing drawings for the investor pitch and factory handover, rather than relying on the early low-fidelity mock-up. Command term focus: JUSTIFY — give valid evidence linking a physical feature to a higher-order goal (e.g. cost, sustainability, stakeholder need). Reveal Answer Structure: For each audience — identify the stakeholder + identify what they need to see/do + explain why the earlier model type could not meet that need + connective linking to outcome. Investors need to judge whether the finished product will look, feel and function like a market-ready item before committing funding (1) ; the low-fidelity card mock-up could never demonstrate real material finish, working electronics or genuine user experience, so only a high-fidelity prototype can convincingly secure investment (1–2) . Separately, the factory in China needs exact, toleranced dimensions to manufacture interchangeable parts at scale (1) ; orthographic drawings — unlike a pictorial mock-up — communicate precise, measurable dimensions and hidden detail using an internationally standardised convention that the factory's machinists and quality-control staff can read without ambiguity (1–2) , reducing costly manufacturing errors (1) . Question 7 [8 marks] Evaluate TrailLight's use of Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) instead of Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) if they decide to 3D-print the final hinge bracket in low-volume production, and design one improvement to their prototyping process for the next product iteration. Command term focus: EVALUATE — weigh advantages against disadvantages and reach a justified conclusion; may extend to DESIGN (identify a weakness and propose an innovation). Reveal Answer Structure: Advantage(s) of SLS + disadvantage(s)/trade-off + comparison to FDM + justified conclusion, then one specific, innovative process improvement. SLS produces stronger, functional end-use parts with no need for support structures, allowing the complex internal geometry an optimised hinge bracket might need after FEA-guided lightweighting (advantage); however, SLS equipment and material costs are significantly higher than FDM, and the slightly grainier surface finish may need secondary finishing for a consumer product (disadvantage). Because the hinge bracket is a structurally critical part rather than a purely cosmetic one, the extra cost of SLS is justified by its superior mechanical performance for this specific component, whereas FDM remains the better (cheaper, faster) choice for early concept iterations (justified conclusion). Improvement: TrailLight could introduce an intermediate FEA-validated functional prototype stage — printing the optimised geometry in cheap FDM first purely to physically validate the FEA prediction before committing to a costlier SLS production run, catching any simulation-to-reality gap earlier and more cheaply.

sections.html:
B2.2 Glossary

Glossary: Topic B2.2 — Modelling and Prototyping

Every key term from this unit, its IB-style definition, and a real-world example that shows the term in use. Click on a term to reveal its definition.

Iterative Design
IB Definition: The act of repeating a process with the aim of approaching a desired goal, target or result.
Real-World Context: Dyson built and tested 5,127 vacuum cleaner prototypes over five years, refining the design each time based on test data.
2D Drawing
IB Definition: A representation of an object on a single flat plane, emphasising clarity, simplicity and standardisation.
Real-World Context: An electrician reads a standardised electrical schematic diagram to wire a building correctly.
3D Model / Drawing
IB Definition: A representation that creates the illusion of depth and volume, helping a viewer understand spatial relationships.
Real-World Context: A photorealistic render shown to a client before an architectural project is built.
Isometric Drawing
IB Definition: A 3D pictorial representation in which all three axes are equally foreshortened, so dimensions stay to scale.
Real-World Context: IKEA instruction booklets use isometric-style views so customers can measure and match parts accurately.
Orthographic Projection
IB Definition: A set of related 2D views (e.g. front, plan, side) used to communicate precise dimensions and detail for manufacturing.
Real-World Context: An architect submits plan, elevation and section drawings for council planning approval.
Assembly Drawing
IB Definition: A drawing showing how different parts of a product fit together in their finished position, often with a parts list.
Real-World Context: Aircraft technicians check an assembly drawing to confirm a replacement part is correctly fitted.
Exploded Drawing
IB Definition: A drawing showing components separated but in their correct relative position, clarifying assembly sequence.
Real-World Context: LEGO and IKEA instructions use exploded views so untrained customers can self-assemble a product.
Low-Fidelity Prototype
IB Definition: A quick, cheap, simple model (e.g. paper or cardboard) used early on to test a basic idea or user interaction.
Real-World Context: IDEO's rough foam-and-wire shopping cart mock-up, built in a single day to test a basket-swap concept.
High-Fidelity Prototype
IB Definition: A detailed prototype that closely resembles the final product in look, feel and functionality.
Real-World Context: A CNC-machined aluminium smartphone housing used to test in-hand feel before mass production.
Aesthetic Prototype
IB Definition: A model focused on visual appearance, form and material characteristics, without functioning like the final product.
Real-World Context: A hand-sculpted clay model used by car studios to refine exterior body-panel curvature.
Functional Prototype
IB Definition: A working model used to test mechanics, interactions and performance.
Real-World Context: An exposed 3D-printed robotic gripper mechanism tested for grip strength before any cosmetic housing is designed.
Scale Model
IB Definition: A smaller or larger representation used to visualise spatial relationships for products too large or too small to test at final size.
Real-World Context: A 1:100 architectural model, or a 25% scale car model tested in a wind tunnel.
Computer-Aided Design (CAD)
IB Definition: The use of computer software to aid the design process.
Real-World Context: An engineer models a plastic enclosure in SolidWorks and exports it directly to FEA and CNC software.
Wireframe Model
IB Definition: The least detailed CAD model, using lines and curves to represent edges, mainly for early conceptualisation.
Real-World Context: A car stylist's first digital sketch of a vehicle's overall silhouette and proportion.
Surface Model
IB Definition: A CAD model defining only the outer shape/contours, with no data on interior mass, but capable of photorealistic rendering.
Real-World Context: A Class-A surfacing render of a car's exterior body panels used for marketing before engineering is finalised.
Solid Model
IB Definition: A complete 3D CAD representation defining both outer and inner surfaces (volume), essential for detailing and simulation.
Real-World Context: A solid-modelled plastic enclosure used to calculate material cost and run an FEA stress test.
Finite Element Analysis (FEA)
IB Definition: Digital model calculation and simulation of unknown factors (e.g. stress, heat) in products using CAD systems.
Real-World Context: GE Aviation used FEA-guided topology optimization to cut a jet engine bracket's weight by around 80%.
Rapid Prototyping
IB Definition: Manufacturing techniques used to produce physical objects quickly for testing, typically from 3D CAD models.
Real-World Context: A desktop 3D printer used to turn an overnight CAD file into a testable physical part by morning.
Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM)
IB Definition: A rapid prototyping technique that melts and extrudes thermoplastic material layer by layer.
Real-World Context: NASA sent an FDM printer to the International Space Station so astronauts can print tools on demand.
Stereolithography (SLA)
IB Definition: A rapid prototyping technique using a laser to cure liquid photopolymer resin into a solid object.
Real-World Context: Jewellery designers SLA-print castable wax-style patterns later cast in silver or gold using lost-wax casting.
Selective Laser Sintering (SLS)
IB Definition: A rapid prototyping technique using a high-power laser to fuse small particles of powder into a 3D object.
Real-World Context: SpaceX and Relativity Space 3D-print entire rocket engines with internal cooling channels using laser-sintered metal powder.
Mock-up
IB Definition: A digital, scale or full-size representation of a product used to test mechanics and gain feedback.
Real-World Context: A card-and-tape mock-up of a folding lantern hinge, built to test the mechanism before CAD modelling begins.
Prototype
IB Definition: A physical or virtual sample built to test a concept or process, or to act as an object to be replicated.
Real-World Context: A working, high-fidelity camping lantern prototype presented to investors before a production run is committed.

sections.title: Read an FEA result critically · B2.2.4
sections.html:
An FEA colour plot estimates a particular quantity under stated assumptions. First read the plot title, legend, unit and scale. A red region may indicate high displacement, high stress or another plotted result; red alone does not mean failure. Check material properties, applied loads, supports and mesh refinement. Compare stress with a suitable material limit and investigate local peaks rather than accepting a screenshot as proof of safety.

Two plots, one component · 8 minutes

Your teacher provides stress and displacement plots for the same bracket. Identify the largest displacement, the highest stress, the supports and load direction. Suggest one strengthening change and explain which result should improve. Then identify one real test needed to check the model assumptions.

syllabus.title: Modelling and prototyping
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How do designers communicate ideas to different stakeholders?

statements.text: Drawings facilitate the discussion of concepts to others for feedback or information.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to construct and interpret 2D drawings and 3D models, including isometric, orthographic projection, assembly and exploded drawings.

statements.text: Physical prototypes are 3D, tangible representations of design or systems and can be developed at a range of fidelity for different users and environments.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to construct and interpret aesthetic and functional prototypes at different levels of fidelity, including the considerations of scale, shape and space.

statements.text: Computer-aided design (CAD) involves the creation, development and analysis of a design outcome using computer software.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to construct and interpret surface, solid and virtual models.

statements.text: Finite element analysis (FEA) is used to simulate how a part or assembly will perform under certain conditions.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to interpret the output from FEA.

statements.text: The increasing effectiveness of rapid prototyping techniques enables designers to create complex physical prototypes for testing.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to construct and interpret CAD models suitable for rapid prototyping.

statements.text: Prototypes are created to gather data and feedback from potential users and clients.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to select and use appropriate drawings, physical prototypes and CAD models to gather relevant data and feedback, which can be used to analyse and develop the design iteratively.

activity.title: Choose the model
activity.materials: Card, paper, CAD access if available
steps: For a desk lamp, list distinct questions about form, reach, structure and light output.
Choose a suitable model or prototype for each question.
Make one quick model and conduct a small test with recorded evidence.
Identify what the model excludes and specify the next test.
activity.debrief: What can a scale model fail to predict at full size?

exam.question: Explain one limitation of a scale model used to test structural performance. [2]
exam.answer: Scaling dimensions changes the relationship between weight, cross-sectional area and volume. A small model may therefore not reproduce full-size stresses or failure behaviour directly.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Phone Stand Drawing Set
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Phone Stand Drawing Set Using isometric dot paper and a simple object (e.g. a phone stand made of 3 parts): Sketch it in isometric. Which to a customer? Why? This directly rehearses the "good choice when..." exam skill.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: The Coffee Cup Carrier Challenge
activities.text: Practical Engagement: The Coffee Cup Carrier Challenge In teams, use identical basic materials (card, tape, foam, string) and 15 minutes to build a low-fidelity prototype of a device to carry three coffee cups one-handed. Test each prototype live, then discuss as a class: what did this rough model let us learn cheaply that we could never have learned from a drawing alone? Follow with the IDEO shopping-cart video above as a professional case study of the same principle.
