searchText: modelling and prototyping b2.2.1 drawings for communication ~90 min lesson 1: drawings for communication every product you own began as an idea inside someone's head. between that idea and the object in your hand sits a chain of drawings, models, digital files and prototypes — each one a translation of the design into a form that a particular audience can understand, test or approve. a structural engineer cannot approve a design from a mood-board render; a customer on kickstarter will not back a product from an orthographic drawing with tolerance callouts. across this whole topic, keep coming back to one idea: every modelling and prototyping method exists to answer a specific question, for a specific audience, at a specific stage of the design cycle. your exam answers should always say who the model is for and what question it answers — that is exactly what separates a level 5–6 evaluate/justify answer from a level 1–2 description. hook: isometric vs. orthographic (8 min) drawings are the oldest and still the fastest way to share a design idea — quick and cheap to produce and revise, so they are used constantly and iteratively throughout the design cycle, from a five-second concept sketch to a fully toleranced manufacturing drawing. before naming any drawing types, watch the clip below and try to predict: which drawing style could a machinist actually measure directly off, and which one is closer to how the human eye sees the object? watch: isometric projection vs. orthographic projection explained . 2d vs. 3d representations 1. 2d drawings definition: a representation of an object on a single flat plane, valued for clarity, simplicity and standardization — because they follow agreed conventions (line types, symbols, dimensioning rules such as iso 128 or bs 8888), a technical drawing produced in hong kong can be read accurately by a manufacturer in shenzhen or germany without translation. context: an electrician wiring a building never sees the finished 3d space when they read the schematic — they read a standardized 2d symbol diagram that strips away everything except the information they need. materials/examples: electrical schematic diagrams, architectural floor plans, technical engineering drawings used on a factory floor. application: good choice when precise dimensions, tolerances or standardized symbols must be communicated to a technically trained audience quickly and cheaply, and spatial/aesthetic appearance is not the priority. 2. 3d models and drawings definition: a representation that creates the illusion of depth and volume on a flat page or screen, so a viewer can understand how a form occupies space without needing to mentally reconstruct it from several 2d views. context: a photorealistic render shown to a client before an architectural project is built lets a non-technical audience judge form and proportion instantly. materials/examples: concept renders, client-facing pictorial visuals, marketing images. application: good choice when the audience is non-technical, or when overall form, proportion and spatial relationship matter more than exact manufacturing dimensions — e.g. a concept render shown to a client for the first time. 3. isometric drawing definition: a 3d pictorial representation in which all three axes are equally foreshortened and set 120° apart. because the foreshortening is equal on every axis, dimensions along each axis remain to scale — you can measure directly off an isometric drawing, unlike a perspective drawing where lines converge toward a vanishing point and distort scale. context: ikea relies on isometric-style pictorial views inside its instruction booklets precisely because dimensions stay proportionally accurate — a customer can recognise which pre-drilled hole lines up with which dowel. materials/examples: isometric dot/grid paper, patent illustrations, self-assembly instructions. application: good choice when you need a 3d pictorial view that can still be measured or scaled accurately — ideal for technical/engineering drawings, patent illustrations and self-assembly instructions. 4. orthographic projection definition: a set of separate, related 2d views — typically front, plan (top) and side elevation — each looking straight along one axis with no perspective distortion. combined with dimension lines, hidden-detail lines and a title block, it communicates precise dimensions a single pictorial view cannot show. context: before a building can be submitted for planning permission, an architect must supply a full orthographic set — plan, elevations and sections — because a single 3d render cannot specify wall thicknesses or window positions with the precision a contractor requires. materials/examples: dimension lines, hidden-detail lines, title blocks, scale rulers, cad drawing sheets. application: good choice when a part or building must be manufactured or constructed to an exact dimension or tolerance — the industry-standard language between designer and manufacturer. 5. assembly drawings definition: a drawing showing how the individual components of a product fit together in their final, joined position, usually alongside a numbered parts list (bill of materials) that references each component. context: aircraft maintenance technicians work from assembly drawings to confirm that a replacement part has been correctly fitted and orientated before an aircraft is certified airworthy again. materials/examples: numbered bill of materials (bom), joined-position cad views. application: good choice when a technician needs to check that parts are correctly located, orientated and fastened relative to each other in the finished product. 6. exploded drawings definition: a drawing that separates the components of a product along an axis while keeping them in their correct relative position and order, usually with numbered call-outs and dashed lines showing the direction of assembly. context: lego and ikea instructions are almost entirely exploded drawings, and repair sites such as ifixit use them in teardown guides so a customer can order the exact numbered spare part they need. materials/examples: numbered call-outs, dashed assembly-direction lines. application: good choice when a non-expert needs to assemble, disassemble or identify spare parts for a product without formal drawing-reading training. practical engagement: phone stand drawing set using isometric dot paper and a simple object (e.g. a phone stand made of 3 parts): sketch it in isometric. produce a 2-view orthographic (front + side) of the same object, with dimensions. draw an exploded view with a numbered parts list. debrief: which drawing would you send to a cnc machinist? which to a customer? why? this directly rehearses the "good choice when..." exam skill. drawing type what it shows best audience / use 2d drawing a single flat plane, using standardized symbols and conventions. technically trained audiences needing precise dimensions or symbols (electricians, machinists). 3d model / drawing depth and volume on a flat page or screen. non-technical stakeholders judging overall form and proportion. isometric drawing 3d pictorial view on three 120° axes, true to scale. technical/patent illustrations and self-assembly instructions that must still be measurable. orthographic projection related front/plan/side 2d views with no perspective distortion. manufacture or construction to an exact dimension or tolerance. assembly drawing components shown in their final, joined position with a parts list. checking parts are correctly located and fastened in the finished product. exploded drawing components separated along an axis but kept in correct relative order. non-experts assembling, disassembling or ordering spare parts. b2.2.2 physical prototypes ~60 min lesson 2: physical prototypes a physical prototype is a tangible, three-dimensional object built to test an idea — and unlike a drawing or digital model, it can be picked up, operated, worn or dropped. that physicality lets designers and users evaluate things a drawing never can: ergonomics, weight, texture, assembly, real mechanical performance. physical prototypes are built at different levels of fidelity (how closely they resemble the finished product) depending on what question they are trying to answer. hook: five days to redesign a shopping cart watch the clip below. note the exact moment the ideo team stops talking about ideas and starts building something rough with their hands — that moment is the whole point of low-fidelity prototyping. watch: abc nightline — ideo shopping cart . levels of fidelity 1. low-fidelity prototypes definition: quick, cheap and simple models — often made from paper, card, foam board or tape — used early in the design process to test a basic concept or a user's first interaction with an idea, before any time is invested in materials, finish or mechanism. context: in their famous 1999 project for abc nightline, ideo redesigned the supermarket shopping cart in five days. on day one, engineers built a rough cardboard, foam and wire mock-up purely to test whether a basket-swap concept even worked — long before anyone worried about colour, material or manufacturing. materials/examples: paper, card, foam board, tape. application: use early, when speed and low cost matter more than realism, to test whether a concept works at all. 2. high-fidelity prototypes definition: detailed versions that closely resemble the final product in look, feel and functionality. because they are expensive and time-consuming to build, they are used later — for advanced user testing, investor pitches, or final stakeholder sign-off before committing to mass-production tooling. context: smartphone manufacturers cnc-machine aluminium "unibody" prototypes that are visually and dimensionally identical to the production model, so designers can test in-hand feel, button travel and weight distribution before committing to expensive injection-mould tooling. materials/examples: cnc-machined final-grade materials, working electronics, near-final finishes. application: use later, when you need to test performance, finish or gain formal approval from a stakeholder who needs to see (almost) the real thing. types of physical models 3. aesthetic prototypes definition: models that focus only on visual appearance — form, proportion, colour and surface finish — without functioning like the final product internally. context: automotive studios (ford, bmw, tesla) still hand-sculpt full-size clay "aesthetic" models of new car bodies, because designers can judge how light reflects across a curved surface far more accurately on a physical clay form than on a screen render. materials/examples: clay, foam, paint, surface-finish samples. application: choose to test look, branding or marketing reaction. 4. functional prototypes definition: working models built to test mechanics, interactions and performance, even if they don't look anything like the finished product. context: a company developing a robotic prosthetic hand will 3d print an ugly, exposed functional prototype of just the gripping mechanism to test grip strength and object recognition, long before any cosmetic skin covering is designed. materials/examples: 3d-printed mechanisms, breadboard electronics, exposed working parts. application: choose to test engineering performance. 5. scale models definition: models built larger or smaller than the real object to visualise spatial relationships for products that are too large or too small to prototype at final size. context: a 1:100 scale architectural model lets a planning committee understand a building's relationship to its street before a single brick is laid, while automotive engineers test 25% scale car models in a wind tunnel because a full-size rolling-road test is vastly more expensive. materials/examples: architectural scale models, wind-tunnel test models. application: choose when the true size of the product makes full-size testing impractical or too costly. practical engagement: the coffee cup carrier challenge in teams, use identical basic materials (card, tape, foam, string) and 15 minutes to build a low-fidelity prototype of a device to carry three coffee cups one-handed. test each prototype live, then discuss as a class: what did this rough model let us learn cheaply that we could never have learned from a drawing alone? follow with the ideo shopping-cart video above as a professional case study of the same principle. model type focus good choice when... low-fidelity speed and low cost over realism. testing whether a basic concept works at all, early in the process. high-fidelity realism in look, feel and function. advanced user testing, investor pitches or final sign-off. aesthetic visual appearance only. testing look, branding and marketing reaction. functional mechanics, interaction and performance. testing engineering performance. scale model spatial relationships at a different size. product is too large or small to test at final size. b2.2.3 computer-aided design (cad) ~60 min lesson 3: computer-aided design (cad) cad is the use of computer software (e.g. solidworks, fusion 360, rhino, sketchup) to visualise, modify and analyse a design before committing to physical production. unlike a physical prototype, a cad file can be changed in seconds, shared instantly across the world, measured with perfect precision, and fed directly into manufacturing (cam) or simulation (fea) software. cad models exist at different levels of geometric detail, and choosing the right one depends on what you need the model to do. 1. wireframe models definition: the least detailed cad models, representing an object using only lines and curves along its edges — essentially a see-through "skeleton" with no surfaces or volume. context: a designer sketching the very first digital concept of a new car's silhouette will often start with wireframe curves to check overall proportion and stance before any surface is applied — the file is tiny and every curve can be reshaped instantly. materials/examples: edge curves only, no surfaces — the lightest possible cad file. application: good for the earliest concept stage and checking basic proportion — but a wireframe cannot be 3d printed, rendered realistically, or used to calculate volume or mass. 2. surface models definition: models that define only the outer "skin" or contours of an object, creating photorealistic images with no data about internal mass or structure — like a hollow shell with zero wall thickness. context: car stylists use high-end surface modelling ("class-a surfacing") to perfect the exact curvature of exterior body panels for a photorealistic marketing render — long before the engineering team has finalised the load-bearing structure hidden underneath. materials/examples: nurbs surfaces, class-a surfacing software. application: good when visual appearance or a marketing/kickstarter image matters more than manufacturability at that stage — but with no defined volume, a surface model cannot be used for fea, mass/cost calculation, or most cnc/3d-printing workflows. 3. solid models definition: complete 3d representations that define both the outer and inner surfaces (the full volume) of an object, so software can calculate mass, volume, centre of gravity and material cost. most professional engineering cad (feature-based, parametric modelling — extrude, revolve, fillet) works this way, and the solid model is normally the "master" file for detailed engineering, fea and manufacturing. context: an engineer designing an injection-moulded plastic enclosure builds it as a solid model so the software can instantly report wall thickness, material volume and cost — and the exact same file exports straight into an fea stress simulation and into the cnc toolpath software that cuts the mould. materials/examples: feature-based parametric operations — extrude, revolve, fillet. application: essential whenever a design will be manufactured, simulated (fea) or costed by material volume. practical engagement: wireframe → surface → solid using free cad software (e.g. tinkercad or fusion 360), build the same simple bracket first as basic sketch geometry (wireframe-like), then loft/extrude it into a solid. try to get a mass/volume readout at each stage and note when it becomes possible — this makes the wireframe → surface → solid progression concrete rather than abstract. cad model detail level can it calculate mass/volume? typical use wireframe edges (lines/curves) only. no earliest concept stage, checking proportion. surface outer "skin," zero wall thickness. no photorealistic renders, marketing, class-a surfacing. solid full internal + external volume. yes engineering, fea, cnc/3d-printing, costing. b2.2.4 finite element analysis (fea) ~60 min lesson 4: finite element analysis (fea) fea is a digital simulation tool that predicts how a part or assembly will perform under real-world physical conditions — stress, heat, vibration, airflow — without building it. the software divides ("discretizes") a solid cad model into thousands of small connected elements (a mesh), applies the loads and constraints a designer specifies, and calculates the resulting stress, strain and deformation across every element. hook: simulating before you build watch the clip below, then answer: what does fea let an engineer find out about a part before a single physical prototype has been built? watch: what is finite element analysis (fea)? explained simply . 1. benefits of fea definition: fea reduces the need for expensive, time-consuming physical prototypes and destructive testing, identifies failure points early — while changes are still cheap — and supports sustainable design by revealing exactly where material can be safely removed without compromising strength (lightweighting). context: formula 1 teams run fea on every carbon-fibre wishbone and chassis component before it is ever machined, because physically building and crash-testing a real part is vastly more expensive than simulating it first. materials/examples: mesh density settings, applied loads and constraints, material property data. application: use when a part's structural or thermal performance needs to be predicted and optimised before committing to expensive tooling or materials. 2. interpreting the results definition: fea results are usually displayed as a colour-coded stress map. as a general convention, red indicates areas of high stress and greatest risk of failure (often at corners, holes or sudden changes in cross-section), while blue indicates low stress, meaning that area is "over-engineered" and a candidate for material reduction. context: it is essential to read the map against its numerical scale bar rather than judging colour alone, and to remember that fea is only as accurate as its mesh density, material data and assumed loads — real designers still validate fea predictions with a small number of physical prototype tests rather than trusting simulation blindly. materials/examples: colour-coded stress maps, numerical scale bars. application: use when a design needs to be made lighter or more sustainable without an expensive trial-and-error cycle of physical prototypes. case study: ge aviation's 80% lighter bracket ge aviation used fea-guided topology optimization to redesign a jet engine bracket, removing material from every low-stress ("blue") region the simulation identified while keeping the high-stress ("red") load paths intact — the result was roughly 80% lighter than the original while meeting the same strength requirements, directly cutting fuel burn and material use. practical engagement: read the stress map look at a simple cantilever bracket stress-map image (search "fea stress map bracket" or use a free fusion 360 simulation study). identify the red zones, the blue zones, and propose one specific change to the geometry that would reduce weight while keeping the red zones intact — connect this explicitly to sustainability and material efficiency. b2.2.5 rapid prototyping effectiveness ~90 min lesson 5: rapid prototyping effectiveness rapid prototyping (rp) covers manufacturing techniques that build a physical object quickly and directly from a digital cad file, layer by layer, without the moulds, jigs or tooling that traditional manufacturing requires. this is why rp is so effective at low volumes: it allows highly complex geometries impossible to machine (such as internal lattices) and lets designers iterate a physical model overnight instead of waiting weeks for tooling. 1. fused deposition modelling (fdm) definition: works by melting a thermoplastic filament (commonly pla, abs or petg) and extruding it through a heated nozzle, building the object layer by layer. context: desktop fdm printers are the workhorse of school workshops and product design studios worldwide because they are cheap to run — nasa has even sent an fdm printer to the international space station so astronauts can print replacement tools on demand instead of waiting months for a resupply launch. materials/examples: pla, abs, petg thermoplastic filament. application: good choice when you need a cheap, fast, reasonably strong functional prototype and can accept visible layer lines and lower dimensional accuracy. 2. stereolithography (sla) definition: uses a uv laser to selectively cure liquid photopolymer resin in a vat into a solid object, layer by layer, producing very high detail and a smooth surface finish. context: jewellery designers 3d-print a wax-like castable resin "former" using sla, then use the traditional lost-wax casting process to cast the exact same intricate form in silver or gold. dental labs use the same resin-printing principle to produce precise models for clear aligners such as invisalign. materials/examples: liquid photopolymer resin, uv laser. application: good choice when fine surface detail and a smooth finish are critical — jewellery, dental models, miniatures — and the part does not need high mechanical strength. 3. selective laser sintering (sls) definition: uses a high-power laser to fuse small particles of powder (typically nylon plastic, or metal powder in the related dmls process) into a solid 3d object. because the surrounding unfused powder itself supports the part during printing, no support structures are needed, allowing complex internal geometry and lattices that other processes cannot produce. context: spacex and relativity space 3d-print entire rocket engines from metal powder using laser-sintering processes, embedding internal cooling channels that would be impossible to machine conventionally, while functional nylon sls parts are widely used for custom prosthetic sockets and drone components. materials/examples: nylon powder, metal powder (dmls). application: good choice when a strong, functional, end-use part with complex internal geometry is needed and support-free printing is an advantage — at a higher equipment cost than fdm or sla. fdm sla sls process melted filament extruded layer by layer uv laser cures liquid resin in a vat laser fuses powdered material (plastic or metal) typical use cheap functional prototypes, jigs, classroom use high-detail aesthetic/dental/jewellery patterns strong end-use functional parts, complex geometry surface finish visible layer lines smooth, highly detailed slightly grainy/porous relative cost low medium high support needed? yes, for overhangs yes, for overhangs no — powder bed self-supports read: fdm vs. sla vs. sls: 3d printing technology comparison (formlabs) . practical engagement: card-sort — match the process given six short product briefs (e.g. "a smooth wax pattern for a gold ring," "a cheap prototype bracket for a school project," "a strong drone arm with an internal lattice to save weight"), match each to fdm, sla or sls, justifying your choice using the comparison table above. this rehearses exactly the "apply the rule to a specific context" ao2 skill used in ib exam questions. b2.2.6 data and feedback ~60 min lesson 6: data, feedback and stakeholder communication a prototype is only useful if it generates data that improves the next version. designers rely on a continuous model → test → refine cycle: build a version, test it against real users or real physical conditions, collect data (both quantitative, such as load-test results or task-completion times, and qualitative, such as user comfort or aesthetic preference), and use that evidence to refine the design before the next iteration. this cycle is what the syllabus term iterative design describes, and it repeats — sometimes hundreds of times — until the final product meets the design specification. 1. the model → test → refine cycle definition: an iterative loop in which designers build a version, test it against real users or physical conditions, collect quantitative and qualitative data, and use that evidence to refine the design before the next iteration. context: sir james dyson built and tested 5,127 prototypes of his cyclone vacuum cleaner separator over five years, measuring dust-separation performance at every stage and refining the geometry based on that data until it out-performed every bagged vacuum on the market. materials/examples: load-test results, task-completion times (quantitative); user comfort or aesthetic preference (qualitative). application: repeats until the final product meets the design specification — this cycle is the syllabus term iterative design. 2. stakeholder communication definition: non-technical stakeholders — clients, investors, everyday users — usually cannot read an orthographic drawing or interpret an fea stress map. presenting a physical or high-quality visual model instead lets these audiences understand shape, proportion, colour and use almost instantly, which is essential for gathering honest, useful feedback and for winning approval or investment. context: crowdfunding campaigns on kickstarter succeed or fail largely on rendered cad images and short functional-prototype demo videos, not technical drawings, because backers are consumers, not engineers — while an architect presenting to a client will often bring a physical scale model into the room alongside renders, because clients read spatial relationships far more easily in a model they can walk around than in a stack of construction drawings. materials/examples: rendered cad images, demo videos, physical scale models. application: choose the model or drawing type to match the audience — technical language and orthographic drawings for engineers, physical models and everyday language for customers. practical engagement: explain it twice role-play in pairs: one student is the "designer" and must explain the same design change twice — once to a "manufacturing engineer" partner (using technical/orthographic language) and once to a "customer" partner (using a physical model or render and everyday language). debrief on how and why the communication method changed for each stakeholder. linking questions use these to bridge b2.2 to other parts of the syllabus stages of the design process? b1.1 user-centred design: why must the choice of model or prototype type be driven by the needs of the user or stakeholder being tested? b3.3 mechanical systems — application and selection: how can fea and functional prototyping be used to validate the performance of a mechanical system before manufacture? c4.1 design for manufacture: how does the choice between rapid prototyping methods (fdm, sla, sls) anticipate the demands of full-scale manufacture? b2.2 exam practice ao1 / ao2 / ao3 exam practice: topic b2.2 the following questions are written in the style of ib dp design technology paper 1 and paper 2, following the command-term logic in cracking the command terms (ao1 knowledge, ao2 application, ao3 synthesis). a short stimulus is provided below; use it to anchor the short-answer and long-answer questions, as the real ib papers do. stimulus traillight is a small design company developing a collapsible, solar-powered camping lantern for backpackers. early in development the team built a rough card-and-tape mock-up of the folding mechanism. mid-way through development, the folding hinge bracket was modelled as a cad solid model and fea tested; the stress map showed a red (high-stress) zone at the hinge pin hole and a large blue (low-stress) zone across the flat base plate. for the final investor pitch, the team produced a high-fidelity, fully working prototype and a set of orthographic manufacturing drawings for their factory in china. section a: multiple choice (ao1) question 1 [1 mark] what is the correct rapid prototyping technique for creating a smooth, castable wax-style pattern for jewellery? fused deposition modelling (fdm) stereolithography (sla) selective laser sintering (sls) of metal powder computer numerical control (cnc) milling command term focus: identify — a simple, direct selection task with no reasoning required. reveal answer b. stereolithography (sla), chosen for its smooth, highly detailed surface finish suited to fine jewellery patterns. [1] question 2 [1 mark] on the fea stress map of traillight's hinge bracket, the red zone at the hinge pin hole indicates: an area of low stress and excess material an area of high stress and risk of failure the exact location the part will be 3d printed an area with no load applied command term focus: identify — recognising a standard convention from the description given. reveal answer b. red conventionally indicates high stress concentration and greatest risk of failure. [1] question 3 [1 mark] which cad model type contains no data about a part's internal mass or volume, and therefore cannot be used to calculate weight or run an fea simulation? wireframe model surface model solid model assembly model command term focus: identify — matching a cad model type to its defining property. reveal answer b. a surface model defines only the outer "skin" of the object, with zero internal volume data. [1] section b: short answer (ao1 / ao2) question 4 [2 marks] outline one reason why traillight's design team built a low-fidelity card-and-tape mock-up before developing the cad solid model of the folding mechanism. command term focus: outline — a brief account combining a feature with its benefit. reveal answer a low-fidelity mock-up is quick and cheap to build (1) , which lets the team test whether the basic folding concept and user interaction works before investing time and money in a detailed, accurate cad model (1) . question 5 [3 marks] explain how the fea results described in the stimulus could support more sustainable design of the hinge bracket. command term focus: explain — a three-step logic chain (a → b → c). reveal answer the fea stress map shows a large blue, low-stress zone across the base plate (a) (1) ; because this material is barely loaded, the designer can remove or thin material from that region without weakening the part (b) (1) ; this reduces the mass of plastic or metal used per lantern, lowering material cost and the product's overall environmental footprint (c) (1) . section c: long answer (ao2 / ao3) question 6 [6 marks] justify traillight's decision to produce a high-fidelity prototype and a set of orthographic manufacturing drawings for the investor pitch and factory handover, rather than relying on the early low-fidelity mock-up. command term focus: justify — give valid evidence linking a physical feature to a higher-order goal (e.g. cost, sustainability, stakeholder need). reveal answer structure: for each audience — identify the stakeholder + identify what they need to see/do + explain why the earlier model type could not meet that need + connective linking to outcome. investors need to judge whether the finished product will look, feel and function like a market-ready item before committing funding (1) ; the low-fidelity card mock-up could never demonstrate real material finish, working electronics or genuine user experience, so only a high-fidelity prototype can convincingly secure investment (1–2) . separately, the factory in china needs exact, toleranced dimensions to manufacture interchangeable parts at scale (1) ; orthographic drawings — unlike a pictorial mock-up — communicate precise, measurable dimensions and hidden detail using an internationally standardised convention that the factory's machinists and quality-control staff can read without ambiguity (1–2) , reducing costly manufacturing errors (1) . question 7 [8 marks] evaluate traillight's use of selective laser sintering (sls) instead of fused deposition modelling (fdm) if they decide to 3d-print the final hinge bracket in low-volume production, and design one improvement to their prototyping process for the next product iteration. command term focus: evaluate — weigh advantages against disadvantages and reach a justified conclusion; may extend to design (identify a weakness and propose an innovation). reveal answer structure: advantage(s) of sls + disadvantage(s)/trade-off + comparison to fdm + justified conclusion, then one specific, innovative process improvement. sls produces stronger, functional end-use parts with no need for support structures, allowing the complex internal geometry an optimised hinge bracket might need after fea-guided lightweighting (advantage); however, sls equipment and material costs are significantly higher than fdm, and the slightly grainier surface finish may need secondary finishing for a consumer product (disadvantage). because the hinge bracket is a structurally critical part rather than a purely cosmetic one, the extra cost of sls is justified by its superior mechanical performance for this specific component, whereas fdm remains the better (cheaper, faster) choice for early concept iterations (justified conclusion). improvement: traillight could introduce an intermediate fea-validated functional prototype stage — printing the optimised geometry in cheap fdm first purely to physically validate the fea prediction before committing to a costlier sls production run, catching any simulation-to-reality gap earlier and more cheaply. b2.2 glossary glossary: title: Material selection

sections.title: Lesson 1: Properties
sections.html:
3.1.1 Properties 1 Hour

Lesson 1: Properties

Lesson Objective 3.1.1

Materials are selected for specific applications based on their properties. Students must be able to identify appropriate materials based on their physical, chemical and mechanical properties.

Hook: The O-Ring Failure

In 1986, the Space Shuttle Challenger disintegrated shortly after launch. The cause was traced back to a single rubber O-ring that failed.

The Science: The launch day was unusually cold. The material lost its elasticity and became brittle in the low temperatures, failing to seal the joint.

Key Lesson: Materials must be selected for specific environmental conditions.

Decoding the Data: Young's Modulus

One of the most critical distinctions in engineering is between Strength and Stiffness.

  • Young’s Modulus (Stiffness): Measures how much a material stretches under load.
  • High Modulus: Steel. It is stiff.
  • Low Modulus: Rubber. It is stretchy.

Case Study: The Formula 1 Monocoque

The Challenge
Protect the driver (High compressive strength) but weigh almost nothing.
The Selection
Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP).
The Why?
Incredible strength-to-weight ratio. Steel is too heavy; Aluminum isn't strong enough per gram.

Deep Dive: The Racing Bicycle Frame

Context: A designer needs a frame that is lightweight (for speed) but stiff (for power transfer).

  • Steel: High tensile strength, durable, but heavy. High Young's Modulus.
  • Aluminium (6061): Lightweight, cheaper, but lower fatigue limit (can crack over time).
  • Carbon Fibre: Extremely high strength-to-weight ratio, anisotropic (strength in specific directions), expensive.

Justification: Carbon fibre is selected despite the cost (3.1.3) because the mechanical properties (Young's Modulus/Weight ratio) are critical for racing.

Activity: The Modulus Match

Decide if the application requires a High or Low Young's Modulus. Click to reveal the answer.

A Diving Board

Reveal Answer
Low Modulus
Needs to bend and return energy (Fiberglass).

A Skyscraper Beam

Reveal Answer
High Modulus
Must not bend under load (Steel).

A Car Bumper

Reveal Answer
Low Modulus
Needs to absorb minor impact (Polymer).

A Bungee Cord

Reveal Answer
Low Modulus
Needs extreme elasticity to stretch (Rubber).

Smartphone Screen

Reveal Answer
High Modulus
Must be rigid and scratch resistant (Glass).

Aircraft Wing Spar

Reveal Answer
High Modulus
Must resist bending during flight (Aluminium).

sections.title: Lesson 2: Aesthetic Characteristics
sections.html:
3.1.2 Aesthetic 1 Hour

Lesson 2: Aesthetic Characteristics

Lesson Objective 3.1.2

Materials are selected for specific applications based on their aesthetic characteristics. Students must be able to identify appropriate materials based on texture, form and colour, which can also be enhanced by using a variety of finishing techniques.

Hook: Apple vs. The Rest

Pass around a plastic laptop and an aluminium MacBook. Ask: Why does the metal feel "premium"?

It's not just the look. Thermal conductivity makes the metal feel cool to the touch. Rigidity makes it feel solid. These are physical properties creating an aesthetic perception.

The Language of Aesthetics

Aesthetic properties describe the visual, tactile, and sensory characteristics that influence user preference.

Property Physical Factors Explanation Design Application
Color Light absorption/reflection, Pigment chemistry. The specific wavelength of light reflected. Critical for branding and signaling. Calming blue for medical devices; High-vis red for safety gear.
Luster / Gloss Refractive index, Surface smoothness. Interaction with light. Ranges from Matte (dull) to High Gloss (reflective). High-gloss car exteriors (premium) vs. Matte dashboards (anti-glare).
Texture Surface roughness, Manufacturing process. The perceived feel (visual or tactile). Soft-touch coating on phones for grip; Brushed metal for industrial look.
Transparency Light transmission, Scattering. Transparent (clear), Translucent (diffused), or Opaque (blocked). Glass windows vs. Translucent plastic light diffusers.
Tactility Thermal conductivity, Friction, Hardness. How it feels: Warm/Cool, Slick/Sticky. Wood (warm) handles vs. Stainless steel (cool) fixtures.
Form Malleability, Ductility, Plasticity. Ability to hold specific geometric shapes. Glass blown into curves; Carbon fiber formed into aerodynamic shapes.
Sound Acoustic properties, Density, Damping. Auditory feedback when struck. A car door closing with a solid "thunk" conveys quality.
Aerospace

The dark color of Carbon Fiber isn't paint; it's the material's identity, symbolizing max strength/min weight.

Medical

Smooth textures are vital for sterilization, but colors must be non-threatening to patients.

Automotive

Paint gloss is controlled not just for looks but for UV durability.

Case Study: The Alessi "Bird" Kettle

Designed by Michael Graves, this is a kitchen icon.

Material Clash:

  • Body: Polished Stainless Steel. Feels Industrial, Clean, Reflective.
  • Whistle: PA Plastic Bird. Feels Playful, Colorful, Tactile.

Analysis: The material choice dictates the personality of the product.

Activity: Mood Boarding

Create a Moodboard for a lunchbox for the following clients. Focus on texture, form, and colour.

Business CEO

Sophisticated, Premium.

Construction Worker

Rugged, Durable.

Toddler

Playful, Safe.

Minimalist Salary Woman

Clean, Eco-conscious.

sections.title: Lesson 3: C.A.S. (Cost, Availability, Sustainability)
sections.html:
3.1.3 Context 1 Hour

Lesson 3: C.A.S. (Cost, Availability, Sustainability)

Lesson Objective 3.1.3

Additional factors influence the selection and application of materials in a specific context. Students must be able identify appropriate materials based on cost, availability and sustainability.

1. Cost

Definition: The total financial expenditure required to acquire, process, and maintain a material throughout its lifecycle (Initial Cost + Life-Cycle Cost).

Context: Engineers must ensure profitability. High-performance materials are often skipped for "good enough" materials to keep the product affordable.

Example: In low-cost housing, Concrete Blocks are selected over Cut Stone due to significantly lower labor and material costs.

2. Availability

Definition: The ease with which a material can be sourced, transported, and supplied consistently.

Context: Supply chains and geography dictate availability. A material might be cheap in one country but impossible to get in another.

Example: Timber is primary in Scandinavia (locally abundant), whereas desert regions like the UAE rely on Steel and Concrete.

3. Sustainability

Definition: Environmental impact, carbon footprint, "Embodied Energy", and recyclability.

Context: Legislation and consumer demand drive the Circular Economy.

Example: Recycled Aluminum requires only 5% of the energy to produce compared to Virgin Aluminum.

The "Material Selection Triangle"

These three factors are interconnected:

  • Sustainability vs. Cost: Sustainable materials (like Mycelium) often cost more due to lack of scale, but may save on waste taxes.
  • Availability vs. Sustainability: Transporting "green" Bamboo globally increases its carbon footprint (Embodied Energy).
  • Cost vs. Availability: Scarcity (Low Availability) causes Price Spikes (High Cost).

Student Activity: The Triple Constraint Challenge

Scenario: Design a High-Volume Shipping Crate for fragile electronics.

Phase 2: The 3-Way Pivot
Option A: Budget King

Priority: COST

Option B: Local Hero

Priority: AVAILABILITY (100-mile radius)

Option C: Eco-Warrior

Priority: SUSTAINABILITY

Phase 3: The Justification Matrix
Priority Primary Material The "Big Trade-off" (Sacrifice)
Cost Low-grade Plastic Low durability; high environmental waste.
Availability Local Timber Higher Density increases shipping fuel costs.
Sustainability Mycelium High Cost; limited production speed.

Animation of a balancing act representing trade-offs.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Primary and Secondary Research
sections.html:
3.1.4 Research 1 Hour

Lesson 4: Primary and Secondary Research

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the difference between primary and secondary research methods in the context of material selection.
  • Justify material choices using Primary and Secondary research.

1. Secondary Research (The "Desktop" Phase)

Definition: Gathering information that already exists. This is usually the first step in the design process to create a shortlist of potential materials.

Context & Methods

In industry, engineers don't test every single material from scratch. They look up data sheets to find materials that theoretically fit the criteria.

Material Databases (e.g., MatWeb, CES EduPack)

Software that allows you to filter materials by property (e.g., "Show me all metals with a melting point above 1000°C").

Ashby Charts

Visual graphs that compare two properties, like Strength vs. Density. This helps spot the best "compromise" material.

Supplier Data Sheets

PDFs provided by manufacturers detailing the exact chemical composition and limits of a specific alloy.

Case Studies

Looking at what competitors use. If 90% of car engines are made of Aluminum alloys, that is strong secondary evidence.

Industry Application: Camping Stove

Example: A designer creating a new Camping Stove.

  • Action: They consult a database to find metals with high Thermal Conductivity and high Melting Points.
  • Result: The research eliminates wood and plastic immediately. It highlights Copper, Aluminum, and Titanium.
  • Justification: "Secondary research confirms that Titanium offers the best strength-to-weight ratio compared to steel, which is critical for hiking portability."

2. Primary Research (The "Hands-On" Phase)

Definition: Generating new data yourself through experiments, testing, or user feedback. This is used to verify the shortlist from your secondary research.

Context & Methods

Data sheets are perfect "in theory," but they don't tell you how a material feels, how it looks when painted, or how it reacts to a specific glue.

Destructive Testing

Applying force until the material breaks.

  • Tensile Testing: Pulling it apart to measure elasticity and ultimate strength.
  • Impact Testing: Hitting it (e.g., Izod test) to measure toughness/brittleness.
Non-Destructive Testing

Measuring without damaging.

  • Visual/Tactile Check: Does it feel "cheap"? Is it too heavy?
  • Hardness Test: Pressing a diamond tip into the surface.
  • User Trials: Giving a prototype to a user to see if it gets hot or slippery.

Industry Application: Camping Stove (Continued)

Example: The same designer with the Camping Stove.

  • Action: They narrow it down to Aluminum (Cheap) and Titanium (Expensive). They buy a sample of both and boil water in them.
  • Result: They find that the thin Aluminum wall dents easily when dropped on a rock (Impact Test), whereas the Titanium scratches but holds its shape.
  • Justification: "Primary testing revealed that while Aluminum was lighter, it failed the impact test simulating a drop on rocks. Therefore, Titanium is selected for the 'Pro' model."

3. How to Structure a Material Justification

When students are asked to "justify" their choice, they should follow this formula:

Claim + Evidence (Primary/Secondary) + Reasoning
Component Explanation Example
The Claim What material did you pick? "I selected ABS Plastic for the vacuum cleaner casing."
Evidence (Secondary) What does the book say? "MatWeb data indicates ABS has high impact resistance and can be injection molded."
Evidence (Primary) What did you find out? "My scratch test showed ABS resisted wear better than HIPS (Polystyrene) when dragged on concrete."
The Reasoning Why does this matter? "Since vacuums often bang into furniture, high impact resistance is more important than the lower cost of HIPS."

4. Student Activity: "The Material Showdown"

Objective: Students must select the best material for a School Cafeteria Tray.

Constraints: Must be durable, easy to clean, lightweight, and cheap.

Step 1: Secondary Research (20 mins)
  • Search online for "common plastic properties."
  • Find Density, Cost, and Melting Point for: Polypropylene (PP), Acrylic, and Polycarbonate.
  • Output: A comparison table.
Step 2: Primary Research (30 mins)
  • Provide samples of these three plastics.
  • Test A (The Scratch Test): Use a key/sandpaper (Hygiene factor).
  • Test B (The Drop Test): Drop from table height (Durability factor).
  • Test C (The Bend Test): Flex them. Does it snap?
Step 3: The Justification

Write a paragraph justifying your choice through primary and secondary research.

Summary of Differences

Feature Secondary Research Primary Research
Source Books, Internet, Standards (ISO). Experiments, Surveys, Observations.
Cost/Time Low cost, fast. High cost, time-consuming.
Purpose To narrow down options (Screening). To verify performance (Validation).
Reliability General (might not apply to your specific use). Specific (applies exactly to your prototype).

4. Student Activity: "The Material Showdown"

Objective: Students must select the best material for a School Cafeteria Tray.

Constraints: Must be durable, easy to clean, lightweight, and cheap.

Step 1: Secondary Research (20 mins)
  • Search online for "common plastic properties."
  • Find Density, Cost, and Melting Point for: Polypropylene (PP), Acrylic, and Polycarbonate.
  • Output: A comparison table.
Step 2: Primary Research (30 mins)
  • Provide samples of these three plastics.
  • Test A (The Scratch Test): Use a key/sandpaper (Hygiene factor).
  • Test B (The Drop Test): Drop from table height (Durability factor).
  • Test C (The Bend Test): Flex them. Does it snap?
Step 3: The Justification

Write a paragraph justifying your choice through primary and secondary research.

sections.html:
Exam Preparation

Practice questions typical of IB Design Technology Paper 1 and 2.

Q1. Define "Young's Modulus".
Indicative answer · reveal after attempting

Young's Modulus is a measure of the stiffness of a solid material. It defines the relationship between stress (force per unit area) and strain (proportional deformation) in a material in the linear elastic regime of a uniaxial deformation.

Q2. Explain why a designer might choose ABS plastic over Timber for a hairdryer casing.
Indicative answer · reveal after attempting

Form: ABS can be injection molded into complex shapes.
Properties: ABS is electrically insulating and heat resistant.
Cost: High volume production makes injection molding cheaper per unit.

sections.title: Young’s modulus engineering quiz — repaired practice
sections.html:
Young’s modulus engineering quiz

Adapted classroom practice. Missing numeric values from the original have been replaced with explicit data. Question 3 now states sample values because composite stiffness depends on direction and construction.

Question 1

A titanium-alloy sample experiences a stress of 400 MPa and a strain of 0.004. Calculate its Young’s modulus.

  1. $100\text{ GPa}$
  2. $10\text{ GPa}$
  3. $160\text{ GPa}$
  4. $1000\text{ GPa}$
Hint

Remember the formula $E = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}$ and that $1\text{ GPa} = 1000\text{ MPa}$.

Answer and rationale

Option A. E = stress / strain = 400 MPa / 0.004 = 100,000 MPa = 100 GPa.

Question 2

You are designing a suspension bridge and need to select a material for the main suspension cables. You are given four materials with the following Young's Modulus values. Which is the most appropriate choice to support massive static loads without significant stretching?

  1. $0.1\text{ GPa}$
  2. $2.0\text{ GPa}$
  3. $70\text{ GPa}$
  4. $210\text{ GPa}$
Hint

Suspension cables must resist immense tension and maintain the structural geometry under heavy traffic.

Answer and rationale

Option D. This high value indicates immense stiffness (typical of structural steel), which is exactly what is needed to prevent the bridge deck from sagging.

Question 3

A supplied data table gives Young’s modulus values: steel 210 GPa; this carbon-fibre composite 150 GPa along its fibres; nylon 3 GPa; rubber 0.01 GPa. Which list orders these samples from highest to lowest modulus?

  1. Steel, Carbon Fiber, Nylon, Rubber
  2. Rubber, Nylon, Carbon Fiber, Steel
  3. Carbon Fiber, Steel, Rubber, Nylon
  4. Steel, Nylon, Carbon Fiber, Rubber
Hint

Think about which material would be hardest to stretch by hand versus which one stretches easily.

Answer and rationale

Option A. For these stated samples and loading direction: 210 > 150 > 3 > 0.01 GPa. Composite stiffness depends on fibre type, orientation and lay-up; this is not a universal ranking.

Question 4

On a standard stress-strain graph, Material X has a very steep linear slope, while Material Y has a very shallow linear slope. What does this indicate about the materials?

  1. Material X has a higher Young's Modulus and is stiffer than Material Y.
  2. Material X has a lower Young's Modulus and is more elastic than Material Y.
  3. Material Y requires more stress to produce the same amount of strain as Material X.
  4. Material Y has a higher Young's Modulus but lower overall strength than Material X.
Hint

The slope of the line in the elastic region of a stress-strain graph represents the material's stiffness.

Answer and rationale

Option A. A steep slope means it takes a large amount of stress to produce a small amount of strain, which is the definition of high stiffness.

Question 5

Why does a pole vaulting pole require a relatively low Young's Modulus compared to a structural column in a building?

  1. The pole needs to bend significantly to store and release elastic potential energy.
  2. The pole must resist all bending forces to maintain its structural integrity during the jump.
  3. A lower Young's Modulus ensures the pole is heavier and provides a better center of gravity.
  4. Structural columns need to be flexible to sway in the wind, whereas poles must be completely rigid.
Hint

Consider the functional purpose of the object: does it need to absorb and return energy, or simply support weight without moving?

Answer and rationale

Option A. A lower Young's Modulus allows the pole to deflect elastically under load and spring back, propelling the athlete.

Question 6

An aerospace engineer is looking at an Ashby chart plotting Young's Modulus on the vertical (Y) axis and Density on the horizontal (X) axis. If they are searching for a material for a drone wing that must be both exceptionally stiff and extremely lightweight, where should they look?

  1. Top-Left Quadrant
  2. Top-Right Quadrant
  3. Bottom-Left Quadrant
  4. Bottom-Right Quadrant
Hint

You want a high value on the vertical axis and a low value on the horizontal axis.

Answer and rationale

Option A. The top-left area contains materials with high values on the Y-axis (stiffness) and low values on the X-axis (weight).

Question 7

A cylindrical structural support has a cross-sectional area of $0.05\text{ m}^2$ and is subjected to a compressive force of $500,000\text{ N}$. What is the stress acting on the support?

  1. $10,000,000\text{ Pa}$
  2. $25,000\text{ Pa}$
  3. $1,000,000\text{ Pa}$
  4. $2,500,000\text{ Pa}$
Hint

The formula for stress is Force divided by Area ($\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$).

Answer and rationale

Option A. Stress is Force divided by Area (), which equals $10,000,000\text{ Pascals}$ ($10\text{ MPa}$).

Question 8

A highly elastic polymer band has an original resting length of $2.0\text{ meters}$. When stretched by a machine, it extends by an additional $0.5\text{ meters}$. What is the strain on the band?

  1. 0.25
  2. 4
  3. 0.5
  4. 2.5
Hint

Strain is the ratio of the change in length to the original length ($\epsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0}$).

Answer and rationale

Option A. Strain = extension / original length = 0.5 / 2.0 = 0.25. Strain is dimensionless.

Question 9

A wire with an original length of $10\text{ m}$ and a cross-sectional area of $0.0001\text{ m}^2$ is pulled with a force of $5,000\text{ N}$, causing it to stretch by $0.01\text{ m}$. What is the Young's Modulus of the wire?

  1. $50\text{ GPa}$
  2. $5\text{ GPa}$
  3. $500\text{ GPa}$
  4. $0.5\text{ GPa}$
Hint

First calculate stress (), then calculate strain ($\Delta L / L_0$), and finally divide stress by strain.

Answer and rationale

Option A. Stress = 5,000 / 0.0001 = 50,000,000 Pa. Strain = 0.01 / 10 = 0.001. E = 50,000,000 / 0.001 = 50,000,000,000 Pa = 50 GPa.

Question 10

A supplier states that a polymer has a Young’s modulus of 4.0 GPa. A test applies a stress of 20 MPa and records a strain of 0.008. Is the test sample stiffer or more flexible than claimed?

  1. More flexible, because the calculated Young's Modulus is $2.5\text{ GPa}$.
  2. Stiffer, because the calculated Young's Modulus is $5.0\text{ GPa}$.
  3. More flexible, because the calculated Young's Modulus is $6.0\text{ GPa}$.
  4. Stiffer, because the calculated Young's Modulus is $1.6\text{ GPa}$.
Hint

Calculate the actual Young's Modulus from the test data and compare it to the supplier's claim. A lower value indicates less stiffness.

Answer and rationale

Option A. The actual YM is $20\text{ MPa} / 0.008 = 2,500\text{ MPa}$ ($2.5\text{ GPa}$). Because this is lower than $4.0\text{ GPa}$, the material is more flexible.

options.rationale: A shallow slope actually means Material Y requires *less* stress to deform compared to Material X.

options.text: Material Y has a higher Young's Modulus but lower overall strength than Material X.
options.rationale: A shallow slope indicates a low Young's Modulus, not a high one.

sourceQuiz.hint: The slope of the line in the elastic region of a stress-strain graph represents the material's stiffness.

sourceQuiz.question: Why does a pole vaulting pole require a relatively low Young's Modulus compared to a structural column in a building?

options.text: The pole needs to bend significantly to store and release elastic potential energy.
options.rationale: A lower Young's Modulus allows the pole to deflect elastically under load and spring back, propelling the athlete.

options.text: The pole must resist all bending forces to maintain its structural integrity during the jump.
options.rationale: If it resisted all bending, it would behave like a rigid column and provide no upward spring for the vaulter.

options.text: A lower Young's Modulus ensures the pole is heavier and provides a better center of gravity.
options.rationale: Young's Modulus is a measure of stiffness, not density or weight.

options.text: Structural columns need to be flexible to sway in the wind, whereas poles must be completely rigid.
options.rationale: While buildings do sway slightly, a vaulting pole must be far more flexible than a primary structural column.

sourceQuiz.hint: Consider the functional purpose of the object: does it need to absorb and return energy, or simply support weight without moving?

sourceQuiz.question: An aerospace engineer is looking at an Ashby chart plotting Young's Modulus on the vertical (Y) axis and Density on the horizontal (X) axis. If they are searching for a material for a drone wing that must be both exceptionally stiff and extremely lightweight, where should they look?

options.rationale: The top-left area contains materials with high values on the Y-axis (stiffness) and low values on the X-axis (weight).
This quadrant would yield materials that are very stiff but also very heavy (high density).
Materials here would be lightweight, but also highly flexible (low stiffness), which would cause a wing to fold in flight.
This quadrant represents materials that are both extremely heavy and highly flexible, which is the opposite of what is needed.

sourceQuiz.hint: You want a high value on the vertical axis and a low value on the horizontal axis.

sourceQuiz.question: A cylindrical structural support has a cross-sectional area of $0.05\text{ m}^2$ and is subjected to a compressive force of $500,000\text{ N}$. What is the stress acting on the support?

options.rationale: Stress is Force divided by Area (), which equals $10,000,000\text{ Pascals}$ ($10\text{ MPa}$).
This would be the result if you multiplied the force by the area instead of dividing.
This implies a decimal error during the division calculation.
This implies a mathematical error likely related to misplacing a decimal point or using the wrong operation.

sourceQuiz.hint: The formula for stress is Force divided by Area ($\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$).

sourceQuiz.question: A highly elastic polymer band has an original resting length of $2.0\text{ meters}$. When stretched by a machine, it extends by an additional $0.5\text{ meters}$. What is the strain on the band?

options.rationale: Strain is the change in length divided by the original length (), which equals .
This is the result of dividing the original length by the extension, which is the inverse of the strain formula.
This is the value of the extension itself, but strain is a ratio of the extension to the original length.
This is the final length of the band, not the strain ratio.

sourceQuiz.hint: Strain is the ratio of the change in length to the original length ($\epsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0}$).

sourceQuiz.question: A wire with an original length of $10\text{ m}$ and a cross-sectional area of $0.0001\text{ m}^2$ is pulled with a force of $5,000\text{ N}$, causing it to stretch by $0.01\text{ m}$. What is the Young's Modulus of the wire?

options.rationale: Stress is $5,000 / 0.0001 = 50,000,000\text{ Pa}$. Strain is . Dividing Stress by Strain gives $50,000,000,000\text{ Pa}$, or $50\text{ GPa}$.
This points to a decimal error in calculating either the stress, the strain, or the final division.
This suggests a decimal place error, likely from improperly converting the raw Pascal value into Gigapascals.
This signifies a miscalculation in the strain ratio or a large unit conversion error.

sourceQuiz.hint: First calculate stress (), then calculate strain ($\Delta L / L_0$), and finally divide stress by strain.

sourceQuiz.question: A supplier guarantees their new polymer has a Young's Modulus of $4.0\text{ GPa}$. Your lab tests a sample, applying a stress of $20\text{ MPa}$ and recording a strain of . Based on these results, is the material stiffer or more flexible than claimed?

options.text: More flexible, because the calculated Young's Modulus is $2.5\text{ GPa}$.
options.rationale: The actual YM is $20\text{ MPa} / 0.008 = 2,500\text{ MPa}$ ($2.5\text{ GPa}$). Because this is lower than $4.0\text{ GPa}$, the material is more flexible.

options.text: Stiffer, because the calculated Young's Modulus is $5.0\text{ GPa}$.
options.rationale: This calculation is incorrect. If the YM were $5.0\text{ GPa}$, it would be stiffer, but the test data does not yield this result.

options.text: More flexible, because the calculated Young's Modulus is $6.0\text{ GPa}$.
options.rationale: A YM of $6.0\text{ GPa}$ would make the material stiffer than claimed, not more flexible, and the calculation is also incorrect.

options.text: Stiffer, because the calculated Young's Modulus is $1.6\text{ GPa}$.
options.rationale: While the calculated value is wrong, a lower value of $1.6\text{ GPa}$ would mean the material is more flexible, not stiffer.

sourceQuiz.hint: Calculate the actual Young's Modulus from the test data and compare it to the supplier's claim. A lower value indicates less stiffness.

syllabus.title: Material selection
syllabus.guidingQuestion: Why is material selection crucial to designers of products?

statements.text: Materials are selected for specific applications based on their properties.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify appropriate materials based on their physical, chemical and mechanical properties.

statements.text: Materials are selected for specific applications based on their aesthetic characteristics.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify appropriate materials based on texture, form and colour, which can also be enhanced by using a variety of finishing techniques.

statements.text: Additional factors influence the selection and application of materials in a specific context.
statements.guidance: Students must be able identify appropriate materials based on cost, availability and sustainability.

statements.text: The selection of materials for a specific purpose can be justified through primary and secondary research.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to justify their choice of materials using appropriate research methods.

steps: Specify measurable requirements for an outdoor bench seat.

exam.question: Explain why material selection should consider the intended manufacturing process. [2]

Objective: Students must select the best material for a School Cafeteria Tray.

Constraints: Must be durable, easy to clean, lightweight, and cheap.

Step 1: Secondary Research (20 mins)
  • Search online for "common plastic properties."
  • Find Density, Cost, and Melting Point for: Polypropylene (PP), Acrylic, and Polycarbonate.
  • Output: A comparison table.
Step 2: Primary Research (30 mins)
  • Provide samples of these three plastics.
  • Test A (The Scratch Test): Use a key/sandpaper (Hygiene factor).
  • Test B (The Drop Test): Drop from table height (Durability factor).
  • Test C (The Bend Test): Flex them. Does it snap?
Step 3: The Justification

Write a paragraph justifying your choice through primary and secondary research.

title: Structural systems application and selection

sections.title: Lesson 1: Structures in Everyday Products
sections.html:
3.2.1 Structures in Everyday Products ~60 min

Lesson 1: Structures in Everyday Products

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
  • Identify the five key forces (tension, compression, bending, shear, torsion) acting on structures within everyday products.
  • Analyse a product to locate likely points of structural failure using sketches, CAD reasoning, or physical inspection.
  • Apply appropriate strengthening techniques to improve a product's structural performance.

Structures aren't confined to buildings and bridges — they exist inside almost every manufactured object you own. A phone case, a backpack strap, a chair leg, and a paperclip are all structures that must survive predictable (and sometimes unpredictable) forces during normal use. Before you can improve a product, you first need to identify which forces are acting on it and where those forces concentrate. This lesson introduces the five fundamental forces and the practical toolkit designers use to strengthen a structure without simply "adding more material everywhere."

Key Terms

TermWorking Definition
TensionA pulling force that stretches or elongates a material.
CompressionA pushing/squashing force that shortens or crushes a material.
BendingA force applied away from a fixed point that causes a material to curve.
ShearA force that causes two adjacent parts of a material to slide past one another in opposite directions.
TorsionA twisting force applied around the longitudinal axis of a material.
Structural SystemThe parts of a product that resist load, including shell, framework, or solid structures.
StrutsStructural members or bracing designed specifically to resist compression.
LaminationBonding multiple layers of material together to increase strength and resistance to bending.
Practical Engagement: Reverse-Engineer a Failure
  1. In pairs, examine an everyday product that has failed structurally (e.g. a cracked phone case, a snapped clothes peg, a broken umbrella rib, a split chair leg — bring a real object or a photo).
  2. Sketch the product and label the force(s) most likely responsible for the failure (tension, compression, bending, shear, or torsion).
  3. Identify the specific point of failure and explain, in structural terms, why that location was the weak point (e.g. thin cross-section, sharp internal corner acting as a stress concentrator, unsupported span).
  4. Propose two strengthening techniques (material change, reinforcement, shape change, thickness increase, or combining structural types) that would prevent a repeat failure, and briefly justify each choice against cost and weight trade-offs.
  5. Share your redesign sketch with another pair and critique each other's reasoning.

Multimedia Resources

  • Internal Forces: Compression, Tension, Bending, Torsion
    Video — clear animated overview of all five forces
  • Strength of Materials in 2 Minutes
    Video — Tension, Compression, Shear, Bending & Torsion explained
  • Best Practices for Adding Ribs & Gussets for Structural Integrity
    Article — Fictiv

Exam Practice

Multiple Choice

1. Which force acts when two adjacent surfaces of a material slide past each other in opposite directions?

  • Tension
  • Torsion
  • Shear
  • Compression
Reveal Answer
C — Shear. [1] Shear occurs when adjacent parts of a material slide past one another in opposite directions.

2. A backpack strap stretching under the weight of books is primarily experiencing:

  • Compression
  • Tension
  • Torsion
  • Shear
Reveal Answer
B — Tension. [1] The strap is being pulled and elongated by the load.

3. Which strengthening technique is most appropriate for reducing bending in a flat plastic shelf, without significantly increasing the amount of material used?

  • Adding ribs
  • Removing all internal supports
  • Using a thinner material
  • Removing the shelf brackets
Reveal Answer
A — Adding ribs. [1] Ribs increase resistance to bending with minimal added material, unlike a solid thickness increase.

4. Identify two forces acting on a bicycle frame when a cyclist rides over a pothole. [2 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Compression — the sudden impact pushes/squashes parts of the frame.

[1] Bending and/or shear — the frame flexes and its tubes experience sliding/curving forces as the wheel drops into and out of the pothole. (Any two valid named forces with a brief link to the scenario.)

5. Describe how changing the shape of a structural component — for example, from a flat panel to a triangulated truss form — can improve its ability to resist bending forces. [4 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] A flat panel resists bending mainly through the stiffness of the material itself.

[1] A triangulated truss converts bending into tension and compression in individual struts.

[1] Triangles are geometrically rigid shapes that don't deform under load the way a flat panel can.

[1] This allows the structure to resist greater bending loads without a large increase in material or weight.

6. A manufacturer's phone case cracks consistently at the corners after drop tests. Explain, using appropriate structural terminology, two design modifications the company could make to reduce the likelihood of failure. [6 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Corners are stress concentrators — sharp internal/external corners cause stress to build up in a small area.

[2] Modification 1: increase the corner radius (rounding/filleting the corner) — this spreads the stress over a larger area rather than concentrating it at a sharp point.

[2] Modification 2: add reinforcement, e.g. a raised rib or thicker material at the corner, or change to a tougher/more flexible material at impact points to absorb energy.

[1] Both modifications reduce the concentration of stress at the point of impact, lowering the likelihood of a crack initiating there.

7. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using a combined frame-and-shell structural system, rather than a single shell structure, in the design of a piece of outdoor furniture. [8 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[2] Advantage: a frame can carry the main structural loads efficiently (e.g. through struts in tension/compression), while a lighter shell can be used purely for weather protection or seating surface, reducing overall material and weight.

[2] Advantage: the frame can be made from a stiff, weather-resistant material (e.g. metal) while the shell uses a different, cheaper or more comfortable material — combining structural types allows material choice to match function.

[2] Disadvantage: a frame-and-shell system typically has more component parts and joints, increasing manufacturing complexity and cost, and creating more potential failure points (e.g. at fixings).

[2] Disadvantage: a single shell structure can be simpler and cheaper to manufacture (e.g. rotationally moulded plastic furniture) and has fewer joints to fail, though it may need more material overall to achieve the same strength. A balanced conclusion referencing the specific outdoor-furniture context scores full marks.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Young's Modulus and Material Stiffness
sections.html:
3.2.2 Young's Modulus and Material Stiffness ~60 min

Lesson 2: Young's Modulus and Material Stiffness

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
  • Define stress, strain, and Young's Modulus, and state the correct units for each.
  • Calculate tensile stress, tensile strain, and Young's Modulus from given data.
  • Select an appropriate material for a design application by comparing Young's Modulus values.

Not all strong materials behave the same way under load. A material can resist breaking (strength) yet still bend or stretch noticeably before it does (low stiffness) — or resist any deformation at all until the moment it snaps (high stiffness, low ductility). Young's Modulus is the specific measurement that lets you compare how stiff different materials are, and it directly informs decisions such as why a skyscraper's frame is steel while a phone case's bumper is a flexible polymer.

Key Terms

TermWorking Definition
Stress (σ)The force applied per unit of cross-sectional area, measured in N/m² (Pascals).
Strain (ε)The ratio of the change in length to the original length; it has no units.
Young's Modulus (E)A measure of the stiffness of an elastic material, defined as tensile stress divided by tensile strain.
StiffnessThe resistance of a material to elastic (recoverable) deformation under an applied load.
Elastic LimitThe maximum stress a material can withstand while still returning to its original shape once the load is removed.
Practical Engagement: Material Selection by Stiffness
  1. Working from a reference table of approximate Young's Modulus values (steel ≈ 200 GPa, aluminium ≈ 69 GPa, wood along the grain ≈ 11 GPa, ABS plastic ≈ 2–3 GPa, rubber ≈ 0.01–0.1 GPa), rank the materials from stiffest to most flexible.
  2. Match each material to the everyday product it is best suited for: skyscraper frame, phone case bumper, bicycle frame, shoe sole, running shoe midsole cushioning. Justify each match with reference to E.
  3. Complete the calculation: a steel test wire has an original length of 2.5 m and a cross-sectional area of 4 × 10⁻⁶ m². Under a 200 N load it stretches by 1.25 mm. Calculate the stress, strain, and Young's Modulus, and check your answer against the accepted value for steel (~200 GPa).
  4. Discuss in groups: why might you deliberately choose a material with a lower Young's Modulus even though a stiffer material is available (e.g. shock absorption, comfort, flexibility for repeated bending)?

Multimedia Resources

  • Understanding Young's Modulus
    Video — The Efficient Engineer: stress-strain curves through to atomic-scale behaviour
  • How Stiffness Is Different From Young's Modulus
    Video — Hooke's Law
  • Young's Modulus of Elasticity
    Video — Khan Academy

Exam Practice

Multiple Choice

1. Young's Modulus is calculated as:

  • strain ÷ stress
  • stress ÷ strain
  • force ÷ area
  • extension ÷ length
Reveal Answer
B — stress ÷ strain. [1]

2. A material with a very high Young's Modulus is best described, in design terms, as:

  • Ductile
  • Flexible
  • Stiff
  • Brittle
Reveal Answer
C — Stiff. [1] A high E means the material strongly resists elastic deformation.

3. Which unit is used to measure tensile stress?

  • Newtons
  • Pascals
  • Metres
  • It has no units
Reveal Answer
B — Pascals. [1] Stress is force per unit area, N/m² = Pa.

4. Define tensile strain and state why it has no units. [2 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Tensile strain is the ratio of the change in length (extension) to the original length.

[1] It has no units because it's a ratio of two lengths (m/m), so the units cancel out.

5. A wire of original length 2.0 m stretches by 4 mm under load. Calculate the tensile strain. [3 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Convert extension to metres: 4 mm = 0.004 m.

[1] Strain = extension ÷ original length = 0.004 ÷ 2.0.

[1] Strain = 0.002 (no units).

6. Explain why steel is typically selected over aluminium for the primary structural frame of a skyscraper, referring to Young's Modulus. [6 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Steel has a much higher Young's Modulus (≈200 GPa) than aluminium (≈69 GPa).

[2] A higher E means steel deforms elastically far less than aluminium under the same stress — it is stiffer.

[2] For a skyscraper, minimising sway/deflection under wind and gravity loads is critical for occupant comfort and structural performance, so the stiffer material is preferred for the primary frame.

[1] A valid trade-off point, e.g. aluminium's lower density could reduce weight, but its lower stiffness makes it less suitable as the primary structural material for a very tall structure.

7. A footwear company wants to redesign a running shoe's midsole to better absorb impact, while a phone company wants a phone case that resists denting. Explain how the Young's Modulus values of suitable materials would differ for each product, and evaluate the trade-offs of selecting a very high versus a very low Young's Modulus material in each case. [8 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[2] The running shoe midsole needs a low Young's Modulus material (flexible, e.g. foamed polymer) so it can compress and absorb impact energy with each step.

[2] The phone case needs a comparatively higher Young's Modulus / tougher material at contact points so it resists denting and holds its shape under impact, rather than permanently deforming.

[2] Trade-off for the midsole: too low an E risks excessive/unstable deformation and poor energy return; too high an E gives poor cushioning and comfort, increasing impact transmitted to the runner.

[2] Trade-off for the phone case: too high an E (very stiff, often brittle) risks cracking on sharp impact rather than absorbing energy; too low an E risks permanent denting/loss of shape. A balanced material choice (or combination of materials) is usually required in both cases.
