sections.title: Lesson 3: Structural Failure and Analysis
sections.html:
3.2.3 Structural Failure and Analysis ~60 min

Lesson 3: Structural Failure and Analysis

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
  • Explain common causes of structural failure: overloading, poor material choice, and issues of size and shape.
  • Interpret colour-coded Finite Element Analysis (FEA) stress maps.
  • Evaluate a real-world structural failure case study to identify design and process lessons.

Every structural failure has a cause that, in hindsight, was often predictable. Modern designers rarely wait for a physical prototype to break before finding out where it is weak — instead, they use Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to simulate real-world forces on a digital model, long before it's manufactured. This lesson connects digital simulation tools to real, high-consequence engineering failures so you understand both how failure happens and how it can be predicted and prevented.

Key Terms

TermWorking Definition
Finite Element Analysis (FEA)Digital model calculation and simulation of unknown factors in products using computer-aided design (CAD) systems.
OverloadingApplying a force to a structure that exceeds its designed working load.
Stress ConcentrationA localised area of a structure (often a sharp corner, hole, or change in cross-section) where stress is significantly higher than the surrounding material.
LightweightingRemoving material from low-stress areas of a structure, identified through analysis such as FEA, to reduce weight and cost without compromising strength.
Practical Engagement: Reading FEA and Learning from Failure
  1. Study an FEA stress map image of a component (e.g. a bracket or beam under load). Identify the blue (low stress), yellow (moderate stress) and red (high stress / likely failure) zones and explain what you should do in each zone as a designer.
  2. Case study: research the 1981 Hyatt Regency walkway collapse. Identify what the original design specified, what change was made during construction, and why that seemingly minor change caused catastrophic failure.
  3. In groups, produce a one-page 'lessons learned' summary connecting the Hyatt Regency case to the general causes of structural failure (overloading, poor material choice, size/shape issues) covered in this topic.
  4. Extension: research how a company (e.g. in the automotive, aerospace, or consumer electronics industry) uses FEA in its product development process, and summarise one concrete example.

Multimedia Resources

  • What Is Finite Element Analysis (FEA)? Explained Simply
    Video
  • Introduction to Finite Element Analysis (FEA) — Beginner's Guide Episode 1
    Video
  • Hyatt Regency Walkway Collapse
    Article — background, causes, and consequences
  • What Is Finite Element Analysis (FEA)?
    Article — Siemens
  • How Is FEA Used for Company Projects in Industry?
    Article — Cad Crowd

Exam Practice

Multiple Choice

1. In a typical FEA stress map, red colouring indicates:

  • No stress
  • Low stress
  • Moderate stress
  • High stress and potential failure
Reveal Answer
D — High stress and potential failure. [1]

2. The 1981 Hyatt Regency walkway collapse was primarily caused by:

  • Poor material selection
  • An unapproved design change that doubled the load on connecting rods
  • An excessively high safety factor
  • Wind-induced oscillation
Reveal Answer
B — An unapproved design change that doubled the load on connecting rods. [1]

3. "Lightweighting" informed by FEA results primarily aims to:

  • Increase the safety factor
  • Remove material from low-stress areas to reduce weight and cost
  • Add material to every surface
  • Increase the surface area of a part
Reveal Answer
B — Remove material from low-stress areas to reduce weight and cost. [1]

4. State two possible causes of structural failure in a product. [2 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Overloading — applying a force that exceeds the designed working load.

[1] Any other valid cause, e.g. poor material choice, or issues of size and shape (such as a stress concentration at a sharp corner).

5. Outline how FEA can help a designer decide where to add or remove material in a component. [4 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] FEA simulates the forces acting on a digital model and displays the resulting stress distribution as a colour-coded map.

[1] Red/high-stress zones show where the component is at greatest risk of failure.

[1] A designer can reinforce or thicken material in those high-stress zones.

[1] Blue/low-stress zones show where material is doing little structural work, so it can be removed (lightweighted) to save weight and cost without compromising strength.

6. Explain how a designer might use FEA colour-coded stress maps to iteratively improve the design of a bicycle helmet. [6 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] A first digital model of the helmet is simulated under a representative impact load.

[1] The updated model is re-simulated, and this cycle repeats — an iterative process — until the stress distribution is acceptable across the whole helmet.

7. With reference to the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse (or another structural failure case you have studied), discuss how a combination of a minor design change and inadequate structural analysis can lead to catastrophic failure. [8 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[2] Description of the case: the original design routed a single long connecting rod through both walkway levels; the construction change split this into two shorter rods, one supporting the other.

[2] This change doubled the load carried by the connecting point on the upper walkway's support beam, which the original design had never been analysed to withstand.

Interpret colour-coded Finite Element Analysis (FEA) stress maps. Evaluate a real-world structural failure case study to identify design and process lessons. Every structural failure has a cause that, in hindsight, was often predictable. sections.title: Lesson 4: Force Diagrams
sections.html:
3.2.4 Force Diagrams ~50 min

Lesson 4: Force Diagrams

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
  • Construct simple force (free body) diagrams to represent external loads on a structure.
  • Identify reaction forces at supports for simply supported and cantilevered beams.
  • Interpret force diagrams to predict where a structure is most likely to fail.

Before a structure is built, tested, or even modelled in CAD, designers often start with a simple hand-drawn force diagram. This visual 'map' of external and internal forces lets you quickly estimate where a structure will experience the greatest stress — without needing complex software. This lesson builds the visual language of force diagrams that underpins later, more complex analysis such as FEA.

Key Terms

TermWorking Definition
Force Diagram (Free Body Diagram)A simplified diagram showing all external forces acting on an isolated structure or component.
Reaction ForceA force exerted by a support in response to an applied load, acting to keep the structure in equilibrium.
Point LoadA force applied at a single, specific location on a structure.
Distributed LoadA force spread evenly (or unevenly) across a length or area of a structure, rather than at a single point.
CantileverA structural member fixed and supported at only one end, with the other end free.
Practical Engagement: Drawing and Interpreting Force Diagrams
  1. Draw a force diagram for a simply supported wall shelf loaded with a single heavy book placed at its centre. Label the applied load and the two reaction forces at the supports.
  2. Redraw the diagram with the book moved to the far outer edge of the shelf (unsupported end). Discuss, using your diagram, why this position increases the risk of the shelf bending or snapping.
  3. Draw a force diagram for a cantilevered diving board fixed at one end, with a person's weight acting at the free end. Identify where the internal bending force is greatest.
  4. Compare your diagrams with a partner and check that reaction forces balance the applied load(s) in each case.

Multimedia Resources

  • How to Draw Bending Moment & Shear Force Diagrams: Simply Supported Beam
    Video
  • Draw Bending Moment & Shear Force Diagrams: Cantilever Beam
    Video
  • Understanding Shear Force and Bending Moment Diagrams
    Article — The Efficient Engineer

Exam Practice

Multiple Choice

1. In a force diagram of a symmetrically loaded, simply supported beam with a single central point load, the reaction force at each support is:

  • Equal to the total load
  • Half the total load (assuming symmetry)
  • Zero
  • Double the total load
Reveal Answer
B — Half the total load (assuming symmetry). [1]

2. A force (free body) diagram is used primarily to:

  • Show the aesthetic design of a product
  • Represent all external forces acting on an isolated object
  • Calculate a material's Young's Modulus
  • Display FEA stress colours
Reveal Answer
B — Represent all external forces acting on an isolated object. [1]

3. A cantilever beam is best described as:

  • Supported at both ends
  • Fixed at one end only, with the other end free
  • Supported only at its centre
  • Entirely unsupported
Reveal Answer
B — Fixed at one end only, with the other end free. [1]

4. Sketch and label a simple force diagram for a wall-mounted shelf with a single load placed at its outer edge (a written description of the diagram is acceptable if you are unable to draw). [3 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] Applied load (point load) correctly shown/described acting downward at the outer edge of the shelf.

[1] Reaction force(s) shown/described acting at the wall-mounted (fixed) support.

[1] A reaction moment shown/described at the fixed support, since the load is offset from the support (this is what distinguishes it from a simple point-load reaction).

5. Identify the two types of reaction that can occur at a fixed (built-in) support. [2 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] A reaction force (resisting linear movement/translation).

[1] A reaction moment (resisting rotation).

6. Explain why force diagrams are a useful tool for designers before physical prototyping begins. [5 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] A force diagram lets a designer estimate where a structure will experience the greatest stress before anything is built.

[1] It requires no complex software or physical materials — just a quick hand sketch.

[1] It helps identify reaction forces at supports, checking that a proposed support arrangement is even viable.

[1] It can reveal likely failure points early, before time and material are spent on a physical prototype.

[1] It provides a foundation for more detailed later analysis, such as FEA, saving time when a more complex simulation is eventually needed.

7. A designer is creating a diving board (a cantilevered beam) fixed at one end. Using a force diagram, explain where the bending force is greatest along its length, and discuss how this should inform the material thickness at different points along the board. [8 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[2] In a cantilever with the load at the free end, the bending force (bending moment) is zero at the free end and increases along the length of the board, reaching its maximum at the fixed end.

[2] This is because the bending moment at any point equals the load multiplied by its distance from that point — the distance (and therefore the moment) is greatest at the fixed support.

[2] The material should therefore be thickest/most reinforced near the fixed end, where bending stress is highest, and can be thinner near the free end, where stress is lowest.

[2] This matches material to where it's structurally needed — reducing unnecessary material (and weight/cost) at the free end while ensuring the fixed end doesn't fail. Credit reference to a tapered board profile as a real-world example of this principle.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Safety Factors
sections.html:
3.2.5 Safety Factors ~50 min

Lesson 5: Safety Factors

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
  • Define Safety Factor (SF) and state its formula.
  • Calculate the safety factor of a structure given ultimate and working load data.
  • Justify an appropriate safety factor for a product based on its level of risk to users.

No designer can predict every variable a product will face — sudden shocks, material defects, or user misuse. The Safety Factor is how you build a deliberate margin of error into a structure, ensuring it can withstand more than its expected everyday load. Understanding how to select and justify an appropriate safety factor is central to responsible, user-focused design.

Key Terms

TermWorking Definition
Safety Factor (SF)The ratio of how much load a structure can bear compared to its normal expected load.
Ultimate (Maximum) LoadThe greatest load a structure can withstand before it fails.
Allowable (Working) LoadThe load a structure is designed and expected to carry during normal use.
Contingency MarginThe additional reserve strength built into a design to account for unpredictable variables such as sudden loads, material defects, or misuse.
Practical Engagement: Calculating and Justifying Safety Factors
  1. Calculate the safety factor for a component with an ultimate load of 900 N and a working load of 300 N. Show your working using the formula SF = Ultimate Load ÷ Allowable Load.
  2. For each of the following products, decide on an appropriate safety factor range and justify your choice by considering the consequences of failure: a passenger aircraft wing, an elevator cable, a children's swing set, a picture frame hook, a pedestrian bridge.
  3. Debate in pairs: is it ever acceptable to reduce a safety factor to save material cost or weight? Consider both commercial and ethical perspectives.
  4. Extension: research the safety factor typically required by regulation or industry standard for one specific product category (e.g. climbing equipment, elevators, playground equipment) and compare it with your own estimate.

Multimedia Resources

  • Factor of Safety Basics Explained in 2 Minutes
    Video
  • Factor of Safety with Examples
    Video
  • Factor of Safety
    Article — Wikipedia

Exam Practice

Multiple Choice

1. The formula for Safety Factor is:

  • Working Load ÷ Ultimate Load
  • Ultimate Load ÷ Working Load
  • Ultimate Load × Working Load
  • Ultimate Load − Working Load
Reveal Answer
B — Ultimate Load ÷ Working Load. [1]

2. A safety factor of 1 means:

  • The structure has ample reserve strength
  • The structure can only just support its expected load, with no margin for error
  • The structure will fail immediately under any load
  • The structure is twice as strong as needed
Reveal Answer
B — The structure can only just support its expected load, with no margin for error. [1]

3. Which product would typically require the highest safety factor?

  • A wooden coat hook
  • A plastic ruler
  • A passenger aircraft wing
  • A picture frame
Reveal Answer
C — A passenger aircraft wing. [1] The consequences of failure are catastrophic and life-threatening, demanding a high safety margin.

4. A component has an ultimate load of 900 N and is designed to work under a load of 300 N. Calculate its safety factor. [2 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] SF = Ultimate Load ÷ Working Load = 900 ÷ 300.

[1] SF = 3.

5. State why furniture typically uses a lower safety factor (1.5–2.5) than a bridge (3–5+). [2 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] The consequences of a furniture item failing are generally lower risk to human life than a bridge failing.

[1] A bridge carries much higher, more variable and less predictable loads (traffic, crowds, weather) and its failure could be catastrophic and affect many people at once, justifying a much larger safety margin.

6. Explain why designers build a safety factor into a structure rather than designing it to withstand exactly the expected working load. [5 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[1] No designer can predict every variable a product will face in real use.

[1] Sudden or unexpected shocks/loads (e.g. dropping, overloading) can exceed the normal expected load.

[1] Material defects from manufacturing can make an individual component weaker than the ideal calculated strength.

[1] User misuse (using a product in a way it wasn't intended for) can apply loads or conditions beyond the design brief.

[1] Designing to exactly the working load leaves no contingency margin for any of these factors, risking failure under real-world conditions.

7. A playground swing set is being redesigned. Explain how the designer should determine an appropriate safety factor, and evaluate the consequences of selecting a safety factor that is too low compared with one that is unnecessarily high. [8 marks]

Reveal Markscheme

[2] The designer should consider the consequences of failure (children's safety, public/high-risk use), likely variability in load (multiple users, dynamic swinging forces, rough use) and relevant regulations/standards for playground equipment.

[2] Too low a safety factor: the structure may fail under realistic but unpredicted loads (e.g. several children swinging at once, a sudden jolt), risking injury — an unacceptable outcome for a product used by children.

[2] Too high a safety factor: the structure becomes unnecessarily heavy, uses more material, and increases manufacturing cost and environmental impact without a proportional safety benefit.

[2] Evaluation: the designer must balance user safety against cost, material use and sustainability — for a high-risk product like a swing set, err toward a higher safety factor within a sensible, standards-informed range rather than minimising cost. Credit reference to relevant safety factor ranges or standards.

sections.html:
B3.2 Glossary

Consolidated Glossary — Topic B3.2

All key terms from the five lessons, in one place. Click a term to reveal its definition.

Tension
IB Definition: A pulling force that stretches or elongates a material.
Real-World Example: A backpack strap stretching under the weight of books.
Compression
IB Definition: A pushing/squashing force that shortens or crushes a material.
Real-World Example: The legs of a chair compressing under a seated person's weight.
Bending Force
IB Definition: A load applied a certain distance from a fixed position that causes a material to curve.
Real-World Example: A shelf sagging in the middle when heavy books are placed away from the wall supports.
Shear
IB Definition: A force that causes two adjacent parts of a material to slide past one another in opposite directions.
Real-World Example: Scissor blades cutting through paper.
Torsion
IB Definition: A twisting force applied around the longitudinal axis of a material.
Real-World Example: A screwdriver shaft twisting as it turns a stiff screw.
Structural System
IB Definition: The parts of a product that resist load, including shell, framework, or solid structures.
Real-World Example: The tubular metal frame of a bicycle, which supports the rider's weight.
Struts
IB Definition: Structural members or bracing designed specifically to resist compression.
Real-World Example: Bracing members in a roof truss that prevent long spans from sagging.
Lamination
IB Definition: Bonding multiple layers of material together to increase strength and resistance to bending.
Real-World Example: Plywood, made from layers of wood glued together for extra strength and stability.
Young's Modulus (E)
IB Definition: A measure of the stiffness of an elastic material, defined as tensile stress divided by tensile strain.
Real-World Example: Selecting steel for a skyscraper's frame because its high Young's Modulus minimises swaying in high winds.
Stress (σ)
IB Definition: The force applied per unit of cross-sectional area, measured in N/m² (Pascals).
Real-World Example: The stress in a climbing rope carrying a climber's body weight.
Strain (ε)
IB Definition: The ratio of the change in length to the original length; it has no units.
Real-World Example: The stretch in a bungee cord expressed as a fraction of its unstretched length.
Stiffness
IB Definition: The resistance of a material to elastic (recoverable) deformation under an applied load.
Real-World Example: A carbon-fibre bicycle frame that flexes very little when pedalled hard.
Elastic Limit
IB Definition: The maximum stress a material can withstand while still returning to its original shape once the load is removed.
Real-World Example: A rubber band that snaps back to shape after mild stretching, but not after being pulled too far.
Finite Element Analysis (FEA)
IB Definition: Digital model calculation and simulation of unknown factors in products using computer-aided design (CAD) systems.
Real-World Example: Simulating stress distribution in a car frame during a crash to identify and reinforce weak points.
Overloading
IB Definition: Applying a force to a structure that exceeds its designed working load.
Real-World Example: Too many passengers standing on one side of a small boat, causing it to capsize.
Stress Concentration
IB Definition: A localised area of a structure where stress is significantly higher than in the surrounding material, often at sharp corners or holes.
Real-World Example: Cracks in a phone case starting at the sharp corner of the camera cut-out.
Lightweighting
IB Definition: Removing material from low-stress areas of a structure, identified through analysis such as FEA, to reduce weight and cost.
Real-World Example: Aircraft components thinned in low-stress zones to reduce fuel consumption.
Force Diagram (Free Body Diagram)
IB Definition: A simplified diagram showing all external forces acting on an isolated structure or component.
Real-World Example: A sketch showing the load and reaction forces on a wall-mounted shelf.
Reaction Force
IB Definition: A force exerted by a support in response to an applied load, keeping the structure in equilibrium.
Real-World Example: The upward force from a table leg supporting the table's weight.
Cantilever
IB Definition: A structural member fixed and supported at only one end, with the other end free.
Real-World Example: A diving board fixed at one end, projecting out over a pool.
Safety Factor (SF)
IB Definition: The ratio of how much load a structure can bear compared to its normal expected load.
Real-World Example: Designing a bridge with an SF of 3 so it can support triple its intended maximum traffic load.
Ultimate (Maximum) Load
IB Definition: The greatest load a structure can withstand before it fails.
Real-World Example: The point at which a rated climbing carabiner finally snaps under test conditions.
Allowable (Working) Load
IB Definition: The load a structure is designed and expected to carry during normal use.
Real-World Example: The maximum recommended number of people for a lift, as stated on its safety plate.

syllabus.title: Structural systems application and selection
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How can structural systems be incorporated into product design?

statements.text: Structures are present in the design of everyday products.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to analyse and model the forces acting on and within the structure of existing products and be able to suggest how existing structures can be strengthened.

statements.text: Young’s Modulus is the measure of stiffness of a material.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to calculate Young’s Modulus using the formula: Young’s Modulus (E) = Tensile Stress (σ)/Tensile Strain (ε), and interpret stress-strain graphs for a given material, identifying the Young’s Modulus, yield strength, ultimate strength and fracture.

statements.text: Structures fail due to overloading, material choice, size and shape.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify why a structure has failed, including interpreting data from finite element analysis (FEA).

statements.text: Forces acting on a structure or within a beam can be represented diagrammatically.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to interpret simple force diagrams for a given structure.

statements.text: Safety factors (SFs) are a way to design in contingency to prevent failure from overloading a structure.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to calculate SFs using the formula: SF = Ultimate Load (Stress)/Allowable Load (Stress); calculate maximum intended loads for given structures; and design structures with an SF.

activity.title: Structure under constraints
steps: Design a paper support for a stated load and fixed material budget.
Compare a braced frame with an unbraced frame. Sketch load paths and joints.
Apply equal incremental loads; record deflection and failure location.
Revise one joint or member using evidence and retest.
activity.debrief: Is the stiffest structure always the best solution?

exam.question: Explain the function of diagonal bracing in a rectangular frame. [2]
exam.answer: It creates triangles and resists racking, reducing changes in the frame’s shape under lateral loads.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Reverse-Engineer a Failure
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Reverse-Engineer a Failure In pairs, examine an everyday product that has failed structurally (e.g. a cracked phone case, a snapped clothes peg, a broken umbrella rib, a split chair leg — bring a real object or a photo). Sketch the product and label the force(s) most likely responsible for the failure (tension, compression, bending, shear, or torsion). Identify the specific point of failure and explain, in structural terms, why that location was the weak point (e.g. thin cross-section, sharp internal corner acting as a stress concentrator, unsupported span). Propose two strengthening techniques (material change, reinforcement, shape change, thickness increase, or combining structural types) that would prevent a repeat failure, and briefly justify each choice against cost and weight trade-offs. Share your redesign sketch with another pair and critique each other's reasoning.
activities.html:
Practical Engagement: Reverse-Engineer a Failure
  1. In pairs, examine an everyday product that has failed structurally (e.g. a cracked phone case, a snapped clothes peg, a broken umbrella rib, a split chair leg — bring a real object or a photo).
  2. Sketch the product and label the force(s) most likely responsible for the failure (tension, compression, bending, shear, or torsion).
  3. Identify the specific point of failure and explain, in structural terms, why that location was the weak point (e.g. thin cross-section, sharp internal corner acting as a stress concentrator, unsupported span).
  4. Propose two strengthening techniques (material change, reinforcement, shape change, thickness increase, or combining structural types) that would prevent a repeat failure, and briefly justify each choice against cost and weight trade-offs.
  5. Share your redesign sketch with another pair and critique each other's reasoning.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Material Selection by Stiffness
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Material Selection by Stiffness Working from a reference table of approximate Young's Modulus values (steel ≈ 200 GPa, aluminium ≈ 69 GPa, wood along the grain ≈ 11 GPa, ABS plastic ≈ 2–3 GPa, rubber ≈ 0.01–0.1 GPa), rank the materials from stiffest to most flexible. Match each material to the everyday product it is best suited for: skyscraper frame, phone case bumper, bicycle frame, shoe sole, running shoe midsole cushioning. Justify each match with reference to E. Complete the calculation: a steel test wire has an original length of 2.5 m and a cross-sectional area of 4 × 10⁻⁶ m². Under a 200 N load it stretches by 1.25 mm. Calculate the stress, strain, and Young's Modulus, and check your answer against the accepted value for steel (~200 GPa). Discuss in groups: why might you deliberately choose a material with a lower Young's Modulus even though a stiffer material is available (e.g. shock absorption, comfort, flexibility for repeated bending)?

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Reading FEA and Learning from Failure
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Reading FEA and Learning from Failure Study an FEA stress map image of a component (e.g. a bracket or beam under load). Identify the blue (low stress), yellow (moderate stress) and red (high stress / likely failure) zones and explain what you should do in each zone as a designer. Case study: research the 1981 Hyatt Regency walkway collapse. Identify what the original design specified, what change was made during construction, and why that seemingly minor change caused catastrophic failure. In groups, produce a one-page 'lessons learned' summary connecting the Hyatt Regency case to the general causes of structural failure (overloading, poor material choice, size/shape issues) covered in this topic. Extension: research how a company (e.g. in the automotive, aerospace, or consumer electronics industry) uses FEA in its product development process, and summarise one concrete example.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Drawing and Interpreting Force Diagrams
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Drawing and Interpreting Force Diagrams Draw a force diagram for a simply supported wall shelf loaded with a single heavy book placed at its centre. Label the applied load and the two reaction forces at the supports. Redraw the diagram with the book moved to the far outer edge of the shelf (unsupported end). Discuss, using your diagram, why this position increases the risk of the shelf bending or snapping. Draw a force diagram for a cantilevered diving board fixed at one end, with a person's weight acting at the free end. Identify where the internal bending force is greatest. Compare your diagrams with a partner and check that reaction forces balance the applied load(s) in each case.

[2] disadvantage: a frame-and-shell system typically has more component parts and joints, increasing manufacturing complexity and cost, and creating more potential failure points (e.g. at fixings). [2] disadvantage: a single shell structure can be simpler and cheaper to manufacture (e.g. rotationally moulded plastic furniture) and has fewer joints to fail, though it may need more material overall to achieve the same strength. a balanced conclusion referencing the specific outdoor-furniture context scores full marks. 3.2.2 young's modulus and material stiffness ~60 min lesson 2: young's modulus and material stiffness by the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: define stress, strain, and young's modulus, and state the correct units for each. calculate tensile stress, tensile strain, and young's modulus from given data. select an appropriate material for a design application by comparing young's modulus values. not all strong materials behave the same way under load. a material can resist breaking (strength) yet still bend or stretch noticeably before it does (low stiffness) — or resist any deformation at all until the moment it snaps (high stiffness, low ductility). young's modulus is the specific measurement that lets you compare how stiff different materials are, and it directly informs decisions such as why a skyscraper's frame is steel while a phone case's bumper is a flexible polymer. key terms term working definition stress (σ) the force applied per unit of cross-sectional area, measured in n/m² (pascals). strain (ε) the ratio of the change in length to the original length; it has no units. young's modulus (e) a measure of the stiffness of an elastic material, defined as tensile stress divided by tensile strain. stiffness the resistance of a material to elastic (recoverable) deformation under an applied load. elastic limit the maximum stress a material can withstand while still returning to its original shape once the load is removed. practical engagement: material selection by stiffness working from a reference table of approximate young's modulus values (steel ≈ 200 gpa, aluminium ≈ 69 gpa, wood along the grain ≈ 11 gpa, abs plastic ≈ 2–3 gpa, rubber ≈ 0.01–0.1 gpa), rank the materials from stiffest to most flexible. match each material to the everyday product it is best suited for: skyscraper frame, phone case bumper, bicycle frame, shoe sole, running shoe midsole cushioning. justify each match with reference to e. complete the calculation: a steel test wire has an original length of 2.5 m and a cross-sectional area of 4 × 10⁻⁶ m². under a 200 n load it stretches by 1.25 mm. calculate the stress, strain, and young's modulus, and check your answer against the accepted value for steel (~200 gpa). discuss in groups: why might you deliberately choose a material with a lower young's modulus even though a stiffer material is available (e.g. shock absorption, comfort, flexibility for repeated bending)? multimedia resources understanding young's modulus video — the efficient engineer: stress-strain curves through to atomic-scale behaviour how stiffness is different from young's modulus video — hooke's law young's modulus of elasticity video — khan academy exam practice multiple choice 1. young's modulus is calculated as: strain ÷ stress stress ÷ strain force ÷ area extension ÷ length reveal answer b — stress ÷ strain. [1] 2. a material with a very high young's modulus is best described, in design terms, as: ductile flexible stiff brittle reveal answer c — stiff. [1] a high e means the material strongly resists elastic deformation. 3. which unit is used to measure tensile stress? newtons pascals metres it has no units reveal answer b — pascals. [1] stress is force per unit area, n/m² = pa. 4. define tensile strain and state why it has no units. [2 marks] reveal markscheme [1] tensile strain is the ratio of the change in length (extension) to the original length. [1] it has no units because it's a ratio of two lengths (m/m), so the units cancel out. 5. a wire of original length 2.0 m stretches by 4 mm under load. calculate the tensile strain. [3 marks] reveal markscheme [1] convert extension to metres: 4 mm = 0.004 m. [1] strain = extension ÷ original length = 0.004 ÷ 2.0. [1] strain = 0.002 (no units). 6. explain why steel is typically selected over aluminium for the primary structural frame of a skyscraper, referring to young's modulus. [6 marks] reveal markscheme [1] steel has a much higher young's modulus (≈200 gpa) than aluminium (≈69 gpa). [2] a higher e means steel deforms elastically far less than aluminium under the same stress — it is stiffer. [2] for a skyscraper, minimising sway/deflection under wind and gravity loads is critical for occupant comfort and structural performance, so the stiffer material is preferred for the primary frame. [1] a valid trade-off point, e.g. aluminium's lower density could reduce weight, but its lower stiffness makes it less suitable as the primary structural material for a very tall structure. 7. a footwear company wants to redesign a running shoe's midsole to better absorb impact, while a phone company wants a phone case that resists denting. explain how the young's modulus values of suitable materials would differ for each product, and evaluate the trade-offs of selecting a very high versus a very low young's modulus material in each case. [8 marks] reveal markscheme [2] the running shoe midsole needs a low young's modulus material (flexible, e.g. foamed polymer) so it can compress and absorb impact energy with each step. [2] the phone case needs a comparatively higher young's modulus / tougher material at contact points so it resists denting and holds its shape under impact, rather than permanently deforming. [2] trade-off for the midsole: too low an e risks excessive/unstable deformation and poor energy return; too high an e gives poor cushioning and comfort, increasing impact transmitted to the runner. [2] trade-off for the phone case: too high an e (very stiff, often brittle) risks cracking on sharp impact rather than absorbing energy; too low an e risks permanent denting/loss of shape. a balanced material choice (or combination of materials) is usually required in both cases. 3.2.3 structural failure and analysis ~60 min lesson 3: structural failure and analysis by the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: explain common causes of structural failure: overloading, poor material choice, and issues of size and shape. interpret colour-coded finite element analysis (fea) stress maps. evaluate a real-world structural failure case study to identify design and process lessons. every structural failure has a cause that, in hindsight, was often predictable. modern designers rarely wait for a physical prototype to break before finding out where it is weak — instead, they use finite element analysis (fea) to simulate real-world forces on a digital model, long before it's manufactured. this lesson connects digital simulation tools to real, high-consequence engineering failures so you understand both how failure happens and how it can be predicted and prevented. key terms term working definition finite element analysis (fea) digital model calculation and simulation of unknown factors in products using computer-aided design (cad) systems. overloading applying a force to a structure that exceeds its designed working load. stress concentration a localised area of a structure (often a sharp corner, hole, or change in cross-section) where stress is significantly higher than the surrounding material. lightweighting removing material from low-stress areas of a structure, identified through analysis such as fea, to reduce weight and cost without compromising strength. practical engagement: reading fea and learning from failure study an fea stress map image of a component (e.g. a bracket or beam under load). identify the blue (low stress), yellow (moderate stress) and red (high stress / likely failure) zones and explain what you should do in each zone as a designer. case study: research the 1981 hyatt regency walkway collapse. identify what the original design specified, what change was made during construction, and why that seemingly minor change caused catastrophic failure. in groups, produce a one-page 'lessons learned' summary connecting the hyatt regency case to the general causes of structural failure (overloading, poor material choice, size/shape issues) covered in this topic. extension: research how a company (e.g. in the automotive, aerospace, or consumer electronics industry) uses fea in its product development process, and summarise one concrete example. multimedia resources what is finite element analysis (fea)? explained simply video introduction to finite element analysis (fea) — beginner's guide episode 1 video hyatt regency walkway collapse article — background, causes, and consequences what is finite element analysis (fea)? article — siemens how is fea used for company projects in industry? article — cad crowd exam practice multiple choice 1. in a typical fea stress map, red colouring indicates: no stress low stress moderate stress high stress and potential failure reveal answer d — high stress and potential failure. [1] 2. the 1981 hyatt regency walkway collapse was primarily caused by: poor material selection an unapproved design change that doubled the load on connecting rods an excessively high safety factor wind-induced oscillation reveal answer b — an unapproved design change that doubled the load on connecting rods. [1] 3. "lightweighting" informed by fea results primarily aims to: increase the safety factor remove material from low-stress areas to reduce weight and cost add material to every surface increase the surface area of a part reveal answer b — remove material from low-stress areas to reduce weight and cost. [1] 4. state two possible causes of structural failure in a product. [2 marks] reveal markscheme [1] overloading — applying a force that exceeds the designed working load. [1] any other valid cause, e.g. poor material choice, or issues of size and shape (such as a stress concentration at a sharp corner). 5. outline how fea can help a designer decide where to add or remove material in a component. [4 marks] reveal markscheme [1] fea simulates the forces acting on a digital model and displays the resulting stress distribution as a colour-coded map. [1] red/high-stress zones show where the component is at greatest risk of failure. [1] a designer can reinforce or thicken material in those high-stress zones. [1] blue/low-stress zones show where material is doing little structural work, so it can be removed (lightweighted) to save weight and cost without compromising strength. 6. explain how a designer might use fea colour-coded stress maps to iteratively improve the design of a bicycle helmet. [6 marks] reveal markscheme [1] a first digital model of the helmet is simulated under a representative impact load. [2] the resulting stress map highlights red (high-stress) zones — likely points of cracking or failure on impact — and blue (low-stress) zones that are structurally over-engineered. [2] the designer reinforces the high-stress zones (e.g. thicker shell, added internal ribs) and removes material from low-stress zones to reduce weight without reducing protection. [1] the updated model is re-simulated, and this cycle repeats — an iterative process — until the stress distribution is acceptable across the whole helmet. 7. with reference to the hyatt regency walkway collapse (or another structural failure case you have studied), discuss how a combination of a minor design change and inadequate structural analysis can lead to catastrophic failure. [8 marks] reveal markscheme [2] description of the case: the original design routed a single long connecting rod through both walkway levels; the construction change split this into two shorter rods, one supporting the other. [2] this change doubled the load carried by the connecting point on the upper walkway's support beam, which the original design had never been analysed to withstand. [2] because the change was not resubmitted for full structural analysis, the increased load and resulting stress concentration went undetected before construction was completed. [2] discussion/evaluation: a seemingly minor change can have a large structural effect if it alters how loads are transferred through a system, which is why any design change — however small it looks — requires re-analysis before it is built. credit any well-reasoned case study with equivalent structural and process reasoning. 3.2.4 force diagrams ~50 min lesson 4: force diagrams by the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: construct simple force (free body) diagrams to represent external loads on a structure. identify reaction forces at supports for simply supported and cantilevered beams. interpret force diagrams to predict where a structure is most likely to fail. before a structure is built, tested, or even modelled in cad, designers often start with a simple hand-drawn force diagram. this visual 'map' of external and internal forces lets you quickly estimate where a structure will experience the greatest stress — without needing complex software. this lesson builds the visual language of force diagrams that underpins later, more complex analysis such as fea. key terms term working definition force diagram (free body diagram) a simplified diagram showing all external forces acting on an isolated structure or component. reaction force a force exerted by a support in response to an applied load, acting to keep the structure in equilibrium. point load a force applied at a single, specific location on a structure. distributed load a force spread evenly (or unevenly) across a length or area of a structure, rather than at a single point. cantilever a structural member fixed and supported at only one end, with the other end free. practical engagement: drawing and interpreting force diagrams draw a force diagram for a simply supported wall shelf loaded with a single heavy book placed at its centre. label the applied load and the two reaction forces at the supports. redraw the diagram with the book moved to the far outer edge of the shelf (unsupported end). discuss, using your diagram, why this position increases the risk of the shelf bending or snapping. draw a force diagram for a cantilevered diving board fixed at one end, with a person's weight acting at the free end. identify where the internal bending force is greatest. compare your diagrams with a partner and check that reaction forces balance the applied load(s) in each case. multimedia resources how to draw bending moment & shear force diagrams: simply supported beam video draw bending moment & shear force diagrams: cantilever beam video understanding shear force and bending moment diagrams article — the efficient engineer exam practice multiple choice 1. in a force diagram of a symmetrically loaded, simply supported beam with a single central point load, the reaction force at each support is: equal to the total load half the total load (assuming symmetry) zero double the total load reveal answer b — half the total load (assuming symmetry). [1] 2. a force (free body) diagram is used primarily to: show the aesthetic design of a product represent all external forces acting on an isolated object calculate a material's young's modulus display fea stress colours reveal answer b — represent all external forces acting on an isolated object. [1] 3. a cantilever beam is best described as: supported at both ends fixed at one end only, with the other end free supported only at its centre entirely unsupported reveal answer b — fixed at one end only, with the other end free. [1] 4. sketch and label a simple force diagram for a wall-mounted shelf with a single load placed at its outer edge (a written description of the diagram is acceptable if you are unable to draw). [3 marks] reveal markscheme [1] applied load (point load) correctly shown/described acting downward at the outer edge of the shelf. [1] reaction force(s) shown/described acting at the wall-mounted (fixed) support. [1] a reaction moment shown/described at the fixed support, since the load is offset from the support (this is what distinguishes it from a simple point-load reaction). 5. identify the two types of reaction that can occur at a fixed (built-in) support. [2 marks] reveal markscheme [1] a reaction force (resisting linear movement/translation). [1] a reaction moment (resisting rotation). 6. explain why force diagrams are a useful tool for designers before physical prototyping begins. [5 marks] reveal markscheme [1] a force diagram lets a designer estimate where a structure will experience the greatest stress before anything is built. [1] it requires no complex software or physical materials — just a quick hand sketch. [1] it helps identify reaction forces at supports, checking that a proposed support arrangement is even viable. [1] it can reveal likely failure points early, before time and material are spent on a physical prototype. [1] it provides a foundation for more detailed later analysis, such as fea, saving time when a more complex simulation is eventually needed. 7. a designer is creating a diving board (a cantilevered beam) fixed at one end. using a force diagram, explain where the bending force is greatest along its length, and discuss how this should inform the material thickness at different points along the board. [8 marks] reveal markscheme [2] in a cantilever with the load at the free end, the bending force (bending moment) is zero at the free end and increases along the length of the board, reaching its maximum at the fixed end. [2] this is because the bending moment at any point equals the load multiplied by its distance from that point — the distance (and therefore the moment) is greatest at the fixed support. [2] the material should therefore be thickest/most reinforced near the fixed end, where bending stress is highest, and can be thinner near the free end, where stress is lowest. [2] this matches material to where it's structurally needed — reducing unnecessary material (and weight/cost) at the free end while ensuring the fixed end doesn't fail. credit reference to a tapered board profile as a real-world example of this principle. 3.2.5 safety factors ~50 min lesson 5: safety factors by the end of this lesson, you'll be able to: define safety factor (sf) and state its formula. calculate the safety factor of a structure given ultimate and working load data. justify an appropriate safety factor for a product based on its level of risk to users. no designer can predict every variable a product will face — sudden shocks, material defects, or user misuse. the safety factor is how you build a deliberate margin of error into a structure, ensuring it can withstand more than its expected everyday load. understanding how to select and justify an appropriate safety factor is central to responsible, user-focused design. key terms term working definition safety factor (sf) the ratio of how much load a structure can bear compared to its normal expected load. ultimate (maximum) load the greatest load a structure can withstand before it fails. allowable (working) load the load a structure is designed and expected to carry during normal use. contingency margin the additional reserve strength built into a design to account for unpredictable variables such as sudden loads, material defects, or misuse. practical engagement: calculating and justifying safety factors calculate the safety factor for a component with an ultimate load of 900 n and a working load of 300 n. show your working using the formula sf = ultimate load ÷ allowable load. for each of the following products, decide on an appropriate safety factor range and justify your choice by considering the consequences of failure: a passenger aircraft wing, an elevator cable, a children's swing set, a picture frame hook, a pedestrian bridge. debate in pairs: is it ever acceptable to reduce a safety factor to save material cost or weight? consider both commercial and ethical perspectives. extension: research the safety factor typically required by regulation or industry standard for one specific product category (e.g. climbing equipment, elevators, playground equipment) and compare it with your own estimate. multimedia resources factor of safety basics explained in 2 minutes video factor of safety with examples video factor of safety article — wikipedia exam practice multiple choice 1. the formula for safety factor is: working load ÷ ultimate load ultimate load ÷ working load ultimate load × working load ultimate load − working load reveal answer b — ultimate load ÷ working load. [1] 2. a safety factor of 1 means: the structure has ample reserve strength the structure can only just support its expected load, with no margin for error the structure will fail immediately under any load the structure is twice as strong as needed reveal answer b — the structure can only just support its expected load, with no margin for error. [1] 3. which product would typically require the highest safety factor? a wooden coat hook a plastic ruler a passenger aircraft wing a picture frame reveal answer c — a passenger aircraft wing. [1] the consequences of failure are catastrophic and life-threatening, demanding a high safety margin. 4. a component has an ultimate load of 900 n and is designed to work under a load of 300 n. calculate its safety factor. [2 marks] reveal markscheme [1] sf = ultimate load ÷ working load = 900 ÷ 300. [1] sf = 3. 5. state why furniture typically uses a lower safety factor (1.5–2.5) than a bridge (3–5+). [2 marks] reveal markscheme [1] the consequences of a furniture item failing are generally lower risk to human life than a bridge failing. [1] a bridge carries much higher, more variable and less predictable loads (traffic, crowds, weather) and its failure could be catastrophic and affect many people at once, justifying a much larger safety margin. 6. explain why designers build a safety factor into a structure rather than designing it to withstand exactly the expected working load. [5 marks] reveal markscheme [1] no designer can predict every variable a product will face in real use. [1] sudden or unexpected shocks/loads (e.g. dropping, overloading) can exceed the normal expected load. [1] material defects from manufacturing can make an individual component weaker than the ideal calculated strength. [1] user misuse (using a product in a way it wasn't intended for) can apply loads or conditions beyond the design brief. [1] designing to exactly the working load leaves no contingency margin for any of these factors, risking failure under real-world conditions. 7. a playground swing set is being redesigned. explain how the designer should determine an appropriate safety factor, and evaluate the consequences of selecting a safety factor that is too low compared with one that is unnecessarily high. [8 marks] reveal markscheme [2] the designer should consider the consequences of failure (children's safety, public/high-risk use), likely variability in load (multiple users, dynamic swinging forces, rough use) and relevant regulations/standards for playground equipment. [2] too low a safety factor: the structure may fail under realistic but unpredicted loads (e.g. several children swinging at once, a sudden jolt), risking injury — an unacceptable outcome for a product used by children. [2] too high a safety factor: the structure becomes unnecessarily heavy, uses more material, and increases manufacturing cost and environmental impact without a proportional safety benefit. [2] evaluation: the designer must balance user safety against cost, material use and sustainability — for a high-risk product like a swing set, err toward a higher safety factor within a sensible, standards-informed range rather than minimising cost. credit reference to relevant safety factor ranges or standards. b3.2 glossary consolidated glossary — topic b3.2 all key terms from the five lessons, in one place. click a term to reveal its definition. tension ib definition: a pulling force that stretches or elongates a material. real-world example: a backpack strap stretching under the weight of books. compression ib definition: a pushing/squashing force that shortens or crushes a material. real-world example: the legs of a chair compressing under a seated person's weight. bending force ib definition: a load applied a certain distance from a fixed position that causes a material to curve. real-world example: a shelf sagging in the middle when heavy books are placed away from the wall supports. shear ib definition: a force that causes two adjacent parts of a material to slide past one another in opposite directions. real-world example: scissor blades cutting through paper. torsion ib definition: a twisting force applied around the longitudinal axis of a material. real-world example: a screwdriver shaft twisting as it turns a stiff screw. structural system ib definition: the parts of a product that resist load, including shell, framework, or solid structures. real-world example: the tubular metal frame of a bicycle, which supports the rider's weight. struts ib definition: structural members or bracing designed specifically to resist compression. real-world example: bracing members in a roof truss that prevent long spans from sagging. lamination ib definition: bonding multiple layers of material together to increase strength and resistance to bending. real-world example: plywood, made from layers of wood glued together for extra strength and stability. young's modulus (e) ib definition: a measure of the stiffness of an elastic material, defined as tensile stress divided by tensile strain. real-world example: selecting steel for a skyscraper's frame because its high young's modulus minimises swaying in high winds. stress (σ) ib definition: the force applied per unit of cross-sectional area, measured in n/m² (pascals). real-world example: the stress in a climbing rope carrying a climber's body weight. strain (ε) ib definition: the ratio of the change in length to the original length; it has no units. real-world example: the stretch in a bungee cord expressed as a fraction of its unstretched length. stiffness ib definition: the resistance of a material to elastic (recoverable) deformation under an applied load. real-world example: a carbon-fibre bicycle frame that flexes very little when pedalled hard. elastic limit ib definition: the maximum stress a material can withstand while still returning to its original shape once the load is removed. real-world example: a rubber band that snaps back to shape after mild stretching, but not after being pulled too far. finite element analysis (fea) ib definition: digital model calculation and simulation of unknown factors in products using computer-aided design (cad) systems. real-world example: simulating stress distribution in a car frame during a crash to identify and reinforce weak points. overloading ib definition: applying a force to a structure that exceeds its designed working load. real-world example: too many passengers standing on one side of a small boat, causing it to capsize. stress concentration ib definition: a localised area of a structure where stress is significantly higher than in the surrounding material, often at sharp corners or holes. real-world example: cracks in a phone case starting at the sharp corner of the camera cut-out. lightweighting ib definition: removing material from low-stress areas of a structure, identified through analysis such as fea, to reduce weight and cost. real-world example: aircraft components thinned in low-stress zones to reduce fuel consumption. force diagram (free body diagram) ib definition: a simplified diagram showing all external forces acting on an isolated structure or component. real-world example: a sketch showing the load and reaction forces on a wall-mounted shelf. reaction force ib definition: a force exerted by a support in response to an applied load, keeping the structure in equilibrium. real-world example: the upward force from a table leg supporting the table's weight. cantilever ib definition: a structural member fixed and supported at only one end, with the other end free. real-world example: a diving board fixed at one end, projecting out over a pool. safety factor (sf) ib definition: the ratio of how much load a structure can bear compared to its normal expected load. real-world example: designing a bridge with an sf of 3 so it can support triple its intended maximum traffic load. ultimate (maximum) load ib definition: the greatest load a structure can withstand before it fails. real-world example: the point at which a rated climbing carabiner finally snaps under test conditions. allowable (working) load ib definition: the load a structure is designed and expected to carry during normal use. real-world example: the maximum recommended number of people for a lift, as stated on its safety plate. finite element analysis (fea) safety factor (sf) structural system young’s modulus tension compression bending force shear torsion struts lamination young's modulus (e) stress (σ) strain (ε) stiffness elastic limit overloading stress concentration lightweighting force diagram (free body diagram) reaction force cantilever ultimate (maximum) load allowable (working) load structures are present in the design of everyday products. young’s modulus is the measure of stiffness of a material. structures fail due to overloading, material choice, size and shape. forces acting on a structure or within a beam can be represented diagrammatically. safety factors (sfs) are a way to design in contingency to prevent failure from overloading a structure.

title: Mechanical systems application and selection

sections.title: Lesson 1: Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio & Efficiency
sections.html:
B3.3.1 Mechanical Advantage (MA) B3.3.2 Velocity Ratio (VR) B3.3.3 Efficiency ~150 min

Lesson 1: Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio & Efficiency

Topic A3.3 introduced how to calculate mechanical advantage for a mechanism in isolation. B3.3 asks a harder, more design-relevant question: given a real brief, which system should a designer specify, and why? This lesson revisits MA alongside two further calculations — velocity ratio and efficiency — and immediately puts each one to work justifying a real design decision.

Hook: From Calculating to Choosing

By the end of Topic B3.3 you will be able to: calculate MA, VR and efficiency for gear, pulley, belt and lever systems; explain how gear and belt systems control the speed, torque and direction of rotary motion; analyse cam profiles and construct simple displacement diagrams; classify lever systems and apply the principle of moments; and — the skill this topic is really about — given a real design brief, select and justify an appropriate mechanical system. Every calculation in this unit exists to serve that final skill.

1. Mechanical Advantage (MA)

Mechanical Advantage

Definition: The factor by which a mechanism multiplies an input effort force to move a load (resistance). It tells a designer how much "easier" a task becomes when a mechanism is introduced between the user and the job to be done.

Context: An MA greater than 1 means the mechanism is multiplying force (good for lifting or gripping); an MA less than 1 means it is trading force for speed or reach instead.

Materials/Examples: Levers, gear trains, pulleys, winches, geared hand tools.

Application: Design consideration: a high MA on paper is worthless if the mechanism is unreliable. A good designer balances MA against friction, added weight, material strength and manufacturing cost to make sure the theoretical advantage survives real-world use.

How MA is found:
  • Gears: MA = teeth on driven gear ÷ teeth on driver gear.
  • Pulleys: MA = number of rope sections supporting the load (a block-and-tackle with 4 supporting ropes has an MA of 4).
  • Levers: MA = length of the effort arm ÷ length of the load arm.

Case Study: Fiskars PowerGear2™ Bypass Pruners

Standard bypass pruning shears are a simple 1st class lever — fine for thin stems, but gardeners with weaker grip strength struggle to cut anything thicker than a pencil. Fiskars redesigned the tool around a compound gear-and-cam mechanism built into the pivot, rather than relying on the handle-arm length alone.

As the handles close, an internal gear track rotates a cam that keeps re-engaging at a mechanically favourable point throughout the cut — Fiskars markets this as delivering up to three times more cutting power than a standard bypass pruner of the same handle length, without needing longer (heavier, harder to control) handles.

Why this system? A gear/cam mechanism packs a high, changing MA into a compact, single-hand tool — something a simple lever geometry alone could not do without making the tool unwieldy. It is a clear example of choosing a mechanism to meet a human-factors constraint (limited hand strength), not just a mechanical one.

Learn more: Fiskars PowerGear™ technology

Worked Example — Compound Lever Pruners: A pruner's compound lever has an effort arm of 160 mm (the handle, measured from the pivot) and a load arm of 20 mm (the blade edge, measured from the same pivot).
MA = Effort arm ÷ Load arm = 160 ÷ 20 = 8
A hand force of just 25 N at the handle therefore produces roughly 200 N of cutting force at the blade — enough to shear through a 15 mm branch that would be impossible to cut with bare secateurs of ordinary leverage.

Your Turn: Design Decision — An Accessible Jar Opener

A client with arthritis in her hands is your target user for the IA. Grip-strength testing shows she can comfortably and safely apply about 15 N of turning force. Lab testing shows a typical stuck jar lid needs about 45 N of turning force at the lid edge to break the vacuum seal.

  1. Calculate the minimum MA the mechanism must provide for your client to open the jar unaided.
  2. Two candidate concepts are on your desk: (a) a long-handled strap wrench, with an effort arm of 180 mm and an effective load arm of 40 mm at the lid; (b) a rotating gear-and-ratchet jar opener that clamps around the lid. Calculate the MA of concept (a). Does it meet the requirement from Q1?
  3. Which system would you select — the lever-based strap wrench or a gear-based rotating opener — for this client? Justify your choice using MA, but also ergonomics, one-handed operation, and the effect of friction between the tool and a wet or textured lid.
Reveal Model Answer

1. Minimum MA = Load ÷ Effort = 45 N ÷ 15 N = 3.

2. MA of the strap wrench = 180 ÷ 40 = 4.5. Since 4.5 > 3, it meets the minimum requirement on paper.

3. Either could be argued, but the gear-and-ratchet opener is often the stronger choice for this client: it clamps and turns with a squeezing or ratcheting action rather than requiring a sustained, precise gripping-and-twisting motion, so it needs less fine motor control from arthritic hands and can be operated one-handed. Its toothed grip also bites into a wet or textured lid more reliably than a smooth strap, whose effective friction — and therefore its real MA — can drop sharply if the lid is damp, echoing the 3.3.1 design consideration that a high MA on paper is worthless if the mechanism is unreliable in real-world conditions.

2. Velocity Ratio (VR)

Velocity Ratio

Definition: Compares how far, or how fast, the input (effort) and output (load) of a mechanism move relative to each other. It is a ratio of distances or speeds, not forces.

Context: For gears, use the number of teeth on the driven and driver gears; for pulleys and belts, use the diameters of the wheels.

Materials/Examples: Gear trains, pulley-and-belt systems, bicycle cassettes.

Application: Rule of thumb: a higher VR gives lower speed but higher torque at the output — exactly what a climbing gear on a bicycle, or the low gear on a winch, is for.

Formula: VR = Teeth on driven gear ÷ Teeth on driver gear  (or, for pulleys/belts, Diameter of driven wheel ÷ Diameter of driver wheel)

Case Study: Shimano™ Bicycle Derailleur Gearing

A road cyclist reaching a steep hill does not pedal harder — they change gear. Shifting to a smaller chainring at the front and a larger sprocket at the back changes the velocity ratio between the pedals (driver) and the rear wheel (driven, via the sprocket).

Climbing gear: 34-tooth chainring, 32-tooth sprocket → VR = 32 ÷ 34 ≈ 0.94. A high VR: each pedal stroke moves the bike only a short distance, but with much less resistance felt at the pedals — ideal for a steep gradient.

Sprint gear: 50-tooth chainring, 11-tooth sprocket → VR = 11 ÷ 50 = 0.22. A low VR: the wheel travels much further per pedal stroke, trading torque for road speed on flat, fast sections.

Why this system? A cassette of 8–12 sprockets lets one rider access a huge range of VR values on demand, rather than needing a different fixed-ratio bike for hills versus flats — a clear case of selecting a system (variable gearing) because the use-context changes minute to minute.

Watch: How Gears Work — 3D Animation.

Worked Example — A Simple Gear Train: A workshop hoist has a driver gear with 60 teeth turning a driven gear with 20 teeth.
VR = Teeth on driven ÷ Teeth on driver = 20 ÷ 60 = 0.33
A VR below 1 means the driven gear turns faster than the driver — here, three times faster (1 ÷ 0.33) for every single turn of the driver. This confirms the rule from 3.3.4: a large driver turning a small driven gear increases output speed.

Your Turn: Design Decision — A Hand-Crank Emergency Radio

Inventor Trevor Baylis's wind-up radio concept — commercialised as the BayGen Freeplay — let users in areas without reliable electricity power a radio by turning a hand crank. The crank must turn a small generator (dynamo) shaft fast to produce a usable voltage, far faster than a hand can comfortably crank it directly.

  1. A single gear stage connects a 15-tooth driver gear (fixed to the hand crank) to a 5-tooth driven gear (fixed to the dynamo shaft). Calculate the VR, and state how many times the dynamo shaft spins for every one turn of the crank.
  2. Testing shows the dynamo needs to spin at least 20 times faster than the crank to charge the internal battery effectively. Does the single gear stage in Q1 meet this? If not, propose and calculate a two-stage (compound) gear train — using two gear pairs in sequence — that achieves at least a 20:1 speed increase.
  3. Why might a designer choose a multi-stage gear train over a single very small driven gear (e.g. a 15-tooth driver against a 0.75-tooth driven gear, which is not physically possible) to achieve a large VR? Consider gear tooth strength and manufacturing limits.
Reveal Model Answer

1. VR = 5 ÷ 15 = 0.33. The dynamo shaft spins 1 ÷ 0.33 = 3 times for every one turn of the crank.

2. No — 3× is far short of the 20× required. A two-stage train of, for example, a 15-tooth driver to a 3-tooth driven gear in each stage (VR = 3 ÷ 15 = 0.2, i.e. a 5× speed increase per stage) gives an overall increase of 5 × 5 = 25×, comfortably exceeding the 20:1 requirement.

3. Gears with very few teeth become structurally weak (the tooth profile becomes "undercut") and are difficult or impossible to manufacture reliably below a practical minimum tooth count. Splitting a large ratio across two moderate, physically realistic stages achieves the same overall speed increase while keeping every gear strong enough to survive repeated use.

3. Efficiency

Efficiency

Definition: Measures how much of the energy put into a system comes out as useful work, after losses to friction, heat, noise or slippage are accounted for. No real mechanism is 100% efficient.

Context: Because friction is what makes a mechanism's real MA fall short of its ideal, theoretical VR, comparing the two gives a quick estimate of efficiency without needing to measure energy directly.

Materials/Examples: Gear trains, belt drives, pulley systems, lever mechanisms.

Application: Improving efficiency: designers reduce energy loss with lubricants, precise alignment, belt/chain tensioners, sealed bearings, or higher-quality (lower-friction, more dimensionally stable) materials.

Formula: Efficiency = (Output energy ÷ Input energy) × 100%
Shortcut (gear/lever/pulley systems): Efficiency ≈ (MA ÷ VR) × 100% — because friction is exactly what makes real MA fall short of the ideal (VR) value, comparing the two gives a fast estimate of efficiency without measuring energy directly.

Case Study: Chain vs. Gates Carbon Belt™ Drive on Bicycles

For over a century almost every bicycle used a steel roller chain, because a well-lubricated chain is extremely efficient — independent lab testing puts a clean, waxed chain at around 98–99% efficient. That efficiency is exactly why racing bikes still use chains: at professional level, a 1–2% power loss is worth avoiding.

But a chain's efficiency depends on it staying clean and lubricated — grit, rain and rust drag it down fast. This is why many commuter and bike-share bicycles now use a carbon-fibre belt drive instead: it needs no oil, doesn't rust, resists dirt, and lasts several times longer than a chain, even though a belt can run marginally less efficient than a pristine, freshly-lubed chain.

Why this system? The choice isn't simply "which is more efficient" — it is which efficiency loss a designer can live with. A racing team chases every fraction of a percent; a bike-share operator trades a small, stable efficiency figure for near-zero maintenance across thousands of bikes.

Read: Are Belt Drivetrains More Efficient Than Chain Drivetrains? (Lab Testing)

Worked Example — Electric Scooter Motor: An e-scooter's hub motor draws 250 W of electrical input power. A dynamometer measures 227.5 W of useful mechanical power actually delivered to the wheel.
Efficiency = (227.5 ÷ 250) × 100 = 91%
The missing 9% is lost mainly as heat in the motor windings and friction in the bearings — which is why the motor casing gets warm after a long ride.

Your Turn: Design Decision — Drivetrain for a City Bike-Share Fleet

You are advising two very different clients. Client A: a city bike-share operator with 5,000 bicycles, parked outdoors year-round, serviced only twice a year, ridden mostly on flat urban streets by casual users. Client B: a track cycling team preparing a bike for a velodrome time trial, where the bike is serviced daily and marginal power gains decide medals.

  1. For each client, recommend a chain-drive or belt-drive system, and justify your choice using efficiency, maintenance frequency, weather exposure, and weight.
  2. A belt-drive test rig measures an MA of 3.8 against a VR of 4.0 for its pulley system. Use the MA ÷ VR shortcut to estimate its efficiency, and comment on whether this supports your recommendation for Client A.
Reveal Model Answer

1. Client A: a belt drive — it needs no lubrication, resists rain, dirt and rust, and lasts far longer between services, which directly cuts the cost of maintaining 5,000 outdoor bikes serviced only twice a year. Client B: a chain drive — a clean, daily-serviced chain reaches a slightly higher efficiency (98–99% vs. a belt's marginally lower figure), and at professional level that small margin can decide a race, while daily servicing removes the chain's usual maintenance disadvantage.

2. Efficiency ≈ (MA ÷ VR) × 100% = (3.8 ÷ 4.0) × 100% = 95%. This is a high efficiency figure, supporting the Client A recommendation: the small ~5% energy loss is a reasonable trade for near-zero maintenance and weather resistance across a large outdoor fleet.

Client B: a chain drive — a clean, daily-serviced chain reaches a slightly higher efficiency (98–99% vs. a belt's marginally lower figure), and at professional level that small margin can decide a race, while daily servicing removes the chain's usual maintenance disadvantage.

2. Efficiency ≈ (MA ÷ VR) × 100% = (3.8 ÷ 4.0) × 100% = 95%. This is a high efficiency figure, supporting the Client A recommendation: the small ~5% energy loss is a reasonable trade for near-zero maintenance and weather resistance across a large outdoor fleet.
