B3.3.4 Rotary Motion: Speed & Direction B3.3.5 Cams and Followers ~120 min

Lesson 2: Controlling Rotary Motion & Cam Systems

Gear and belt systems don't just transmit rotary motion — designers manipulate them deliberately to change its speed, torque and direction to suit a specific task. Cams take that manipulation a step further, converting continuous rotation into precisely timed reciprocating movement.

1. Manipulating Rotary Motion

Speed, Torque & Direction Control

Definition: The deliberate use of gear or pulley size and arrangement to change a rotary output's speed, torque or direction relative to its input.

Context: The same physical gear train can be arranged to prioritise speed, torque, or a change of direction, depending entirely on which gear the designer chooses as driver and which as driven.

Materials/Examples: Gearboxes, pulley-and-belt drives, idler gears, crossed belts.

Application: Selecting the right arrangement is a core AO2 design-technology skill — the same components, arranged differently, serve completely different purposes.

  • Increasing speed: a large driver gear turns a smaller driven gear (the driven gear spins faster, with less torque).
  • Increasing torque: a small driver gear turns a larger driven gear (the driven gear spins slower, with more force).
  • Reversing direction: insert an idler gear between the driver and driven gear (gears mesh in pairs, so each mesh flips rotation direction — an idler flips it back), or cross a belt in a pulley system.

Case Study: Two-Speed Cordless Drill/Driver Gearbox

A cordless drill/driver has a small switch marked "1" and "2" that changes an internal planetary gear train — engineers designed this because drilling and driving screws have opposite mechanical requirements.

Gear 1 (low): a large gear reduction between motor and chuck. Output speed is low, but torque is high — needed to drive a long screw into hardwood without stalling the motor or stripping the screw head.

Gear 2 (high): a smaller gear reduction. Output speed is high, torque is lower — ideal for quickly drilling a clean hole in thin material, where high torque is not the limiting factor.

Why this system? A single fixed gear ratio would compromise both tasks. Two selectable ratios let one motor serve two very different jobs — a direct, everyday example of choosing VR to match torque and speed to the task, not just to the motor's natural output.

Worked Example — Gear Ratios for Speed vs. Torque:
Drill gear 1 (low): 12-tooth driver, 48-tooth driven → VR = 48 ÷ 12 = 4. High VR: torque is multiplied roughly 4×, speed is quartered.
Drill gear 2 (high): 12-tooth driver, 16-tooth driven → VR = 16 ÷ 12 ≈ 1.33. Lower VR: less torque multiplication, closer to the motor's natural speed.
Reversing direction: fitting a 20-tooth idler gear between the 12-tooth driver and 48-tooth driven gear does not change the VR calculation (idlers are not counted in the ratio) — it only flips the direction of the output shaft, exactly as a car's reverse gear uses an idler to send the output the opposite way to the engine's fixed rotation direction.

Your Turn: Design Decision — A Powered Wheelchair Drivetrain

Your client's motor has a no-load speed of 3000 rpm and delivers 0.5 Nm of torque at the motor shaft. The design brief requires: enough torque at the wheels to climb a standard 1:12 accessibility ramp, which testing shows needs at least 15 Nm at the wheel; and a comfortable top speed on flat pavement, corresponding to a wheel speed of around 40 rpm.

  1. Calculate the torque multiplication (VR) needed to satisfy the ramp requirement (15 ÷ 0.5).
  2. Calculate the speed reduction (VR) needed to bring the wheel down to 40 rpm from the motor's 3000 rpm.
  3. Compare your two answers. Can a single fixed gear ratio satisfy both the ramp-climbing torque and the flat-ground speed target? If not, would you propose a two-speed gearbox (like the drill above), or an electronic motor controller that varies current instead of using a mechanical ratio change? Justify your choice, linking to B3.4 (electronic systems).
Reveal Model Answer

1. Torque ratio needed = 15 ÷ 0.5 = 30:1.

2. Speed reduction needed = 3000 ÷ 40 = 75:1.

3. Because 75:1 is greater than the 30:1 minimum, gearing purely for the flat-ground speed target (75:1) automatically delivers more than enough torque for the ramp (0.5 × 75 = 37.5 Nm > 15 Nm needed), so a single fixed-ratio gearbox can technically satisfy both requirements. However, many designers would still favour a two-speed gearbox, or better, an electronic motor controller that varies current to adjust torque and speed on demand (linking to B3.4): this avoids permanently carrying unnecessary torque headroom, allows finer real-time control between "ramp mode" and "cruise mode," and accounts for the fact that a real motor's available torque changes with load and speed, unlike the idealised no-load figures given here.

2. Cams and Followers

Cam and Follower

Definition: Cams convert continuous rotary motion into reciprocating motion (repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down movement) through a follower that rides on the cam's edge, or cam profile.

Context: Designers describe a follower's motion in three phases across one rotation of the cam: rise, dwell and fall.

Materials/Examples: Camshafts, automatic dispensing mechanisms, sewing machine feed dogs, pear/snail/eccentric cam profiles.

Application: Chosen whenever a repeating, precisely-timed reciprocating movement — including genuine pauses — must be driven from a continuously rotating shaft.

  • Rise: the follower is pushed outward/upward as the cam profile radius increases.
  • Dwell: the follower stays still while the cam profile radius is momentarily constant.
  • Fall: the follower drops back as the profile radius decreases (often helped by gravity or a return spring).

Displacement diagrams plot follower displacement (y-axis) against the cam's angle of rotation, 0°–360° (x-axis). Before a cam profile is ever cut, engineers plan the exact timing of rise, dwell and fall on this diagram — it is the cam's motion "blueprint."

Case Study: The Car Engine Camshaft

Inside a petrol or diesel engine, a rotating camshaft opens and closes the intake and exhaust valves at exactly the right moment in each cylinder's four-stroke cycle — get the timing wrong by even a few degrees and engine performance and emissions suffer badly.

Each lobe on the camshaft is a precision cam profile: the rise opens the valve, a brief dwell holds it fully open, and the fall (assisted by a valve spring) snaps it shut. Engineers use displacement diagrams to plan valve "duration" and "overlap" — how long each valve stays open and how much the intake and exhaust valves overlap being open together — because this directly affects power, fuel economy and emissions.

Why this system? A cam-driven valvetrain guarantees the exact same, repeatable, high-speed timing thousands of times per minute — something no human-operated or simple crank-driven system could achieve reliably at engine speeds.

Watch: How Do Cam and Follower Mechanisms Work?

Worked Example — Reading a Displacement Diagram: A cam completes rise over 0°–60°, dwell (open) over 60°–120°, fall over 120°–180°, and dwell (closed) over 180°–360°.
If the cam rotates at 30 rpm (0.5 revolutions per second), one full rotation takes 2 seconds. The follower is therefore held open for (120° − 60°) ÷ 360° × 2 s ≈ 0.33 seconds, and closed for (360° − 180°) ÷ 360° × 2 s = 1 second before the next rise begins.

Discussion: Designing a Dwell

A circular (eccentric) cam gives smooth, continuous follower motion with no true dwell at all. Why might a designer deliberately choose an irregular profile — a pear or snail shape — instead, even though it is harder and more expensive to manufacture precisely?

Your Turn: Design Decision — An Automatic Pet Feeder

A motor rotates a cam once every 8 hours to release one measured portion of food, three times a day. The mechanism must: stay closed and store food for a long period; then rise quickly to open a dispensing flap for about 2 seconds; hold the flap open (dwell) for 3 seconds so food can fall through; then fall quickly to close and stay closed until the next 8-hour cycle.

  1. Sketch (in words or as a simple diagram) the shape of the displacement diagram this cam needs, labelling the rise, dwell (open), fall and dwell (closed) sections and their approximate angular ranges.
  2. Two cam-profile types are available: a circular (eccentric) cam, which gives smooth, continuous motion with no dwell period at all; and a pear/snail-shaped cam, which can be profiled to include a genuine dwell. Which would you choose for this feeder, and why?
  3. What risk is there for the pet (and the mechanism) if the fall phase is too slow, or if the follower does not fully return during the long "closed" dwell?
Reveal Model Answer

1. The full cycle (8 hours = 28,800 seconds) is represented by the full 0–360° rotation, but the active phases (rise ~2 s, open dwell 3 s, fall ~2 s ≈ 7 s total) occupy only a tiny fraction of that — roughly 0.02% of the rotation. The displacement diagram is therefore an almost flat line at "closed" for nearly the entire 360°, with a very narrow spike showing a sharp rise, a brief open dwell, and a sharp fall clustered together at one point in the rotation.

2. The pear/snail-shaped cam. It can be profiled to include a genuine dwell (a constant-radius section) at both the open and closed positions, which the feeder needs to hold the flap open long enough for food to fall through and closed for the rest of the cycle. A circular cam gives continuous motion with no true dwell, so the flap would never reliably stay fully open or fully closed.

3. A slow fall, or a follower that doesn't fully return, could leave the flap slightly open during the long closed dwell — risking pests or moisture reaching the stored food, food spoilage, or food continuing to trickle out and overfeeding the pet. Repeated imperfect seating of the follower could also accelerate wear and eventually cause the mechanism to jam.

Reversing DirectionIdler gear, or a crossed beltA car's reverse gear idler
Rise / Dwell / FallThe three phases of follower motion in one cam rotationAn engine valve opening, holding, and closing

sections.title: Lesson 3: Levers, Moments & Applying Mechanical Systems
sections.html:
B3.3.6 Levers and Moments Synthesis & Linking Questions ~90 min

Lesson 3: Levers, Moments & Applying Mechanical Systems

A lever is one of the oldest mechanisms known, magnifying force through the placement of three points: the fulcrum (pivot), the load (resistance to be moved), and the effort (input force). This final lesson formalises lever classification and the principle of moments, then steps back to connect the whole of B3.3 to the rest of the syllabus — and to the IA.

1. Lever Classes

Lever

Definition: A rigid bar pivoting on a fulcrum, with effort applied to move a load. Its class depends on where the fulcrum sits relative to the load and effort.

Context: The same three-point arrangement — fulcrum, load, effort — can be reordered in three ways, and each ordering suits a different design purpose.

Materials/Examples: Scissors, wheelbarrows, tweezers, crowbars, the human forearm.

Application: MA = length of the effort arm ÷ length of the load arm, for any lever class.

ClassArrangementReal-World Example
1st classFulcrum is between the effort and the load.Scissors, a see-saw, a claw hammer removing a nail.
2nd classLoad is between the fulcrum and the effort.A wheelbarrow — the wheel is the fulcrum, the load sits in the middle, effort is at the handles.
3rd classEffort is between the fulcrum and the load.Tweezers, a fishing rod, the human forearm (elbow = fulcrum, biceps = effort, hand = load).

Case Study: 3rd-Class Lever Design in Prosthetic Limbs

The human forearm is a natural 3rd class lever: the elbow (fulcrum) is at one end, the biceps (effort) pulls close to the elbow, and the hand (load) is far away. This is mechanically "inefficient" (MA is always less than 1 — the biceps must pull much harder than the weight held in the hand) but it buys something more valuable: speed and range of movement at the hand for only a small muscle contraction.

Prosthetics engineers deliberately copy this 3rd class arrangement in running blades (such as Össur's Flex-Foot Cheetah) and body-powered prosthetic hands: replicating the lever class of the limb being replaced means the device moves and "feels" the way the user's brain and remaining muscles already expect, rather than fighting against decades of learned motion.

Why this system? This is a case where a designer deliberately chooses a mechanically "weak" (MA < 1) lever class, because matching natural human biomechanics is more important than maximising force multiplication — a strong reminder that MA is never the only design criterion.

Worked Example — Wheelbarrow (2nd Class Lever): A wheelbarrow's wheel axle (fulcrum) sits 0.25 m from the centre of the load; the effort is applied at the handles, 1.15 m from the fulcrum.
MA = Effort arm ÷ Load arm = 1.15 ÷ 0.25 = 4.6
A gardener lifting a 200 N load of soil only needs to apply about 43 N at the handles (200 ÷ 4.6) — the 2nd class arrangement (load between fulcrum and effort) is exactly what makes wheelbarrows liftable by one person.

Your Turn: Design Decision — A Foot-Pedal Bin Lid

You are designing a step-on pedal mechanism to lift a bin lid weighing an equivalent of 6 N at the hinge, measured 90 mm from the hinge (fulcrum). The foot pedal will be positioned 220 mm from the hinge, on the opposite side of the mechanism to the lid.

  1. Identify the class of lever this arrangement represents (consider where the fulcrum, load and effort each sit).
  2. Calculate the MA of this pedal system, and the force a user's foot must apply to lift the lid.
  3. A wheelchair-using client finds the pedal hard to reach and needs the required foot force reduced further. Propose one specific dimensional change to the mechanism, and recalculate the MA and required force to show the improvement.
Reveal Model Answer

1. 1st class lever — the fulcrum (hinge) sits between the load (lid, 90 mm to one side) and the effort (pedal, 220 mm to the other side).

2. MA = Effort arm ÷ Load arm = 220 ÷ 90 = 2.44. Required foot force = Load ÷ MA = 6 ÷ 2.44 ≈ 2.5 N.

3. Extending the pedal's distance from the hinge, e.g. to 350 mm, gives MA = 350 ÷ 90 ≈ 3.89, reducing the required foot force to 6 ÷ 3.89 ≈ 1.5 N — a meaningfully lighter action for a user with reduced leg strength or reach, at the cost of a longer, more space-consuming pedal arm.

2. Moments

Moments

Definition: A lever balances (or moves) according to the principle that moment = force × distance from the fulcrum.

Context: This is the physical reasoning behind the MA formula in 3.3.1 — a longer effort arm creates a larger moment for the same force, which is why MA = effort arm ÷ load arm.

Materials/Examples: Spanners, see-saws, torque wrenches.

Application: Pushing at the very end of a long spanner handle, rather than near its head, creates a larger moment for the same applied force — the everyday intuition that underlies every lever calculation in this unit.

Synthesis and Linking Questions

Use these as discussion prompts, exit tickets, or extension tasks to connect B3.3 to other parts of the DP Design Technology course — exactly the kind of cross-topic reasoning that Paper 1 and Paper 2 long-answer questions reward.

C1.2 Inclusive Design: How does mechanical advantage enable an inclusive design strategy for elderly or impaired users? (e.g. reducing the force required to open a heavy door.)
B3.1 Material Selection: Why is it critical to select appropriate materials (like hardened steel for gears) so that mechanisms operate at full functionality over a long period?
B2.2 Modelling: To what extent can mechanical systems be effectively mocked up and tested using low-fidelity physical prototypes or CAD simulations?
B3.4 Electronics: How can mechanical systems be combined with electronic systems (sensors and microcontrollers) to create convergent technologies like robotics?

Teaching Note: Alignment with the Internal Assessment (IA)

The six "Your Turn" design-decision scenarios in this topic are written in the same voice as an IA justification paragraph — an MA/VR/efficiency calculation, followed by a reasoned system choice. Consider having students convert one scenario answer directly into IA Criterion D prose as a modelling exercise.

  • Criterion C (Ideation): If applicable to the product being redesigned, students must apply knowledge of mechanical systems to develop feasible ideas and functional models.
  • Criterion D (Designing): Students must present detailed applications of mechanical systems, including technical drawings and justified component choices, to communicate the final solution to a third-party manufacturer.

sections.title: Exam Practice: Topic B3.3
sections.html:
B3.3 Exam Practice AO1 / AO2 / AO3

Exam Practice: Topic B3.3

Three multiple-choice questions, two short-answer questions and two long-answer (extended-response) questions, calibrated to the command terms and Paper 1/Paper 2 style used in the IB DT specimen papers. Sample/indicative answers for teacher use follow each question.

Section A: Multiple Choice (3 questions, 1 mark each)

Question 1 — context: A popular stand mixer, such as the KitchenAid Artisan™, uses an internal gear system between the motor and the beater shaft. This gear system causes the beater to spin on its own axis while also orbiting in a circle around the mixing bowl (a planetary gear arrangement) — a much slower rotation than the motor itself produces.

1(a). What is the primary purpose of the gear system fitted between the motor and the beater shaft?

  • To decrease torque and increase rotational speed
  • To reverse the direction of rotation only
  • To increase torque while reducing rotational speed
  • To convert rotary motion into reciprocating motion
Reveal Answer
C. To increase torque while reducing rotational speed. A gear reduction between a fast motor and a slow beater shaft always trades speed for torque — that torque is what lets the mixer work thick dough. [1]

1(b). Which material property is most important when selecting the alloy used to manufacture the mixer's internal gears?

  • Optical transparency
  • Hardness and wear resistance
  • Thermal expansion coefficient
  • Electrical conductivity
Reveal Answer
B. Hardness and wear resistance. Gears mesh under repeated, high load — hardness and wear resistance (not conductivity or transparency) determine whether the teeth survive years of use. [1]

1(c). A planetary gear system, as used in this mixer, causes the beater to:

  • Rotate on its own axis only
  • Orbit around the bowl only
  • Both rotate on its own axis and orbit around the bowl
  • Move in a straight reciprocating line
Reveal Answer
C. Both rotate on its own axis and orbit around the bowl. That combined spin-and-orbit motion is the defining feature of a planetary gear train, and is exactly why it achieves thorough bowl coverage. [1]

Section B: Short Answer (2 questions)

Question 2 [2 marks]

Describe how a rear derailleur gear system on a road bicycle allows a cyclist to select an appropriate gear ratio when climbing a steep hill.

Reveal Answer

[2] Command term Describe (Action + Mechanism + Result): shifting to a smaller chainring and/or larger rear sprocket (Action) increases the velocity ratio between pedals and rear wheel (Mechanism), so each pedal stroke needs less force even though the bike covers less distance per stroke (Result). 1 mark for identifying the gear change; 1 mark for linking it to reduced effort/increased VR.

Question 3 [4 marks]

A wheelbarrow has its wheel axle (fulcrum) positioned 0.25 m from the centre of the load, and the effort is applied at the handles, 1.15 m from the fulcrum.

  • (a) Identify the class of lever demonstrated by a wheelbarrow. [1]
  • (b) Calculate the mechanical advantage of this wheelbarrow system. [2]
  • (c) State one design reason why a wheelbarrow uses this lever class rather than a 1st class arrangement. [1]
Reveal Answer

(a) 2nd class lever. [1]

(b) MA = 1.15 ÷ 0.25 = 4.6. 1 mark for correct substitution, 1 mark for the correct answer. [2]

(c) Any reasonable justification, e.g. "the load sits close to the fulcrum/wheel, so a single person can lift a heavy load with a comparatively small effort force at the handles." [1]

Section C: Long Answer (2 questions)

Question 4 [6 marks]

Evaluate the choice of a belt-drive system over a traditional chain-drive system for a fleet of 5,000 public bike-share bicycles used outdoors year-round.

Reveal Answer

[6] Command term Evaluate (Strength/Opportunity, Limitation/Threat, Comparison, Synthesis/Conclusion):

Strength: belt drives need no lubrication, resist rain, dirt and rust, and last far longer between services than a chain — directly reducing the operating cost of servicing 5,000 outdoor bikes only twice a year.

Limitation: a belt drive can be marginally less efficient than a perfectly clean, lubricated chain, and typically requires a splittable frame to fit at all.

Comparison: a chain would need frequent cleaning/oiling to avoid rust and wear in an outdoor, low-maintenance context — the opposite of what a bike-share fleet needs.

Synthesis: for this specific context (outdoor, high-use, minimal servicing), the small efficiency trade-off is outweighed by drastically lower maintenance costs and downtime, so a belt drive is the more suitable system — though a professional racing team, prioritising marginal performance gains under daily maintenance, would reasonably choose the opposite.

Question 5 [6 marks]

Justify the use of a cam-and-follower mechanism, rather than a simple continuously-rotating motor and flap, in the design of an automatic pet feeder that must open briefly at three fixed times each day.

Reveal Answer

[6] Command term Justify (Point, Evidence/Mechanism, Consequence/Impact):

Point: the feeder must stay firmly closed for long dwell periods (storing food safely, keeping pests out) and open only briefly and repeatably at three exact times.

Evidence/Mechanism: a cam profile can be shaped to include genuine dwell periods (a constant-radius section) at both the open and closed positions, which a simple continuously-rotating flap or basic crank cannot reliably provide without added electronic timing.

Impact/Justification: because the cam's rise/dwell/fall timing is fixed mechanically in the shape of the profile itself, the feeder repeats the same precise open/close cycle every rotation without relying on additional sensors or software — a robust, low-cost, low-power solution appropriate for a simple consumer product.

Full marks require a balanced or extended point, e.g. briefly noting a limitation (the fixed profile cannot easily change portion size/timing without physically changing the cam) to reach the top of the mark band.

sections.title: Glossary: Topic B3.3 — Mechanical Systems: Application and Selection
sections.html:
B3.3 Glossary

Glossary: Topic B3.3 — Mechanical Systems: Application and Selection

Every key term used across 3.3.1–3.3.6, with its IB-style definition and a real-world example drawn from the case studies and scenarios in this topic. Click on a term to reveal its definition.

Mechanical advantage (MA)
IB Definition: The ratio of output (load) force to input (effort) force in a mechanical system.
Real-World Example: A long-handled crowbar lifting a heavy paving stone with minimal hand force.
Velocity ratio (VR)
IB Definition: The ratio of the distance (or speed) moved by the effort to the distance (or speed) moved by the load.
Real-World Example: Calculating how many times a bicycle's rear wheel turns for each single turn of the pedals.
Efficiency
IB Definition: The percentage of input energy converted into useful output work, after losses to friction, heat or slippage.
Real-World Example: A belt-driven bicycle losing a small percentage of pedalling power to belt flex, compared with a lubricated chain.
Driver (gear/pulley)
IB Definition: The gear or pulley that receives the input effort and drives the rest of the system.
Real-World Example: The chainring on a bicycle, turned directly by the pedals.
Driven (gear/pulley)
IB Definition: The gear or pulley that receives motion from the driver and produces the output.
Real-World Example: The rear sprocket on a bicycle cassette, turned by the chain from the chainring.
Idler gear
IB Definition: A gear placed between the driver and driven gear that reverses output direction without changing the velocity ratio.
Real-World Example: The gear used in a car's manual gearbox to provide reverse without reversing the engine itself.
Gear-driven system
IB Definition: A system transmitting power from a driver to a driven part using interlocking gears.
Real-World Example: A bicycle's internal hub gears, or a cordless drill's two-speed gearbox.
Belt-driven system
IB Definition: A drive system where a belt transfers power between at least two pulleys.
Real-World Example: A washing machine's motor turning the drum via a belt, which absorbs shock and runs quietly.
Pulley system (block and tackle)
IB Definition: A system of one or more pulleys and a rope, where MA depends on the number of rope sections supporting the load.
Real-World Example: A four-rope block and tackle used to lift a car engine out of its bay with an MA of 4.
Torque
IB Definition: A rotational (twisting) force that causes an object to rotate about an axis.
Real-World Example: The high torque delivered by a drill's low gear setting when driving a long screw into hardwood.
Cam
IB Definition: A mechanical component that transforms rotary motion into reciprocating (linear, back-and-forth) motion.
Real-World Example: The camshaft lobes inside a car engine that open and close the intake and exhaust valves.
Follower
IB Definition: The component that rests against a cam's profile and moves as the cam rotates beneath it.
Real-World Example: The valve stem pushed open and released by a rotating camshaft lobe.
Cam profile
IB Definition: The precise outline shape of a cam, which determines the timing and pattern of the follower's motion.
Real-World Example: A pear/snail-shaped cam profile chosen to give a pet feeder a true dwell period while its flap stays open.
Displacement diagram
IB Definition: A graph plotting a follower's displacement against the cam's angle of rotation (0°–360°), used to plan motion timing.
Real-World Example: An engineer plotting valve rise, dwell and fall against crankshaft angle before cutting a camshaft.
Rise / dwell / fall
IB Definition: The three phases of follower motion: moving outward (rise), staying still (dwell), and returning (fall).
Real-World Example: A pet feeder flap that rises to open, dwells briefly so food can drop, then falls to close again.
Reciprocating motion
IB Definition: Repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down linear motion.
Real-World Example: The up-and-down motion of an engine valve, produced from the camshaft's continuous rotation.
Lever
IB Definition: A rigid bar that pivots about a fulcrum to magnify an effort force acting on a load.
Real-World Example: A pair of scissors (1st class), a wheelbarrow (2nd class), or a fishing rod (3rd class).
Fulcrum
IB Definition: The fixed pivot point about which a lever rotates.
Real-World Example: The wheel axle of a wheelbarrow, or the elbow joint in a human forearm.
1st class lever
IB Definition: A lever arrangement where the fulcrum sits between the effort and the load.
Real-World Example: A pair of scissors, or a see-saw.
2nd class lever
IB Definition: A lever arrangement where the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort.
Real-World Example: A wheelbarrow, where the load sits between the wheel (fulcrum) and the handles (effort).
3rd class lever
IB Definition: A lever arrangement where the effort sits between the fulcrum and the load.
Real-World Example: The human forearm, and prosthetic limbs deliberately designed to copy it, such as running blades.
Moment
IB Definition: The turning effect of a force, equal to force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from the fulcrum.
Real-World Example: The larger moment created by pushing at the very end of a long spanner handle rather than near its head.

Pulley system (block and tackle) IB Definition: A system of one or more pulleys and a rope, where MA depends on the number of rope sections supporting the load. Real-World Example: A four-rope block and tackle used to lift a car engine out of its bay with an MA of 4. Torque IB Definition: A rotational (twisting) force that causes an object to rotate about an axis. Real-World Example: The high torque delivered by a drill's low gear setting when driving a long screw into hardwood. Cam IB Definition: A mechanical component that transforms rotary motion into reciprocating (linear, back-and-forth) motion. Real-World Example: The camshaft lobes inside a car engine that open and close the intake and exhaust valves. Follower IB Definition: The component that rests against a cam's profile and moves as the cam rotates beneath it. Real-World Example: The valve stem pushed open and released by a rotating camshaft lobe. Cam profile IB Definition: The precise outline shape of a cam, which determines the timing and pattern of the follower's motion. Real-World Example: A pear/snail-shaped cam profile chosen to give a pet feeder a true dwell period while its flap stays open. Displacement diagram IB Definition: A graph plotting a follower's displacement against the cam's angle of rotation (0°–360°), used to plan motion timing. Real-World Example: An engineer plotting valve rise, dwell and fall against crankshaft angle before cutting a camshaft. Rise / dwell / fall IB Definition: The three phases of follower motion: moving outward (rise), staying still (dwell), and returning (fall). Real-World Example: A pet feeder flap that rises to open, dwells briefly so food can drop, then falls to close again. Reciprocating motion IB Definition: Repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down linear motion. Real-World Example: The up-and-down motion of an engine valve, produced from the camshaft's continuous rotation. Lever IB Definition: A rigid bar that pivots about a fulcrum to magnify an effort force acting on a load. Real-World Example: A pair of scissors (1st class), a wheelbarrow (2nd class), or a fishing rod (3rd class). Fulcrum IB Definition: The fixed pivot point about which a lever rotates. Real-World Example: The wheel axle of a wheelbarrow, or the elbow joint in a human forearm. 1st class lever IB Definition: A lever arrangement where the fulcrum sits between the effort and the load. Real-World Example: A pair of scissors, or a see-saw. 2nd class lever IB Definition: A lever arrangement where the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort. Real-World Example: A wheelbarrow, where the load sits between the wheel (fulcrum) and the handles (effort). 3rd class lever IB Definition: A lever arrangement where the effort sits between the fulcrum and the load. Real-World Example: The human forearm, and prosthetic limbs deliberately designed to copy it, such as running blades. Moment IB Definition: The turning effect of a force, equal to force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from the fulcrum. Real-World Example: The larger moment created by pushing at the very end of a long spanner handle rather than near its head.

sourceDocuments: B3.3 Mechanical Systems: Application and Selection

syllabus.title: Mechanical systems application and selection
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How can mechanical systems be incorporated into product design?

statements.text: Mechanical advantage of a system can be calculated.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to calculate mechanical advantage in gear, pulley, belt and lever systems.

statements.text: Velocity ratios for gear-, pulley- and belt-driven systems can be calculated.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to calculate velocity ratios for gear-, pulley- and belt-driven systems.

statements.text: Efficiency can be calculated.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to calculate efficiency for gear- and belt-driven systems.

statements.text: Gear- and belt-driven systems are used to change the direction, speed, power and efficiency of a rotary motion.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to calculate gear ratios and belt-driven system ratios considering the use of drive and driven gears, calculate the speed of rotation of a gear system at several points, including initial input and final output speed, and construct systems that use gears to increase or decrease speed and motion.

statements.text: Cams and followers are used to change rotary motion to reciprocating motion.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to analyse how cam systems translate rotary motion into reciprocating motion, construct mechanical systems that use cams, and interpret diagrams that represent the use of cams in a system.

statements.text: Levers reduce the effort needed to exert a force and move a load.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to analyse the Load (L), Effort (E) and Fulcrum, calculate Load (L) and Effort (E), construct mechanical systems that use levers, and interpret diagrams that represent the use of levers in a system.

activity.title: Select a motion solution
activity.materials: Card, split pins, mechanism reference sheets
steps: A product must turn continuous rotary input into repeated linear movement. Generate two mechanisms.
Sketch and label input, output and movement direction.
Compare compactness, friction, motion profile, maintenance and safety.
Build a card model of one option and justify its selection.
activity.debrief: How does the required output motion determine mechanism choice?

exam.question: Explain why a cam and follower may be chosen for repeated non-uniform movement. [2]
exam.answer: The cam profile determines the follower displacement through a rotation, allowing rise, fall and dwell periods to be tailored to the task.

activities.title: Your Turn: Design Decision — An Accessible Jar Opener
activities.text: Your Turn: Design Decision — An Accessible Jar Opener A client with arthritis in her hands is your target user for the IA. Grip-strength testing shows she can comfortably and safely apply about 15 N of turning force. Lab testing shows a typical stuck jar lid needs about 45 N of turning force at the lid edge to break the vacuum seal. Calculate the minimum MA the mechanism must provide for your client to open the jar unaided. Two candidate concepts are on your desk: (a) a long-handled strap wrench, with an effort arm of 180 mm and an effective load arm of 40 mm at the lid; (b) a rotating gear-and-ratchet jar opener that clamps around the lid. Calculate the MA of concept (a). Does it meet the requirement from Q1? Which system would you select — the lever-based strap wrench or a gear-based rotating opener — for this client? Justify your choice using MA, but also ergonomics, one-handed operation, and the effect of friction between the tool and a wet or textured lid. Reveal Model Answer 1. Minimum MA = Load ÷ Effort = 45 N ÷ 15 N = 3 . 2. MA of the strap wrench = 180 ÷ 40 = 4.5 . Since 4.5 > 3, it meets the minimum requirement on paper. 3. Either could be argued, but the gear-and-ratchet opener is often the stronger choice for this client: it clamps and turns with a squeezing or ratcheting action rather than requiring a sustained, precise gripping-and-twisting motion, so it needs less fine motor control from arthritic hands and can be operated one-handed. Its toothed grip also bites into a wet or textured lid more reliably than a smooth strap, whose effective friction — and therefore its real MA — can drop sharply if the lid is damp, echoing the 3.3.1 design consideration that a high MA on paper is worthless if the mechanism is unreliable in real-world conditions.

2. MA of the strap wrench = 180 ÷ 40 = 4.5. Since 4.5 > 3, it meets the minimum requirement on paper.

3. Either could be argued, but the gear-and-ratchet opener is often the stronger choice for this client: it clamps and turns with a squeezing or ratcheting action rather than requiring a sustained, precise gripping-and-twisting motion, so it needs less fine motor control from arthritic hands and can be operated one-handed. activities.title: Your Turn: Design Decision — A Hand-Crank Emergency Radio
activities.text: Your Turn: Design Decision — A Hand-Crank Emergency Radio Inventor Trevor Baylis's wind-up radio concept — commercialised as the BayGen Freeplay — let users in areas without reliable electricity power a radio by turning a hand crank. The crank must turn a small generator (dynamo) shaft fast to produce a usable voltage, far faster than a hand can comfortably crank it directly. A single gear stage connects a 15-tooth driver gear (fixed to the hand crank) to a 5-tooth driven gear (fixed to the dynamo shaft). Calculate the VR, and state how many times the dynamo shaft spins for every one turn of the crank. Testing shows the dynamo needs to spin at least 20 times faster than the crank to charge the internal battery effectively. Does the single gear stage in Q1 meet this? If not, propose and calculate a two-stage (compound) gear train — using two gear pairs in sequence — that achieves at least a 20:1 speed increase. Why might a designer choose a multi-stage gear train over a single very small driven gear (e.g. a 15-tooth driver against a 0.75-tooth driven gear, which is not physically possible) to achieve a large VR? Consider gear tooth strength and manufacturing limits. Reveal Model Answer 1. VR = 5 ÷ 15 = 0.33. The dynamo shaft spins 1 ÷ 0.33 = 3 times for every one turn of the crank. 2. No — 3× is far short of the 20× required. A two-stage train of, for example, a 15-tooth driver to a 3-tooth driven gear in each stage (VR = 3 ÷ 15 = 0.2, i.e. a 5× speed increase per stage) gives an overall increase of 5 × 5 = 25× , comfortably exceeding the 20:1 requirement. 3. Gears with very few teeth become structurally weak (the tooth profile becomes "undercut") and are difficult or impossible to manufacture reliably below a practical minimum tooth count. Splitting a large ratio across two moderate, physically realistic stages achieves the same overall speed increase while keeping every gear strong enough to survive repeated use. Background: Objects of Engineering — the BayGen Freeplay wind-up radio (IMechE Archive)

  2. Testing shows the dynamo needs to spin at least 20 times faster than the crank to charge the internal battery effectively. Does the single gear stage in Q1 meet this? activities.title: Your Turn: Design Decision — Drivetrain for a City Bike-Share Fleet
activities.text: Your Turn: Design Decision — Drivetrain for a City Bike-Share Fleet You are advising two very different clients. Client A: a city bike-share operator with 5,000 bicycles, parked outdoors year-round, serviced only twice a year, ridden mostly on flat urban streets by casual users. Client B: a track cycling team preparing a bike for a velodrome time trial, where the bike is serviced daily and marginal power gains decide medals. For each client, recommend a chain-drive or belt-drive system, and justify your choice using efficiency, maintenance frequency, weather exposure, and weight. A belt-drive test rig measures an MA of 3.8 against a VR of 4.0 for its pulley system. Use the MA ÷ VR shortcut to estimate its efficiency, and comment on whether this supports your recommendation for Client A. Reveal Model Answer 1. Client A: a belt drive — it needs no lubrication, resists rain, dirt and rust, and lasts far longer between services, which directly cuts the cost of maintaining 5,000 outdoor bikes serviced only twice a year. Client B: a chain drive — a clean, daily-serviced chain reaches a slightly higher efficiency (98–99% vs. a belt's marginally lower figure), and at professional level that small margin can decide a race, while daily servicing removes the chain's usual maintenance disadvantage. 2. Efficiency ≈ (MA ÷ VR) × 100% = (3.8 ÷ 4.0) × 100% = 95% . This is a high efficiency figure, supporting the Client A recommendation: the small ~5% energy loss is a reasonable trade for near-zero maintenance and weather resistance across a large outdoor fleet.

activities.title: Your Turn: Design Decision — A Powered Wheelchair Drivetrain
activities.text: Your Turn: Design Decision — A Powered Wheelchair Drivetrain Your client's motor has a no-load speed of 3000 rpm and delivers 0.5 Nm of torque at the motor shaft. The design brief requires: enough torque at the wheels to climb a standard 1:12 accessibility ramp, which testing shows needs at least 15 Nm at the wheel; and a comfortable top speed on flat pavement, corresponding to a wheel speed of around 40 rpm. Calculate the torque multiplication (VR) needed to satisfy the ramp requirement (15 ÷ 0.5). Calculate the speed reduction (VR) needed to bring the wheel down to 40 rpm from the motor's 3000 rpm. Compare your two answers. Can a single fixed gear ratio satisfy both the ramp-climbing torque and the flat-ground speed target? If not, would you propose a two-speed gearbox (like the drill above), or an electronic motor controller that varies current instead of using a mechanical ratio change? Justify your choice, linking to B3.4 (electronic systems). Reveal Model Answer 1. Torque ratio needed = 15 ÷ 0.5 = 30:1 . 2. Speed reduction needed = 3000 ÷ 40 = 75:1 . 3. Because 75:1 is greater than the 30:1 minimum, gearing purely for the flat-ground speed target (75:1) automatically delivers more than enough torque for the ramp (0.5 × 75 = 37.5 Nm > 15 Nm needed), so a single fixed-ratio gearbox can technically satisfy both requirements. However, many designers would still favour a two-speed gearbox, or better, an electronic motor controller that varies current to adjust torque and speed on demand (linking to B3.4): this avoids permanently carrying unnecessary torque headroom, allows finer real-time control between "ramp mode" and "cruise mode," and accounts for the fact that a real motor's available torque changes with load and speed, unlike the idealised no-load figures given here.

activities.title: Your Turn: Design Decision — An Automatic Pet Feeder
activities.text: Your Turn: Design Decision — An Automatic Pet Feeder A motor rotates a cam once every 8 hours to release one measured portion of food, three times a day. The mechanism must: stay closed and store food for a long period; then rise quickly to open a dispensing flap for about 2 seconds; hold the flap open (dwell) for 3 seconds so food can fall through; then fall quickly to close and stay closed until the next 8-hour cycle. Sketch (in words or as a simple diagram) the shape of the displacement diagram this cam needs, labelling the rise, dwell (open), fall and dwell (closed) sections and their approximate angular ranges. Two cam-profile types are available: a circular (eccentric) cam, which gives smooth, continuous motion with no dwell period at all; and a pear/snail-shaped cam, which can be profiled to include a genuine dwell. Which would you choose for this feeder, and why? What risk is there for the pet (and the mechanism) if the fall phase is too slow, or if the follower does not fully return during the long "closed" dwell? Reveal Model Answer 1. The full cycle (8 hours = 28,800 seconds) is represented by the full 0–360° rotation, but the active phases (rise ~2 s, open dwell 3 s, fall ~2 s ≈ 7 s total) occupy only a tiny fraction of that — roughly 0.02% of the rotation. The displacement diagram is therefore an almost flat line at "closed" for nearly the entire 360°, with a very narrow spike showing a sharp rise, a brief open dwell, and a sharp fall clustered together at one point in the rotation. 2. The pear/snail-shaped cam. It can be profiled to include a genuine dwell (a constant-radius section) at both the open and closed positions, which the feeder needs to hold the flap open long enough for food to fall through and closed for the rest of the cycle. A circular cam gives continuous motion with no true dwell, so the flap would never reliably stay fully open or fully closed. 3. A slow fall, or a follower that doesn't fully return, could leave the flap slightly open during the long closed dwell — risking pests or moisture reaching the stored food, food spoilage, or food continuing to trickle out and overfeeding the pet. Repeated imperfect seating of the follower could also accelerate wear and eventually cause the mechanism to jam.

activities.title: Your Turn: Design Decision — A Foot-Pedal Bin Lid
activities.text: Your Turn: Design Decision — A Foot-Pedal Bin Lid You are designing a step-on pedal mechanism to lift a bin lid weighing an equivalent of 6 N at the hinge, measured 90 mm from the hinge (fulcrum). The foot pedal will be positioned 220 mm from the hinge, on the opposite side of the mechanism to the lid. Identify the class of lever this arrangement represents (consider where the fulcrum, load and effort each sit). Calculate the MA of this pedal system, and the force a user's foot must apply to lift the lid. A wheelchair-using client finds the pedal hard to reach and needs the required foot force reduced further. Propose one specific dimensional change to the mechanism, and recalculate the MA and required force to show the improvement. Reveal Model Answer 1. 1st class lever — the fulcrum (hinge) sits between the load (lid, 90 mm to one side) and the effort (pedal, 220 mm to the other side). 2. MA = Effort arm ÷ Load arm = 220 ÷ 90 = 2.44 . Required foot force = Load ÷ MA = 6 ÷ 2.44 ≈ 2.5 N . 3. Extending the pedal's distance from the hinge, e.g. to 350 mm, gives MA = 350 ÷ 90 ≈ 3.89, reducing the required foot force to 6 ÷ 3.89 ≈ 1.5 N — a meaningfully lighter action for a user with reduced leg strength or reach, at the cost of a longer, more space-consuming pedal arm.

designer specify, and why? this lesson revisits ma alongside two further calculations — velocity ratio and efficiency — and immediately puts each one to work justifying a real design decision. hook: from calculating to choosing by the end of topic b3.3 you will be able to: calculate ma, vr and efficiency for gear, pulley, belt and lever systems; explain how gear and belt systems control the speed, torque and direction of rotary motion; analyse cam profiles and construct simple displacement diagrams; classify lever systems and apply the principle of moments; and — the skill this topic is really about — given a real design brief, select and justify an appropriate mechanical system. every calculation in this unit exists to serve that final skill. 1. mechanical advantage (ma) mechanical advantage definition: the factor by which a mechanism multiplies an input effort force to move a load (resistance). it tells a designer how much "easier" a task becomes when a mechanism is introduced between the user and the job to be done. context: an ma greater than 1 means the mechanism is multiplying force (good for lifting or gripping); an ma less than 1 means it is trading force for speed or reach instead. materials/examples: levers, gear trains, pulleys, winches, geared hand tools. application: design consideration: a high ma on paper is worthless if the mechanism is unreliable. a good designer balances ma against friction, added weight, material strength and manufacturing cost to make sure the theoretical advantage survives real-world use. how ma is found: gears: ma = teeth on driven gear ÷ teeth on driver gear. pulleys: ma = number of rope sections supporting the load (a block-and-tackle with 4 supporting ropes has an ma of 4). levers: ma = length of the effort arm ÷ length of the load arm. case study: fiskars powergear2™ bypass pruners standard bypass pruning shears are a simple 1st class lever — fine for thin stems, but gardeners with weaker grip strength struggle to cut anything thicker than a pencil. fiskars redesigned the tool around a compound gear-and-cam mechanism built into the pivot, rather than relying on the handle-arm length alone. as the handles close, an internal gear track rotates a cam that keeps re-engaging at a mechanically favourable point throughout the cut — fiskars markets this as delivering up to three times more cutting power than a standard bypass pruner of the same handle length, without needing longer (heavier, harder to control) handles. why this system? a gear/cam mechanism packs a high, changing ma into a compact, single-hand tool — something a simple lever geometry alone could not do without making the tool unwieldy. it is a clear example of choosing a mechanism to meet a human-factors constraint (limited hand strength), not just a mechanical one. learn more: fiskars powergear™ technology worked example — compound lever pruners: a pruner's compound lever has an effort arm of 160 mm (the handle, measured from the pivot) and a load arm of 20 mm (the blade edge, measured from the same pivot). ma = effort arm ÷ load arm = 160 ÷ 20 = 8 a hand force of just 25 n at the handle therefore produces roughly 200 n of cutting force at the blade — enough to shear through a 15 mm branch that would be impossible to cut with bare secateurs of ordinary leverage. your turn: design decision — an accessible jar opener a client with arthritis in her hands is your target user for the ia. grip-strength testing shows she can comfortably and safely apply about 15 n of turning force. lab testing shows a typical stuck jar lid needs about 45 n of turning force at the lid edge to break the vacuum seal. calculate the minimum ma the mechanism must provide for your client to open the jar unaided. two candidate concepts are on your desk: (a) a long-handled strap wrench, with an effort arm of 180 mm and an effective load arm of 40 mm at the lid; (b) a rotating gear-and-ratchet jar opener that clamps around the lid. calculate the ma of concept (a). does it meet the requirement from q1? which system would you select — the lever-based strap wrench or a gear-based rotating opener — for this client? justify your choice using ma, but also ergonomics, one-handed operation, and the effect of friction between the tool and a wet or textured lid. reveal model answer 1. minimum ma = load ÷ effort = 45 n ÷ 15 n = 3 . 2. ma of the strap wrench = 180 ÷ 40 = 4.5 . since 4.5 > 3, it meets the minimum requirement on paper. 3. either could be argued, but the gear-and-ratchet opener is often the stronger choice for this client: it clamps and turns with a squeezing or ratcheting action rather than requiring a sustained, precise gripping-and-twisting motion, so it needs less fine motor control from arthritic hands and can be operated one-handed. its toothed grip also bites into a wet or textured lid more reliably than a smooth strap, whose effective friction — and therefore its real ma — can drop sharply if the lid is damp, echoing the 3.3.1 design consideration that a high ma on paper is worthless if the mechanism is unreliable in real-world conditions. 2. velocity ratio (vr) velocity ratio definition: compares how far, or how fast, the input (effort) and output (load) of a mechanism move relative to each other. it is a ratio of distances or speeds, not forces. context: for gears, use the number of teeth on the driven and driver gears; for pulleys and belts, use the diameters of the wheels. materials/examples: gear trains, pulley-and-belt systems, bicycle cassettes. application: rule of thumb: a higher vr gives lower speed but higher torque at the output — exactly what a climbing gear on a bicycle, or the low gear on a winch, is for. formula: vr = teeth on driven gear ÷ teeth on driver gear  (or, for pulleys/belts, diameter of driven wheel ÷ diameter of driver wheel) case study: shimano™ bicycle derailleur gearing a road cyclist reaching a steep hill does not pedal harder — they change gear. shifting to a smaller chainring at the front and a larger sprocket at the back changes the velocity ratio between the pedals (driver) and the rear wheel (driven, via the sprocket). climbing gear: 34-tooth chainring, 32-tooth sprocket → vr = 32 ÷ 34 ≈ 0.94. a high vr: each pedal stroke moves the bike only a short distance, but with much less resistance felt at the pedals — ideal for a steep gradient. sprint gear: 50-tooth chainring, 11-tooth sprocket → vr = 11 ÷ 50 = 0.22. a low vr: the wheel travels much further per pedal stroke, trading torque for road speed on flat, fast sections. why this system? a cassette of 8–12 sprockets lets one rider access a huge range of vr values on demand, rather than needing a different fixed-ratio bike for hills versus flats — a clear case of selecting a system (variable gearing) because the use-context changes minute to minute. watch: how gears work — 3d animation. worked example — a simple gear train: a workshop hoist has a driver gear with 60 teeth turning a driven gear with 20 teeth. vr = teeth on driven ÷ teeth on driver = 20 ÷ 60 = 0.33 a vr below 1 means the driven gear turns faster than the driver — here, three times faster (1 ÷ 0.33) for every single turn of the driver. this confirms the rule from 3.3.4: a large driver turning a small driven gear increases output speed. your turn: design decision — a hand-crank emergency radio inventor trevor baylis's wind-up radio concept — commercialised as the baygen freeplay — let users in areas without reliable electricity power a radio by turning a hand crank. the crank must turn a small generator (dynamo) shaft fast to produce a usable voltage, far faster than a hand can comfortably crank it directly. a single gear stage connects a 15-tooth driver gear (fixed to the hand crank) to a 5-tooth driven gear (fixed to the dynamo shaft). calculate the vr, and state how many times the dynamo shaft spins for every one turn of the crank. testing shows the dynamo needs to spin at least 20 times faster than the crank to charge the internal battery effectively. does the single gear stage in q1 meet this? if not, propose and calculate a two-stage (compound) gear train — using two gear pairs in sequence — that achieves at least a 20:1 speed increase. why might a designer choose a multi-stage gear train over a single very small driven gear (e.g. a 15-tooth driver against a 0.75-tooth driven gear, which is not physically possible) to achieve a large vr? consider gear tooth strength and manufacturing limits. reveal model answer 1. vr = 5 ÷ 15 = 0.33. the dynamo shaft spins 1 ÷ 0.33 = 3 times for every one turn of the crank. 2. no — 3× is far short of the 20× required. a two-stage train of, for example, a 15-tooth driver to a 3-tooth driven gear in each stage (vr = 3 ÷ 15 = 0.2, i.e. a 5× speed increase per stage) gives an overall increase of 5 × 5 = 25× , comfortably exceeding the 20:1 requirement. 3. gears with very few teeth become structurally weak (the tooth profile becomes "undercut") and are difficult or impossible to manufacture reliably below a practical minimum tooth count. splitting a large ratio across two moderate, physically realistic stages achieves the same overall speed increase while keeping every gear strong enough to survive repeated use. background: objects of engineering — the baygen freeplay wind-up radio (imeche archive) 3. efficiency efficiency definition: measures how much of the energy put into a system comes out as useful work, after losses to friction, heat, noise or slippage are accounted for. no real mechanism is 100% efficient. context: because friction is what makes a mechanism's real ma fall short of its ideal, theoretical vr, comparing the two gives a quick estimate of efficiency without needing to measure energy directly. materials/examples: gear trains, belt drives, pulley systems, lever mechanisms. application: improving efficiency: designers reduce energy loss with lubricants, precise alignment, belt/chain tensioners, sealed bearings, or higher-quality (lower-friction, more dimensionally stable) materials. formula: efficiency = (output energy ÷ input energy) × 100% shortcut (gear/lever/pulley systems): efficiency ≈ (ma ÷ vr) × 100% — because friction is exactly what makes real ma fall short of the ideal (vr) value, comparing the two gives a fast estimate of efficiency without measuring energy directly. case study: chain vs. gates carbon belt™ drive on bicycles for over a century almost every bicycle used a steel roller chain, because a well-lubricated chain is extremely efficient — independent lab testing puts a clean, waxed chain at around 98–99% efficient. that efficiency is exactly why racing bikes still use chains: at professional level, a 1–2% power loss is worth avoiding. but a chain's efficiency depends on it staying clean and lubricated — grit, rain and rust drag it down fast. this is why many commuter and bike-share bicycles now use a carbon-fibre belt drive instead: it needs no oil, doesn't rust, resists dirt, and lasts several times longer than a chain, even though a belt can run marginally less efficient than a pristine, freshly-lubed chain. why this system? the choice isn't simply "which is more efficient" — it is which efficiency loss a designer can live with. a racing team chases every fraction of a percent; a bike-share operator trades a small, stable efficiency figure for near-zero maintenance across thousands of bikes. read: are belt drivetrains more efficient than chain drivetrains? (lab testing) worked example — electric scooter motor: an e-scooter's hub motor draws 250 w of electrical input power. a dynamometer measures 227.5 w of useful mechanical power actually delivered to the wheel. efficiency = (227.5 ÷ 250) × 100 = 91% the missing 9% is lost mainly as heat in the motor windings and friction in the bearings — which is why the motor casing gets warm after a long ride. your turn: design decision — drivetrain for a city bike-share fleet you are advising two very different clients. client a: a city bike-share operator with 5,000 bicycles, parked outdoors year-round, serviced only twice a year, ridden mostly on flat urban streets by casual users. client b: a track cycling team preparing a bike for a velodrome time trial, where the bike is serviced daily and marginal power gains decide medals. for each client, recommend a chain-drive or belt-drive system, and justify your choice using efficiency, maintenance frequency, weather exposure, and weight. a belt-drive test rig measures an ma of 3.8 against a vr of 4.0 for its pulley system. use the ma ÷ vr shortcut to estimate its efficiency, and comment on whether this supports your recommendation for client a. reveal model answer 1. client a: a belt drive — it needs no lubrication, resists rain, dirt and rust, and lasts far longer between services, which directly cuts the cost of maintaining 5,000 outdoor bikes serviced only twice a year. client b: a chain drive — a clean, daily-serviced chain reaches a slightly higher efficiency (98–99% vs. a belt's marginally lower figure), and at professional level that small margin can decide a race, while daily servicing removes the chain's usual maintenance disadvantage. 2. efficiency ≈ (ma ÷ vr) × 100% = (3.8 ÷ 4.0) × 100% = 95% . this is a high efficiency figure, supporting the client a recommendation: the small ~5% energy loss is a reasonable trade for near-zero maintenance and weather resistance across a large outdoor fleet. concept formula real-world example mechanical advantage (ma) ma = load ÷ effort compound-lever pruners cutting an 8× multiplied force at the blade velocity ratio (vr) vr = teeth (driven) ÷ teeth (driver) a bicycle derailleur trading vr for climbing torque vs. sprint speed efficiency efficiency = (output ÷ input) × 100% a belt drive trading a few % efficiency for near-zero maintenance b3.3.4 rotary motion: speed & direction b3.3.5 cams and followers ~120 min lesson 2: controlling rotary motion & cam systems gear and belt systems don't just transmit rotary motion — designers manipulate them deliberately to change its speed, torque and direction to suit a specific task. cams take that manipulation a step further, converting continuous rotation into precisely timed reciprocating movement. 1. manipulating rotary motion speed, torque & direction control definition: the deliberate use of gear or pulley size and arrangement to change a rotary output's speed, torque or direction relative to its input. context: the same physical gear train can be arranged to prioritise speed, torque, or a change of direction, depending entirely on which gear the designer chooses as driver and which as driven. materials/examples: gearboxes, pulley-and-belt drives, idler gears, crossed belts. application: selecting the right arrangement is a core ao2 design-technology skill — the same components, arranged differently, serve completely different purposes. increasing speed: a large driver gear turns a smaller driven gear (the driven gear spins faster, with less torque). increasing torque: a small driver gear turns a larger driven gear (the driven gear spins slower, with more force). reversing direction: insert an idler gear between the driver and driven gear (gears mesh in pairs, so each mesh flips rotation direction — an idler flips it back), or cross a belt in a pulley system. case study: two-speed cordless drill/driver gearbox a cordless drill/driver has a small switch marked "1" and "2" that changes an internal planetary gear train — engineers designed this because drilling and driving screws have opposite mechanical requirements. gear 1 (low): a large gear reduction between motor and chuck. output speed is low, but torque is high — needed to drive a long screw into hardwood without stalling the motor or stripping the screw head. gear 2 (high): a smaller gear reduction. output speed is high, torque is lower — ideal for quickly drilling a clean hole in thin material, where high torque is not the limiting factor. why this system? a single fixed gear ratio would compromise both tasks. two selectable ratios let one motor serve two very different jobs — a direct, everyday example of choosing vr to match torque and speed to the task, not just to the motor's natural output. worked example — gear ratios for speed vs. torque: drill gear 1 (low): 12-tooth driver, 48-tooth driven → vr = 48 ÷ 12 = 4 . high vr: torque is multiplied roughly 4×, speed is quartered. drill gear 2 (high): 12-tooth driver, 16-tooth driven → vr = 16 ÷ 12 ≈ 1.33 . lower vr: less torque multiplication, closer to the motor's natural speed. reversing direction: fitting a 20-tooth idler gear between the 12-tooth driver and 48-tooth driven gear does not change the vr calculation (idlers are not counted in the ratio) — it only flips the direction of the output shaft, exactly as a car's reverse gear uses an idler to send the output the opposite way to the engine's fixed rotation direction. your turn: design decision — a powered wheelchair drivetrain your client's motor has a no-load speed of 3000 rpm and delivers 0.5 nm of torque at the motor shaft. the design brief requires: enough torque at the wheels to climb a standard 1:12 accessibility ramp, which testing shows needs at least 15 nm at the wheel; and a comfortable top speed on flat pavement, corresponding to a wheel speed of around 40 rpm. calculate the torque multiplication (vr) needed to satisfy the ramp requirement (15 ÷ 0.5). calculate the speed reduction (vr) needed to bring the wheel down to 40 rpm from the motor's 3000 rpm. compare your two answers. can a single fixed gear ratio satisfy both the ramp-climbing torque and the flat-ground speed target? if not, would you propose a two-speed gearbox (like the drill above), or an electronic motor controller that varies current instead of using a mechanical ratio change? justify your choice, linking to b3.4 (electronic systems). reveal model answer 1. torque ratio needed = 15 ÷ 0.5 = 30:1 . 2. speed reduction needed = 3000 ÷ 40 = 75:1 . 3. because 75:1 is greater than the 30:1 minimum, gearing purely for the flat-ground speed target (75:1) automatically delivers more than enough torque for the ramp (0.5 × 75 = 37.5 nm > 15 nm needed), so a single fixed-ratio gearbox can technically satisfy both requirements. however, many designers would still favour a two-speed gearbox, or better, an electronic motor controller that varies current to adjust torque and speed on demand (linking to b3.4): this avoids permanently carrying unnecessary torque headroom, allows finer real-time control between "ramp mode" and "cruise mode," and accounts for the fact that a real motor's available torque changes with load and speed, unlike the idealised no-load figures given here. 2. cams and followers cam and follower definition: cams convert continuous rotary motion into reciprocating motion (repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down movement) through a follower that rides on the cam's edge, or cam profile. context: designers describe a follower's motion in three phases across one rotation of the cam: rise, dwell and fall. materials/examples: camshafts, automatic dispensing mechanisms, sewing machine feed dogs, pear/snail/eccentric cam profiles. application: chosen whenever a repeating, precisely-timed reciprocating movement — including genuine pauses — must be driven from a continuously rotating shaft. rise: the follower is pushed outward/upward as the cam profile radius increases. dwell: the follower stays still while the cam profile radius is momentarily constant. fall: the follower drops back as the profile radius decreases (often helped by gravity or a return spring). displacement diagrams plot follower displacement (y-axis) against the cam's angle of rotation, 0°–360° (x-axis). before a cam profile is ever cut, engineers plan the exact timing of rise, dwell and fall on this diagram — it is the cam's motion "blueprint." case study: the car engine camshaft inside a petrol or diesel engine, a rotating camshaft opens and closes the intake and exhaust valves at exactly the right moment in each cylinder's four-stroke cycle — get the timing wrong by even a few degrees and engine performance and emissions suffer badly. each lobe on the camshaft is a precision cam profile: the rise opens the valve, a brief dwell holds it fully open, and the fall (assisted by a valve spring) snaps it shut. engineers use displacement diagrams to plan valve "duration" and "overlap" — how long each valve stays open and how much the intake and exhaust valves overlap being open together — because this directly affects power, fuel economy and emissions. why this system? a cam-driven valvetrain guarantees the exact same, repeatable, high-speed timing thousands of times per minute — something no human-operated or simple crank-driven system could achieve reliably at engine speeds. watch: how do cam and follower mechanisms work? worked example — reading a displacement diagram: a cam completes rise over 0°–60°, dwell (open) over 60°–120°, fall over 120°–180°, and dwell (closed) over 180°–360°. if the cam rotates at 30 rpm (0.5 revolutions per second), one full rotation takes 2 seconds. the follower is therefore held open for (120° − 60°) ÷ 360° × 2 s ≈ 0.33 seconds , and closed for (360° − 180°) ÷ 360° × 2 s = 1 second before the next rise begins. discussion: designing a dwell a circular (eccentric) cam gives smooth, continuous follower motion with no true dwell at all. why might a designer deliberately choose an irregular profile — a pear or snail shape — instead, even though it is harder and more expensive to manufacture precisely? your turn: design decision — an automatic pet feeder a motor rotates a cam once every 8 hours to release one measured portion of food, three times a day. the mechanism must: stay closed and store food for a long period; then rise quickly to open a dispensing flap for about 2 seconds; hold the flap open (dwell) for 3 seconds so food can fall through; then fall quickly to close and stay closed until the next 8-hour cycle. sketch (in words or as a simple diagram) the shape of the displacement diagram this cam needs, labelling the rise, dwell (open), fall and dwell (closed) sections and their approximate angular ranges. two cam-profile types are available: a circular (eccentric) cam, which gives smooth, continuous motion with no dwell period at all; and a pear/snail-shaped cam, which can be profiled to include a genuine dwell. which would you choose for this feeder, and why? what risk is there for the pet (and the mechanism) if the fall phase is too slow, or if the follower does not fully return during the long "closed" dwell? reveal model answer 1. the full cycle (8 hours = 28,800 seconds) is represented by the full 0–360° rotation, but the active phases (rise ~2 s, open dwell 3 s, fall ~2 s ≈ 7 s total) occupy only a tiny fraction of that — roughly 0.02% of the rotation. the displacement diagram is therefore an almost flat line at "closed" for nearly the entire 360°, with a very narrow spike showing a sharp rise, a brief open dwell, and a sharp fall clustered together at one point in the rotation. 2. the pear/snail-shaped cam. it can be profiled to include a genuine dwell (a constant-radius section) at both the open and closed positions, which the feeder needs to hold the flap open long enough for food to fall through and closed for the rest of the cycle. a circular cam gives continuous motion with no true dwell, so the flap would never reliably stay fully open or fully closed. 3. a slow fall, or a follower that doesn't fully return, could leave the flap slightly open during the long closed dwell — risking pests or moisture reaching the stored food, food spoilage, or food continuing to trickle out and overfeeding the pet. repeated imperfect seating of the follower could also accelerate wear and eventually cause the mechanism to jam. concept key idea real-world example increasing speed large driver → small driven gear cordless drill's high-speed setting increasing torque small driver → large driven gear cordless drill's low-speed/high-torque setting reversing direction idler gear, or a crossed belt a car's reverse gear idler rise / dwell / fall the three phases of follower motion in one cam rotation an engine valve opening, holding, and closing displacement diagram plots follower displacement against cam angle (0–360°) planning valve timing in a camshaft, or flap timing in a pet feeder b3.3.6 levers and moments synthesis & linking questions ~90 min lesson 3: levers, moments & applying mechanical systems a lever is one of the oldest mechanisms known, magnifying force through the placement of three points: the fulcrum (pivot), the load (resistance to be moved), and the effort (input force). this final lesson formalises lever classification and the principle of moments, then steps back to connect the whole of b3.3 to the rest of the syllabus — and to the ia. 1. lever classes lever definition: a rigid bar pivoting on a fulcrum, with effort applied to move a load. its class depends on where the fulcrum sits relative to the load and effort. context: the same three-point arrangement — fulcrum, load, effort — can be reordered in three ways, and each ordering suits a different design purpose. materials/examples: scissors, wheelbarrows, tweezers, crowbars, the human forearm. application: ma = length of the effort arm ÷ length of the load arm, for any lever class. class arrangement real-world example 1st class fulcrum is between the effort and the load. scissors, a see-saw, a claw hammer removing a nail. 2nd class load is between the fulcrum and the effort. a wheelbarrow — the wheel is the fulcrum, the load sits in the middle, effort is at the handles. 3rd class effort is between the fulcrum and the load. tweezers, a fishing rod, the human forearm (elbow = fulcrum, biceps = effort, hand = load). case study: 3rd-class lever design in prosthetic limbs the human forearm is a natural 3rd class lever: the elbow (fulcrum) is at one end, the biceps (effort) pulls close to the elbow, and the hand (load) is far away. this is mechanically "inefficient" (ma is always less than 1 — the biceps must pull much harder than the weight held in the hand) but it buys something more valuable: speed and range of movement at the hand for only a small muscle contraction. prosthetics engineers deliberately copy this 3rd class arrangement in running blades (such as össur's flex-foot cheetah) and body-powered prosthetic hands: replicating the lever class of the limb being replaced means the device moves and "feels" the way the user's brain and remaining muscles already expect, rather than fighting against decades of learned motion. why this system? this is a case where a designer deliberately chooses a mechanically "weak" (ma < 1) lever class, because matching natural human biomechanics is more important than maximising force multiplication — a strong reminder that ma is never the only design criterion. worked example — wheelbarrow (2nd class lever): a wheelbarrow's wheel axle (fulcrum) sits 0.25 m from the centre of the load; the effort is applied at the handles, 1.15 m from the fulcrum. ma = effort arm ÷ load arm = 1.15 ÷ 0.25 = 4.6 a gardener lifting a 200 n load of soil only needs to apply about 43 n at the handles (200 ÷ 4.6) — the 2nd class arrangement (load between fulcrum and effort) is exactly what makes wheelbarrows liftable by one person. your turn: design decision — a foot-pedal bin lid you are designing a step-on pedal mechanism to lift a bin lid weighing an equivalent of 6 n at the hinge, measured 90 mm from the hinge (fulcrum). the foot pedal will be positioned 220 mm from the hinge, on the opposite side of the mechanism to the lid. identify the class of lever this arrangement represents (consider where the fulcrum, load and effort each sit). calculate the ma of this pedal system, and the force a user's foot must apply to lift the lid. a wheelchair-using client finds the pedal hard to reach and needs the required foot force reduced further. propose one specific dimensional change to the mechanism, and recalculate the ma and required force to show the improvement. reveal model answer 1. 1st class lever — the fulcrum (hinge) sits between the load (lid, 90 mm to one side) and the effort (pedal, 220 mm to the other side). 2. ma = effort arm ÷ load arm = 220 ÷ 90 = 2.44 . required foot force = load ÷ ma = 6 ÷ 2.44 ≈ 2.5 n . 3. extending the pedal's distance from the hinge, e.g. to 350 mm, gives ma = 350 ÷ 90 ≈ 3.89, reducing the required foot force to 6 ÷ 3.89 ≈ 1.5 n — a meaningfully lighter action for a user with reduced leg strength or reach, at the cost of a longer, more space-consuming pedal arm. 2. moments moments definition: a lever balances (or moves) according to the principle that moment = force × distance from the fulcrum. context: this is the physical reasoning behind the ma formula in 3.3.1 — a longer effort arm creates a larger moment for the same force, which is why ma = effort arm ÷ load arm. materials/examples: spanners, see-saws, torque wrenches. application: pushing at the very end of a long spanner handle, rather than near its head, creates a larger moment for the same applied force — the everyday intuition that underlies every lever calculation in this unit. synthesis and linking questions use these as discussion prompts, exit tickets, or extension tasks to connect b3.3 to other parts of the dp design technology course — exactly the kind of cross-topic reasoning that paper 1 and paper 2 long-answer questions reward. c1.2 inclusive design: how does mechanical advantage enable an inclusive design strategy for elderly or impaired users? (e.g. reducing the force required to open a heavy door.) b3.1 material selection: why is it critical to select appropriate materials (like hardened steel for gears) so that mechanisms operate at full functionality over a long period? b2.2 modelling: to what extent can mechanical systems be effectively mocked up and tested using low-fidelity physical prototypes or cad simulations? b3.4 electronics: how can mechanical systems be combined with electronic systems (sensors and microcontrollers) to create convergent technologies like robotics?
