to decrease torque and increase rotational speed to reverse the direction of rotation only to increase torque while reducing rotational speed to convert rotary motion into reciprocating motion reveal answer c. to increase torque while reducing rotational speed. a gear reduction between a fast motor and a slow beater shaft always trades speed for torque — that torque is what lets the mixer work thick dough. [1] 1(b). which material property is most important when selecting the alloy used to manufacture the mixer's internal gears? optical transparency hardness and wear resistance thermal expansion coefficient electrical conductivity reveal answer b. hardness and wear resistance. gears mesh under repeated, high load — hardness and wear resistance (not conductivity or transparency) determine whether the teeth survive years of use. [1] 1(c). a planetary gear system, as used in this mixer, causes the beater to: rotate on its own axis only orbit around the bowl only both rotate on its own axis and orbit around the bowl move in a straight reciprocating line reveal answer c. both rotate on its own axis and orbit around the bowl. that combined spin-and-orbit motion is the defining feature of a planetary gear train, and is exactly why it achieves thorough bowl coverage. [1] section b: short answer (2 questions) question 2 [2 marks] describe how a rear derailleur gear system on a road bicycle allows a cyclist to select an appropriate gear ratio when climbing a steep hill. reveal answer [2] command term describe (action + mechanism + result): shifting to a smaller chainring and/or larger rear sprocket (action) increases the velocity ratio between pedals and rear wheel (mechanism), so each pedal stroke needs less force even though the bike covers less distance per stroke (result). 1 mark for identifying the gear change; 1 mark for linking it to reduced effort/increased vr. question 3 [4 marks] a wheelbarrow has its wheel axle (fulcrum) positioned 0.25 m from the centre of the load, and the effort is applied at the handles, 1.15 m from the fulcrum. (a) identify the class of lever demonstrated by a wheelbarrow. [1] (b) calculate the mechanical advantage of this wheelbarrow system. [2] (c) state one design reason why a wheelbarrow uses this lever class rather than a 1st class arrangement. [1] reveal answer (a) 2nd class lever. [1] (b) ma = 1.15 ÷ 0.25 = 4.6. 1 mark for correct substitution, 1 mark for the correct answer. [2] (c) any reasonable justification, e.g. "the load sits close to the fulcrum/wheel, so a single person can lift a heavy load with a comparatively small effort force at the handles." [1] section c: long answer (2 questions) question 4 [6 marks] evaluate the choice of a belt-drive system over a traditional chain-drive system for a fleet of 5,000 public bike-share bicycles used outdoors year-round. reveal answer [6] command term evaluate (strength/opportunity, limitation/threat, comparison, synthesis/conclusion): strength: belt drives need no lubrication, resist rain, dirt and rust, and last far longer between services than a chain — directly reducing the operating cost of servicing 5,000 outdoor bikes only twice a year. limitation: a belt drive can be marginally less efficient than a perfectly clean, lubricated chain, and typically requires a splittable frame to fit at all. comparison: a chain would need frequent cleaning/oiling to avoid rust and wear in an outdoor, low-maintenance context — the opposite of what a bike-share fleet needs. synthesis: for this specific context (outdoor, high-use, minimal servicing), the small efficiency trade-off is outweighed by drastically lower maintenance costs and downtime, so a belt drive is the more suitable system — though a professional racing team, prioritising marginal performance gains under daily maintenance, would reasonably choose the opposite. question 5 [6 marks] justify the use of a cam-and-follower mechanism, rather than a simple continuously-rotating motor and flap, in the design of an automatic pet feeder that must open briefly at three fixed times each day. reveal answer [6] command term justify (point, evidence/mechanism, consequence/impact): point: the feeder must stay firmly closed for long dwell periods (storing food safely, keeping pests out) and open only briefly and repeatably at three exact times. evidence/mechanism: a cam profile can be shaped to include genuine dwell periods (a constant-radius section) at both the open and closed positions, which a simple continuously-rotating flap or basic crank cannot reliably provide without added electronic timing. impact/justification: because the cam's rise/dwell/fall timing is fixed mechanically in the shape of the profile itself, the feeder repeats the same precise open/close cycle every rotation without relying on additional sensors or software — a robust, low-cost, low-power solution appropriate for a simple consumer product. full marks require a balanced or extended point, e.g. briefly noting a limitation (the fixed profile cannot easily change portion size/timing without physically changing the cam) to reach the top of the mark band. b3.3 glossary glossary: topic b3.3 — mechanical systems: application and selection every key term used across 3.3.1–3.3.6, with its ib-style definition and a real-world example drawn from the case studies and scenarios in this topic. click on a term to reveal its definition. mechanical advantage (ma) ib definition: the ratio of output (load) force to input (effort) force in a mechanical system. real-world example: a long-handled crowbar lifting a heavy paving stone with minimal hand force. velocity ratio (vr) ib definition: the ratio of the distance (or speed) moved by the effort to the distance (or speed) moved by the load. real-world example: calculating how many times a bicycle's rear wheel turns for each single turn of the pedals. efficiency ib definition: the percentage of input energy converted into useful output work, after losses to friction, heat or slippage. real-world example: a belt-driven bicycle losing a small percentage of pedalling power to belt flex, compared with a lubricated chain. driver (gear/pulley) ib definition: the gear or pulley that receives the input effort and drives the rest of the system. real-world example: the chainring on a bicycle, turned directly by the pedals. driven (gear/pulley) ib definition: the gear or pulley that receives motion from the driver and produces the output. real-world example: the rear sprocket on a bicycle cassette, turned by the chain from the chainring. idler gear ib definition: a gear placed between the driver and driven gear that reverses output direction without changing the velocity ratio. real-world example: the gear used in a car's manual gearbox to provide reverse without reversing the engine itself. gear-driven system ib definition: a system transmitting power from a driver to a driven part using interlocking gears. real-world example: a bicycle's internal hub gears, or a cordless drill's two-speed gearbox. belt-driven system ib definition: a drive system where a belt transfers power between at least two pulleys. real-world example: a washing machine's motor turning the drum via a belt, which absorbs shock and runs quietly. pulley system (block and tackle) ib definition: a system of one or more pulleys and a rope, where ma depends on the number of rope sections supporting the load. real-world example: a four-rope block and tackle used to lift a car engine out of its bay with an ma of 4. torque ib definition: a rotational (twisting) force that causes an object to rotate about an axis. real-world example: the high torque delivered by a drill's low gear setting when driving a long screw into hardwood. cam ib definition: a mechanical component that transforms rotary motion into reciprocating (linear, back-and-forth) motion. real-world example: the camshaft lobes inside a car engine that open and close the intake and exhaust valves. follower ib definition: the component that rests against a cam's profile and moves as the cam rotates beneath it. real-world example: the valve stem pushed open and released by a rotating camshaft lobe. cam profile ib definition: the precise outline shape of a cam, which determines the timing and pattern of the follower's motion. real-world example: a pear/snail-shaped cam profile chosen to give a pet feeder a true dwell period while its flap stays open. displacement diagram ib definition: a graph plotting a follower's displacement against the cam's angle of rotation (0°–360°), used to plan motion timing. real-world example: an engineer plotting valve rise, dwell and fall against crankshaft angle before cutting a camshaft. rise / dwell / fall ib definition: the three phases of follower motion: moving outward (rise), staying still (dwell), and returning (fall). real-world example: a pet feeder flap that rises to open, dwells briefly so food can drop, then falls to close again. reciprocating motion ib definition: repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down linear motion. real-world example: the up-and-down motion of an engine valve, produced from the camshaft's continuous rotation. lever ib definition: a rigid bar that pivots about a fulcrum to magnify an effort force acting on a load. real-world example: a pair of scissors (1st class), a wheelbarrow (2nd class), or a fishing rod (3rd class). fulcrum ib definition: the fixed pivot point about which a lever rotates. real-world example: the wheel axle of a wheelbarrow, or the elbow joint in a human forearm. 1st class lever ib definition: a lever arrangement where the fulcrum sits between the effort and the load. real-world example: a pair of scissors, or a see-saw. 2nd class lever ib definition: a lever arrangement where the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort. real-world example: a wheelbarrow, where the load sits between the wheel (fulcrum) and the handles (effort). 3rd class lever ib definition: a lever arrangement where the effort sits between the fulcrum and the load. real-world example: the human forearm, and prosthetic limbs deliberately designed to copy it, such as running blades. moment ib definition: the turning effect of a force, equal to force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from the fulcrum. real-world example: the larger moment created by pushing at the very end of a long spanner handle rather than near its head. belt-driven system cam gear-driven system lever mechanical advantage pulley reciprocating motion velocity ratios mechanical advantage (ma) velocity ratio (vr) efficiency driver (gear/pulley) driven (gear/pulley) idler gear pulley system (block and tackle) torque follower cam profile displacement diagram rise / dwell / fall fulcrum 1st class lever 2nd class lever 3rd class lever moment mechanical advantage of a system can be calculated. velocity ratios for gear-, pulley- and belt-driven systems can be calculated. efficiency can be calculated. gear- and belt-driven systems are used to change the direction, speed, power and efficiency of a rotary motion. cams and followers are used to change rotary motion to reciprocating motion. levers reduce the effort needed to exert a force and move a load.

title: Electronic systems application and selection

sections.title: Lesson 1: Electronics in Everyday Products & Diagnostics
sections.html:
3.4.1 Electronics in Products 3.4.2 Diagnostic Apparatus Duration: 3 Hours

Lesson 1: Electronics in Everyday Products & Diagnostics

Deconstructing electronic architecture into clear functional blocks and utilizing specialized bench apparatus to diagnose, verify, and quantify electronic performance.

1. System Architecture in Consumer Devices

Definition: The functional breakdown of an electronic device into sequential operational stages: Power Supply → Input/Sensor → Microcontroller Processing → Actuator Output.

Context: Modern consumer products rely on modular architecture where discrete subsystems pass data and power safely.

Materials/Examples: Smart kettles, digital alarm clocks, electric toothbrushes, thermal hair dryers.

Application: Allows designers to isolate potential component failures and optimize sub-circuits independently.

2. Diagnostic Testing Apparatus

Definition: Specialized electronic test equipment used to measure static electrical parameters and dynamic voltage signals over time.

Context: Digital Multimeters measure static values (V, I, R), while Oscilloscopes map voltage trends across microsecond intervals to analyze transient waveforms and signals.

Materials/Examples: Digital Multimeters (DMM), Cathode-Ray/Digital Storage Oscilloscopes.

Application: Verifying pulse-width modulation (PWM) motor control signals, checking power rails, and identifying circuit short-circuits.

Case Study: Dyson Supersonic™ Hair Dryer Diagnostics

Dyson engineers integrated a glass bead thermistor measuring air temperature 40 times per second directly to a microprocessor. Diagnostic technicians utilize oscilloscopes to monitor the precise Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) wave sent to the high-speed V9 digital motor, ensuring immediate duty-cycle adjustments prevent thermal damage.

Activity: Teardown & Bench Diagnostics

In small groups, disassemble a retired electronic device (e.g., smoke detector or cordless mouse). Trace physical board pathways, measure power rail DC voltages using a DMM, and probe motor or speaker output pins with an oscilloscope to visually record output waveforms during activation.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Electrical Calculations & Component Networks
sections.html:
3.4.3 Ohm's & Power Laws 3.4.4 Component Networks Duration: 3 Hours

Lesson 2: Electrical Calculations & Component Networks

Quantitative circuit analysis focusing on voltage drops, current distribution, power dissipation, and mathematical modeling of resistor/capacitor networks.

1. Fundamental Circuit Laws

Definition: Mathematical relationships governing current (), voltage (), resistance (), and electrical power ().

Context: Ohm's Law () and Power Laws () govern current limits and heat generation in product enclosures.

Materials/Examples: Current-limiting resistors, heating elements, surface-mount resistors.

Application: Sizing components safely to avoid thermal breakdown or component burnout.

2. Resistor & Capacitor Network Calculations

Definition: Calculating equivalent electrical values across combined series and parallel component topologies.

Context: Resistors in series sum directly (), whereas parallel resistors inverse-sum (). Capacitors show the exact opposite mathematical behavior.

Materials/Examples: Decoupling capacitor banks, high-voltage battery cell arrays.

Application: Designing power management circuits, smoothing ripple voltages, and building specific voltage divider networks.

Component Class Series Connection Formula Parallel Connection Formula Key Functional Purpose
Resistors $R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \dots$ $\frac{1}{R_{total}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} + \dots$ Limits current flow, divides voltages.
Capacitors $\frac{1}{C_{total}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3} + \dots$ $C_{total} = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + \dots$ Stores charge, filters signal noise.

Case Study: Tesla Model S Battery Management System (BMS)

The Tesla battery pack configures thousands of individual lithium-ion cells in series (stepping up total pack voltage to ~400V) and parallel (increasing current capacity). Parallel capacitor networks filter high-frequency transient spikes during regenerative braking bursts to prevent cell overheating.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Flow Diagrams & System Schematics
sections.html:
3.4.5 Flow Diagrams 3.4.6 Circuit Schematics Duration: 3 Hours

Lesson 3: Flow Diagrams & System Schematics

Standardized visual representations mapping system-level decision trees and detailed physical electronic component connections.

1. Software Control Flow Diagrams

Definition: Graphical mapping using standardized ANSI shapes to outline firmware logic prior to coding.

Context: Ovals signal Start/End; Rectangles denote internal Processing; Diamonds denote conditional Decisions; Parallelograms indicate Input/Output operations.

Materials/Examples: System flowcharts, algorithmic state machines.

Application: Establishes clear software execution loops and fault routines for embedded controllers.

2. Electrical System Schematics

Definition: Standardized schematic diagrams detailing exact physical interconnections between electronic symbols.

Context: Utilizes standardized schematic symbols for components such as NPN/PNP transistors, flyback diodes, op-amps, and IC chips.

Materials/Examples: Schematic CAD tools (EDA), PCB layouts.

Application: Guides PCB design, physical breadboarding, and manufacturing assembly.

Case Study: Bosch Smart Washing Machine Logic

Bosch engineers draw comprehensive flow diagrams to enforce safety subroutines. For example, the software evaluates if door status is CLOSED and water level is HIGH before permitting the drum motor relay to energize.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Digital Inputs (Sensors), Control & Logic
sections.html:
3.4.7 Sensors 3.4.8 Control Circuits 3.4.9 Digital Logic Duration: 4 Hours

Lesson 4: Digital Inputs (Sensors), Control & Logic

Interfacing analog/digital sensors with microcontrollers and implementing combinational digital logic gates for decision-making.

1. Environmental Sensors

Definition: Input transducers converting physical quantities into measurable electrical signals.

Context: Includes accelerometers (tilt/motion), ultrasonic transducers (distance), LDRs (light), soil moisture probes, hygrometers (humidity), pressure sensors, microphones, and IR sensors.

Materials/Examples: DHT11 humidity sensors, HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance modules.

Application: Translating real-world environmental phenomena into micro-voltage changes.

2. Combinational Digital Logic

Definition: Binary decision circuits processing discrete High (1) and Low (0); nominal voltages depend on the hardware (for example, 3.3 V or 5 V logic) state inputs via Boolean logic.

Context: AND gates require all inputs High; OR gates require any input High; NOT gates invert incoming logic signals.

Materials/Examples: 74HC series ICs, programmable PIC microcontrollers.

Application: Hardware interlocks, safety systems, and automated device control.

Input A Input B AND Output () OR Output () NOT A Output ()
00001
01011
10010
11110

Case Study: Apple Watch Fall Detection & SOS

The Apple Watch combines accelerometer data sampling at 800 Hz. If a hard impact is detected (Input 1) AND zero motion is registered for 60 seconds (Input 2), the digital logic triggers an emergency alert sequence.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Digital System Outputs & Wireless Communication
sections.html:
3.4.10 System Outputs 3.4.11 Wireless Protocols Duration: 3 Hours

Lesson 5: Digital System Outputs & Wireless Communication

Selecting electromechanical actuators for physical movement and evaluating wireless communication standards based on energy, range, and bandwidth budgets.

1. Output Actuator Integration

Definition: Subsystems converting electronic control signals into physical motion, light, sound, or high-power switching.

Context: Includes servo motors (precise angular control), fluid pumps, LCD panels, buzzers, and relays (isolating low-voltage logic from high-voltage AC loads).

Materials/Examples: Electromechanical relays, solid-state relays, piezoelectric buzzers.

Application: Executing physical work safely in automated devices.

2. Wireless Communication Standards

Definition: Standardized protocols enabling networked data transfer between electronic hardware nodes.

Context: Protocols are selected based on key design trade-offs between battery consumption, operating distance, and bandwidth.

Materials/Examples: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), Wi-Fi (802.11), 5G Cellular Networks.

Application: IoT products, wearable devices, remote monitoring, and smart home eco-systems.

Protocol Operating Range Power Draw Data Rate Primary Product Context
Bluetooth (BLE) Short (~10 m) Very Low Moderate (~1-2 Mbps) Wearable fitness trackers, wireless audio
Wi-Fi Medium (~50-100 m) High High (~100+ Mbps) Smart home hubs, HD video streaming
5G Cellular Global / Cellular wide Moderate to High Ultra-High (~1+ Gbps) Autonomous vehicles, remote smart cities

Case Study: Rachio Smart Sprinkler Controller

The Rachio irrigation controller pulls weather data via Wi-Fi, driving 24V AC water valves safely via electromechanical relays. Direct smartphone configuration utilizes BLE during installation.

Exam Practice & Assessment

IB-style exam questions mapping to Assessment Objectives AO1, AO2, and AO3.

Section A: Multiple Choice Questions

Q1. A remote environmental sensor runs on a coin-cell battery 50m from a receiver. It transmits 10 bytes of data once per hour and must last two years. Which protocol is most suitable?

  • 5G Cellular
  • High-Speed Wi-Fi
  • Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)
  • Satellite Uplink
Reveal Answer

Correct Answer: C — Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)

BLE is optimized for low power consumption, short range, and tiny data payloads. Wi-Fi draws far too much energy for a multi-year coin-cell application.

Q2. Two resistors are connected in parallel. This network is placed in series with a resistor. What is total circuit resistance?

Reveal Answer

Correct Answer: B —

Parallel calculation: $\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{100} + \frac{1}{100} = \frac{2}{100} \implies R_p = 50\,\Omega$. Series calculation: .

Section B: Short Answer Questions

Q3. An LED indicator operates at and (). The power rail is . Calculate: (1) required current-limiting resistor, and (2) resistor power dissipation.

Reveal Answer
  • Voltage drop across resistor: [1]
  • Resistance: [1]
  • Power dissipation: (or ) [2]

Q4. Explain the functional difference between an electromechanical relay and a microcontroller pin when controlling a AC pump.

Reveal Answer
  • Microcontroller Pin: Provides low-voltage DC logic signals () at small milliamp levels; cannot drive high AC loads directly without destruction [1].
  • Relay: Uses the low-voltage signal to magnetically switch physically isolated high-voltage ( AC) contacts safely [1].

sections.title: Glossary of Terms
sections.html:
Glossary of Terms

Click on a term to reveal its definition.

AND gate

IB Definition: A basic digital logic gate that requires two or more inputs and a single output.

Real-World Context: A security alarm sounding only if motion is detected AND the system is armed.

Bluetooth

IB Definition: A standard for short-distance wireless communication between electronic devices.

Real-World Context: Connecting wireless ear-buds to a smartphone.

Current

IB Definition: The flow of electric charge through a conductive circuit.

Real-World Context: Selecting fuse wire ratings to prevent heat electrical fires.

Multimeter

IB Definition: An instrument used to measure current, voltage, and resistance.

Real-World Context: Checking if a circuit battery retains sufficient charge.

Oscilloscope

IB Definition: An instrument used to display and analyze electrical signal waveforms over time.

Real-World Context: Inspecting high-frequency PWM motor control signals.

Series Circuit

IB Definition: A circuit where components are connected end-to-end along a single path.

Real-World Context: Traditional string fairy lights where one faulty bulb breaks the entire loop.

sections.html:
Electronic systems: repaired calculation practice

Newly specified replacement questions for incomplete source items. These are classroom practice, not official IB questions.

1. Resistor networks [3 marks]

Two 100 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. This network is in series with a 200 Ω resistor. Calculate the total resistance.

Worked answer

1/Rp = 1/100 + 1/100; Rp = 50 Ω [2]. Rtotal = 50 + 200 = 250 Ω [1].

2. LED current limiting [4 marks]

An LED has a forward voltage of 2.0 V at a current of 20 mA. The supply is 5.0 V. Calculate the required series resistance and the resistor's power dissipation.

Worked answer

Voltage across resistor = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 V [1]. I = 0.020 A; R = 3.0 / 0.020 = 150 Ω [1]. P = VI = 3.0 × 0.020 = 0.060 W [2]. A practical rating must exceed 0.060 W; 0.25 W gives margin.

3. Relay control [2 marks]

Explain why a 3.3 V microcontroller pin cannot directly power a 230 V AC pump, and how an appropriately rated relay module can control it.

Answer guidance

The pin supplies a low-voltage, limited-current logic signal, which cannot supply the pump's operating voltage or current [1]. A correctly designed relay driver/module uses that signal to switch separately supplied, appropriately rated pump contacts, providing isolation [1]. This is a schematic task; use low-voltage classroom models.

sections.title: Boolean logic and memory · B3.4.9
sections.html:
Boolean variables take values 0 or 1. AND is written A · B, OR is written A + B, and NOT A can be written ¬A. Boolean OR is inclusive: 1 + 1 = 1 in this notation. A truth table lists every input combination and its output.

A combinational circuit depends only on the present inputs. For example, motor enable Y = DoorClosed · StartPressed permits operation only when both inputs are 1. A sequential circuit also depends on stored state: a push-to-start controller remembers that Start was pressed until Stop is pressed. Identical present inputs can therefore produce different outputs depending on earlier events.

Build the interlock · 8 minutes

Define A = door closed, B = start pressed, C = emergency stop pressed. Construct the eight-row truth table for Y = A · B · ¬C. Sketch the gates and test every row. Extend the idea: describe the additional stored state needed if a brief Start press should keep the motor running after Start is released.

Output check

For rows ABC = 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111, outputs are 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. A latch or program state can remember Running; Stop must reset that state.

sections.title: Circuit calculations restored · B3.4.3–4
sections.html:
Ohm’s law: V = IR. Electrical power: P = VI. Resistors in series add: Rtotal = R₁ + R₂. For parallel resistors, 1/Rtotal = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂. Capacitors reverse these network rules: capacitances add in parallel; reciprocals add in series.

Repaired classroom question 1

Two 100 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. Their combination is in series with a 220 Ω resistor. Calculate total resistance.

Worked solution

1/Rp = 1/100 + 1/100, so Rp = 50 Ω. Rtotal = 50 + 220 = 270 Ω.

Repaired classroom question 2

A 5 V supply powers an LED with forward voltage 2 V at 20 mA. Calculate the ideal series resistance and resistor power dissipation.

Worked solution

Resistor voltage = 5 − 2 = 3 V. I = 0.020 A. R = 3/0.020 = 150 Ω. P = VI = 3 × 0.020 = 0.060 W. A practical component selection also needs a suitable power-rating margin.

Network challenge · 5 minutes

Calculate the equivalent capacitance of 10 μF and 20 μF in parallel, then in series. Explain which stores more charge at the same voltage.

Check

Parallel: 30 μF. Series: 1/C = 1/10 + 1/20, giving approximately 6.67 μF. For fixed voltage, Q = CV, so the parallel combination stores more charge.

sections.title: Wireless choices need evidence · B3.4.11
sections.html:
Compare Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and 5G using product requirements: energy budget, range, data rate, available infrastructure and connectivity cost. Bluetooth commonly supports nearby device links; Wi-Fi uses a local network; 5G uses cellular infrastructure. Actual range and power depend on the hardware, operating mode, interference and environment. A named protocol alone does not guarantee a stated range or battery life.

Protocol pitch · 6 minutes

Choose a link for a wearable sending tiny data packets to a phone, a mains-powered classroom camera on an existing network, and a remote mobile tracker. State two reasons for each choice and one test or specification you need before committing.

syllabus.title: Electronic systems application and selection
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How can electronic systems be incorporated into product design?

statements.text: Electronics are present in the design of many everyday products.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to analyse simple electronic products and circuits to identify the main component parts that enable them to perform a specific function.

statements.text: Design and manufacture of electronic products requires the use of specialized apparatus.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe how to use basic electronic measuring apparatus, including multi- meters, on voltage, current and resistance ranges, and oscilloscopes to observe waveforms.

statements.text: Voltage (V) in a circuit is calculated by a combination of current (I) and resistance (R), and electrical power (P) is calculated by a combination of voltage (V) and current (I).
statements.guidance: Students must be able to calculate power, voltage, current and resistance in a circuit, considering V = IR and P = VI by rearranging equations and substituting values.

statements.text: Resistors and capacitors can be used in series or parallel in a circuit for different purposes.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to calculate resistance and capacitance in series and parallel in a circuit.

statements.text: Electronic systems are used to perform a specific function, which can be mapped using a flow diagram.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to construct flow diagrams (using appropriate symbols) to model a programmable system that controls an electronic device.

statements.text: System diagrams depict the components and the arrangement of circuits.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to construct diagrams for simple circuits that use resistors, capacitors, switches, relays, diodes, transistors, operational amplifiers, integrated circuits, and input and output devices.

statements.text: Digital systems at the first stage of the input–process–output model use inputs to sense changes in their environment.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to determine the use of sensors to collect and input information into a digital system, including accelerometer (motion), ultrasonic (distance or proximity), photoresistor (light), voltage (moisture), hygrometer (humidity and air temperature), pressure (barometric), microphone (sound) and infrared (radiation or heat).

statements.text: Digital systems at the second stage of the input–process–output model use control circuits to monitor and control.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to create simple circuits that use microcontrollers as a programmable integrated circuit (PIC) with appropriate software to carry out a predetermined task.

statements.text: Digital systems use logic to compare input data.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to describe digital systems in terms of the binary number system, Boolean algebra, logic gates such as AND, OR and NOT, combinational logic circuits and sequential logic circuits, and be able to construct truth tables for a digital circuit.

statements.text: Digital systems at the third stage of the input–process–output model use the output to communicate to or control their environment.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to determine appropriate output devices to communicate information or physically control an environment, including motors (including servos and pumps), LCD display (communication and light), buzzer (sound) and relay (mechanical).

statements.text: Digital systems can communicate with each other using embedded systems.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to compare the protocol embedded systems used to communicate with other systems (Wi-Fi vs Bluetooth vs 5G).

title: Production systems

sections.title: Lesson 1: Production System Uniqueness
sections.html:
4.1.1 Production System Uniqueness ~15 min (with 4.1.2) Prior knowledge: none assumed

Lesson 1: Production System Uniqueness

Production systems are matched to the product being made. Before designers can choose a manufacturing technique, they need to be able to identify and describe the systems available and recognise which real products come from each.

Hook (5 min)

Show two images side by side: a hand-stitched leather bag and a robotic car-assembly line. Ask: "Which took longer to make one unit? Which could make one million units fastest?" Take quick verbal answers — no wrong answers, just surfaces the craft-vs-automation spectrum students are about to formalise.

Engagement: Production System Card Sort

In pairs, students receive six system-name cards and arrange them along a spectrum from most human-controlled to most machine-controlled. For each, they write one sentence naming a real product made that way. Cold-call three pairs to defend their placement — this is where the key terms craft, mechanized, automated, and CIM get repeated aloud and stick.

The Six Production Systems

1. Craft Production

Definition: Small-scale production centred on manual skill and a strong human element; produces customised, high-quality goods.

Example: A hand-stitched leather bag, made start to finish by one artisan.

2. Mechanized Production

Definition: A volume process using machines controlled by humans — a mix of manual and automated work.

Example: A human-operated textile loom weaving fabric on a production floor.

3. Automated Production

Definition: A volume process where machines, controlled by computers, perform all or nearly all tasks, cutting human error and boosting precision.

Example: Robotic arms welding and assembling smartphones on a production line.

4. Assembly-Line Production

Definition: A volume process where the product moves continuously along a conveyor, gaining components at each workstation.

Example: A car body moving down the line as doors, engines and seats are fitted in sequence.

5. Hybrid Production Systems

Definition: A combination of systems used to make a single product.

Example: 3D printing a prototype, then injection moulding the same part for mass production.

6. Computer Integrated Manufacturing (CIM)

Definition: A fully automated system where computers integrate production, business and manufacturing processes end-to-end.

Example: A smart factory with real-time inventory tracking and automated quality control.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Balance of Machinery Use
sections.html:
4.1.2 Balance of Machinery Use ~15 min (with 4.1.1)

Lesson 2: Balance of Machinery Use

Every system sits somewhere on a spectrum between manufacturer (human) and tools/machinery. Designers must be able to argue the advantages and disadvantages of each.

Discuss (2 min quick-fire pair talk)

"Would you rather buy a mass-produced watch for $30 or a hand-crafted one for $300? What are you actually paying for?" Surfaces value, consistency, and the human element as discussion threads.

Advantages & Disadvantages by System

1. Craft

Advantage: Highly customised, high perceived value, flexible design changes.

Disadvantage: Slow, expensive per unit, inconsistent between units.

2. Mechanized

Advantage: Faster than craft, retains some skilled judgement.

Disadvantage: Still limited by operator speed and fatigue.

3. Automated

Advantage: Very high precision, consistent quality, low labour cost per unit.

Disadvantage: High capital cost, inflexible to design change, job displacement.

4. Assembly-line

Advantage: High throughput, specialised efficient workstations.

Disadvantage: Monotonous labour; a stoppage at one station halts the whole line.

5. Hybrid

Advantage: Combines the strengths of each stage of manufacture.

Disadvantage: Complex to plan and coordinate; multiple skill sets needed.

6. CIM

Advantage: End-to-end efficiency, real-time data, minimal human error.

Disadvantage: Extremely high setup cost, requires specialist maintenance.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Scale of Production
sections.html:
4.1.3 Scale of Production ~15 min

Lesson 3: Scale of Production

Production systems are also selected according to the required volume of output.

Engagement: Match the Scale

Rapid-fire round: call out a product (custom wedding dress, an iPhone, a limited sneaker drop, A4 printer paper, a Formula 1 chassis). Students hold up one of five scale cards simultaneously. Discuss any disagreements — the most productive disagreement is usually mass vs. mass customization.

The Five Scales of Production

1. One-off Production

Definition: An individual, often craft-produced article, or a prototype for larger-scale production.

Example: A custom-built superyacht.

2. Batch Production

Definition: A limited, set number of items produced together, balancing customisation and efficiency.

Example: A limited-edition run of sneakers.

3. Mass Production

Definition: Large volumes of standardised products on production lines, giving high output per worker.

Example: Identical smartphones made for a global market.

4. Mass Customization

Definition: A sophisticated approach that customises individual products while keeping mass-production efficiency.

Example: Nike By You — customers choose colours/materials on a mass-produced shoe platform.

5. Continuous Production

Definition: Manufacture or processing without interruption, ideal for constant high demand.

Example: Rolling aluminium sheet around the clock.

Watch (2 min)

Mass Customisation (Operations Management) — a short explainer distinguishing mass customization from standard mass production.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Factors Influencing Choice
sections.html:
4.1.4 Factors Influencing Choice ~15 min

Lesson 4: Factors Influencing Choice

Selecting and justifying a manufacturing technique depends on several interacting factors.

1. Type of Product (Part) Being Manufactured

A single injection-moulded bracket vs. a load-bearing structural beam demand very different processes.

2. Type of Material(s) Used

Thermoplastics suit injection moulding; hardwoods suit craft joinery.

3. Scale of Production (Volume)

A prototype (one-off) vs. a global product line (mass) need entirely different systems.

4. Production System Constraints

Available machinery, factory layout, and workforce skill limit what is feasible.

5. Cost and Environmental Considerations

Tooling cost, energy use, material waste, and end-of-life impact all weigh into the decision.

Engagement: You Decide

In groups of three, students receive one product brief (e.g. "500 identical ceramic mugs for a café chain" or "a one-off prosthetic hand fitted to a single patient"). Groups recommend a production system and scale, justifying the choice against at least three of the factors above, then pitch it to the class in 30 seconds. This is where Discuss and Justify command-term language gets practised out loud.

Example brief

500 identical ceramic mugs for a café chain — moderate volume, standardised product, low unit cost required → batch production is the likely fit, balancing tooling cost against the need for some customisation (chain branding) without full mass-production infrastructure.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Deconstruction and Design
sections.html:
4.1.5 Deconstruction and Design ~15 min (with 4.1.6)

Lesson 5: Deconstruction and Design

Designing a production system requires understanding the product and its components in depth. Students must be able to deconstruct a multi-component product and analyse how each part was made and how it functions within the assembly.

Engagement: Deconstruction Lab

In pairs, carefully take apart a simple multi-component object (a retractable pen works well: spring, ink cartridge, click mechanism, moulded barrel). For each component, students record in a table: component name, likely material, likely production method, and its function in the assembly.

Tools needed: a small screwdriver set, plastic pry tools; no live tools or heat required.

Case study: the retractable pen

A retractable pen alone typically reveals injection moulding (barrel, clip), metal forming (spring), and precision assembly (click mechanism) — three different processes in one cheap object.

Recording Table (worked example)

ComponentLikely materialLikely production methodFunction in assembly
BarrelThermoplastic (e.g. polypropylene)Injection mouldingHouses and protects internal components; provides grip
ClipThermoplastic or metalInjection moulding / metal stampingSecures pen to pocket or notebook
SpringSteel wireMetal forming (coiling)Provides the retracting force in the click mechanism
Click mechanismThermoplastic / metalInjection moulding + precision assemblyExtends and retracts the ink cartridge on demand
Ink cartridgePlastic tube + metal tip/ballExtrusion + precision metal machiningStores and delivers ink to the writing surface

Optional extension viewing

For a look at high-speed automated assembly in a real factory: BMW Car Factory ROBOTS — Fast Manufacturing.

sections.title: Lesson 6: Impact on Aesthetics and Function
sections.html:
4.1.6 Impact on Aesthetics and Function ~15 min (with 4.1.5)

Lesson 6: Impact on Aesthetics and Function

The production system and manufacturing technique used constrain and shape a product's final look, feel and performance — designers must be able to discuss this relationship.

1. Aesthetics

Injection moulding gives smooth, seamless surfaces; hand-craft leaves visible tool marks and asymmetry that signal authenticity and value.

2. Function

Automated CNC machining achieves tolerances a human hand cannot, enabling precision parts (e.g. surgical instruments); assembly-line standardisation ensures every unit performs identically.

3. Trade-off

A hand-built product may be structurally stronger through skilled craft joinery, but an automated one is more dimensionally consistent across thousands of units.

Discuss

Return to the deconstructed object from Lesson 5: "Which component would look or perform differently if it had been hand-crafted instead of moulded? What would be gained, and what would be lost?"

Linking Questions (extension / revision)

  • A2.2 Prototyping: To what extent are prototyping techniques becoming production systems?
  • B3.1 Material Selection: How does material selection impact the cost of using different production systems?
  • C3.2 Life-cycle Analysis: To what extent does the selection of a production system affect the outcome of a life-cycle analysis?
  • C4.1 Design for Manufacture: To what extent does the choice of design for manufacture (DfM) strategies affect the feasibility of certain production systems?

sections.title: Exam Practice — Topic 4.1 Production Systems
sections.html:
Exam Prep Topic 4.1 Production Systems

Exam Practice — Topic 4.1 Production Systems

Complete individually. Questions are written in IB command-term style. Suggested timing: MCQs as an in-class exit ticket (5 min); short-answer and long-answer questions for homework or the following lesson (20 min).

Section A: Multiple Choice (1 mark each)

1. Which production system involves machines performing all or nearly all tasks, controlled by computers, with minimal human involvement?

  • Mechanized production
  • Automated production
  • Craft production
  • Batch production
Reveal Answer
B. Automated production. [1] By definition, automated production uses computer-controlled machines for nearly all tasks, minimising human involvement.

2. A company manufactures a limited run of 200 numbered watches to mark an anniversary. This is best described as:

  • Mass production
  • Continuous production
  • Batch production
  • One-off production
Reveal Answer
C. Batch production. [1] A set, limited number of identical items (200) made together is the defining feature of batch production, distinguishing it from a single one-off item or a continuous/mass run.

3. Which factor is LEAST likely to influence the choice of a manufacturing technique for a new product?

  • The material(s) used in the product
  • The scale of production required
  • The favourite colour of the lead designer
  • Cost and environmental considerations
Reveal Answer
C. The favourite colour of the lead designer. [1] Personal preference for colour has no bearing on material, scale, system constraints, cost or environmental factors that determine manufacturing technique.

Section B: Short Answer (3–5 marks each)

4. Identify and describe two differences between mechanized production and automated production. [4]

Reveal Markscheme

Award up to [4] for two clearly identified and described differences (1 mark identification + 1 mark description, per difference):

  • Mechanized production is controlled by a human operator, whereas automated production is controlled by computers with minimal human involvement. [2]
  • Mechanized output speed and consistency are limited by operator skill and fatigue; automated production achieves higher precision and consistent quality regardless of fatigue. [2]

Accept other valid differences (e.g. capital cost, flexibility to design change) with clear description.

5. Describe, using an example, what is meant by mass customization, and explain how it differs from standard mass production. [5]

Reveal Markscheme
  • Definition: mass customization produces individualised products while retaining the efficiency of mass production. [1]
  • Valid example, e.g. Nike By You, where customers select colours/materials on a standardised shoe platform. [1]
  • Mass production makes identical, standardised units with no customer input, prioritising cost and speed. [1]
  • Mass customization allows customer input/personalisation at some stage while still using largely standardised, efficient processes. [1]
  • Recognises the trade-off: mass customization is more flexible than mass production but typically at a slightly higher cost/complexity. [1]

Section C: Long Answer / Extended Response (8–10 marks each)

6. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using assembly-line production for a company manufacturing a consumer product of your choice. Your answer should refer to cost, quality consistency, and flexibility. [8]

Reveal Markscheme

Indicative content (assess using level-of-response markbands, up to [8]):

  • Named product clearly identified (e.g. a car, a smartphone) and linked throughout the answer.
  • Cost: lower unit cost at high volumes due to specialised workstations and division of labour; high initial setup cost for the line and tooling.
  • Quality consistency: standardisation across workstations gives uniform quality between units; a fault at one station can affect every unit until caught.
  • Flexibility: difficult and costly to reconfigure the line for design changes or new models; a stoppage at any one station halts the entire line.
  • Balanced discussion weighing advantages against disadvantages, with a brief concluding judgement, is required for the top band (7–8 marks).

7. To what extent does the choice of production system affect the aesthetics and function of a final product? Support your answer with reference to at least two named production systems and specific real-world products. [10]

Reveal Markscheme

Indicative content (assess using level-of-response markbands, up to [10]):

  • At least two named systems compared (e.g. craft production vs. automated CNC machining, or injection moulding vs. hand-craft joinery), each linked to a specific real-world product.
  • Aesthetics: injection moulding/automation gives smooth, seamless, uniform surfaces; hand-craft leaves visible tool marks/asymmetry often valued for authenticity.
  • Function: automated/CNC systems achieve tight tolerances enabling precision performance (e.g. surgical instruments); assembly-line standardisation ensures identical performance across units; craft methods can allow bespoke structural strength for a single item.
  • "To what extent" requires a judgement: production system is a major but not sole influence — material choice, design intent, and cost constraints also shape outcomes.
  • Top band (9–10) requires a sustained, well-supported evaluation with a clear, justified conclusion.

[1] Personal preference for colour has no bearing on material, scale, system constraints, cost or environmental factors that determine manufacturing technique. Section B: Short Answer (3–5 marks each) 4. Identify and describe two differences between mechanized production and automated production. [4] Reveal Markscheme Award up to [4] for two clearly identified and described differences (1 mark identification + 1 mark description, per difference): Mechanized production is controlled by a human operator, whereas automated production is controlled by computers with minimal human involvement. [2] Mechanized output speed and consistency are limited by operator skill and fatigue; automated production achieves higher precision and consistent quality regardless of fatigue. [2] Accept other valid differences (e.g. capital cost, flexibility to design change) with clear description. 5. Describe, using an example, what is meant by mass customization, and explain how it differs from standard mass production. [5] Reveal Markscheme Definition: mass customization produces individualised products while retaining the efficiency of mass production. [1] Valid example, e.g. Nike By You, where customers select colours/materials on a standardised shoe platform. [1] Mass production makes identical, standardised units with no customer input, prioritising cost and speed. [1] Mass customization allows customer input/personalisation at some stage while still using largely standardised, efficient processes. [1] Recognises the trade-off: mass customization is more flexible than mass production but typically at a slightly higher cost/complexity. [1] Section C: Long Answer / Extended Response (8–10 marks each) 6. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using assembly-line production for a company manufacturing a consumer product of your choice. Your answer should refer to cost, quality consistency, and flexibility. [8] Reveal Markscheme Indicative content (assess using level-of-response markbands, up to [8] ): Named product clearly identified (e.g. a car, a smartphone) and linked throughout the answer. Cost: lower unit cost at high volumes due to specialised workstations and division of labour; high initial setup cost for the line and tooling. Quality consistency: standardisation across workstations gives uniform quality between units; a fault at one station can affect every unit until caught. Flexibility: difficult and costly to reconfigure the line for design changes or new models; a stoppage at any one station halts the entire line. Balanced discussion weighing advantages against disadvantages, with a brief concluding judgement, is required for the top band (7–8 marks). 7. To what extent does the choice of production system affect the aesthetics and function of a final product? Support your answer with reference to at least two named production systems and specific real-world products. [10] Reveal Markscheme Indicative content (assess using level-of-response markbands, up to [10] ): At least two named systems compared (e.g. craft production vs. automated CNC machining, or injection moulding vs. hand-craft joinery), each linked to a specific real-world product. Aesthetics: injection moulding/automation gives smooth, seamless, uniform surfaces; hand-craft leaves visible tool marks/asymmetry often valued for authenticity. Function: automated/CNC systems achieve tight tolerances enabling precision performance (e.g. surgical instruments); assembly-line standardisation ensures identical performance across units; craft methods can allow bespoke structural strength for a single item. "To what extent" requires a judgement: production system is a major but not sole influence — material choice, design intent, and cost constraints also shape outcomes. Top band (9–10) requires a sustained, well-supported evaluation with a clear, justified conclusion.

sections.title: Glossary — Topic 4.1 Production Systems
sections.html:
Glossary

Glossary — Topic 4.1 Production Systems

Click on a term to reveal its definition.

Production System

Definition: The organisation of how products are manufactured, including facilities, machinery and equipment.

Example: A car manufacturer's entire factory floor layout, robotics, and worker stations combined.

Craft Production

Definition: Small-scale production centred on manual skills and a human element, focused on customised, high-quality products.

Example: A luthier hand-building an acoustic guitar.

Mechanized Production

Definition: A volume production process involving machines controlled by humans; a mix of manual and automated components.

Example: A worker operating a power loom in a textile mill.

Automated Production

Definition: A volume production process where machines perform all or nearly all tasks, controlled by computers, reducing human error and increasing precision.

Example: Robotic arms spot-welding car frames at a Tesla gigafactory.

Assembly-line Production

Definition: Volume production where products move continuously along a conveyor while components are added at successive workstations.

Example: The original Ford Model T production line.

Hybrid Production Systems

Definition: A combination of manufacturing systems required to make a single product.

Example: A 3D-printed prototype tooling used to injection-mould the final plastic part.

Computer Integrated Manufacturing (CIM)

Definition: A fully automated manufacturing system using computers to integrate production, business and manufacturing processes.

Example: A smart factory that automatically reorders raw materials when inventory sensors run low.

One-off Production

Definition: An individual, often craft-produced article, or a prototype for larger-scale production.

Example: A bespoke superyacht built for a single client.

Batch Production

Definition: Limited volume production where a set number of items are produced, balancing customisation and efficiency.

Example: A seasonal batch of 5,000 limited-edition trainers.

Mass Production

Definition: Production of large amounts of standardised products on production lines, permitting high rates of production per worker.

Example: Millions of identical smartphones assembled for global release.

Mass Customization

Definition: A sophisticated approach to producing customised products while maintaining mass-production efficiency.

Example: Nike By You, where customers personalise colourways on a standardised shoe platform.

Continuous Production

Definition: A method used to manufacture or process materials without interruption; ideal for high-demand products.

Example: Round-the-clock rolling of aluminium sheet at a smelting plant.

syllabus.title: Production systems
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How is the ideal production system determined for a product?

statements.text: Production systems can be unique and specific to the type of product being manufactured.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify the most effective type of production system (craft, mechanized, automated, assembly line, hybrid production systems and computer integrated manufacturing (CIM)) used in the manufacture of a given product.

statements.text: Production systems can be categorized based on the balance between the manufacturer and the tools and machinery they use.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each production system, including craft production, mechanization, automation, assembly line, hybrid production systems and CIM.

statements.text: Production systems are selected according to the required scale of production.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to determine appropriate manufacturing techniques for each scale of production, including one-off production, batch production, mass production, mass customization and continuous production.

statements.text: Various factors influence the choice of manufacturing techniques.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss factors that influence choices of manufacturing techniques, including type of product (part) being manufactured, type of material(s) used in production, scale of production, production system, cost constraints and environmental considerations. Students must be able to justify the selection of appropriate manufacturing techniques for the production of a product.

statements.text: The design of a production system requires an understanding of a product, its component parts and the manufacturing techniques used.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to deconstruct and analyse multi-component products to determine how they were made and their relevance within the assembly and function of a product.

statements.text: The design of a product is influenced by the limitations of a production system and manufacturing techniques.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss how production methods can influence the function and aesthetics of a product.

activity.title: Paper factory
steps: Make identical folded paper products first as individual one-off work, then in a small batch.
Divide the process into stations and run a short production line.
Record throughput, work in progress, errors and waiting time.
Identify a bottleneck; change one station and compare the evidence.
activity.debrief: When can a faster station fail to improve total throughput?

exam.question: Explain one reason for using batch production rather than continuous production. [2]
exam.answer: Batch production supports different product variants or intermittent demand; equipment can be changed between batches rather than being dedicated to one uninterrupted output.
exam.label: Additional teacher-authored exam-style practice; indicative answer

activities.title: Engagement: Production System Card Sort
activities.text: Engagement: Production System Card Sort In pairs, students receive six system-name cards and arrange them along a spectrum from most human-controlled to most machine-controlled. For each, they write one sentence naming a real product made that way. Cold-call three pairs to defend their placement — this is where the key terms craft , mechanized , automated , and CIM get repeated aloud and stick.

activities.title: Discuss (2 min quick-fire pair talk)
activities.text: Discuss (2 min quick-fire pair talk) "Would you rather buy a mass-produced watch for $30 or a hand-crafted one for $300? What are you actually paying for?" Surfaces value, consistency, and the human element as discussion threads.

activities.title: Engagement: Match the Scale
activities.text: Engagement: Match the Scale Rapid-fire round: call out a product (custom wedding dress, an iPhone, a limited sneaker drop, A4 printer paper, a Formula 1 chassis). Students hold up one of five scale cards simultaneously. Discuss any disagreements — the most productive disagreement is usually mass vs. mass customization.

activities.title: Engagement: You Decide
activities.text: Engagement: You Decide In groups of three, students receive one product brief (e.g. "500 identical ceramic mugs for a café chain" or "a one-off prosthetic hand fitted to a single patient"). Groups recommend a production system and scale, justifying the choice against at least three of the factors above, then pitch it to the class in 30 seconds. This is where Discuss and Justify command-term language gets practised out loud.

activities.title: Engagement: Deconstruction Lab
activities.text: Engagement: Deconstruction Lab In pairs, carefully take apart a simple multi-component object (a retractable pen works well: spring, ink cartridge, click mechanism, moulded barrel). For each component, students record in a table: component name, likely material, likely production method, and its function in the assembly. Tools needed: a small screwdriver set, plastic pry tools; no live tools or heat required.

a mix of manual and automated components. example: a worker operating a power loom in a textile mill. automated production definition: a volume production process where machines perform all or nearly all tasks, controlled by computers, reducing human error and increasing precision. example: robotic arms spot-welding car frames at a tesla gigafactory. assembly-line production definition: volume production where products move continuously along a conveyor while components are added at successive workstations. example: the original ford model t production line. hybrid production systems definition: a combination of manufacturing systems required to make a single product. example: a 3d-printed prototype tooling used to injection-mould the final plastic part. computer integrated manufacturing (cim) definition: a fully automated manufacturing system using computers to integrate production, business and manufacturing processes. example: a smart factory that automatically reorders raw materials when inventory sensors run low. one-off production definition: an individual, often craft-produced article, or a prototype for larger-scale production. example: a bespoke superyacht built for a single client. batch production definition: limited volume production where a set number of items are produced, balancing customisation and efficiency. example: a seasonal batch of 5,000 limited-edition trainers. mass production definition: production of large amounts of standardised products on production lines, permitting high rates of production per worker. example: millions of identical smartphones assembled for global release. mass customization definition: a sophisticated approach to producing customised products while maintaining mass-production efficiency. example: nike by you, where customers personalise colourways on a standardised shoe platform. continuous production definition: a method used to manufacture or process materials without interruption; ideal for high-demand products. example: round-the-clock rolling of aluminium sheet at a smelting plant. assembly-line production automated production computer integrated manufacturing (cim) continuous production craft production batch production hybrid production system mechanized production mass production one-off production production system hybrid production systems mass customization production systems can be unique and specific to the type of product being manufactured. production systems can be categorized based on the balance between the manufacturer and the tools and machinery they use. production systems are selected according to the required scale of production. various factors influence the choice of manufacturing techniques. the design of a production system requires an understanding of a product, its component parts and the manufacturing techniques used. the design of a product is influenced by the limitations of a production system and manufacturing techniques.

title: Responsibility of the designer

sections.title: Unit Overview
sections.html:
Unit Overview

Welcome to Unit C1.1: Responsibility of the Designer! In this unit, we will explore the critical role designers play in shaping our world through product development. You'll discover that designing is more than just aesthetics and function; it involves a deep responsibility to clients, communities, and the environment.

Across several parts, we'll delve into ethical considerations, safety standards, and the complex challenge of obsolescence. By the end, you'll be able to outline a designer's multifaceted responsibilities and connect these crucial concepts to other areas of design technology. Let's uncover how thoughtful design can lead to innovative and continuously evolving products for a changing world! 💡

Recommended Time Allocation: Multiple sessions

Lesson Objectives:

  • Outline a designer's responsibility to the client, community, and environment, referencing the Triple Bottom Line.
  • Discuss how safety standards and codes of practice ensure user well-being.
  • Analyze the different types of obsolescence (planned, style, technological, functional, social).
  • Evaluate how obsolescence impacts the Triple Bottom Line (TBL).
  • Use linking questions to connect your understanding of designer responsibility to other areas of the syllabus.

sections.title: Part 1: The Designer's Triple Responsibility
sections.html:
Part 1: The Designer's Triple Responsibility

Focus: 1.1.1 Client Needs and Environmental Considerations.

Introduction & Hook: Impact Spectrum Analysis ⚖️

Activity: Think-Pair-Share

In pairs, brainstorm three products for each category:

  • A product with a significant positive impact (e.g., LifeStraw, solar-powered lights).
  • A product with a significant negative impact (e.g., single-use plastic packaging, fast fashion items).
  • A product with a mixed impact (e.g., an electric car - reduces emissions but has battery disposal issues).

After your brainstorming, we'll share examples as a class. This activity will immediately frame the designer's role as one of navigating complex ethical trade-offs, moving beyond a simple good/bad dichotomy.

Core Concepts: The Triple Bottom Line

We will introduce the designer's core responsibilities: to the Client, the Community, and the Environment. It's crucial for designers to critically analyze how their decisions affect not just the end-user but also the wider world.

Framework Introduction: The Triple Bottom Line (TBL)

The Triple Bottom Line (TBL) is a framework for measuring success across three interconnected pillars:

  • People (Social): How does the design impact the community? Is it safe? Does it improve lives? Does it consider social and cultural implications, promoting fairness and well-being?
  • Planet (Environmental): What is the product's environmental footprint? This involves considering material selection, manufacturing processes, energy efficiency, lifespan, and end-of-life options like recycling or safe disposal.
  • Profit (Economic): Is the product economically viable for the client and the market? Does it generate revenue, create jobs, and contribute to economic prosperity?

Video Source: Ellen MacArthur Foundation

sections.title: Part 2: Ensuring Safety & Setting Standards
sections.html:
Part 2: Ensuring Safety & Setting Standards

Focus: 1.1.2 Safety Standards.

Discussion & Scenario: Who is Responsible?

Prompt for Discussion:

"A new electric scooter is released. Its battery has a tendency to overheat and catch fire. Who is responsible? The user? The retailer? The manufacturer? The designer?"

This discussion will naturally lead to the conclusion that the designer has a primary ethical and professional responsibility to prevent harm by adhering to established standards and codes of practice.

Case Studies: Automotive and Children's Products

The automotive industry provides a powerful example of ergonomics in action, particularly concerning safety. Engineers and designers meticulously study human physiology and the physics of a crash to create vehicles that protect occupants. This involves everything from designing crumple zones that absorb impact to creating intuitive dashboards that minimize driver distraction.

Automotive Safety

The automotive industry provides a powerful example of ergonomics in action, particularly concerning safety. Engineers and designers meticulously study human physiology and the physics of a crash to create vehicles that protect occupants. This involves everything from designing crumple zones that absorb impact to creating intuitive dashboards that minimize driver distraction.

  • The Incredible Engineering That Helps You Survive Car Crashes: This video from the channel "It's Okay To Be Smart" provides a deep dive into the physics of car crashes and how engineers use real-world crash testing to design vehicles that keep you safe. It explains the importance of crumple zones and how they hack Newton's laws to absorb and dissipate crash energy.
  • How a car's design helps make it safer in a crash: From "The Globe and Mail", this video shows a Subaru crash test at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) and explains the various design elements that contribute to a car's safety in a collision.
  • Volvo ES90 | Safety and Design: This video from Volvo Cars focuses on how they integrate safety from the very beginning of the design process, demonstrating their commitment to both design aesthetics and occupant protection.

Children's Products

Designing products for children presents a unique set of ergonomic and safety challenges. Since children are still developing and have different physical dimensions and cognitive abilities than adults, designers must consider factors like choking hazards, sharp edges, and non-toxic materials. Regulatory bodies like the CPSC play a crucial role in setting the standards that ensure these products are safe.

  • Toy Safety Hangout: Hosted by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), this video provides insights from a CPSC engineer and a spokeswoman on the various toy hazards to look for. It's a great resource for understanding the official safety standards and regulations that designers must follow, from small parts and choking hazards to flammability and lead content in paint.
  • For more insights on the business and design side of toy creation, this website provides a great resource for understanding toy safety regulations and essential considerations for designers. You can find their blog on the topic here: Toy Safety: Essential Considerations for Toy Creators and Designers.

Activity: Safety Sleuths 🕵️

Task: Evaluate Product Safety

In small groups, you will be provided with a common product (or images of one), such as a child's toy or a kitchen appliance. We will reference specific standards like those for Toy Design Safety or Automobile Design Safety as examples.

Safety & Standards Checklist: You will use a simplified checklist to evaluate your product. Standards provide minimum requirements and testing protocols:

  • Are there any sharp edges or small parts (potential choking hazard)?
  • Are the materials non-toxic and safe for intended use?
  • Are there clear instructions and warnings for use (demonstrating user-centered design)?
  • Is the electronic wiring properly insulated and protected?

Key Takeaway:

This activity makes the abstract concept of "standards" tangible and demonstrates how they are applied in practice to mitigate risks and ensure user well-being.

sections.title: Part 3: The Challenge of Obsolescence
sections.html:
Part 3: The Challenge of Obsolescence

Focus: 1.1.3 Obsolescence and its impact on the TBL.

Core Concepts: The Five Types of Obsolescence

We will define and provide clear, modern examples for each of the five types of obsolescence:

  • Planned Obsolescence: A product is intentionally designed with a limited useful lifespan, encouraging replacement (e.g., non-replaceable smartphone batteries; printers with planned component failure).
  • Technological Obsolescence: A new technology or superior product feature supersedes an existing one, making the older product less desirable or useful (e.g., landline phones replaced by smartphones; DVDs replaced by streaming services).
  • Style Obsolescence: Changes in fashions, trends, or aesthetics make a product appear outdated or undesirable, even if it is still functional (e.g., "fast fashion" clothing; older car models whose aesthetics fall out of favor).
  • Functional Obsolescence: The product wears out, breaks down, or its parts become unavailable, making it difficult or impossible to repair (e.g., an appliance for which spare parts are no longer manufactured; software that is no longer compatible with modern operating systems).
  • Social Obsolescence: External social, cultural, or environmental factors decrease the product's value or desirability (e.g., a gas-guzzling car in an era of high fuel prices and environmental consciousness; products associated with outdated social norms).

Activity: Obsolescence Impact Analysis 🌍

Task: Analyze TBL Impact

As a class, we will watch a short video on planned obsolescence and e-waste. Following the video, we will hold a class discussion or a brief debate on the topic: "How does planned obsolescence impact the three pillars of the Triple Bottom Line?"

  • Economic Impact: Consider increased sales for manufacturers versus loss of consumer trust and the financial burden on consumers.
  • Environmental Impact: Discuss increased waste and resource consumption versus the potential for new, more efficient technology.
  • Social Impact: Explore the promotion of a "throwaway culture" and potential inequalities versus job creation and innovation in new industries.

Goal: This activity encourages you to analyze the complex, multifaceted impacts of design decisions related to a product's lifespan.

Part 4: Synthesis & Linking Questions

Introduction to Linking Questions: We will explain that Linking Questions are a key skill in IB DP Design Technology. They help you connect different parts of the syllabus to form a holistic understanding of design, showing how topics like materials, ergonomics, and sustainability are all interrelated.

Group Discussion: Connecting Concepts

In small groups, choose and discuss one of the following linking questions. Be prepared to share one key point with the class:

  • How does the classification and properties of materials affect the designer’s ability to meet their responsibilities to minimize negative impacts on the communities they design for? (A3.1)
  • How does the designer mitigate the impact of social, style, functional and technological obsolescence when using a design for sustainability strategy? (C2.1)
  • To what extent are there differences between the responsibility of the designer and the responsibility of the design student as they engage with the design process? (B2.1)
