searchText: inclusive design 1.2.1 fundamental principles of inclusive design ~45 min lesson 1: fundamental principles of inclusive design inclusive design — also called universal design — means creating products, services, and environments that are usable by the widest possible range of people, regardless of age, ability, or circumstance, without the need for special adaptation. this lesson introduces the vocabulary that separates inclusive design from assistive technology, and the three payoffs that make accessibility a design driver rather than a compliance checkbox. 1. inclusive design vs assistive technology definition: inclusive design builds accessibility into the mainstream product itself, so it is usable by the widest possible range of people without special adaptation. this sits opposite "assistive technology," which is built specifically and only for a defined disabled user group. context: a dedicated jar-opening grip tool sold only in mobility-aid shops is assistive technology; a peeler with an oversized, soft, ridged handle sold to everyone is inclusive design solving the same underlying problem. materials/examples: single-purpose aids (braille labellers, jar-opener grips) vs mainstream products with accessibility built in (soft-grip peelers, lever door handles). application: helps a designer decide, at the very start of a brief, whether the goal is a specialist product for one group or a better mainstream product for everyone. 2. the curb-cut effect definition: the phenomenon where a feature designed for people with disabilities ends up benefiting a much larger population — flexible, adaptable solutions help everyone, not just people with a diagnosed impairment. context: kerb ramps were built for wheelchair users but are now used constantly by parents with strollers, delivery workers with trolleys, and travellers with roller bags. materials/examples: kerb ramps, automatic doors, closed captions, voice assistants. application: used to justify accessibility investment to stakeholders by showing the societal benefit extends well beyond the originally targeted user group. 3. business impact & innovation pressure definition: designing for accessibility expands the addressable market and frequently forces genuine innovation, because solving a hard constraint for one group usually produces a better product for all groups — accessibility constraints are a design driver, not just a compliance checkbox. context: oxo good grips was not marketed as a "disability product" — it was sold as a better peeler for everyone, and became one of the best-selling kitchen tool ranges in the world. materials/examples: market-expansion case studies, constraint-driven ideation exercises. application: reframes an accessibility requirement in a design brief as an opportunity for innovation rather than a limitation to work around. case study: oxo good grips in 1990, sam farber watched his wife betsey, who had mild arthritis, struggle to grip a thin-handled vegetable peeler. working with smart design, they developed a peeler with an oversized, soft, ridged handle designed for a user with reduced grip strength. it wasn't marketed as a "disability product" — it was sold as a better peeler for everyone, and it became one of the best-selling kitchen tool ranges in the world. read: the untold story of the vegetable peeler that changed the world — fast company . practical engagement: "adapt or include?" sort in pairs, students are given eight product photos (e.g. a single-purpose jar-opener grip aid, oxo peeler, a standard round door knob, a lever door handle, a wheelchair ramp bolted onto stairs, a low-floor bus, a large-button "senior" phone, a smartphone with adjustable text size). for each, they classify it as assistive technology (built only for an impaired user) or inclusive design (built into the mainstream product for everyone) and justify the call in one sentence. debrief: which inclusive examples also work better for a non-impaired user in a specific situation (e.g. carrying shopping bags, wearing gloves)? concept definition why it matters inclusive design building accessibility into the mainstream product itself, usable by the widest range of people. removes the need for a separate, stigmatising "disability product." assistive technology a product built specifically and only for a defined disabled user group. necessary where a mainstream solution cannot serve a specific need, but reaches a smaller market. curb-cut effect a feature designed for disabled users ends up benefiting a much larger population. shows accessibility investment as broad societal and commercial benefit, not niche cost. 1.2.2 classification of users and impairments ~45 min lesson 2: classification of users and impairments to design inclusively, a team must first understand the range of ways a person can be excluded from using a product. the syllabus groups impairments into three categories — physical, sensory, and cognitive — and a crucial exam-relevant nuance is that impairment is not always permanent. 1. physical impairment definition: a limitation affecting movement, strength, coordination, or dexterity. context: arthritis reducing a user's ability to twist a round door knob or grip a thin peeler handle. materials/examples: arthritis, paralysis, muscle weakness, limb differences. application: drives grip, handle, and control designs that require force or fine motor control. 2. sensory impairment definition: a limitation affecting the processing of external stimuli such as vision, hearing, touch, or balance. context: colour blindness affecting a user's ability to distinguish a red "stop" icon from a green "go" icon. materials/examples: colour blindness, total blindness, hearing loss, reduced finger sensitivity. application: drives contrast, sound, haptic, and multi-sensory redundancy in interface design. 3. cognitive impairment definition: a limitation affecting mental functions such as problem-solving, learning, memory, or attention. context: dementia affecting a care-home resident's ability to remember to switch off a kettle. materials/examples: dyslexia, alzheimer's, adhd, brain injuries affecting decision-making. application: drives simplification, memory aids, and automatic safety features such as shut-off timers. 4. the persona spectrum: permanent, temporary, situational definition: microsoft's "persona spectrum" model splits each impairment category into permanent, temporary, and situational versions of the same limitation — impairment is not always permanent, and designing for the permanent case also serves a much larger group of temporarily or situationally impaired users. context: a permanently one-armed user, a user with a temporary arm injury, and a new parent holding a baby in one arm all need the same one-handed product solution. materials/examples: persona spectrum diagrams mapping permanent/temporary/situational states across each impairment category. application: prevents a design team from under-serving demand by wrongly assuming only permanently impaired users need a feature. category impacts examples physical movement, strength, coordination, dexterity arthritis, paralysis, muscle weakness, limb differences sensory processing external stimuli (vision, hearing, touch, balance) colour blindness, total blindness, hearing loss, reduced finger sensitivity cognitive mental functions — problem-solving, learning, attention dyslexia, alzheimer's, adhd, brain injuries affecting decision-making case study: closed captions closed captions on streaming video were originally a sensory-impairment accommodation for d/deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers. today the majority of their use is situational — watching in a noisy gym, a quiet office, or a language that isn't the viewer's first — showing how a single accessibility feature serves permanent, temporary, and situational users simultaneously. practical engagement: "impairment simulation circuit" four stations, 5 minutes each: smear petroleum jelly on safety glasses and try to read a medicine label (sensory — vision). wear thick gardening gloves and try to send a text message (physical — dexterity). follow a six-step instruction sheet while a partner reads distracting numbers aloud (cognitive — attention). use one hand only to open a snack packet and pour a drink (physical — limb difference/situational). students log the specific point of failure at each station and one design change that would remove it. 1.2.3 the "myth of average" ~45 min lesson 3: the "myth of average" designing for the "average" (50th percentile) user is a seductive shortcut — and a well-documented design failure mode. the core statistical problem: almost nobody is average across multiple variables simultaneously. hook: the cockpit built for no one in 1950, the us air force measured 4,063 pilots on 10 body dimensions to build a single "average" cockpit. before reading on — how many of those 4,063 pilots do you think fell within the middle 30% of the range on all 10 dimensions at once? 1. the statistical problem of "average" definition: a person might have average height but above-average arm reach and below-average hand width; the more variables a product depends on, the smaller the fraction of the population that is "average" on all of them at once. context: standard classroom/office chair height sized for the 50th-percentile adult leaves shorter students' feet dangling and forces taller students into cramped knee angles — even though almost none of the affected students would be classified as having a "disability." materials/examples: anthropometric data sets, multi-variable percentile analysis. application: warns designers against sizing a product to a single "average" figure drawn from one variable in isolation. 2. the 1950 us air force cockpit study definition: the origin case for the "myth of average" outside design — a fixed cockpit sized to the average pilot on 10 dimensions was found to fit zero of the pilots tested on all 10 simultaneously. context: lieutenant gilbert daniels checked how many of the 4,063 pilots fell within the middle 30% of the range on all 10 dimensions at once — the answer was zero. the average cockpit fit no one, and was contributing to a spike in fatal crashes caused by pilots unable to reach controls or see instruments properly. the air force scrapped the fixed cockpit and mandated adjustability instead. materials/examples: daniels' 1950 anthropometric survey, the resulting shift to adjustable seats, pedals and harnesses. application: the canonical exam example for why "design for average" fails, and why adjustability replaced it. 3. trade-offs: cost vs inclusivity definition: designers must weigh inclusivity against real constraints: cost, manufacturing complexity, and aesthetics. a single fixed size is always cheaper to tool and manufacture than an adjustable range — exactly why the "design for average" trap is so persistent commercially, even though it predictably fails a majority of real users. context: a manufacturer choosing one fixed chair height for an entire school saves on tooling and stock-keeping, but guarantees a poor fit for a large proportion of students. materials/examples: cost-per-unit vs adjustability-mechanism comparisons. application: frames the decision to design for average, or to invest in adjustability, as an explicit trade-off to justify in an exam answer — not an oversight. case study: the standard classroom chair a chair sized for the 50th-percentile adult leaves shorter students' feet dangling — reducing lower-back support and circulation — and forces taller students into cramped knee angles, even though almost none of the affected students would be classified as having a "disability." the failure is statistical, not medical. practical engagement: "cockpit problem" data exercise students measure four variables across the class (hand span, forearm length, seated eye height, standing reach) and plot how many classmates fall within the middle 30% on all four simultaneously, replicating a miniature version of daniels' 1950 finding. almost always, the number is far smaller than students predict beforehand — making the statistical point experientially rather than just conceptually. further reading: the end of average (todd rose) — background on the flaw of designing for "the average" . 1.2.4 "design for extremes" strategy ~45 min lesson 4: "design for extremes" strategy rather than designing for the average, designers deliberately design for the extremes of the user population — typically the 5th and 95th percentile (or, for higher-stakes safety products, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentile). the logic: if a product, combined with a range of adjustability, fits the shortest and tallest, strongest and weakest users at the boundaries of the "normal" distribution, it will fit almost everyone in between. watch: why accessible design is for everyone — stefanie reid, ted. 1. design for extremes: core logic definition: a strategy of designing products to function for users at the low and high ends of the population range (typically 5th–95th or 2.5th–97.5th percentile), so that, combined with adjustability, the product fits nearly everyone between. context: a modern car seat adjusts fore-aft, seat height, backrest angle, and lumbar support, and the steering column tilts and telescopes — fitting the 5th-percentile female driver and the 95th-percentile male driver, with everyone else accommodated by the adjustable range between them. materials/examples: 5th/95th percentile anthropometric targets, adjustability mechanisms. application: replaces the single "average" figure from lesson 3 with two boundary figures plus a range in between. 2. advantages definition: inclusivity — accommodates atypical body sizes and many users with disabilities without a separate product line. wider market appeal — an adjustable product reaches more customer segments. safety — reduces risk by explicitly testing for the most vulnerable users. context: automotive crash-test programmes test both a 5th-percentile female and a 95th-percentile male dummy, because a restraint system tuned only to an average-sized occupant can injure people at either end of the range. materials/examples: crash-test dummy ranges, adjustable product lines replacing multiple fixed-size skus. application: the strongest justification points to use in an exam "justify" or "evaluate" response. 3. disadvantages definition: increased cost — more material, more testing, and mechanical adjustability mechanisms raise unit cost. complexity — more moving parts can mean more points of failure and confusion. over-engineering — features for the extreme user can clutter the interface for the majority "middle" user who never touches them. context: a chair with six separate adjustment levers is harder to operate correctly than one with none — the very adjustability meant to include more users can itself become a usability barrier. materials/examples: multi-lever office chairs, feature-heavy control panels. application: the balancing counter-argument required for a fully evaluated exam response. case study: automotive seating and steering columns a modern car seat adjusts fore-aft, seat height, backrest angle, and lumbar support, and the steering column tilts and telescopes — a direct application of designing to fit the 5th-percentile female driver and the 95th-percentile male driver, with everyone else accommodated by the adjustable range between them. the trade-off is real: this adjustability adds motors, rails, and cost that a single fixed seat would not need. practical engagement: "design the extremes" brief in groups, students are given a product brief (e.g. a public library self-checkout kiosk) and two user profiles at the percentile extremes (a seated wheelchair user at low reach height; a standing 95th-percentile-height user). they sketch one adjustable or dual-mode feature that satisfies both extremes, then list one cost or complexity trade-off their solution introduces. advantages of design for extremes disadvantages of design for extremes inclusivity — accommodates atypical body sizes and disabilities without a separate product line wider market appeal — reaches more customer segments than a single fixed size safety — explicitly tests for the most vulnerable users at the boundaries increased cost — more material, testing, and adjustability mechanisms complexity — more moving parts, more points of failure, more user confusion over-engineering — extreme-user features can clutter or bulk up the product for the middle majority 1.2.5 real-world applications and synthesis ~45 min lesson 5: real-world applications and synthesis bringing the strategies together, several everyday products show inclusive design and design-for-extremes operating side by side. this lesson links c1.2 outward to mechanical systems, electronic systems, ergonomics, and user-centred research across the syllabus. 1. door handles — mechanical advantage definition: lever-style handles require only a downward push (achievable with a closed fist, elbow, or forearm) rather than the grip-and-twist motion a round knob demands, which fails for users with arthritis, limited grip strength, or hands full of shopping bags. context: this links directly to b3.3 mechanical systems : the lever provides mechanical advantage, converting a small downward force into enough torque to release the latch. materials/examples: lever-style door handles vs round door knobs. application: a concrete, exam-ready example connecting inclusive design to mechanical principles. 2. smartphones — accessibility features gone mainstream definition: voice commands, screen magnification, colour-correction filters, and haptic feedback were originally accessibility features for sensory- and physical-impairment users, and are now used constantly by the general population. context: voice commands are used while driving; screen magnification is used by anyone in bright sunlight — a further curb-cut effect example. materials/examples: voice assistants, screen magnifiers, colour-correction filters, haptic feedback. application: shows how a single accessibility feature can serve permanent, temporary, and situational users at once (lesson 2's persona spectrum). 3. low-placed sinks and countertops — trade-offs definition: low-placed sinks and countertops are needed for wheelchair-user knee clearance and reach, but they create a genuine trade-off: a sink low enough for a wheelchair user can be uncomfortably low for a very tall standing user. context: height-adjustable counters are the more complete inclusive solution — a direct application of the design-for-extremes-plus-adjustability logic from lesson 4. materials/examples: fixed low counters vs height-adjustable counters. application: a useful example for exam questions asking students to identify a trade-off in an inclusive design solution. practical engagement: "redesign the handle" mini-challenge students are given a round door knob and asked to redesign it as a lever handle on paper, labelling (a) the impairment category it addresses, (b) the mechanical principle enabling the improvement, and (c) one population beyond disabled users who also benefits (e.g. someone carrying groceries). linking questions use these to bridge c1.2 to other parts of the syllabus and to build the kind of cross-topic thinking paper 2 extended-response questions reward. a1.1 ergonomics: to what extent is a deep understanding of ergonomics (reach, clearance, strength) vital for inclusive design? a2.1 user-centred research: how can designers use user-centred research methods to remove personal bias and understand diverse needs? b3.3 mechanical systems: how does mechanical advantage (e.g. levers) improve accessibility for impaired users? b3.4 electronic systems: how can sensors and microcontrollers enhance products to be more inclusive? c1.3 beyond usability (hl): to what extent does the attract/converse/transact (act) model promote inclusive design? c1.2 exam practice ao1 / ao2 / ao3 exam practice: topic c1.2 the following questions are written in the style of ib dp design technology paper 1 and paper 2. a stimulus is provided below; use it to anchor every question, as the real ib papers do. stimulus: "clearpour" a homeware company, clearpour, is developing an electric kettle for use in residential care homes. the design brief requires it to be usable by residents with a wide range of physical, sensory, and cognitive abilities, as well as by staff. the design team began with field research and interviews inside two care homes before generating any concepts. the final prototype uses a large, high-contrast on/off switch, a wide double-handed grip moulded from a soft-touch material, and an automatic shut-off after 90 seconds of boiling. section a: multiple choice (ao1) question 1 [1 mark] which category of impairment is the clearpour kettle's high-contrast on/off switch primarily designed to address? physical sensory cognitive situational examiner insight: a direct ao1 recall/identify question — high contrast addresses the processing of a visual stimulus, the definition of a sensory impairment. reveal answer b. sensory. [1] question 2 [1 mark] the clearpour design team's decision to visit care homes and interview residents and staff before generating concepts is best classified as which stage of user-centred design? concept research implementation launch examiner insight: tests whether students can place field research and interviews correctly within the five-stage ucd model from a2.1 — gathering data before any concepts are proposed is research. reveal answer b. research. [1] question 3 [1 mark] clearpour's soft-touch, wide double-handed grip is an example of which design strategy? designing for the 50th-percentile average user designing for extremes population stereotyping secondary research examiner insight: the wide, soft grip accommodates users at the low end of grip-strength ability rather than an average user — the definition of designing for extremes. reveal answer b. designing for extremes. [1] section b: short answer (ao1 / ao2) question 4 [2 marks] state the two impairment categories, other than sensory, that a designer must consider when creating an inclusive product. examiner insight: ao1 — technical terms only, no explanation needed. the first two correct terms earn both marks. reveal answer 1. physical; 2. cognitive. [2] question 5 [2 marks] outline how clearpour's automatic shut-off feature benefits a user with a cognitive impairment such as early-stage dementia. examiner insight: ao2 outline — a brief account connecting a feature to a specific benefit (feature + benefit), not a full explanation chain. reveal answer the automatic shut-off removes the need for the user to remember to turn the kettle off (1 mark) , preventing the safety risk of the kettle boiling dry or overheating if the user forgets or is distracted (1 mark) . [2] section c: long answer (ao2 / ao3) question 6 [6 marks] justify clearpour's decision to conduct field research and interviews in care homes rather than relying on a survey sent to residents' families. examiner insight: ao3 justify — give valid evidence supporting a conclusion, linking the method choice to a higher-order goal. use a point–evidence–explain chain and address the comparison explicitly. reveal answer field research and interviews allow designers to directly observe residents' physical struggles (e.g. tremors, grip weakness) and hear staff's first-hand safety concerns, which a family-completed survey cannot capture because the intended end-users themselves are often not the respondents. interviews also allow follow-up questions that surface pain points the designer did not anticipate, whereas a survey's fixed questions can only confirm existing assumptions. because the population includes users with cognitive impairments who may not be able to reliably self-report on a written survey, direct field observation produces more valid and complete data. on balance, the depth and accuracy of firsthand field research justifies its higher time cost, especially for a safety-critical product used by a vulnerable population. [6] question 7 [8 marks] evaluate the effectiveness of clearpour's "design for extremes" approach to the grip and handle, and design one further modification that would improve the kettle's inclusivity for a user with a visual impairment. examiner insight: ao3 evaluate + design — weigh strengths against limitations with a final judgement (evaluate), then solve a specific new problem by identifying a weakness and innovating (design). both command terms must be addressed for full marks. reveal answer evaluate (5 marks): the wide double-handed grip and soft-touch material accommodate users with reduced grip strength or arthritis (physical impairment), and the dual-handed structure also spreads the weight of a full kettle, reducing strain — likely also benefiting non-impaired elderly staff carrying a heavy, hot object. however, the stimulus gives no evidence that the extremes of the sensory or cognitive spectrum were tested against, suggesting the strategy was applied narrowly to physical impairment only. a fully evaluated design-for-extremes approach should test at the percentile extremes across every relevant impairment type, not just one. design (3 marks): adding raised, tactile bumps or braille markings at the fill-line and around the power switch would let a visually impaired resident locate the correct water level and controls by touch, addressing the sensory-impairment gap identified in the evaluation above. ib definition: a strategy of designing products to function for users at the low and high ends of the population range (typically 5th–95th or 2.5th–97.5th percentile), so that, combined with adjustability, the product fits nearly everyone between. real-world context: automotive seating and steering columns adjust to fit both a 5th-percentile female driver and a 95th-percentile male driver. adjustability ib definition: a design feature allowing a product to be physically reconfigured by the user to suit their own body or preference. real-world context: a pneumatic office-chair height lever. population stereotype ib definition: an assumption about how a population as a whole is likely to interpret or respond to a design cue, used to make interfaces intuitive. real-world context: using red for "stop/delete" buttons because most users associate red with danger. mechanical advantage ib definition: the factor by which a mechanism (such as a lever) multiplies an input force. real-world context: a lever-style door handle converts a small downward push into enough torque to release the latch, unlike a round knob. design for extremes inclusive design (universal design) user-centred research methods curb-cut effect assistive technology physical impairment sensory impairment cognitive impairment persona spectrum 50th percentile ("average") user anthropometric title: Beyond usability

sections.title: Lesson 1: From Usable to Desirable
sections.html:
1.3.1 The Four-Pleasure Framework ~3 hours

Lesson 1: From Usable to Desirable

A supermarket kettle and a premium brushed-steel kettle can boil the same litre of water in the same 90 seconds. Both are perfectly usable. Yet people queue up to pay ten times more for the second one. Usability (A1.1, B1.1) explains why a product works — Beyond Usability explains why people fall in love with it. Designer and cognitive scientist Don Norman put it bluntly: attractive things work better, because positive emotion widens the way people think, makes them more tolerant of small faults, and more likely to persevere when something goes wrong.

The Core Shift

Usability asks: "can they use it?" Beyond Usability asks: "do they want it, enjoy using it, and feel it says something about who they are?" HL students use two frameworks to answer that question analytically rather than just intuitively: the Four-Pleasure Framework and the Attract/Converse/Transact (ACT) Model.

In 2000, consultant Patrick W. Jordan adapted the anthropologist Lionel Tiger's idea that human pleasure operates on four levels, and turned it into a practical design tool. The Four-Pleasure Framework gives designers a checklist for auditing the emotional experience of a product across four distinct channels: the body (physio), other people (socio), the mind (psycho), and personal values (ideo). A genuinely well-loved product rarely succeeds on just one channel — it layers several together.

PleasureChannelOne-line test
Physio-pleasureThe senses / the bodyDoes it feel, sound, or smell good to use?
Socio-pleasureOther peopleDoes it connect me to others or signal status?
Psycho-pleasureThe mindDoes it make me feel clever, in control, or intrigued?
Ideo-pleasureValues / identityDoes it reflect who I am or what I believe in?

1. Physio-Pleasure

Definition: Sensory pleasure derived from touch, smell, hearing, or taste, or satisfaction from the physical effectiveness of an object.

Context: Design cues include textures, material finishes, weights, ergonomic grips, sounds and physical sensations (A1.1 Ergonomics; B3.1 Material Selection). Sony's PlayStation 5 DualSense controller uses a textured, non-slip grip and adaptive triggers that physically stiffen to simulate the tension of drawing a bowstring — players report that the haptic feedback alone changed how "real" a game felt, entirely independent of the graphics.

Materials/Examples: Textured grips, vibration motors, adaptive triggers, material finishes.

Application: Drives choices about surface texture, weight distribution, sound design, and haptic feedback in any physical or interactive product.

Try This — Blindfolded Materials Lab

In small groups, collect 5–6 unlabelled material samples or small products (e.g. brushed aluminium, cork, soft-touch rubber, cold glass, raw plywood). Blindfold one member and have them handle each sample for 10 seconds, rating physio-pleasure from 1 (unpleasant) to 5 (delightful) without knowing what the material is.

As a group, identify which specific sensory property drove each high or low score — weight, temperature, grain, or texture — and record it. Debrief: name one product you own that wins purely on physio-pleasure, and identify the material or mechanism responsible.

2. Socio-Pleasure

Definition: Pleasure derived from social interaction, communication, or a sense of belonging to a social group.

Context: Design cues include shared experiences, collaborative features, connectivity, leaderboards, and status symbols. Apple Watch's Activity Sharing feature turns a private fitness routine into a public, slightly competitive conversation: friends see each other's daily activity rings and can send a "cheer" or a friendly "taunt" when someone is falling behind. Strava's "kudos" and segment leaderboards, and Duolingo's weekly leagues, work on the same principle — the underlying function hasn't changed, but wrapping it in a social layer measurably increases how often people use the product.

Materials/Examples: Leaderboards, shared activity feeds, connectivity features, status symbols.

Application: Used to add a competitive or belonging layer on top of an otherwise solitary product function.

Try This — Add the Social Layer

In pairs, choose a deliberately solitary, unglamorous product: a toothbrush, a running shoe, a house plant pot, or a water bottle. Sketch and describe ONE new feature that would inject socio-pleasure into it, without changing its core function.

Pitch your idea to another pair in 60 seconds. The class votes on the most convincing pitch and explains why it would actually change behaviour.

3. Psycho-Pleasure

Definition: Pleasure derived from cognition, discovery, learning, and other activities that satisfy the intellect.

Context: Design cues include intuitive interfaces that reduce cognitive load, clever problem-solving features, and satisfying micro-interactions. The dashboard of a pre-2010 luxury car could carry 40+ physical buttons for climate, audio, and navigation — each one a small decision the driver had to locate under time pressure. The Tesla Model 3 collapses almost all of that into a single, logically nested touchscreen menu: fewer physical choices, less hunting, less cognitive load, and a genuine feeling of mastery once the layout "clicks." At the other end of the complexity scale, a wordless LEGO or IKEA instruction booklet delivers the same psycho-pleasure through pure visual clarity — no reading required, no ambiguity, a small dopamine hit at every completed step (B2.2 Modelling and Prototyping).

Materials/Examples: Simplified touchscreen menus, wordless instruction booklets, intuitive nested menus.

Application: Drives interface simplification and the reduction of unnecessary decisions or steps in a task.

Try This — Cognitive Load Redesign

In groups, examine a photo or real example of a deliberately confusing interface (an old universal remote, a flashing microwave clock, a cluttered vending machine). Count the number of buttons, steps, or decisions required to complete one simple task (e.g. "set the clock").

Redesign the interface to complete the same task in the fewest possible steps. Sketch your new layout and label which buttons or steps you eliminated and why.

4. Ideo-Pleasure

Definition: Pleasures linked to ideals, aesthetics, culture, or personal values. It builds a profound emotional attachment by appealing to the customer's belief systems.

Context: Design cues include sustainable or organic materials, cultural icons, retro references, or products that represent a philosophical or political stance. An eco-friendly reusable water bottle made from biodegradable materials rarely out-performs a cheap plastic bottle on pure function — both hold and dispense water. What it sells is a value: "I am the kind of person who reduces plastic waste." Outdoor brand Patagonia pushed ideo-pleasure to its logical extreme in 2011 with a now-famous advertisement literally titled "Don't Buy This Jacket," urging customers to consider the environmental cost of consumption before buying — a message that, paradoxically, deepened brand loyalty rather than harming sales. A restored VW camper van is the classic IB example: mechanically it is slower, thirstier, and less reliable than almost any modern car, yet its owners pay a premium for the counter-culture identity and nostalgia the vehicle represents.

Materials/Examples: Biodegradable materials, retro styling, sustainability messaging, cultural/political statements.

Application: Used to build brand loyalty and emotional attachment by aligning a product with the user's self-image and values.

Try This — Value Audit

Individually, identify one object you personally own that you feel some pride or identity attachment to (a phone case, a pair of shoes, a bag, a water bottle). In two sentences, name the value or belief it signals about you, and name the specific design cue (material, branding, imagery, form) responsible for that signal.

Share with a partner: would you feel the same attachment to a functionally identical but visually generic version of the same object? Why or why not?

Synthesis: The Four-Pleasure Product Teardown

A single well-designed product almost always layers more than one pleasure at once. This closing task asks students to map all four onto one real, complex product.

Try This — Four-Pleasure Product Teardown

In groups of 3–4, each group is assigned one complex real product: a smartphone, an e-bike, a games console, or a coffee machine. Draw a 2×2 grid labelled Physio / Socio / Psycho / Ideo. For each quadrant, identify ONE specific, named design feature of the product that targets that pleasure.

Rank the four pleasures from strongest to weakest for your product, and propose one redesign that would strengthen the weakest quadrant. A spokesperson presents the group's strongest and weakest pleasure category to the class in under 90 seconds.

Background reading: People-Centred Designing: 11.1 The Four Pleasures — OpenLearn (The Open University), on Jordan's framework.

sections.title: Lesson 2: The Attract/Converse/Transact (ACT) Model
sections.html:
1.3.2 The Attract/Converse/Transact (ACT) Model ~3 hours

Lesson 2: The Attract/Converse/Transact (ACT) Model

Where the Four-Pleasure Framework audits a single moment of use, the ACT model tracks a product's entire relationship with a user over time — from the first glance in a shop window, through the daily experience of operating it, to whether it can actually be trusted to do its job. The three stages echo (without being identical to) Don Norman's influential three levels of emotional processing: visceral (instant, appearance-based), behavioral (felt during use), and reflective (long-term meaning and self-image).

Watch: 3 Ways Good Design Makes You Happy — Don Norman, TED. The psychological basis behind the ACT model.

AttractConverseTransact
Visceral / aesthetic levelBehavioral / interaction levelFunctional / usefulness level
"I want it!""How does it feel?""Does it work well?"
First impression: appearance, form, sound, finish — before any interaction occurs.Felt experience of usability during operation: intuitive controls, physical feedback, guidance.Does the product reliably and efficiently perform its core task and satisfy the practical need?

1. Attract

Definition: The visceral, aesthetic stage — the first impression a product makes through appearance, form, sound, and finish, before the customer has touched or operated it.

Context: A retro, all-metal camera body with analogue-style dials draws the eye on a shop shelf before the customer has touched a single button.

Materials/Examples: Product form, finish, colour, packaging, shop-window presence.

Application: Governs the "I want it" moment that gets a product picked up or clicked on in the first place.

2. Converse

Definition: The behavioral, interaction stage — the felt experience of usability during operation, including intuitive controls, physical feedback, and guidance.

Context: Each dial on a premium camera gives a satisfying, weighted mechanical click as settings change, and the shutter makes a crisp, reassuring sound — the camera feels considered in the hand.

Materials/Examples: Tactile dials, button feedback, sound design, control weighting.

Application: Governs "how does it feel" — the moment-to-moment interaction quality that keeps a product satisfying to use.

3. Transact

Definition: The functional, usefulness stage — whether the product reliably and efficiently performs its core task and satisfies the practical need it was bought for.

Context: Ultra-fast, reliable autofocus and long battery life mean a camera actually captures the shot when it matters, satisfying the practical need it was bought for.

Materials/Examples: Reliability, functional performance, battery life, core-task success rate.

Application: Governs long-term trust — a product can win Attract and Converse and still fail here if it doesn't actually work.

Walking Through the ACT Model: A Premium Digital Camera

  • Attract: a retro, all-metal body with analogue-style dials draws the eye on a shop shelf before the customer has touched a single button.
  • Converse: each dial gives a satisfying, weighted mechanical click as settings change, and the shutter makes a crisp, reassuring sound — the camera feels considered in the hand.
  • Transact: ultra-fast, reliable autofocus and long battery life mean the camera actually captures the shot when it matters, satisfying the practical need it was bought for.

Case Study: When ACT Fails — Juicero

In 2016, Silicon Valley start-up Juicero launched a $700 (later $400) Wi-Fi-connected juicer with a sleek, minimalist design that drew rave early press coverage and over $120 million in investment — a textbook Attract stage. Pressing the machine's handle down to extract juice from proprietary packets felt smooth and premium: a strong Converse stage too.

Then, in April 2017, Bloomberg journalists showed that the pre-packaged juice pouches could be squeezed by hand, just as fast, with no machine at all. The product had almost nothing left to offer at the Transact stage — it did not do its practical job any better than a human hand. Juicero cut its price and folded within months.

Discussion: Can a strong Attract and Converse stage ever compensate for a weak Transact stage in the long term? What does this suggest about the order of priority a designer should give the three stages?

Full case background: Wikipedia — Juicero.

Try This — The Product Journey Map

In groups, choose one real product you own or know well. Complete a three-stage journey map: one sentence plus one quick sketch for Attract, Converse, and Transact.

Be honest — if one stage is genuinely weak in your product, say so and explain why the product still succeeds (or doesn't). Gallery walk: post your map and read three other groups'. Vote on the product with the strongest full journey across all three stages.

Linking C1.3 to the Rest of the Course

To reach the top mark bands, HL students must connect Beyond Usability to other syllabus areas rather than treating it as an isolated topic.

A1.1 Ergonomics: Ergonomic elements — touch, sound, smell, and visual aesthetics — are the direct gateways for triggering physio-pleasure.
B3.1 Material Selection: Choosing distinctive materials (cool brushed aluminium vs warm, organic cork) is a primary way designers evoke physio-pleasure (sensory touch) or ideo-pleasure (sustainability).
C1.2 Inclusive Design: The ACT model directly supports universal accessibility by ensuring products are not merely usable by diverse populations, but equally desirable and attractive to them.
IA Criterion E (Presenting a Redesign): HL students can use the Four-Pleasure or ACT frameworks to justify why a final redesigned solution is emotionally superior to the original, not just functionally adequate.

Pressing the machine's handle down to extract juice from proprietary packets felt smooth and premium: a strong Converse stage too. Then, in April 2017, Bloomberg journalists showed that the pre-packaged juice pouches could be squeezed by hand, just as fast, with no machine at all. The product had almost nothing left to offer at the Transact stage — it did not do its practical job any better than a human hand. Juicero cut its price and folded within months. Discussion: Can a strong Attract and Converse stage ever compensate for a weak Transact stage in the long term? What does this suggest about the order of priority a designer should give the three stages? Full case background: Wikipedia — Juicero . Try This — The Product Journey Map In groups, choose one real product you own or know well. Complete a three-stage journey map: one sentence plus one quick sketch for Attract, Converse, and Transact. Be honest — if one stage is genuinely weak in your product, say so and explain why the product still succeeds (or doesn't). Gallery walk: post your map and read three other groups'. Vote on the product with the strongest full journey across all three stages. Linking C1.3 to the Rest of the Course To reach the top mark bands, HL students must connect Beyond Usability to other syllabus areas rather than treating it as an isolated topic. A1.1 Ergonomics: Ergonomic elements — touch, sound, smell, and visual aesthetics — are the direct gateways for triggering physio-pleasure. B3.1 Material Selection: Choosing distinctive materials (cool brushed aluminium vs warm, organic cork) is a primary way designers evoke physio-pleasure (sensory touch) or ideo-pleasure (sustainability). C1.2 Inclusive Design: The ACT model directly supports universal accessibility by ensuring products are not merely usable by diverse populations, but equally desirable and attractive to them. IA Criterion E (Presenting a Redesign): HL students can use the Four-Pleasure or ACT frameworks to justify why a final redesigned solution is emotionally superior to the original, not just functionally adequate.

sections.html:
C1.3 Exam Practice AO1 / AO2 / AO3

Exam Practice: Topic C1.3

The following questions are written in the style of IB DP Design Technology Paper 1 and Paper 2 (HL). A stimulus is provided below; use it to anchor every question, as the real IB papers do.

Stimulus: "Solstice"

"Solstice" is a premium electric commuter bicycle. It has a retro-styled frame made from 80% recycled aluminium, a mechanical pedal-assist dial that clicks between five power modes, a companion smartphone app that lets riders compare weekly distance totals with friends on a shared leaderboard, and a torque-sensing motor with regenerative braking that reliably extends range on hilly commutes.

Section A: Multiple Choice (AO1)

Question 1 [1 mark]

Identify the pleasure type MOST directly targeted by the Solstice's pedal-assist dial, which gives a satisfying, weighted click as riders shift between power modes, and its cool, smooth anodised aluminium frame.

  • Socio-pleasure
  • Psycho-pleasure
  • Physio-pleasure
  • Ideo-pleasure

Examiner insight: A quick "point and name" task from a diagram/description — no explanation required.

Reveal Answer
C. Physio-pleasure — the description is entirely about touch (dial click, cool metal), the sensory channel. [1]

Question 2 [1 mark]

A customer sees an online advert for the Solstice and feels drawn to its retro, minimalist silhouette before ever touching the bike. Identify the stage of the ACT model this reaction occurs at.

  • Converse
  • Transact
  • Usability
  • Attract

Examiner insight: Match the described moment (pre-interaction, appearance-based) to the correct named stage.

Reveal Answer
D. Attract — the visceral, aesthetic first impression before any interaction has occurred. [1]

Question 3 [1 mark]

The Solstice companion app lets riders compare weekly distance totals with friends on a shared leaderboard. Identify what this feature is primarily designed to trigger.

  • Physio-pleasure
  • Ideo-pleasure
  • Socio-pleasure
  • Usability

Examiner insight: Match the design feature (comparison with friends) to its pleasure category.

Reveal Answer
C. Socio-pleasure — the leaderboard creates social comparison and a sense of belonging to a group of riders. [1]

Section B: Short Answer (AO1 / AO2)

Question 4 [3 marks]

List the three stages of the Attract/Converse/Transact model, in the correct order.

Examiner insight: AO1 recall — give the sequence with no explanation. The order matters as much as the terms.

Reveal Answer

1. Attract; 2. Converse; 3. Transact. [3]

Question 5 [3 marks]

Outline how the Solstice's use of 80% recycled aluminium in its frame contributes to ideo-pleasure for environmentally conscious commuters.

Examiner insight: A brief account connecting the feature to the benefit — Feature + Value link + brief mechanism.

Reveal Answer

The Solstice's frame is made from 80% recycled aluminium (1), which appeals to a rider's personal value of environmental responsibility and reduced resource consumption (1). This gives the bike emotional meaning beyond simple transport, i.e. ideo-pleasure, deepening the rider's attachment to the product (1). [3]

Section C: Long Answer (AO2 / AO3)

Question 6 [6 marks]

Justify the inclusion of a mechanical, tactile pedal-assist dial rather than a fully digital touchscreen control on the Solstice, with reference to the Four-Pleasure Framework.

Examiner insight: AO3 — build a logical chain (Point → Evidence → Explain) and acknowledge the trade-off with the alternative (a touchscreen), rather than only listing an advantage. Structure: (Point: mechanical dial's physio-pleasure benefit) + (Evidence/mechanism: reliability in gloves/weather, tactile confirmation without looking) + (Flip side: what a touchscreen would offer instead) + (Synthesis/conclusion).

Reveal Answer

A mechanical dial provides strong physio-pleasure through tactile, weighted feedback that a rider can feel and confirm without looking down (Point), which is safer and more reliable in cold weather or with gloved hands, when a capacitive touchscreen may not register a press at all (Evidence). On the other hand, a touchscreen could offer richer psycho-pleasure through detailed, glanceable information such as live battery range (Flip side). However, for a product whose primary use context is an outdoor, weather-exposed commute, the reliability and immediacy of physio-pleasure through a mechanical control outweighs the extra information density of a screen, justifying Solstice's design choice (Synthesis). [6]

Question 7 [8 marks]

Evaluate the effectiveness of the Solstice's design in achieving the Transact stage of the ACT model for daily commuters, and design ONE modification that would improve psycho-pleasure for an inexperienced or elderly rider.

Examiner insight: AO3 — a full "critical appraisal." Requires a strength, a limitation, a comparison/synthesis, and a concrete, justified design modification (linking to C1.2 Inclusive Design for full marks). Structure: Strength (evidence for Transact) + Limitation (evidence against, for a specific user group) + Synthesis/judgement + Design modification with justification.

Reveal Answer

The Solstice largely succeeds at the Transact stage for the general commuter: the torque-sensing motor with regenerative braking reliably extends range on hilly routes, meaning the bike consistently performs its core function of getting a rider to work without failure (Strength). However, for an inexperienced or elderly rider, the companion app's leaderboard and multiple power-mode settings may increase cognitive load rather than reduce it, weakening psycho-pleasure and, by extension, the felt reliability of the whole system for that user group (Limitation). On balance, the Solstice's core mechanical Transact performance is strong, but its digital layer is not yet inclusive of all user personas (Synthesis). A justified modification would be an optional "Easy Mode" on the companion app: a single high-contrast screen showing only battery range and current power mode, hiding the leaderboard and secondary statistics by default. This reduces the number of decisions the rider must process (psycho-pleasure), while linking directly to the C1.2 principle that products should be inclusive without singling users out, since "Easy Mode" remains available to any rider who chooses it (Design modification + justification). [8]

sections.title: Glossary: Topic C1.3 — Beyond Usability
sections.html:
C1.3 Glossary

Glossary: Topic C1.3 — Beyond Usability

Every key term from this unit, its IB-style definition, and a real-world example that shows the term in use. Click on a term to reveal its definition.

Attract/Converse/Transact (ACT) Model
IB Definition: A framework for creating designs that improve the relationship between users and a product by intentionally triggering emotional responses.
Real-World Context: A premium digital camera with a retro, tactile aesthetic (Attract), a satisfying mechanical click of the dials (Converse), and ultra-fast, reliable autofocus (Transact).
Four-Pleasure Framework
IB Definition: A framework that encourages design for pleasure and emotion, encompassing socio-pleasure, physio-pleasure, psycho-pleasure, and ideo-pleasure.
Real-World Context: Evaluating a smart kettle for physical comfort (physio), smart-home connectivity (socio), ease of temperature programming (psycho), and energy-saving values (ideo).
Ideo-Pleasure
IB Definition: Pleasures linked to ideals, aesthetics, culture, or values.
Real-World Context: Driving a vintage VW camper van, where the cultural identity and "idea" of the vehicle bring more pleasure than its mechanical utility.
Physio-Pleasure
IB Definition: Sensory pleasure derived from touch, smell, hearing, or taste, or satisfaction from the effectiveness of an object.
Real-World Context: The smooth, weighted glide of a premium fountain pen over high-quality paper, or the haptic feedback of a PlayStation DualSense controller.
Psycho-Pleasure
IB Definition: Pleasure derived from cognition, discovery, knowledge, and other things that satisfy the intellect.
Real-World Context: Completing a difficult level in an educational puzzle game, or navigating a Tesla's simplified single-touchscreen dashboard.
Socio-Pleasure
IB Definition: Pleasure derived from a sense of belonging to a social group or social interaction.
Real-World Context: Apple Watch's Activity Sharing feature, or multiplayer gaming systems designed to keep teams communicating in real time.
Usability
IB Definition: How effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily a user can interact with a product.
Real-World Context: A website checkout process that requires only three clicks, minimising user errors and friction.

Pleasures linked to our ideal, aesthetically, culturally and otherwise.

Types of pleasure that come from cognition, discovery, knowledge and other things that satisfy the intellect.

syllabus.title: Beyond usability
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How do designers go beyond accessibility and usability to address a wider range of issues to improve products and services?

statements.text: The four-pleasure framework can act as a critical component to determine how users interpret and interact with a product.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline how the four-pleasure framework can be used to create designs that intentionally trigger socio-, physio-, psycho- and ideo-pleasure responses.

statements.text: The attract/converse/transact (ACT) model is a framework used by designers to improve the relationship between a user and a product.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to suggest how the ACT model can be used as a framework for creating products that intentionally trigger positive emotional responses, considering desirability, usability and usefulness.

activity.title: Pleasure beyond function
steps: Compare two products that perform a similar function but evoke different responses.
Assign evidence to physio-, socio-, psycho- and ideo-pleasure.
Map one product through attract, converse and transact.
Redesign one feature for a chosen emotional response and justify it for a specified user.
activity.debrief: Can emotional attachment support a longer product life?

exam.question: Distinguish physio-pleasure from socio-pleasure. [2]
exam.answer: Physio-pleasure comes from sensory or bodily experience, such as a comfortable grip. Socio-pleasure comes from social interaction or belonging associated with a product.
exam.label: Additional teacher-authored exam-style practice; indicative answer

activities.title: Try This — Blindfolded Materials Lab
activities.text: Try This — Blindfolded Materials Lab In small groups, collect 5–6 unlabelled material samples or small products (e.g. brushed aluminium, cork, soft-touch rubber, cold glass, raw plywood). Blindfold one member and have them handle each sample for 10 seconds, rating physio-pleasure from 1 (unpleasant) to 5 (delightful) without knowing what the material is. As a group, identify which specific sensory property drove each high or low score — weight, temperature, grain, or texture — and record it. Debrief: name one product you own that wins purely on physio-pleasure, and identify the material or mechanism responsible.

activities.title: Try This — Add the Social Layer
activities.text: Try This — Add the Social Layer In pairs, choose a deliberately solitary, unglamorous product: a toothbrush, a running shoe, a house plant pot, or a water bottle. Sketch and describe ONE new feature that would inject socio-pleasure into it, without changing its core function. Pitch your idea to another pair in 60 seconds. The class votes on the most convincing pitch and explains why it would actually change behaviour.

activities.title: Try This — Cognitive Load Redesign
activities.text: Try This — Cognitive Load Redesign In groups, examine a photo or real example of a deliberately confusing interface (an old universal remote, a flashing microwave clock, a cluttered vending machine). Count the number of buttons, steps, or decisions required to complete one simple task (e.g. "set the clock"). Redesign the interface to complete the same task in the fewest possible steps. Sketch your new layout and label which buttons or steps you eliminated and why.

activities.title: Try This — Value Audit
activities.text: Try This — Value Audit Individually, identify one object you personally own that you feel some pride or identity attachment to (a phone case, a pair of shoes, a bag, a water bottle). In two sentences, name the value or belief it signals about you, and name the specific design cue (material, branding, imagery, form) responsible for that signal. Share with a partner: would you feel the same attachment to a functionally identical but visually generic version of the same object? Why or why not?

activities.title: Try This — Four-Pleasure Product Teardown
activities.text: Try This — Four-Pleasure Product Teardown In groups of 3–4, each group is assigned one complex real product: a smartphone, an e-bike, a games console, or a coffee machine. Draw a 2×2 grid labelled Physio / Socio / Psycho / Ideo. For each quadrant, identify ONE specific, named design feature of the product that targets that pleasure. Rank the four pleasures from strongest to weakest for your product, and propose one redesign that would strengthen the weakest quadrant. A spokesperson presents the group's strongest and weakest pleasure category to the class in under 90 seconds.

searchText: beyond usability 1.3.1 the four-pleasure framework ~3 hours lesson 1: from usable to desirable a supermarket kettle and a premium brushed-steel kettle can boil the same litre of water in the same 90 seconds. both are perfectly usable. yet people queue up to pay ten times more for the second one. usability (a1.1, b1.1) explains why a product works — beyond usability explains why people fall in love with it . designer and cognitive scientist don norman put it bluntly: attractive things work better, because positive emotion widens the way people think, makes them more tolerant of small faults, and more likely to persevere when something goes wrong. the core shift usability asks: "can they use it?" beyond usability asks: "do they want it, enjoy using it, and feel it says something about who they are?" hl students use two frameworks to answer that question analytically rather than just intuitively: the four-pleasure framework and the attract/converse/transact (act) model . generic kettle — perfectly usable designer kettle — same function, radically different emotional appeal in 2000, consultant patrick w. jordan adapted the anthropologist lionel tiger's idea that human pleasure operates on four levels, and turned it into a practical design tool. the four-pleasure framework gives designers a checklist for auditing the emotional experience of a product across four distinct channels: the body (physio), other people (socio), the mind (psycho), and personal values (ideo). a genuinely well-loved product rarely succeeds on just one channel — it layers physically stiffen to simulate the tension of drawing a bowstring — players report that the haptic feedback alone changed how "real" a game felt, entirely independent of the graphics. debrief: name one product you own that wins purely on physio-pleasure, and identify the material or mechanism responsible. 2. socio-pleasure definition: pleasure derived from social interaction,
