social layer measurably increases how often people use the product. materials/examples: leaderboards, shared activity feeds, connectivity features, status symbols. application: used to add a competitive or belonging layer on top of an otherwise solitary product function. friends comparing fitness results try this — add the social layer in pairs, choose a deliberately solitary, unglamorous product: a toothbrush, a running shoe, a house plant pot, or a water bottle. sketch and describe one new feature that would inject socio-pleasure into it, without changing its core function. pitch your idea to another pair in 60 seconds. the class votes on the most convincing pitch and explains why it would actually change behaviour. 3. psycho-pleasure definition: pleasure derived from cognition, discovery, learning, and other activities that satisfy the intellect. context: design cues include intuitive interfaces that reduce cognitive load, clever problem-solving features, and satisfying micro-interactions. the dashboard of a pre-2010 luxury car could carry 40+ physical buttons for climate, audio, and navigation — each one a small decision the driver had to locate under time pressure. the tesla model 3 collapses almost all of that into a single, logically nested touchscreen menu: fewer physical choices, less hunting, less cognitive load, and a genuine feeling of mastery once the layout "clicks." at the other end of the complexity scale, a wordless lego or ikea instruction booklet delivers the same psycho-pleasure through pure visual clarity — no reading required, no ambiguity, a small dopamine hit at every completed step (b2.2 modelling and prototyping). materials/examples: simplified touchscreen menus, wordless instruction booklets, intuitive nested menus. application: drives interface simplification and the reduction of unnecessary decisions or steps in a task. an interface with too many decisions a cluttered remote control a confusing ticket machine try this — cognitive load redesign in groups, examine a photo or real example of a deliberately confusing interface (an old universal remote, a flashing microwave clock, a cluttered vending machine). count the number of buttons, steps, or decisions required to complete one simple task (e.g. "set the clock"). redesign the interface to complete the same task in the fewest possible steps. sketch your new layout and label which buttons or steps you eliminated and why. 4. ideo-pleasure definition: pleasures linked to ideals, aesthetics, culture, or personal values. it builds a profound emotional attachment by appealing to the customer's belief systems. context: design cues include sustainable or organic materials, cultural icons, retro references, or products that represent a philosophical or political stance. an eco-friendly reusable water bottle made from biodegradable materials rarely out-performs a cheap plastic bottle on pure function — both hold and dispense water. what it sells is a value: "i am the kind of person who reduces plastic waste." outdoor brand patagonia pushed ideo-pleasure to its logical extreme in 2011 with a now-famous advertisement literally titled "don't buy this jacket," urging customers to consider the environmental cost of consumption before buying — a message that, paradoxically, deepened brand loyalty rather than harming sales. a restored vw camper van is the classic ib example: mechanically it is slower, thirstier, and less reliable than almost any modern car, yet its owners pay a premium for the counter-culture identity and nostalgia the vehicle represents. materials/examples: biodegradable materials, retro styling, sustainability messaging, cultural/political statements. application: used to build brand loyalty and emotional attachment by aligning a product with the user's self-image and values. restored vw camper van — identity and nostalgia over reliability try this — value audit individually, identify one object you personally own that you feel some pride or identity attachment to (a phone case, a pair of shoes, a bag, a water bottle). in two sentences, name the value or belief it signals about you, and name the specific design cue (material, branding, imagery, form) responsible for that signal. share with a partner: would you feel the same attachment to a functionally identical but visually generic version of the same object? why or why not? synthesis: the four-pleasure product teardown a single well-designed product almost always layers more than one pleasure at once. this closing task asks students to map all four onto one real, complex product. try this — four-pleasure product teardown in groups of 3–4, each group is assigned one complex real product: a smartphone, an e-bike, a games console, or a coffee machine. draw a 2×2 grid labelled physio / socio / psycho / ideo. for each quadrant, identify one specific, named design feature of the product that targets that pleasure. rank the four pleasures from strongest to weakest for your product, and propose one redesign that would strengthen the weakest quadrant. a spokesperson presents the group's strongest and weakest pleasure category to the class in under 90 seconds. background reading: people-centred designing: 11.1 the four pleasures — openlearn (the open university) , on jordan's framework. 1.3.2 the attract/converse/transact (act) model ~3 hours lesson 2: the attract/converse/transact (act) model where the four-pleasure framework audits a single moment of use, the act model tracks a product's entire relationship with a user over time — from the first glance in a shop window, through the daily experience of operating it, to whether it can actually be trusted to do its job. the three stages echo (without being identical to) don norman's influential three levels of emotional processing: visceral (instant, appearance-based), behavioral (felt during use), and reflective (long-term meaning and self-image). watch: 3 ways good design makes you happy — don norman, ted. the psychological basis behind the act model. attract converse transact visceral / aesthetic level behavioral / interaction level functional / usefulness level "i want it!" "how does it feel?" "does it work well?" first impression: appearance, form, sound, finish — before any interaction occurs. felt experience of usability during operation: intuitive controls, physical feedback, guidance. does the product reliably and efficiently perform its core task and satisfy the practical need? 1. attract definition: the visceral, aesthetic stage — the first impression a product makes through appearance, form, sound, and finish, before the customer has touched or operated it. context: a retro, all-metal camera body with analogue-style dials draws the eye on a shop shelf before the customer has touched a single button. materials/examples: product form, finish, colour, packaging, shop-window presence. application: governs the "i want it" moment that gets a product picked up or clicked on in the first place. 2. converse definition: the behavioral, interaction stage — the felt experience of usability during operation, including intuitive controls, physical feedback, and guidance. context: each dial on a premium camera gives a satisfying, weighted mechanical click as settings change, and the shutter makes a crisp, reassuring sound — the camera feels considered in the hand. materials/examples: tactile dials, button feedback, sound design, control weighting. application: governs "how does it feel" — the moment-to-moment interaction quality that keeps a product satisfying to use. 3. transact definition: the functional, usefulness stage — whether the product reliably and efficiently performs its core task and satisfies the practical need it was bought for. context: ultra-fast, reliable autofocus and long battery life mean a camera actually captures the shot when it matters, satisfying the practical need it was bought for. materials/examples: reliability, functional performance, battery life, core-task success rate. application: governs long-term trust — a product can win attract and converse and still fail here if it doesn't actually work. walking through the act model: a premium digital camera a retro-styled premium digital camera attract: a retro, all-metal body with analogue-style dials draws the eye on a shop shelf before the customer has touched a single button. converse: each dial gives a satisfying, weighted mechanical click as settings change, and the shutter makes a crisp, reassuring sound — the camera feels considered in the hand. transact: ultra-fast, reliable autofocus and long battery life mean the camera actually captures the shot when it matters, satisfying the practical need it was bought for. case study: when act fails — juicero in 2016, silicon valley start-up juicero launched a $700 (later $400) wi-fi-connected juicer with a sleek, minimalist design that drew rave early press coverage and over $120 million in investment — a textbook attract stage. pressing the machine's handle down to extract juice from proprietary packets felt smooth and premium: a strong converse stage too. then, in april 2017, bloomberg journalists showed that the pre-packaged juice pouches could be squeezed by hand, just as fast, with no machine at all. the product had almost nothing left to offer at the transact stage — it did not do its practical job any better than a human hand. juicero cut its price and folded within months. discussion: can a strong attract and converse stage ever compensate for a weak transact stage in the long term? what does this suggest about the order of priority a designer should give the three stages? full case background: wikipedia — juicero . try this — the product journey map in groups, choose one real product you own or know well. complete a three-stage journey map: one sentence plus one quick sketch for attract, converse, and transact. be honest — if one stage is genuinely weak in your product, say so and explain why the product still succeeds (or doesn't). gallery walk: post your map and read three other groups'. vote on the product with the strongest full journey across all three stages. linking c1.3 to the rest of the course to reach the top mark bands, hl students must connect beyond usability to other syllabus areas rather than treating it as an isolated topic. a1.1 ergonomics: ergonomic elements — touch, sound, smell, and visual aesthetics — are the direct gateways for triggering physio-pleasure. b3.1 material selection: choosing distinctive materials (cool brushed aluminium vs warm, organic cork) is a primary way designers evoke physio-pleasure (sensory touch) or ideo-pleasure (sustainability). c1.2 inclusive design: the act model directly supports universal accessibility by ensuring products are not merely usable by diverse populations, but equally desirable and attractive to them. ia criterion e (presenting a redesign): hl students can use the four-pleasure or act frameworks to justify why a final redesigned solution is emotionally superior to the original, not just functionally adequate. c1.3 exam practice ao1 / ao2 / ao3 exam practice: topic c1.3 the following questions are written in the style of ib dp design technology paper 1 and paper 2 (hl). a stimulus is provided below; use it to anchor every question, as the real ib papers do. stimulus: "solstice" "solstice" is a premium electric commuter bicycle. it has a retro-styled frame made from 80% recycled aluminium, a mechanical pedal-assist dial that clicks between five power modes, a companion smartphone app that lets riders compare weekly distance totals with friends on a shared leaderboard, and a torque-sensing motor with regenerative braking that reliably extends range on hilly commutes. section a: multiple choice (ao1) question 1 [1 mark] identify the pleasure type most directly targeted by the solstice's pedal-assist dial, which gives a satisfying, weighted click as riders shift between power modes, and its cool, smooth anodised aluminium frame. socio-pleasure psycho-pleasure physio-pleasure ideo-pleasure examiner insight: a quick "point and name" task from a diagram/description — no explanation required. reveal answer c. physio-pleasure — the description is entirely about touch (dial click, cool metal), the sensory channel. [1] question 2 [1 mark] a customer sees an online advert for the solstice and feels drawn to its retro, minimalist silhouette before ever touching the bike. identify the stage of the act model this reaction occurs at. converse transact usability attract examiner insight: match the described moment (pre-interaction, appearance-based) to the correct named stage. reveal answer d. attract — the visceral, aesthetic first impression before any interaction has occurred. [1] question 3 [1 mark] the solstice companion app lets riders compare weekly distance totals with friends on a shared leaderboard. identify what this feature is primarily designed to trigger. physio-pleasure ideo-pleasure socio-pleasure usability examiner insight: match the design feature (comparison with friends) to its pleasure category. reveal answer c. socio-pleasure — the leaderboard creates social comparison and a sense of belonging to a group of riders. [1] section b: short answer (ao1 / ao2) question 4 [3 marks] list the three stages of the attract/converse/transact model, in the correct order. examiner insight: ao1 recall — give the sequence with no explanation. the order matters as much as the terms. reveal answer 1. attract; 2. converse; 3. transact. [3] question 5 [3 marks] outline how the solstice's use of 80% recycled aluminium in its frame contributes to ideo-pleasure for environmentally conscious commuters. examiner insight: a brief account connecting the feature to the benefit — feature + value link + brief mechanism. reveal answer the solstice's frame is made from 80% recycled aluminium (1) , which appeals to a rider's personal value of environmental responsibility and reduced resource consumption (1) . this gives the bike emotional meaning beyond simple transport, i.e. ideo-pleasure, deepening the rider's attachment to the product (1) . [3] section c: long answer (ao2 / ao3) question 6 [6 marks] justify the inclusion of a mechanical, tactile pedal-assist dial rather than a fully digital touchscreen control on the solstice, with reference to the four-pleasure framework. examiner insight: ao3 — build a logical chain (point → evidence → explain) and acknowledge the trade-off with the alternative (a touchscreen), rather than only listing an advantage. structure: (point: mechanical dial's physio-pleasure benefit) + (evidence/mechanism: reliability in gloves/weather, tactile confirmation without looking) + (flip side: what a touchscreen would offer instead) + (synthesis/conclusion). reveal answer a mechanical dial provides strong physio-pleasure through tactile, weighted feedback that a rider can feel and confirm without looking down (point), which is safer and more reliable in cold weather or with gloved hands, when a capacitive touchscreen may not register a press at all (evidence). on the other hand, a touchscreen could offer richer psycho-pleasure through detailed, glanceable information such as live battery range (flip side). however, for a product whose primary use context is an outdoor, weather-exposed commute, the reliability and immediacy of physio-pleasure through a mechanical control outweighs the extra information density of a screen, justifying solstice's design choice (synthesis). [6] question 7 [8 marks] evaluate the effectiveness of the solstice's design in achieving the transact stage of the act model for daily commuters, and design one modification that would improve psycho-pleasure for an inexperienced or elderly rider. examiner insight: ao3 — a full "critical appraisal." requires a strength, a limitation, a comparison/synthesis, and a concrete, justified design modification (linking to c1.2 inclusive design for full marks). structure: strength (evidence for transact) + limitation (evidence against, for a specific user group) + synthesis/judgement + design modification with justification. reveal answer the solstice largely succeeds at the transact stage for the general commuter: the torque-sensing motor with regenerative braking reliably extends range on hilly routes, meaning the bike consistently performs its core function of getting a rider to work without failure (strength). however, for an inexperienced or elderly rider, the companion app's leaderboard and multiple power-mode settings may increase cognitive load rather than reduce it, weakening psycho-pleasure and, by extension, the felt reliability of the whole system for that user group (limitation). on balance, the solstice's core mechanical transact performance is strong, but its digital layer is not yet inclusive of all user personas (synthesis). a justified modification would be an optional "easy mode" on the companion app: a single high-contrast screen showing only battery range and current power mode, hiding the leaderboard and secondary statistics by default. this reduces the number of decisions the rider must process (psycho-pleasure), while linking directly to the c1.2 principle that products should be inclusive without singling users out, since "easy mode" remains available to any rider who chooses it (design modification + justification). [8] c1.3 glossary glossary: topic c1.3 — beyond usability every key term from this unit, its ib-style definition, and a real-world example that shows the term in use. click on a term to reveal its definition. attract/converse/transact (act) model ib definition: a framework for creating designs that improve the relationship between users and a product by intentionally triggering emotional responses. real-world context: a premium digital camera with a retro, tactile aesthetic (attract), a satisfying mechanical click of the dials (converse), and ultra-fast, reliable autofocus (transact). four-pleasure framework ib definition: a framework that encourages design for pleasure and emotion, encompassing socio-pleasure, physio-pleasure, psycho-pleasure, and ideo-pleasure. real-world context: evaluating a smart kettle for physical comfort (physio), smart-home connectivity (socio), ease of temperature programming (psycho), and energy-saving values (ideo). ideo-pleasure ib definition: pleasures linked to ideals, aesthetics, culture, or values. real-world context: driving a vintage vw camper van, where the cultural identity and "idea" of the vehicle bring more pleasure than its mechanical utility. physio-pleasure ib definition: sensory pleasure derived from touch, smell, hearing, or taste, or satisfaction from the effectiveness of an object. real-world context: the smooth, weighted glide of a premium fountain pen over high-quality paper, or the haptic feedback of a playstation dualsense controller. psycho-pleasure ib definition: pleasure derived from cognition, discovery, knowledge, and other things that satisfy the intellect. real-world context: completing a difficult level in an educational puzzle game, or navigating a tesla's simplified single-touchscreen dashboard. socio-pleasure ib definition: pleasure derived from a sense of belonging to a social group or social interaction. real-world context: apple watch's activity sharing feature, or multiplayer gaming systems designed to keep teams communicating in real time. usability ib definition: how effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily a user can interact with a product. real-world context: a website checkout process that requires only three clicks, minimising user errors and friction. attract/converse/ transact model (act) four-pleasure framework ideo-pleasure physio-pleasure psycho-pleasure socio-pleasure usability attract/converse/transact (act) model the four-pleasure framework can act as a critical component to determine how users interpret and interact with a product. the attract/converse/transact (act) model is a framework used by designers to improve the relationship between a user and a product.

title: Design for sustainability

sections.title: Lesson Overview
sections.html:
Lesson Overview

This lesson provides an engaging and interactive approach to understanding the core principles and frameworks of sustainable design, using real-world case studies to reinforce key concepts.

Learning Objectives:

  • Discuss strategies to achieve sustainability, including waste, pollution, and energy consumption.
  • Analyze sustainable products to demonstrate how they meet Datchefski's five principles.
  • Explain the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) and the relationship between People, Planet, and Profit, including inherent conflicts and compromises.
  • Evaluate how the TBL can help designers prioritize needs to discover design opportunities.
  • Apply their knowledge to answer IB-style exam questions.

sections.title: Part 1: Sustainability
sections.html:
Part 1: Sustainability

Focus: Rethinking our approach to product lifecycles.

Discussion: A Guiding Question

Activity: Class Brainstorm

Begin by discussing the guiding question: "What does 'sustainability' mean to you?" and "What products do you believe are 'sustainable'?"

Strategies for Achieving Sustainability

To design effectively for the future, designers must implement specific strategies at every stage of a product's lifecycle.

Material Selection

Choosing renewable, recycled, or biodegradable materials reduces waste and environmental impact. Using fewer materials ensures a lower carbon footprint.

Energy Efficiency

Designing products that require less energy during production, operation, and disposal. Opting for renewable energy sources in manufacturing is key.

Waste Reduction

Reducing material waste during manufacturing. Strategies include designing for disassembly, modular design, and minimizing excess packaging.

Longevity & Durability

Creating long-lasting, repairable, and upgradable products prevents unnecessary waste. Durability reduces the need for frequent replacements.

End-of-Life Considerations

Designing for reuse, recycling, or biodegradability. Products should be designed with circular economy principles in mind to avoid landfills.

Ethical & Social Responsibility

Consider ethical manufacturing, fair labor practices, and social impact, ensuring production does not harm communities or exploit workers.

Core Concepts: The 4 R's

The foundational strategies of sustainable design in this context are Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, and Repurpose. These principles guide designers and consumers in minimizing environmental impact.

Case Study: Patagonia's "Worn Wear" Program

Reduce:

Patagonia encourages customers to buy less by creating high-quality, durable products that last a long time.

Reuse:

The "Worn Wear" program promotes repair, resale, and extending the life of products, which significantly reduces the carbon footprint. The company offers free repairs and an online marketplace for used gear.

Recycle:

Patagonia manages a take-back program for old products that have reached the end of their useful life, breaking them down to retrieve raw materials like polyester for future manufacturing.

Repurpose (Could also be Rethink or Repair):

Items that are beyond repair are repurposed into new products. For example, fabric from damaged jackets can be salvaged to create bags or unique "ReCrafted" garments, giving the material a new function.

Activity: Watch & Discuss

Watch the video below on the "Worn Wear" program and discuss which of the 4 R's are most prominent in the initiative.

sections.title: Part 2: Datchefski's Five Principles
sections.html:
Part 2: Datchefski's Five Principles

Focus: A holistic framework for sustainable product design.

Datchefski's Five Principles (30 Minutes)

Core Understanding: Introduce Edwin Datchefski's five principles of sustainable design: Cyclic, Solar, Safe, Efficient, and Social. These principles provide a holistic framework for creating environmentally responsible products.

The 5 Principles Explained

Cyclic

Products should be made from renewable or recyclable materials so they can be reused or returned to nature without causing harm. This promotes a closed-loop system where materials continuously circulate rather than becoming waste.

Solar

The manufacturing and use of the product should rely on renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind, or hydro power, to reduce reliance on fossil fuels and lower carbon emissions.

Safe

Products should be non-toxic and harmless to humans and ecosystems throughout their lifecycle. This means avoiding hazardous chemicals, pollutants, and materials that can cause long-term damage.

Efficient

The design should maximize functionality while minimizing resource consumption. This includes reducing material waste, optimizing energy use, and ensuring efficient manufacturing, transportation, and disposal.

Social

Sustainable design should benefit people by promoting fair labor practices, ethical sourcing, and community well-being. The product should be made under fair working conditions, respect human rights, and contribute positively to society.

Activity: Analyzing a Sustainable Product

Product: Herman Miller Aeron Chair. This iconic office chair is a great example of a product designed with sustainability in mind.

  • Cyclic: The chair is made from recycled aluminum and recyclable plastic components and is designed for easy disassembly at the end of its life.
  • Solar: Herman Miller has committed to using 100% renewable energy for their manufacturing.
  • Safe: It is made from non-toxic materials, ensuring it poses no harm to people or the environment during its use or disposal.
  • Efficient: The design minimizes material use while maintaining durability and performance.
  • Social: The company adheres to fair labor practices and supports communities through its foundation.

The Sustainable Sketchbook Sprint

Watch this video to see how a professional designer, Reid Schlegel, uses a sketchbook for ideation and concept development. Pay attention to how he uses mind maps, sketches, and annotations to refine his ideas.

Materials

  • Sketchbooks or A3 Paper: The primary canvas for ideation.
  • Markers, Pens, Colored Pencils: To create visually engaging and distinct drawings.
  • Post-it Notes: For quick annotations, brainstorming, and principle labeling.
  • Datschefski's Principles Reference Sheet: A printed guide to all five principles for easy reference.

The Process

Warm-up: "The Ugly Idea" (5 minutes)

Students individually draw the "ugliest" or most unsustainable version of a common product (e.g., a plastic fork, a cheap umbrella). This low-stakes exercise gets their creative juices flowing without the pressure of perfection.

Product Selection & Analysis (10 minutes)

Students choose one product from a provided list of "unsustainable culprits" (e.g., a disposable razor, a plastic laundry detergent bottle, a single-use coffee pod). On their sketchbook, they first draw the existing product and list its unsustainable qualities.

Ideation Session: "The Mind-Map & Principle-Mapping" (20 minutes)

Mind-Map: Students create a mind-map around their chosen product. Central to the mind-map is the product's function (e.g., "washing clothes"). Branches extend to problems, user needs, and potential solutions.

Principle-Mapping: They then create a new page, dedicating a section to each of Datschefski's principles. For each principle, they brainstorm and sketch ideas that would redesign the product. For example, under "Solar," they might sketch a sun-powered detergent pod dispenser. Under "Cyclic," they might draw a bottle that can be refilled at a station.

Proposal Development: "The One-Pager" (15 minutes)

Students select their strongest ideas and synthesize them into a single, cohesive proposal on one page of their sketchbook. This page should be a visual and textual pitch for their redesigned product. It should include:

  • A hero sketch of the final product.
  • Key features highlighted with arrows and text.
  • Annotations that explicitly link each feature to one or more of Datschefski's principles.
  • A brief, compelling title for the new product.
Critique & Feedback: "Gallery Walk" (10 minutes)

Students display their proposals. Others walk around, viewing the ideas and using Post-it notes to provide constructive feedback and ask questions. This peer-review process, central to design critiques, helps refine and strengthen the proposals.

Benefits

  • Focus on Concept over Craft: This activity prioritizes the quality and originality of the ideas, not the ability to build a physical prototype.
  • Structured Creativity: Techniques like mind-mapping and sketching provide a framework for students to channel their creativity effectively.
  • Documentation: The sketchbook serves as a portfolio piece, documenting their design process and thought-flow.
  • Iterative Thinking: By generating multiple ideas and then synthesizing them, students learn an essential skill of the design process: iteration.

Annotations that explicitly link each feature to one or more of Datschefski's principles. A brief, compelling title for the new product. Critique & Feedback: "Gallery Walk" (10 minutes) Students display their proposals. Others walk around, viewing the ideas and using Post-it notes to provide constructive feedback and ask questions. This peer-review process, central to design critiques, helps refine and strengthen the proposals. Benefits Focus on Concept over Craft: This activity prioritizes the quality and originality of the ideas, not the ability to build a physical prototype. Structured Creativity: Techniques like mind-mapping and sketching provide a framework for students to channel their creativity effectively. Documentation: The sketchbook serves as a portfolio piece, documenting their design process and thought-flow. Iterative Thinking: By generating multiple ideas and then synthesizing them, students learn an essential skill of the design process: iteration.

sections.title: Part 3: The Triple Bottom Line (TBL)
sections.html:
Part 3: The Triple Bottom Line (TBL)

Focus: Balancing People, Planet, and Profit.

Core Understanding: The Three P's

The Triple Bottom Line (TBL) is a framework that measures a product's success not just by financial metrics, but also by its social and environmental impact. It is a key tool for designers to evaluate the holistic impact of their work.

  • People (Social): How the design impacts human well-being, fair labor, and community engagement.
  • Planet (Environmental): The product's ecological footprint, including resource use, pollution, and waste.
  • Profit (Economic): The financial performance and long-term viability of the product.

Case Study: IKEA's Sustainable Sourcing

Conflict and Compromise

IKEA's commitment to using wood from more sustainable sources can create a conflict between the Planet and Profit. While using responsibly sourced materials may increase initial costs, it can also lead to long-term profitability by attracting environmentally-conscious consumers and reducing risks associated with illegal logging. This demonstrates how a short-term conflict can lead to a long-term win for all three pillars.

Multimedia Resource: TBL Explained

Watch this video to get a clear, visual summary of the Triple Bottom Line and its application in business and design.

sections.title: Extended Exam Practice
sections.html:
Extended Exam Practice

Let's test your understanding with some practice questions. Remember to use specific examples and terminology from the unit in your answers.

Multiple Choice Questions (Paper 1 Style)

1. Which of the following best describes the "Cyclic" principle of Datchefski's sustainable design?

A. The use of clean, renewable energy sources throughout a product's lifecycle.
B. The creation of products that can be fully recycled or composted with no waste.
C. The development of products that use the least amount of energy and materials possible.
D. The assurance that a product's creation supports basic human rights.

2. A company decides to use sustainably sourced bamboo for a new line of cutting boards. While this increases the material cost, it attracts a new segment of environmentally conscious consumers, leading to an overall increase in sales. This scenario best exemplifies the relationship between which two aspects of the Triple Bottom Line?

A. Planet and People
B. People and Profit
C. Planet and Profit
D. People, Planet, and Profit

Short Answer Questions (Paper 2 Style)

1. Explain the importance of the "Rethink" strategy in sustainable design. Use a specific example of a product that required a fundamental rethinking of its design to become more sustainable. [4 marks]

Reveal Answer

The "Rethink" strategy involves a fundamental redesign of a product or system to challenge and improve existing unsustainable practices. It is important because it goes beyond incremental changes like recycling and instead seeks to eliminate the root causes of unsustainability, leading to a more significant positive impact.

Example: The shift from single-use coffee cups to reusable keep cups or "Cup-to-Go" systems. Rather than focusing on making the disposable cup more recyclable (a "Recycle" approach), the "Rethink" strategy questions the need for a disposable cup at all. This led to the development of durable, reusable alternatives that fundamentally change the consumption model, significantly reducing waste and resource consumption.

2. Analyze how the Triple Bottom Line can help a designer to prioritize the needs of a community when designing a public-use product, such as a bench. [5 marks]

Reveal Answer

The TBL provides a structured way to evaluate trade-offs and prioritize needs for a public-use product like a bench:

  • People: A designer would prioritize the community's social needs by ensuring the bench is ergonomically sound, accessible to all (including the elderly or those with mobility issues), and made from non-toxic materials. The design should also foster social interaction and a sense of community ownership, preventing it from becoming a social nuisance.
  • Planet: The designer must consider the bench's environmental impact by selecting sustainable materials (e.g., FSC-certified wood or recycled plastic), minimizing waste during manufacturing, and ensuring the product is durable and repairable to extend its lifespan.
  • Profit: While not a direct consumer product, the bench still has an economic aspect. The designer must ensure the materials and manufacturing are cost-effective for the municipality, the maintenance is low, and the product's longevity reduces the need for frequent replacement, offering long-term economic value.

By using the TBL, a designer can see that a low-cost bench (Profit) made from unsustainable materials (bad for Planet) that is uncomfortable (bad for People) is not a true success. The framework helps prioritize the social and environmental needs of the community alongside economic viability.

Long Answer Questions (Paper 2 Style)

1. How important is material selection when creating products that are designed to be sustainable? [8 marks]

2. To what extent is the responsibility for design for sustainability the designer's alone? Justify your answer with reference to key stakeholders, such as manufacturers, consumers, and governments. [10 marks]

glossary.term: Datschefski’s five principles of sustainable design
glossary.definition: Five principles that facilitate a holistic approach to sustainable design. Cyclic: The product is made from organic materials, and is recyclable or compostable, or is made from minerals that are continuously cycled in a closed loop. Solar: The product uses solar energy or other forms of renewable energy that are cyclic and safe, both during use and manufacture. Safe: The product is non-toxic in use and disposal, and its manufacture does not involve toxic releases or the disruption of ecosystems. Efficient: The product’s efficiency in manufacture and use is improved by a factor. Social: The product and its components and raw materials are manufactured under fair and just operating conditions for the workers involved and the local communities.
In the context of design, sustainability seeks to eliminate a negative impact on the environment, health and well-being of users.
An expanded spectrum of values and criteria for measuring organizational success: economic (profit), environmental (planet) and social (people).

syllabus.title: Design for sustainability
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How can design for sustainability ensure we meet our current needs without compromising our future existence?

statements.text: Design for sustainability involves the choices and decisions made for developing designs (products) and design methodologies.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss strategies to achieve sustainability and the importance of decision- making when addressing issues related to sustainable design, including waste, pollution and energy consumption.

statements.text: The five principles of sustainable design are that a product must be cyclic (create no waste), solar (use clean energy), safe (cause no harm), efficient (use the least amount of energy and materials as possible) and social (support basic human rights) (Datchefski, 1999).
statements.guidance: Students must be able to analyse sustainable products to demonstrate how they meet Datchefski’s principles.

statements.text: The triple bottom line (TBL) measures levels of success of a product in relation to social (people), economic (profit) and environmental (planet), which are key responsibilities of a designer.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the TBL and the relationship between the three Ps (people, profit, planet), which includes conflict and compromise.

statements.text: Designers make decisions by considering the balance between the three Ps of the TBL.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain how the TBL can help designers to prioritize the needs of clients, communities and the environment to discover design opportunities.

activity.title: Five-principle redesign
steps: Select a familiar product and map its material, energy and user impacts.
Assess it against cyclic, solar, safe, efficient and social principles.
Propose a specific improvement for two principles.
Explain one trade-off across people, planet and profit; identify evidence needed to judge the result.
activity.debrief: Why does one green feature not prove a product is sustainable?

exam.question: Explain how the triple bottom line broadens an evaluation of a product. [3]
exam.answer: It considers social effects on people, environmental effects on the planet and economic performance or profit. A judgement must consider trade-offs across all three rather than cost alone.

solutions. principle-mapping: they then create a new page, dedicating a section to each of datschefski's principles. for each principle, they brainstorm and sketch ideas that would redesign the product. for example, under "solar," they might sketch a sun-powered detergent pod dispenser. under "cyclic," they might draw a bottle that can be refilled at a station. proposal development: "the one-pager" (15 minutes) students select their strongest ideas and synthesize them into a single, cohesive proposal on one page of their sketchbook. this page should be a visual and textual pitch for their redesigned product. it should include: a hero sketch of the final product. key features highlighted with arrows and text. annotations that explicitly link each feature to one or more of datschefski's principles. a brief, compelling title for the new product. critique & feedback: "gallery walk" (10 minutes) students display their proposals. others walk around, viewing the ideas and using post-it notes to provide constructive feedback and ask questions. this peer-review process, central to design critiques, helps refine and strengthen the proposals. benefits focus on concept over craft: this activity prioritizes the quality and originality of the ideas, not the ability to build a physical prototype. structured creativity: techniques like mind-mapping and sketching provide a framework for students to channel their creativity effectively. documentation: the sketchbook serves as a portfolio piece, documenting their design process and thought-flow. iterative thinking: by generating multiple ideas and then synthesizing them, students learn an essential skill of the design process: iteration. part 3: the triple bottom line (tbl) focus: balancing people, planet, and profit. core understanding: the three p's the triple bottom line (tbl) is a framework that measures a product's success not just by financial metrics, but also by its social and environmental impact. it is a key tool for designers to evaluate the holistic impact of their work. people (social): how the design impacts human well-being, fair labor, and community engagement. planet (environmental): the product's ecological footprint, including resource use, pollution, and waste. profit (economic): the financial performance and long-term viability of the product. case study: ikea's sustainable sourcing conflict and compromise ikea's commitment to using wood from more sustainable sources can create a conflict between the planet and profit . while using responsibly sourced materials may increase initial costs, it can also lead to long-term profitability by attracting environmentally-conscious consumers and reducing risks associated with illegal logging. this demonstrates how a short-term conflict can lead to a long-term win for all three pillars. multimedia resource: tbl explained watch this video to get a clear, visual summary of the triple bottom line and its application in business and design. extended exam practice let's test your understanding with some practice questions. remember to use specific examples and terminology from the unit in your answers. multiple choice questions (paper 1 style) 1. which of the following best describes the "cyclic" principle of datchefski's sustainable design? a. the use of clean, renewable energy sources throughout a product's lifecycle. b. the creation of products that can be fully recycled or composted with no waste. c. the development of products that use the least amount of energy and materials possible. d. the assurance that a product's creation supports basic human rights. 2. a company decides to use sustainably sourced bamboo for a new line of cutting boards. while this increases the material cost, it attracts a new segment of environmentally conscious consumers, leading to an overall increase in sales. this scenario best exemplifies the relationship between which two aspects of the triple bottom line? a. planet and people b. people and profit c. planet and profit d. people, planet, and profit short answer questions (paper 2 style) 1. explain the importance of the "rethink" strategy in sustainable design. use a specific example of a product that required a fundamental rethinking of its design to become more sustainable. [4 marks] reveal answer the "rethink" strategy involves a fundamental redesign of a product or system to challenge and improve existing unsustainable practices. it is important because it goes beyond incremental changes like recycling and instead seeks to eliminate the root causes of unsustainability, leading to a more significant positive impact. example: the shift from single-use coffee cups to reusable keep cups or "cup-to-go" systems. rather than focusing on making the disposable cup more recyclable (a "recycle" approach), the "rethink" strategy questions the need for a disposable cup at all. this led to the development of durable, reusable alternatives that fundamentally change the consumption model, significantly reducing waste and resource consumption. 2. analyze how the triple bottom line can help a designer to prioritize the needs of a community when designing a public-use product, such as a bench. [5 marks] reveal answer the tbl provides a structured way to evaluate trade-offs and prioritize needs for a public-use product like a bench: people: a designer would prioritize the community's social needs by ensuring the bench is ergonomically sound, accessible to all (including the elderly or those with mobility issues), and made from non-toxic materials. the design should also foster social interaction and a sense of community ownership, preventing it from becoming a social nuisance. planet: the designer must consider the bench's environmental impact by selecting sustainable materials (e.g., fsc-certified wood or recycled plastic), minimizing waste during manufacturing, and ensuring the product is durable and repairable to extend its lifespan. profit: while not a direct consumer product, the bench still has an economic aspect. the designer must ensure the materials and manufacturing are cost-effective for the municipality, the maintenance is low, and the product's longevity reduces the need for frequent replacement, offering long-term economic value. by using the tbl, a designer can see that a low-cost bench (profit) made from unsustainable materials (bad for planet) that is uncomfortable (bad for people) is not a true success. the framework helps prioritize the social and environmental needs of the community alongside economic viability. long answer questions (paper 2 style) 1. how important is material selection when creating products that are designed to be sustainable? [8 marks] 2. to what extent is the responsibility for design for sustainability the designer's alone? justify your answer with reference to key stakeholders, such as manufacturers, consumers, and governments. [10 marks] datschefski’s five principles of sustainable design sustainability triple bottom line (tbl) design for sustainability involves the choices and decisions made for developing designs (products) and design methodologies. the five principles of sustainable design are that a product must be cyclic (create no waste), solar (use clean energy), safe (cause no harm), efficient (use the least amount of energy and materials as possible) and social (support basic human rights) (datchefski, 1999). the triple bottom line (tbl) measures levels of success of a product in relation to social (people), economic (profit) and environmental (planet), which are key responsibilities of a designer. designers make decisions by considering the balance between the three ps of the tbl.

title: Design for a circular economy

sections.title: Lesson Overview
sections.html:
Lesson Overview

Key Takeaway

The Circular Economy is a deliberate, design-driven strategy that shifts from the traditional take-make-dispose model to a regenerative system focused on eliminating waste, circulating materials, and regenerating nature.

Learning Objectives:

  • Compare and contrast the linear economy and the circular economy, explaining why the latter is restorative and regenerative by design.
  • Discuss and apply design strategies for eliminating waste, including longevity, upgradability, disassembly, and dematerialization.
  • Analyze the role of biodegradable materials and the "R" strategies (reuse, repair, recondition, recycling) in closing the loop.
  • Explain the reliance of the circular economy on renewable energy sources.

sections.title: Part 2: Eliminating Waste: The Concept2 RowErg Case Study
sections.html:
Part 2: Eliminating Waste: The Concept2 RowErg Case Study

Focus: Strategies to design out waste and pollution from the start.

No problem at all. In IB Design Technology, shifting between topics often means looking at the same product through a slightly different lens. While the previous focus was on recovery (end-of-life), Topic 2.2.2 focuses on prevention.

The goal here is to design the product so that waste and pollution are never created in the first place. Here is how the Concept2 RowErg serves as a perfect case study for Eliminating Waste and Pollution.

1. Longevity

Definition: Making products durable and long-lasting.

If a product breaks after two years, you have to manufacture a new one. That doubles the manufacturing pollution and waste. Longevity is the single most effective way to eliminate waste.

  • Mechanical Simplicity: The Concept2 relies on air resistance (a fan) and a chain. It avoids complex, fragile gearboxes or friction belts that wear out quickly.
  • Material Selection: It utilizes an aluminum monorail with a stainless steel track. This prevents rust and corrosion (pollution from degradation) and ensures the machine lasts for decades, even in humid environments like rowing boathouses.

Impact on Waste: By lasting 20+ years, one Concept2 prevents the manufacture (and eventual disposal) of 3 or 4 cheaper, lower-quality rowing machines.

2. Upgradability

Definition: Designing products that can be easily upgraded with new components.

Usually, when technology improves, the old hardware becomes "obsolete waste." Concept2 eliminates this waste by separating the technology (the monitor) from the mechanics (the frame).

The Monitor Strategy: The mechanics of rowing haven't changed, but digital connectivity has. Concept2 allows you to put their newest Performance Monitor (PM5) on a rower built in 1993 (Model C).

Eliminating Waste: Instead of throwing away a 60lb metal machine because it doesn't have Bluetooth, the user simply swaps the 1lb plastic monitor. This saves the landfill from 59lbs of unnecessary waste.

3. Disassembly

Definition: Designing products that are easy to take apart for repair or recycling.

If you cannot take a product apart, you usually cannot repair it (leading to waste) and you cannot separate materials for recycling (leading to pollution).

Standard Fasteners: Concept2 uses standard hex bolts and screws. There are no "tamper-proof" screws, and more importantly, no glues or adhesives used to bond the structural components.

Pollution Prevention: Because the steel, aluminum, and plastic can be separated in minutes using basic tools, these materials don't end up in a landfill leaking toxins. They are easily sorted into pure recycling streams.

4. Dematerialization

Definition: Reducing the amount of material used in a product's design. This principle asks: How can we provide the same function using less physical stuff?

Air vs. Weight: Many gym machines use heavy iron stacks or magnetic flywheels to create resistance. The Concept2 uses Air Resistance. The flywheel is essentially a light plastic fan. It generates resistance through fluid dynamics rather than heavy mass.

Structural Optimization: The main rail is an aluminum extrusion. It is hollow. By using a specific geometric profile (an I-beam shape), it provides immense strength to hold a heavy user without needing a solid block of metal. This significantly reduces the raw material extraction and the energy (pollution) required to transport the machine.

Teacher's Exam Tip: The "Why" Matters

In a Paper 2 exam, if you are asked about Dematerialization, don't just say "It uses less material." You must explain the consequence regarding waste and pollution.

Weak: "The Concept2 uses a hollow rail so it is lighter."

Strong: "The Concept2 exemplifies dematerialization by using a hollow extruded aluminum rail. This reduces the volume of raw material extraction required for manufacture and lowers the shipping weight, thereby reducing the carbon footprint (pollution) associated with distribution."

Summary: Strategies to Eliminate Waste

Strategy Concept2 Application Pollution/Waste Outcome
Longevity Uses mechanical simplicity and rust-resistant materials (Aluminum). Prevents manufacturing pollution of replacement units (1 machine vs 4).
Upgradability Modular design separates Tech (Monitor) from Mechanics (Frame). Prevents 59lbs of structural waste when tech becomes obsolete.
Disassembly Standard fasteners; no glues/adhesives. Prevents toxic landfill leaching; allows pure recycling streams.
Dematerialization Hollow extrusion rail & air resistance (fan) vs heavy weights. Reduces extraction impact and distribution carbon footprint.

sections.title: Part 3: Biodegradable Materials within the Circular Economy (C2.2.3)
sections.html:
Part 3: Biodegradable Materials within the Circular Economy (C2.2.3)

Focus: Understanding the Biological Cycle and Regenerative Design.

1. The Linear Problem

The Hook

Imagine Styrofoam packing peanuts floating in the ocean. Now ask yourself: "If I bury this Styrofoam in the ground, what does it look like in 500 years?"

In a Linear Economy (Take-Make-Dispose), materials that cannot decompose become "monstrous hybrids"—materials that clog up the system and pollute the environment forever.

2. Theory: The Butterfly Diagram

To understand the solution, we look at the "Butterfly Diagram". This model splits the circular economy into two distinct cycles:

Technical Cycle

For non-renewables (metals, plastics). We keep them in the loop via repair, reuse, and remanufacture. These materials should never enter the biosphere.

Biological Cycle

For biodegradable materials. They flow back into the system to regenerate nature. They are capable of being decomposed by bacteria or living organisms.

Why do we prefer Biodegradable Materials?

  • Regeneration: They turn waste into food (nutrients) for the soil.
  • Independence: They reduce reliance on finite, geopolitical resources (like oil).
  • Safety: They reduce toxic leakage into the environment (no microplastics).

3. Case Study: Ecovative Mycelium

How do we replace Styrofoam? Ecovative Design uses mushroom roots (mycelium) to grow packaging.

How it works:

  1. Waste as Input: Farmers sell crop waste (corn stalks) to Ecovative.
  2. Inoculation: Ecovative cleans it and adds mycelium (mushroom roots).
  3. Growth: The mix is put into a mold (e.g., a corner protector) and grows in the dark for 4-5 days. (Self-assembly!)
  4. Baking: It is heated to stop growth.
  5. End of Life: The user breaks the foam into their garden. It biodegrades in 45 days, fertilizing the soil.

4. Critical Discussion

Discussion: Why isn't everything Mycelium?

"Given the environmental benefits, why hasn't all Styrofoam been replaced by Mycelium yet?"

Reveal Factors
  • Cost: Oil-based plastic is artificially cheap due to scale and subsidies.
  • Scalability: Growing packaging takes days; stamping plastic takes seconds.
  • Durability: Biodegradable materials can degrade too early if stored improperly (high humidity/moisture).

Exam Revision: Linear vs. Circular

Feature Linear Economy (Standard) Circular Economy (Biodegradable)
Source Finite (Oil) Renewable (Plants/Fungi)
Production Energy Intensive (Extraction) Low Energy (Biological Growth)
End of Life Waste (Landfill/Incineration) Nutrient (Compost/Soil Food)
System Impact Depletes Natural Capital Regenerates Natural Capital

Formative Assessment

Sketch a simple flow chart comparing the life cycle of a Styrofoam Cup vs. a PLA (Corn starch) Cup or Mycelium Block. Ensure you clearly label where the material goes at the "End of Life" stage.

sections.title: Part 4: Recovery and Restoration (C2.2.4) - The Technical Cycle
sections.html:
Part 4: Recovery and Restoration (C2.2.4) - The Technical Cycle

Focus: The hierarchy of value in the Technical Cycle (Fixing vs. Smashing).

1. The Theory: Hierarchy of Value

While the previous topic focused on the Biological Cycle (rotting), this topic focuses on the Technical Cycle (fixing). The goal is to keep products at their highest value for as long as possible.

Restoration (Higher Value)

Keeping the product as a product (Repair, Reuse, Recondition). This saves the massive energy originally used to manufacture it.

Recovery (Lower Value)

Smashing it back down to raw materials (Recycling). This destroys the "value add" of the manufacturing process and requires energy to process.

2. Case Study: The Fairphone (Consumer Electronics)

The Fairphone is the gold standard case study for this topic. It is the world's first modular smartphone designed specifically for user repair and longevity, directly addressing the linear nature of modern electronics.

Defining the Confusing Terms (Technical Cycle)

Term IB Definition The Fairphone Example
Repair Fixing a broken product to extend its life. Modular Design: If the camera breaks, the user unclips it and snaps in a new one. No glue; only standard screws.
Recondition Restoring a product to a "like-new" condition. "New Life" Edition: Fairphone takes back old phones, tests every part, replaces the battery/screen, and sells it again with a warranty.
Reuse Using a product again in its original form. Hand-me-down: Because software is supported for 7+ years, a parent can give their old phone to a child, and it still works perfectly.
Recycle Processing waste materials into new materials. Urban Mining: When a module is dead, Fairphone sends it to a smelter to extract gold, tungsten, and cobalt for new phones.

Teacher's Cheat Sheet: "Recondition" vs. "Repair"

This is the most common point of confusion for students.

  • Repair: Happens during the user's ownership. (e.g., I replace the screen on my phone so I can keep using it).
  • Recondition: Happens between owners. (e.g., A company takes a phone, cleans/fixes it, and sells it to a new customer).

3. Take-Back Legislation

The "Stick" - WEEE Directive

The Law: The WEEE Directive (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) in the EU forces manufacturers to be financially responsible for their product when it becomes waste.

Design Impact: Because Fairphone knows they have to pay to recycle the phone, they design it for Design for Disassembly. If they glued it shut (like competitors), it would cost them more to separate materials.

4. Critical Discussion

Commercial Tension

"If Repair and Restoration are so good for the planet, why do major companies (like Apple/Samsung) make it so hard to do?"

Reveal Reasons
  • Planned Obsolescence: Selling a new phone is often more profitable than fixing an old one.
  • IP Protection: Manufacturers don't want third parties seeing or tampering with their internal tech.
  • Aesthetics: Glued glass and sealed unibodies look "sleeker" and thinner than devices with visible screws and clips.

Formative Assessment: The Toaster Challenge

Look at a photo of a cheap, plastic toaster that is molded shut. Propose 3 design changes that would move it from a Linear to a Circular product, specifically addressing:

  • Repair: (e.g., Use screws instead of glue/snaps).
  • Recondition: (e.g., Use durable materials like stainless steel that can be polished).
  • Recycle: (e.g., Mark plastic types for sorting).

sections.title: Part 5: Renewable Energy: The Engine of Circularity (C2.2.5)
sections.html:
Part 5: Renewable Energy: The Engine of Circularity (C2.2.5)

Focus: Why the system must run on renewables to be truly circular.

1. The Core Concept: "Clean Loops"

The Problem with Recycling

People often think "Circular Economy = Recycling". This is incorrect.

Recycling requires massive amounts of energy (melting, shredding, washing). If you recycle a plastic bottle using energy from burning coal, you are still depleting a finite resource and polluting the biosphere. This is a "Dirty Loop".

A truly circular system must run on renewable energy to decouple economic growth from finite resource consumption.

2. Case Study: IKEA's "Energy Independence"

IKEA provides the perfect case study because they utilize all five energy sources listed in the syllabus across their operations. Their goal is to be "Climate Positive" by 2030, meaning they are not just a furniture retailer, but an energy producer.

Energy Source How IKEA uses it (Real World) Circular Economy Connection
1. Biomass The Sawdust Loop: Factories burn wood waste (sawdust) to heat the factory and dry paint. Waste = Food. Turning a material waste product into an energy resource on-site.
2. Solar Rooftop Real Estate: 900,000+ panels on flat store roofs power lights and checkouts. Distributed Energy. Generating energy exactly where it is used reduces transmission losses.
3. Wind Off-site Investment: 500+ wind turbines generate power to "offset" grid electricity. Scalability. Shows circular companies must invest in infrastructure, not just products.
4. Geothermal Store Heating/Cooling: Boreholes under car parks store heat in summer/retrieve in winter. Efficiency. Reduces HVAC energy demand by 50-70%, making renewable energy go further.
5. Hydro The Nordic Advantage: Purchasing "Green Energy Certificates" from the hydro-heavy Nordic grid. Location Strategy. Placing energy-intensive manufacturing near abundant renewable sources.

3. Critical Discussion: Reliability & "The Mix"

The Intermittency Challenge

"Why doesn't IKEA just run the factory on Solar panels?"

Answer: The sun doesn't shine at night, but the factory runs 24/7. This is why Biomass and Hydro are critical—they provide "Baseload" power (steady energy) that solar/wind cannot. A robust circular economy needs a mix of renewable sources to be reliable.

Formative Assessment: The Energy Map

Draw a diagram of a theoretical factory and label where you would apply the 5 energy sources based on the IKEA model:

Reveal Answer
  • Roof → Solar
  • Car Park/Ground → Geothermal
  • Waste Stream → Biomass
  • Grid Connection → Wind/Hydro

Cheat Sheet: Key Exam Arguments

When discussing why the circular economy relies on renewables, ensure you hit these three points:

  • Restoration: Fossil fuels are extractive (take-make-waste). Renewable energy is restorative (natural flows).
  • Resilience: Decentralized energy (like solar on the roof) makes the business less vulnerable to oil price shocks.
  • Zero Emissions: To regenerate nature, we must eliminate the greenhouse gases associated with manufacturing.

sections.title: Extended Exam Practice
sections.html:
Extended Exam Practice

Test your understanding with these practice questions. Remember to use specific terminology and strategies from the unit.

Multiple Choice Questions (Paper 1 Style)

1. Which concept most accurately describes the 'REUSE' objective of a circular economy?

A. Transforming old material into a new product of lower quality.
B. Fixing a broken component to restore the product to a functional state.
C. Using a product again in its original form for the same or a different function.
D. Returning a product to the manufacturer for complete renewal to 'like-new' condition.

2. Which design consideration is most directly addressed by a product being designed for disassembly in a circular economy?

A. Facilitating material segregation and high-purity recycling/repair.
B. Reducing the total amount of raw material used in the product.
C. Ensuring the energy used in the manufacturing process is renewable.
D. Making the product aesthetically appealing to encourage consumers to buy less often.

Short Answer Questions (Paper 2 Style)

1. Identify and outline two specific design strategies that aim to eliminate waste and pollution in the product phase, providing a brief example for each. [4 marks]

Reveal Answer

Strategy 1: Longevity

Outline: Making products durable and long-lasting to extend the use phase, reducing the need for replacement.

Example: Designing a high-quality stainless steel kettle with replaceable heating elements, rather than a cheaper, non-repairable plastic alternative.

Strategy 2: Disassembly

Outline: Designing products that are easy to take apart using standard tools (like screws or snap-fits) to facilitate easy repair or high-purity recycling.

Example: The modular design of the Fairphone, where the screen or battery can be replaced by the user with a single screwdriver.

2. To what extent does material selection affect a product's suitability as part of a circular economy? (B3.1) [4 marks]

Reveal Answer

Material selection is fundamental to a product's circularity. The choice determines the potential for resource recovery and pollution.

  • Selecting pure, easily separable materials (e.g., single-polymer plastics, virgin metals) or biodegradable materials ensures high-quality recycling or natural regeneration at end-of-life.
  • Conversely, using composite materials, adhesives, or mixed plastics creates materials that are difficult or impossible to recycle economically, forcing them into a residual waste stream, which is characteristic of the linear economy.

Long Answer Questions (Paper 2 Style)

1. Explain what a "Linear Economy" is and compare it with the benefits of a circular economy for both the manufacturer and the environment. [10 marks]

Reveal Answer

The Linear Economy:

The linear economy follows the traditional, unsustainable model of Take-Make-Dispose. It assumes that resources are infinite and disposal space is limitless. This model relies heavily on the constant extraction of virgin materials, leading to significant environmental degradation at both the start (extraction and production) and end (landfill/waste) of the product's life cycle.

Benefits of the Circular Economy:

For the Manufacturer/Business:

  • Resource Security: Reduces dependence on volatile global raw material markets, providing greater stability in production costs and supply chain resilience.
  • New Revenue Streams: Manufacturers can generate income from product maintenance, repair services, offering 'Product-as-a-Service' models, or selling high-quality recovered materials.
  • Brand Value: Enhances reputation and brand loyalty among environmentally conscious consumers, meeting regulatory requirements (e.g., EPR).

For the Environment:

  • Waste Elimination: By design, products are constantly cycled (reused, repaired, remanufactured), minimizing the amount of material sent to landfill.
  • Pollution Reduction: Less extraction of raw materials and decreased manufacturing of new goods results in lower greenhouse gas emissions and reduced pollution of water and air.
  • Regenerative Design: Emphasizes the use of renewable energy and the safe return of biological materials to the biosphere, actively restoring and regenerating natural capital.

2. Evaluate how the suitability of a product for a circular economy can be determined through product analysis and evaluation (C3.1) and discuss the likely outcome of a Life-Cycle Analysis (LCA) for such a product (C3.2). [10 marks]

Reveal Answer

Product Analysis & Evaluation (C3.1) for Circularity:

Suitability is determined by evaluating the product's design against circularity metrics, often using frameworks like the 9R Hierarchy (Refuse, Rethink, Reduce, Reuse, Repair, etc.). Key evaluation criteria include:

  • Repairability/Disassembly Score: Assessing if the product can be easily separated using simple tools (screws over glue/welds), which is vital for component repair or high-fidelity material segregation.
  • Material Purity: Analyzing the Bill of Materials to ensure components are made of single-stream materials that are easily recycled without complex separation processes.
  • Longevity of Critical Components: Evaluating if high-wear parts (e.g., batteries, filters, seals) are designed for easy replacement, preventing the premature obsolescence of the entire product.
  • Hazardous Content: Checking for the presence of toxic or hazardous materials that would complicate recycling or make safe regeneration impossible.
Life-Cycle Analysis (LCA) Outcome (C3.2):

A Life-Cycle Analysis (LCA) measures the environmental impact of a product from its inception ("cradle") to its final destination ("grave" for linear, "cradle" for circular). Products optimized for a circular economy are highly likely to result in a significantly **positive LCA outcome** compared to linear products.

  • Decoupling Impact: The circular model breaks the link between consumption and resource extraction. The LCA of a circular product dramatically reduces the impact scores associated with the most polluting phases: Raw Material Extraction and End-of-Life Disposal.
  • Impact Shifting: Instead of high-impact extraction, the LCA measures the lower impact of Recovery/Processing (refurbishment, recycling). By keeping materials in use, the environmental cost is amortized over multiple product lives, yielding a far lower per-unit impact over time.

sections.title: Glossary of Terms
sections.html:
Glossary of Terms

Key definitions for Topic 2.2. Click the buttons to reveal the standard IB definitions.

Circular Economy
Click to Reveal Definition
A system that is restorative and regenerative by design, looking beyond the current take-make-waste extractive industrial model.
Linear Economy
Click to Reveal Definition
An economy based on the make, use, dispose model.
Longevity
Click to Reveal Definition
Designing products to have a long life span.
Upgradability
Click to Reveal Definition
Designing products so that parts can be replaced or updated to extend the product's life.
Disassembly
Click to Reveal Definition
Designing a product so that it can be easily taken apart for repair or recycling.
Dematerialization
Click to Reveal Definition
The reduction of the total material and energy throughput of any product and service.
Biodegradable
Click to Reveal Definition
A material that can be broken down by bacteria or other living organisms.
Technical Cycle
Click to Reveal Definition
The cycle of the circular economy involving the circulation of technical nutrients (materials that cannot biodegrade).
Biological Cycle
Click to Reveal Definition
The cycle of the circular economy involving the flow of biological nutrients (biodegradable materials).
Repair
Click to Reveal Definition
The reconstruction or renewal of any part of an existing structure or device.
Recondition
Click to Reveal Definition
Rebuilding a product so that it is in an "as new" condition, and is generally used for car engines and tires.
Reuse
Click to Reveal Definition
Use of a product in the same context or in a different context.
Recycle
Click to Reveal Definition
Refers to using the materials from obsolete products to create other products.
Renewable Energy
Click to Reveal Definition
Energy from a source that is not depleted when used, such as wind or solar power.
Take-back Legislation
Click to Reveal Definition
Take-back Legislation; Laws that require manufacturers to “take back” products at the end of their lifecycle for disposal or recycling. Also known as “extended producer responsibility.

syllabus.title: Design for a circular economy
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How do designers minimize waste and reduce product waste and pollution?

statements.text: A circular economy is a closed-loop system where resources are continuously repurposed.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to compare and contrast a linear approach and the circular economy.

statements.text: The aim of the circular economy is to eliminate waste and pollution throughout all stages of a product’s life cycle.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss how designers can design products in ways that eliminate waste and pollution, including designing for longevity, upgradability, disassembly and dematerialization.

statements.text: An objective of the circular economy is to incorporate biodegradable materials.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss why biodegradable materials are a preferred material in a circular economy model.

statements.text: An objective of the circular economy is to recover and restore products, components and materials.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss how designers can consider the recovery and restoration of products, components and materials through take-back legislation, reuse, repair, recondition or recycling.

statements.text: The circular economy relies on the use of renewable energy.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify renewable energy sources and discuss why the circular economy relies on the use of renewable energy.

activity.title: Close the loop
activity.materials: Discarded packaging or images, sticky notes
steps: Draw the present take–make–dispose pathway for a product.
Add routes for maintenance, reuse, repair, refurbishment, remanufacture and recycling where appropriate.
Identify the joining and material choices that enable or block these routes.
Propose a take-back arrangement and test its feasibility for a named stakeholder.
activity.debrief: Why can recycling be a weaker option than retaining a working product?

exam.question: Explain how modular design can support a circular economy. [2]
exam.answer: Modules can be repaired, replaced or upgraded separately, preserving the value of remaining components and keeping products in use longer.

activities.text: Introduction & Linear Audit Quickly list the items in your pencil case or bag. Discuss the "fate" of the materials (e.g., disposable pens, plastic bottles). This represents the traditional Take-Make-Dispose linear approach.

activities.title: The Hook
activities.text: The Hook Imagine Styrofoam packing peanuts floating in the ocean. Now ask yourself: "If I bury this Styrofoam in the ground, what does it look like in 500 years?" In a Linear Economy (Take-Make-Dispose), materials that cannot decompose become "monstrous hybrids"—materials that clog up the system and pollute the environment forever.

activities.title: The Problem with Recycling
activities.text: The Problem with Recycling People often think "Circular Economy = Recycling" . This is incorrect. Recycling requires massive amounts of energy (melting, shredding, washing). If you recycle a plastic bottle using energy from burning coal, you are still depleting a finite resource and polluting the biosphere. This is a "Dirty Loop". A truly circular system must run on renewable energy to decouple economic growth from finite resource consumption.
