searchText: design for a circular economy lesson overview key takeaway the circular economy is a deliberate, design-driven strategy that shifts from the traditional take-make-dispose model to a regenerative system focused on eliminating waste, circulating materials, and regenerating nature . learning objectives: compare and contrast the linear economy and the circular economy , explaining why the latter is restorative and regenerative by design. discuss and apply design strategies for eliminating waste , including longevity , upgradability , disassembly , and dematerialization . analyze the role of biodegradable materials and the "r" strategies (reuse, repair, recondition, recycling) in closing the loop. explain the reliance of the circular economy on renewable energy sources . part 1: hook: from line to loop (c2.2.1) focus: understanding the transition from a linear to a regenerative system. activity: linear audit (0-5 min) introduction & linear audit quickly list the items in your pencil case or bag. discuss the "fate" of the materials (e.g., disposable pens, plastic bottles). this represents the traditional take-make-dispose linear approach. conceptual video & discussion (5-15 min) watch this short animation which clearly contrasts the linear model with the concept of a closed loop. part 2: eliminating waste: the concept2 rowerg case study focus: strategies to design out waste and pollution from the start. no problem at all. in ib design technology, shifting between topics often means looking at the same product through a slightly different lens. while the previous focus was on recovery (end-of-life), topic 2.2.2 focuses on prevention. the goal here is to design the product so that waste and pollution are never created in the first place. here is how the concept2 rowerg serves as a perfect case study for eliminating waste and pollution. 1. longevity definition: making products durable and long-lasting. if a product breaks after two years, you have to manufacture a new one. that doubles the manufacturing pollution and waste. longevity is the single most effective way to eliminate waste. mechanical simplicity: the concept2 relies on air resistance (a fan) and a chain. it avoids complex, fragile gearboxes or friction belts that wear out quickly. material selection: it utilizes an aluminum monorail with a stainless steel track. this prevents rust and corrosion (pollution from degradation) and ensures the machine lasts for decades, even in humid environments like rowing boathouses. impact on waste: by lasting 20+ years, one concept2 prevents the manufacture (and eventual disposal) of 3 or 4 cheaper, lower-quality rowing machines. 2. upgradability definition: designing products that can be easily upgraded with new components. usually, when technology improves, the old hardware becomes "obsolete waste." concept2 eliminates this waste by separating the technology (the monitor) from the mechanics (the frame). the monitor strategy: the mechanics of rowing haven't changed, but digital connectivity has. concept2 allows you to put their newest performance monitor (pm5) on a rower built in 1993 (model c). eliminating waste: instead of throwing away a 60lb metal machine because it doesn't have bluetooth, the user simply swaps the 1lb plastic monitor. this saves the landfill from 59lbs of unnecessary waste. 3. disassembly definition: designing products that are easy to take apart for repair or recycling. if you cannot take a product apart, you usually cannot repair it (leading to waste) and you cannot separate materials for recycling (leading to pollution). standard fasteners: concept2 uses standard hex bolts and screws. there are no "tamper-proof" screws, and more importantly, no glues or adhesives used to bond the structural components. pollution prevention: because the steel, aluminum, and plastic can be separated in minutes using basic tools, these materials don't end up in a landfill leaking toxins. they are easily sorted into pure recycling streams. figure 1: concept2 schematic demonstrating design for disassembly and standardized parts. 4. dematerialization definition: reducing the amount of material used in a product's design. this principle asks: how can we provide the same function using less physical stuff? air vs. weight: many gym machines use heavy iron stacks or magnetic flywheels to create resistance. the concept2 uses air resistance . the flywheel is essentially a light plastic fan. it generates resistance through fluid dynamics rather than heavy mass. structural optimization: the main rail is an aluminum extrusion. it is hollow. by using a specific geometric profile (an i-beam shape), it provides immense strength to hold a heavy user without needing a solid block of metal. this significantly reduces the raw material extraction and the energy (pollution) required to transport the machine. teacher's exam tip: the "why" matters in a paper 2 exam, if you are asked about dematerialization, don't just say "it uses less material." you must explain the consequence regarding waste and pollution. weak: "the concept2 uses a hollow rail so it is lighter." strong: "the concept2 exemplifies dematerialization by using a hollow extruded aluminum rail. this reduces the volume of raw material extraction required for manufacture and lowers the shipping weight, thereby reducing the carbon footprint (pollution) associated with distribution." summary: strategies to eliminate waste strategy concept2 application pollution/waste outcome longevity uses mechanical simplicity and rust-resistant materials (aluminum). prevents manufacturing pollution of replacement units (1 machine vs 4). upgradability modular design separates tech (monitor) from mechanics (frame). prevents 59lbs of structural waste when tech becomes obsolete. disassembly standard fasteners; no glues/adhesives. prevents toxic landfill leaching; allows pure recycling streams. dematerialization hollow extrusion rail & air resistance (fan) vs heavy weights. reduces extraction impact and distribution carbon footprint. part 3: biodegradable materials within the circular economy (c2.2.3) focus: understanding the biological cycle and regenerative design. 1. the linear problem the hook imagine styrofoam packing peanuts floating in the ocean. now ask yourself: "if i bury this styrofoam in the ground, what does it look like in 500 years?" in a linear economy (take-make-dispose), materials that cannot decompose become "monstrous hybrids"—materials that clog up the system and pollute the environment forever. 2. theory: the butterfly diagram to understand the solution, we look at the "butterfly diagram". this model splits the circular economy into two distinct cycles: figure 2: the butterfly diagram distinguishing technical and biological cycles. technical cycle for non-renewables (metals, plastics). we keep them in the loop via repair, reuse, and remanufacture. these materials should never enter the biosphere. biological cycle for biodegradable materials . they flow back into the system to regenerate nature. they are capable of being decomposed by bacteria or living organisms. why do we prefer biodegradable materials? regeneration: they turn waste into food (nutrients) for the soil. independence: they reduce reliance on finite, geopolitical resources (like oil). safety: they reduce toxic leakage into the environment (no microplastics). 3. case study: ecovative mycelium how do we replace styrofoam? ecovative design uses mushroom roots (mycelium) to grow packaging. how it works: waste as input: farmers sell crop waste (corn stalks) to ecovative. inoculation: ecovative cleans it and adds mycelium (mushroom roots). growth: the mix is put into a mold (e.g., a corner protector) and grows in the dark for 4-5 days. (self-assembly!) baking: it is heated to stop growth. end of life: the user breaks the foam into their garden. it biodegrades in 45 days, fertilizing the soil. 4. critical discussion discussion: why isn't everything mycelium? "given the environmental benefits, why hasn't all styrofoam been replaced by mycelium yet?" reveal factors cost: oil-based plastic is artificially cheap due to scale and subsidies. scalability: growing packaging takes days; stamping plastic takes seconds. durability: biodegradable materials can degrade too early if stored improperly (high humidity/moisture). exam revision: linear vs. circular feature linear economy (standard) circular economy (biodegradable) source finite (oil) renewable (plants/fungi) production energy intensive (extraction) low energy (biological growth) end of life waste (landfill/incineration) nutrient (compost/soil food) system impact depletes natural capital regenerates natural capital formative assessment sketch a simple flow chart comparing the life cycle of a styrofoam cup vs. a pla (corn starch) cup or mycelium block . ensure you clearly label where the material goes at the "end of life" stage. part 4: recovery and restoration (c2.2.4) - the technical cycle focus: the hierarchy of value in the technical cycle (fixing vs. smashing). 1. the theory: hierarchy of value while the previous topic focused on the biological cycle (rotting), this topic focuses on the technical cycle (fixing). the goal is to keep products at their highest value for as long as possible. restoration (higher value) keeping the product as a product (repair, reuse, recondition). this saves the massive energy originally used to manufacture it. recovery (lower value) smashing it back down to raw materials (recycling). this destroys the "value add" of the manufacturing process and requires energy to process. figure 3: the "power of the inner loop". the tighter the circle (repair/reuse), the better it is for the environment compared to the outer circle (recycling). (refer to the technical cycle in figure 2). 2. case study: the fairphone (consumer electronics) the fairphone is the gold standard case study for this topic. it is the world's first modular smartphone designed specifically for user repair and longevity, directly addressing the linear nature of modern electronics. defining the confusing terms (technical cycle) term ib definition the fairphone example repair fixing a broken product to extend its life. modular design: if the camera breaks, the user unclips it and snaps in a new one. no glue; only standard screws. recondition restoring a product to a "like-new" condition. "new life" edition: fairphone takes back old phones, tests every part, replaces the battery/screen, and sells it again with a warranty. reuse using a product again in its original form. hand-me-down: because software is supported for 7+ years, a parent can give their old phone to a child, and it still works perfectly. recycle processing waste materials into new materials. urban mining: when a module is dead, fairphone sends it to a smelter to extract gold, tungsten, and cobalt for new phones. teacher's cheat sheet: "recondition" vs. "repair" this is the most common point of confusion for students. repair: happens during the user's ownership. (e.g., i replace the screen on my phone so i can keep using it). recondition: happens between owners. (e.g., a company takes a phone, cleans/fixes it, and sells it to a new customer). 3. take-back legislation the "stick" - weee directive the law: the weee directive (waste electrical and electronic types for sorting). part 5: renewable energy: the engine of circularity (c2.2.5) focus: why the system must run on renewables to be truly circular. 1. the core concept: "clean loops" the problem with recycling people often think "circular economy = recycling" . this is incorrect. recycling requires massive amounts of energy (melting, shredding, washing). if you recycle a plastic bottle using energy from burning coal, you are still depleting a finite resource and polluting the biosphere. this is a "dirty loop". a truly circular system must run on renewable energy to decouple economic growth from finite resource consumption. 2. case study: ikea's "energy independence" ikea provides the perfect case study because they utilize all five energy sources listed in the syllabus across their operations. their goal is to be "climate positive" by 2030, meaning they are not just a furniture retailer, but an energy producer . energy source how ikea uses it (real world) circular economy connection 1. biomass the sawdust loop: factories burn wood waste (sawdust) to heat the factory and dry paint. waste = food. turning a material waste product into an energy resource on-site. 2. solar rooftop real estate: 900,000+ panels on flat store roofs power lights and checkouts. distributed energy. generating energy exactly where it is used reduces transmission losses. 3. wind off-site investment: 500+ wind turbines generate power to "offset" grid electricity. scalability. shows circular companies must invest in infrastructure, not just products. 4. geothermal store heating/cooling: boreholes under car parks store heat in summer/retrieve in winter. efficiency. reduces hvac energy demand by 50-70%, making renewable energy go further. 5. hydro the nordic advantage: purchasing "green energy certificates" from the hydro-heavy nordic grid. location strategy. placing energy-intensive manufacturing near abundant renewable sources. 3. critical discussion: reliability & "the mix" the intermittency challenge "why doesn't ikea just run the factory on solar panels?" answer: the sun doesn't shine at night, but the factory runs 24/7. this is why biomass and hydro are critical—they provide "baseload" power (steady energy) that solar/wind cannot. a robust circular economy needs a mix of renewable sources to be reliable. formative assessment: the energy map draw a diagram of a theoretical factory and label where you would apply the 5 energy sources based on the ikea model: reveal answer roof → solar car park/ground → geothermal waste stream → biomass grid connection → wind/hydro cheat sheet: key exam arguments when discussing why the circular economy relies on renewables, ensure you hit these three points: restoration: fossil fuels are extractive (take-make-waste). renewable energy is restorative (natural flows). resilience: decentralized energy (like solar on the roof) makes the business less vulnerable to oil price shocks. zero emissions: to regenerate nature, we must eliminate the greenhouse gases associated with manufacturing. extended exam practice test your understanding with these practice questions. remember to use specific terminology and strategies from the unit. multiple choice questions (paper 1 style) 1. which concept most accurately describes the 'reuse' objective of a circular economy? a. transforming old material into a new product of lower quality. b. fixing a broken component to restore the product to a functional state. c. using a product again in its original form for the same or a different function. d. returning a product to the manufacturer for complete renewal to 'like-new' condition. 2. which design consideration is most directly addressed by a product being designed for disassembly in a circular economy? a. facilitating material segregation and high-purity recycling/repair. b. reducing the total amount of raw material used in the product. c. ensuring the energy used in the manufacturing process is renewable. d. making the product aesthetically appealing to encourage consumers to buy less often. short answer questions (paper 2 style) 1. identify and outline two specific design strategies that aim to eliminate waste and pollution in the product phase, providing a brief example for each. [4 marks] reveal answer strategy 1: longevity outline: making products durable and long-lasting to extend the use phase, reducing the need for replacement. example: designing a high-quality stainless steel kettle with replaceable heating elements, rather than a cheaper, non-repairable plastic alternative. strategy 2: disassembly outline: designing products that are easy to take apart using standard tools (like screws or snap-fits) to facilitate easy repair or high-purity recycling. example: the modular design of the fairphone, where the screen or battery can be replaced by the user with a single screwdriver. 2. to what extent does material selection affect a product's suitability as part of a circular economy? (b3.1) [4 marks] reveal answer material selection is fundamental to a product's circularity. the choice determines the potential for resource recovery and pollution. selecting pure, easily separable materials (e.g., single-polymer plastics, virgin metals) or biodegradable materials ensures high-quality recycling or natural regeneration at end-of-life. conversely, using composite materials, adhesives, or mixed plastics creates materials that are difficult or impossible to recycle economically, forcing them into a residual waste stream, which is characteristic of the linear economy . long answer questions (paper 2 style) 1. explain what a "linear economy" is and compare it with the benefits of a circular economy for both the manufacturer and the environment. [10 marks] reveal answer the linear economy: the linear economy follows the traditional, unsustainable model of take-make-dispose . it assumes that resources are infinite and disposal space is limitless. this model relies heavily on the constant extraction of virgin materials, leading to significant environmental degradation at both the start (extraction and production) and end (landfill/waste) of the product's life cycle. benefits of the circular economy: for the manufacturer/business: resource security: reduces dependence on volatile global raw material markets, providing greater stability in production costs and supply chain resilience. new revenue streams: manufacturers can generate income from product maintenance, repair services, offering 'product-as-a-service' models, or selling high-quality recovered materials. brand value: enhances reputation and brand loyalty among environmentally conscious consumers, meeting regulatory requirements (e.g., epr). for the environment: waste elimination: by design, products are constantly cycled (reused, repaired, remanufactured), minimizing the amount of material sent to landfill. pollution reduction: less extraction of raw materials and decreased manufacturing of new goods results in lower greenhouse gas emissions and reduced pollution of water and air. regenerative design: emphasizes the use of renewable energy and the safe return of biological materials to the biosphere, actively restoring and regenerating natural capital. 2. evaluate how the suitability of a product for a circular economy can be determined through product analysis and evaluation (c3.1) and discuss the likely outcome of a life-cycle analysis (lca) for such a product (c3.2). [10 marks] reveal answer product analysis & evaluation (c3.1) for circularity: suitability is determined by evaluating the product's design against circularity metrics, often using frameworks like the 9r hierarchy (refuse, rethink, reduce, reuse, repair, etc.). key evaluation criteria include: repairability/disassembly score: assessing if the product can be easily separated using simple tools (screws over glue/welds), which is vital for component repair or high-fidelity material segregation. material purity: analyzing the bill of materials to ensure components are made of single-stream materials that are easily recycled without complex separation processes. longevity of critical components: evaluating if high-wear parts (e.g., batteries, filters, seals) are designed for easy replacement, preventing the premature obsolescence of the entire product. hazardous content: checking for the presence of toxic or hazardous materials that would complicate recycling or make safe regeneration impossible. life-cycle analysis (lca) outcome (c3.2): a life-cycle analysis (lca) measures the environmental impact of a product from its inception ("cradle") to its final destination ("grave" for linear, "cradle" for circular). products optimized for a circular economy are highly likely to result in a significantly **positive lca outcome** compared to linear products. decoupling impact: the circular model breaks the link between consumption and resource extraction. the lca of a circular product dramatically reduces the impact scores associated with the most polluting phases: raw material extraction and end-of-life disposal . impact shifting: instead of high-impact extraction, the lca measures the lower impact of recovery/processing (refurbishment, recycling). by keeping materials in use, the environmental cost is amortized over multiple product lives, yielding a far lower per-unit impact over time. glossary of terms key definitions for topic 2.2. click the buttons to reveal the standard ib definitions. circular economy click to reveal definition a system that is restorative and regenerative by design, looking beyond the current take-make-waste extractive industrial model. linear economy click to reveal definition an economy based on the make, use, dispose model. longevity click to reveal definition designing products to have a long life span. upgradability click to reveal definition designing products so that parts can be replaced or updated to extend the product's life. disassembly click to reveal definition designing a product so that it can be easily taken apart for repair or recycling. dematerialization click to reveal definition the reduction of the total material and energy throughput of any product and service. biodegradable click to reveal definition a material that can be broken down by bacteria or other living organisms. technical cycle click to reveal definition the cycle of the circular economy involving the circulation of technical nutrients (materials that cannot biodegrade). biological cycle click to reveal definition the cycle of the circular economy involving the flow of biological nutrients (biodegradable materials). repair click to reveal definition the reconstruction or renewal of any part of an existing structure or device. recondition click to reveal definition rebuilding a product so that it is in an "as new" condition, and is generally used for car engines and tires. reuse click to reveal definition use of a product in the same context or in a different context. recycle click to reveal definition refers to using the materials from obsolete products to create other products. renewable energy click to reveal definition energy from a source that is not depleted when used, such as wind or solar power. take-back legislation click to reveal definition take-back legislation; laws that require manufacturers to “take back” products at the end of their lifecycle for disposal or recycling. also known as “extended producer responsibility. biodegradable material circular economy dematerialization linear approach/ economy renewable energy sources take-back legislation linear economy longevity upgradability disassembly biodegradable technical cycle biological cycle repair recondition reuse recycle renewable energy a circular economy is a closed-loop system where resources are continuously repurposed. the aim of the circular economy is to eliminate waste and pollution throughout all stages of a product’s life cycle. an objective of the circular economy is to incorporate biodegradable materials. an objective of the circular economy is to recover and restore products, components and materials. the circular economy relies on the use of renewable energy.

title: Product analysis and evaluation

sections.title: Unit Overview
sections.html:
Unit Overview

Welcome to Unit C3.1: Product Analysis and Evaluation! In this unit, we will explore the critical processes designers use to understand the strengths, weaknesses, and potential for improvement in existing products. This is a fundamental skill for any aspiring designer, enabling you to make informed decisions for future development.

Across several sessions, you will learn to identify key stakeholders, apply powerful analytical tools like SWOT analysis, engage in hands-on testing and reverse engineering, and develop "constructive discontent" to drive innovation. By the end of this unit, you will be able to dissect products with a keen eye, identify market opportunities, and suggest meaningful improvements. Let's start uncovering the hidden value in everyday objects! 🔍

Recommended Time Allocation: Multiple sessions

Lesson Objectives:

  • Discuss the purpose of product analysis and its importance in the design development cycle.
  • Identify a wide range of stakeholders and explain their relevance to product development.
  • Apply a SWOT analysis to a given product, considering function, performance, usability, features, and materials.
  • Use data from testing and reverse engineering to identify areas for product improvement.
  • Analyze products with "constructive discontent" to identify unmet user needs.
  • Compare competing products to identify market opportunities and areas for innovation.

sections.title: Session 1: The "Why" and "Who" of Product Analysis
sections.html:
Session 1: The "Why" and "Who" of Product Analysis

Focus: 3.1.1 Purpose of Analysis, 3.1.2 Stakeholders, 3.1.6 Constructive Discontent, 3.1.7 Product Understanding.

Introduction & Hook: The Frustration Inventory

Activity: Constructive Discontent

Let's begin with the concept of Constructive Discontent. Take out an everyday object you have with you (e.g., a pen, a water bottle, your phone case, a backpack). In pairs, identify at least three things that are frustrating, inefficient, or could be better about that product.

After your discussion, we will share some of your findings as a class. This exercise immediately frames product analysis not as an abstract exercise, but as a critical tool for identifying problems and driving improvement, which is its core purpose.

Core Concepts: Purpose and Stakeholders

We will formally define Product Analysis as a systematic process to understand a product's strengths and weaknesses, ultimately informing its future development.

Stakeholder Mapping Activity:

We will introduce the concept of Stakeholders. On a whiteboard, we will place a picture of a common product (e.g., a bicycle). Your task will be to brainstorm every single person or group who has an interest in that product. We'll guide you to include:

  • Users: (e.g., The cyclist, a child learning to ride)
  • Designers & Engineers: (The people who created it)
  • Manufacturers: (The companies and factory workers who built it)
  • Retailers: (The bike shop selling the product)
  • Maintenance/Repair Personnel: (The mechanics who fix it)
  • Government/Safety Bodies: (Organizations setting safety standards and regulations)
  • Recyclers/Disposers: (Those involved in the product's end-of-life)

Key Takeaway:

This visual exercise demonstrates that a product's success depends on meeting the needs of a wide and varied group of people, not just the end-user.

Activity 1: Stakeholder Perspectives

Task: Prioritizing Needs

In small groups, each group will be assigned a different stakeholder from the mapping activity (e.g., "You are the manufacturer," "You are the parent buying the bike for a child").

Scenario: "A new version of this bicycle is being designed." Each group must list their top 3 priorities and concerns for the new design from their assigned perspective.

Presentations & Discussion: Each group will briefly present their list. We will observe how a "user" group might prioritize comfort and style, while a "manufacturer" group prioritizes cost-effective materials and ease of assembly. This activity highlights potential conflicts and the need for a balanced approach in design.

Introduction & Hook: The Frustration Inventory Activity: Constructive Discontent Let's begin with the concept of Constructive Discontent . Take out an everyday object you have with you (e.g., a pen, a water bottle, your phone case, a backpack). In pairs, identify at least three things that are frustrating, inefficient, or could be better about that product. After your discussion, we will share some of your findings as a class. This exercise immediately frames product analysis not as an abstract exercise, but as a critical tool for identifying problems and driving improvement, which is its core purpose. Core Concepts: Purpose and Stakeholders We will formally define Product Analysis as a systematic process to understand a product's strengths and weaknesses, ultimately informing its future development. Stakeholder Mapping Activity: We will introduce the concept of Stakeholders . On a whiteboard, we will place a picture of a common product (e.g., a bicycle). Your task will be to brainstorm every single person or group who has an interest in that product. We'll guide you to include: Users: (e.g., The cyclist, a child learning to ride) Designers & Engineers: (The people who created it) Manufacturers: (The companies and factory workers who built it) Retailers: (The bike shop selling the product) Maintenance/Repair Personnel: (The mechanics who fix it) Government/Safety Bodies: (Organizations setting safety standards and regulations) Recyclers/Disposers: (Those involved in the product's end-of-life) Key Takeaway: This visual exercise demonstrates that a product's success depends on meeting the needs of a wide and varied group of people, not just the end-user. Activity 1: Stakeholder Perspectives Task: Prioritizing Needs In small groups, each group will be assigned a different stakeholder from the mapping activity (e.g., "You are the manufacturer," "You are the parent buying the bike for a child"). Scenario: "A new version of this bicycle is being designed." Each group must list their top 3 priorities and concerns for the new design from their assigned perspective. Presentations & Discussion: Each group will briefly present their list. We will observe how a "user" group might prioritize comfort and style, while a "manufacturer" group prioritizes cost-effective materials and ease of assembly. This activity highlights potential conflicts and the need for a balanced approach in design.

sections.title: Session 2: The Analyst's Toolkit: SWOT & Competitive Analysis
sections.html:
Session 2: The Analyst's Toolkit: SWOT & Competitive Analysis

Focus: 3.1.3 SWOT Analysis, 3.1.5 Opportunities for Improvements.

Recap & Introduction

We will quickly review the concepts of stakeholders and constructive discontent from our last session. Then, we will introduce SWOT Analysis as a structured tool used by designers and businesses to formalize the analysis process and identify strategic directions.

Core Concepts: Mastering SWOT Analysis

We will clearly define the four components of SWOT:

  • Strengths (Internal, Positive): What does the product do well? What are its advantages?

    Example: Durable materials, intuitive interface, strong brand recognition.

  • Weaknesses (Internal, Negative): Where does the product fall short? What are its disadvantages or areas for improvement?

    Example: Poor battery life, uncomfortable grip, high manufacturing cost.

  • Opportunities (External, Positive): What external market trends, technologies, or gaps can the product or company leverage for growth?

    Example: Growing demand for sustainable products, emergence of new materials, underserved market segment.

  • Threats (External, Negative): What external factors could negatively impact the product or company?

    Example: A cheaper competing product is released, rising material costs, changing consumer preferences, new regulations.

Guided Practice: As a class, we will perform a SWOT analysis on a well-known, simple product, like a standard coffee shop paper cup. This will help you understand how to apply each component.

Activity 2: Hands-On SWOT Analysis

Task: Product SWOT and Competitive Comparison

In your groups (the same as Session 1), each group will receive a different but related product (e.g., Group A gets an Apple mouse, Group B gets a Logitech mouse, Group C gets a basic Dell mouse).

Analysis: Each group will perform a detailed SWOT analysis on their assigned product, thoroughly considering its function, performance, usability, features, and materials.

Competitive Comparison: Once your SWOT analysis is complete, you will share your key "Strengths" and "Weaknesses" with the other groups. This will naturally lead to a comparative analysis, where you can see how one product's weakness is another's strength. This exercise is the foundation for identifying significant opportunities for improvement and innovation in the market.

sections.title: Session 3: From Analysis to Action: Testing & Redesign
sections.html:
Session 3: From Analysis to Action: Testing & Redesign

Focus: 3.1.4 Testing and Reverse Engineering, 3.1.5 Improvements.

Introduction to Testing & Reverse Engineering

Let's consider: "How did the designers of an ergonomic mouse know it was comfortable? How did they test its click-rate?" This introduces the critical need for generating hard data through various forms of testing.

We will define Reverse Engineering as the process of systematically disassembling a product to understand how it was made, how it functions, and the materials and components used. We will explain that this is a key method for gathering tangible data for a comprehensive product analysis.

Activity 3: The Teardown

Task: Hands-On Disassembly and Analysis

You will be provided with a simple, safe-to-disassemble mechanical product (e.g., a retractable ballpoint pen, a PEZ dispenser, a wind-up toy).

Procedure:

  • Initial Testing: Before disassembly, test the product's function, performance, and usability, noting your initial findings and any "constructive discontent."
  • Disassembly: Carefully take the product apart, laying out the components in an "exploded view" (like a diagram). Identify each part and hypothesize its function and material.
  • Analysis: Based on your disassembly, how does the internal mechanism work? Are there any signs of wear or potential failure? How does its construction relate to the strengths and weaknesses you identified earlier?

Goal: This hands-on activity provides concrete, tangible data that moves your analysis beyond simple observation to a deeper understanding of the product's construction and function. This data is crucial for identifying specific areas that require improvement.

Unit Synthesis: Recommendations for the Future

Final Task: Design Improvement Proposal

You will compile all your work from the three sessions (your Stakeholder notes, SWOT analysis, and Reverse Engineering findings) for your specific product.

The Challenge: Write a concluding paragraph that answers the guiding question of this unit: "Based on your complete analysis, what are the top three recommendations you would give to the design team for the next version of this product, and why?" Justify each recommendation with specific evidence from your analysis.

sections.title: Extended Exam Practice
sections.html:
Extended Exam Practice

Let's test your understanding with some practice questions across different formats. Remember to use specific examples and terminology from the unit in your answers.

Multiple Choice Questions

1. Which of the following is an internal factor considered in a SWOT analysis?

  • A. Changes in consumer buying habits.
  • B. The release of a new, innovative competitor product.
  • C. A product's strong brand reputation and loyal customer base.
  • D. New government regulations affecting manufacturing.

2. The primary purpose of applying "constructive discontent" during product analysis is to:

  • A. Criticize the original designers unfairly.
  • B. Identify existing problems and unmet user needs for improvement.
  • C. Focus only on the positive aspects of a product.
  • D. Increase the product's market share by highlighting flaws.

Short Answer Questions

1. Identify three different stakeholders for a smartphone and briefly explain why each stakeholder is important in the context of the phone's design and development.

Reveal Answer

Award [1] for identifying each relevant stakeholder and [1] for a clear explanation of their importance, up to [3 max].

Stakeholder 1: End Users

Importance: Users are the most crucial stakeholders. Their needs, behaviors, and feedback on usability, features, and satisfaction directly determine the product's success. Designers must understand how users will interact with the phone to create a useful and desirable product.

Stakeholder 2: Manufacturers/Engineers

Importance: These stakeholders are concerned with the feasibility of producing the design. They provide expertise on materials, production processes, and cost, ensuring the design is practical and can be manufactured efficiently and profitably.

Stakeholder 3: Retailers/Distributors

Importance: Retailers and distributors are important for market success. They are concerned with the product's packaging, logistics, and marketability. Their feedback can influence design decisions related to size, durability, and brand appeal.

2. Define Reverse Engineering and explain how it helps in gathering data for product improvement.

Reveal Answer

Award [1] for a correct definition of Reverse Engineering and [1] for a clear explanation of how it helps with product improvement [2 max].

Definition:

Reverse engineering is a method used to understand how an existing product was made by disassembling it.

How it Helps:

It allows designers to analyze a product's components, materials, manufacturing techniques, and internal workings. This provides valuable data to understand its strengths and weaknesses, which can then be used to identify opportunities for improvement. For example, by disassembling a competitor's product, a company can discover a more efficient way to assemble their own, which reduces cost.

Longer Answer Questions

1. You are tasked with analyzing a new ergonomic desk chair. Discuss how you would use a SWOT analysis and identify at least three relevant stakeholders to inform your evaluation. Provide specific examples for each element of the SWOT and for each stakeholder's concerns.

Reveal Answer

Award [1] for discussing the use of SWOT analysis and identifying stakeholders, [1] for each clear example for the SWOT analysis, and [1] for each clear example of a stakeholder's concerns, up to [4 marks].

To analyze the ergonomic desk chair, a SWOT analysis would be used to provide a structured evaluation. The information for this analysis would be gathered from a range of stakeholders.

SWOT Analysis Examples:

Strengths: The chair has a comfortable, adjustable lumbar support system and a wide range of height settings, making it highly adaptable for different users.

Weaknesses: The material used for the seat is not breathable, causing the user to sweat during prolonged use, and the armrests are difficult to adjust.

Opportunities: There is a growing market for home office products due to remote work, and there is an opportunity to sell to a corporate market. The chair could be improved by using a more breathable material or by adding more intuitive armrest controls.

Threats: A competitor has just released a cheaper chair with similar features, and there are new government regulations concerning the use of certain plastics in furniture.

Stakeholder Examples:

End Users: A user's main concern would be usability and comfort. They might provide feedback on whether the chair is comfortable for long periods and if the controls are easy to understand and adjust.

Manufacturer: The manufacturer would be concerned with the cost of materials and the ease of production. They might point out that the complex adjustment mechanism is expensive to produce.

Retailer: The retailer would be concerned with the chair's marketability and packaging. They might suggest that the chair is too heavy or bulky for efficient shipping, which could increase costs.

2. Explain why it is important to gather information from a range of stakeholders during a product analysis exercise. Use examples of potential conflicting priorities that different stakeholders might have regarding a common product.

Reveal Answer

Award [1] for explaining why it's important to gather info from a range of stakeholders, and [1] for each clear example of conflicting priorities with a common product, up to [4 marks].

It is crucial to gather information from a range of stakeholders during product analysis because each group has a different perspective and set of priorities. A product's success is not determined by its function alone but by how well it meets the needs of all involved parties, from the user to the manufacturer to the retailer.

Conflicting Priorities Example: A Smartphone

User vs. Manufacturer: The user wants a smartphone with the largest, highest-resolution screen and the longest battery life possible. However, the manufacturer's priority is to produce a phone that is cost-effective and easy to manufacture. This creates a conflict, as a larger screen or a more powerful battery can increase the cost and complexity of manufacturing.

Designer vs. Marketer: The designer's priority is to create a product that is both aesthetically pleasing and highly functional, perhaps using a sleek, unibody design with a non-removable battery for better aesthetics. The marketer's priority is to appeal to a broad market, which might include users who prefer the practicality of a replaceable battery.

Retailer vs. Engineer: The retailer wants a product that is packaged in a small box for efficient shelf space and shipping. The engineer wants a larger package to protect a fragile device during transit. This creates a conflict between logistics and product safety.

We will discuss strategies for answering these questions effectively, focusing on structure, use of terminology, and illustrative examples.

sections.title: Glossary of Key Terms for C3.1 (SL & HL)
sections.html:
Glossary of Key Terms for C3.1 (SL & HL)

Here are the key terms from our unit to help you remember important concepts:

Product Analysis

A systematic process to understand a product's strengths and weaknesses, ultimately informing its future development.

Context: A core activity for designers to learn from existing products. Example: Disassembling a competitor's product to understand its construction and materials.

Stakeholders

Any person, group, or organization who has an interest or concern in a product, project, or company.

Context: Their diverse needs and perspectives must be considered in design. Example: Users, manufacturers, retailers, government regulators, and recyclers for a mobile phone.

SWOT Analysis

A strategic planning tool used to identify a product's (or company's) Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats.

Context: Helps in understanding the internal and external factors affecting a product. Example: Analyzing a new electric scooter's powerful motor (Strength), limited range (Weakness), growing urban demand (Opportunity), and competing models (Threat).

Strengths (SWOT)

Internal, positive attributes of a product that give it an advantage over others.

Context: What the product does well. Example: A smartphone's advanced camera features, durable construction, or user-friendly interface.

Weaknesses (SWOT)

Internal, negative attributes of a product that put it at a disadvantage.

Context: Areas where the product falls short. Example: A laptop's short battery life, heavy weight, or high price point compared to competitors.

Opportunities (SWOT)

External, positive factors or trends that a product could exploit to its advantage.

Context: Favorable external conditions. Example: A rising consumer demand for eco-friendly packaging, or new technological advancements that could be integrated.

Threats (SWOT)

External, negative factors or trends that could pose challenges or harm to a product.

Context: Unfavorable external conditions. Example: Intense competition, changes in economic conditions, or new regulations that make a product obsolete.

Constructive Discontent

An attitude of actively seeking out problems and inefficiencies in existing products, not just to complain, but to identify areas for improvement and innovation.

Context: A mindset for designers to drive meaningful product development. Example: Feeling frustrated by a clumsy can opener and then sketching ideas for a more ergonomic design.

Product Improvement

Modifications or enhancements made to an existing product to enhance its performance, usability, aesthetics, sustainability, or cost-effectiveness.

Context: The ultimate goal of product analysis and evaluation. Example: Updating a smartphone with a faster processor, a better camera, or a longer-lasting battery.

Testing

Systematic procedures used to collect data on a product's performance and usability.

Context: Can include user tests, durability tests, and functionality tests to gather objective data on a product's effectiveness.

Reverse Engineering

A method used to understand how an existing product was made by systematically disassembling it to analyze its components, materials, and internal workings.

Context: Provides critical data on manufacturing techniques and can reveal why a product succeeds or fails in its design. Example: Taking apart a mechanical toy to see how its gears and springs function together.

Market Opportunity

A favorable external condition that a product or company can leverage for growth and success.

Context: Often revealed through SWOT and competitive analysis. Example: A gap in the market for high-quality, eco-friendly water bottles presents a market opportunity for a new product.
sections.text: Glossary of Key Terms for C3.1 (SL & HL) Here are the key terms from our unit to help you remember important concepts: Product Analysis A systematic process to understand a product's strengths and weaknesses, ultimately informing its future development. Context: A core activity for designers to learn from existing products. Example: Disassembling a competitor's product to understand its construction and materials. Stakeholders Any person, group, or organization who has an interest or concern in a product, project, or company. Context: Their diverse needs and perspectives must be considered in design. Example: Users, manufacturers, retailers, government regulators, and recyclers for a mobile phone. SWOT Analysis A strategic planning tool used to identify a product's (or company's) Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats. Context: Helps in understanding the internal and external factors affecting a product. Example: Analyzing a new electric scooter's powerful motor (Strength), limited range (Weakness), growing urban demand (Opportunity), and competing models (Threat). Strengths (SWOT) Internal, positive attributes of a product that give it an advantage over others. Context: What the product does well. Example: A smartphone's advanced camera features, durable construction, or user-friendly interface. Weaknesses (SWOT) Internal, negative attributes of a product that put it at a disadvantage. Context: Areas where the product falls short. Example: A laptop's short battery life, heavy weight, or high price point compared to competitors. Opportunities (SWOT) External, positive factors or trends that a product could exploit to its advantage. Context: Favorable external conditions. Example: A rising consumer demand for eco-friendly packaging, or new technological advancements that could be integrated. Threats (SWOT) External, negative factors or trends that could pose challenges or harm to a product. Context: Unfavorable external conditions. Example: Intense competition, changes in economic conditions, or new regulations that make a product obsolete. Constructive Discontent An attitude of actively seeking out problems and inefficiencies in existing products, not just to complain, but to identify areas for improvement and innovation. Context: A mindset for designers to drive meaningful product development. Example: Feeling frustrated by a clumsy can opener and then sketching ideas for a more ergonomic design. Product Improvement Modifications or enhancements made to an existing product to enhance its performance, usability, aesthetics, sustainability, or cost-effectiveness. Context: The ultimate goal of product analysis and evaluation. Example: Updating a smartphone with a faster processor, a better camera, or a longer-lasting battery. Testing Systematic procedures used to collect data on a product's performance and usability. Context: Can include user tests, durability tests, and functionality tests to gather objective data on a product's effectiveness. Reverse Engineering A method used to understand how an existing product was made by systematically disassembling it to analyze its components, materials, and internal workings. Context: Provides critical data on manufacturing techniques and can reveal why a product succeeds or fails in its design. Example: Taking apart a mechanical toy to see how its gears and springs function together. Market Opportunity A favorable external condition that a product or company can leverage for growth and success. Context: Often revealed through SWOT and competitive analysis. Example: A gap in the market for high-quality, eco-friendly water bottles presents a market opportunity for a new product.

syllabus.title: Product analysis and evaluation
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How does product analysis and evaluation inform various stakeholders and aid in a product’s future development?

statements.text: Product analysis and evaluation is a process that involves examining a product performance to determine its strengths and weaknesses, and identify opportunities for improvement.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss the purpose of a product analysis exercise and why it is important for product design development.

statements.text: As part of the product analysis process, a product should be tested and information gathered from a range of stakeholders.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify the various stakeholders, such as users, manufacturers and engineers, that will help in any future development of a product.

statements.text: A SWOT analysis is a standard product analysis tool that is used to identify a product’s strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to analyse a product using a SWOT analysis based on function, performance, usability, features and materials.

statements.text: Function, performance and usability can be established using data generated through testing and reverse engineering.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to use data generated from relevant testing and/or reverse engineering to identify areas of the product that require improvement and to determine how well the product meets the needs of the user.

statements.text: Weaknesses identified in a product or range of products can lead to opportunities for product improvement.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to compare competing and similar products to identify opportunities for further product improvements.

statements.text: Constructive discontent can be used to identify areas where the product is not meeting the needs of its users and to determine how it can be improved to meet those needs.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to identify areas where a product is not meeting the needs of its users.

statements.text: Product analysis enables designers to understand a product better.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss the purpose of a product analysis task and why it is important for product design development.

activity.title: Evidence-led product review
steps: Write three measurable criteria for the same user and task.
Test both products under the same conditions and record results.
Build a SWOT analysis that separates product strengths and weaknesses from external opportunities and threats.
Recommend an improvement using the evidence and state a test limitation.
activity.debrief: What separates a justified evaluation from a list of opinions?

exam.question: Explain how reverse engineering can inform product improvement. [2]
exam.answer: Disassembly reveals components, joints and manufacturing choices. This evidence can identify problems such as difficult repair or excess material and guide redesign.

activities.title: Activity: Constructive Discontent
activities.text: Activity: Constructive Discontent Let's begin with the concept of Constructive Discontent . Take out an everyday object you have with you (e.g., a pen, a water bottle, your phone case, a backpack). In pairs, identify at least three things that are frustrating, inefficient, or could be better about that product. After your discussion, we will share some of your findings as a class. This exercise immediately frames product analysis not as an abstract exercise, but as a critical tool for identifying problems and driving improvement, which is its core purpose.

activities.title: Task: Prioritizing Needs
activities.text: Task: Prioritizing Needs In small groups, each group will be assigned a different stakeholder from the mapping activity (e.g., "You are the manufacturer," "You are the parent buying the bike for a child"). Scenario: "A new version of this bicycle is being designed." Each group must list their top 3 priorities and concerns for the new design from their assigned perspective. Presentations & Discussion: Each group will briefly present their list. We will observe how a "user" group might prioritize comfort and style, while a "manufacturer" group prioritizes cost-effective materials and ease of assembly. This activity highlights potential conflicts and the need for a balanced approach in design.

activities.title: Task: Product SWOT and Competitive Comparison
activities.text: Task: Product SWOT and Competitive Comparison In your groups (the same as Session 1), each group will receive a different but related product (e.g., Group A gets an Apple mouse, Group B gets a Logitech mouse, Group C gets a basic Dell mouse). Analysis: Each group will perform a detailed SWOT analysis on their assigned product, thoroughly considering its function, performance, usability, features, and materials. Competitive Comparison: Once your SWOT analysis is complete, you will share your key "Strengths" and "Weaknesses" with the other groups. This will naturally lead to a comparative analysis , where you can see how one product's weakness is another's strength. This exercise is the foundation for identifying significant opportunities for improvement and innovation in the market.

activities.title: Task: Hands-On Disassembly and Analysis
activities.text: Task: Hands-On Disassembly and Analysis You will be provided with a simple, safe-to-disassemble mechanical product (e.g., a retractable ballpoint pen, a PEZ dispenser, a wind-up toy). Procedure: Initial Testing: Before disassembly, test the product's function, performance, and usability, noting your initial findings and any "constructive discontent." Disassembly: Carefully take the product apart, laying out the components in an "exploded view" (like a diagram). Identify each part and hypothesize its function and material. Analysis: Based on your disassembly, how does the internal mechanism work? Are there any signs of wear or potential failure? How does its construction relate to the strengths and weaknesses you identified earlier? Goal: This hands-on activity provides concrete, tangible data that moves your analysis beyond simple observation to a deeper understanding of the product's construction and function. This data is crucial for identifying specific areas that require improvement .

activities.title: Final Task: Design Improvement Proposal
activities.text: Final Task: Design Improvement Proposal You will compile all your work from the three sessions (your Stakeholder notes, SWOT analysis, and Reverse Engineering findings) for your specific product. The Challenge: Write a concluding paragraph that answers the guiding question of this unit: "Based on your complete analysis, what are the top three recommendations you would give to the design team for the next version of this product, and why?" Justify each recommendation with specific evidence from your analysis.

searchText: product analysis and evaluation unit overview welcome to unit c3.1: product analysis and evaluation ! in this unit, we will explore the critical processes designers use to understand the strengths, weaknesses, and potential for improvement in existing products. this is a fundamental skill for any aspiring designer, enabling you to make informed decisions for future development. across several sessions, you will learn to identify key stakeholders, apply powerful analytical tools like swot analysis, engage in hands-on testing and reverse engineering, and develop "constructive features, and materials. use data from testing and reverse engineering to identify areas for product improvement . analyze products with " constructive discontent " to identify unmet user needs. compare competing products to identify market opportunities and areas for innovation. session 1: the "why" and "who" of product analysis focus: 3.1.1 purpose of analysis, 3.1.2 stakeholders, 3.1.6 reputation and loyal customer base. d. new government regulations affecting manufacturing. 2. the primary purpose of applying " constructive discontent " during product analysis is to: a. criticize most crucial stakeholders. their needs, behaviors, and feedback on usability, features, and satisfaction directly determine the product's success. designers must understand how users will interact with the phone to create a useful and desirable product. stakeholder 2: manufacturers/engineers importance: these stakeholders are concerned with the feasibility of producing the design. they provide expertise on materials, production processes, and cost, ensuring the design is practical and can be manufactured efficiently and profitably. stakeholder 3: retailers/distributors importance: retailers and distributors are important for market success. they are concerned with the product's packaging, logistics, and marketability. their feedback can influence design decisions related to size, durability, and brand appeal. 2. define reverse engineering and explain how it helps in gathering data for product improvement . reveal answer award [1] for a correct definition of reverse engineering and [1] for a clear explanation of how it helps with product improvement [2 max]. definition: reverse engineering is a method used to understand how an existing product was made by disassembling it. how it helps: it allows designers to analyze a product's components, materials, manufacturing techniques, and internal workings. this provides valuable data to understand its strengths and weaknesses, which can then be used to identify opportunities for improvement. for example, by disassembling a competitor's product, a company can discover a more efficient way to assemble their own, which reduces cost. longer answer questions 1. you are tasked with analyzing a new ergonomic desk chair. discuss how you would use a swot analysis and identify at least three relevant stakeholders to inform your evaluation. provide specific examples for each element of the swot and for each stakeholder's concerns. reveal answer award [1] for discussing the use of swot analysis and identifying stakeholders, provide a structured evaluation. the information for this analysis would be gathered from a range of stakeholders. swot analysis examples: strengths: the chair has a comfortable, adjustable lumbar support system and a wide range of height settings, making it highly adaptable for different users. weaknesses: the material used for the seat is not breathable, causing the user to sweat during prolonged use, and the armrests are difficult to adjust. opportunities: there is a growing market for home office products due to remote work, and there is an opportunity to sell to a corporate market. the chair could be improved by using a more breathable material or by adding more intuitive armrest controls. threats: a competitor has just released a cheaper chair with similar features, and there are new government regulations concerning the use of certain plastics in furniture. stakeholder examples: end users: a user's main concern would be usability and comfort. they might provide feedback on whether the chair is comfortable for long periods and if the controls are easy to understand and adjust. manufacturer: the manufacturer would be concerned with the cost of materials and the ease of production. they might point out that the complex adjustment mechanism is expensive to produce. retailer: the retailer would be concerned with the chair's marketability and packaging. they might suggest that the chair is too heavy or bulky for efficient shipping, which could increase costs. 2. explain why it is important to gather information from a range of stakeholders during a product analysis exercise. use examples of potential conflicting priorities that different stakeholders might have regarding a common product. reveal answer award [1] for explaining why it's important to gather info from a range of stakeholders, and [1] for each clear example of conflicting priorities with a common product, up to [4 marks]. it is crucial to gather information from a range of stakeholders during product analysis because each group has a different perspective and set of priorities. a product's success is not determined by its function alone but by how well it meets the needs of all involved parties, from the user to the manufacturer to the retailer. conflicting priorities example: a smartphone user vs. manufacturer: the user wants a smartphone with the largest, highest-resolution screen and the longest battery life possible. however, the manufacturer's priority is to produce a phone that is cost-effective and easy to manufacture. this creates a conflict, as a larger screen or a more powerful battery can increase the cost and complexity of manufacturing. designer vs. marketer: the designer's priority is to create a product that is both aesthetically pleasing and highly functional, perhaps using a sleek, unibody design with a non-removable battery for better aesthetics. the marketer's priority is to appeal to a broad market, which might include users who prefer the practicality of a replaceable battery. retailer vs. engineer: the retailer wants a product that is packaged in a small box for efficient shelf space and shipping. the engineer wants a larger package to protect a fragile device during transit. this creates a conflict between logistics and product safety. we will discuss strategies for answering these questions effectively, title: Life-cycle analysis

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.html:
Overview

What You Will Learn

Unit Objectives

By the end of this C3.2 study guide, you should be able to:

  • Define Life-Cycle Analysis (LCA) and explain its purpose in factually evaluating the environmental impact of a product.
  • Understand the differences between "open loop" (cradle-to-grave) and "closed loop" (cradle-to-cradle) life cycles.
  • Analyze a product's life through its five inventory stages: Raw Material Extraction, Manufacture, Distribution, Use, and Disposal.
  • Evaluate the environmental impacts present at each stage, which include global warming potential, pollution, ecotoxicity, and resource depletion.
  • Understand why designers have an ethical responsibility to ensure a positive LCA outcome through strategic material selection and Design for Manufacture (DfM).

sections.title: Introduction to LCA & Systems Thinking
sections.html:
Section 1 45 Mins

Introduction to LCA & Systems Thinking

When we design or buy a product, we often only see the final result. However, an LCA replaces assumptions with factual evidence regarding sustainability.

Shifting How We Think About Design

Using an LCA shifts how we think about design models:

  • The Linear Model (Open Loop)

    This is the traditional "take-make-dispose" model, also known as Cradle-to-Grave.

  • The Circular Model (Closed Loop)

Think About It: The Product Autopsy

Take an ordinary white cotton T-shirt.

Cotton cultivation and textile processing can consume significant water; impacts depend on location, farming and production methods.

Mentally "autopsy" a piece of your clothing by working backward from the moment it is thrown away. Try to list every assumed environmental cost involved in its creation, such as pesticides for cotton, fuel for shipping, and electricity for sewing.

sections.title: The Five Inventory Stages
sections.html:
Section 2 1 Hour

The Five Inventory Stages

Designers must account for both materials and energy usage across all five stages of a product's life to conduct a thorough analysis.

Stage Description Associated Impacts
1. Raw Material Extraction The sourcing and refining of materials from the earth. Resource depletion, habitat destruction, ecotoxicity.
2. Manufacture The process of shaping and assembling the final product. High energy usage, water consumption, waste generation.
3. Distribution & Transport The logistics and packaging phase to get the product to consumers. Major source of greenhouse gas emissions (GWP).
4. Use and Maintenance Energy consumption or repairs required while owned by the consumer. Electricity grid reliance, water usage (e.g., washing clothes).
5. Disposal / Recycling The end of the product's life. Landfill space, incineration pollution, or (ideally) material recovery.

Activity: Stage Mapping & Debate

Choose a modern product, like an electric vehicle battery, a PlayStation controller, or a fast-fashion jacket. Map out its five stages and try to identify which stage has the highest environmental footprint.

Debate Question:

Should designers focus primarily on creating more sustainable products, or should the focus be on changing user habits to consume less?

sections.title: The Designer’s Responsibility
sections.html:
Section 3 45 Mins

The Designer’s Responsibility

Core Principle

The designer has a professional and ethical duty to achieve a relatively positive LCA. Decisions made during the design phase drastically alter the product's environmental footprint across its entire life cycle.

1. Material Selection: Closing the Loop

The goal here is to shift from a linear economy (take-make-waste) to a circular economy. Choosing renewables or recyclates isn't just about "being green"; it’s about reducing the energy-intensive extraction of raw materials.

Why it’s Pertinent: Virgin plastics require the extraction and refining of petroleum, a process with high embodied energy and CO₂ emissions.

The "LCA" Impact: Using recycled content significantly lowers the "Global Warming Potential" (GWP) in the raw material acquisition phase.

Examples in Practice:
  • Recycled PET (rPET): Using rPET for textile fibers or packaging instead of virgin polyester.
  • Bio-based Polymers: Specifying PLA (Polylactic Acid) derived from corn starch for short-life consumer goods.
  • Mono-materiality: Designing a sneaker entirely from one type of plastic (like TPU) so it is 100% recyclable at the end of its life, rather than a mix of leather, foam, and rubber that cannot be separated.

2. Manufacturing Techniques: Energy Efficiency

Once materials are chosen, the conversion of that material into a part is the next energy hurdle. Designers often overlook that the shape of a part dictates the method of making it.

Why it’s Pertinent: High-heat processes (like glass blowing or aluminum smelting) or high-pressure processes (like heavy injection molding) consume massive amounts of electricity.

The "LCA" Impact: This addresses the "Production" phase. Choosing a process that operates at lower temperatures or requires fewer steps reduces the cumulative energy demand.

Examples in Practice:
  • Cold Forming vs. Hot Forging: Using cold-rolled steel processes where possible to avoid the energy required to heat billets.
  • Additive Manufacturing (3D Printing): For complex, low-volume aerospace parts, 3D printing can be more efficient because it only uses the material needed, whereas CNC machining might turn 70% of a metal block into waste "chips."
  • Low-Pressure Molding: Using natural fiber composites that can be molded at lower temperatures compared to traditional glass-reinforced plastics.

3. Design for Manufacture (DfM): Waste Reduction

DfM is often viewed through the lens of cost-cutting, but in LCA, waste is a carbon footprint with no utility. If you design a part that requires 20% of the material to be trimmed off and thrown away, you are essentially paying for the carbon of material that never reaches the customer.

Why it’s Pertinent: Complexity is the enemy of sustainability. More parts mean more tools, more assembly energy, and more potential for failure.

The "LCA" Impact: This reduces impact across both the "Manufacturing" and "End-of-Life" phases.

Examples in Practice:
  • Part Consolidation: Designing a single complex injection-molded housing that replaces five separate parts and ten screws. This reduces assembly time and the energy used by assembly robots.
  • Nesting Optimization: In laser cutting or textile pattern making, designing shapes that "interlock" on a sheet to minimize the "skeletal waste" left behind.
  • Snap-fits vs. Adhesives: Using mechanical snap-fits instead of glue. Glues "contaminate" materials, making them impossible to recycle. Snap-fits allow for easy disassembly and material recovery.

Summary Table: Designer Influence on LCA

Decision Area LCA Phase Targeted Primary Environmental Benefit
Material Selection Raw Material Extraction Reduced resource depletion & lower embodied carbon.
Mfg. Techniques Production / Processing Reduced energy consumption and carbon emissions.
DfM / Waste Manufacturing & End-of-Life High material yield and ease of circular recovery.

sections.title: Test Your Knowledge
sections.html:
Assessment Prep

Test Your Knowledge

Review these questions based on the content above. Attempt to answer them before revealing the key.

Multiple Choice

1. Which of the following best describes a "closed loop" life cycle?

  1. A product that is highly durable but ends up in landfill.
  2. A sustainable model where end-of-life materials are processed back into the cycle.
  3. A manufacturing process with zero emissions.
  4. The linear take-make-dispose model.
Reveal Answer
Answer: B

2. During which LCA stage is packaging primarily evaluated?

  1. Raw Material Extraction
  2. Manufacture
  3. Distribution and Transport
  4. Use and Maintenance
Reveal Answer
Answer: C

Written Response

3. Outline the difference between an 'open loop' and a 'closed loop' LCA. (2 marks)
Answer Guideline:
An open loop LCA assesses environmental impacts from cradle to grave, ending in disposal. A closed loop LCA uses a cradle-to-cradle approach, where materials recovered at the end of a product's life are processed and fed back into a new manufacturing cycle.
4. State two environmental factors that are factually examined during an LCA. (2 marks)
Answer Guideline:
Any two of the following: Global warming potential, air/water/soil pollution, ecotoxicity, or resource depletion.
5. Explain how decisions made during material selection and use phases impact the LCA of a hiking jacket. (4 marks)
Answer Guideline:
  • Material Selection: Choosing renewable, recycled, or non-toxic materials reduces resource depletion and ecotoxicity during extraction and processing.
  • Use Phase: If the jacket requires frequent washing at high temperatures or uses non-durable materials requiring constant repair, the energy and water consumption during the consumer use phase will increase the product's overall environmental footprint.
6. Discuss how a designer can use Design for Manufacture (DfM) to achieve a positive LCA outcome. (6 marks)
Answer Guideline:
  • Designers have early-stage control over the environmental fate of a product.
  • Reference specific DfM strategies, particularly Design for Disassembly, ensuring products can be easily taken apart at the "grave" stage.
  • Reducing the number of materials, avoiding permanent glues, and designing modular parts allows for easier material recovery and recycling.
  • Choosing low-energy manufacturing techniques directly alters the carbon footprint.

sections.title: Glossary of Key Terms
sections.html:
Reference

Glossary of Key Terms

Click on any term below to reveal its exact definition along with a real-world application.

Life-Cycle Analysis (LCA)

Definition: A factual technique to evaluate a product's environmental impact across its entire existence, from raw material to disposal.

Real-World Example Measuring the exact amount of CO2 emitted to mine lithium, assemble a phone, ship it, charge it for 3 years, and eventually recycle it.
Open Loop (Cradle-to-Grave)

Definition: A linear product life cycle that ends with the product being disposed of (the "grave").

Real-World Example A single-use plastic grocery bag that is manufactured, used once, and thrown into a landfill.
Closed Loop (Cradle-to-Cradle)

Definition: A sustainable cycle where a product's end-of-life materials are recovered and processed into new products.

Real-World Example An aluminum can that is melted down and turned into a brand new aluminum can over and over again.
Ecotoxicity

Definition: The potential for biological, chemical, or physical stressors to damage local ecosystems.

Real-World Example Harmful chemical dyes from a textile factory running off into a local river, killing fish and plant life.
Global Warming Potential (GWP)

Definition: A measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps in the atmosphere, used in LCAs to evaluate climate impact.

Real-World Example The methane emitted from agricultural farming required to create leather for shoes.
Design for Disassembly (DfD)

Definition: A manufacturing strategy aimed at creating products that can be easily and safely taken apart at the end of their life for recycling or repair.

Real-World Example A laptop held together with standard screws instead of industrial glue, allowing the battery to be easily separated from the plastic casing.

sections.title: From inventory to evidence · C3.2.1–2
sections.html:
An inventory records material and energy inputs and outputs across extraction, manufacture, distribution, use and maintenance, and end of life. Compare products delivering the same function, over a stated service period. Keep the system boundary and assumptions consistent.

Impact categories describe different consequences. Global warming potential concerns greenhouse-gas effects; air, water and soil pollution concern releases to those environments; ecotoxicity concerns harm to ecosystems; resource depletion concerns use of finite resources. A single carbon total does not show every impact.

Classroom LCA lab · 15 minutes

The following invented data are only for practising comparison. Two lamps each provide the required classroom task lighting for 1,000 hours. Lamp A uses 20 kWh and has an embodied footprint of 8 kg CO₂e. Lamp B uses 10 kWh and has an embodied footprint of 12 kg CO₂e. Assume electricity contributes 0.5 kg CO₂e per kWh and ignore other stages for this simplified exercise.

Calculate both totals. Then calculate the energy-emissions factor at which their totals become equal. Explain why this simplified result cannot establish which lamp is more sustainable overall.

Evidence check

A: 8 + 20 × 0.5 = 18 kg CO₂e. B: 12 + 10 × 0.5 = 17 kg CO₂e. Equality: 8 + 20f = 12 + 10f, giving f = 0.4 kg CO₂e/kWh. The decision could change with electricity source, useful life, repair needs, toxicity, resource use or the omitted transport and end-of-life stages.

syllabus.title: Life-cycle analysis
syllabus.guidingQuestion: Why should designers consider the effects a product has on the environment?

statements.text: A life-cycle analysis (also known as the five stages of life-cycle analysis) helps designers factually analyse a product’s entire life cycle in terms of sustainability.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain and discuss life-cycle analysis considerations, such as global warming potential, air, water and soil pollution, ecotoxicity and resource depletion, that cause environmental impact.

statements.text: Designers evaluate the environmental impacts of a product or service. In the case of a product, the environmental impact is assessed from raw material extraction and processing (cradle), through the manufacture, distribution and use, to the recycling or final disposal of the materials (grave).
statements.guidance: Students must be able to explain the life-cycle analysis inventory stages (cradle-to-grave) and the materials and energy usage that go into these processes: raw material extraction; manufacture; distribution and transport; use and maintenance; and disposal and recycling.

activity.title: Life-cycle boundary debate
steps: Choose a single-use and reusable option and define a fair functional unit.
Set a cradle-to-grave boundary including materials, manufacture, transport, use and disposal.
Compare illustrative impacts and vary washing or transport assumptions.
State how the conclusion depends on data quality, use frequency and omitted impacts.
activity.debrief: How could a changed system boundary reverse an LCA conclusion?

exam.question: Explain why a functional unit is needed in a comparative LCA. [2]
exam.answer: It defines the same service or function for both options, so impacts are compared on an equivalent basis rather than per unequal product.
