operates at lower temperatures or requires fewer steps reduces the cumulative energy demand. examples in practice: cold forming vs. hot forging: using cold-rolled steel processes where possible to avoid the energy required to heat billets. additive manufacturing (3d printing): for complex, low-volume aerospace parts, 3d printing can be more efficient because it only uses the material needed, whereas cnc machining might turn 70% of a metal block into waste "chips." low-pressure molding: using natural fiber composites that can be molded at lower temperatures compared to traditional glass-reinforced plastics. 3. design for manufacture (dfm): waste reduction dfm is often viewed through the lens of cost-cutting, but in lca, waste is a carbon footprint with no utility. if you design a part that requires 20% of the material to be trimmed off and thrown away, you are essentially paying for the carbon of material that never reaches the customer. why it’s pertinent: complexity is the enemy of sustainability. more parts mean more tools, more assembly energy, and more potential for failure. the "lca" impact: this reduces impact across both the "manufacturing" and "end-of-life" phases. examples in practice: part consolidation: designing a single complex injection-molded housing that replaces five separate parts and ten screws. this reduces assembly time and the energy used by assembly robots. nesting optimization: in laser cutting or textile pattern making, designing shapes that "interlock" on a sheet to minimize the "skeletal waste" left behind. snap-fits vs. adhesives: using mechanical snap-fits instead of glue. glues "contaminate" materials, making them impossible to recycle. snap-fits allow for easy disassembly and material recovery. summary table: designer influence on lca decision area lca phase targeted primary environmental benefit material selection raw material extraction reduced resource depletion & lower embodied carbon. mfg. techniques production / processing reduced energy consumption and carbon emissions. dfm / waste manufacturing & end-of-life high material yield and ease of circular recovery. assessment prep test your knowledge review these questions based on the content above. attempt to answer them before revealing the key. multiple choice 1. which of the following best describes a "closed loop" life cycle? a product that is highly durable but ends up in landfill. a sustainable model where end-of-life materials are processed back into the cycle. a manufacturing process with zero emissions. the linear take-make-dispose model. reveal answer answer: b 2. during which lca stage is packaging primarily evaluated? raw material extraction manufacture distribution and transport use and maintenance reveal answer answer: c written response 3. outline the difference between an 'open loop' and a 'closed loop' lca. (2 marks) answer guideline: an open loop lca assesses environmental impacts from cradle to grave, ending in disposal. a closed loop lca uses a cradle-to-cradle approach, where materials recovered at the end of a product's life are processed and fed back into a new manufacturing cycle. 4. state two environmental factors that are factually examined during an lca. (2 marks) answer guideline: any two of the following: global warming potential, air/water/soil pollution, ecotoxicity, or resource depletion. 5. explain how decisions made during material selection and use phases impact the lca of a hiking jacket. (4 marks) answer guideline: material selection: choosing renewable, recycled, or non-toxic materials reduces resource depletion and ecotoxicity during extraction and processing. use phase: if the jacket requires frequent washing at high temperatures or uses non-durable materials requiring constant repair, the energy and water consumption during the consumer use phase will increase the product's overall environmental footprint. 6. discuss how a designer can use design for manufacture (dfm) to achieve a positive lca outcome. (6 marks) answer guideline: designers have early-stage control over the environmental fate of a product. reference specific dfm strategies, particularly design for disassembly, ensuring products can be easily taken apart at the "grave" stage. reducing the number of materials, avoiding permanent glues, and designing modular parts allows for easier material recovery and recycling. choosing low-energy manufacturing techniques directly alters the carbon footprint. reference glossary of key terms click on any term below to reveal its exact definition along with a real-world application. life-cycle analysis (lca) definition: a factual technique to evaluate a product's environmental impact across its entire existence, from raw material to disposal. real-world example measuring the exact amount of co2 emitted to mine lithium, assemble a phone, ship it, charge it for 3 years, and eventually recycle it. open loop (cradle-to-grave) definition: a linear product life cycle that ends with the product being disposed of (the "grave"). real-world example a single-use plastic grocery bag that is manufactured, used once, and thrown into a landfill. closed loop (cradle-to-cradle) definition: a sustainable cycle where a product's end-of-life materials are recovered and processed into new products. real-world example an aluminum can that is melted down and turned into a brand new aluminum can over and over again. ecotoxicity definition: the potential for biological, chemical, or physical stressors to damage local ecosystems. real-world example harmful chemical dyes from a textile factory running off into a local river, killing fish and plant life. global warming potential (gwp) definition: a measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps in the atmosphere, used in lcas to evaluate climate impact. real-world example the methane emitted from agricultural farming required to create leather for shoes. design for disassembly (dfd) definition: a manufacturing strategy aimed at creating products that can be easily and safely taken apart at the end of their life for recycling or repair. real-world example a laptop held together with standard screws instead of industrial glue, allowing the battery to be easily separated from the plastic casing. an inventory records material and energy inputs and outputs across extraction, manufacture, distribution, use and maintenance, and end of life. compare products delivering the same function, over a stated service period. keep the system boundary and assumptions consistent. impact categories describe different consequences. global warming potential concerns greenhouse-gas effects; air, water and soil pollution concern releases to those environments; ecotoxicity concerns harm to ecosystems; resource depletion concerns use of finite resources. a single carbon total does not show every impact. classroom lca lab · 15 minutes the following invented data are only for practising comparison. two lamps each provide the required classroom task lighting for 1,000 hours. lamp a uses 20 kwh and has an embodied footprint of 8 kg co₂e. lamp b uses 10 kwh and has an embodied footprint of 12 kg co₂e. assume electricity contributes 0.5 kg co₂e per kwh and ignore other stages for this simplified exercise. calculate both totals. then calculate the energy-emissions factor at which their totals become equal. explain why this simplified result cannot establish which lamp is more sustainable overall. evidence check a: 8 + 20 × 0.5 = 18 kg co₂e. b: 12 + 10 × 0.5 = 17 kg co₂e. equality: 8 + 20f = 12 + 10f, giving f = 0.4 kg co₂e/kwh. the decision could change with electricity source, useful life, repair needs, toxicity, resource use or the omitted transport and end-of-life stages. cradle-to-cradle cradle-to-grave life-cycle analysis life-cycle analysis (lca) open loop (cradle-to-grave) closed loop (cradle-to-cradle) ecotoxicity global warming potential (gwp) design for disassembly (dfd) a life-cycle analysis (also known as the five stages of life-cycle analysis) helps designers factually analyse a product’s entire life cycle in terms of sustainability. designers evaluate the environmental impacts of a product or service. in the case of a product, the environmental impact is assessed from raw material extraction and processing (cradle), through the manufacture, distribution and use, to the recycling or final disposal of the materials (grave).

title: Design for manufacture strategies

sections.title: Lesson 1: What is Design for Manufacture? & Design for Process
sections.html:
4.1.1 What is DfM? 4.1.2 Design for Process ~50 mins

Lesson 1: What is Design for Manufacture? & Design for Process

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to define Design for Manufacture (DfM) and its three strategies, and explain and apply Design for Process using a real product example.

1. What is Design for Manufacture?

Definition: Design for Manufacture (DfM) occurs when designers create products specifically for the optimum use of existing manufacturing capability.

Context: Rather than designing a product first and figuring out how to make it afterwards, DfM builds manufacturing, assembly and end-of-life thinking into the design process from day one — saving cost, time and material, and reducing environmental impact.

Three strategies: Design for Process (can it be made?), Design for Assembly (can it be put together efficiently?), Design for Disassembly (can it be taken apart again at end of life?).

Quick Engagement: Sort the Strategy

In pairs, you'll be given six short product-design decisions (e.g. "adding a draft angle to a moulded case", "replacing 12 screws with 2 snap-fit clips", "using solder instead of screws on a circuit board"). Sort each decision into Design for Process, Design for Assembly or Design for Disassembly and justify your choice aloud — this is a chance to surface what you already know (and any misconceptions) before we dive into the content below.

2. Design for Process

Definition: Design for Process ensures a product can be effectively made using a specific manufacturing technique.

Goal: to guarantee compatibility between the design and the chosen production method (e.g. injection moulding, casting, 3D printing, CNC machining).

Materials/Examples: Designing an injection-moulded plastic part with uniform wall thickness prevents warping and defects while speeding up the cooling cycle.

Application: Designers add a small "draft angle" (typically 1–3°) to vertical faces so the finished part releases cleanly from the mould without dragging or damage.

Real-World Example

Injection-moulded parts with uniform wall thickness and a small draft angle release cleanly from the mould, avoiding warping, sink marks and dragging damage — keeping cycle times low and scrap rates down.

Practical Engagement: Draft Angle Detective

You'll be shown two CAD renders or physical mouldings of the same simple container — one with 0° draft (straight vertical walls) and one with a 2° draft angle. In small groups, predict what happens when each is ejected from a two-part mould, sketch the mould halves separating, and explain — using the terms draft angle, wall thickness, warping and cycle time — why the drafted version is manufacturable at scale and the other is not.

Extension: calculate how a 0.5 mm inconsistency in wall thickness could cause sink marks or warping on cooling.

Watch/read: Hubs — What is a Draft Angle in Injection Moulding? (video + guide)

sections.title: Lesson 2: Design for Assembly & Design for Disassembly
sections.html:
4.1.3 Design for Assembly 4.1.4 Design for Disassembly ~50 mins

Lesson 2: Design for Assembly & Design for Disassembly

You'll explain and apply Design for Assembly and Design for Disassembly using real products, and evaluate how these choices affect environmental impact.

3. Design for Assembly

Definition: Design for Assembly considers how components are combined at various stages — component-to-component, or subassemblies into a final product.

Goal: to simplify and speed up the assembly process, reducing labour costs and manufacturing time.

Materials/Examples: IKEA flat-pack furniture is designed for efficient assembly by the end-user, using a minimal number of standard fasteners (typically cam locks, dowels and hex-key bolts) and clear pictogram instructions so no specialist skill is required.

Application: Some newer ranges use wedge-dowel joints that need no tools at all.

Practical Engagement: Snap-Fit vs Screw Race

Working in pairs, assemble a small model (or a set of LEGO/snap-fit blocks representing a sub-assembly) using only snap-fit connections while your partner assembles an equivalent structure using screws and a screwdriver. Time both.

Discuss: which was faster and why; what happens if a snap-fit part is assembled wrong (can it be corrected)? which method would a factory producing 10,000 units/day prefer, and why does that same choice make disassembly for repair harder or easier later?

Watch/read: IKEA Museum — The Story of the Flat-Pack

4. Design for Disassembly

Definition: Designing a product so it can be easily and economically taken apart at the end of its functional life.

Goal: to allow components to be reused or repaired, and materials to be separated and recycled efficiently.

Materials/Examples: The Fairphone uses standard screws and modular components — such as a replaceable camera module and a user-removable battery — instead of permanent adhesives.

Application: This allows owners to repair the device with a basic screwdriver rather than sending it to landfill.

Case Study: The Fairphone

Standard screws and swappable modules (camera, battery) instead of glue mean the Fairphone can be repaired with common tools — a direct demonstration of Design for Disassembly enabling "Right to Repair."

Practical Engagement: Teardown & Repairability Score

Watch a short teardown clip of the Fairphone (or a comparable modular product) and, using an iFixit-style 1–10 repairability rubric, score the product on: ease of opening the case, fastener type (adhesive vs screw), modularity of parts, and availability of spare parts.

Then repeat the exercise from memory for a typical sealed/glued smartphone and compare your scores, justifying the gap using DfD terminology (modular, standard fasteners, right to repair).

Watch/read: Fast Company — How Fairphone designed a more repairable, sustainable smartphone

sections.title: Lesson 3: Environmental Impact, Synthesis & The Toaster Challenge
sections.html:
4.1.5 Environmental Impact Synthesis & Application ~50 mins

Lesson 3: Environmental Impact, Synthesis & The Toaster Challenge

You'll evaluate how DfM choices affect environmental impact and the circular economy, link DfM to other areas of the syllabus, and apply all three strategies to redesign a product.

5. Environmental Impact

Definition: The selection of DfM strategies has a direct effect on the environmental footprint of a product's manufacture, use and disposal.

Sustainability: designers use DfM — especially Design for Disassembly — to facilitate material recovery and reduce waste.

Circular Economy: DfM is essential for "closing the loop," ensuring high-value materials can be reclaimed rather than ending up in landfill.

Practical Engagement: The Urban Mining Calculator

Here's the statistic: a tonne of discarded circuit boards can contain roughly 100 times more gold than a tonne of newly mined gold ore, and hundreds of millions of unused smartphones in the EU alone hold gold and other metals worth over US$1 billion.

In groups, estimate how much of that value is actually recoverable from (a) a glued, sealed phone and (b) a modular, screw-together phone, then discuss why Design for Disassembly is the strategy that most directly determines whether "urban mining" is economically viable.

Watch/read: Dassault Systèmes — What is Urban Mining?

Synthesis and Linking Questions

Use these to connect DfM to other areas of the syllabus and to prepare for Paper 3 case-study reasoning:

  1. A3.3 / B3.3 (Mechanical Systems): Why is a design for assembly strategy critical when designing complex moving mechanical parts?
  2. B2.2 (Modelling): How do designers use physical and virtual modelling to resolve assembly issues before mass production?
  3. B3.1 (Material Selection): To what extent does the choice of material (e.g. a composite vs. a metal) limit or enable specific DfM strategies?
  4. C2.2 (Circular Economy): To what extent is design for disassembly the most important factor in ensuring a product can enter a circular economy?
  5. C3.2 (Life-Cycle Analysis): How does a successful DfM strategy lead to a more positive outcome in a product's LCA?

Practical Learning Experience: The Toaster Challenge

The Task: You're shown a photo of a budget, mass-produced toaster that is ultrasonically welded (moulded shut).

The Objective: Propose three specific design changes that would move the product from a linear economy model to a circular economy model.

Application: justify each change using correct DfM terminology:

  • Change 1 (Disassembly): replace welded joints with standard hex-head screws to allow for heater-element repair.
  • Change 2 (Assembly): use modular internal wiring looms to speed up factory assembly.
  • Change 3 (Process): redesign the outer shell for injection moulding using a single recyclable polymer (e.g. polypropylene) to ensure material purity during recycling.

Deliverable: a one-page annotated sketch or exploded diagram of the redesigned toaster, with each change labelled and linked to its DfM strategy and its environmental benefit.

sections.title: Exam Practice
sections.html:
Exam Practice

Answer using full IB Design Technology command-term technique. Mark allocations are shown in brackets.

Section A — Multiple Choice (1 mark each)

1. A remote control is redesigned to use snap-fit clips instead of 20 separate screws. This is an example of:

  • Design for Process
  • Design for Assembly
  • Design for Disassembly
  • Design for Recycling
Reveal Answer
Answer: B. Snap-fit clips replacing multiple screws reduces assembly time and labour — the defining goal of Design for Assembly.

2. A draft angle is added to the vertical walls of an injection-moulded casing. Its primary purpose is to:

  • Increase the wall thickness for strength
  • Allow the part to release cleanly from the mould
  • Add a decorative textured finish
  • Reduce the amount of plastic used
Reveal Answer
Answer: B. The draft angle lets the moulded part eject cleanly without dragging or damaging the mould — a Design for Process consideration.

3. Which feature of the Fairphone best demonstrates Design for Disassembly?

  • An ultrasonically welded outer casing
  • Standard screws and a modular, replaceable camera unit
  • A permanently glued battery
  • Single-use, non-recyclable packaging
Reveal Answer
Answer: B. Standard screws and modular, replaceable parts allow the device to be taken apart and repaired at end of life.

Section B — Short Answer

4. Describe two features of a product that has been designed for assembly. [4]

Reveal Answer
Award marks for identifying a valid feature (e.g. use of standard/minimal fasteners, snap-fit joints, colour-coded or symmetrical parts, sub-assemblies built off-line) plus a linked explanation of how it speeds up or simplifies assembly.
2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for explanation).

5. Outline how design for process can reduce manufacturing costs, using an example. [4]

Reveal Answer
Award marks for outlining a process-compatibility feature (e.g. draft angles, uniform wall thickness, minimising tool changes) and linking it to a cost mechanism — faster cycle times, less scrap/rework, longer tool life, fewer defects. Credit any valid manufacturing example (injection moulding, die casting, CNC).

Section C — Extended Response

6. Justify the choice of using standard screws and modular components in a smartphone design intended for a circular economy. [6]

Reveal Answer
  • Identify strategy: state that this represents Design for Disassembly.
  • Justify (repair): modular parts allow for easy repair and upgradability, extending the product's functional lifespan.
  • Justify (tools): standard screws ensure the user can take the device apart with common tools, supporting the "Right to Repair."
  • Justify (recycling): easy separation of materials (no glue) allows for "urban mining," where high-value metals like gold and cobalt can be recovered at end-of-life.
  • Conclusion: link these factors back to a positive Life-Cycle Analysis (LCA) and the reduction of e-waste.

7. "Design for disassembly is the most important DfM strategy in ensuring a product can enter a circular economy." Discuss the extent to which you agree with this statement. [8]

Reveal Answer
  • For: without disassembly, materials cannot be separated at end-of-life regardless of how efficiently the product was manufactured or assembled — contamination (e.g. glued composites) makes high-value recycling/urban mining impossible, directly blocking the circular economy.
  • Against: Design for Process and Design for Assembly also matter — e.g. using a single recyclable polymer (process) ensures material purity even before disassembly is considered; poor assembly design (excess fasteners, mixed materials) can make disassembly uneconomical even if theoretically possible.
  • Balanced conclusion: the three strategies are interdependent — a circular product typically needs process (material purity), assembly (efficient, minimal-fastener build) and disassembly (recoverability) working together; disassembly is often the most visible strategy for a circular economy but is enabled by the other two. Accept well-argued responses that favour either side, provided they are substantiated with examples (Fairphone, toaster, smartphone).

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
Glossary

Click on a term to reveal its definition.

Design for Manufacture (DfM)
IB Definition: Designers design specifically for optimum use of existing manufacturing capability.
Real-World Application: Optimising a bracket design to be CNC machined with minimal material waste.
Design for Process
IB Definition: Design that enables the product to be manufactured using a specific manufacturing process.
Real-World Application: Shaping a part with a "draft angle" so it releases easily from a mould.
Design for Assembly
IB Definition: Design that takes account of assembly at various levels, e.g. component-to-component or subassemblies.
Real-World Application: Using snap-fit joints instead of 20 separate screws to build a remote control.
Design for Disassembly
IB Definition: Designing a product so it can easily and economically be taken apart, components reused or repaired, and materials recycled.
Real-World Application: The Concept2 RowErg, bolted together (not glued) to allow decades of maintenance and parts replacement.
Draft Angle
IB Definition: A slight taper (typically 1–3°) applied to the vertical faces of a moulded part to allow clean release from the mould.
Real-World Application: A drafted plastic bucket wall vs. a straight-walled one that jams and drags in the mould.
Snap-Fit Joint
IB Definition: A moulded feature that allows two parts to be pushed together and held without additional fasteners.
Real-World Application: The clip that holds a toy's battery cover shut without screws.
Subassembly
IB Definition: A group of components pre-built as a unit before being combined into the final product.
Real-World Application: A car door pre-fitted with its window mechanism before being attached to the chassis.
Modular Design
IB Definition: Designing a product from separable, self-contained units that can be replaced or upgraded independently.
Real-World Application: The Fairphone's swappable camera and battery modules.
Right to Repair
IB Definition: The principle/movement advocating that consumers and independent repairers should be able to fix products using standard tools and available parts.
Real-World Application: Legislation requiring manufacturers to sell spare parts and repair manuals to the public.
Circular Economy
IB Definition: An economic model in which materials and products are kept in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair and recycling, minimising waste.
Real-World Application: A phone manufacturer that takes back old handsets to recover metals for new ones.
Linear Economy
IB Definition: A "take-make-dispose" economic model where raw materials are extracted, made into products, and discarded after use.
Real-World Application: A glued, sealed toaster that is thrown away and landfilled after one component fails.
Urban Mining
IB Definition: The recovery of valuable metals and materials (e.g. gold, cobalt, copper) from discarded electronic products rather than from natural ore.
Real-World Application: Recovering gold from circuit boards in old smartphones — at a far higher concentration than gold ore.
Life-Cycle Analysis (LCA)
IB Definition: A method of assessing the environmental impact of a product across its entire life, from raw material extraction to disposal.
Real-World Application: Comparing the LCA of a repairable Fairphone against a sealed, non-repairable competitor.

syllabus.title: Design for manufacture strategies
syllabus.guidingQuestion: How can the evolution of production systems transform the way products are designed and manufactured, and transform the efficient disposal of products?

statements.text: Design for manufacture (DfM) comprises of three strategies.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline design for process, design for assembly and design for disassembly strategies.

statements.text: Design for process considers how products are made using a specific manufacturing technique.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline the advantages of design for process and explain how a product could be designed using this strategy.

statements.text: Design for assembly considers how components of a product are combined.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline the advantages of design for assembly and explain how a product could be designed using the design for assembly strategy.

statements.text: Design for disassembly considers how components of a product can be separated.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to outline the advantages of design for disassembly and explain how a product could be designed using this strategy.

statements.text: The selection of DfM strategies has a direct effect on the environmental impact of the manufacture, use and disposal of a product.
statements.guidance: Students must be able to discuss how designers use DfM strategies to reduce the environmental impact of the manufacture, use and disposal of products.

activity.title: Design for assembly sprint
activity.materials: Two small assemblies or photographs, paper
steps: Count parts, fastener types, assembly directions and tool changes.
Sketch a redesign that reduces unnecessary parts or simplifies assembly.
Estimate assembly operations before and after; record assumptions.
Evaluate the effects on disassembly, repair, tooling and product performance.
activity.debrief: When might reducing part count make repair more difficult?

exam.question: Explain one benefit of standardizing components in manufacture. [2]
exam.answer: Using common components can reduce procurement variety and inventory costs while simplifying assembly and replacement, provided the components meet the requirements.
exam.label: Additional teacher-authored exam-style practice; indicative answer

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Draft Angle Detective
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Draft Angle Detective You'll be shown two CAD renders or physical mouldings of the same simple container — one with 0° draft (straight vertical walls) and one with a 2° draft angle. In small groups, predict what happens when each is ejected from a two-part mould, sketch the mould halves separating, and explain — using the terms draft angle, wall thickness, warping and cycle time — why the drafted version is manufacturable at scale and the other is not. Extension: calculate how a 0.5 mm inconsistency in wall thickness could cause sink marks or warping on cooling.

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Snap-Fit vs Screw Race
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Snap-Fit vs Screw Race Working in pairs, assemble a small model (or a set of LEGO/snap-fit blocks representing a sub-assembly) using only snap-fit connections while your partner assembles an equivalent structure using screws and a screwdriver. Time both. Discuss: which was faster and why; what happens if a snap-fit part is assembled wrong (can it be corrected)? which method would a factory producing 10,000 units/day prefer, and why does that same choice make disassembly for repair harder or easier later?

activities.title: Practical Engagement: Teardown & Repairability Score
activities.text: Practical Engagement: Teardown & Repairability Score Watch a short teardown clip of the Fairphone (or a comparable modular product) and, using an iFixit-style 1–10 repairability rubric, score the product on: ease of opening the case, fastener type (adhesive vs screw), modularity of parts, and availability of spare parts. Then repeat the exercise from memory for a typical sealed/glued smartphone and compare your scores, justifying the gap using DfD terminology (modular, standard fasteners, right to repair).

activities.title: Practical Engagement: The Urban Mining Calculator
activities.text: Practical Engagement: The Urban Mining Calculator Here's the statistic: a tonne of discarded circuit boards can contain roughly 100 times more gold than a tonne of newly mined gold ore, and hundreds of millions of unused smartphones in the EU alone hold gold and other metals worth over US$1 billion. In groups, estimate how much of that value is actually recoverable from (a) a glued, sealed phone and (b) a modular, screw-together phone, then discuss why Design for Disassembly is the strategy that most directly determines whether "urban mining" is economically viable.

activities.title: Practical Learning Experience: The Toaster Challenge
activities.text: Practical Learning Experience: The Toaster Challenge The Task: You're shown a photo of a budget, mass-produced toaster that is ultrasonically welded (moulded shut). The Objective: Propose three specific design changes that would move the product from a linear economy model to a circular economy model. Application: justify each change using correct DfM terminology: Change 1 (Disassembly): replace welded joints with standard hex-head screws to allow for heater-element repair. Change 2 (Assembly): use modular internal wiring looms to speed up factory assembly. Change 3 (Process): redesign the outer shell for injection moulding using a single recyclable polymer (e.g. polypropylene) to ensure material purity during recycling. Deliverable: a one-page annotated sketch or exploded diagram of the redesigned toaster, with each change labelled and linked to its DfM strategy and its environmental benefit.

The Task: You're shown a photo of a budget, mass-produced toaster that is ultrasonically welded (moulded shut).

The Objective: Propose three specific design changes that would move the product from a linear economy model to a circular economy model.

Application: justify each change using correct DfM terminology:

  • Change 1 (Disassembly): replace welded joints with standard hex-head screws to allow for heater-element repair.
  • Change 2 (Assembly): use modular internal wiring looms to speed up factory assembly.
  • Change 3 (Process): redesign the outer shell for injection moulding using a single recyclable polymer (e.g. polypropylene) to ensure material purity during recycling.

Deliverable: a one-page annotated sketch or exploded diagram of the redesigned toaster, with each change labelled and linked to its DfM strategy and its environmental benefit.

than ending up in landfill. practical engagement: the urban mining calculator here's the statistic: a tonne of discarded circuit boards can contain roughly 100 times more gold than a tonne of newly mined gold ore, and hundreds of millions of unused smartphones in the eu alone hold gold and other metals worth over us$1 billion. in groups, estimate how much of that value is actually recoverable from (a) a glued, sealed phone and (b) a modular, screw-together phone, then discuss why design for disassembly is the strategy that most directly determines whether "urban mining" is economically viable. watch/read: dassault systèmes — what is urban mining? synthesis and linking questions use these to connect dfm to other areas of the syllabus and to prepare for paper 3 case-study reasoning: a3.3 / b3.3 (mechanical systems): why is a design for assembly strategy critical when designing complex moving mechanical parts? b2.2 (modelling): how do designers use physical and virtual modelling to resolve assembly issues before mass production? b3.1 (material selection): to what extent does the choice of material (e.g. a composite vs. a metal) limit or enable specific dfm strategies? c2.2 (circular economy): to what extent is design for disassembly the most important factor in ensuring a product can enter a circular economy? c3.2 (life-cycle analysis): how does a successful dfm strategy lead to a more positive outcome in a product's lca? practical learning experience: the toaster challenge the task: you're shown a photo of a budget, mass-produced toaster that is ultrasonically welded (moulded shut). the objective: propose three specific design changes that would move the product from a linear economy model to a circular economy model. application: justify each change using correct dfm terminology: change 1 (disassembly): replace welded joints with standard hex-head screws to allow for heater-element repair. change 2 (assembly): use modular internal wiring looms to speed up factory assembly. change 3 (process): redesign the outer shell for injection moulding using a single recyclable polymer (e.g. polypropylene) to ensure material purity during recycling. deliverable: a one-page annotated sketch or exploded diagram of the redesigned toaster, with each change labelled and linked to its dfm strategy and its environmental benefit. exam practice answer using full ib design technology command-term technique. mark allocations are shown in brackets. section a — multiple choice (1 mark each) 1. a remote control is redesigned to use snap-fit clips instead of 20 separate screws. this is an example of: design for process design for assembly design for disassembly design for recycling reveal answer answer: b. snap-fit clips replacing multiple screws reduces assembly time and labour — the defining goal of design for assembly. 2. a draft angle is added to the vertical walls of an injection-moulded casing. its primary purpose is to: increase the wall thickness for strength allow the part to release cleanly from the mould add a decorative textured finish reduce the amount of plastic used reveal answer answer: b. the draft angle lets the moulded part eject cleanly without dragging or damaging the mould — a design for process consideration. 3. which feature of the fairphone best demonstrates design for disassembly? an ultrasonically welded outer casing standard screws and a modular, replaceable camera unit a permanently glued battery single-use, non-recyclable packaging reveal answer answer: b. standard screws and modular, replaceable parts allow the device to be taken apart and repaired at end of life. section b — short answer 4. describe two features of a product that has been designed for assembly. [4] reveal answer award marks for identifying a valid feature (e.g. use of standard/minimal fasteners, snap-fit joints, colour-coded or symmetrical parts, sub-assemblies built off-line) plus a linked explanation of how it speeds up or simplifies assembly. 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for explanation). 5. outline how design for process can reduce manufacturing costs, using an example. [4] reveal answer award marks for outlining a process-compatibility feature (e.g. draft angles, uniform wall thickness, minimising tool changes) and linking it to a cost mechanism — faster cycle times, less scrap/rework, longer tool life, fewer defects. credit any valid manufacturing example (injection moulding, die casting, cnc). section c — extended response 6. justify the choice of using standard screws and modular components in a smartphone design intended for a circular economy. [6] reveal answer identify strategy: state that this represents design for disassembly. justify (repair): modular parts allow for easy repair and upgradability, extending the product's functional lifespan. justify (tools): standard screws ensure the user can take the device apart with common tools, supporting the "right to repair." justify (recycling): easy separation of materials (no glue) allows for "urban mining," where high-value metals like gold and cobalt can be recovered at end-of-life. conclusion: link these factors back to a positive life-cycle analysis (lca) and the reduction of e-waste. 7. "design for disassembly is the most important dfm strategy in ensuring a product can enter a circular economy." discuss the extent to which you agree with this statement. [8] reveal answer for: without disassembly, materials cannot be separated at end-of-life regardless of how efficiently the product was manufactured or assembled — contamination (e.g. glued composites) makes high-value recycling/urban mining impossible, directly blocking the circular economy. against: design for process and design for assembly also matter — e.g. using a single recyclable polymer (process) ensures material purity even before disassembly is considered; poor assembly design (excess fasteners, mixed materials) can make disassembly uneconomical even if theoretically possible. balanced conclusion: the three strategies are interdependent — a circular product typically needs process (material purity), assembly (efficient, minimal-fastener build) and disassembly (recoverability) working together; disassembly is often the most visible strategy for a circular economy but is enabled by the other two. accept well-argued responses that favour either side, provided they are substantiated with examples (fairphone, toaster, smartphone). glossary click on a term to reveal its definition. design for manufacture (dfm) ib definition: designers design specifically for optimum use of existing manufacturing capability. real-world application: optimising a bracket design to be cnc machined with minimal material waste. design for process ib definition: design that enables the product to be manufactured using a specific manufacturing process. real-world application: shaping a part with a "draft angle" so it releases easily from a mould. design for assembly ib definition: design that takes account of assembly at various levels, e.g. component-to-component or subassemblies. real-world application: using snap-fit joints instead of 20 separate screws to build a remote control. design for disassembly ib definition: designing a product so it can easily and economically be taken apart, components reused or repaired, and materials recycled. real-world application: the concept2 rowerg, bolted together (not glued) to allow decades of maintenance and parts replacement. draft angle ib definition: a slight taper (typically 1–3°) applied to the vertical faces of a moulded part to allow clean release from the mould. real-world application: a drafted plastic bucket wall vs. a straight-walled one that jams and drags in the mould. snap-fit joint ib definition: a moulded feature that allows two parts to be pushed together and held without additional fasteners. real-world application: the clip that holds a toy's battery cover shut without screws. subassembly ib definition: a group of components pre-built as a unit before being combined into the final product. real-world application: a car door pre-fitted with its window mechanism before being attached to the chassis. modular design ib definition: designing a product from separable, self-contained units that can be replaced or upgraded independently. real-world application: the fairphone's swappable camera and battery modules. right to repair ib definition: the principle/movement advocating that consumers and independent repairers should be able to fix products using standard tools and available parts. real-world application: legislation requiring manufacturers to sell spare parts and repair manuals to the public. circular economy ib definition: an economic model in which materials and products are kept in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair and recycling, minimising waste. real-world application: a phone manufacturer that takes back old handsets to recover metals for new ones. linear economy ib definition: a "take-make-dispose" economic model where raw materials are extracted, made into products, and discarded after use. real-world application: a glued, sealed toaster that is thrown away and landfilled after one component fails. urban mining ib definition: the recovery of valuable metals and materials (e.g. gold, cobalt, copper) from discarded electronic products rather than from natural ore. real-world application: recovering gold from circuit boards in old smartphones — at a far higher concentration than gold ore. life-cycle analysis (lca) ib definition: a method of assessing the environmental impact of a product across its entire life, from raw material extraction to disposal. real-world application: comparing the lca of a repairable
